Procurement & Security Onboarding: Timing and Pricing Checkpoint

Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-10-19
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Carter (Redwood AE), Ravi Shah (Redwood SE), Laura Kim (Pinecrest - Head Procurement), Dr. Amir Patel (CTO), Sofia Lopez (Security), Evan Brooks (Vendor Ops)

Summary:
Quick procurement checkpoint focused on MSA/DPA redlines, SLA expectations, pricing approval path, and technical onramp for a private/dedicated sandbox. Customer reiterated need for KMS/HSM integration and clear data residency options. Redwood AE/SE outlined next steps, sprint timeline, and pilot acceptance criteria.

Topics:
- MSA/DPA redlines and timeline
- Pricing and committed capacity options (dedicated vs hosted burst)
- Security ask: KMS, encryption-at-rest, audit logs, SOC 2 scope
- Sandbox access, benchmarks and acceptance criteria
- Procurement approval path and internal stakeholders

00:00:00 Jamie Carter: okay everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you taking the time today, we packed a lot into the invite so we're gonna try to run through MSA redline status, pricing routes and then technical follow up. um Ravi and I will split, i'll cover procurement and pricing and Ravi will jump in on KMS and sandbox stuff.

00:00:18 Laura Kim: thanks Jamie, yep we wanted a short checkpoint — procurement is on a tight calendar, our finance committee meets next week so any gating docs we can get this week would help.

00:00:27 Jamie Carter: understood. quick question, Laura, do you expect the legal team to want custom language around data retention and deletion for PHI? or is standard DPA usually ok?

00:00:36 Laura Kim: short answer: we handle PHI so, yes they will want explicit deletion windows and also what happens on termination. we flagged KMS and key custody as big items too.

00:00:46 Ravi Shah: (SE) hi all, hi Laura — so on KMS we support two patterns: customer-managed keys in their cloud KMS for hosted and also bring-your-own-key to our private deployment. we treat the decryption keys never at rest in the control plane, and we can integrate with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and Azure Key Vault. There are some HSM handoffs for on-prem but we can get you specific runbook.

00:01:12 Dr. Amir Patel: quick clarifying q — our security team insists on HSM-backed signing for audit logs, is that part of the default?

00:01:20 Ravi Shah: not in the default hosted offering — audit logs are tamper-evident and forwarded to your SIEM, but we can enable HSM-backed signing in our private deployments or as a dedicated option. it does add a bit of operational lead time, maybe 2-4 weeks to configure with the vendor's key management.

00:01:40 Laura Kim: timeline-wise that's ok if we get it documented in the MSA as a deliverable or milestone. finance wants price certainty though: can you recap pricing options, committed vs burst?

00:01:52 Jamie Carter: sure. high level we have three lanes: 1) Hosted pay-as-you-go (fastest to start, variable cost), 2) Dedicated reserved capacity (committed monthly and cheaper per token, predictable), and 3) Private (VPC/on-prem) which includes a platform fee plus support tier. For your PHI workload we usually see dedicated or private. We can structure a 12-month commit with step-down unit pricing if you sign to a reserved capacity.

00:02:20 Evan Brooks: any minimum commit? our budget team wants to avoid large upfront.

00:02:25 Jamie Carter: typical minimum is modest — we can propose a pilot commit for 3 months with an option to convert to annual. i'll send a pricing sheet with a pilot option that shows per-token economics and committed-break-even.

00:02:36 Sofia Lopez: for the SLA side, do you have a guaranteed p99 latency SLA for dedicated nodes? we need to know fallbacks in case of regional outages.

00:02:45 Ravi Shah: p99 latency SLA is available for dedicated reseller contracts; exact ms target depends on model and sequence length. we also support automated fallback to compatible model variant and cross-region failover. i'll include runbook notes on routing, and what to expect for KV cache warmup after a failover.

00:03:05 Dr. Amir Patel: our main risk is quality regressions when you fallback to a quantized variant — can you lock model versioning?

00:03:12 Jamie Carter: yes you can pin model versions and rollout policies. Redwood Optimize will also surface quality regressions by prompt set so you can catch it in early testing.

00:03:22 Laura Kim: legal asked if you will accept a limited liability carve-out for regulatory fines — we have some push back on unlimited liability.

00:03:30 Jamie Carter: fair. our standard MSA has caps tied to fees paid, but we can discuss escalation language with your counsel. i'll flag that as an item to annotate in the redline.

00:03:40 Laura Kim: great. can you share your SOC 2 report? and do you have any FedRAMP discussions?

00:03:47 Ravi Shah: we can share SOC 2 Type II report under an NDA — i'll drop the link. for FedRAMP we do not have an attestation yet; we have customers running in FedRAMP moderate paths through our private deployments but it's not a certified offering from Redwood.

00:04:05 Sofia Lopez: okay — we need to confirm with our audit team if SOC 2 is sufficient or if we'll require additional evidentiary material.

00:04:12 Jamie Carter: under stand. next let's talk about the sandbox and benchmarks — we promised a dedicated sandbox for your pilot, and a benchmark plan to validate latency and cost per token under your sequence distribution. Ravi?

00:04:22 Ravi Shah: yes. sandbox will be a dedicated pool with pinned model and KV lengths matching your workload. proposed acceptance criteria: 1) p95/p99 latency under X ms, 2) inference stability (no OOMs) for 8-hour sustained run, 3) accuracy regression below agreed delta on 500 eval prompts. We'll provide credentials and a short-runbook for KMS test keys.

00:04:50 Evan Brooks: how long to stand up the sandbox?

00:04:53 Ravi Shah: typically 3-5 business days for hosted sandbox with customer-managed KMS; if you want an isolated private deployment it can be 2-3 weeks depending on network setup and HSM provisioning.

00:05:03 Laura Kim: budget people will push back on the private option cost — is there a middle ground?

00:05:08 Jamie Carter: yes, dedicated in-cloud will hit a middle ground: predictable pricing without the full private platform fee. we can propose a 3-month dedicated pilot with commitment credit toward an annual reserved contract.

00:05:18 Dr. Amir Patel: about data residency — our regs require PHI to remain in our US region. do you support region pinning?

00:05:25 Ravi Shah: absolutely, region pinning is supported for dedicated and private. hosted API has region options but not strict residency guarantees unless on a dedicated pool in that region.

00:05:35 Laura Kim: okay that's good. legal also asked about data deletion on termination and proof of deletion.

00:05:40 Jamie Carter: we'll add deletion attestation language to the DPA. we can include a process for certified deletion and an export of logs showing deletion events.

00:05:50 Sofia Lopez: and audit logs retention?

00:05:52 Ravi Shah: default 90 days for application logs, but for dedicated/private we can extend retention and forward to your SIEM. logs are immutable once written but we can provide retention controls and signed timestamps.

00:06:10 Laura Kim: good. quick operational question: what's the escalation path if we find a production-quality regression during the pilot?

00:06:17 Jamie Carter: we'll set up a joint war room with our SEs and CSM. the MSA will include a remediation timeline and rollback policy; for pilots we do priority engineering support to remediate within X business days — we'll define exact SLA in the redline.

00:06:32 Evan Brooks: last thing — procurement wants to see a clean price sheet and an annotated MSA redline by end of week.

00:06:39 Jamie Carter: understood — i'll put the redline and pilot pricing in an email after this call.

00:06:44 Ravi Shah: i'll attach the sandbox runbook, KMS integration step-by-step, and a sample benchmark script.

00:06:50 Dr. Amir Patel: sounds good. i also want a short 30- to 60-minute bench test with our sample prompts to check model fidelity before procurement signs off.

00:06:58 Jamie Carter: we'll schedule that. aim for next Wednesday? tentative 2027-10-27?

00:07:03 Laura Kim: next Wednesday works for timing for our team.

00:07:06 Jamie Carter: perfect. any other blockers or open questions?

00:07:10 Sofia Lopez: just one — can you send the SOC 2 and the DPA redline to our security alias? names: security@pinecrest-health.com?

00:07:17 Jamie Carter: yes i'll cc that alias on the redline email.

00:07:20 Laura Kim: and also copy our procurement mailbox so it lands in the right review queue.

00:07:24 Jamie Carter: will do.

00:07:26 [mix of chatter as wrap-up]

00:07:40 Jamie Carter: OK recap: redline + pricing sheet by Jamie this week, Ravi shares KMS/runbook and sandbox playbook, customer to confirm PHI mapping and sign-off owners. we'll book the bench test for 2027-10-27. if anything changes we'll update the calendar invite.

00:08:00 Laura Kim: thank you all, this was helpful.

00:08:05 Meeting End

Notes on transcription: occasional recognition errors (HSM sometimes transcribed as "H S M"), speaker overlaps, and proper nouns may be slightly off in places. The audio was clear for most speakers but there were brief packet drop artifacts at 00:04:00.

Pilot go-decision matrix and cutover responsibilities

Weekly POC sync focused on final go/no-go decision matrix, defining cutover responsibilities, canary thresholds, A/B split plan, and monitoring/runbook handoff. Agreement to run a dry-run on 2026-06-26, Redwood to deliver updated runbook and dashboard links. Next step: pricing + commitment conversation after successful dry-run.
go/no-go decision matrix
cutover runbook
canary thresholds and rollback conditions
A/B traffic split plan
dashboards and alerts
SLO acceptance criteria
ownership during quiet window
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-24
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Alex Martinez, Priya Nair (Redwood); Jordan Li, Maya Thompson, Samir Patel (AstraFold)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Final pilot checks, decide go/no-go gating, agree runbook owners and dry-run schedule.

00:00 Alex: okay everyone uh thanks for joining i think we have about 50 minutes, i'll kick off. quick agenda - walk through the decision matrix, owners for the cutover runbook, canary thresholds, monitoring, then decide dry-run date.
00:18 Jordan: yeah thanks Alex, appreciate it. we're heads down on the last integration bits, a few questions on traffic shaping and the kv cache warmup.
00:30 Priya: great, i'll cover kv cache warmup and the auto-prefix cache thing, we have a small warmup job that primes the caches to avoid initial latency spikes. sometimes the transcription says K-V cash which is fun but yes it's K-V cache.
00:47 Maya: quick context - our SLA goal is 99.9 for p95 response under normal load, our internal perf tests show we're hitting p95 around 220ms on the hosted variant but with dedicated we saw mid 140s in your benchmarks.
01:05 Alex: right, and that matches the model families we suggested. for the pilot we default to the dedicated pool with fallback to hosted for burst traffic, unless you prefer routing by cost.
01:22 Jordan: we prefer predictable latency so dedicated makes sense. one of our concerns is canary thresholds - what metrics should we gate on? latency, error rate, and quality spike?
01:40 Priya: recommended three-tier gate: latency (p95 > 300ms is fail), error rate (5xx > 0.5% over 5 minutes is fail), and quality/regression check (sampled prompts with human raters or automatic eval; if top-level metric drops by more than 3% compared to baseline fail). note that automatic eval can be noisy, so we'll bias to manual review for first canary.
02:05 Samir: for the error rate threshold - is 0.5% tight for our traffic volume? at peak 50 RPS that's like, what, a few errors. we want to avoid false positives during transient spikes.
02:20 Priya: good point - we recommend a rolling window and a secondary tier - orange threshold at 1% triggers slower ramp but doesn't abort, red threshold at 2% aborts immediate. so a graduated approach.
02:38 Maya: can you repeat the ramp steps for an A/B test? we want to start small and double every 10 minutes?
02:45 Alex: our suggestion: A/B staged ramp - 1% -> 5% -> 10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%. timing can be 10-15 minutes between steps and each step needs green checks from the three gates. if a gate trips we hold and investigate for up to 30 minutes then decide rollback.
03:10 Jordan: sounds sensible. who's on call to make the go/no-go decision during quiet window? we need named owners.
03:20 Alex: proposal: Redwood SE (Priya) monitors infra and model-side metrics, AstraFold SRE (Samir) owns service telemetry and rollback triggers, Jordan as project lead makes the final go/no-go with input from Maya for quality. we can put this in the runbook.
03:40 Samir: ok, i'll take the SRE lead. Priya, you'll run the model dashboards. Jordan, you want me to ping you at each ramp step or only for anomalies?
03:50 Jordan: ping at each ramp step and for anomalies, please. that's our preference.
04:00 Priya: we'll add Slack hooks and a dedicated channel for the cutover. also add an on-call rotation if this moves to production.
04:13 Maya: monitoring - what dashboards will you hand over? we need per-route p50/p95/p99, token counts, model memory, KV hit rate, and cost-per-request estimates.
04:25 Priya: yes we'll provide a dashboard template: latency, error rate, throughput, KV hit rate, GPU utilization, and sampling of outputs for quality. links will be in the runbook. Redwood will maintain the dashboard during pilot; after launch we will hand over a view-only link and the alert rules.
04:45 Jordan: about data residency and logs - AstraFold needs request logs retained for 90 days and we need SOC2 paperwork for audit.
04:55 Alex: Redwood is SOC2 compliant and we can enable longer audit retention as an add-on. for private deployment customers we also support VPC peering and KMS integration for key management.
05:10 Maya: one more legal note - PII redaction is required for a subset of our payloads. is there an easy way to do that?
05:20 Priya: we have pre-processing hooks and can support a redaction layer client-side or via the gateway. we'll add an example sanitizer snippet to the runbook.
05:35 Jordan: can we run a dry-run with traffic mirroring first before any user-visible switch?
05:42 Alex: absolutely - traffic mirroring for a baseline run is low risk. suggested plan: mirroring for 24 hours, then a scheduled dry-run where we do a full staged ramp against a canary slice, then the actual cutover next week if green.
06:05 Samir: timeline? we want the production cutover by end of next week if possible.
06:12 Alex: proposed schedule - mirroring 2026-06-25 02:00 UTC for 24 hours, dry-run 2026-06-26 03:00 UTC (quiet window), final cutover 2026-07-01 03:00 UTC (quiet window). does that work?
06:28 Maya: the 03:00 UTC quiet window is fine for our global team.
06:35 Jordan: ok confirm the mirroring and dry-run. we will need the runbook and the dashboard links before the dry-run.
06:42 Priya: Redwood will deliver updated runbook by 2026-06-26 00:00 UTC (so you have it before dry-run) and dashboard links by 2026-06-25 18:00 UTC.
06:52 Alex: i'll also share the pricing impact of routing fallback to hosted for bursts by EOD tomorrow.
07:00 Jordan: now let's talk rollback scenarios - full rollback vs degrade-to-hosted fallback. which do you recommend?
07:12 Priya: for user-facing apps we recommend degrade-to-hosted fallback (graceful degradation) where we route a percentage to hosted variant automatically if canary triggers. full rollback is heavier and requires state reconciliation for KV cache; that'll be fallback plan B.
07:30 Samir: for cache state - if we rollback, how do we ensure correctness? we have ephemeral session tokens stored in Redis.
07:38 Priya: we advise session reconciliation scripts in the runbook and a KV cache priming step before traffic flip. we'll include the exact commands.
07:50 Maya: alerting - who gets paged for what thresholds? Samir to page infra, Priya to page model/SE, Alex to page AE for stakeholder updates?
08:02 Alex: yes that's fine. we'll codify escalation matrix.
08:10 Jordan: are there any blockers from Redwood side for the dry-run?
08:15 Priya: no blockers, we have capacity reserved. need the final route definitions and example payloads from your side to prime KV cache.
08:28 Jordan: action - Maya to share route list and sample payloads by 2026-06-24 EOD.
08:35 Maya: yes will do.
08:40 Jordan: next topic - evaluation / quality checks during canary. do you have a sample prompt set?
08:46 Priya: we'll share the canary prompt set and automatic eval harness. for first canary we want human spot checks of 50 samples every ramp step.
09:00 Maya: okay that sounds manageable.
09:06 Jordan: security review - any extra steps for KMS? we use AWS KMS and need CMK usage logs forwarded to our SIEM.
09:15 Alex: Redwood supports AWS KMS integration and can configure audit log forwarding to your SIEM via our log exporter. we'll include the config snippet in the runbook.
09:28 Samir: what about rate limiting - do you have per-customer quotas? during pilot we might burst beyond expected.
09:35 Priya: we have per-api-key rate limits and can set soft quotas during pilot to avoid throttling. we can also configure graceful 429 handling and retries.
09:48 Maya: regression alerting - if quality drops but latency is fine, what's the recommended action?
09:55 Priya: pause ramp and escalate to human review; if the drop is persistent beyond 15 minutes rollback or route back to previous model.
10:08 Jordan: ok good. any risks you want to call out?
10:12 Alex: main risks - cache warmup causing initial latency spike, noisy automatic eval false positives, and insufficient observability on token-level cost. mitigation: dry-run mirroring, manual review for first canary, and token-level dashboard.
10:30 Maya: question - can we enable verbose sampling for the dry-run to capture edge cases?
10:35 Priya: yes we'll enable increased sampling and redact PII as per the sanitizer.
10:42 Jordan: timeline recap?
10:45 Alex: mirroring starts 2026-06-25 02:00 UTC; runbook by 2026-06-26 00:00 UTC; dry-run 2026-06-26 03:00 UTC; final cutover target 2026-07-01 03:00 UTC.
10:58 Maya: agreed.
11:05 Jordan: any ask on pricing?
11:10 Alex: i'll share hosted fallback cost delta and a proposed reserved capacity delta for dedicated by tomorrow EOD.
11:20 Samir: we may need a short SLO clause in the pilot contract for response time guarantees during the quiet window.
11:28 Alex: Redwood legal can draft a 2-week pilot SLO guarantee; i'll loop in sales ops after this call.
11:40 Maya: final check - do we have a checklist for pre-cutover smoke tests?
11:45 Priya: yes we'll include smoke tests: basic end-to-end, latency/throughput at ramp steps, KV hit rate check, sample qualitative checks.
11:58 Jordan: perfect. i think that's everything.
12:03 Alex: great recap - i'll list owners and action items in the runbook. any final comments?
12:10 Maya: none from me.
12:12 Jordan: no, thanks everyone.
12:15 Alex: thanks all, we will reconvene after dry-run results.

Questions (logged):
- How do we handle PII redaction in sampled payloads? (answered: pre-processing hooks and sanitizer examples included)
- What's the exact error threshold logic? (answered: rolling window + orange/red tiers)

Action items (brief):
- Maya Thompson: share route list and sample payloads by 2026-06-24 EOD
- Priya Nair (Redwood): deliver updated runbook by 2026-06-26 00:00 UTC and dashboard links by 2026-06-25 18:00 UTC
- Alex Martinez: share pricing delta for hosted fallback by 2026-06-25 EOD
- Jordan Li: confirm quiet window schedule and reviewer list by 2026-06-25 12:00 UTC

End of transcript.
Redwood to deliver updated cutover runbook by 2026-06-26 00:00 UTC
Redwood to share dashboard links by 2026-06-25 18:00 UTC
AstraFold to provide route list and sample payloads by 2026-06-24 EOD
Dry-run scheduled for 2026-06-26 03:00 UTC (quiet window)
Pricing delta for hosted fallback from Redwood by 2026-06-25 EOD
Maya Thompson: share route list and sample payloads by 2026-06-24 EOD
Priya Nair: deliver updated runbook by 2026-06-26 00:00 UTC and dashboard links by 2026-06-25 18:00 UTC
Alex Martinez: share pricing delta for hosted fallback by 2026-06-25 EOD
Jordan Li: confirm quiet window schedule and reviewer list by 2026-06-25 12:00 UTC
Samir Patel: own SRE on-call during dry-run (confirm rotation)

document.content:
Private Connectivity & Runtime Orchestration Lab

Deep technical session focused on Private VPC connectivity for Redwood Private deployment. Main topics: PrivateLink setup patterns, NAT and egress design, DNS resolution and Route53 endpoints, KV-cache/batching behavior over VPC, and quantization/runtime tuning to hit p50/p99 latency SLOs.
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-17 14:00 PT
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Laura Chen, Marcus Hale, Diego Alvarez (Redwood); Priya Raman, Evan Liu, Sarah Gomez, Tom Becker (Aegis)

Summary: quick run-through of network topology, then live Q&A and lab-style troubleshooting. Marcus to demo a PrivateLink attach and show KV cache latency numbers under simulated egress constraints.

---
00:00:03 Laura (Redwood AE): ok folks, thanks for joining everyone, um, we wanted to keep this pretty hands on — we're going to start with the target topology you sent over, and then walk through where latency tends to show up with inference workloads
00:00:18 Priya (Aegis CTO): sounds good, we have about 30 minutes of context and then we wanted to dive into the lab, we sent the diagram in the invite, hope that helps
00:00:27 Marcus (Redwood SE): yep we have it, thanks. quick call out, i'll focus on PrivateLink attachment patterns and the egress hairpin/NAT behavior — diego will cover runtime tuning and KV cache impacts later
00:00:40 Evan (Aegis Infra): quick note: our prod VPC is NAT gw behind TGW, MTU is currently 1500, and we do have strict egress inspection via a proxy appliance in a different AZ
00:00:52 Sarah (Aegis Security): and we need to confirm encryption at rest + KMS integration for dedicated instances, also audit logs forwarded to our ELK
00:01:05 Laura: great. quick agenda — 1) PrivateLink and route table patterns, 2) DNS and Route53 resolver behavior, 3) NAT/hairpin issues and how they affect KV cache/batching, 4) runtime/quantization tradeoffs, 5) next steps and pilot plan

00:04:12 Marcus: ok, so on PrivateLink there are two common patterns we recommend for Private deployment — one is endpoint-per-subnet where each customer subnet has a VPC Endpoint that terminates to our PrivateLink service; the other is centralised endpoint + TGW route propagation. each has tradeoffs.
00:04:37 Tom (Aegis ML Eng): for us, least blast radius is endpoint-per-subnet, because we segment models by subnet, but that increases number of endpoints and, you know, route table management complexity
00:04:51 Marcus: exactly. also if you're using our Dedicated pool per-model segmentation, the per-subnet endpoint gives cleaner isolation. centralised is easier for egress control and observability though.
00:05:15 Evan: when you say endpoint, do we need to open specific SG ports? we have strict SG rules
00:05:22 Marcus: yes — we recommend allowing HTTPS/443 from your app subnets to the endpoint's SG; the endpoint's SG then allows to our service side. we can provide IaC snippets for the SGs. note: if you have a proxy appliance in path, the TLS terminates there which can break mTLS unless you do tcp passthrough. we've seen cases where proxy does SNI stripping.

00:08:50 Diego (Redwood SRE): jumping into KV cache — the biggest gotcha is that KV cache hits only help if requests are routed to the same model host/backplane. if PrivateLink + TGW or NAT routes cause failover to a different AZ or a fallback model variant, you lose warm KV state and see a p99 spike.
00:09:10 Priya: so hairpinned egress — when our service calls out to the internet for auxiliary tooling — would that impact the model's KV cache?
00:09:20 Diego: indirectly, yes. the problem is request affinity. if your egress path causes the load balancer or router to reassign requests across different host pools, the runtime loses locality. also increased RTT from proxy/NAT adds per-token latency.
00:09:34 Marcus: we've measured scenarios where an extra 40-80ms of NAT/proxy RTT turned a p99 from 320ms to ~460ms for 256 token completions — mostly due to synchronous fetches for streaming handoff and smaller batching windows.

00:12:55 Evan: detail question — we saw packet drops and retransmits sometimes, is MTU mismatch a real issue? our appliances use 1400 path MTU in some paths
00:13:03 Diego: yes very much. fragmentation increases CPU in NIC and increases latency. for heavy batching (large prompt+response), we encourage path MTU consistency; we also support gRPC chunking but TLS+proxy can still fragment. if you have MTU < 1500, tell us and we'll test with smaller frame sizes in the runtime kernel.
00:13:40 Tom: ok, how about DNS? we use Route53 inbound endpoints to resolve private hostnames — will PrivateLink still need public DNS entries?
00:13:50 Marcus: you can keep private Route53 records and create a private hosted zone. for PrivateLink our service publishes VPC endpoint DNS names that resolve to the ENIs in our VPC. if you use Route53 Resolver endpoints, ensure conditional forwarding to our resolver IPs. otherwise you'll hit the public resolver and may get public IPs that break routing.

00:16:10 Sarah: can you explain the flow when we use a forward proxy — we see TLS inspection there, how does that play with the Redwood runtime's streaming?
00:16:22 Marcus: TLS inspection often breaks http/2 and streaming because it inserts buffering. streaming needs end-to-end TCP flow semantics; when proxy buffers and reassembles, it increases tail latency and can break chunked transfer semantics. if you must have inspection, we recommend whitelisting endpoint ARNs and bypassing payload inspection for inference traffic, or using a TLS passthrough to preserve mTLS between your app and our endpoint.

00:19:05 Priya: on the dedicated trial, we want to validate throughput and ensure no cold-start hit during burst periods — what's your recommended test harness?
00:19:15 Diego: we usually run a two-phase test: 1) steady-state load to measure throughput and token efficiency (batching windows, KV hit rates), 2) burst tests with sudden ramp to simulate scale-ups and see how batch accumulation and autoscaler behaves. we'll provide a script that simulates your token distribution and prompt lengths.
00:19:33 Marcus: and instrument p50/p95/p99 and KV hit ratio; if you see p99 spikes during ramp it's usually egress or affinity issues not the runtime itself.

00:22:40 Tom: quick quantization question — we plan to run some models at int8 or 4-bit quant, any gotchas on quality vs latency when you run in private?
00:22:51 Diego: quantization reduces memory and can speed things up especially for throughput-heavy workloads; however for some decoder-only models 4-bit can introduce subtle quality regressions. our Optimize tool provides per-prompt evals. note: quantized kernels may change compute pattern which interacts with dynamic batching; sometimes quantized faster per-token but batching needs to be tuned differently to avoid tail latency increases.
00:23:22 Marcus: small add — quantized models have different kernel selection; if you mix quantized and full-precision hosts in the same pool, affinity rules should pin similar requests to like hosts to avoid big variance.

00:26:02 Evan: about KV cache eviction — if we have many short-lived sessions, does that pollute the cache?
00:26:10 Diego: yes, LRU eviction will evict older prefixes. we have a configurable cache size per host; for private Dedicated pools you can increase the cache budget. also using request-level affinity (sticky sessions) helps keep hot prefixes together.

00:28:20 Marcus: demo time — i'm going to show a PrivateLink attach; please bear with the screen share. (several seconds of typing) ok — create VPCE endpoint in the us-west-2 subnet, attach SG allow 443 from app-subnet, add route table entry for 10.2.0.0/16 to point to the endpoint. after that we configure the endpoint service in our account and accept connection on our side.
00:29:05 Evan: i see, in our environment we have an enforced proxy so the VPCE attachment still goes via the proxy, which we've seen cause SNI strip. how would we side-step that?
00:29:12 Marcus: two options: 1) allow direct egress to the VPCE SG from your app subnets (bypass proxy for inference traffic), or 2) run the proxy in TCP passthrough mode for VPCE traffic so TLS isn't terminated at the proxy. Option 1 is simpler but requires exception gating.

00:31:40 Priya: what's best practice for NAT? single NAT in a public subnet vs per-AZ NATs?
00:31:48 Diego: per-AZ NATs reduce cross-AZ hairpinning and improve latency; single NAT causes egress hotspots and cross-AZ packets that break affinity. we strongly recommend per-AZ NATGW if you have AZ-isolated model hosts. Also consider SNAT port exhaustion — for high QPS we add Elastic IP pools and scale NAT instances accordingly.

00:34:50 Tom: i want to measure end-to-end token latency under two conditions — with KV warm and with cold. how do we capture that?
00:35:00 Marcus: we provide a harness that runs sequential warmup requests and then measures single request latency distribution. we'll also add instrumentation for kv_hit boolean in traces so you can filter traces. remember streaming adds a small constant overhead but lowers perceived latency for end-users.

00:37:20 Evan: any recommendations for aperture size for batching? our request size distribution is heavy on short prompts ~20-30 tokens
00:37:29 Diego: for short prompts you want smaller max batch size but aggressive batching window (10-30ms) to accumulate enough tokens. continuous batching helps — runtime fills a batch up to token budget, not just request count. for many small prompts the token budgeting approach is more efficient.

00:40:10 Laura: question from sales ops — what happens if a route table gets misconfigured and traffic egresses to public internet?
00:40:18 Marcus: then you'll hit our public hosted endpoints and may incur different routing, increased latency, and potential data egress footprints. we recommend strict route table testing in a staging VPC first. we can also provide a conditional alert that flags when requests are routing to public IPs.

00:43:05 Priya: can we pin model versions and have controlled rollouts, so we can validate KV and quantization changes gradually?
00:43:14 Laura: yes — Redwood supports canary rollouts and A/B with automatic fallback. for private Dedicated pools you can pin host pools to model revisions and apply traffic split rules. we'll include a rollout plan in the pilot doc.

00:45:50 Sarah: auditors will ask about logs — do you provide per-request audit log with identity and prompt hashes? how long retained?
00:46:00 Diego: we can forward audit logs to your S3 or SIEM; retention and redaction policies are configurable. for sensitive data we recommend hashing or redacting prompt content before forwarding; we also integrate with customer KMS for envelope encryption.

00:48:30 Marcus: quick note — we've seen customers accidentally double-encrypt when proxy performs TLS termination; when that happens client cert validation can fail at our side for mTLS. best practice: either full end-to-end TLS with no interception or perform mutual TLS between app and endpoint and have proxy operate as pure TCP forwarder.

00:51:05 Tom: let's simulate a problematic path — do you have a quick test for detecting hairpin?
00:51:13 Diego: yes run traceroute from app-host to endpoint IP and check whether it traverses the NAT GW or jumps AZs. also we provide a small agent that emits a synthetic request with a header that our backplane logs and returns which host handled it so you can verify affinity.

00:54:00 Evan: we want to try the Dedicated trial next week, how long to set up?
00:54:08 Marcus: usually 24-48 hours to provision the Dedicated pool and another 24 to attach PrivateLink and validate. we'll prioritize if you sign the trial agreement.

00:55:40 Priya: any security checklist / items we need to complete before the trial?
00:55:48 Laura: yes, we'll share a short security checklist — SAML SSO integration, KMS key arn, CIDR ranges, SIEM log endpoint, and any compliance docs. Sarah, we'll route the SOC2/ISO docs to you via the share link.

01:00:02 Diego: final runtime note — for quantized models please include representative prompt sets in the evals. we can run A/B with full precision and quantized kernels and provide diff reports on token-level perplexity and sampling quality metrics. small prompt sets may not reveal edge cases.

01:03:15 Marcus: last thing — when we run the burst test, expect autoscaler to bring up hosts which causes cold KV cache, so we recommend a rolling buffer that pre-warms with a subset of traffic. we can script a warmup to reduce cold-start p99 spikes.
01:05:30 Priya: awesome — this was super helpful. recap — Laura will send runbook and pricing, Marcus will provision the Dedicated trial, Diego will provide the test harness and traceroute agent, Tom to send prompt corpus and traffic profile.
01:06:02 Laura: and we'll schedule the follow-up for a live trial run on 2027-11-24.
01:06:12 Evan: thanks everyone, we'll get the CIDRs and logs over by Monday.
01:06:25 Sarah: thanks — appreciate the clarity on TLS/proxy patterns.
01:06:40 Laura: thanks all, talk soon.

---
Notes on transcription: occasional label mismatches (speaker IDs), and some technical terms may be slightly garbled (e.g., KV cache noted as "K-V chache" in raw transcript). We captured the key artifacts and action items above.

document.content:
Pilot velocity handoff / weekly tuning sync

Meeting header:
- Date: 2027-12-01
- Start: 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~49 minutes
- Attendees: Ethan Cole (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Alex Ramirez (Peregrine Infra), Priya Desai (Peregrine ML), Liam Chen (Peregrine Platform)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Weekly pilot sync focused on latency velocity handoff. Reviewed this week's TTFT/uplift numbers, streaming handshake variance, sequence-length distribution impact, and kernel choice trade-offs. Agreed to run microburst load-shaper tests, share kernel perf spreadsheet, and propose dates for a short Dedicated trial. Discussed security/residency briefly (VPC + KMS) and an ask for audit logs retention.

Topics covered:
- TTFT metrics and P95/P99 variance
- Streaming start/keepalive handshake jitter
- Seqlen distribution (median vs 95th) and cost implications
- Kernel selection: flash-attn vs tiled GEMM vs fallback paths
- Microburst hedging and priority routing
- Next steps for Dedicated trial and artifacts to share

Action items (extracted): see metadata action_items above.

Transcript:
[00:00] Ethan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick check-in — how's week two of the pilot looking from your side, Alex?
[00:24] Alex: Yeah, thanks. So overall it's been okay. We saw median token time drop with the new batch policy, but there's still these spikes last Thursday — p95 shot up to like 230 ms on average for small responses.
[00:45] Maya: Right, that matches the traces we pulled. Median TTFT around 78 ms per token for the short path, but the variance cluster — the microbursts — pushed the tail up. We think it's a mixture of KV-cache warmup and a kernel-path oscillation at certain seqlens.
[01:12] Priya: Quick clarification — when you say "short path" do you mean the streaming early-response path? Our chat flows hit both streaming and non-streaming routes.
[01:24] Maya: Good call — yes, short path = streaming-first-token route. Non-streaming generation tends to amortize some costs so the profile is different.
[01:36] Liam: We pushed more traffic through the streaming endpoint this week to mimic mobile clients. Noted the p95 spikes after about 800 qps bursts.
[01:50] Ethan: OK. Two threads to follow: first, kernel selection and fallback — Maya, can you remind everyone of the options we tested?
[02:02] Maya: Sure. We have the default fused-attn (flash-attn optimized kernels), a tiled GEMM path that is more stable across seqlen but slightly higher median, and a quant-friendly path for int8 which reduces GPU memory and improves throughput but has slightly higher latency jitter on small sequences. We also prototyped a hybrid fallback that switches to tiled GEMM when queue depth passes a threshold.
[02:32] Alex: The hybrid fallback looked promising in the lab. In our env, though, the oscillation happened where the runner kept flipping between kernels every 20-30ms and that caused CPU interrupts we didn't expect.
[02:45] Maya: Yep that's a real risk — kernel thrash. Our suggestion is to use a hysteresis window: only switch after sustained crossing of the threshold for N requests or M ms. We'll include parameters in the sheet.
[03:06] Ethan: Sounds good. Second thread: streaming handshake jitter — Priya, you had some logs showing the handshake latency drift?
[03:16] Priya: Yeah. In the traces the early streaming frames sometimes get delayed by 120-180ms when queue depth grows. We suspect connection ramping plus our prefix cache misses. There's also a few HTTP keepalive churns on your side (maybe client side) — I'm still investigating.
[03:36] Maya: Two mitigations: aggressive prefix/KV warm caching for hot routes, and a small pre-emptive slot for the very first token on streaming routes (we call it the "boost slot"), so it avoids scheduling behind large batched jobs. It costs a tiny bit on throughput but cuts TTFT tails.
[04:00] Liam: That boost slot would need policy knobs; we don't want to starve heavy batch jobs during our peak hours.
[04:08] Ethan: Totally. We can gate boost slots by customer tier or route label. We'll propose defaults but you can tune.
[04:18] Alex: One operational ask — can we get raw perf logs? The dashboard has aggregates but we want the traces mapped to request IDs.
[04:30] Maya: Yes, we'll share the raw logs plus a kernel mapping CSV — which kernel executed per request, seqlen, lat, mem footprint.
[04:40] Priya: That'll help a lot. Also, on seqlen distribution — our median is 256 tokens, but the 95th is close to 1600 because of long analytic queries. How does that affect kernel picks?
[04:56] Maya: Significant. For long seqlens the fused-attn is great and efficient, but for mid-range (500-900) the tiled GEMM sometimes wins, especially when KV cache hits are high. The decision boundary changes with quantization and batch size. We'll include plots in the spreadsheet.
[05:18] Ethan: FYI on Dedicated trial: we can run a 2-week reserved pool for you to validate tail behavior under isolation. That also lets you try different compilation flags and quant profiles without noisy neighbors.
[05:31] Liam: Perfect. What are the constraints? Cost/lead time?
[05:36] Ethan: We'll propose dates and a cost estimate — it scales by GPU type and hours. For a fair trial we'd recommend one V100-class equivalent per shard but with our scheduler tuned for low latency, not max throughput.
[05:50] Alex: Another question — security and logs. We need KMS integration and a longer audit-retention window for model calls. Is that supported in the Private plane?
[06:02] Maya: Yes, Private (VPC) supports KMS and you can configure audit retention up to X months (we'll confirm exact number in the security pack). For Hosted we have encrypted-at-rest and short-term audit retention; Dedicated offers extended retention as an add-on.
[06:20] Priya: Great. Please send the SOC2 artifacts again — we gave them to procurement but they asked for a few clarifications around SAML assertions.
[06:29] Ethan: Will do, I'll attach the latest package and note the SAML snippet.
[06:34] [07:00] Speaker 2 (unlabeled, minor crosstalk): -- yeah mm-hm
[07:15] Maya: Back to performance — we ran a microburst sim on our side that mimics a 2s 5k qps spike. Results: with the hybrid fallback and a 150ms hysteresis, p95 stayed under 260ms; without it p95 hit ~420ms.
[07:40] Alex: Those numbers align with what we saw in our infra. Can you share those raw traces?
[07:47] Maya: Yes. Also note we saw an edge case where the quant-int8 path caused a small accuracy drift on a handful of prompts — Priya flagged this.
[07:57] Priya: Right, we saw subtle tokenization shifts on financial tickers in int8; not acceptable for some routes. We need route-aware quantization policies.
[08:10] Ethan: Route-aware quantization — good point. We can pin high-criticality routes to full-precision or to validated quant profiles.
[08:19] Liam: On routing, can we route by latency SLO? Like if a route needs sub-200ms p95 we send it through the boost slot + fresher KV cache pool.
[08:29] Maya: Yes, we support policy-based routing. We'll propose a default policy DSL snippet and an example set for your three main routes.
[08:38] Alex: One small thing — the dashboard's sequence length histogram is useful but we need it per-route not global.
[08:45] Ethan: Noted. We'll add per-route seqlen histograms to the export we send.
[08:52] [09:10] Priya: Regarding microburst test plan — are you able to run it on our Dedicated trial or do you want us to run locally?
[09:19] Maya: Ideally both. We can run an initial sim on our infra against a dedicated pool, then you run it in your staging to validate network effects. We'll share the load-shaper script.
[09:30] Alex: Ok. Also curious about cost impact if we enable boost slots for 20% of streaming traffic. Any ballpark?
[09:40] Ethan: Roughly 6-10% increase in unit cost for those priority slots depending on traffic profile. We'll model that in the spreadsheet for your actual seqlen distribution.
[09:53] Liam: For the kernel oscillation issue, do you recommend we tweak our autoscaler thresholds? We saw thrash when autoscaler scaled up then down quickly.
[10:03] Maya: Yes, smooth autoscaler policies (longer cooldown) can prevent oscillation. Also the kernel hysteresis helps because switching between kernels less often reduces the observed thrash.
[10:14] Alex: If we accept a small cost increase, we could lock priority routes to the low-latency path permanently.
[10:21] Priya: That would solve it for critical flows. But we'd still want to test long-tail analytic queries separately.
[10:28] Maya: Agreed. Separate class for analytics: schedule them on batch-optimized nodes during off-peak.
[10:35] Ethan: Quick logistics — I'll send the spreadsheet, the load-shaper script (link: https://redwood.internal/pilot/microburst-script), and a proposed Dedicated trial calendar. Any dates in early Dec we should avoid?
[10:50] Liam: End of week Dec 10-12 is baseline load testing window for our infra team, avoid those.
[10:57] Ethan: Noted. We'll avoid that slot.
[11:02] Priya: One question on tracing IDs — can trace IDs carry customer request context so we can correlate with our logs?
[11:10] Maya: Yes, we can optionally pass a request_id header through the runtime and echo it back in traces. We'll include config details in the log export.
[11:20] Alex: Great. Also, procurement asked for a short technical memo summarizing the Dedicated trial constraints and rollback policy.
[11:28] Ethan: We'll draft that and send it to procurement.
[11:34] [11:55] Maya: Ok to recap?
[11:37] Ethan: Yeah go ahead.
[11:38] Maya: Recap: 1) Maya/Ethan share kernel perf sheet + raw logs by 12/03. 2) Peregrine runs microburst test in staging with our script and reports back on 12/08. 3) AE proposes 2-week Dedicated trial dates outside Dec 10-12. 4) Priya will flag any quant-related accuracy problems per-route. 5) Liam will deliver per-route seqlen histograms by 12/02.
[11:59] Priya: That matches.
[12:02] Alex: Thanks all, appreciate the detail.
[12:06] Ethan: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts and a calendar invite for the trial planning call.
[12:12] Liam: Thanks. Bye.
[12:15] End of call.

Notes on transcript quality: Several short crosstalk interruptions and occasional mis-transcripts (e.g., "KV cash" or "flash-attn" spelled out differently) may appear in exported auto-transcript. Shared artifacts referenced: kernel-performance spreadsheet (link), microburst load-shaper script (link), SOC2/security pack (will be attached).

Final explicit next steps (human readable):
- Ethan: Share kernel perf spreadsheet + raw traces (due 2027-12-03).
- Maya: Provide hybrid-fallback hysteresis parameter recommendations (due 2027-12-06).
- Priya: Run microburst tests with provided script in stage and share results (due 2027-12-08).
- Liam: Send per-route seqlen histograms and topology note (due 2027-12-02).
- AE: Propose Dedicated trial dates and cost estimate (ASAP, avoid 2027-12-10 to 2027-12-12).

2026-01-14 Staging catalog assay and pin approval sync

Weekly POC sync focused on candidate model comparison across catalog, pin approval process, and rollback/fallback runbook. Reviewed latest batch of latency/quality numbers, flagged two models for soft-pin+, agreed on an emergency fallback path and security checklist requests.
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-14 15:00 PST | Duration: 52 min | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Lucas (Redwood SE), Riya, Tom; Priya (NimbleHealth ML), Ben (CTO), Hannah (SRE), Oscar (Product)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll try to keep this tight, we've got 50 minutes. quick roll call?
[00:12] Priya Rao: Hi, Priya here. I'll lead the run for the synthetic tests this week.
[00:17] Ben Morales: Ben here. focused on the ops questions and timeline.
[00:21] Hannah Li: Hannah, SRE. mainly interested in cutover mechanics and emergency swap.
[00:30] Maya Chen: Great. quick agenda: one, review the catalog comparison Riya sent; two, confirm which two candidates we soft-pin in staging; three, talk through rollback / fallback; four, security asks. Lucas, you want to kick off the perf highlights?
[00:45] Lucas O'Neal: Sure. so we ran the batch through the staging fleet, three variants: rdx-7b-quant, rdx-13b-q4, and an external 14b baseline. latency medians: rdx-7b around 38ms per token in our continuous-batching emulation; 13b q4 was 62ms median; external 14b baseline came in 74ms but had slightly higher quality on open-ended prompts. throughputs looked consistent with sequence length distribution you shared. note: KV cache warmup was faster on the rdx-13b for the first 50 requests — though the transcript capture sometimes shows KV *cash* which is odd in the logs.
[01:30] Priya Rao: When you say quality, are we using our rubric or Redwood's default? I'm seeing different rank order depending on the eval set.
[01:38] Lucas O'Neal: Good point — we ran both. the weighted score in the shared sheet uses your eval set at 60% and natively measured perplexity & edit-distance at 40%. I'll post both sheets. link: https://redwood-prod-shared/benchmarks/NH-9982 (internal link).
[01:52] Oscar Vega: Quick Q — the external model spikes on hallucination in the policy questions; that's a showstopper for us.
[02:00] Maya Chen: Right, that's why we were focusing on the rdx variants; they trade a little latency for consistency.
[02:06] Ben Morales: Cost delta between 7b quant and 13b q4? We're watching run-rate.
[02:12] Riya Patel: 7b quant is about 0.6x the token cost vs 13b q4 in our config; 13b gives better NLU in the complex dialog flows so it's a product decision. we added a column for cost in the sheet.
[02:26] Hannah Li: Ops concerns: if we pin to 13b q4, what's the emergency fallback? do we failover to hosted Redwood or to rdx-7b within our Dedicated pool?
[02:35] Lucas O'Neal: Two-tiered plan recommended: soft-fallback -> route 10% traffic to rdx-7b (same pool) when latency or NPS degrades, hard fallback -> route fully to hosted compatible variant in another region or to pre-warmed rdx-7b. We'll provide the routing policy snippet for your gateway.
[02:53] Priya Rao: That snippet will help — please include TTLs and grace periods. we want automated rollback if error-rate > 5% for 2 mins.
[03:02] Lucas O'Neal: noted; we usually recommend a 1-min lookback with a 3-minute confirmation window for canaries, but we'll match your SLOs.
[03:12] Ben Morales: On the pin, do we need legal signoff or is product ok to approve the staging pin?
[03:18] Maya Chen: For staging pin approvals, product + ops is usually fine; for production pin we ask for security + legal to ack due to data residency and audit log requirements.
[03:28] Hannah Li: Speaking of security, we've got two doc asks: SOC 2 Type II evidence and KMS key usage diagram. also SSO/SAML integration flow.
[03:37] Tom Alvarez: I'll attach the security pack to the ticket; Maya will follow up with the KMS diagram.
[03:45] Maya Chen: Yep, I'll share the KMS/HSM integration doc and a sample audit log extract.
[03:50] Oscar Vega: Any blockers on private deployment? we might need a VPC egress policy tweak to allow the staging connectors.
[03:56] Lucas O'Neal: There's a small firewall rule — we'll send a snippet. for on-prem option the packaging is larger; we don't recommend it for this pilot.
[04:04] Priya Rao: Back to the results, the embeddings regression from last week — did we isolate to quantization noise?
[04:12] Lucas O'Neal: We looked; embeddings drifted slightly on 7b quant during long-context QA. seems like a quantization calibration issue. we have a fix candidate (recalibration pass on the tokenizer embedding layer) — we'll test it in the next build.
[04:30] Ben Morales: How confident are you in the rollback? Last time the manual cutover took 25 minutes and we had session loss.
[04:37] Lucas O'Neal: We're adding session sticky fallback: client continuity token is preserved by routing layer during soft migration. hard swap will require TTL expiration but we can reduce TTLs to minimize impact.
[04:52] Priya Rao: Ok. For the pin matrix, what's your recommendation? we have three columns: soft-pin, hard-pin, and blocklist.
[05:00] Maya Chen: Recommendation from Redwood: soft-pin the rdx-13b-q4 as primary candidate with rdx-7b-quant as fast fallback. blocklist the external 14b due to hallucination and inconsistent latency spikes. that gets us quality and an escape hatch.
[05:16] Hannah Li: Can we have a staged rollout: 0->10->50->100 over 48 hours? with automatic revert on error?
[05:25] Lucas O'Neal: Yep. we support canary progression policies and automatic rollback if error thresholds hit. we'll provide the config YAML.
[05:34] Priya Rao: We'll also run the synthetic routing test to validate the sticky token behavior.
[05:40] Maya Chen: Good. quick note on metrics: we'll surface token-level latency, 99th, error-rate, and quality regression alerts tied to your eval set.
[05:50] Ben Morales: Will cost attribution be per route/model so we can bill feature owners?
[05:55] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Console gives token-level cost breakdown by route/model and teams. we'll turn that on for your account.
[06:02] Oscar Vega: Timeline: assuming we soft-pin by next Tuesday staging, when can we do prod freeze?
[06:08] Maya Chen: If staging looks good and you sign off on pin matrix, prod freeze and canary next week (ETA earliest 2026-01-27).
[06:15] Priya Rao: That works.
[06:18] Hannah Li: One more question: audit logs retention, do you support configurable retention for Private? we need 7 years for certain audits.
[06:26] Riya Patel: Private deployments support configurable retention; hosted has limits but we offer add-on long-term retention. we'll include exact retention SLAs in the security pack.
[06:36] Ben Morales: Any red flags on data residency? our EU customers must remain in EU region.
[06:41] Lucas O'Neal: You can pin region; routing policy supports geo-fencing. we'll map models to regions and fallbacks respect data residency.
[06:50] Priya Rao: Sweet. action items recap?
[06:56] Maya Chen: Maya to push pin matrix & pinned YAML, Lucas to push rollback runbook & routing snippet, Priya to run synthetic test, Hannah and Lucas to schedule tabletop.
[07:05] Hannah Li: I'll send available windows for the week of Jan 26.
[07:10] Maya Chen: Great. anything else?
[07:13] Ben Morales: Quick mention — we're also evaluating Anthropic for a separate internal pilot; not blocking but wanted to be transparent.
[07:20] Maya Chen: Thanks. we'll include a brief competitor comparison in the matrix.
[07:25] Priya Rao: One small transcript note — in the doc there's a line that says "KV cash" which is just a typo.
[07:30] Lucas O'Neal: haha, yes — KV cache.
[07:34] Maya Chen: Alright, we'll finish with next steps and I'll follow up with links: pin matrix, benchmark sheet, security pack.
[07:43] Tom Alvarez: I'll log the notes in the CRM and attach the artifacts.
[07:47] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. end.

References and artifacts mentioned:
- Pin approval matrix (sheet): https://redwood-prod-shared/benchmarks/NH-9982/pin-matrix
- Benchmark detail (latency/quality): link above
- Security pack placeholder: https://redwood-sec/NH-9982/security-pack
- Routing snippet (to be posted): will be added to the ticket

Transcript notes: occasional mis-transcriptions and shorthand; speaker labels sometimes generic (Speaker 6), filler words left in place.

Redwood to share updated pin matrix and weighted perf table (Maya) by 2026-01-19
NimbleHealth to run synthetic routing test against soft-fallback (Priya) by 2026-01-21

document.content:
Lumen Legaltech - Security review: audit logs + config change controls (Dedicated autoscaling)

Lumen Legaltech reviewed Redwood’s approach to auditability for Dedicated autoscaling configuration and scaling decisions, with emphasis on compliance needs (change traceability, retention, export). Redwood confirmed that scaling policy updates are captured as audit events with actor identity (user/service), before/after diffs, request IDs, and enforcement outcomes. Redwood also described decision/audit events emitted by the autoscaler (requested desired vs bounded desired, clamp reason, predictive vs reactive signal source, staleness/fallback). Lumen asked about RBAC granularity, separation of duties, and whether Redwood support staff can modify customer bounds. Redwood outlined role-based controls in Console/API, optional approval workflows via customer process, and that Redwood internal access is controlled and logged. Next steps: share draft audit event schema and retention options, confirm Lumen’s required retention period (12 vs 24 months), and schedule a follow-up focused on SIEM export + evidence collection for audits.
Redwood (Kevin Osei) to share audit log export options (HTTP webhook vs S3-style delivery) and current retention defaults by tier.
Redwood (Benji Okafor) to send draft event shape for scaling policy change + autoscaler decision events (fields + example payloads).
Lumen (Ava Chen) to confirm required retention period (12/24 months) and whether immutable/WORM storage is required for their audits.
Lumen (Priya Desai) to list required RBAC roles (who can edit bounds, who can view audit logs, who can enable predictive mode).
Redwood (Marcus Lin) to provide Trust Center links / SOC 2 report access instructions and confirm audit log access controls for support personnel.
Schedule 30-min follow-up next week to walk through event samples and how they map to Lumen evidence checklist.
Do audit logs include before/after for min/max bounds and predictive mode toggles?
Can Redwood employees change customer scaling bounds, and is that logged distinctly from customer-initiated changes?
What is the default retention and can we extend to 24 months for regulated workloads?
Can audit logs be exported to our SIEM (Splunk) with guaranteed delivery semantics?
Do you log autoscaler decisions (i.e., why you scaled) or only config changes?
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Lumen Legaltech - Security review: audit logs + config change controls (Dedicated autoscaling)
Date: 2025-07-22
Time: 4:00 PM PT
Duration: 47 minutes
Recorder: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
- Liam O'Rourke (Redwood Inference, TAM)
- Marcus Lin (Redwood Inference, Security)
- Kevin Osei (Redwood Inference, Audit Log Export/SIEM)
- Benji Okafor (Redwood Inference, Platform/Control Plane)
- Ava Chen (Lumen Legaltech, Security & GRC)
- Mark Feld (Lumen Legaltech, Compliance)
- Priya Desai (Lumen Legaltech, Platform Engineering)
- Jonah Brooks (Lumen Legaltech, Procurement Ops)

---

[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, cool. Folks can hear me okay?

[00:03] Ava Chen: Yep, loud and clear.

[00:05] Liam O'Rourke: Great. Thanks everyone. Today we wanted to focus on audit logs and config changes around Dedicated autoscaling, right. Specifically, the min/max bounds feature you all asked about, and predictive scaling toggle. Marcus and Kevin are here for security and export/retention, Benji for the actual API side.

[00:23] Mark Feld: Perfect.

[00:25] Priya Desai: Yeah, we have an internal checklist. We can just run down it.

[00:28] Liam O'Rourke: Sounds good. Ava do you want to kick us off with the top questions?

[00:33] Ava Chen: Sure. So, for us the big thing is change traceability. If someone changes autoscaling policy—min bound, max bound, cool-down, turning on predictive—do we have an audit record with who did it, when, and what exactly changed, like before and after.

[00:50] Benji Okafor: Yep. So there are two buckets: configuration changes and scaling decisions. For configuration, updates to the scaling policy are done via Console or API endpoint. Those are persisted, and we emit an audit event on write.

[01:05] Ava Chen: When you say audit event, what’s in it?

[01:07] Benji Okafor: Actor identity, so user ID if it’s a human via Console, or service account if via API token; the org/account ID, deployment ID, region; timestamp; request ID; and we capture a diff-like structure. In practice it’s “before” and “after” snapshots of the policy object.

[01:29] Mark Feld: Snapshot of the whole object or just the changed fields?

[01:32] Benji Okafor: Whole object, but we also include changed field paths for easy indexing. Like scaling_policy.min_replicas changed from 4 to 8.

[01:43] Priya Desai: Does that include predictive mode? Like “predictive.enabled = true” type of thing.

[01:49] Benji Okafor: Exactly.

[01:51] Ava Chen: Okay. Next: retention. We typically require 1 year minimum, sometimes 2 years depending on the client matter. What’s default retention and can it be extended.

[02:02] Kevin Osei: Today for Dedicated enterprise tiers we default to 400 days in-platform for audit events. For some customers we do 730 days with an add-on, but we generally recommend export to your own storage for long-term retention and immutability.

[02:20] Jonah Brooks: 400 days is… oddly specific.

[02:23] Kevin Osei: Yeah. It’s basically 13 months. Covers “one year plus some audit lag.”

[02:29] Ava Chen: If we export, what are the options? We use Splunk. We can do webhooks, or S3 with a forwarder.

[02:37] Kevin Osei: Both patterns are supported depending on deployment mode. For Hosted and Dedicated, we support near-real-time delivery via HTTPS endpoint, signed payloads. And we have a bucket delivery option that’s like “we drop JSON lines files” on a cadence. Some customers then ingest to Splunk via a collector.

[02:58] Ava Chen: And delivery guarantees? Like, at least once, exactly once?

[03:02] Kevin Osei: It’s at-least-once. Events have idempotency keys (event_id) so you can de-dupe. We retry on non-2xx with exponential backoff.

[03:13] Mark Feld: Are these “audit logs” different from app logs?

[03:16] Marcus Lin: Yes, separated streams. Audit is change events, access events, and some control-plane decisions. It’s not request payloads or prompt data.

[03:25] Priya Desai: That’s good. We don’t want prompts in audit logs.

[03:28] Liam O'Rourke: Yep, that’s been a consistent ask.

[03:33] Ava Chen: Okay, now RBAC. Who in our org can see audit logs, who can edit scaling policy. We need separation: operators can view, only platform admins can change.

[03:45] Benji Okafor: In Console we have roles at the project/account scope. Roughly: Viewer, Operator, Admin. Viewer can read configs and view audit logs. Operator can do operational actions like view metrics, but cannot change scaling policy by default. Admin can update scaling policy.

[04:05] Ava Chen: “By default” meaning configurable?

[04:08] Benji Okafor: Yeah, you can also use custom roles via RBAC policy if you’re on the enterprise plan. Under the hood it’s permission-based: “dedicated.scalingPolicy.write” etc.

[04:22] Priya Desai: Is API token scopeable to just one deployment? We try to avoid broad tokens.

[04:28] Benji Okafor: Yes. Tokens can be constrained to deployment IDs and environments. And service accounts have their own audit identity.

[04:38] Mark Feld: We also need to know if Redwood staff can change these settings. Like, can Support log in and edit our bounds.

[04:46] Marcus Lin: Good question. So, Redwood internal access is tightly controlled. For Dedicated, support cannot casually edit customer scaling policies. If there is a break-glass scenario, there is a privileged workflow requiring approval, and actions are logged. Those logs are in our internal audit system, and customer-visible audit events would show “actor_type=redwood_operator” and the reason code.

[05:09] Ava Chen: So we would see that in our audit export.

[05:12] Marcus Lin: Yes, the same audit stream. The event includes “actor,” “channel,” and a justification field. We don’t put sensitive internal ticket content, but we tag the internal case ID.

[05:23] Jonah Brooks: That’s important for us. A lot of vendors say “we can but we won’t.”

[05:27] Marcus Lin: Understood. We try to make it explicit and inspectable.

[05:33] Priya Desai: Switching to the autoscaler decision logging—do you log when the system scales? We’ve been burned where scaling happens and we can’t explain why.

[05:42] Benji Okafor: Yes, we log the scaling decisions as a separate event type. It includes “requested_desired_replicas” from the policy evaluator, then “bounded_desired_replicas” after applying min/max. And the clamp reason: e.g. “clamped_to_max” or “clamped_to_min.”

[06:02] Ava Chen: Wait, what generates requested desired? Is that prediction or reactive signals.

[06:07] Benji Okafor: Both. The autoscaler loop computes a desired value based on reactive signals—queue depth, saturation, latency—and optionally includes a forecast input if predictive mode is enabled. The audit event records which signals were used and their “staleness.” If the forecast is stale or missing, it falls back to reactive.

[06:29] Priya Desai: That’s the thing we want documented. Like, if the predictor was down, we don’t want it scaling to zero.

[06:35] Benji Okafor: Right, and we had a pilot bug in a different account where null forecast caused an unsafe downscale. That’s fixed: null forecast is treated as “no forecast,” and min bound is always applied. Also, scale-to-zero is not allowed for Dedicated unless explicitly configured, and for your tier it would be disabled.

[06:58] Mark Feld: Do you include the reason in human terms? Or it’s just numbers.

[07:02] Benji Okafor: Both. There’s a “reason_code” field and a “reason_detail” string. Example: “reactive_queue_depth_high; bounded at max=24”

[07:13] Ava Chen: Okay. Another compliance item: we need “who viewed audit logs” sometimes. Do you log access to audit logs?

[07:21] Marcus Lin: We do, yes. Access events include read actions in Console for sensitive pages (audit log viewer, token management, scaling policy). For API access, we log token usage metadata. Again, no prompt contents, just the fact of access and which resource.

[07:41] Priya Desai: Is that also exportable?

[07:44] Kevin Osei: Yes, same export pipeline. Event type differs: “audit_log.read” versus “scaling_policy.update” etc.

[07:52] Ava Chen: Good.

[08:00] Liam O'Rourke: Maybe we should anchor back on Dedicated specifics. You all asked about min/max bounds because of budget controls, but here we’re focusing on the security posture: you want assurance that those are hard enforced and any change is traceable.

[08:14] Mark Feld: Exactly. And we also need to know retention and if we can do WORM.

[08:19] Kevin Osei: If you export to your storage, you can configure WORM/immutability on your side. On our bucket delivery, we don’t currently offer customer-managed WORM in Redwood-managed storage. But we can deliver to your bucket in your cloud account for Private; for Dedicated, it’s typically our managed pipeline to your endpoint.

[08:40] Ava Chen: Okay, so for Dedicated we should do webhook -> Splunk, then store raw events in an immutable index.

[08:46] Kevin Osei: That’s the usual pattern.

[08:49] Priya Desai: Are events signed? We need integrity.

[08:53] Kevin Osei: Yes, we sign payloads, and include a signature header. We can also do mTLS for the webhook.

[09:03] Ava Chen: Nice.

[09:05] Marcus Lin: Also, all audit events are generated server-side; clients can’t spoof them.

[09:10] Ava Chen: Right.

[09:12] Priya Desai: On RBAC, what about SSO? We require SAML.

[09:16] Marcus Lin: We support SAML SSO with SCIM for provisioning. RBAC ties to groups. Many enterprise customers map “Platform-Admins” group to Admin role, etc.

[09:31] Mark Feld: And do you support MFA.

[09:33] Marcus Lin: Yes. If SSO enforced, you inherit your IdP MFA policy.

[09:39] Ava Chen: Cool. Let’s talk about config change controls. We have an internal change management process that requires approvals. Do you have any in-product approval workflow?

[09:51] Liam O'Rourke: Today we don’t have a two-person approval flow in Console. Most customers handle that by restricting write permissions and requiring changes go through Terraform or API with your CI approvals.

[10:04] Benji Okafor: And just to add: we have Terraform support for scaling policy fields—min, max, predictive toggle—so you can put it into GitOps. That gives you an audit trail in your repo plus our audit event.

[10:20] Priya Desai: That’s actually ideal for us.

[10:22] Jonah Brooks: Procurement note: we will likely ask that to be in scope for the enterprise agreement.

[10:28] Liam O'Rourke: We can loop legal in later, sure.

[10:33] Ava Chen: Another question: if someone changes max bound, do you rate limit changes? We’ve seen systems where people spam config and it causes instability.

[10:43] Benji Okafor: Yes, we enforce throttling on policy updates. If someone tries to update repeatedly, we reject with a 429-ish error and also emit an audit warning event “scaling_policy.update_throttled.”

[10:59] Ava Chen: Nice. That helps.

[11:03] Priya Desai: On decision events, can we correlate to deployment metrics? Like we want to see “scale event at 10:05, queue depth rising.”

[11:12] Benji Okafor: Yes, events include a trace/correlation ID, and the autoscaler also emits metrics for “desired vs bounded replicas.” In Grafana you can line up the timeline. I can share example dashboards.

[11:28] Liam O'Rourke: We’ll send the dashboard spec link too.

[11:33] Mark Feld: Do you keep these decision logs for same retention as audit logs?

[11:38] Kevin Osei: Yes, same pipeline and retention settings.

[11:44] Ava Chen: Okay. Let’s get into data residency. If our Dedicated deployment is in us-west, where do audit logs live.

[11:53] Marcus Lin: The control plane logs are stored in region-aligned infrastructure. For export, we deliver from that region to your endpoint. If you need strict residency guarantees, we can document the specific region mapping.

[12:09] Priya Desai: We’ll need that documented.

[12:11] Liam O'Rourke: Got it.

[12:14] Ava Chen: We also have to answer: do you log any customer data in these events. Like deployment names could contain client names.

[12:22] Benji Okafor: We include deployment_id, not freeform deployment display names, in the audit event. In Console you may label deployments, but the event payload uses IDs. If you want, we can add a field to include display name, but by default it’s not included.

[12:39] Mark Feld: Prefer not.

[12:40] Benji Okafor: Same.

[12:43] Ava Chen: Good. Another item: do you log changes coming from Redwood automation? Like if the platform changes defaults.

[12:51] Benji Okafor: Platform defaults changing generally does not mutate your policy object. But if we change something that affects behavior, we publish release notes and it’s versioned. Your explicit bounds always win. If there is a migration that writes fields, we emit an audit event with actor_type=system and includes the migration version.

[13:12] Ava Chen: That’s what I want to hear.

[13:14] Priya Desai: Can you give an example of the audit event types? Just list them.

[13:20] Benji Okafor: Sure. “scaling_policy.create”, “scaling_policy.update”, “scaling_policy.delete” (rare), “scaling_decision.emitted”, “scaling_bound_hit” as a counter event, “forecast.input_stale” when predictive enabled but stale, and “audit_log.read”. Plus the general “token.create/rotate” events.

[13:45] Kevin Osei: And “export.delivery_failed” is another one if your endpoint starts returning errors.

[13:52] Ava Chen: Great. I’ll map those.

[13:56] Mark Feld: On the predictive mode: if we don’t enable it, do we still see forecast-related events.

[14:02] Benji Okafor: No, you won’t. Predictive signal ingestion is gated and the events only appear if enabled.

[14:08] Ava Chen: And enabling predictive mode itself is audited.

[14:11] Benji Okafor: Yep.

[14:14] Liam O'Rourke: Maybe we should also cover who can enable predictive mode. Some customers treat it as a higher-risk setting.

[14:20] Priya Desai: Yes, we’d want only Admin to do that.

[14:23] Benji Okafor: That’s the default. And we can also add an org-level policy: predictive mode can’t be enabled unless account flag is on. So you’d have to request it.

[14:35] Ava Chen: That’s good. So you basically have a feature flag gate.

[14:38] Benji Okafor: Exactly.

[14:41] Mark Feld: Another compliance question: can we export audit logs to our eDiscovery system? Meaning do you have an API to query historical events.

[14:50] Kevin Osei: Yes, there’s an API for querying audit events by time range, type, deployment_id, actor. It’s paginated. For bulk eDiscovery we recommend export rather than API.

[15:08] Ava Chen: Okay.

[15:10] Priya Desai: Switching a bit—one of our concerns is config drift. If Terraform is source of truth, will Console edits create drift.

[15:19] Liam O'Rourke: It can, like any system. Most customers lock down Console writes and treat Terraform as the only writer.

[15:26] Benji Okafor: Also, the audit event includes “channel=console|api|terraform” depending on how it was made. Terraform uses API under the hood but tags a user-agent and we set channel.

[15:39] Priya Desai: Perfect.

[15:41] Ava Chen: Can you talk about how you store the audit logs? Encryption, keys.

[15:47] Marcus Lin: Audit logs are encrypted at rest. For Dedicated, we use cloud KMS. For Private deployments, we can integrate with customer-managed KMS depending on the packaging. Access is restricted and logged.

[16:03] Mark Feld: Any chance of customer-managed keys for Dedicated.

[16:07] Marcus Lin: Not today as a standard feature, but we can discuss as part of enterprise requirements. Many customers are satisfied with export to their own storage as the compliance control.

[16:19] Ava Chen: Okay, so for our audit scope we can treat “authoritative” retention as in our own environment.

[16:25] Marcus Lin: Exactly.

[16:28] Jonah Brooks: I have a question on contractual language. If we set max bounds, are those hard enforced? Because that’s part of our budget control.

[16:37] Benji Okafor: Yes. Hard invariant: never exceed max, never go below min. There are special cases like region capacity shortage where we might not be able to meet min, but we never exceed max. If min can’t be met, we surface a degraded state and alert.

[16:56] Priya Desai: And that degraded state is visible in logs/metrics?

[17:00] Benji Okafor: Yes, metric and event: “min_unmet_due_to_capacity_shortage” with region.

[17:08] Ava Chen: Is that an audit event or operational event.

[17:10] Benji Okafor: It’s in the decision/audit stream because it’s important for postmortems.

[17:17] Marcus Lin: And from compliance standpoint, it’s not a user-initiated change. It’s an operational state event.

[17:24] Ava Chen: Got it.

[17:26] Liam O'Rourke: We’re at about halfway. Any other checklist items, Ava?

[17:31] Ava Chen: Yeah, last couple. One: do we get timestamps in UTC?

[17:36] Kevin Osei: ISO-8601 with offset, but effectively UTC. You can choose to normalize.

[17:41] Ava Chen: Two: can we include our own change ticket ID as metadata when updating scaling policy. For example, “CHG-1234”.

[17:50] Benji Okafor: Not in the core schema today, but we have a “client_request_context” string field that can carry metadata. Some customers put their change ticket there. It is included in the audit event.

[18:03] Priya Desai: That’s excellent.

[18:05] Mark Feld: Great for evidence.

[18:08] Ava Chen: Last: we want to ensure audit logs can’t be deleted by our own admins. Like, an admin could cover their tracks.

[18:16] Kevin Osei: In Redwood, audit logs are append-only. You can’t delete or modify entries via API/Console. In your own Splunk, that depends on your controls.

[18:28] Marcus Lin: And internal Redwood policies prevent tampering; we can share that as part of SOC 2 controls documentation.

[18:36] Ava Chen: Okay.

[18:38] Liam O'Rourke: Before we wrap, do you want to ask about competitor comparisons? Not required but sometimes helps.

[18:44] Priya Desai: We’ve looked at Bedrock and Azure OpenAI. Mostly they don’t give us the autoscaling knobs we want. On audit logs, they do CloudTrail-ish logs, but it’s not tied to model serving decisions.

[18:58] Benji Okafor: Yeah, we try to connect the “what changed” and “what the autoscaler did” so you can explain behavior.

[19:05] Mark Feld: That’s key.

[19:08] Ava Chen: Can you send a sample? Even redacted. Like one scaling policy update event, one decision event.

[19:16] Benji Okafor: Yep, I’ll send a couple examples.

[19:19] Kevin Osei: And I’ll send export docs plus how to verify signatures.

[19:24] Marcus Lin: I’ll send Trust Center links and the section that mentions audit logging access controls.

[19:31] Liam O'Rourke: Great. Anything else?

[19:34] Ava Chen: That’s it. We’ll confirm 24 month retention requirement. Might be a must.

[19:41] Jonah Brooks: And I’ll note it for contract.

[19:44] Liam O'Rourke: Cool. We’ll schedule a 30-min follow up next week. Thanks all.

[19:50] Priya Desai: Thanks.

[19:51] Mark Feld: Thank you.

[19:52] Ava Chen: Thanks.

---

Auto-generated notes (Fireflies)
- Action items captured in meeting: send audit event schema + samples; send export/signing docs; confirm retention requirements; schedule follow-up.
- Keywords detected: audit logs, RBAC, SAML, SCIM, Splunk, retention, autoscaling bounds, predictive scaling.
