Pilot queue-shape snapshot & backpressure review

Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-11-18
- Start: 15:00 PT
- Duration: ~52 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Noah (CSM); Sara (AuroraPay Head of Platform), Diego (SRE), Ellen (ML Eng)

Summary:
- Quick snapshot of pilot steady-state; main focus on queue shape and emergent backpressure at 3k RPS equivalency, looking at continuous batching behaviour and concurrency targets. Agree to run per-variant latency sweeps and validate replay.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: okay uh let's get started, thanks everyone for joining, we wanted to do a... quick snapshot of where the pilot is at after the traffic ramp last week. um Sara, you good to kick off with what you saw on your side?
[00:12] Sara: yeah thanks Maya, so we ramped to roughly 3k rps equivalency using our thin-client replay, mostly short prompts, average length ~80 tokens. we noticed a tail rise in latency around the 95/99, and at times the queue length spikes which then causes a couple request retries from the client.
[00:26] Diego: yeah (interruption) the interesting bit is we start to see backpressure in our service mesh rather than in Redwood's route — requests pile in the ingress, then some get dropped. it could be how we shaped concurrency on our side.
[00:40] Liam: right, we've seen similar patterns; continuous batching is trying to amortize tokens but when concurrency is capped too low you'll get long queueing windows that blow up pctile. couple questions, do you have the KV cache enabled in these runs?
[00:52] Ellen: we tested two toggles: KV cache on and KV off. most of the bulk replay used KV on. toggling it off made the P95 worse by about 18% for the biggest model.
[01:04] Liam: that aligns. another knob is batch max latency vs batch size, we can nudge batch cap from 20ms to 40ms to reduce request batching frequency which sometimes helps tail.
[01:16] Maya: quick note — we've uploaded a snapshot deck to the shared drives, link: drive.redwood/pilot/aft-queue-snapshot (see notes).
[01:24] Sara: cool, we'll pull it after. Diego, do you have the ingress metrics?
[01:28] Diego: yes, I can show a clip, um (pauses) but in short the ingress queue climbs at the same cadence as the spike in Redwood's accept rate; when we hit about 60 concurrent connections per instance the mesh starts to shard requests and latency cascades.
[01:44] Noah: that could be related to your service concurrency shaping; if you can raise the per-instance concurrency and let Redwood handle soft queuing the system might smooth out.
[01:53] Ellen: question on that — we have strict SLA on worker thread counts, can't just blast concurrency up without mem impacts. is there a recommended concurrency target?
[02:02] Liam: for the model family you're running, we'd typically start with per-vCPU concurrency 4-6 for lower-latency variants and 2-3 for larger when KV is enabled. but more important is the total in-flight tokens; if we keep average in-flight under 120k tokens across the pool the P95 tends to behave.
[02:18] Sara: the numbers help, can you put that in the sheet?
[02:21] Liam: yes i'll put a chart, i'll run model-variant sweeps for P50/P95/P99 and include with kv on/off.
[02:28] Diego: one thing we saw — once reply queueing starts the client retries are exacerbating the burst; so we need to coordinate retry backoffs too. our replay script is currently aggressive.
[02:40] Ellen: we can soften the retry policy, add exponential. however we still want to test Redwood burst/fallback behaviour — do you have a fallback policy we can trigger?
[02:49] Maya: yes we do; in pilot config we can route to a cheaper quantized variant automatically when latency exceeds threshold. it's controlled by the routing policy in the pilot config. we can demo that.
[02:58] Sara: did you see any quality regressions when falling back? we need accuracy to remain close for user flows.
[03:04] Liam: in our internal tests quality delta was small for summary tasks, larger for open-ended creative completions. we can add a short eval set from AuroraPay (like 20 prompts) to measure delta.
[03:14] Ellen: we'll put together that eval set, should be representative of billing descriptions and short replies.
[03:21] Noah: action: Ellen to share eval set and test harness link.
[03:25] Diego: another datapoint — when we tried to increase batch max latency it helped throughput but increased median by ~30ms which is okay for most flows but not for auth flows. we need route-level policies.
[03:38] Maya: yes route-level concurrency and batch overrides are supported, you can pin auth route to a low-latency profile. we'll add recommended configs to the deck.
[03:46] Sara: what about KV cache TTL? any sweet spots?
[03:50] Liam: short TTLs help if your prompts vary, but for repeated prefixes a longer TTL gives large wins. for your workload with heavy repeated header patterns, increasing TTL to 2 minutes reduced token generation 7-9%.
[04:04] Ellen: noted. will tune.
[04:07] Maya: okay let's talk concrete next steps — Liam you'll run the latency sweeps and share CSVs, attach batch cap experiments. Ellen will run replay with softened retry and share logs. Maya will send updated pilot pricing including burst capacity and fallback policy options.
[04:22] Sara: timeline — can we get the CSVs and pricing by EOW? means 11/23?
[04:27] Maya: yes we can do 11/20 for pricing, 11/23 for the sweeps.
[04:31] Diego: can we also get an example route config snippet for setting per-route batch windows? that's helpful for our infra team.
[04:37] Liam: i'll add samples to the sheet and the deck.
[04:40] Ellen: one more ask — security quiz: do you have a link for audit logs retention in Private mode? we might need the compliance add-on.
[04:47] Maya: sure i'll drop the security pack link (SOC2 + audit log retention) in the CRM and add contact for security team.
[04:53] Sara: awesome. last thing — can we schedule a focused follow-up after you upload sweeps? maybe 30 minutes next wednesday?
[04:59] Maya: yes let's tentatively put 11/25 14:00 PT. we'll confirm in invite.
[05:05] Noah: cool, thanks everyone.

End recap (auto):
- Run per-variant P50/P95/P99 latency sweeps with KV on/off (Liam)
- Soften replay retries and share logs (Ellen)
- AE to share pilot pricing with burst options and security pack (Maya)
- Add route-level batch/concurrency examples to deck (Liam)
- Schedule follow-up for 2026-11-25 14:00 PT

References & shared artifacts:
- deck: drive.redwood/pilot/aft-queue-snapshot
- results sheet: drive.redwood/pilot/aft-queue-results.csv
- replay script: gitlab.aurorapay/replay/thin-client-v3

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-transcription of acronyms (K V cache -> KV cache), some speaker overlap labeled as interruptions.

Quant Probe Weekly Checkin - latency vs quality

Weekly POC sync focused on INT8/FP8 performance deltas vs. quality. Discussed a small regression on multi-turn prompts, tail latency spikes with batching, and next-step smoke tests on dedicated capacity. Action items assigned for micro-benchmarks, sample prompt set, and a VPC peering test.
Redwood to share updated micro-benchmarks (latency tail and p50/p95) by 2026-01-20
Customer to run small smoke test on dedicated pool next week and report throughput numbers
Schedule on-prem checklist review if infra green by 2026-01-27
Samira Khan - rerun INT8 traces with prefix caching on (due 2026-01-20)
Maya Patel - provide 200 sample prompts that trigger hallucination cases (due 2026-01-18)
Jordan Li - provision VPC peering test environment and share logs (due 2026-01-22)
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-15
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Samira Khan (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SA), Maya Patel (StrataScale ML), Jordan Li (StrataScale Infra), Priya Nair (StrataScale PM)

Auto Summary: quick recap of last week's INT8 run, new FP8 baseline, a couple of regressions on long-form multi-turn, plan to run dedicated smoke test and share updated metrics.

[00:00] Alex (AE): okay hi everyone thanks for joining on the 15th, um, quick roll call and then we'll jump in.
[00:12] Maya (ML Eng): hey loud and clear, Maya here. we got Jordan and Priya on.
[00:16] Jordan (Infra): yep here.
[00:20] Samira (SE): Samira from Redwood, I have the perf sheets up. quick note, some numbers were re-run this morning after the fix for KV cache eviction.
[00:30] Alex: cool, let's do a 2 min recap of results then dig into the regression cases.

[01:05] Samira: so summary first - INT8 run 2026-01-13 gives about 1.9x token throughput vs FP16 baseline at our standard batch, cost down ~44% on token units, p50 latency improved but p95 has a small increase, around +18-22% on long sequences. FP8 baseline from yesterday looks promising for throughput but shows slightly higher variance in the SNR metric we use for completion fidelity.

[02:10] Maya: what's the SNR again? sorry, sometimes the metric name gets swapped in our notes.
[02:14] Diego: it's the signal-to-noise—or our proxy for semantic fidelity—lower means more hallucination, uh we compute it from entailment scores over the prompt set.
[02:24] Maya: ok got it. the issue we saw on multi-turn earlier, is it the same one? responses becoming terse after turn three?

[03:00] Samira: yes that symptom. We traced it to two possible contributors: tokenization side-effects with int8 quant tables and the KV cache mismatch when prefix caching is off. when prefix cache is disabled, the runtime rebuilds keys which seems to amplify rounding.
[03:22] Jordan: does that mean our prefix caching in the prod-like bench was off? because our smoke-setup in our env had caching disabled for correctness checks.
[03:31] Samira: correct — your smoke runs had caching off on purpose, so we need to rerun with cache on to compare apples-to-apples.

[04:00] Priya (Product): quick question on deployment mode — are we still on hosted for the baseline or did Redwood spin up a dedicated pool for these runs?
[04:09] Alex: baseline INT8 and FP8 runs were on hosted but with dedicated-like instance types; we can run the dedicated pool smoke by next week per the plan.

[04:40] Maya: on hallucinations, I uploaded 40 failure examples to the shared drive, but I'll push another 160 that cover multi-turn, low-resource prompts, and the edge-case legalese.

[05:15] Samira: great, that helps. We'll run sensitivity sweeps over quant thresholds—per-layer scale tweaks and calibration windows. We think a per-layer calibration (couple layers) drops hallucination delta by ~0.8-1.2% in our internal tests.

[06:00] Speaker 4 (contractor?): one thing we noticed, the batching policy in your runtime — when it aggregates variable-length requests — p95 jumps. is that configurable at the client level?
[06:12] Diego: yes, we expose batching config via route policy; you can tune max batch size, max latency window, and prefer small-batches-for-latency. For the pilot, we recommend a two-tier policy: small-latency for interactive routes and large-batch for offline.

[06:40] Jordan: can that be per-model variant? our plan is to have an FP8 fallback and INT8 primary, so routing needs to be aware.
[06:49] Samira: yes routing supports tiered variants — we can do model-variant routing by priority and model compatibility. Automatic fallback also possible when capacity low.

[07:20] Maya: any notes on encryption/KMS when we go dedicated or on-prem? we need to confirm our compliance team that keys stay in our HSM.
[07:30] Alex: Redwood supports KMS integrations and HSM-backed keys for Private installs. we'll share the security brief.

[08:05] Priya: will the logs have user-level traces for audit? SOC2 asks for retention details.
[08:12] Diego: yes, we can configure audit logs and retention windows. for the pilot we kept 30 days but enterprise can do longer.

[09:00] Samira: back to the perf deltas — attached link: spreadsheet/quant-probe-jan13.csv (note: link in notes). Important: one anomaly flagged — a subset of prompts with long numeric sequences under INT8 had token-level mistransforms, suspected due to the quant rounding in fast-float path.

[09:42] Maya: numeric sequences… that might impact our reports generator. we'll add 20 more examples focusing on numeric tables.

[10:15] Alex: can you describe the mismatch in more detail Samira? is it repeatable?
[10:20] Samira: somewhat repeatable — in about 2% of these long-numeric prompts the output swapped digits or truncated chunks. We think enabling subword-stability heuristics during detokenization reduces that by half. We'll push a patch to the tokeniser and rerun the INT8 trace.

[11:05] Jordan: side note — our infra wanted to know if the dedicated pool can be pinned to a region and if we can reserve capacity for the pilot window.
[11:14] Alex: yes we can pin region and reserve a small commit for the pilot week; we'll send options and pricing in the follow-up.

[12:00] Diego: also FYI we saw a small tail spike when KV cache misses went above 15% — this was in your smoke env where caching was off. So expectation: with caching on, p95 should normalize close to baseline.

[13:00] Maya: do you have a simple test harness to measure cache hit ratio? our team can run it locally.
[13:08] Samira: yes, we'll share a small python harness and a test script (link: github.com/redwood/mini-bench) with run instructions.

[14:00] Priya: on the quality metric, are we running human evals or only automated entailment checks?
[14:08] Maya: we did a small human eval batch of 100 but that method is expensive, so mainly automated plus a targeted human subset for regression.

[15:00] Samira: recommended next experiments: 1) INT8 with prefix caching on + tokeniser patch, 2) FP8 variant with per-layer calibration windows, 3) dedicated pool smoke test with two routing policies. We'll collect p50/p95, throughput, SNR delta, and hallucination examples.

[15:50] Maya: can you include memory usage deltas as well? our capacity planner needs that.
[15:55] Samira: yes memory and GPU util will be in the spreadsheet.

[16:30] Jordan: for the dedicated smoke, do you need us to open peering or will Redwood use a temporary VPN?
[16:37] Alex: VPC peering is easiest, Jordan. we'll provide CIDR ranges and the config. We'll also do a VPN option if you prefer.

[17:10] Priya: timeline wise — if we get the smoke by 1/20 and we like the deltas, can we plan a short on-prem feasibility review before EOD 1/27?
[17:19] Alex: that sounds doable. we'll tentatively pencil in 1/27 for an infra deep dive.

[18:00] Samira: quick note — competitor mention, Lambda did some public numbers that look close on throughput but they don't have the per-route observability we show. (murmurs)

[18:25] Maya: ok good to know.

[19:10] Diego: wrapping up — I'll enumerate concrete changes we'll run: tokeniser patch, per-layer INT8 calibration, FP8 alpha run, and dedicated smoke with caching on.

[20:00] Alex: let's capture action items — Samira will share updated micro-benchmarks by 1/20, Maya to upload full prompt set by 1/18, Jordan to spin up VPC peering test by 1/22. Also Redwood to share lane-level routing policy examples.

[20:45] Priya: any blockers from Redwood side we should be aware of?
[20:50] Samira: none immediate; we are waiting for your sample prompts and your green on peering.

[21:30] Maya: one last thing — can you include a short note on fallback behaviour if INT8 triggers a quality alert in prod? we'd like auto-fallback to FP8 for critical routes.
[21:45] Alex: yes that's standard — we can configure automatic variant fallback with alerts. we'll include a config snippet.

[22:10] Alex: great thanks everyone, we'll follow-up in email and share links to the updated sheets and harness. next sync same time next week unless we meet earlier for the infra deep dive.

Meeting end: 16:52 UTC

Links mentioned: spreadsheet: /quant-probe-jan13.csv; harness: github.com/redwood/mini-bench; security brief: redwood.com/security/brief (placeholder)

Transcript notes: occasional mis-transcriptions present, speaker overlap at times noted as 'Speaker 4'.

Sprint 5 pilot tuning and decision readout - Ventra Labs

Sprint 5 readout covering benchmark delta vs their incumbent: p95 latency improvements and throughput scaling. Discussed dedicated capacity ask, security requirements (SOC2, KMS, VPC), and next steps to finalize pilot->contract decision. Action items assigned for pricing, docs, and final 24h load run.
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-19
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Marcus Li (Redwood AE), Samantha Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Menon (Ventra CTO), Ethan Shaw (Ventra Lead ML), Lena Ortiz (Ventra Cloud)

[00:00] Marcus: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Marcus from Redwood here, and Samantha our SE is with me. Quick check, is this still a good time for the Ventra team?
[00:08] Priya: Yes, we are good. We've got about 45 minutes. Want to keep it focused on the tuning readout and next steps.
[00:14] Marcus: Perfect. I'll say the agenda is: short results summary, deep dive on a couple of perf points (latency p95, throughput sustain), security checklist, then a runbook and decision timeline. Samantha, do you want to kick us off with the numbers?
[00:25] Samantha: Yeah, sure. So quick reminder of the test harness — this was the 512-token prompt mix you gave us, the realtime small-batch workload matching your QA profile. We ran three 30-minute steady-state runs, two burst runs, and one 24-hour ramp.
[00:38] Ethan: quick note — the 24-hour ramp had the synthetic user patterns from Monday's logs, which include the longer context items.
[00:46] Samantha: Right. OK, high-level: for the primary model variant you provided (vt-large-quant), our p95 latency observed was ~180 ms at 512 tokens (seq=512) under steady state. The incumbent that you sent benchmarks for was averaging p95 ~420 ms on the same workload. Throughput wise, our cluster sustained ~240 req/s with 99% success and tail no more than 3% retry, whereas incumbent sustained around 110-130 req/s before queuing effects.
[01:15] Priya: Wait, 180ms p95, that's pretty big improvement. Is that with prefix caching enabled? I thought you said the KV cache helps a lot for our workload.
[01:24] Samantha: Yes, we had prefix/KV cache on for repeated conversation flows — that's responsible for a chunk of delta on short-prompt cases. For the longer contexts the improvement is still present - we saw about 2x reduction in per-token compute due to optimized kernels and 8-bit friendly quant paths.
[01:38] Lena: Could you clarify the test infra? Was this hosted or dedicated nodes? Network distance matters for our region.
[01:45] Samantha: Good question. These runs were on Redwood Dedicated pre-prod nodes in us-east-1, same region you've been testing in. We provisioned a 4-GPU pool with the autoscaler disabled to get deterministic numbers.
[01:55] Ethan: there's a small transcription glitch in the last deck notes but — were the GPU types A100s or H100s? That matters for our cost model.
[02:04] Marcus: They were H100s with cut kernels for int8 ops — but it's worth noting we also ran a spot of A100s to compare. H100 had better p95 and higher throughput for these sequence lengths, so the headline numbers we shared come from H100 runs.
[02:18] Priya: Good. On cost, how much better is serving cost per 1M tokens? I know exact numbers change but a rough delta vs incumbent helps the finance team.
[02:27] Marcus: Ballpark: with our batching and KV savings for this workload, per-token CPU/GPU charge is about 25-35% lower than the incumbent in your baseline, before factoring reserved capacity discounts. With a dedicated-month commit the delta widens to ~40-50% depending on quant profile. We'll put exacts in the follow-up quote.
[02:42] Lena: On the dedicated slots ask — Priya mentioned wanting a hard SLA for latency. Do you have SLO examples you can commit in a pilot contract?
[02:51] Samantha: For pilot we generally offer best-effort latency targets; for Dedicated with a monthly commit we can offer an SLA with p99 or p95 targets and credits. For this workload we can propose p95 < 220 ms as a starting SLA for the dedicated configuration used in the runs. Exact terms in commercial doc.
[03:06] Ethan: We hit some jitter spikes in the ramp test at around hour 9 — any idea why? There were garbage collection style pauses in logs.
[03:14] Samantha: I pulled the trace — looks like a combination of kernel warmup during an autoscaler event and one of the nodes reloading a quantized weight shard. We added a pre-warm in the configured runbook to mitigate that; with pre-warm the spikes dropped to noise. We'll include the trace link in the follow-up.
[03:28] Priya: ok, safety/security: our legal team needs SOC2 Type II, KMS/HSM integration, and audit logs for inference requests. Also data residency — we need logs to stay in the US. Can you satisfy those?
[03:41] Marcus: Yes — Redwood has SOC2 Type II and we can provide the report. KMS integrations are supported (both AWS KMS and customer-managed HSMs for the Private option). Audit logs and retention settings are configurable; for the Dedicated offering logs can be routed to your Kinesis/CloudWatch or exported to your S3 in-region. We'll share the SOC2 report and a short KMS integration note.
[03:58] Lena: For VPC peering and network policy, what's the typical lead time to get Private control plane + VPC peering in place? We are on a compliance window tight schedule.
[04:07] Marcus: For Private (VPC) deployments the typical setup is 2-3 weeks once we have the network info and security contacts. If you want on-prem air-gapped it's longer. For Dedicated with VPC peering we can usually do initial peering in 5-7 business days assuming there's no network ACL surprises.
[04:21] Priya: Great. On the incumbent comparison, we ran a few end-to-end user flows and got some parity on quality — any risk of output drift after quantization/latency tuning?
[04:31] Samantha: We did a suite of eval prompts (your golden set) after quantization and routing changes. The measured semantic similarity and task accuracy stayed within your tolerance (we saw a mean relative delta of ~0.8% on intent accuracy). We can lock in an eval set as part of the QA gate for rollout.
[04:45] Ethan: we want to try a final 24-hour full traffic replay with your service in dedicated mode before sign-off. Can you run that?
[04:51] Marcus: Yes — we can schedule a 24-hour run next week. We'll need your replay artifacts and a target window. We recommend running the 24-hour in the same region and with the dedicated pool configuration to replicate production.
[04:59] Priya: timeline-wise, our procurement wants a commercial term by end of next week. Is that realistic?
[05:05] Marcus: We can get a dedicated capacity quote and a pilot-to-contract schedule over by Thursday if you share volumes and commit targets by Tuesday.
[05:12] Priya: We'll aim for that.
[05:15] Samantha: Quick technical aside — routing: we propose a fallback to a smaller but cheaper model variant when load exceeds threshold. That gave you minimal user impact in tests. The playbook for fallbacks is in the doc I attached earlier.
[05:27] Ethan: In the fallback runs, what's the observed quality delta, and do you have automatic A/B rollback if quality drifts?
[05:33] Samantha: Fallback delta on your eval set was small — usually under 2% on the tasks that matter. We support automatic rollback policies if the monitoring detects a drop in quality tied to prompt set metrics. We'll hook into your observability for those alerts.
[05:45] Lena: And how granular is RBAC for logs and token-level auditing? We need separate teams to see different sets of logs.
[05:51] Marcus: RBAC is role-based and can integrate with SSO/SAML; token-level trace can be projected only to specific auditors. We can map to least privilege.
[05:58] Priya: Alright let's be concrete on actions.

[06:00] Marcus: I'll recap: Redwood to send dedicated capacity quote and per-token economics, include SLA language draft, and attach SOC2 and KMS notes. We'll also schedule the 24-hour final load run for next week pending artifacts from Ventra. Samantha will share the perf traces and routing playbook with annotations on the jitter fix. Ventra will provide the replay artifacts, target window, and the list of eval prompts for gating.
[06:21] Priya: That works. Ethan will own the replay artifacts. Lena will coordinate network windows and security contacts. We aim to decide by end of next week.
[06:30] Marcus: Any other blockers?
[06:33] Ethan: Just one more thing — can you add an estimated ramp cost for monthly commit, like 6-month vs 12-month? Finance wants that sensitivity.
[06:40] Marcus: Yes, we'll include 6/12 month commit pricing and show unit economics at 0.5x, 1x, and 2x of baseline traffic.
[06:47] Priya: Okay thanks all.

[06:50] Speaker 2: [inaudible - brief cross talk]
[06:53] Samantha: I'll also attach a quick runbook for the pre-warm step that eliminated the hour-9 spike and a small note on kernel warmup behavior.
[06:59] Marcus: Great. Let's do a quick restate of next steps and owners.

[07:03] Marcus: Action items — I'll follow with a formal quote and SLA terms by 2026-05-22. Samantha will share the traces and the playbook today. Ethan will upload replay artifacts by 2026-05-21. Lena will confirm a 2-hour VPC peering window and security contact by 2026-05-21. Priya will send a short vendor checklist from legal so we can align contract items.
[07:28] Priya: Sounds good. Any final questions?
[07:32] Lena: None from infra.
[07:34] Ethan: All good.
[07:36] Marcus: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the doc bundle and propose the 24-hour window. Decision meeting tentatively 2026-05-26 at 14:00 UTC.
[07:44] Priya: We'll take that. Thanks everyone.
[07:46] Marcus: Bye all.

End of transcript.

Notes: transcript contains occasional automated speaker mislabels and a couple of inaudible markers. Links mentioned during the call: perf-traces (link), SOC2-report (link), playbook-prewarm (link), dedicated-quote-draft (link).
Marcus - send dedicated capacity quote, per-token economics, and SLA draft by 2026-05-22
Samantha - share perf traces, routing playbook, and pre-warm runbook today (2026-05-19)
Ethan - upload replay artifacts and baseline logs by 2026-05-21
Lena - confirm VPC peering window and security contact by 2026-05-21
Priya - provide vendor checklist from legal by 2026-05-21
Marcus - schedule final decision meeting 2026-05-26 14:00 UTC
Marcus: send detailed pricing and dedicated capacity quote by 2026-05-22
Samantha: share SOC2 report excerpt, KMS integration notes, and perf traces by 2026-05-19
Ethan: provide 3 representative inference workloads and baseline logs by 2026-05-21
Lena: confirm VPC peering window and supply network contacts by 2026-05-21
Priya: send legal vendor checklist for contract alignment by 2026-05-21

ReefPoint Throughput & Latency Assessment

Intro + workload profile. Customer wants p95 < 200ms for streaming chat, 1000 concurrent users, fallback to cheaper quantized model under heavy burst. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC) tradeoffs and benchmarking plan.
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-27
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Jared (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Lina (ReefPoint CTO), Marcus (Head ML Infra), Sasha (SRE), Tomas (Data Eng)

[00:00] Jared: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick intro — Im Jared, AE at Redwood, and Priya our senior SE is here to dig into your latency and throughput goals. Lina, want to kick us off with the big picture?

[00:18] Lina: Sure. Quick context: ReefPoint is building a clinician-facing chat assistant, mostly server-side streaming to UI. Goal is p95 latency that feels instant — rough target is under 200ms for streaming token delivery in typical sessions. We also need to support sustained spikes during morning rounds, estimate up to 1,000 concurrent sessions with avg 20 tokens/sec each during peak bursts.

[00:44] Priya: Thanks. Couple clarifying q's: when you say streaming p95 <200ms is that end-to-end from request to first token, or per-token increment? Also how big are your typical prompts and completions?

[01:03] Lina: Good point. We mean first-byte latency for streaming (first token) should be under 200ms p95, and subsequent token churn ideally low-latency as well. Average prompt length: 120 tokens, expected completion ~60 tokens on average, but some sessions hit 400-600 tokens if a clinician is doing long notes.

[01:29] Marcus: I also want to call out infra constraints. We're keen to avoid data egress if possible — prefer VPC/private deployment. We have on-prem KMS via HashiVault and strict firewall rules; any hosted solution needs to support private peering or a private deployment. Cost is a factor — we looked at Megalith and QuickServe but their hosted pricing blew past our forecasts.

[02:00] Jared: Understood. We can run hosted, dedicated reserved capacity, or private (VPC/on-prem). For your p95 targets and concurrency, Dedicated or Private typically gives the most predictable tail latency. Hosted can work if we provision the right instance shapes and use pinning. For streaming, small batch sizes are important to keep first-token latency low.

[02:23] Priya: A few engineering notes — streaming latency is dominated by model kv-cache warmup and kernel scheduling at small batch sizes. For p95 under 200ms we'll look at: model variant (quantized vs fp16), continuous batching window, and whether we can use prefix caching for repeated prompts. Do you have a high-percentile prompt reuse pattern?

[02:47] Tomás: Some reuse, yes. About 15% of sessions reuse templates. Also important: our traffic pattern is spiky — long tails during morning rounds and more sparse evenings. We can supply 72h logs.

[03:05] Sasha: From SRE perspective, we need graceful degradation. If we hit capacity we want an automatic fallback to a smaller quantized model with slightly lower quality rather than throttling users. Also audit logs and per-request tracing is non-negotiable.

[03:22] Priya: Makes sense. Redwood has a fallback routing policy — we can route to a cheaper quantized variant or to a queue with fast 429/retry semantics. And we have token-level audit logging and tracing hooks for integrations. We'll share the docs.

[03:40] Marcus: On the KMS side, can we bring our HashiVault keys? We need envelope encryption with customer-managed keys.

[03:48] Jared: Yes, for private deployments you can bring your own keys (BYOK) and we support HSM-backed flows. Hosted requires managed keys but we support tenant-level customer KMS integrations for Dedicated. We'll include the KMS matrix in the security brief.

[04:06] Lina: For benchmarking we care about both steady-state throughput and burst p95. Can you propose a test harness? We want a token/sec baseline and p95 per-token latency at multiple concurrencies — 100, 500, 1k, and 2k if possible.

[04:25] Priya: We'll share an ops-benchmark.csv and a test harness we usually use (Griffin harness) — it's a small runner that simulates streaming clients and measures first-byte and per-token latency. Plan: run the harness against a hosted endpoint with synthetic prompts, then repeat on Dedicated and a Private sandbox if you want. We'll collect p50/p95/p99 and tail token throughput.

[04:52] Tomas: How do you handle KV cache across requests? We're worried about cold starts hurting p95 when users jump into long sessions.

[05:00] Priya: The runtime supports prefix/KV caching on a per-session basis; persistent session caches can be pinned to a warm instance to avoid cold starts for frequent users. For less frequent sessions we rely on fast kernel paths — quantized execution can be faster per token in some model variants but sometimes increases first-token latency due to dequantization steps. So there's a tradeoff.

[05:28] Marcus: Cost question: what's the unit cost difference between hosted and dedicated for a workload like ours? Ballpark is fine.

[05:34] Jared: Ballpark — hosted pay-as-you-go will be higher per-token in heavy steady-state compared to Dedicated reserved pools. With Dedicated you commit to GPUs and get better unit economics, and Private is similar but adds infra & support fees. We'll put together a cost estimate after we see your traffic sample.

[05:50] Sasha: Are there known cases where streaming p95 <200ms doesn't hold despite using Dedicated? What usually breaks?

[05:58] Priya: Common failure modes: very long sequences that cause KV cache pressure, sudden spikes that overwhelm a single instance group before autoscaling kicks in, and suboptimal batching windows that aggregate too many requests. We mitigate with autoscale policies, pre-warming, and smaller batching windows for low-latency routes. We can configure canary flows so critical traffic goes to pinned capacity.

[06:22] Lina: For our compliance team, do you have SOC2 + ISO docs? Also need an audit log format example.

[06:30] Jared: Yes, we'll attach SOC2 and an example audit log export. We can also show log entries with request ids and token counts.

[06:38] Tomás: One last technical: do you support model quantization mixes? Like running 8-bit for streaming but 4-bit for background batch reranking?

[06:46] Priya: Yes, the runtime supports multiple quantization profiles and we can route requests based on policy (latency-sensitive vs cost-sensitive). Background reranking can use heavier quantization or CPU-backed evaluation depending on the pipeline.

[07:00] Jared: Let's outline the benchmark plan so everyone's aligned. Step 1: Customer sends 72h traffic and prompt set. Step 2: Redwood runs a hosted sim to get a baseline. Step 3: If baseline shows deficits, we spin up Dedicated pool sized for your 1k concurrency and run comparison. Step 4: If private is required, we'll mirror the Dedicated config into your VPC and run the same sims.

[07:28] Marcus: Sounds good. For the Dedicated sizing, do you have a formula or rule-of-thumb we can use before the sim?

[07:35] Priya: Rule-of-thumb: estimate tokens/sec at peak, then map to model tokens/sec capability per GPU for your chosen model. Example: a ada-like open model might do X tokens/sec on a T4, but modern Llama variants on A100 do far better. We'll provide a matrix with tokens/sec per GPU for common models. That'll let you rough out GPU counts.

[07:58] Lina: Can you also include streaming p95 numbers per model in that matrix? We need to see first-byte p95 at 1k concurrency.

[08:07] Priya: We'll include first-byte p95 and per-token throughput measured under the harness. Important caveat: p95 scales with sequence length distribution. We'll run multiple distributions.

[08:22] Jared: Operational questions: do you want dedicated ingress endpoints per region for lower latency to clinicians?

[08:29] Sasha: Yes, multi-region closer to our primary hospitals would help. We have priority regions in West-US and EU-West. Private deployment must support cross-region peering or we do separate private pods.

[08:45] Priya: Cross-region can be done with smart routing and model variants. We can pin capacity in both regions and sync model artifacts; failover works with automatic fallback if one region is overloaded.

[09:01] Tomás: About the benchmark artifacts — how will results be shared? Simple csv + graphs? We prefer a short slide with p95/p50/p99 and a raw csv.

[09:10] Jared: We'll share csv plus a one-pager and a short recording of the run. We'll also push the raw harness logs.

[09:17] Lina: Ok timeline — we want results before our procurement review on Sept 14. Is that feasible?

[09:23] Jared: Yes: collect logs by Sept 3, run hosted baseline the week of Sept 6, and Dedicated run the week of Sept 13. That gives you numbers before the 14th. We'll confirm scheduling offline.

[09:35] Brief pauses and some cross-talk about calendar slots...

[10:02] Priya: Quick technical nit — when we measure token/sec please ensure we capture p95 of the inter-token arrival times for streaming clients; that often shows microbursts.

[10:15] Marcus: Will the benchmarking also measure cold-start tail latency after a scale-to-zero event? We need to understand cold path in off-hours.

[10:22] Priya: Yes we'll include cold-start tests; we'll simulate a cold pool with reclaimed KV cache and measure full session p95. We'll annotate which numbers are warm vs cold.

[10:36] Tomás: Any limitations on prompt types? We have some structured JSON prompts and also free-text notes.

[10:43] Priya: That's fine. We'll run both structured and free-text distributions. If you can highlight the few heavy prompts that are 400-600 tokens that will help tune caching.

[10:58] Sasha: For security review — we'll need an architecture diagram showing where logs are stored and how PII is redacted.

[11:06] Jared: We'll include a redaction example and where logs live for each deployment mode.

[11:14] Lina: Great. Any other blockers?

[11:18] Marcus: None from infra side besides confirming KMS and peering but that's in the action items.

[11:24] Jared: Ok final recap: Redwood to share benchmark harness and ops-benchmark template, security + SOC2 + KMS doc, and a rough tokens/sec per-GPU matrix. Customer to share logs and prompt sets by Sept 3. Priya will schedule benchmark runs.

[11:41] Meeting ends with thanks and agreement to sync on calendar invites.

Notes: Transcript has minor ASR errors — some proper nouns normalized. References: shared: ops-benchmark.csv, shared: redwood-soc2-brief.pdf

document.content:
Verdance Systems — LLM portout strategy and eval checklist

Meeting Header
Date: 2026-01-27
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 mins
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Verdance - Head of ML), Jonas Reed (Verdance - Platform), Sara Liu (Verdance - Security)

Summary:
Short kick-off to understand Verdance's plan to move off OpenAI for core product generation and evaluate options (Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private). They run a mix of API and self-hosted vLLM for cost reasons. Main concerns: parity on outputs, latency, tokenization differences, KMS, and an enterprise procurement timeline.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, this is Priya our solutions engineer. How are you Maya, Jonas, Sara?
[00:10] Maya: Doing good, thanks. We're excited but also, you know, cautious. We've been running production on OpenAI for the last 9 months and—there's a lot to untangle.
[00:20] Priya: Totally, and congrats on scaling. What are the immediate pain points? Cost, latency, control?
[00:30] Jonas: Cost and the black box feeling. We run a bunch of batch jobs with vllm on prem and some latency-critical endpoints on OpenAI. The big ask is: can Redwood mirror our current latency SLOs and output quality, and what breaks when we change tokenizers or quantize?
[00:45] Alex: Good, so two parallel threads: functional parity (quality/regression) and infra fit (latency & ops). On parity—what model families are you using? Are you on GPT-4 style APIs or Claude-like?
[00:58] Maya: We're primarily on OpenAI GPT-4o for generation and using small Claude-2 for some assistant tasks. Also running Llama-2-13b quantized on vLLM for internal tools.
[01:12] Priya: Ok so a mix. When you say 'run Llama-2-13b on vLLM', is that on-prem GPU clusters? And what's your tokenizer mismatch risk—are you doing prompt engineering that relies on exact token offsets?
[01:27] Jonas: Yes, on-prem clusters, Kubernetes. Token offsets matter for our snippet extraction; we've had subtle shifts moving between TGI and vllm, like off-by-one token splits, which causes some downstream matching to flake.
[01:42] Sara: For security, we need SSO (SAML), KMS integration, SOC2 evidence, and audit logs. Also data residency for EU customers—we need EU-only processing for certain tenants.
[01:55] Alex: All standard asks. Redwood Private does customer-managed VPC and on-prem connectors, KMS/HSM integrations, and we can document SOC2 artifacts. For EU residency, we can pin region routing and restrict models to region-specific pools.
[02:10] Maya: From a parity standpoint, we ran a small eval where Redwood's hosted model produced more repetition on long-form completion compared to OpenAI, any recs?
[02:20] Priya: We usually see that differences come from decoding defaults and tokenizer differences. We can match temps/top_p and also provide model-specific sampling profiles. Also, Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles and batching configs without regressing quality—this is where an eval set helps.
[02:36] Jonas: Can you run an A/B with our eval set? We want to see not just log-prob metrics but downstream metrics (like entity extraction F1) and edge-case prompts.
[02:46] Alex: Absolutely. Typical PoC: you provide 10-50 representative prompts and expected outputs, we run parity sweeps across hosted/dedicated/private variants and share a regression report. We can also run a throughput test on your sample traffic.
[03:00] Sara: On encryption, do you have in-transit and at-rest covered? And keys—can we bring our own keys?
[03:08] Priya: TLS for transit, AES-256 for rest, and yes BYOK through KMS/HSM integrations. For Redwood Private we support customer keys, and for Dedicated we have optional KMS link ups.
[03:20] Maya: Procurement-wise, timeline is tight—finance wants a vendor with an enterprise contract by end of Q1. We'll need pricing and compliance docs.
[03:32] Alex: We'll send a two-path pricing: hosted per-token with committed discounts and a dedicated reserved capacity quote with monthly commits. Also include private licensing terms.

-- TIMESTAMPED DISCUSSION (more verbatim, with transcription artifacts) --
[03:45] Jonas: One weird thing we saw was vllm mem growth after a long prefix cache, is that something Redwood handles with automatic KV pruning?
[03:55] Priya: Yes, we have KV cache eviction policies and continuous batching that trims KV when we hit thresholds. Sometimes it's tuned per workload—like very long-context summarization needs a different policy.
[04:10] Jonas: Hmm okay. When you say 'continuous batching', do you mean requests are batched cross-tenant? We can't have cross-tenant mixing.
[04:18] Priya: No, not mixing. Batching is tenant-isolated. The runtime opportunistically aggregates within the same customer pool to improve GPU utilization.
[04:30] Maya: For evaluation, how do you handle deterministic vs non-deterministic outputs? We need repeatability for tests.
[04:38] Priya: We can run deterministic sampling (fixed seeds / greedy) for eval parity. For production, you can choose stochastic decoding. Our eval harness preserves randomness controls.
[04:48] Sara: Logs: can we get request-level audit logs for every generation including input, model version, and token counts? We require 12 months retention for certain customers.
[04:58] Alex: Yes, we have configurable retention. For Private you can set retention policies and export logs to your SIEM. For hosted, we provide logs with retention up to X days by default and extended retention as an add-on.
[05:12] Maya: What about model pinning during rollouts? We want to canary a new quantized variant in dedicated before flipping prod.
[05:22] Priya: Rollouts are supported: canary, A/B, automatic fallbacks. You can pin model versions at route-level. We also have automated regression alerts tied to your eval sets.

[05:40] Jonas: Tokenization mismatch—if we move from OpenAI to a Redwood-curated LLM, how do you help map tokens? We have a lot of prompt templates.
[05:50] Priya: We provide tokenizer diff reports and a migration guide per model pair. In many cases it's whitespace splitting differences; we can suggest prompt rewrites and sampling configs.
[06:05] Maya: Costs—what's the delta going from OpenAI usage at scale to Redwood Hosted? We need a TCO with dedicated reserved capacity scenarios.
[06:15] Alex: We'll build a TCO doc. Short answer: hosted is competitive, but for sustained high throughput dedicated reduces per-token cost via reserved GPU amortization.

[06:30] Sara: Any compliance red flags? If we need FedRAMP down the road, is Redwood on that path?
[06:38] Alex: We're SOC2 and have enterprise controls; FedRAMP is a bigger lift—it's not on our immediate roadmap but we can discuss third-party hosting options and dedicated on-prem splits for that compliance.
[06:52] Jonas: For the PoC benchmarking—can you run vllm/TGI parity? We want to see if TGI fast-chat style optimizations map over.
[07:00] Priya: We can. We'll include runs on both vLLM and TGI-style runtime variants. Small note: names sometimes get mis-typed in tools—vllm vs v-L-L-M—our docs cover that.
[07:12] Maya: On the product side, if we need to call external tools or function-calling, does Redwood support structured output and tool calling?
[07:20] Priya: Yes, streaming + function calling + structured outputs supported—payloads include model-confidence and token usage headers.
[07:32] Sara: Any SLA for latency? We need a P50/P95 target, especially for synchronous endpoints.
[07:40] Alex: For hosted we publish latency profiles per model; for Dedicated we can guarantee P95 under the reserved capacity contract and include SLOs in the SLA.

[07:55] Maya: Ok, what's the usual PoC length? We were thinking 2-4 weeks.
[08:02] Alex: Typical is 2-6 weeks depending on breadth. For you, with eval parity and perf tests, 3 weeks seems feasible—week 1 onboarding and dataset ingest, week 2 parity runs, week 3 tuning & final report.
[08:18] Jonas: Are there any known gotchas moving prompts that rely on stop-token heuristics?
[08:24] Priya: Stop token behavior can vary by runtime; we'll run stop-token normalization in the harness.
[08:32] Maya: Okay great. One more question—billing granularity. If we burst beyond reserved capacity, how is that handled?
[08:40] Alex: There's burst capacity options and overage billing; we'll include that in the quote. Dedicated pools have burst to shared capacity subject to policy.

[08:52] Sara: Also need to know about access controls—RBAC, SSO, and audit trail for model deploys.
[08:58] Priya: RBAC is route and project scoped; we integrate with SAML SSO and can log deploy events.

Recap / Next Steps:
[09:10] Alex: Recap: Verdance will share a set of 10 eval prompts + expected outcomes and sample traffic profile. Redwood will send: pricing (hosted + dedicated + private), compatibility checklist, and a PoC plan with timelines. Priya will prepare vLLM/TGI parity notes and a sample runbook.
[09:30] Maya: We'll try to get the prompts and traffic slice by Monday.
[09:36] Jonas: Procurement is target end of Q1 so we'll need to move fast.

Action Items:
- Alex: Send pricing + reserved capacity options and compliance docs by 2026-02-02
- Priya: vLLM/TGI parity notes, tokenizer diff guide, and PoC runbook by 2026-02-05
- Maya: Provide evaluation prompts (10-20) and sample traffic profile by 2026-02-01

Artifacts referenced:
- Redwood Compatibility Checklist (link shared in chat)
- PoC template and benchmark spreadsheet (will be shared)

End of transcript

Tenant access model and quota strategy discussion - Cythera Systems

Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-03-26
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Tomás (Redwood SE), Aisha (Cythera VP Platform), Ravi (SRE), Lena (Security), Oliver (Dev)

Auto Summary: Quick demo of org/project key approaches, discussion of quota models for multi-tenant traffic, RBAC and billing segmentation options, and an initial POC plan for Dedicated capacity. Security questions around KMS / audit trails, and a tentative next step to run a POC next week.

Topics covered: tenant access models, rate limiting patterns (burst vs sustained), fairshare vs capacity lanes, project key vs org key tradeoffs, billing segmentation, KV/prefix cache impacts on cost, SSO/KMS and audit requirements, POC scope and metrics.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Maya, AE on the account, and Tomás is our SE who will walk through the console and the quota model.
[00:12] Aisha (Cythera): Hi, thanks. We have a short-ish agenda: we want to understand how Redwood would let us map our internal tenants (teams + external customers) to keys and quotas, and how billing and access controls work.
[00:22] Tomás (Redwood): Great, we'll do a short demo of the Console and then talk through patterns. One note — terminology can be a bit fuzzy, so when we say "org key" we mean a top-level key that can issue project keys and act as a billing anchor; "project key" is scoped narrower and useful for customers or services.
[00:38] Ravi (Cythera): Quick Q — we currently have a hybrid model: most traffic goes through our internal gateway to a k8s-hosted model, but we're evaluating dedicated capacity for steady inference (and hosted API for dev). Our main constraints are burst protection, cost predictability, and separation of logs for compliance.
[00:55] Maya (Redwood): Totally. We'll show both routing and quota controls so you can keep dev traffic on hosted and route production to Dedicated.
[01:05] Tomás (Redwood): Jumping into the Console — you can set rate limits at the org level, or create project-level quotas. People often combine: org-level soft quotas for overall spend, and project keys for per-tenant concurrency and burst windows.
[01:24] Oliver (Cythera): If we create a project key per customer, how do we handle per-customer billing? We need clear invoice lines.
[01:33] Tomás (Redwood): Two patterns: one is to have the org key be the billing entity and use project keys tagged with metadata for invoice grouping. The Console exposes cost breakdowns by key tag, so you can export csv for billing. The other is multi-org setup if customers must be totally siloed (different contracts).
[01:50] Lena (Cythera): About audit logs — we need immutable logs with user identity for every request. Does Redwood surface request-level logs in the private deployment? And is that compatible with our KMS/HSM for key wrapping?
[02:05] Tomás (Redwood): In Private and Dedicated, you get request traces and can ship logs to your SIEM. For KMS, we support customer-managed keys for secrets — wrapping provider depends on the deployment (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or HSM integrations). Audit trail tie-in is supported; we'll share the SOC2 artifacts.
[02:22] Aisha (Cythera): Good. On quota behaviour — we have big spikes from some partners that, if not limited, blow out our bill. What's Redwood's approach to backpressure?
[02:33] Tomás (Redwood): We use token/leaky-bucket style counters per key with configurable burst window and sustained rate. There are also capacity lanes — you can reserve Dedicated capacity for VIP tenants so they get guaranteed throughput, and everything else is behind fairshare. Fallback policies let you route to lower-cost quantized variants if Dedicated is saturated.
[02:52] Ravi (Cythera): How deterministic is quota enforcement under high concurrency? We can't have soft enforcement that lets 10x bursts through for a minute.
[03:00] Tomás (Redwood): Enforcement is at the routing layer next to the runtime, so it's low-latency and deterministic — we try to avoid leaky implementations where bursts slip by. You can set hard concurrency caps and burst capacity separately.
[03:14] Maya (Redwood): I'll add that the Console shows a simulated policy impact — you can run a "what-if" on a traffic trace and see dropped tokens, estimated cost, and latency tail changes. That tool helped a customer rework their burst windows.
[03:27] Aisha (Cythera): Nice. Can we see an example policy?
[03:31] Tomás (Redwood): Sure — demo time. (screen-share noises) Here is an org policy: default 'sustained' 10 rps per project, burst 100 tokens with a 30s decay. For a VIP tag we pin a Dedicated lane with reserved 200 rps. You can also create sticky routing rules so requests from certain IP ranges or header tokens always hit the VIP lane.
[03:58] Oliver (Cythera): That sticky routing — does it depend on a cookie or header? We have mobile clients that can't hold long-lived cookies.
[04:06] Tomás (Redwood): We use header-based project keys or hashed device ids as sticky keys. For mobile, we recommend short-lived project keys minted by your auth service.
[04:16] Ravi (Cythera): What's the cost delta if we pin 2 GPUs for VIP lane vs letting requests be elastic?
[04:24] Maya (Redwood): Depends on utilization pattern. If VIPs are heavy and steady, reserved Dedicated is often cheaper per token because batching and KV cache improve throughput. If it's spiky and low utilization, hosted with throttles may be better. We'll include a modeled cost calc with your traffic profile.
[04:40] Lena (Cythera): On encryption, we need per-tenant data separation and encryption-in-transit+at-rest. Also an option to disable telemetry export to 3rd party logs.
[04:52] Tomás (Redwood): Private deployment supports customer-controlled network boundaries and controls for log egress. You can restrict what telemetry leaves and we can push only aggregated metrics if required.
[05:03] Aisha (Cythera): Ok, quick clarifying question — for internal teams we want lax quotas; for external partners we want hard caps and billing per-request. How to make the policy model flexible?
[05:14] Tomás (Redwood): You can build hierarchical policies: org defaults, project overrides, and route-level rules. Also, tags allow cost centers to be attached so billing is automatic. We also support quotas tied to usage windows (daily/monthly) if you need invoiceable caps.
[05:29] Ravi (Cythera): What about key sprawl — we fear many project keys floating around. Is there tooling to rotate, revoke, and auto-expire keys?
[05:36] Tomás (Redwood): Yes, the Console has a key lifecycle UI: rotate, revoke, set TTLs, and audit key usage. You can also mint ephemeral keys via API if you prefer ephemeral auth.
[05:47] Oliver (Cythera): How does the KV/prefix cache interact with multi-tenant fairness? If a tenant hits cache warm for long sessions, do they hog GPU memory?
[05:58] Tomás (Redwood): Good point. Our runtime isolates KV cache per model instance and can set per-tenant cache quotas. We also have eviction strategies that free low-recently-used keys. In Dedicated pools you can pin cache sizes per lane.
[06:14] Aisha (Cythera): Can you walk through a simple POC plan where we push our typical 5-min burst patterns?
[06:20] Maya (Redwood): Sure. Proposed POC: 7 days, dedicated staging pool mirrored to your region, ingest your traffic trace, run with two policy sets (org-pinned VIPs vs project-key-per-customer), measure tail latency (95/99), cost per token, and cache hit rate. We then iterate.
[06:38] Ravi (Cythera): For the traffic trace ingestion, does Redwood need raw requests or synthetic replay?
[06:44] Tomás (Redwood): We can replay synthetic traces derived from your telemetry. If you can provide anonymized logs with headers + token counts and timestamps, that's enough. We also offer a small client for live traffic shadowing.
[06:55] Lena (Cythera): On the security questionnaire — does Redwood support SAML/SSO for the Console? And can we enforce RBAC so only allowed users can create org keys?
[07:07] Tomás (Redwood): Yes SAML/SSO + SCIM provisioning are available. RBAC is granular: you can limit key creation, quota editing, and visibility. We'll send the entitlement matrix.
[07:18] Aisha (Cythera): Can we do per-tenant data retention controls? For example some customers require shorter retention of prompts/logs.
[07:25] Tomás (Redwood): You can set retention policies by tag or project, or opt out of storing prompts entirely for certain keys. In Private, that's enforced on your side too.
[07:34] Maya (Redwood): Quick aside — one pattern we recommend: use org key to manage billing and master config, issue project keys per external customer with TTL and a tag for billing. Internal services can be under a separate project namespace with higher burst windows.
[07:50] Ravi (Cythera): If we do that, is there a chance project keys get used in ways to bypass org-level throttles?
[07:57] Tomás (Redwood): Policies are evaluated in order: org hard caps apply first, then project overrides can relax but not exceed hard org limits unless you explicitly allow it. We can also set a guardrail that enforces cost thresholds.
[08:12] Oliver (Cythera): Any gotchas with SDKs and token handling for mobile apps?
[08:17] Tomás (Redwood): Keep tokens short-lived, use your auth service to mint ephemeral tokens, and use header-based identification rather than embedding keys in app bundles.
[08:26] Aisha (Cythera): Let's talk about billing visibility — can we get per-route and per-model cost dashboards to attribute costs to product teams?
[08:34] Tomás (Redwood): Yes, Console has cost dashboards broken down by key, route, model, and time window. You can export csv and hook to your billing pipeline.
[08:43] Maya (Redwood): We're about to show a short simulation — what-if you set per-project daily caps and a VIP lane; watch how the simulated request queue fills and which requests get routed to fallback models.
[08:55] (screen share; simulated heatmap noises)
[09:03] Tomás (Redwood): See here — the simulation highlights red when queue delay exceeds threshold; you can tune burst window or enable fallback to a quantized variant that uses less memory and costs less per token.
[09:16] Ravi (Cythera): For fallback model quality differences, can we set automatic evals to monitor regressions if fallback is used more than X%?
[09:25] Tomás (Redwood): Yes — Redwood Optimize can run evals on a prompt set and alert if quality drops past a threshold tied to a rollout or fallback usage. Another option is canary routing where a small percentage uses the quantized model first.
[09:39] Lena (Cythera): We may require additional logging of user identities in audit records. Is that supported without leaking PII?
[09:46] Tomás (Redwood): We can log identity tokens or hashed IDs, and you control retention and redaction rules. We'll align on a hashed-ID scheme so PII isn't stored.
[09:57] Aisha (Cythera): Ok this has been super helpful. Couple of follow-ups: 1) cost modeling with our trace; 2) the POC scope; 3) security artifact handoff.
[10:07] Maya (Redwood): Yep — we'll send an email summarizing those items.
[10:11] Oliver (Cythera): One last question — if a tenant starts DOSing the API, are there automated mitigations beyond rate limiting? e.g., IP blacklists or token revocation?
[10:20] Tomás (Redwood): You can revoke keys instantly and block IP ranges at the gateway; additionally, our autoscaler has rules to shed non-VIP traffic under overload. We also integrate with WAFs for known bad actors.
[10:33] Ravi (Cythera): Great. Can you also confirm latency SLOs if we run on Dedicated? We need 95th < 120ms for small prompts.
[10:41] Tomás (Redwood): For short prompts on our Dedicated pools we can hit 95th under 100-120ms depending on model and sequence length. We'll include measured samples from similar customers.
[10:51] Maya (Redwood): Quick recap and blockers: Cythera to share traffic trace + security constraints. Redwood to share pricing, KV-cache benchmarks, and SOC2 artifacts. Agree on 7-day POC start target next week if logs available.
[11:07] Aisha (Cythera): Sounds good. If you can include a short example config showing org policy + project override that'd help our infra team.
[11:14] Tomás (Redwood): Will do — I'll paste a sample YAML with policy precedence and an example of sticky routing rules.
[11:21] Maya (Redwood): Cool — thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email and set up the POC kickoff.
[11:26] (meeting ends)

Action items (brief):
- Maya: pricing + SLA + sample org/project policy YAML, due 2026-04-02.
- Tomás: KV-cache latency CSV + sample trace + policy YAML, due 2026-03-30.
- Cythera (Ravi/Lena): Provide anonymized traffic trace + security questionnaire answers, due 2026-03-29.

Notes on transcript quality: medium — there are a few places with brief crosstalk and some product names transcribed incorrectly (e.g., "kv cash" occasionally).

References shared during call: Console screenshots (link placeholder), sample policy YAML (link placeholder), SOC2 summary deck (link placeholder), POC checklist (link placeholder).

Oxford Avenue Labs - Quicklaunch vs Private Pilot Discovery

Initial discovery to understand Oxford Avenue Labs' usage patterns and whether they can start on Redwood hosted API for fast time-to-first-token or need a private/dedicated pilot due to data residency and compliance. Discussed quickstart credits, expected QPS, latency SLOs, SOC 2/KMS needs, and next steps for pricing and demo. Consensus: try hosted quicklaunch for first integration while evaluating private pilot for regulated PII pipelines.
Customer leans toward hosted quickstart for speed with a parallel private pilot for PII. Key technical asks: p95 latency <600ms, 80 qps steady, KV cache behaviour, KMS/SSO integration. Redwood to provide pricing, private runbook, SOC2 docs, and schedule a cache/batching demo.
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-16
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 44 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jules Wang (Redwood SE), Talia Romero (Redwood CSM), Paul Winters (CTO, Oxford Ave), Maria Gomez (Lead ML Eng), Kevin Lau (Infra), Anika Rao (PM)

Auto Summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect): discussed quickstart credits, hosted API path to first token, potential private pilot for regulated data. Action items noted.

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Samir from Redwood Inference, and with me is Jules, our solutions engineer, and Talia from customer success. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Paul: Good, thanks. Excited to talk through options. We've been evaluating a few runtimes and wanted to see how Redwood maps to our infra and compliance constraints.
[00:18] Jules: Great. Quick agenda: understand your stack, constraints (latency, privacy), demo the quickstart path and discuss dedicated/private pilots and costs. We'll also cover security controls like SSO, KMS, audit logs.
[00:28] Maria: For context, our main thing is a customer-facing assistant that does pricing suggestions and document summarization. We expect p95 latency under 600ms for the critical path and QPS around 80 steady, spiky to 250 during peaks. We also have a pipeline that processes invoices containing PII — that's why data residency matters.
[00:48] Samir: Thanks, that's helpful. Just to clarify — is the PII pipeline the same traffic that will hit the public API, or is it a batch offline job?
[00:54] Kevin: It's a mix. Most is offline batch, but occasionally some redaction/lookup flows will need inference in near-real-time and must be within our EU region.
[01:05] Samir: OK. Two natural paths: 1) start with Redwood hosted API to get to first token quickly — we give trial credits and SDKs so your engineers can prototype in a day or two; 2) parallel evaluation of Dedicated or Private (VPC) for the PII flows, which gives you control over residency, KMS, and network isolation.
[01:25] Anika: What's the typical time-to-first-token for teams using the quickstart?
[01:29] Jules: Most engineering teams can get a hello-world call in a few hours, and a basic integration in 1-2 days if you use our SDK. With our free credits we can simulate realistic traffic for a week. Note: time-to-first-token depends on model choice and prompt pipeline.
[01:46] Maria: Can you do a hosted flow but ensure data doesn't get stored or used for model training?
[01:51] Samir: Yes — by default hosted customers can opt-out of training and we surface data retention controls; for regulated customers we recommend Dedicated or Private. There was a small typo in some docs where we wrote Rewood but that's just the auto transcript :)
[02:03] Paul: Do you have SOC 2 and ISO docs we can hand to security?
[02:07] Talia: Absolutely. We'll send SOC 2 type II report and an ISO summary. Jules will include a private deployment runbook and KMS integration notes.
[02:15] Kevin: For KMS, can we use our cloud provider KMS or do you have customer-managed HSM?
[02:20] Jules: You can bring your own KMS in Private deployments; Dedicated has integrations for customer-managed keys in supported clouds. Our on-prem option supports HSM for air-gapped setups.
[02:30] Maria: On performance — you mentioned KV cache and batching. We use long context windows for some summarization jobs, and we'd like to avoid paying heavy per-token costs if possible.
[02:39] Jules: Right — we have automatic prefix/KV caching to save repeated context, and smart batching. For your workload, we might recommend a quantized model for cheaper tokens, and a lower-latency variant pinned for the critical path.
[02:54] Maria: How much of a token cost delta are we looking at when moving from hosted baseline to dedicated with quantization?
[02:59] Samir: Ballpark — 20-40% unit cost reduction depending on batching efficiency and sequence lengths; dedicated also gives you reserved capacity so you can meet throughput SLAs. We'll share a modeled spreadsheet.
[03:12] Paul: Are there any trade-offs in quality with quantization? Our summarization needs to be pretty accurate.
[03:17] Jules: There's sometimes a mild drop but we have quantization profiles and eval tooling to guard against regressions. Redwood Optimize flags quality regressions tied to prompt sets. We can run a small eval on your prompt set to verify.
[03:29] Anika: What does the onboarding process look like if we start hosted but want to transition to Private later?
[03:35] Samir: We keep model versioning and rollout policies consistent across modes, so you can pin model versions and move traffic gradually. Typical flow: quickstart on hosted, pilot traffic to dedicated for throughput, then private pilot for compliance-sensitive pipelines.
[03:48] Paul: Any customers who did that pattern? See a couple of names in your materials but curious for a quick example.
[03:54] Samir: One customer in fintech started on hosted for prototyping, then reserved dedicated capacity for production, and then set up a private VPC for regulated flows. We'll anonymize the case study and share it.
[04:05] Maria: On the SDKs — do you support python and our Node stack?
[04:08] Jules: Yes Python, Node, and REST. We also have sample repos for serverless and k8s sidecar patterns.
[04:15] [04:15] — short cross talk / background noise — Kevin: sorry, had a quick timeline Q — we plan an internal spike next sprint, want to know if we can get a performance benchmark run?
[04:22] Samir: Yes — we can run a benchmark with your sample prompts using our hosted perf harness or spin a dedicated perf run. We'd need traffic profile and sample prompts.
[04:30] Kevin: We'll send p95 targets and a 24-hour traffic sample.
[04:33] Maria: Also, do you have RBAC for routes and token-level cost tracing? We need to show cost attribution to product teams.
[04:39] Talia: We have token-level cost breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and tracing hooks. RBAC is available for admin roles and you can restrict keys to models/routes.
[04:47] Anika: On pricing — are free credits standard, and how much?
[04:51] Samir: New orgs get trial credits (amount varies by program) — typically enough to run a week of integration and a small load test. For pilots we can extend credits; committed capacity discounts apply for Dedicated.
[05:01] Paul: For private pilot cost modeling, do you also provide a reference infra cost estimate?
[05:06] Jules: Yes — the runbook will include estimated GPU counts, expected utilization, and infra TCO. We'll include network/hardware licensing notes.
[05:14] Maria: Security-wise, our legal team will ask about audit logging and retention.
[05:18] Talia: Audit logs are available in both Dedicated and Private; hosted has retention windows and export hooks to your SIEM. We'll attach the exact retention policy.
[05:26] [05:26] Maria: Quick aside — is there an on-prem option for completely air-gapped? We have some customers that demand that.
[05:31] Jules: Yes, on-prem air-gapped deployment is part of our private offering — longer lead time but possible.
[05:36] Paul: If we start hosted, will switching to private require changing client code?
[05:40] Samir: Minimal. The API and SDK are consistent. You might change endpoint and auth, but payloads and models remain the same. We try to keep that transition smooth.
[05:50] Anika: What do you need from us to start the quickstart?
[05:54] Samir: Sign-up, we grant credits, share a sample prompt, and a short integration guide. For more realistic tests, share traffic profile and target SLOs.
[06:03] Paul: Sounds good. On team responsibilities, who will be our point for technical questions?
[06:07] Jules: Jules will be SE contact for technical integration. Talia will coordinate docs and SOC 2 artifacts. Samir will own commercial/pricing.
[06:16] [06:16] Maria: A few nitty bits — latency targets: p50 under 200ms desirable, p95 under 600ms; throughput: steady 80 qps, burst 250. We have some long seq cases with ~6k tokens occasionally.
[06:30] Jules: Noted — 6k tokens is sizable; we'll check supported model configs and caching strategy for that. Longer contexts may push latency.
[06:37] Paul: We also want to add a security review as part of procurement. What's the expected timeline for that?
[06:41] Talia: We typically provide security artifacts within 48 hours and coordinate a security review call if needed.
[06:47] Anika: Any limitation on data residency in hosted mode?
[06:50] Samir: Hosted runs in multiple regions; you can pin region in requests, but for hard residency needs we recommend Private.
[06:58] [06:58] — short pause — background — Samir: OK let's talk immediate next steps and decide on a path.
[07:04] Paul: I think we want to do a fast path: start hosted quickstart with credits to validate product integration and UX, and run a small production-like test for the non-PII traffic. For the PII flows we'll scope a private pilot.
[07:18] Samir: Perfect. We'll enable trial credits and send a quickstart checklist. Jules will coordinate the private runbook and perf eval.
[07:25] Maria: We'll prepare sample prompts and a 24-hour traffic dump.
[07:28] Kevin: Also want a bench where we test KV cache behaviour with repeated prompts.
[07:32] Jules: We'll include KV cache examples — sometimes transcribed as K-V cash in the auto notes, ha.
[07:36] Anika: For the follow-up demo, can we see an example of the rollout and canary tooling?
[07:40] Samir: Yes, we'll show canary/A-B, automatic fallback to compatible model variants, and the Console dashboards.
[07:48] Paul: Great, let's lock a follow-up for next week.
[07:51] Samir: We'll propose a 45-min technical demo next Tue or Wed.
[07:55] Talia: I'll include SOC 2, ISO, and audit log retention docs in the follow-up email.
[08:01] [08:01] — wrap up — Samir: Thanks everyone. Quick recap: start hosted quickstart with credits; customer to send prompts and traffic profile; Redwood to send pricing, private runbook, SOC 2/ISO; schedule follow-up demo focusing on caching, batching, and rollout.
[08:20] Paul: Thanks, talk soon.

Meeting end.
