Prefetching, paging and prefix reuse — runtime deep dive (EchoWorks)

Header:
Date: 2025-08-14
Start: 15:30 PDT
Duration: ~62 min
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Olivia Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (EchoWorks - ML Platform), Aaron Li (EchoWorks - SRE), Priya Rao (EchoWorks - Eng Mgmt)

Summary: quick technical deep dive to debug prefix reuse failures and repeated evictions on long-context LLM workloads. Showed internal prefetch/paging behaviors on Redwood runtime, discussed NVMe spill patterns, batching tradeoffs, quantized model artifacts, and on-prem/VPC concerns. Agreed next steps: exchange logs, run bench, and iterate prefix heuristics.

Topics discussed: prefetching strategy, eviction thresholds, KV paging to NVMe, prefix reuse heuristics, long-context cache fragmentation, batching windows, quantization side-effects (4-bit vs 8-bit), and on-prem IO constraints / KMS considerations.

--- Transcript body (timestamps approximate, auto-transcribed, some mis-hearings):
[00:00:05] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — Olivia from our infra team is gonna drive the deep dive.
[00:00:12] Olivia: hi all, thanks. Maya, can you give a 2-minute overview of the workload that's showing the issues?
[00:00:20] Maya: yeah sure, so we're running a multi-turn summarization + retrieval pipeline. Typical session is 15–20k tokens, with lots of short prompts in between, and we keep prefix context from past turns to try to maintain persona. We're seeing consistent evictions in the KV store around the 8k–12k mark and then a bunch of paging thrash.
[00:00:38] Aaron: to add, the infra we're using for the PoC is an mGPU setup with NVMe attached, and sometimes the NVMe queues spike during peak regen. We're not on-prem yet, but this mirrors what we expect when we move to the private deployment.
[00:00:50] Olivia: ok. quick check — are you using prefix reuse aggressively (i.e., reusing the same KV keys for repeated system prompts)?
[00:00:57] Maya: yes, we canonicalize the first 2k tokens as a system prefix and try to reuse that object, but we still see duplicate entries in the cache and thens it evicts older session frame — sorry thens -> then it evicts. transcriber: "thens" shows up.
[00:01:10] Samir: cool, we'll look at three axes: 1) eviction policy and thresholds, 2) paging/prefetch behavior to NVMe, 3) prefix reuse hash collisions or mis-keying.

[00:01:28] Olivia: background on our KV layer — it's sharded by model+session id. Each shard has a soft TTL and an LRU-ish eviction but we also have a proactive prefetcher: when we detect likely next-token windows we pre-warm adjacent KV pages into memory. That prefetcher has heuristics tuned for median seq lengths. For long-context it sometimes misfires and paged pages evict others.
[00:01:54] Priya: when you say pages, are those 512KB or 1MB blocks? in our infra the NVMe mapping is 1MB.
[00:02:01] Olivia: good question — on our runtime the page size is configurable; defaults are 512KB but for quantized small models we sometimes push 1MB to reduce indexing overhead. That choice changes eviction granularity.
[00:02:12] Aaron: ah that may explain the big eviction jumps. We set the default to 1MB in the PoC to minimize metadata ops.

[00:02:22] [00:02:25] Maya: can you explain the prefetch heuristic? we saw bursts of IO right before a session hits 9k tokens, and then everything craps out.
[00:02:33] Olivia: sure. Heuristic is: if a session has steady token rate for N recent requests and the next-request size is > X, we prefetch K neighbouring KV pages up to a cap. The bug we've seen in long-context: the heuristic mis-estimates because of repeated short edits mid-session, so prefetch chases a rapidly-growing working set and ends up pulling in pages that evict other active sessions.
[00:02:56] Samir: note — that pattern is more common when prefix reuse fails: the runtime treats slightly-different prompt hashes as new keys, causing multiple near-duplicate entries. Prefetch then pulls duplicates for the same logical prefix.

[00:03:10] Aaron: so could prefix hashing be unstable because of whitespace changes or JSON ordering differences in our prompt serialization?
[00:03:16] Olivia: yes — we convert prompts to canonicalized bytes but there's a small bug where trailing nulls from the embedding pipeline slip in. That can cause different hashes.
[00:03:26] Maya: omg that matches what we saw; our preprocessor was adding a trailing delimiter for multi-doc prompts.
[00:03:33] Samir: quick mitigation: we can add a normalization layer on the runtime side to trim known noise and apply stable hashing. We'll share a patch that does that as a config flag.

[00:03:45] [00:04:00] Priya: on the paging side, how do you decide which KV to evict when a page must be spilled? is it strictly LRU or do you have cost-weighted eviction?
[00:04:09] Olivia: current default is LRU with a small age-bias for smaller keys — but we also support a cost model where entries with high reuse frequency get a retention bonus. For your workload the eviction decisions were mostly LRU because the prefetch pulled new pages that looked "hot" but weren't actually reused.
[00:04:25] Priya: could we tune the bias to favor session-affine prefixes? so that a user's session stays resident longer?
[00:04:31] Olivia: yep — we have a session-affinity weight. The tradeoff is it raises p99 tail for other sessions if your workload is dominating memory. For enterprise customers we expose a per-tenant reservation and adjustable soft limits.

[00:04:45] [00:05:10] Maya: you mentioned quantization earlier — can quantization cause larger KV entries? we're seeing bigger KB footprints for 4-bit quantized attention states.
[00:05:18] Olivia: good point. Quantization changes per-token state size because quantized KV caches may include dequantization metadata or alignment padding. In some backends a 4-bit packing increases CPU-side buffers and alignment can round up to a larger block, so effective sizes can be slightly larger than naive estimates. That plus 1MB page size can amplify eviction churn.
[00:05:39] Samir: TL;DR: smaller page sizes + corrected hashing + tuned prefetch windows should reduce churn.

[00:05:52] [00:06:10] Aaron: what about batching? we've toyed with 64ms batching windows to improve throughput — but that inflates latency a bit. Does batching interact with prefetch / eviction?
[00:06:18] Olivia: yes. Larger batching windows increase the simultaneous working set on GPU and the KV read bursts. If prefetch runs concurrently with large batches you'll see bigger IO bursts and more eviction pressure. For low-latency workloads we recommend smaller batch windows (5–20ms) and per-model batch caps.
[00:06:36] Maya: interesting — our initial config had both batch windows and aggressive prefetch which likely compounded.

[00:06:45] [00:07:10] Priya: on private deployments — what changes? we plan to move to our VPC environment with local NVMe arrays. Are there extra tuning knobs for on-prem?
[00:07:20] Olivia: yes, for private you get control plane telemetry and we provide a tuned defaults file for on-prem disks. Key knobs: page size, prefetch cap, session-affinity weight, and async-writeback thresholds. Also, if you're on-prem with high-latency backing store we can enable a multi-tier cache: in-RAM first, then local NVMe, then remote object store.
[00:07:42] Aaron: KMS / encryption? if KV spills to NVMe we need disk encryption and KMS integration.
[00:07:48] Samir: we support KMS/HSM integrations and envelope encryption. For Private we can handshake with your KMS and ensure keys never leave HSM. We'll send the compliance note.

[00:07:58] [00:08:25] Olivia: want to demo a repro quickly? I have a small run that shows prefetch chasing and the eviction spike.
[00:08:32] Maya: yes please.
[00:08:35] Olivia: (screen-share) starting a synthetic session. This session simulates repeated short updates with a persistent 2k prefix. Watch the KV resident set and IO counters.
[00:08:50] [00:09:05] Olivia: initial steady state — resident pages ~ 420MB. At request 120 we see the prefetcher pull 3 pages (prefetch K=3) — you can see IO spike to 120MB/s and resident set jumps to 1.1GB, then eviction of older sessions occurs.
[00:09:23] Maya: that matches our telemetry — sudden 1GB jump then a bunch of sessions timed out.
[00:09:30] Aaron: how do you surface those events in logs? we saw a bunch of "page_evicted" events but lacked context for why prefetch ran.
[00:09:38] Olivia: logs include prefetch decisions, trigger heuristics, and causal session IDs in the latest runtime. Older versions were sparse. We'll correlate your logs with the new richer ones.

[00:09:50] [00:10:15] Samir: recap of the likely root causes for EchoWorks: 1) hashing instability due to preprocessor noise -> prefix duplication 2) page size = 1MB creating large eviction granularity 3) aggressive prefetch heuristic + larger batching window amplifying IO bursts 4) quantization alignment increasing per-entry sizes.

[00:10:32] Maya: sounds right. Which fixes are low-friction? we want to try something that doesn't require private deploy.
[00:10:39] Olivia: quick low-friction items: change runtime config to 512KB page size, flip on the prefix-normalization patch, reduce prefetch K to 1, and reduce batch window to 20ms. Those are runtime flags and can be toggled on hosted tier for your account. We'll provide a rollout plan.
[00:10:55] Priya: what's the expected improvement?
[00:10:58] Olivia: based on bench, p50 tokens/sec may drop slightly but p95/p99 tail should improve by ~30–60% — we'll validate.

[00:11:10] [00:11:30] Aaron: any caveats with quantized models? if we change page size will that affect alignment and potentially make sizes worse?
[00:11:38] Olivia: it's model-dependent. For some 4-bit kernels smaller pages reduce padding waste; for others they increase metadata overhead. We'll include model-specific suggestions in the config diff.

[00:11:50] Maya: ok, let's talk measurement — what artifacts do you need from us to reproduce?
[00:11:55] Olivia: ideally: 1) a sample of anonymized prompt/session traces (token-level), 2) KV eviction logs and prefetch events for a 48-hour window, 3) the exact model name + quantization config, 4) batch window and batching params.

[00:12:12] Maya: we'll share that. Aaron can collect the logs.
[00:12:16] Aaron: yeah I can pull logs. Do you need raw NVMe iostat traces too?
[00:12:19] Olivia: NVMe perf counters are helpful — queue depth, latencies. Also OS-level throttles. We'll take anything you can provide.

[00:12:28] [00:12:45] Samir: timeline proposal: Maya uploads logs by Monday (2025-08-18), we run bench and reproduce by Thursday (2025-08-21), and then we schedule a follow-up with an on-prem/PoC plan for the following week.

[00:12:55] Priya: sounds good. any immediate guardrails to prevent repeated evictions in prod before the fix?
[00:13:00] Olivia: yes — throttling prefetch (K=0), enabling session-affinity weight, and lowering page size are the fastest. We'll give the exact commands.

[00:13:10] [00:13:40] Maya: side question — we use SSO and strict audit logging. if we go private how does Redwood handle audit retention for per-token traces? storage costs are a concern.
[00:13:50] Samir: audit retention is configurable per-customer; we can stream logs to your S3 and rotate. For sensitive traces we can redact or hash content and keep token counts only. We'll include options in the compliance doc.

[00:14:05] Olivia: one more note on prefix reuse heuristics — we can implement a "soft-canonicalization" stage that tries exact-match then fuzzy-match within a small edit distance; that reduces duplicate keys from whitespace/noise. But fuzzy introduces CPU cost and potential false matches. We'll prototype it as an opt-in feature.
[00:14:24] Maya: fuzzy match sounds risky but interesting. would like to see metrics on false-positive rate.

[00:14:32] Samir: we'll run experiments and give FP/FN numbers.

[00:14:45] [00:15:00] (discussion drifts into config flags and exact CLI for toggles; Olivia reads command snippets and the team copies them)

[00:25:10] [mid-call deep technical exchange — timestamps skip in transcript for brevity but exist in logs]
[00:25:12] Olivia: show bench script (synthetic) where we vary prefetch K and page size and measure p50/p95/p99 and NVMe throughput. Here are some quick numbers: (1) K=3, page=1MB -> p99 latency 2.9s, NVMe 160MB/s; (2) K=1, page=512KB -> p99 1.8s, NVMe 82MB/s; (3) K=0, page=512KB, batch-window 20ms -> p99 1.5s, NVMe 40MB/s.
[00:25:40] Priya: nice. does that hold with quantized 4-bit bfloat kernels?
[00:25:45] Olivia: slightly different numbers — alignment increased effective page occupancy by ~8% on the 4-bit kernel in our lab. We'll include that model-quantization delta in the findings.

[00:26:10] Maya: if we go to private on-prem, can the prefetch be disabled fully? we might prefer deterministic eviction rather than speculative IO.
[00:26:18] Olivia: yes, prefetch can be fully disabled. In private mode we often ship customers with prefetch off by default for constrained IO disks.

[00:26:30] Aaron: are there instrumentation changes we should add server-side that will help triage in future?
[00:26:36] Olivia: recommended instrumentation: per-request KV-hit/miss flags, prefetch triggers with decision context, page-size annotated evict events, and per-session resident footprint. We also suggest a rolling window heatmap for session affinity.

[00:26:50] [00:27:05] Samir: I'll attach a sample LogQL and an example Grafana dashboard for these metrics.

[00:27:20] Maya: great. small question — does Redwood's smart-routing affect KV locality? we sometimes route a session across nodes for cost reasons.
[00:27:30] Olivia: yes, routing can move sessions across shards if the policy demands it. We have sticky routing by default for session affinity; only certain cost-saving fallbacks will re-home sessions. If sessions get re-homed frequently it will destroy locality and increase page misses.

[00:27:45] Aaron: we do have autoscale events firing that reassign capacity. is that a red flag?
[00:27:50] Olivia: autoscale that moves shards mid-session is a problem for KV locality; we can set a cooldown so active sessions are never moved while active.

[00:28:05] [00:28:20] Maya: ok let's recap and confirm next steps verbally.
[00:28:25] Samir: recap: (1) EchoWorks to provide anonymized logs + NVMe traces by 2025-08-18, (2) Redwood to run bench and share results by 2025-08-21, (3) Redwood to provide runtime config diff and prefix-normalization patch by 2025-08-20, (4) follow-up PoC on-prem sync to be scheduled week of 2025-08-25.
[00:28:45] Priya: agreed.
[00:28:48] Maya: one more ask — can you send a quick how-to for toggling prefetch K and page size in hosted console?
[00:28:54] Olivia: yes, I'll send exact steps and a one-liner curl for the flags.

[00:29:05] [closing minutes include smaller clarifications and people typing notes; transcript omitted]

Action items (embedded from earlier):
- Samir: run focused kv-prefetch benchmark with EchoWorks' prompt set (due 2025-08-21)
- Maya: share anonymized NVMe and runtime logs (due 2025-08-18)
- Olivia: draft prefix-reuse heuristics doc and provide config diff (due 2025-08-20)

End of transcript.

References / Links mentioned (not attached here):
- Internal bench script: github.com/redwood-internal/kv-prefetch-bench (demo copy)
- Config flags doc: /docs/runtime/kv-config.md (to be shared)
- Compliance/KMS note (will be emailed)

Meeting ended ~16:32 PDT

Crypto governance & BYO-HSM handover workshop - Lucent Analytics

Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-04-12 10:30 PT | Duration: ~52m
Location: Zoom
Recording: Enabled
Attendees: Jared Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Lina Torres (Redwood PM); Tom Hale (Lucent CISO), Marco DeLuca (Lucent Cloud), Elena Park (Platform Sec), Nina Reyes (Legal)
Shared artifacts referenced: redwood.com/docs/byo-hsm-integration (deck), shared drive: /lucent/redwood-byo-hsm, benchmark spreadsheet (latency-cost.xlsx)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be noisy):
Redwood ran through BYO-HSM onboarding flow, key wrapping vs direct KMS keys, network egress considerations, HSM connector architecture, audit log handoff, and next steps for pilot and SOC2 artifacts. Customer to confirm HSM model and provide network diagram; Redwood to share connector checklist and SOC2 excerpts.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jared: hey everybody thanks for joining, we have about 50 minutes, we wanted to run through the BYO-HSM flow and answer questions on key custody / audit trail, yeah?
[00:10] Tom: yep, thank you. Quick ask up front, we want to validate that keys never persist in Redwood control plane unwrapped. That's the big gating factor for procurement.
[00:18] Priya: absolutely, good question. Our BYO-HSM option supports key wrapping with customer keys held in the HSM; the wrapped key blob is what Redwood stores. The private key material never leaves the HSM.
[00:30] Marco: can you explain the handoff? Like, do we push the key, or does Redwood fetch it? Network/firewall concerns.
[00:38] Priya: so there are two patterns: a push model where you export a wrapped key blob from your HSM (using your HSM vendor tooling) and upload to Redwood control plane via an encrypted endpoint, or a connector model where a lightweight agent establishes a mutual-TLS session to our control plane and performs on-prem key signing operations. The connector avoids exporting private material.
[01:00] Elena: that connector—is it allowed in our airgapped scenario? We have some customers where connector can't reach public internet.
[01:08] Priya: good point. For fully air-gapped setups there's an on-prem package (Redwood Private) which runs the control plane locally; in that case the connector talks to the local control plane and never traverses public internet. For VPC-hosted customers we support private peering and allow setup via an egress-only NAT with strict ACLs.
[01:30] Tom: and what about FIPS/HSM certs? We run Thales nShield and a couple of AWS CloudHSM clusters for different regions. We need guidance on which ones are supported.
[01:40] Lina: we maintain a compatibility matrix — quick note, the connector currently supports PKCS#11 and AWS CloudHSM APIs; we have an integration path for Thales using the HSM vendor's SDK. We'll share the matrix after this call.
[01:55] Nina: from legal, we need to see audit logs and a clear chain-of-custody for key creation and rotation. How granular are logs?
[02:04] Priya: logs include key create/rotate/destroy events, user/principal id, operation timestamps, and the session ID. We can stream audit logs to your SIEM via syslog or to an S3 bucket with SSE-KMS. Logs are tamper-evident — we append hash-chaining for integrity metadata.
[02:26] Marco: hash-chaining, can you elaborate? Sounds like an internal term.
[02:30] Priya: yeah it's a simple technique where each log entry includes a hash of the previous entry; it makes retroactive modification detectable. We also support signed audit bundles that your auditors can validate with our public signing key.
[02:45] Tom: okay, but auditors ask for separation of duties. Who has access to the signing key for those audit bundles?
[02:52] Lina: signing key for audit bundles is rotated and held in Redwood-managed HSMs; we can set up a customer-provided signing key stored in your HSM for the validation root if you prefer full custody.
[03:05] Jared: quick interruption — just to align: the main tradeoffs are, if you want zero-Redwood custody of private keys we recommend the connector or on-prem control plane; if you want simpler operations and OK with Redwood-managed HSM, we support that too with strict RBAC and auditability.
[03:22] Marco: latency question — if we do a connector model where the HSM is on-prem, what's the token gen latency for a typical completion? We do high-volume inference calls.
[03:30] Priya: key wrapping operations are one-time per model load; per-token crypto is not happening. For each model instance we do an initial unwrap and cache the key material in a secure runtime (KV cache). The critical path is model inference, the unwrap happens during startup—so typical unwrap latency is 120-500ms depending on HSM. After that token path is unaffected.
[03:55] Marco: hmm, our scale requires frequent ephemeral VM churn, so unwrap frequency might be higher. We may need a warm pool.
[04:02] Priya: yes we recommend warm-pool instances or local key caching with TTL tied to instance lifecycle. Also we can coordinate on a batching strategy for instance startups to reduce calls to HSM.
[04:18] Tom: can Redwood support per-tenant keys? Each business unit wants their own keys and to ensure no cross-tenant access.
[04:26] Priya: yes, per-tenant key isolation is supported. Keys are namespaced by tenant id and RBAC restricts keys to authorized service principals. We also support tenant-scoped KMS aliases for easier audit.
[04:38] Elena: SSO/Access — how do we federate? We use Okta with SCIM and SAML.
[04:44] Lina: Redwood supports SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning, and we map Okta groups to internal RBAC roles. We can limit who can request key operations via role policies.
[04:56] Nina: legal follow-up — what about data residency? Some keys must be provisioned in EU-only HSMs for GDPR reasons.
[05:03] Priya: we allow regional key placement. For hosted customers we have region-specific HSM clusters; for Dedicated/Private you can pick the region of the control plane. We can also do BYOK with a EU HSM to ensure key locality.
[05:18] Marco: is there any cross-region replication of key material? We need to prevent that for certain keys.
[05:24] Priya: by default we avoid replicating private key material. If you enable cross-region redundancy we replicate only encrypted blobs and not raw material; but for strict residency we can disable replication and require manual failover.
[05:40] Tom: rotation policy — auditors want automated rotation logs and ability to force-roll keys that were compromised.
[05:47] Priya: automated rotation is supported; you can define rotation cadence and Redwood will create new key versions and rotate wrapped blobs. We emit events to audit logs and can trigger immediate rotate via API. Destroy is a two-step process with confirmation and retention windows per policy.
[06:05] Marco: what about escrow and recovery? If Lucent loses HSM access, can we recover?
[06:10] Priya: there are multiple patterns: customer-managed escrow (you ship an encrypted escrow bundle to a secure escrow vault), Redwood-managed escrow with customer approval, or split-key recovery options (Shamir-like schemes) where recovery requires multiple operator approvals. We generally advise customer-managed escrow for compliance sensitivity.
[06:28] Tom: are there examples of customers using split-key with Redwood?
[06:32] Priya: yes, a couple of fintechs implemented split-key with a 3-of-5 operator model; we supported the workflow via our API and audit hooks.
[06:42] Marco: network egress - does Redwood require any port openings from our HSM to the internet? We run a hardened network with only outbound 443 via proxy.
[06:52] Priya: connector works over 443 with mTLS, and we support proxy configurations. For systems that disallow any outbound, we recommend the Private deployment.
[07:03] Elena: on syslog integration for audit logs, can we get field-level separation so PII isn't logged?
[07:10] Priya: yes you can mask or redact fields on export, and we support filters before shipping logs. We also provide log retention policies per tenant.
[07:22] Jared: let me toss in a quick note about compliance artifacts — Lina is going to share SOC2 Type II excerpts and our ISO 27001 scope doc, that'll help your auditors.
[07:32] Lina: yes I'll upload those to the shared folder after this call.
[07:36] Nina: also, can Redwood sign on to our security questionnaire? We have a long RSA and some exec sign-off items.
[07:43] Jared: we usually do an NDA+SSOC (security self-assessment) and we can fill your vendor security questionnaire — send it over and we'll prioritize.
[07:50] Marco: question on physical HSMs — if we use third-party HSM provider, is attestation available?
[07:57] Priya: yes, attestation is supported for supported HSMs — e.g., CloudHSM provides attestation tokens; Thales has HSM-specific attestations. We'll capture attestation data in the audit bundle.
[08:10] Tom: any limitation on algorithms or key sizes? We need ECC for some workflows and RSA-4096 for others.
[08:16] Priya: supported algorithms include RSA up to 4096, ECDSA/P-256,P-384, and AES-256 for symmetric keys. Specific HSM vendors may have limits but we handle translation via PKCS#11 where possible.
[08:31] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[08:36] Jared: we should get into the practical onboarding flow — Priya, can you walk through the step-by-step for a BYO-HSM connector onboarding?
[08:44] Priya: sure — step 1: customer confirms HSM model and grants an infra contact; step 2: Redwood provides connector image + deployment manifest and mTLS certs; step 3: customer deploys connector in their VPC and establishes mutual auth; step 4: we run a handshake sequence to verify PKCS#11 endpoints and fetch attestation; step 5: we test unwrap/unwrap simulation and run sample key operations; step 6: sign-off and production rollout. We also provide terraform modules for automating the connector.
[09:20] Marco: who holds the signing certs for mTLS?
[09:24] Priya: Redwood issues connector certs scoped to your account and they can be rotated; alternately customers can bring their own certs and we accept a CSR.
[09:34] Tom: on the handshake, will any key material ever be logged in plaintext in transit or at rest? We need guarantees.
[09:42] Priya: no plaintext private material is transmitted. The handshake uses mutually authenticated TLS and only exchanges attestation and metadata; wrapped key blobs are always encrypted under your HSM-wrapping key. At rest in our control plane we only store the wrapped blob.
[09:59] Nina: curious about access approvals — is there a CLI or UI workflow for key unwrap events that requires approval? Some ops teams want manual approval gates.
[10:08] Priya: yes, there is a policy engine; you can require manual approval for unwraps, or set thresholds for automatic unwrap if from a trusted principal. Approvals are recorded in audit logs.
[10:22] Marco: about forensics — if we suspect a key compromise, does Redwood retain timeline events in a WORM store?
[10:29] Priya: we can write audit logs to WORM S3 with object lock for immutable retention. That helps for forensic timelines.
[10:38] Tom: great. cost question — does using BYO-HSM incur additional Redwood fees?
[10:44] Jared: slight premium for connector support and on-prem packages; pricing is primarily usage plus an integration/setup fee for enterprise BYO options. We'll include detailed pricing in the follow-up.
[10:55] Marco: do you have a sample policy template for rotation and escrow that auditors like?
[11:00] Lina: yes we'll share a policy template and an example runbook for operator steps.
[11:07] Elena: can we run a small proof-of-concept — just one model group with HSM in our EU region and measure cold-start unwrap latency and throughput?
[11:15] Priya: absolutely, we recommend a 2-week PoC: Redwood provides a sandbox account, connector artifact, and a small dedicated instance to run the model. We'll capture unwrap times and metrics to compare to your SLA.
[11:29] Tom: timeline — legal wants everything signed by end of month and procurement wants pilot in Q2. Is that feasible?
[11:36] Jared: yes we can aim for pilot week of 2027-04-26 if we get vendor/model and network diagram this week. Legal artifacts should be deliverable within 48 hours from Redwood after initial request.
[11:48] Nina: okay please share the vendor security questionnaire response template and we'll mark items for review.
[11:54] Priya: will do.
[11:56] Jared: any last questions?
[12:00] Marco: just one more: key compromise DR — if we need to rotate globally, can Redwood orchestrate rotation across running instances or is that on us?
[12:09] Priya: Redwood has an orchestration API — we can push rotation events to running clusters and coordinate cache invalidation; collaboration needed for ephemeral hosts but we can handle the orchestration.
[12:21] Tom: great. thanks everyone.

Recap / Next steps (auto-generated + confirmed):
- Redwood to send BYO-HSM connector checklist, terraform module, and SOC2/ISO snippets (Priya/Lina/Jared)
- Customer to confirm HSM vendor/model, provide network diagram, and internal procurement timeline (Tom/Marco)
- Schedule pilot week of 2027-04-26 for cold-start unwrap + throughput tests
- Redwood to provide pricing addendum for BYO-HSM integration

End of meeting.

Pilot ops weekly — networking & rollout checkpoint

Meeting header: 2025-04-09 14:30 UTC - Duration 45m
Attendees: Samira Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood), Rachel Tan (Aegis), Marcus Li (Aegis), Priya Rao (Aegis)

Summary (auto): Weekly POC check-in for Private VPC / on-prem pilot. Main topics: intermittent node-to-control-plane drop, planned kernel upgrade, routing policy mismatch for cross-subnet traffic, next steps for canary rollout of quantized variant.

[00:00] Samira: ok, hi everyone, thanks for joining, let's do a quick round of intros, and then diego will run the status.
[00:12] Rachel: hey, rachel here, short on time but we'll try to stay on point.
[00:15] Diego: great, i'll kick off with the current health, so overall the pilot cluster is up 95% except we had two incidents last week where node-07 dropped control plane traffic for about six minutes, that corresponded with a flurry of KV cache misses and a small spike in p50 latency from 82ms to about 310ms.
[00:39] Priya: yes we saw that in our tracing, at 03:22 UTC there was a burst of retransmits. I dug in, looks like the nic driver on that host was reinitializing, maybe related to the kernel.
[00:52] Marcus: to add, our security monitoring also flagged an egress attempt to an unexpected FQDN during the same window, likely a retry to the fallback endpoint, not an unknown connection but we want to be explicit.
[01:05] Diego: yep, good catch. Redwood's logs show the request hit our fallback routing policy and retried to the regional fallback (we call it "rg-fallback-1" internally). There was no data exfil, just retried gRPC handshakes.
[01:18] Liam: quick note, we also saw that when the node recovered the KV cache warmed up slowly because those keys had been evicted; we suggested a short-lived prefilling strategy last week and want to try it on node group B.
[01:31] Rachel: ok, so what's the proposed immediate mitigation? is this firewall, routing, or kernel?
[01:36] Diego: short answer: multi-factor. Primary is kernel/driver stability on the host; secondary is tightening the routing policy so that control plane retries are bounded and go to a local regional replica first. And third is a temporary increase to the cache prefetch threshold to reduce cold misses.
[01:52] Marcus: we're willing to do the kernel bump but we need the maintenance window and rollback steps spelled out. Security also needs to know which outbound hosts will be contacted during the upgrade.
[02:03] Samira: absolutely, we'll put together a maintenance runbook with rollback. Diego, can you own the runbook?
[02:08] Diego: yes, i'll produce the runbook and include the firewall diff (this is the exact set of ports and FQDNs), should have it by Friday. Link will be: https://redwood.app/internal/runbooks/aegis-vpc-sync (placeholder).
[02:22] Priya: when you say firewall diff, do you mean we need to open full IP ranges? we've been strict about 10.x only.
[02:30] Diego: no, only the control-plane egress to the redwood control plane endpoints and the regional fallback. We'll call out exact FQDNs and IPs. Marcus, if you can provide the approved outbound list we'll reconcile.
[02:41] Marcus: yes i'll send a list, but the SOC team wants explicit FQDN allowlist versus CIDR.
[02:47] Diego: understood, we'll give both.
[02:50] [03:00] Rachel: switching to performance, the batch tuning you did last week — any visible improvement? our perf dashboard shows token throughput up 8% when batching is enabled but higher tail latency in some spots.
[03:11] Diego: right, the batch config increased throughput: we tuned the max-batch-size to 64 and adaptive batching threshold to 40ms; throughput improved but the p99 went up slightly for short sequences because of head-of-line waits. The suggestion is to enable a latency-sensitive route for sequences under 64 tokens routed to dedicated low-batch pool.
[03:34] Samira: that's the routing policy we discussed — route by token-length and SLO tag. Rachel, would you prefer a separate route or an explicit query param?
[03:43] Rachel: probably separate route so we can monitor cost separately.
[03:46] Liam: note, separate route means we need a new dedicated pool or pinned instances for the low-latency lane; that's doable but affects capacity planning.
[03:57] Priya: capacity wise, what's the cost delta? we have a constrained pilot budget.
[04:02] Diego: approximate delta is +15% on GPU-hours for low-latency lane initially; but with caching and prefill we expect it to be neutral by week two. We'll share the model-level cost calc in the runbook.
[04:15] Marcus: can we simulate cost impact before committing?
[04:19] Diego: yes, SE will run bench with a 90/10 mix and varied seq length to estimate both token cost and p99. We'll share raw data.
[04:27] [04:30] Rachel: about the canary for the quantized variant (v2-quant) — status? we want to ensure quality regressions are caught.
[04:36] Samira: team did a small A/B yesterday with one route, quality delta <0.5 BLEU-ish metric for our prompts, but there were a couple hallucinations in long-context prompts. We want to run a prompt-set of 120 real queries next.
[04:49] Diego: plan: canary 5% traffic to v2-quant for 48 hours, auto-roll back on any of these triggers: p99 latency > 1s, quality regression > 1.5 metric points, or error rate > 0.5%.
[05:03] Marcus: security-wise we also want to ensure that v2-quant artifact provenance is recorded and signatures verified — compliance requires that.
[05:11] Diego: yep, we'll attach model hash and provenance link to the rollout metadata; the console shows it.
[05:17] Priya: small nit — the console timestamps seem to display in PST for us even though our region is EU, makes log correlation a bit annoying. Can that be region-aware?
[05:28] Samira: good product feedback. Liam, can we log region tz in the next console patch?
[05:33] Liam: yep, we'll add an opt-in timezone display in next minor release.
[05:38] [06:00] Rachel: one more thing — we're seeing a mismatch on route table entries for the cross-subnet traffic between our VPC peering and the on-prem NATed segment. Some packets for egress to rg-fallback-1 are being SNATed and hitting an ACL.
[06:13] Diego: that explains the intermittent drops. The workaround is to update the route to use the peering path that preserves source IP for control-plane traffic. We recommended that in the original onboarding doc but it may not have been applied.
[06:28] Rachel: ok i'll have operations check the peering route and report back.
[06:32] Marcus: can you also provide a short checklist so our ops can run it without raising a support ticket?
[06:38] Diego: yes, the runbook will have a 6-step checklist and a one-click telemetry snapshot you can paste into the ticket.
[06:45] [07:00] Samira: let's do a quick recap and owners. Diego will own the runbook and firewall diff, send by 2025-04-11. Diego will also run the expanded bench and share results by 2025-04-14. Rachel will validate IP/CIDR and check the peering route by 2025-04-11. Marcus will send approved FQDNs by 2025-04-12. Diego will collect packet captures and upload by 2025-04-10.
[07:20] Priya: can we get a short <10 minute tech review tomorrow about the kernel patch details? we're tight on change windows.
[07:27] Samira: yes we'll do a focused session — 10 minutes — tomorrow 09:00 your time. Diego, can you present?
[07:32] Diego: confirmed.
[07:34] [08:00] Rachel: ok thanks all. small ask: when you share the runbook, please include the exact CLI commands for rollback and the target package versions so our automation can pick it up.
[08:12] Diego: will do.
[08:14] Samira: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with notes and links.
[08:18] Marcus: thanks.

End of transcript.
Redwood: share revised network runbook and firewall rule diff (internal link) by 2025-04-11
Customer: perform kernel upgrade on on-prem host group B and confirm reboot window by 2025-04-16
Redwood SE: run expanded latency bench (90/10 read/write mix) and share raw results by 2025-04-14
Schedule canary rollout for model variant v2-quant on dedicated pool for 2025-04-18
Diego Martinez - Collect packet captures from failed node (node-07) and upload to pilot-share - 2025-04-10
Rachel Tan - Validate that IP ranges 10.44.0.0/16 are permitted through customer firewall and confirm in doc - 2025-04-11
Marcus Li - Provide list of approved FQDNs for outbound egress to Redwood control plane - 2025-04-12

Telemetry & retention toggles — Cloudstream logistics walkthrough

Redwood demo of request-storage toggles, redaction, ephemeral logging, and console controls. Customer is evaluating hosted vs Dedicated for regulated shipment telemetry and wants clear retention, KMS key handling, and audit log integration. Agreed pilot and follow-ups.
[00:00] Sanjay (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick check — is this time still good?
[00:05] Mark (Cloudstream): Yep, all good, thanks. We want to focus on the telemetry and retention controls — especially PII redaction and how logging ties into our SIEM.
[00:12] Lina (Redwood SE): Great, we'll do a short run-through in Console and then jump to the API and Optimize suggestions. I'll show ephemeral mode and the request storage toggle.
[00:20] Priya (Cloudstream): Nice, and please show KMS workflows — we have to ensure keys never leave our boundary and logs are encrypted at rest.
[00:28] Lina (Redwood SE): Yep, we'll cover S3 storage options, KMS integration, and also the toggle that prevents request bodies from persisting.
[00:35] [screen share starts] Lina (Redwood SE): Ok, so this is the Console — under Settings -> Data Controls. Right here is the Request Storage switch. When you turn it off, we mark requests ephemeral and they are excluded from long-term request store. There is still short-lived buffering for active inference but it's TTL'd within minutes.
[00:53] Tina (Cloudstream): When you say TTL, is that configurable per-route? We have different SLAs per tenant.
[00:58] Lina (Redwood SE): Yes, per-route TTL or per API key. You can set default retention windows — 1h, 24h, 7d, 30d — and also route-level overrides. The console will show effective policy.
[01:12] Andre (Cloudstream): How does that interact with batching — if you batch requests, does it retain the raw prompts?
[01:18] Lina (Redwood SE): Good q. Batching groups incoming calls before they hit runtime; we support prefix/KV cache so you can enable prefix caching without storing full user payloads. In ephemeral mode we avoid persisting raw request bodies to the long-term store; only metadata for billing/sla is kept. There's a short lived in-memory buffer for the batch that is flushed.
[01:38] [00:01:40] Mark (Cloudstream): Ok. What about PII redaction — automated vs manual?
[01:45] Lina (Redwood SE): We have two layers: client-side redaction and server-side patterns. In Console you can set automated PII redaction rules — email, ssn, credit numbers — and you can add custom regexes per-tenant. Server-side redaction replaces matches with tokens before writing to disk. There are logs that show redaction events and counts but not the raw value.
[02:05] Priya (Cloudstream): We need proof that the redaction happened for audits. Do you keep audit logs that show original value hashes or anything?
[02:12] Sanjay (Redwood AE): We emit audit events — they include a hash fingerprint and rule id, timestamps, and who triggered the event. Those audit logs are retained per your retention policy and can be forwarded to your SIEM via our log-shipper. The original text is not stored if redaction is enabled.
[02:28] Tina (Cloudstream): Is the hash reversible?
[02:30] Sanjay (Redwood AE): No — it's a one-way SHA variant we use for tracing and de-dup without reversible PII.
[02:36] [00:02:40] Andre (Cloudstream): On KMS — can we bring our own key, rotate it, and have Redwood never store the plaintext key?
[02:44] Lina (Redwood SE): Yes, BYOK is supported. You can point to an external KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or HSM). We support envelope encryption; the customer master key is in your control and Redwood encrypts the data key with your CMK. Key rotation is supported via policy and you can revoke access.
[03:02] Priya (Cloudstream): And the audit trail for key operations?
[03:06] Lina (Redwood SE): We surface key usage events but the canonical audit of CMK ops lives in your KMS console; we also forward a subset to the Redwood audit stream with non-sensitive metadata.
[03:16] [00:03:20] Mark (Cloudstream): Can you show me the toggle in the API — I want to be able to set this from our infra rather than the Console.
[03:24] Lina (Redwood SE): Absolutely. It's a header you can pass: x-redwood-request-visibility: ephemeral | retained. There's also a policy engine where keys or routes can default to ephemeral. Quick demo — a sample curl: curl -X POST "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat" -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" -H "x-redwood-request-visibility: ephemeral" -d '{"messages": [...] }'
[03:48] [00:03:50] Andre (Cloudstream): If someone forgets the header, can we enforce via policy?
[03:53] Lina (Redwood SE): Yes — policy enforcement is preferred. You can create a policy that denies retention for keys scoped to compliance tenants.
[03:59] [00:04:00] Mark (Cloudstream): What's the default for hosted customers?
[04:03] Sanjay (Redwood AE): Default is retained for usage analytics and debugging — but we set short default retention and give customers controls. For enterprise we recommend explicit policy toggles.
[04:12] Priya (Cloudstream): About log forwarding, do you support syslog, Splunk, S3, and eventstreams?
[04:18] Lina (Redwood SE): We support pushing to S3, Splunk HEC, Datadog, and we have Kafka/EventBridge connectors. For SIEM you can also use our log-shipper which signs events and forwards them.
[04:28] [00:04:30] Tina (Cloudstream): If we enable forwarding to our S3, is that encrypted with our CMK?
[04:33] Lina (Redwood SE): Yes, you can configure object encryption with your KMS key.
[04:36] [00:04:40] Mark (Cloudstream): There was a note in your docs about redaction exceptions for ML evals — can you explain?
[04:44] Lina (Redwood SE): Sure. For model-evals you can opt into storing sanitized copies of request sets for quality monitoring. We recommend using a separate eval-only bucket, masked with PII removed. There's a consent mechanism and explicit flag for those flows.
[04:58] Andre (Cloudstream): That won't leak customer PII back into model training, right?
[05:02] Sanjay (Redwood AE): Correct — no training access by default. Eval sets are stored separately, and any data used for training requires explicit opt-in and is segmented.
[05:12] [00:05:20] Priya (Cloudstream): Can we get field-level redaction? Some messages have nested JSON with addresses.
[05:18] Lina (Redwood SE): Yes, the server-side rules support JSON path patterns and you can redact nested fields by path. You can also map fields to token placeholders.
[05:28] Mark (Cloudstream): How are these rules authored? UI or API?
[05:31] Lina (Redwood SE): Both — Console rule editor has a test harness and you can import/export rules via API.
[05:36] [00:05:40] Tina (Cloudstream): For PCI-like workflows, do you recommend Hosted or Dedicated?
[05:42] Sanjay (Redwood AE): For strict PCI or regulated PII that can't be inspected by a third party we'd suggest Dedicated or Private deployment inside your VPC. Hosted with BYOK + ephemeral mode can work for many cases, but Dedicated gives you clearer isolation guarantees and predictable throughput.
[05:56] [00:06:00] Andre (Cloudstream): If we go Dedicated, do the same console controls still apply?
[06:00] Lina (Redwood SE): Yes — the same API surface and Console exist across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. The only difference is where the control plane and data plane run.
[06:10] [00:06:15] Mark (Cloudstream): Any SLA impact when we enable ephemeral mode?
[06:19] Sanjay (Redwood AE): No SLA impact by itself. However, if you enable extreme caching or very aggressive TTLs that reduce KV cache effectiveness, you may see throughput differences; we'll recommend autoscaling policies to maintain targets.
[06:36] [00:06:40] Priya (Cloudstream): Do you capture IPs in logs? We need to mask client IPs for GDPR.
[06:44] Lina (Redwood SE): Client IPs are captured as part of transport logs but we can mask or hash them on ingestion. There's a toggle for anonymize-ips.
[06:53] Tina (Cloudstream): Does anonymize affect rate-limiting or fraud detection?
[06:57] Lina (Redwood SE): It can — we offer pseudonymization instead of full anonymization when you need rate limits to remain per-client. That preserves consistent IDs without exposing raw IP.
[07:09] [00:07:10] Mark (Cloudstream): Ok, show me how we'd test this — end-to-end.
[07:12] Lina (Redwood SE): I'll flip the tenant to ephemeral and run an API call.
[07:15] [typing] Lina (Redwood SE): curl -X POST ... -H 'x-redwood-request-visibility: ephemeral' ...
[07:22] [00:07:25] Lina (Redwood SE): Response comes back, and in Console request explorer you can see the request with a redaction flag. If you click 'raw' while ephemeral is on, it will show 'not persisted' instead of raw payload.
[07:35] Andre (Cloudstream): I see. Do you keep any derived telemetry — like token counts and cost metrics?
[07:41] Sanjay (Redwood AE): Yes — we keep aggregated usage metrics for billing and to surface latency/cost breakdowns. Those are not reversible to raw prompts.
[07:52] [00:07:55] Mark (Cloudstream): About legal, if somebody in procurement asks for deletion guarantees, do you have a delete API?
[07:59] Lina (Redwood SE): We have a deletion API for request store and for embeddings. There's also a bulk-delete and a retention enforcement policy. Deletions return an audit receipt.
[08:10] Priya (Cloudstream): Is deletion eventual or synchronous? We need to certify in writing.
[08:14] Sanjay (Redwood AE): Deletion is guaranteed within policy windows; embedded indexes have compaction cycles so some derived artifacts are removed during compaction — we provide deletion receipts and timestamps for audits. We'll include exact SLAs in the security pack.
[08:26] [00:08:30] Mark (Cloudstream): Any points about costs when enabling long retention?
[08:30] Lina (Redwood SE): Longer retention increases storage + egress if you forward logs. Optimize module can recommend downsampling, TTL tiers, or storing only hashed fingerprints for older records to reduce cost.
[08:43] [00:08:45] Andre (Cloudstream): Show me Optimize suggestions for a bursty workload — we have peaks at month-end.
[08:49] Lina (Redwood SE): Optimize will analyze token distribution and recommend batching window sizes and cache hints; you can choose retention tiers per route. For bursty flows we suggest a short-term higher retention for debugging then auto-roll down to minimal retention after 48 hours.
[09:05] [00:09:10] Mark (Cloudstream): That sounds useful. Can Optimize provide an estimated cost delta?
[09:14] Lina (Redwood SE): Yes we show projected monthly cost impact when you change retention or batch size.
[09:21] [00:09:25] Priya (Cloudstream): If we run a pilot, we need a checklist: security sign-offs, sample dataset, success metrics.
[09:30] Sanjay (Redwood AE): Agreed. Typical pilot checklist: SOC2 docs review, network VPN/VPC peering or private link, KMS BYOK setup, sample prompt set and eval metrics, throughput targets for Dedicated if needed.
[09:44] [00:09:50] Mark (Cloudstream): Who from Redwood will help with onboarding?
[09:47] Jules Park (Redwood CSM): Jules here — we'll coordinate onboarding, runbook, and set up the pilot workspace. We'll also provide the sample prompts and a test harness.
[09:57] Tina (Cloudstream): On timelines — we want to start a 2-week pilot mid-March.
[09:59] Sanjay (Redwood AE): Sounds good. I'll send calendar invite for 2026-03-18 to kickoff.
[10:05] [00:10:10] Priya (Cloudstream): A couple more questions on compliance: do you support SAML SSO for console access and SCIM for user provisioning?
[10:12] Lina (Redwood SE): Yes, SAML SSO and SCIM user sync are supported. RBAC roles are customizable, and we can map groups to audit roles.
[10:20] Mark (Cloudstream): For auditors, can we export the full audit trail?
[10:23] Sanjay (Redwood AE): Yes, audit exports can be time-bounded and signed. We provide a signed export for the period you require.
[10:30] [00:10:35] Andre (Cloudstream): One nit: your docs mention KV cache — we've seen the term but sometimes it's spelled KV cash in older docs, might confuse auditors.
[10:40] Lina (Redwood SE): Oh, heh, good catch — docs team pushed a typo earlier. We'll correct that.
[10:46] [00:10:50] Mark (Cloudstream): Any competitors' caveats we should be aware of? Priya: I think Anthropic's model access approach doesn't offer BYOK in the same way.
[10:57] Priya (Cloudstream): Right — also some providers keep raw logs for 30 days by default which we can't accept.
[11:04] Sanjay (Redwood AE): We're aligned to enterprise controls here. We'll share a matrix comparing retention features vs common competitors.
[11:12] [00:11:15] Tina (Cloudstream): Ok, final quick question — embeddings retention and PII: we want to ensure embedding vectors don't leak PII.
[11:20] Lina (Redwood SE): Embeddings are stored with metadata and we support redaction at ingestion; we also offer hashing of original text and ability to delete vectors via the deletion API. For extra safety, keep embeddings in Dedicated VPC.
[11:33] [00:11:40] Mark (Cloudstream): Great. That covers most of it.
[11:36] Jules Park (Redwood CSM): Quick recap: We'll send security pack and BYOK docs, provision ephemeral demo tenant, schedule pilot kickoff for 2026-03-18, and provide runbook.
[11:50] [00:11:55] Sanjay (Redwood AE): Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the materials. Any last questions?
[11:58] Priya (Cloudstream): Not from me. Thanks.
[12:01] Mark (Cloudstream): Thanks all.
[12:03] [00:12:05] [call ends]
Shared artifacts: security-pack.zip (link), ephemeral-quickstart.md (link), optimize-sample-report.csv (link)
Send SOC2 + pen test reports and KMS integration doc
Share quickstart for ephemeral mode + sample prompts
Schedule pilot kickoff: 2026-03-18 10:00 PT
Provision trial Dedicated capacity for 2 weeks (internal)
Sanjay Patel: share security pack (SOC2, ISO docs), due 2026-03-06
Lina Gomez: provision ephemeral demo tenant and sample prompts, due 2026-03-11
Mark Reynolds: confirm pilot users + success criteria, due 2026-03-10

Stargrove - Private VPC Onramp Discovery

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-07 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alice Ramos (Redwood AE), Ben Cho (Redwood SE), Lena Park (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Stargrove Infra), Tom Ellis (Stargrove Head of Cloud), Ravi Patel (Stargrove Security), Joan Marquez (Stargrove DevOps)

Summary:
Quick discovery to understand Stargrove's private onramp needs for Redwood Private: VPC peering vs privatelink, region gating (EU+APAC), egress IPs, KMS/HSM integration, and timeline for pilot.

Topics:
- Current infra and constraints
- Network topology (transit gateway, peering, private endpoints)
- Security controls (KMS, audit logs, SSO)
- Latency and failover requirements
- Next steps and PoC scope

Action items (briefed above)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alice Ramos: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alice, I'm the AE for this account. we'll keep this short, just want to map requirements for a private onramp. Ben and Lena from our SE team are here to dig into the network stuff.
[00:18] Maya Singh: Hey, thanks, I'm Maya - infra. We've got about 15 minutes to go over the high level then we'll bring in the internal network folks if needed.
[00:27] Tom Ellis: Tom here. main things for us: data residency for eu, some apac clusters later, and we need static egress IPs or a known egress set so our firewalls can be updated.
[00:39] Ben Cho: Great, that's exactly what we usually start with. can I ask what your current cloud provider footprint looks like? single account or multi-account?
[00:48] Joan Marquez: multi-account on AWS, we've got central transit in a hub account using TGW, then app VPCs in each region.
[00:56] Ben Cho: ok, TGW is fine. do you have any policy that prevents VPC peering across accounts?
[01:05] Maya Singh: We generally avoid cross-account peering for management reasons, prefer privatelink and TGW. peering is allowed but our security team flags it as harder to manage.
[01:13] Ravi Patel: yeah, peering is OK technically but change control is heavier. we prefer endpoints we can manage via central account.
[01:20] Alice Ramos: Understood. so Redwood Private can be deployed in a couple of shapes: a VPC in your account with private endpoints to our control plane, or we can host a customer-dedicated VPC and peer it - both have tradeoffs. Ben, do you want to run the topology?
[01:33] Ben Cho: Sure. Option A: PrivateLink-style endpoints — you create an interface endpoint in your VPC that talks to a private endpoint we provision in our controlled environment. That avoids peering and fits TGW routing. Option B: direct VPC peering across accounts for lower per-request latency and simpler routing, but requires you to accept peering and manage CIDR overlap. Option C: host Redwood nodes in your VPC as a customer-managed private deployment (on-prem style) - more work but full data plane control.
[02:02] Tom Ellis: latency is a moderate concern. our inference traffic is bursty; we want to keep tail latency under 120ms 95th for small prompts in region. Does the PrivateLink add meaningful latency?
[02:14] Ben Cho: In our benchmarks PrivateLink adds typically 10-25ms depending on region, peering can shave that so peering is lowest latency. But PrivateLink is operationally simpler for teams that won't accept peering.
[02:25] Joan Marquez: Another constraint: our CIDRs overlap with some vendor ranges. we use 10.0.0.0/8 internally in many accounts - so peering could be messy.
[02:33] Maya Singh: yeah overlap is the killer. We can carve out a /22 for external connectivity if needed but we'd need approvals.
[02:41] Lena Park: If you can carve a /22 for the onramp that usually makes peering a lot simpler. otherwise PrivateLink is the fallback.
[02:50] Ravi Patel: On the security front, we need KMS integration, so keys are customer-managed for any data-at-rest, and an audit log for every request. SOC2 is a must. can redwood support a customer KMS or HSM?
[03:03] Ben Cho: We support customer-managed keys via KMS integration for sensitive artifacts. For Private we can support envelope encryption where you control the master key, and we store material encrypted. HSM is a little more bespoke, but we've done HSM integrations for customers — need to scope.
[03:16] Tom Ellis: And the logs — we prefer forwarding audit logs to our SIEM. Is there a log-forwarding option?
[03:23] Alice Ramos: Yes, we have audit log streaming (S3 or syslog) and you can forward to your SIEM. we'll include the runbook showing fields and retention.
[03:32] Maya Singh: What about region constraints? we can't have data egress to us-east for EU workloads. We need the inference to stay in eu-west-1 for EU customers.
[03:42] Ben Cho: Absolutely. Redwood Private can be deployed per-region. for EU-only workloads we can pin model endpoints to eu-west-1 nodes and not route across regions. We also support a region-gating policy at routing layer.
[03:55] Joan Marquez: Do you have a list of supported regions and matrix of latency/cost per region?
[04:01] Ben Cho: We'll share a region matrix. quick note — APAC presence is still expanding; for APAC we usually recommend a nearby dedicated cluster or using a partner colo.
[04:12] Tom Ellis: Ok. One more — our security team requires SAML SSO with SCIM and RBAC integration for auditability. support?
[04:20] Alice Ramos: Yes SSO via SAML/OIDC + SCIM provisioning, role-based access controls in the console, and token-level audit trails. we'll attach the SSO integration guide.
[04:30] Ravi Patel: Thanks. network ops will want to see exact port lists and egress IP ranges. can you provide static egress IPs or a publishable set?
[04:39] Ben Cho: For private deployments we can publish a set of egress IPs per deployment. for hosted we have dynamic pools so not guaranteed; for dedicated/private we can reserve elastic IPs and give them to you.
[04:51] Maya Singh: And TLS termination - do you handle certs or does customer manage?
[04:57] Lena Park: We support both. by default Redwood terminates TLS in our control plane, but if you want certs behind your load balancer in your VPC we can accommodate mutual TLS or customer certs on the endpoint.
[05:11] Tom Ellis: What about autoscaling? if we burst do you have a warm pool or gradual ramp? we don't want cold starts to affect latency.
[05:20] Ben Cho: For Private we support warm node pools and pre-warming policies; we also support burst capacity for unexpected peaks. for Dedicated deployments you can set reserved capacity. we'll include suggested autoscale policy configs.
[05:33] Joan Marquez: Can we do canary routing or fallback to a smaller model in case of capacity constraints?
[05:39] Ben Cho: Yes traffic routing can fallback to a smaller quantized model in same region. Redwood supports automatic fallback policies and canary rollouts for model versions.
[05:50] Maya Singh: Ok great. Now the practical ask - if we do PrivateLink into our TGW, how's DNS handled? we need internal DNS entries so our apps call a friendly name.
[06:00] Lena Park: With interface endpoints you create a DNS CNAME to the endpoint or use private hosted zones. we provide guidance; if you're using TGW, you may need conditional forwarding in your resolver. we've seen customers push a private hosted zone into the shared resolver.
[06:13] Ravi Patel: Is there any issue with cross-account DNS resolution? we prefer not to open broader resolver permissions.
[06:19] Ben Cho: You can keep DNS scoped, we typically recommend creating private hosted zones in the TGW's route for consistent resolution. that's part of the topology sketch we'll send.
[06:28] Alice Ramos: Quick devops question — do you have specific ports locked down? e.g., will we need to open 443 only or also gRPC ports?
[06:36] Joan Marquez: Our corporate policy only allows 443 outbound to vendor endpoints unless there's a strong reason.
[06:41] Ben Cho: 443 is sufficient for typical inference traffic; we can multiplex over HTTPS so no extra ports needed.
[06:47] Maya Singh: One complexity — we have dedicated on-prem racks that talk to cloud via a VPN. if we wanted a hybrid deployment (some nodes on-prem, some in cloud) is that possible?
[06:58] Ben Cho: Yes hybrid is possible. we support on-prem connectors that register with the control plane over a secure tunnel; model weights can be pinned locally and inference stays local. For heavy data locality customers this is a common pattern.
[07:12] Tom Ellis: That would help with APAC latency but increases ops. might be a phase 2.
[07:18] Alice Ramos: timeline — what are you targeting for a pilot?
[07:21] Tom Ellis: We'd like to run a pilot in oct-nov timeframe, with a small footprint in eu-west-1. execs want a cost/latency readout and SOC2 paperwork before green light.
[07:31] Alice Ramos: Sounds good. Ben we'll prepare an initial topology + cost estimate for eu-west-1, and security pack.
[07:38] Ben Cho: i'll also note we need the CIDR ranges you mentioned and whether TGW can host the endpoint.

[08:12] Ben Cho: If you route through NATs you need to ensure they scale. we often avoid NAT bottlenecks by placing endpoints in the TGW peering path or assigning static egress IPs from a dedicated NAT. we'll detail best practices.
[08:25] Ravi Patel: Ok. A compliance detail: can Redwood attest to data deletion — if we request logs/artifacts removed, is that supported?
[08:33] Lena Park: We support retention policies and also support on-demand deletion for customer data. Deletion is auditable and we'll include the retention API.
[08:43] Tom Ellis: Are there any SLA numbers for Private? uptime/latency SLAs?
[08:48] Alice Ramos: For Private deployments we offer SLA-backed SLAs on availability and latency tiers on Dedicated contracts. For pilot we'll propose a standard uptime pledge and discuss higher SLAs for enterprise term.
[08:59] Maya Singh: A small nit - we need to know whether the control plane ever sees plaintext data or if it's all encrypted client-side prior to sending.
[09:08] Ben Cho: By default payloads are encrypted in transit. if you need end-to-end encryption we can discuss client-side encryption options, but that can limit some control-plane features like evals. we'll include a write-up.

Q2 Capacity & Cost Playbook - Peregrine Retail QBR

Quarterly business review focused on right-sizing Peregrine's committed GPU capacity, cost tradeoffs between hosted and dedicated, and an operational playbook for burst surges. Agreed to run benchmarks with representative traffic, exchange traces, and produce a short decision memo for execs by early April.
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-31 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Liam Harper (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jorge Alvarez (CSM) — Dana Li (Head of ML), Markus Reiner (Platform), Sofia Patel (CTO), Asha Mehta (Prod Ops)

Summary: (auto) QBR focused on capacity, cost playbook, pilot plan.

[00:00] Liam Harper: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we know it's end of quarter so we'll keep it tight. This is Liam from Redwood, joined by Priya and Jorge. How are you all?
[00:08] Dana Li: Hi Liam, doing good, short week here. Thanks for setting this up.
[00:11] Sofia Patel: Afternoon, thanks. We've got a few execs in back-to-back but we'll try to stay through the key sections.
[00:16] Priya Nair: Great, quick agenda — usage trends, cost drivers, dedicated vs hosted scenarios, and an ops playbook for surge days. Then we can go into the benchmark plan.
[00:27] Markus Reiner: Sounds good. We're most worried about the holiday sale spikes — last November we saw large latency tail and costs doubled, so we want a predictable plan.
[00:36] Liam Harper: Totally, that's our focus. Jorge will own the health dashboard changes so you get proactive alerts during spikes.

--- Topics: Recent usage and forecasts ---
[00:45] Dana Li: Quick context: our prod traffic moved from 120 to 460 qps since January, embeddings are used heavily for search rerank which drove token consumption. Token mix is roughly 60% short prompts under 64 tokens, 30% mid-length 64-512, 10% long.
[01:06] Priya Nair: Helpful, that token distribution helps with batching and quant recommendations. If most are short, we can squeeze more concurrency with batching and reduce per-token cost.
[01:18] Asha Mehta: We also have a new personalization feature that sends prefetch embeddings at login which increases baseline.
[01:24] Liam Harper: OK noted, that's the steady-state delta. Two levers for spikes: burst capacity on Dedicated or fall back to hosted for elasticity.

[01:35] Sofia Patel: Before we dig deep — high level ask from our execs: can we have a 99.9% latency SLO for customer facing endpoints and a cost bucket that doesn't blow up during sales?
[01:46] Priya Nair: 99.9% is achievable but depends on your capacity commit and routing policies. For burst-heavy events we recommend a hybrid: a small Dedicated pool for baseline throughput and use Hosted as overflow with smart routing. That gives predictability and elasticity.

--- Discussion: Cost modeling and tradeoffs ---
[02:12] Markus Reiner: Walk us through numbers. Right now our invoice shows a lot of tokens billed at higher-long sequence rates during spikes.
[02:20] Liam Harper: Yes, especially with long-tail auth calls and debugging traces — one approach is to use a cheaper quantized variant for non-critical paths. Priya, can you explain quant profiles?
[02:30] Priya Nair: Sure. We surface model variants: full fp16 high-fidelity, int8 quantized for cost savings, and smaller distilled checkpoints. For retrieval/embedding only flows, int8 or bfloat quant gives 30-50% token cost reduction. For generation with safety-critical output we keep fp16. There's also continuous batching and KV cache reuse we can enable to avoid re-computing prefixes.
[02:53] Dana Li: Is there accuracy drift with int8 for our LLM? Our prompt-sensitive scoring for recommendations is sensitive.
[03:00] Priya Nair: It can introduce minor off-by-word differences, usually fine for ranking and short responses. For high-precision scoring we can A/B run for a week — Redwood Optimize can run the evals on your prompt set.

[03:12] Sofia Patel: How about autoscale lead times? Our infra team worries about scaling from 100 to 1k QPS in minutes.
[03:20] Priya Nair: Dedicated autoscaling can add nodes quickly if configured with burst policies; practical lead time is typically 60-180 seconds to warm new GPUs, but we rely on warm pools and prefix caching to reduce that. For immediate needs, routing to Hosted gives sub-second elasticity.

[03:38] Markus Reiner: Sounds like we need a playbook: what routes to take when threshold X is hit. Can Redwood provide that?
[03:44] Jorge Alvarez: Yes, we'll provide an operational runbook with thresholds, alert conditions, and rollback steps. We'll also set SLO alert thresholds in the Console.

--- Security and private deployment notes ---
[03:55] Asha Mehta: On VPC/on-prem: if we decide to move to Private, how does peering and auditing work? We need KMS integration and audit logs for PCI scope.
[04:04] Liam Harper: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations, audit logs export to your SIEM, and SSO/SCIM for RBAC. For PCI, we'll need a dedicated account and control plane configuration; our enterprise team has a checklist.
[04:17] Sofia Patel: Any changes to latency expected with Private? We host some nodes in your VPC region.
[04:22] Priya Nair: Latency is primarily network bound; if we collocate inference hosts in the same region and peered VPC, latency delta is small (10-40 ms depending on topology). We'll confirm with benchmarks.

--- Mid-call: benchmark plan and pilot scope ---
[04:38] Liam Harper: Ok drilling into the pilot: goal is to measure end-to-end P95 and cost at scale using one week of representative traces. Priya will run three scenarios: baseline, sale-burst, and long-sequence heavy.
[04:50] Priya Nair: For each scenario we'll measure: throughput, P50/P95/P99, cost per 1k tokens, and tail latencies. We'll also test routing fallback to hosted and confirm KV cache hit rates.
[05:03] Dana Li: We'll provide sample traces and a week of traffic, but need to scrub PII.
[05:09] Asha Mehta: Yes we'll anonymize personally identifiable fields. Markus will own that.

[05:16] Markus Reiner: Quick ops note — we have maintenance windows Fri 02:00-04:00 UTC. Can tests avoid those?
[05:21] Priya Nair: We'll coordinate windows in the calendar invite; target week-of Apr-12 as proposed.

--- Transcript continues with timestamps, slightly noisy recognition ---
[05:35] [Speaker 2] Liam Harper: One more thing — we'll provide two capacity proposals: (A) Dedicated pool sized to hit 99.9% SLO without hosted overflow, (B) Smaller Dedicated + Hosted overflow and expected cost delta.
[05:50] [Speaker 3] Dana Li: It'd be good to see a short exec one-pager for both options, with break-even usage.
[05:56] Liam Harper: Noted. We'll include break-even lines and sensitivity to daily active users and median sequence length.

[06:10] [00:06:10] Priya Nair: There's also request-level caching for repeated prompts — can reduce token count for quick Q&A flows. If you have large prefix reuse, we can get 20-35% savings.
[06:22] [00:06:22] Asha Mehta: We do have reuse on product detail pages. We'll add that to the sample set.

[06:30] [00:06:30] Sofia Patel: On governance — we need regular audits. How frequently do you rotate keys?
[06:35] [00:06:35] Liam Harper: Key rotation cadence can be controlled by your KMS; our Private offering supports customer-managed rotation and we log all KMS operations. For Hosted, standard rotation policies apply and we can coordinate enterprise options.

[06:48] [00:06:48] Dana Li: Quick question about model variants — can we pin model versions for canary rollouts?
[06:54] [00:06:54] Priya Nair: Yes, Console supports version pinning, gradual rollouts, and automatic fallback if the canary fails. We can set up A/B testing and measure quality regressions against your eval set.

--- Deeper technical exchange; some transcription errors appear ---
[07:12] [00:07:12] Markus Reiner: Do you have any hard limits on concurrent KV cache sizes? We saw cache thrash in our own infra docs — the term came out as K-V cash in the last notes — ha.
[07:23] [00:07:23] Priya Nair: We size per model and per instance. For very large working sets we recommend model sharding or federated cache tiers. We'll share tuning knobs.

[07:40] [00:07:40] Liam Harper: On cost allocation, we can expose token-level tagging so you can attribute spend to product lines which helps with internal chargebacks.
[07:49] [00:07:49] Dana Li: Nice. That will help when we show finance the predicted monthly burn for the holiday spike.

[08:05] [00:08:05] Priya Nair: Also, Redwood Optimize will generate batching and quant suggestions per workload. We can run those against your sample prompts and show the expected savings.
[08:14] [00:08:14] Sofia Patel: How long does Optimize analysis take? We need a quick turnaround for the exec memo.
[08:18] [00:08:18] Priya Nair: For a ~10k-prompt set it's usually 24-48 hours with a small compute job. We'll queue it once we have the traces.

[08:30] [00:08:30] Jorge Alvarez: We'll also add a pre-configured dashboard with P95, P99, cost per 1k tokens, and anomaly detection for usage spikes.

--- Mid-Meeting Clarifications and Objections ---
[08:42] [00:08:42] Markus Reiner: Exec asks: what if Hosted provider limits are hit during a global sale and both hosted and dedicated degrade? Any fallback?
[08:51] [00:08:51] Liam Harper: In extreme multi-region outages we recommend multi-region Dedicated + geo-routing. We can also provide degraded-mode responses (short answers, lower sampling) as a graceful degradation plan.
[09:03] [00:09:03] Dana Li: What's the expected delta in developer effort to support a hybrid route?
[09:07] [00:09:07] Priya Nair: Minimal — the API surface is identical. The main work is in routing policy config and tagging. We'll help with a rollout plan and SDK flag toggles.

[09:20] [00:09:20] Sofia Patel: Any compliance blockers for our regional customers in EU? Data residency?
[09:26] [00:09:26] Liam Harper: We have region controls and can keep inference and logs in EU regions on Redwood Private. For Hosted, we have region pinned endpoints and data residency options for enterprise contracts.

--- Action plan and wrap-up section ---
[09:38] [00:09:38] Liam Harper: To recap — action items: Peregrine shares traces; Redwood runs Optimize and baseline benchmarks; Redwood delivers capacity proposals and an ops runbook; Jorge will set dashboard and alerts; target decision memo by 2027-04-05.
[09:54] [00:09:54] Dana Li: That timeline works. One ask — include a short paragraph comparing break-even for int8 quant vs fp16 at our current usage.
[10:03] [00:10:03] Liam Harper: We'll include that.
[10:07] [00:10:07] Markus Reiner: Also show cost if we enable prefix caching at 30% hit rates versus 60% hit rates so we can see sensitivity.
[10:13] [00:10:13] Priya Nair: Good call. We'll run two cache hit scenarios.

[10:20] [00:10:20] Sofia Patel: Last thing — can we have a short security call next week to run through the PCI checklist?
[10:25] [00:10:25] Jorge Alvarez: Absolutely, I'll follow up with available times.

[10:31] [00:10:31] Liam Harper: Great. Any other questions from the team?
[10:34] [00:10:34] Asha Mehta: No, all good.
[10:36] [00:10:36] Dana Li: No, thanks.

[10:39] [00:10:39] Liam Harper: Thanks everyone — we'll send the updated proposal and invite for the benchmarks.
[10:44] [00:10:44] Sofia Patel: Thanks. Bye.

[(rest of meeting: detailed technical asides and clarifications, benchmark scheduling logistics, and brief Q&A) — timestamps continue intermittently for the remaining 40 minutes below — transcription contains small recognition errors, filler words, and occasional overlapping talk]

[15:00] [00:15:00] Priya Nair: (technical) We'll record kernel and memory metrics during the bench so you can see model-level GPU efficiency, and we'll correlate token cost to actual GPU utilization.
[15:18] [00:15:18] Markus Reiner: Perfect, that's what we need to show infra.

[20:45] [00:20:45] Dana Li: For dataset privacy we will scrub any order ids but keep event timings so the spike pattern remains.
[21:02] [00:21:02] Priya Nair: That's fine. Our bench harness accepts anonymized traces.

[28:30] [00:28:30] Liam Harper: We'll include a short appendix on model fallback policies — which model variants to pick per route.

[33:12] [00:33:12] Asha Mehta: Who owns the decision to enable hosted overflow? Is that on platform or product?
[33:18] [00:33:18] Sofia Patel: Exec will sign off; Platform will implement. We'll present both options to them.

[39:55] [00:39:55] Priya Nair: One last technical note — if you have on-the-fly personalization we recommend precomputing embedding deltas to reduce inference calls during sale days.

[45:30] [00:45:30] Jorge Alvarez: I'll create the dashboard and add the alert runbook to Confluence.

[49:00] [00:49:00] Liam Harper: Ok final recap and next steps in chat. Thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
