document.content:
Pinecrest Biotech - p95 streaming & concurrency discovery

Initial discovery focused on Pinecrest's target p95 latency for streaming inference, concurrency needs for clinical real-time assistants, and options across Redwood Hosted/Dedicated/Private. Customer has strict data residency and SOC2 requirements; they are evaluating a pilot against a 500ms p95 target for 2k-token streaming responses at 75 concurrent streams with burst to 200 concurrent. Action: send benchmark template, share SOC2/KMS docs, schedule pilot kickoff.
Lena Ortiz: send performance benchmarking spreadsheet and example prompt set by 2028-03-01
Amir Shah: draft streaming token/sec test plan and cluster config suggestions by 2028-03-03
Anika Bose (Pinecrest): share representative prompt set (25 prompts) and current perf logs by 2028-03-02
Schedule Dedicated pilot kickoff (requested date window 2028-03-07 to 2028-03-09)
Provide SOC2 and KMS/HSM integration docs
Provision test API key and 100k test tokens for benchmarking
Share sample performance dashboard and tracing snippet
[00:00] Lena (Redwood): Hi everyone — thanks for joining, I'm Lena, AE on this account. Happy to kick off. Am I okay to introduce Amir who's going to take the technical deep dive?
[00:12] Amir (Redwood-SE): Hey, hi — Amir here. We'll talk through latency and throughput tradeoffs, streaming behavior, and deployment options (hosted/dedicated/private).
[00:18] Dr. Maya (Pinecrest): Thanks. Quick context: Pinecrest builds an on-call clinical assistant that summarizes patient notes and streams step-by-step guidance to clinicians — low-latency is critical. We target p95 under 500 milliseconds for the typical 1.5–2k token output, and often have 75 sustained concurrent clinicians, with expected bursts up to ~200.
[00:40] Carlos (Pinecrest): We run a mix of cloud infra and our own GPU rack for other workloads, currently using Triton for some models. We don't want to manage kernel-level infra for this if we can avoid it. Also, data residency — all patient data must stay in our VPC or on-prem.
[01:05] Lena: Great, so main constraints are 500ms p95 for ~2k tokens, 75 steady concurrency, burst to 200, and VPC/on-prem requirement. Is that right?
[01:12] Dr. Maya: Yes that's right. Also SOC2 Type II required, SSO via SAML, and KMS integration for keys.
[01:22] Amir: Cool. Quick question on model: are you looking at smaller encoder-decoder models or large decoder-only? Which model family are you evaluating?
[01:30] Anika (Pinecrest): We're experimenting with a 30B LLM tuned for clinical summarization, quantized to 4-bit for cost. In experiments we see decent quality but latency increases with bigger contexts. We also have a shorter prompt path for high-priority alerts.
[01:46] Amir: OK — 30B quantized is a reasonable sweet spot. For streaming 2k tokens — two knobs matter: per-token generation latency (kernel perf and kv-cache) and application-level batching/concurrency.
[01:58] Speaker 4: [murmur]
[02:02] Amir: To hit 500ms p95 for 2k tokens you basically need sustained token throughput ~4k–6k tokens/sec end-to-end when you account for network/overhead, depending on decoding method. Does that align with your internal numbers?
[02:16] Anika: Our rough internal is more like 2–3k tokens/sec for single-stream on our quantized stack, p95 around 700–900ms at 2k tokens. So we'd need about 2x improvement.
[02:30] Lena: Important note: hosted vs dedicated changes the math. Redwood Hosted can give you fastest time-to-value and we tune kernels per model, but Dedicated (reserved GPU pools) gives you more predictable tail at scale and you can isolate KV/cache warming. Private (VPC/on-prem) gives full data residency but may require additional tuning for kernel choices.
[02:58] Dr. Maya: Curious on the warm vs cold cache behavior — our clinicians will open a patient record and then stream — some prompts share prefixes, others are unique. How much does KV cache reduce p95 in your experience?
[03:15] Amir: KV cache can dramatically reduce repeated prefix costs. For streaming where outputs are generated token-by-token, if you can reuse the KV for the shared prompt prefix, you save the encode cost; we've seen 20–40% p95 improvement in many workloads. But cache hit rate depends on prompt similarity and session design.
[03:34] Carlos: What about batching? I assume batching helps throughput but hurts single-stream p95?
[03:41] Amir: Exactly. Continuous batching increases aggregate tokens/sec (good for cost), but batching delay must be bounded for low p95. Our runtime supports adaptive batching: it will only batch up to a per-request max latency budget, so you get some throughput benefit without blowing p95.
[03:56] Dr. Maya: We prefer consistent p95 over cost savings — clinicians can't wait. So we'd likely pick policies that prioritize latency.
[04:05] Anika: Also interested in fallback behaviors — if Dedicated capacity is saturated, what's the fallback?
[04:11] Lena: You can configure automatic fallback to a cheaper model variant or a different region. For mission-critical clinical flows you can configure prioritized capacity and autoscale thresholds; we also support canary rollouts and graceful degradation (e.g., shorten response length or switch to a compact model).
[04:28] Amir: One note — switching to a smaller model reduces quality; for clinical summarization that can change safety. So we recommend canary A/B tests and quality monitors tied to prompt sets.
[04:40] Carlos: Security check — if we pick Redwood Private VPC, is audit loging and KMS integration available? We need HSM-backed keys in our KMS.
[04:50] Lena: Yes, Private includes customer-managed KMS/HSM integration and retention of audit logs in your environment. We also provide SOC2 artifacts for hosted and support dedicated compliance packages for Private. We'll share the docs.
[05:01] Dr. Maya: Thanks. On specifics — could you walk through a sizing example? Say 75 concurrent steady streams, each producing 15 tokens/sec on average, bursts to 200 where tokens/sec doubles. How do we map that to GPU counts and latency?
[05:15] Amir: Sure — simplistic mapping: tokens/sec per GPU depends on model and quantization. For a 30B 4-bit quantized model we might see 30k–60k tokens/sec on an A100-like instance with optimized kernels for streaming; that translates to roughly 400–800 sustained single-streams at 15 tokens/sec for throughput alone, but tail behavior and context length reduce effective capacity. For p95 < 500ms you need headroom — so for 75 steady streams you'd be safe on Dedicated with 1–2 GPUs depending on real decoding speed and KV cache hit. For bursts to 200, we'd recommend autoscale + burst buffer capacity or an extra GPU standby to absorb the burst.
[06:05] Anika: That seems optimistic vs our numbers. We only saw 10k tokens/sec on our quantized Triton racks. Are your kernels that much faster?
[06:14] Amir: Two factors: kernel-level optimizations (attention kernels, fused ops), and runtime KV cache and continuous decoding pipelines. Also, metric differences: we report raw decode token/sec excluding some wrapper overhead; your Triton pipeline might include copying, grpc overhead, and data pre/post-processing. We'll run a benchmark to align numbers.
[06:33] Speaker 4: [crosstalk]
[06:38] Lena: We'll provide a benchmark template so we can replicate your current test and then run Redwood-hosted comparatives. That will help identify where the 2x gap is.
[06:47] Dr. Maya: On data residency, if we do Hosted for the benchmark, can we mask or synthetic-ize data? Also, how do you handle PHI during tests?
[06:56] Lena: Synthetic prompts are fine and preferred for hosted initial tests. For real PHI we recommend Private or Dedicated with VPC peering. For hosted we can also sign a BAA as part of an enterprise agreement but Private affords the strongest controls.
[07:13] Amir: Also note, network latency from clinician device to region matters for p95. If clinicians are in eastern US, pick the same region; regional routing reduces network tail.
[07:24] Carlos: We have clinicians across US timezones; can we route by region automatically?
[07:28] Amir: Yes — smart routing policies can send requests to nearest region and fall back to nearest available capacity. That reduces p99 network spikes.
[07:36] Dr. Maya: Can you explain streaming framing and server-sent events? We need token-by-token echoes to the UI fast.
[07:42] Amir: Redwood supports chunked HTTP streaming and gRPC streaming. For SSE/HTTP chunking we push tokens as they're produced. The per-token latency includes model decode time and network flush frequency; flushing too often increases overhead. We recommend batching small groups of tokens per network flush (e.g., every 20–50ms) to balance latency and throughput.
[08:05] Anika: What's the overhead of continuous batching on single-stream p95?
[08:09] Amir: If you set batching window to 20ms, you might incur ~20ms of added latency worst-case plus decode time. But that helps throughput by allowing other requests to piggyback. Again, adaptive batching attempts to keep within your SLO.
[08:20] Lena: Quick poll — are you leaning Hosted for faster trial or Dedicated/Private because of data controls?
[08:26] Dr. Maya: For a proof-of-concept we might start with Hosted with synthetic prompts to validate latency. For production we'd likely need Private or Dedicated in our VPC.
[08:37] Carlos: Agreed — but we'd want to validate the kernel perf first.
[08:41] Amir: Good. For the benchmark we'll need: your prompt set, typical context lengths, target p95, concurrency profile (ramp up pattern), and output length distribution.
[08:52] Anika: We can share a redacted prompt set and a small sample of logs. We'll aim to get that by next Thursday.
[08:59] Lena: Perfect. We will also share a sample dashboard with token-level latency and p95 plots to match your telemetry.
[09:07] Dr. Maya: A question on model variants — can Redwood run quantized 4-bit models with KV cache intact?
[09:13] Amir: Yes, our runtime supports 4-bit quantized weights and the KV caching remains the same; some quantization schemes trade a bit of per-token time for reduced memory. We will include a quantization profile recommendation in the test plan.
[09:27] Carlos: Regarding SLOs — do you offer an SLA for p95 or uptime for Dedicated?
[09:31] Lena: Dedicated has SLA options for uptime and latency targets depending on contract tier. For p95 latency contractual SLOs we typically define measurement windows and allowed degradation; this is something we can scope in an enterprise agreement.
[09:44] Speaker 4: [laughter]
[09:47] Anika: Another operational question: do you provide token-level tracing to correlate spikes to prompt or model behavior?
[09:53] Amir: Yes — Redwood Console provides per-request traces, tokenization breakdown, model step timing, and per-route metrics. We can instrument your test prompts to tag where spikes occur.
[10:06] Dr. Maya: How do you handle throttles? We can't have requests dropped mid-stream.
[10:11] Amir: Throttling policy is configurable. For mission-critical streams we can enable prioritized lanes, queueing with guaranteed retries, or graceful truncation fallback that returns partial summary instead of dropping. We avoid mid-stream drops by design.
[10:25] Carlos: For sizing again — is there a recommended margin of safety for the fleet? 30%?
[10:30] Amir: We typically recommend 30–50% headroom for streaming workloads because tails can be spiky and decoding cost can vary with token content. For your clinical case I'd push toward 50% to start, then optimize once we have benchmark data.
[10:44] Lena: Quick note on billing: Hosted is usage-based per token, Dedicated is committed reserved capacity with overage billing options, Private has platform fees plus infra costs. We'll send a pricing matrix.
[10:56] Dr. Maya: Could Redwood provide a short-run dedicated pilot (1–2 GPUs) for us to test in our VPC?
[11:03] Lena: Yes — we can provision a Dedicated sandbox in your VPC or a Private deployment for a pilot. We'll propose a Dedicated pilot to start because it's faster operationally and still gives isolation.
[11:14] Anika: If we do Dedicated, how quickly can autoscale respond to bursts? Seconds? Minutes?
[11:20] Amir: Autoscale depends on provisioning model and cloud capacity. We have rapid scaling for short bursts via warm pools (seconds to low minutes) and longer provisioning for adding new GPU nodes (minutes). For predictable bursts we'd recommend warm standby capacity or burst credits.
[11:36] Dr. Maya: Any hidden gotchas with tokenization differences across models which might affect token counts and cost?
[11:42] Amir: Yes — tokenization differences can change token counts by up to 10–20% depending on model tokenizer. We'll standardize on the tokenizer used in the model during the benchmark.
[11:51] Carlos: Ok, can we see a sample benchmark plan now?
[11:54] Amir: I'll describe at a high level: 1) replicate your current test in Hosted Redwood with synthetic prompts, 2) run single-stream latency tests across prompt lengths, 3) ramp concurrency tests to 75 then burst to 200 while measuring p50/p95/p99 and token/sec, 4) test KV cache hit/miss by grouping similar prefixes, 5) try quantization variant and record quality delta. We'll provide exact scripts.
[12:25] Anika: How do we measure p95 for streaming? Do you measure until stream end or rolling p95 per N tokens?
[12:32] Amir: We measure end-to-end p95 for the full response completion. For longer outputs we also provide per-token latency distributions so you can see if later tokens have different tails.
[12:45] Dr. Maya: Good. One more question — do you support client-side aggregation to reduce network chattiness? Like chunking tokens into 50-token batches?
[12:53] Amir: Yes, client-side can aggregate but that increases perceived latency. We generally recommend server-side controlled flush intervals to manage network overhead while maintaining low apparent latency.
[13:05] Lena: We're about halfway through — any outstanding security questions?
[13:09] Carlos: Need the SOC2 artifact and our legal will want deployment architecture for Private.
[13:13] Lena: We'll attach SOC2 report and sample architecture.
[13:17] Dr. Maya: Timeline: if benchmarks look good we'd like a pilot in March and production by June. Can Redwood support that?
[13:24] Lena: Yes — typical pilot-to-prod timeline for Dedicated/Private is 6–12 weeks depending on integrations; March pilot and June prod is achievable.
[13:33] Speaker 4: [mutter]
[13:36] Amir: A practical suggestion — start the benchmark on Hosted with synthetic prompts this week, then move to Dedicated sandbox in your VPC for PHI-sensitive tests. That reduces risk and speeds feedback.
[13:49] Anika: Sounds good. On quality monitoring — can Redwood tie regressions to prompt sets so we can roll back models?
[13:55] Amir: Yes, Redwood Optimize can create prompt-based evals and alert on regressions per rollout. We'll include an eval harness in the plan.
[14:06] Dr. Maya: Anything else on concurrency shaping?
[14:09] Amir: Just that request prioritization and graceful degradation are key: for example, mark clinical-critical flows as high-priority and enable fallback rules for lower-priority batch jobs.
[14:21] Carlos: Ok let's capture next steps.
[14:24] Lena: Action items recap — I'll send the perf spreadsheet and SOC2/KMS docs; Amir will send the benchmark plan; Anika will share prompts and sample logs. We'll try to kick off the Hosted benchmark the week of 2028-03-01 and schedule a Dedicated pilot for the week of 2028-03-07.
[14:40] Dr. Maya: That aligns. Thank you.
[14:43] Lena: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the artifacts.
[14:48] [END OF TRANSCRIPT]

Notes on transcript quality: Autogenerated transcript had a few mis-hearings on kernel names (Triton vs Tri-ton) and product names (Redwood Dedicated sometimes heard as Redwood Dedicate). There is occasional speaker label drift.

References mentioned during call: "performance benchmarking spreadsheet (link)"; "SOC2 report (link)"; "KMS/HSM integration doc (link)"; "sample Redwood Console dashboard (link)"

Skybound — time-to-first-token playbook & credits discussion

Intro discovery for Skybound's quickstart path: evaluate Redwood hosted for initial PLG trial, discuss free credits, TTFT (time-to-first-token) and privacy constraints; surface security checklist and next steps for a short pilot.
PLG quickstart and free credits
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private fit
Security/compliance (SOC2, SSO, KMS)
Time-to-first-token (sandbox account, SDKs)
Perf expectations and sample workloads
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-01-05 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52m
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes

Attendees:
- Maya Chen (Redwood AE)
- Owen Brooks (Redwood SE)
- Luis Ortega (Skybound, CTO)
- Nadia Li (Skybound, Lead ML Eng)
- Samir Rao (Skybound, Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Discussed onboarding playbook, asked about private deployment windows and credit allocation; agreed to pilot with hosted API first and dial to dedicated if throughput increases.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, this is Owen our SE. How's everyone's morning?
[00:10] Luis: Morning. All good. Just back from a late deploy, so, uh, hoping this call is short.
[00:15] Owen: Cool, we'll keep it tight. Quick agenda — we want to understand your success criteria, give a sense for time-to-first-token using the hosted API, and cover security questions.
[00:25] Samir: Sounds good. High level — our product team wants a way to prototype features with minimal infra work. PLG quickstart sounds like the right fit.
[00:34] Nadia: And we need to be clear on what data hits the service — not allowed to store pII, and we have to meet our SOC2 pre-audit before April.
[00:42] Maya: Totally, that's expected. For PLG, we typically provision a sandbox org with free credits — that gets you to a first call within an hour usually. Owen will walk through the SDK path.
[00:55] Owen: Briefly — we have REST plus SDKs (python/js). The SDK will create an API key that you can swap in your staging. There's a one-click sandbox provision we can do; it maps to a hosted tenant with isolated usage.
[01:10] Luis: One thing — our traffic shape could spike for short bursts. How do you handle burst vs sustained throughput?
[01:18] Owen: Hosted has autoscaling but there are soft rate limits on free sandboxes. For predictable throughput at scale you move to Dedicated — reserved GPUs, predictable qps. For the pilot, hosted with burst allowances is usually fine.
[01:30] Samir: What's the typical latency for a 1k token generation? We care about sub-1s (laughs).
[01:36] Owen: Heh, sub-1s for 1k is optimistic; for a 1k token response it's more like 700–1200 ms per 256 tokens depending on model and hardware and seq length. Also depends on quantization and model variant. We can run a small benchmark with your prompt set.
[01:56] Speaker 1: sorry echoing — can you repeat the kernel bit?
[02:02] Owen: Sure, the runtime picks kernels based on model, sequence length distribution, and hardware — it's basically the back-end optimizer.
[02:12] Nadia: We use a custom reranker and want embeddings too. Any constraints?
[02:18] Maya: Embeddings are supported via the same API. We can share guidance on batching and cost trade-offs.
[02:25] Luis: On compliance, we need to know about data at rest encryption and KMS integration — and whether we can have keys in our KMS for dedicated/private.
[02:34] Owen: For hosted, we encrypt data at rest and in transit; customer-managed keys (KMS) are available for Private deployments and for Dedicated with an enterprise contract. Hosted can also do KMS for enterprise customers, we just need to scope it in the contract.
[02:48] Maya: Also note we have audit logs and token-level cost breakdowns in the console.
[02:54] Samir: Good. Who else on their side needs to be involved? Finance for credits, SecOps for the SOC2 checklist, and platform for any private network access.
[03:04] Luis: Yep. Next, the TTFT — what steps should we expect from us to first token?
[03:10] Owen: Typical path: 1) Create sandbox org (we can do during or immediately after this call), 2) we provision free credits and seed you with example prompts and SDK snippet, 3) you run sample calls, 4) we run an optional small perf test. That is usually achievable in under 2 hours for an engineer once they have the key.
[03:29] Samir: Is there an onboarding doc or playbook?
[03:32] Maya: Yes, we have a Quickstart playbook. Owen — I'll drop the link.
[03:36] Owen: I'll share the quickstart repo and a short checklist. One thing to watch — rate limits on the sandbox default to conservative values to prevent noisy tenants; we can bump them for your pilot after a short validation.
[03:50] Nadia: For the pilot, we want to run 10k token-generations/day across 2 models and a nightly batch of embeddings. Will that blow the sandbox?
[03:58] Owen: That should be fine under credits, but if you need sustained throughput we recommend Dedicated. For now, credits plus a slightly increased sandbox quota should cover it.
[04:08] Luis: If we outgrow hosted, what's the migration path to Dedicated or Private? Downtime?
[04:14] Owen: Migration is primarily configuration and routing; you can pin model versions and route traffic to Dedicated nodes with cutover policies. We do canary first. Downtime is minimal — typically a few minutes for DNS and route changes.
[04:26] Samir: Any regulatory blockers for UE data residency? We have EU customers.
[04:31] Owen: We run in multiple regions. If residency is required, you can pick a region for the deployment or choose Private. We can surface region-specific logs and retention settings.
[04:41] Luis: On pricing — how are credits valued and how do we translate to monthly cost later?
[04:46] Maya: Credits map to tokens/embedding units. We'll send a simple mapping sheet tailored to your expected token usage. For Dedicated it's a commitment-based monthly contract.
[04:56] Speaker 2: (mumble) what about sso?
[05:00] Maya: We support SAML/SSO and SCIM for provisioning in enterprise orgs. That's part of the enterprise onboarding.
[05:08] Nadia: For the security docs, do you have SOC2 and pen test reports to share?
[05:12] Owen: Yes — SOC2 Type II, ISO doc bundles, and a pen-test summary. I'll include those links.
[05:20] Samir: Great. Can we do a short demo of the sandbox API now?
[05:24] Owen: We can, but maybe better to provision first. If you want, Maya can provision the sandbox now and email the creds.
[05:31] Maya: Happy to. Luis, what's the email list for sandbox access?
[05:36] Luis: Send to me and Nadia — louis@skybound.ai and nadia@skybound.ai. Samir cc: samir@skybound.ai.
[05:44] Maya: I'll provision after the call and send the quickstart and a short checklist. Owen will attach perf bench template.
[05:50] Owen: I'll also ask for a small prompt corpus from Nadia to run a benchmark.
[05:55] Nadia: I'll share a redacted set, maybe 50 prompts.
[05:59] Luis: Timeline — we want a pilot live in the next 2 weeks. Is that realistic?
[06:04] Maya: Yes. Sandbox provision today, pilot validation next week, and can expand to a paid pilot or Dedicated after that.
[06:11] Owen: We'll also include guidance on batching and quantization settings to control cost.
[06:16] Samir: Any competitors you've seen customers compare you to?
[06:20] Maya: We often see comparisons to some managed endpoints and vendor X for pricing, and self-hosted open runtimes for private deployments.
[06:27] Luis: Cool. Anything else?
[06:30] Maya: I'll recap next steps in email.
[06:33] (end of call)

Notes on transcription quality: occasional speaker mislabels and some garbled words around kernel/quantization section.

ArgentWave - latency economics & streaming discovery

Discovery focused on p95 latency targets for streaming generation, concurrency model, and a proposed token/sec benchmark across hosted vs dedicated vs private where data residency/KMS matters.
Header: Date: 2026-03-21 16:00 UTC | Duration: 48 mins | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes
Attendees: Liam (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Hannah (Redwood CSM), Maya (ArgentWave CTO), Jules (ML Eng), Noah (Platform Eng), Rita (PM)

Auto-Summary (auto): Discussed p95 targets of 150-250ms for short-response streaming, long-form streaming p95 goals ~700-900ms per turn, concurrency expectations during surge, and a benchmark plan across hosted/dedicated/private. Security questions noted (SOC2, KMS, SAML).

[00:00] Liam: Hey everyone thanks for joining on time, quick intros, we'll try to focus on latency and throughput and then get into streaming token/sec stuff, uh Priya will walk through how we benchmark.
[00:18] Maya: Thanks Liam, we appreciate it. To set context, ArgentWave is rolling out a realtime summarization feature in Q3, target is p95 end-to-end under 300ms for short snippets (<=128 tokens) and acceptable burst to 200 concurrent users. We also have longer workflows for meeting notes where streaming matters.
[00:36] Priya: Cool, that helps. Quick clarifying q — when you say 300ms p95, is that server-side only or end-to-end with network?
[00:45] Maya: End-to-end ideally, but we know network varies. For this talk think server-side p95 target 150-200ms for short snippets, we can add 100ms of client/network.
[01:05] Jules: Also caveat — our frontend does partial rendering so streaming latency matters a lot, token-by-token arrival speed influences UX.
[01:18] Priya: Makes sense. At a high level we support three modes: hosted (our API), dedicated (reserved GPU pools), and private (VPC/on-prem). Each has tradeoffs for latency predictability and data control.
[01:30] Noah: Curious about predictability. During business hours our traffic has diurnal spikes and occasional burst events from internal jobs, we need predictable p95 not just average.
[01:42] Liam: Right, that’s exactly why customers look at dedicated or private — you get reserved capacity and predictable tail. But hosted has quick start and can hit low p95 with smart routing and cache.
[01:56] [noise] Rita: Quick question on cost — how much does burst handling on hosted cost vs dedicated monthly commit?
[02:05] Liam: Short answer: hosted is pay-as-you-go; burst can be handled with burst credits but sustained bursts usually move to dedicated for lower unit cost. We'll send a pricing comparison.
[02:20] Priya: Back to latency: for streaming we measure token throughput in two ways: tokens/sec (steady-state) and token latency (time from request start to first token and inter-token gap). For p95 UX you care about first-token and p95 inter-token gap.
[02:36] Jules: And what about KV cache/prefix caching? We have a lot of repeated context across users so caching could help.
[02:45] Priya: Yes, we do prefix and KV caching in the runtime — that reduces per-token compute and gives big wins on p95 for repeated prompts. For dedicated you can also pin cache in local instance for hot keys.
[02:57] Maya: Do you do automatic batching? We can't have batching increase tail latency beyond p95 targets.
[03:05] Priya: We do continuous batching with latency SLO controls; the runtime will batch within configured latency windows, and we expose batching config and predicted impact. So you can set batching windows tight for p95.
[03:18] Noah: On the private deployment side, what's the network topology expectation and KMS integration?
[03:26] Hannah: For private we provide a control plane and customer-managed networking. We integrate with customer KMS/HSM via standard APIs, support for AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and on-prem HSM options. We also keep audit logs for each request.
[03:40] Jules: Any SOC2 or ISO attestations? Our compliance team will ask.
[03:45] Hannah: Yes, Redwood is SOC2 Type II, and we have SOC2 documentation for customers. For private deployments we have additional controls and can provide architecture review.
[03:56] [crosstalk] Maya: Okay good. On model side — we want to try both base fp16 and 4-bit quantized variants. How does that affect p95 and token/sec?
[04:08] Priya: Quantization reduces memory and increases throughput but may add some decoding overhead depending on kernels. In practice you often see 1.4-2x tokens/sec improvement and small latency delta per token; we can profile. For streaming small models tend to hit first-token faster.
[04:24] Liam: For bench plan we'll test three variants: full fp16, 4-bit quant, and a streaming-optimized runtime with prefix cache. We'll run on hosted and a dedicated mirror.
[04:35] Rita: How long does a benchmark take, and what do you need from us?
[04:40] Priya: Ideally we get your 2k prompt set and a small traffic profile (concurrency bursts, distribution of prompt lengths). Benchmark typically runs several hours to sample tails; we'll do a 1–3 hour run and send raw results + dashboards.
[04:56] Maya: Sounds good. For success criteria, product team wants <300ms end-to-end for short, and 95th percentile inter-token gap under 80ms for streaming.
[05:08] Priya: Noted. We'll capture both server-side and synthetic end-to-end. Server-side p95 goal for short will be targeted at 140-180ms for fp16 and hopefully under 120ms with tuning. Quant results TBD.
[05:23] [00:05:23] Jules: What about multiplexing/connection limits? Our frontend opens many long-lived streaming connections.
[05:31] Liam: We support HTTP/2 and websockets for streaming. For large fanout we recommend using a connection proxy or edge multiplexing to avoid socket exhaustion, and Redwood can recommend connection pooling patterns.
[05:44] Noah: Any throttling or rate-limiting policy we should be aware of?
[05:50] Hannah: By default hosted has rate limits per account; dedicated supports higher qps and custom quotas. You can set per-route quotas and automatic fallback to smaller model variants.
[06:02] Maya: Can fallback be automated? We want graceful degradation to a cheaper model if demand spikes.
[06:07] Priya: Yes, we have routing policies — you can define cost or latency tiers and automatic fallback to a compatible model variant or region. That keeps the system online.
[06:18] [06:18] Rita: About metrics — we need token-level traces, per-request latency breakdown by stage (queue, compute, decode). Is that available in Redwood Console?
[06:28] Liam: Yes, Console exposes token-level cost/latency breakdowns, traces and model-level dashboards. We can give you read-only access to a sample tenant.
[06:38] Jules: On the private side, can we run the same Console integrations or do we need local observability?
[06:45] Hannah: Private provides a control plane that can integrate with your observability stack and we can push metrics to Prometheus/Grafana and provide logs to your SIEM.
[06:55] Maya: Security follow-ups — SAML/SSO and RBAC for teams?
[07:01] Hannah: We support SAML/SSO and fine-grained RBAC; for private we can map to your IdP.
[07:08] [07:08] Priya: Quick note on kernel selection: for certain sequence lengths and architectures we pick optimized kernels, that sometimes changes perf curves — we'll include kernel-level notes in the benchmark results.
[07:22] Jules: Is the benchmark reproducible in our environment? Like can we run the same runner on our infra for private testing?
[07:29] Priya: Yes, we provide a benchmark harness (python runner + config) you can run against our hosted endpoint, a dedicated mirror, or your private cluster. We'll include instructions.
[07:41] [07:41] Noah: Latency SLOs — what SLA coverage exists for p95 latency?
[07:47] Liam: Hosted has best-effort latency SLOs, Dedicated includes SLA-backed uptime and tail latency targets depending on commit tier. We'll share the SLA doc.
[07:58] Rita: And pricing for dedicated — commitment levels and burst credits?
[08:03] Liam: We'll share a table — typical pattern is monthly committed capacity + burst buffer at a premium. Also optional autoscale policies.
[08:14] [08:14] Maya: For long-form streaming (meeting notes) we care about throughput: tokens/sec sustained at 1–2k tokens/sec when batching across many rooms. Can Redwood sustain that on hosted?
[08:27] Priya: Sustained 1–2k tokens/sec is feasible, but hosted multi-tenant environment may add variability. For steady-state at scale we usually recommend dedicated pools to meet sustained throughput with lower variance.
[08:39] Jules: Do you support offloading decode to CPU if GPU gets saturated? We have hybrid infra sometimes.
[08:45] Priya: We have execution paths optimized for both GPU and CPU, but offloading can increase latency; typically we keep decoding on GPU for streaming use cases.
[08:56] [08:56] Noah: Any special considerations for TLS termination in private deployments?
[09:02] Hannah: For private you control TLS at the edge; we can support mTLS between control plane and data plane if needed.
[09:10] Rita: Will you share a sample benchmark report?
[09:14] Priya: Yes — we'll include raw traces, p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec histograms, and kernel profiling.
[09:22] [09:22] Maya: Ok to get into specifics — our prompt distribution: 60% short (<128 tokens), 30% medium (128-512), 10% long (512-2k). Concurrency model: baseline 300 concurrent, burst to 2k for 5-10 minutes.
[09:38] Priya: That's very helpful. We'll simulate traffic with those distributions and a burst pattern. Also test cold-starts for new models and KV cache warm vs cold.
[09:51] Jules: What's the cold-start penalty typically?
[09:54] Priya: Cold-start for large models can add 800ms-2s depending on warmed kernels and cache. We offer warmed instances for dedicated to avoid cold-starts.
[10:06] [10:06] Liam: Quick objection we hear — customers worry quantization will degrade quality. How do you evaluate quality regressions?
[10:14] Maya: Yes quality is a big concern, we can't drop below a certain rouge/accuracy threshold on summarization.
[10:20] Priya: We'll do automated evals on your prompt set and also manual spot checks; Redwood Optimize gives quantization recommendations and regression alerts tied to evals.
[10:33] Hannah: Also you can enable canary rollouts so you test quantized variant on a percentage of traffic and measure regressions.
[10:42] [10:42] Noah: Networking question: during bursts can routing fallback to another region? We have failover needs.
[10:49] Liam: Yes, smart routing can fallback by region or model variant; you can set policies with allowable latency increase during fallback.
[10:58] Rita: How long to stand up a dedicated mirror for benchmark?
[11:02] Priya: We can provision a dedicated mirror in 2–3 business days depending on commit and capacity. For immediate testing we run hosted mirror tests that approximate dedicated.
[11:12] Maya: If we choose private, what's the timeline for deployment? We're aiming to start pilot in 6–8 weeks if everything aligns.
[11:19] Hannah: Private timelines vary but 6–10 weeks is common for VPC-based deployments after contract and infra prep.
[11:27] [11:27] Priya: For the immediate next step we'll run a hosted benchmark and a dedicated mirror run; deliverables will include p50/p95/p99 for first-token and inter-token gaps, tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens for each config, and a decision recommendation.
[11:43] Jules: Can you also include a model of monthly cost given our traffic profile?
[11:47] Liam: Yes — we'll produce a cost model.
[11:50] Maya: Great. Any privacy/data residency concerns with hosted? We have EU customers and need data staying in-region.
[11:58] Hannah: Hosted can pin region; we have Europe regions and can route traffic to EU data centers. For strict residency private is the preferred option.
[12:09] [12:09] Rita: One more on audit logs — retention and format?
[12:13] Hannah: Audit logs can be pushed to your SIEM, retention configurable as an add-on.
[12:19] Priya: Ok final check — what do you want us to prioritize in the benchmark? p95 tails vs cost vs quality?
[12:26] Maya: Priority order: 1) p95 streaming inter-token gap and first-token, 2) sustained tokens/sec during bursts, 3) quality regressions under quantization, 4) cost estimate.
[12:38] Liam: Perfect. We'll follow that order.
[12:42] [12:42] Action recap: Priya runs benchmark, Liam sends pricing and SLA docs, Maya sends prompt corpus. We'll reconvene after results.
[12:51] Maya: Thanks all, this was helpful.
[12:54] Liam: Thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invite for deep-dive and send docs.
[12:59] [End of recording]

document.content:
Capacity sprint kickoff - Sycamore AI POC

Kickoff for a 4-week capacity sprint POC. Aligned on success criteria (latency SLOs, cost targets, quality gates), discussed workload characteristics and proposed reserved+burst architecture. Agreed benchmarks, synthetic trace plan, and timeline. Redwood to run initial load test and share pricing/security docs.
POC scope & timeline
Workload profiling: RT vs batch, seq lengths
Reserved GPU sizing and burst pool strategy
Fallback policies and graceful degradation
Benchmarks: p50/p95/p99 targets, throughput
Security/Compliance asks: SOC2, VPC, KMS
Next steps and deliverables
Jordan Lee - Send POC pricing breakdown + reserved capacity options (due 2026-09-28)
Maya Patel - Share benchmark runbook and sample synthetic trace generator (due 2026-09-27)
Alex Kim - Provide 7-day production query sample and sequence length histogram (due 2026-09-29)
Omar Hassan - Confirm VPC peering requirements and outbound egress policy (due 2026-09-30)
Priya Rao - Provide evaluation prompt set (1000 prompts) and quality pass criteria (due 2026-10-01)
Redwood to stand up an isolated POC environment with reserved GPU pool (proposal in email)
Customer to share traffic traces and evaluation prompts
Schedule bench run week of 2026-10-04 to exercise reserved+burst path
Security review: Redwood to send SOC2/ISO pack and SSO/SAML docs
[00:00:02] Jordan Lee: Alright everybody, thanks for joining. Quick roll call - Jordan from Redwood, Maya SE, Chris on the call.
[00:00:12] Alex Kim: Hey all, Alex here. We wanted to get the POC scoped so we can validate burst strategy for our real-time features.
[00:00:20] Maya Patel: Awesome. Priya, Omar, Tess — do you want to add context on the workload?
[00:00:28] Priya Rao: Sure, so two main surfaces: one is a low-latency inference path for live product (think sub-second targets) and the other is async batch re-ranking that can tolerate higher latency. The live path is 70% of requests but lighter tokens, average seq len ~ 120 tokens. Batch jobs average 1,200 tokens.
[00:00:45] Omar Hassan: Our peak qps is spiky — we see 300 to 1,200 reqs/sec during sale events for a 10–15 minute window. Outside those windows it's 60–100 rps.
[00:00:58] Jordan Lee: Thanks, that helps. So POC goal is to prove a reserved GPU pool can handle baseline RT and that a burst pool covers spikes with graceful fallback. Success criteria we propose: p95 < 300ms for RT under steady load, p95 < 500ms during burst, 99% availability, and cost per 1M tokens below your target.
[00:01:16] Tess Li: On cost, we need to see the numbers. We have a tight threshold — if the burst cost spikes too much it's a problem.
[00:01:23] Chris Nguyen: Totally. We'll present a reserved + burst pricing model. Also options: warm standby instances vs cold queueing for bursts, which have different cost/latency tradeoffs.
[00:01:35] [00:01:40] Priya Rao: Can you run benchmarks against our model? We use a 13B opt variant internally but can test 7B and 13B. Quality delta between 7B and 13B matters for our product.
[00:01:52] Maya Patel: Yes, we'll run both and include quantized 4-bit variants. Note: quantization will reduce cost but sometimes adds subtle quality regressions — we'll include evals against your prompt set.
[00:02:05] Alex Kim: Important: we need VPC/on-prem style network. We'll want peering + private endpoints and KMS/HSM for keys. SOC2 evidence too.
[00:02:15] Jordan Lee: Understood. We'll attach the SOC2 pack and SSO instructions; we support customer-managed KMS for Private deployments. For Hosted POC we can do VPC peering and private endpoints.
[00:02:27] Omar Hassan: For fallback policy: if reserved pool hits capacity, what's the immediate behavior? Queue? Switch to smaller model? Route to another region?
[00:02:36] Maya Patel: Good question — typical recommended policy is tiered fallback: 1) short queue with tokenized reject after X ms, 2) fallback to a smaller/quantized model variant (e.g., 13B -> 7B quant), 3) route to a lower-cost region if latency allows. We can codify that in the POC runbook.
[00:02:52] [00:02:57] Alex Kim: How long to spin up burst GPUs? Cold start times are a concern.
[00:03:01] Chris Nguyen: Warm pools solve that — keeping a small number of GPUs pre-initialized reduces spin-up to ~10–20s, cold cold starts can be 2–4 minutes depending on image pulls and model load. We should capture warm pool sizing in the benchmark.
[00:03:16] Priya Rao: Also KV cache warmup for chat-like workloads — cold KV cache will blow latency on long conversations.
[00:03:24] Maya Patel: We'll instrument prefix/KV cache warm times. Redwood runtime supports automatic KV caching and prefix reuse; we'll include metrics for cache hit ratio.
[00:03:33] Tess Li: For the POC we want a clear pass/fail — maybe quality gate 95% on the prompt eval, p95 latency under 300ms for baseline, and cost under $X per 1M tokens.
[00:03:44] Jordan Lee: Agreed. We'll draft an objective table.
[00:03:50] [00:03:55] Omar Hassan: On autoscale, what cooldowns do you recommend? We don't want oscillation.
[00:03:59] Maya Patel: Typical cooldown 60–120s for horizontal scale, with smoothing windows (e.g., 60s moving average). For GPU-backed services, vertical or warm-pool strategies tend to be better than very aggressive HPA.
[00:04:12] Alex Kim: We'll need traces with 95th/99th percentile breakdowns and token-level cost.
[00:04:17] Chris Nguyen: We'll attach a benchmark spreadsheet with columnar breakdown: tokens, p50/p95/p99, cost per token, GPU utilization. Link: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/sycamore-initial (shared doc).
[00:04:31] [00:04:36] Priya Rao: For dataset — we'll provide seven days of anonymized traces and a 1k prompt eval set.
[00:04:42] Jordan Lee: Timeline proposal: Week 0 (this week) integrate auth + VPC; Week 1 baseline runs with reserved pool; Week 2 burst & warm-pool experiments; Week 3 production-like traffic and final report. That fits 3–4 weeks.
[00:04:59] Tess Li: Who leads the bench runs?
[00:05:02] Maya Patel: Redwood will run the bench runs in collaboration with Sycamore. We'll schedule daily stand-ups the bench week.
[00:05:09] [00:05:15] Alex Kim: Ok, security: SOC2, ISO certs, SSO, RBAC and audit logs. Also long-term logs retention for compliance — we want 365-day audit logs.
[00:05:25] Jordan Lee: We have audit logs and can configure retention tiers; we'll include options and costs in the pack.
[00:05:31] Priya Rao: On metrics: we'll want tracer for token-level timing and per-request model routing decisions (why did a request go to fallback).
[00:05:40] Chris Nguyen: We can surface per-request routing metadata and a model selection trace.
[00:05:45] [00:05:51] Omar Hassan: Edge case: what happens if a single customer tenant spikes and wipes the reserved pool — can we isolate?
[00:05:57] Maya Patel: Yes, we support per-tenant quotas and burst budgets. For Dedicated pools you can have reserved capacity per-tenant and separate burst budgets so noisy neighbors don't affect others.
[00:06:08] Jordan Lee: Let's talk numbers — rough sizing. Based on 70% RT at avg 120 tokens, 300 RPS steady baseline means ~36k tokens/sec = 2.16M tokens/min, which is large. We need to convert to GPU throughput.
[00:06:22] Priya Rao: Our current production average is much lower but we plan to scale. The POC will test 1000 RPS spikes.
[00:06:29] Maya Patel: For rough guidance, a 80GB A100 equivalent can handle approximate X tokens/sec depending on model; we'll run micro-benchmarks to map your sequence length distribution to tokens/sec per GPU. We'll include batch sizes and concurrency tuning.
[00:06:45] [00:06:50] Alex Kim: Can Redwood provide a recommended reserved GPU count and a recommended burst pool size?
[00:06:55] Jordan Lee: Yes — after we run the initial profiling on your trace, we will propose (A) reserved pool for steady-state latency targets, (B) burst pool with warm nodes to cover the top 95th percentile spike, and (C) a small cold fallback for extreme spikes. We'll provide cost scenarios for each.
[00:07:11] Tess Li: Any restraints on data residency? We need EU region support for some tenants.
[00:07:15] Chris Nguyen: We support region pinning and can run POC in EU region for those tenants. We'll note latency differences.
[00:07:22] [00:07:28] Priya Rao: Benchmarks should include quantized parameter sweeps because quality vs cost will be a tradeoff.
[00:07:34] Maya Patel: We'll include 8-bit and 4-bit quant sweeps and provide measured quality deltas on your eval set.
[00:07:40] Jordan Lee: Ok, recap of deliverables: pricing and reserved proposal, bench runbook + synthetic traces, SOC2/security pack, and a schedule for the 4-week sprint.
[00:07:51] Alex Kim: Sounds good. Also, please include warm-pool vs pre-warmed docker image cost comparison.
[00:07:56] Chris Nguyen: We'll add that to the spreadsheet.
  [00:08:03] Tess Li: Thanks all. We'll sync via email and Slack for the next steps.
  [00:08:09] Jordan Lee: Great, next meeting — bench kickoff — tentative 2026-10-04.
  [00:08:15] [END OF TRANSCRIPT EXCERPT]

Note: Transcript truncated for storage; full Fireflies export contains per-second timestamps and raw speech markers. Occasional transcription errors: 'KV' rendered as 'K-V' or 'K V', 'SOC2' sometimes 'sock two'. Also some speaker labels may shift in the raw file.

POC scoping — Veritas Labs: Quality & Performance Runbook

Kickoff for a 6-week POC focused on quality and perf benchmarking. Agreed success criteria (latency, hallucination thresholds, throughput), agreed golden prompt set creation approach and regression cadence; plan to run three model/quantization variants, initial benchmark in 2 weeks, weekly syncs. Action items: pricing + contract, security docs, benchmark spreadsheet, golden prompt template.
Success criteria: latency, throughput, hallucination tolerance
Workload sizing: QPS, peak traffic estimates, batch expectations
Benchmark plan: model variants, golden prompts, regression tests
Scoring approach: automatic metrics + small human eval
Timelines: 2-week benchmark, 6-week pilot, weekly check-ins
Security / compliance notes: data residency, audit logs, SSO
Meeting header: 2027-01-19 16:00 UTC | Duration ~46m | Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Maya (Veritas Head of ML), Tom (CTO), Alice (Data Eng)
[00:00] Samira: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. quick roll call?
[00:10] Maya: Maya here. hi.
[00:12] Tom: Tom on behalf of devops.
[00:15] Alice: Alice here.
[00:18] Daniel: Daniel, Redwood SE. good to meet you all.
[00:22] Samira: Cool. high-level agenda — align on success criteria for the POC, workload sizing, runbook for benchmarks, and who owns what for golden prompts and regression tests.
[00:35] Maya: Sounds good. our main goal is to validate both quality and cost claims. We need to be convinced latency won't blow up and hallucinations are within acceptable bounds.
[00:45] Tom: And from infra side we need to see predictable throughput so we can commit to integrating the API into our pipeline.
[00:52] Daniel: Great. can you remind us of expected traffic patterns? rough numbers will drive model selection and batching policy.
[01:00] Alice: Sure — baseline is ~8k inference calls per day, majority are short prompts, peak about 150 rps during business hours, and batchable bursts up to 300 rps for nightly processing.
[01:17] Samira: Okay that's helpful. for the POC we usually mirror a representative 24–48 hour window and run a load test. we aim to measure p50/p90/p99 latency and tokens/sec cost.
[01:30] Maya: Success criteria — we were thinking p90 generation latency under 350ms for 512 tokens, hallucination rate under 2% on the golden set, and throughput of 200 rps sustained for 30s without errors. are those reasonable?
[01:45] Daniel: p90 < 350ms is achievable on Redwood hosted for many model variants but depends on model size and quantization. especially if you want int8 quant, we can test. Hallucination under 2% is tougher — depends on prompt engineering and evaluation rubric.
[02:03] Tom: How do you measure hallucination? is it automated or manual?
[02:08] Daniel: Mixed approach — automated checks for hallucinations where we can (factuality detectors, embedding similarity to sources), plus human adjudication on a sampled subset of outputs. we propose a weighted score: 70% automatic heuristics, 30% human review for the golden prompts.
[02:25] Maya: That weighting seems fair given time constraints. what's the golden prompt set size you recommend?
[02:30] Samira: We typically ask for 300–500 golden prompts covering edge cases and common flows; you can start with a smaller seed of ~150 and expand during the pilot.
[02:40] Alice: We can prepare 200 initial prompts spanning billing questions, compliance excerpts, and device-specific troubleshooting.
[02:46] Daniel: Perfect. We'll provide a template that includes input, expected intent, allowed variability in answer, and hallucination flags.
[02:55] Maya: On benchmarks — can you walk through the variants you'll run?
[03:00] Daniel: Yes. run three variants: 1) baseline open model (fp16), 2) quantized int8 variant, and 3) a smaller faster model for fallback. for each we measure latency distribution, tokens-per-second cost, and quality metrics on the golden set.
[03:16] Tom: Do you run KV cache or persistent prefix caching in the POC to simulate production?
[03:21] Daniel: We can enable prefix/KV cache for session-based workloads. we'll simulate your cache hit rates — you can provide a representative distribution or we can instrument a trace.
[03:30] Samira: For timelines: initial benchmark run within 10 business days, then a 4-week tuning sprint, and pilot wrap at 6 weeks. weekly standup/check-in, and an internal results doc after each run.
[03:45] Maya: 10 business days to first benchmark is fine. would you need any access to our infra for VPC testing?
[03:52] Samira: For private deployment or VPC you'll need to sign an onboarding checklist; for hosted it's all API keys. for security review we'll send SOC2 docs and network diagrams.
[04:02] Tom: We require audit logs and SSO support. do you provide SAML and role-based access?
[04:07] Daniel: Yes, SAML SSO, RBAC, and audit logs are part of Redwood Dedicated/Private. we'll attach the security package in the followup.
[04:20] Alice: About scoring approach — you mentioned embeddings. can you be specific?
[04:25] Daniel: We'll compute cosine similarity between output embeddings and reference documents for factuality signals, and use answer overlap heuristics for format checks. then combine with human labels to produce a composite quality score 0–100. we'll share the exact spreadsheet.
[04:40] Maya: What's an acceptable composite score threshold?
[04:43] Daniel: We usually aim for >=85 on golden prompts to pass. but that can be adjusted per-customer depending on tolerance.
[04:50] Samira: Budget constraints? any hard limits?
[04:52] Maya: We have a pilot budget target of ~$15k for the 6-week POC. if costs exceed that we need to know early.
[04:58] Samira: We'll provide an estimate for the three variants including token cost and infra. also options for Dedicated reserved capacity if cost predictability matters.
[05:08] Tom: Regression tests — frequency?
[05:10] Daniel: Weekly automated regression runs against the golden set and a monthly human audit. if you use continuous prompts, we can run incremental checks on new samples.
[05:22] Alice: For format checks, we need strict JSON output for downstream parsers. can models be constrained?
[05:28] Daniel: Yes, we support structured output and validators. we can instrument schema checks and fallbacks if schema fails. we'll include tooling to surface format failures in the dashboard.
[05:40] Maya: For the golden prompts, who owns labeling? We'll need to provide expected outputs but don't have bandwidth for full human adjudication.
[05:48] Samira: We'll split tasks — Veritas supplies the seed prompts and expected intents; Redwood supports human labeling for a sample set (we can propose 200 labels) as part of the pilot scope.
[05:58] Maya: That helps. about telemetry and tracing — we need per-route latency and token-level cost attribution.
[06:06] Daniel: Redwood Console provides token-level breakdown, per-route latencies, and traces. we can share sample screenshots and a live demo in the next call.
[06:18] Tom: Any requirements for data residency? we have EU-only customers.
[06:22] Samira: Yes, we can pin regions and provide Private deployment options. for hosted we have EU regions; for strict residency we'll recommend Private.
[06:31] Alice: On model rollouts — can we do canary and automatic fallback if latency spikes?
[06:35] Daniel: Absolutely. Redwood supports canary rollouts, A/B, and automatic fallback to a cheaper/smaller model when tail latency exceeds thresholds.
[06:45] Maya: Great. let's talk about the acceptance criteria one more time and make them concrete.
[06:50] Samira: Draft acceptance criteria: 1) p90 generation latency <= 350ms for 512-token prompts on chosen variant; 2) golden set composite quality >=85; 3) hallucination <=2% on golden set; 4) monthly cost projection within pilot budget +/- 20%; 5) structured format adherence >=99% for JSON outputs.
[07:12] Tom: We want load durability: sustain 200 rps for 30s with <=1% error rate.
[07:18] Daniel: we'll put those as SLIs in the runbook.
[07:22] Alice: For scoring, will you provide the rubric?
[07:25] Daniel: Yes, we'll share a scoring sheet that shows component weights: factuality heuristics 40%, format/intent 30%, human adjudication 30% (sampled).
[07:36] Maya: Are you planning to run any adversarial prompts to check hallucination modes?
[07:40] Daniel: Yes — we'll include a small adversarial set to stress-test the model during the tuning sprint.
[07:47] Samira: Logistics — we need to exchange a security questionnaire and a sample data dump for realistic traces. any PII concerns?
[07:56] Maya: We'll scrub PII, but may need to test with synthetic PII-like tokens.
[08:01] Samira: that's fine — just flag anything sensitive and we'll follow your retention rules.
[08:09] Alice: How do you handle KV cache in the benchmarks — warm vs cold cache?
[08:13] Daniel: We'll run both cold-start and warmed-cache scenarios; we'll document cache-hit percentages.
[08:20] Tom: What does instrumentation look like for your metrics? prometheus or logs?
[08:25] Daniel: We can export metrics via Prometheus or provide CSV/JSON exports. Console has dashboards too.
[08:33] Maya: Ok, where do we sign up for the initial benchmark? timeline spelled out again please.
[08:38] Samira: Step 1: Veritas uploads golden prompt seed + workload traces (3 business days). Step 2: Redwood configures POC environment and runs initial benchmark (within 10 business days). Step 3: tuning sprint 2–4 weeks. Step 4: wrap & handoff at week 6.
[08:56] Alice: Are there any prerequisites from our side for the first run besides prompts and traces?
[08:59] Daniel: API keys, sample configs, and dataset slices. we'll provide a checklist.
[09:05] Maya: Competitors — we've had talks with Vendor X and looked at Vertex; why Redwood for this use-case?
[09:12] Samira: We emphasized production-first tooling, consistent runtime across hosted and private, and cost-optimization levers like batching and prefix caching. plus the console for token-level cost attribution.
[09:25] Tom: Pricing model — do you offer committed reserved capacity for pilot?
[09:29] Samira: We can propose a short-term reserved slot for Dedicated if you want predictable throughput; otherwise hosted pay-as-you-go for the POC. we'll include both options in the pricing sheet.
[09:41] Maya: Our key stakeholders — legal and security will want SOC2 docs; ops will want load test results, and product wants human eval reports.
[09:49] Samira: We'll attach SOC2 and SAML configs. Daniel will share the benchmark plan and a shared spreadsheet for results.
[09:57] Daniel: I'll also include the golden prompt template and an initial scoring rubric.
[10:03] Maya: Good. any open technical risks we should call out?
[10:07] Daniel: Biggest risks: mismatch between seed prompts and production distribution, and hallucination detection coverage — some hallucinations are hard to detect automatically. Also cost blow-ups from high token generations if prompts are not constrained.
[10:21] Alice: We'll scope prompt length caps and sampling in the trace so you can estimate token counts.
[10:27] Samira: perfect. going to capture action items as we speak.
[10:32] [10:32] Action item moment — Samira: send pricing/contract draft. Daniel: send benchmark spreadsheet and golden prompt template. Maya: provide seed prompt set and traces. Alice: identify PII constraints and region requirements.
[10:50] Maya: timeline ok, we'll target to upload seeds by end of this week.
[10:56] Tom: let's schedule weekly 30-minute syncs — same time next week?
[10:59] Samira: yes. I'll send calendar invites.
[11:05] Maya: any final clarifying q's?
[11:08] Alice: just one — do you have recommended human labeling tool?
[11:12] Daniel: we commonly use internal labeling or third-party Labeledly (transcription error: "labelly") — we can recommend options and integrate outputs.
[11:22] Samira: ok thank you all. we'll follow up with the security pack, pricing, and the benchmark sheet. recap and next steps in the follow-up email.
[11:32] Maya: thanks.
[11:34] Tom: thanks everyone.
[11:36] Alice: bye.
[45:12] Meeting adjourned.
Samira to send pricing options (hosted + Dedicated) and contract draft (due 2027-01-21)
Daniel to share benchmark spreadsheet, golden prompt template, and scoring rubric (due 2027-01-20)
Veritas to upload seed prompts and 48h workload traces (target by 2027-01-22)
Samira to attach SOC2 + security pack and SAML config docs (due 2027-01-21)
Schedule weekly 30-minute syncs; first follow-up in 7 days (Samira to send invite)
Samira: Send pricing and contract options (2027-01-21)
Daniel: Deliver benchmark spreadsheet + golden prompt template + rubric (2027-01-20)
Maya: Provide seed prompts (150-200) and POC traces (2027-01-22)
Alice: Confirm PII rules and region requirements (2027-01-21)
Samira: Send calendar invites for weekly check-ins (2027-01-20)
Include golden prompt template with expected output schema and hallucination flags; plan for mixed automated + human evaluation; run cold and warm cache scenarios; attach cost projection table for three model variants.

document.content:
Pricing approval & DPA exception triage — HeliosIQ

Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-15
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Rivera (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Dana Ortiz (HeliosIQ Procurement), Ravi Shah (HeliosIQ InfoSec), Marta Lopez (HeliosIQ Engineering)

Summary:
Quick triage between procurement and security on DPA exceptions, finalize pricing route (annual commit vs usage + burst), confirm KMS/SSO requirements and next steps to get pilot signed off.

Topics:
- DPA exception list and redline path
- SLA commitments (uptime, p50/p95 latency targets)
- Billing model: committed annual vs committed monthly + burst pricing
- Key management (BYOK/HSM) and audit log retention
- Pilot scope and technical checkpoints

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick round of intros, I'm Alex, AE at Redwood, Samir our systems SE is here as well.
[00:12] Dana (HeliosIQ): Hi, Dana here, procurement. We have Ravi from security and Marta from engineering on call too.
[00:18] Samir (Redwood): Hi all. I think agenda was to triage a couple DPA exceptions and lock down pricing path for the pilot.
[00:26] Dana: Correct. Our legal / procurement asked for a fast read on what exceptions are live and whether you can accept our proposed data residency clause and extended audit retention.
[00:35] Alex: Totally. We pulled together a proposed DPA with three areas we usually flag: encryption keying, subprocessor list, and audit log retention. Samir, want to cover the technical constraints?
[00:45] Samir: Sure. For the BYOK request you raised — Redwood supports customer-managed keys via KMS and we have an HSM-backed option for Dedicated/private deployments. On hosted, we offer a KMS integration but there are some egress logging nuances; the logs are accessible but for full HSM custody you'd be looking at Dedicated or Private.
[00:59] Ravi: That nuance is game-changing for us. Our compliance team insists on HSM-backed keys with separation of duties and monthly key rotation logs. Are those logs available for export to our SIEM?
[01:09] Samir: Yes, logs can be exported. The export path is S3-compatible with encrypted transport; push to customer's bucket is supported. Small note: the field names in logs right now reflect internal naming — we can map them, but that mapping work is part of the pilot setup.
[01:26] Marta: When you say "push to our bucket" do you mean you store copies or you only forward events? We need to understand retention — our legal wants seven years, which is higher than your default.
[01:38] Alex: Seven years is outside of our standard offering. We typically retain audit logs for two years in hosted, and up to five years in Dedicated with a governance add-on. We'll need to flag that as an exception and map the cost/operational burden.
[01:52] Dana: Understood. Can we put that as a DPA exception request and you give us a price delta? Procurement prefers a single contract rather than tooling add-ons if possible.
[02:02] Alex: Yes, we can present options. We usually show two paths: 1) accept standard retention and a contractual SLA, or 2) bespoke retention for an additional fee and technical handoff to run the export pipeline. We'll quantify in the redline.
[02:16] Ravi: Next on SLA — your doc lists 99.9% and an SLO for p95 latency on standard chat calls. Our product team expects <120ms p50 for authentication related inference paths. Is that realistic on hosted?
[02:28] Samir: That's tight for hosted at peak concurrency, especially if you hit longer seq lengths. For p50 120ms we usually recommend Dedicated with GPU pinning and tuned batching. On hosted we can get close for typical profiles, but we can't guarantee it under bursty loads.
[02:42] Marta: Pinning and Dedicated means we commit to reserved capacity, right? How large is the minimum?
[02:48] Samir: We have bundle sizes. For the latency SLO you want, a small Dedicated pool (4 GPUs) with the right model variant and quantization profile is usually adequate. I can run a sizing estimate once you share expected QPS and token distribution.
[03:02] Dana: Procurement will need a firm unit price for the committed option and a separate burst rate. Can you provide an annual commit vs month-to-month comparison?
[03:11] Alex: Yes. We'll provide a rate-card: committed annual discounted rate, monthly committed, and a burst rate per 1k tokens above committed throughput. We'll also include a pilot-only rate so you can test before committing.
[03:23] Dana: Great. On the DPA redlines — our legal wants to add a clause for audit rights and third-party audits annually. How do you handle that?
[03:33] Alex: We accept third-party audits for Dedicated/Private under an enterprise agreement; for hosted we provide SOC 2 reports and can provide an attestation package. For annual third-party audits on our platform on your behalf, that's typically a custom addendum.
[03:47] Ravi: Also encryption-at-rest — standard AES-256 is fine but we need proof of key separation and periodic role-based access reports in the contract.
[03:56] Samir: We can provide role-based access control logs. The names/IDs in the logs may appear as internal service principals — we will map and produce a manifest. That mapping is typically an engineering effort during onboarding.
[04:09] Dana: Would that mapping be part of the standard onboarding or a billable service?
[04:14] Alex: For enterprise customers it can be included in onboarding up to a fixed scoping window (e.g., 40 hours). Anything beyond we quote. We'll note that in the redline.
[04:25] [05:00] Speaker 2: (crosstalk)
[04:58] Marta: I have a technical question — latency aside, how do you handle KV cache and multi-tenant prefix caching? We want to ensure inference consistency across sessions.
[05:10] Samir: Good question. Our runtime uses prefix-level KV caching; for Dedicated we can do namespace isolation so cache isn't shared across tenants. On hosted, cache is tenant-separated logically but we don't expose cache controls to customers. If you need deterministic cache behavior, Dedicated or Private is recommended.
[05:26] Marta: So for the pilot, we should probably run on Dedicated to mirror production.
[05:31] Alex: Makes sense. We'll dimension the pilot to reflect production constraints.
[05:36] Dana: Back to pricing: procurement has an internal approval cut-off next Thursday, so if we can get pricing and the DPA redline by Wednesday we can queue it. Is that feasible?
[05:47] Alex: We can aim for that. I'll circulate a DPA with our standard positions and highlight the three exceptions: 1) 7-year log retention, 2) BYOK HSM proof obligations, and 3) annual third-party audit clause.
[05:59] Dana: Perfect. On the BYOK HSM — is that available on hosted with a partner KMS or only Dedicated/Private?
[06:08] Samir: Hosted supports customer-managed keys via cloud KMS (AWS KMS/GCP KMS) where Redwood holds no copy of the key material; HSM-backed BYOK (with hardware key custody) is only fully supported on Dedicated/Private deployments where you can control physical keying or connect to your HSM via VPN.
[06:26] Ravi: We will need an architectural diagram showing where key material lives and where the logs flow. Can you include that in the security packet?
[06:34] Samir: Yes, I'll attach a diagram and a short runbook of key lifecycle events.
[06:38] Alex: We'll also include a sample SLA with p50/p95 numbers for both hosted and Dedicated, and an appendix describing fallback behavior if capacity is constrained.
[06:49] Dana: Talk to me about fallback — our product team will not accept silent degradations. We need clear fallbacks and a plan for model variant substitution.
[06:58] Samir: Redwood has a smart routing/fallback policy: requests can be routed by latency, cost, region, or a strict policy; we support automatic fallback to a compatible model variant and notification hooks. That behavior will be in the contract under the availability and graceful degradation clause.
[07:14] Marta: Are you able to guarantee no output quality regression if you fallback to a smaller model? We rely on specific prompt behaviors.
[07:22] Samir: We can't guarantee identical outputs across model families; what we do is include an A/B test and rollout policy so you can define which endpoints are allowed to fallback and which are strict. For the pilot we'll train against your test prompts and capture quality metrics.
[07:36] Dana: On billing — we need a sample invoice layout showing committed vs burst charges and any add-on fees for retention or mapping work.
[07:45] Alex: We'll provide that. The finance team typically shows invoicing by line item: base committed capacity, token usage overage, add-ons (log retention, mapping hours), and professional services.
[07:57] Ravi: Also include the KMS audit trail. That ties into our SOX obligations.
[08:03] Alex: Understood.
[08:06] [08:30] Speaker 3: (inaudible)
[08:28] Dana: A little process note — if procurement gets the redlined DPA and pricing by Wednesday, I can route internally for a final sign-off to our CISO and CFO. After that, we want a 30-day pilot starting payments-on-commit for a small pool.
[08:42] Alex: Sounds good. We commonly do a 30-day pilot with a short payment or deposit and then convert to committed term if metrics meet your gates.
[08:52] Marta: What instruments are available for the onboarding pilot? Do you give a sandbox token or a dedicated cluster?
[08:59] Samir: For the pilot we can either spin up a small Dedicated cluster for deterministic testing or provide a scoped hosted environment with priority routing. Given your latency needs, I'd recommend the small Dedicated cluster.
[09:12] Dana: Okay we'll note that as preferred.
[09:17] Alex: Let's talk timelines: I'll aim to get the redline and rate-card by 2025-06-18. Samir will provide the pilot access and the security packet by 2025-06-19. Ravi, Dana — you'll review and flag any showstopper items.
[09:31] Ravi: One more ask — can you include in the packet a short section on vendor incident timelines (RTO/RPO) and breach notification commitments? Our legal needs specific hours.
[09:41] Samir: Yes, we have standard breach notification timelines in our playbook; we'll include an excerpt indicating notification within 72 hours and dedicated post-incident reports. We can negotiate shorter windows in an enterprise agreement.
[09:53] Dana: That should be explicit in the redline.
[09:57] Alex: Absolutely.
[10:00] [10:30] Speaker 1: (pause)
[10:27] Marta: Technical nit — do you support SAML 2.0 or only OIDC for SSO?
[10:31] Samir: Both. SAML and OIDC supported for SSO; provisioning via SCIM is available for Dedicated and Private.
[10:39] Marta: Good. We'll need a SCIM connector if we go Dedicated.
[10:44] Alex: Another procurement question — payment terms: net-30 is standard; we can discuss net-45/60 for Enterprise with committed spend. Any constraints?
[10:55] Dana: Net-30 preferred; CFO may negotiate net-45 depending on commitment size. We'll flag after pricing.
[11:03] Alex: Okay.
[11:05] [11:40] Speaker 4: (background noise)
[11:38] Dana: Any competitor considerations — our engineering team mentioned InferenceCorp pitched on-prem with a big discount but lacked autoscaling and caching features. Do you have a doc comparing hosted vs on-prem tradeoffs?
[11:53] Samir: Yes, we have a short TCO playbook that compares Hosted/Dedicated/Private, latency and ops tradeoffs, and the unit economics. I'll attach that.
[12:02] Dana: Please do.
[12:05] Alex: Quick recap for next steps: (1) Redwood sends DPA redline and pricing worksheet by 2025-06-18; (2) Redwood SE sends security packet, architectural diagram, and pilot access window by 2025-06-19; (3) HeliosIQ confirms internal approvers and final decision timeline by 2025-06-17.
[12:25] Dana: That's accurate.
[12:27] Ravi: We'll also mark the audit log and retention ask as priority and get you the retention spec by 2025-06-20.
[12:35] Alex: Great. Any other questions?
[12:39] Marta: One request — can you run a quick throughput bench with our representative prompt set? If you can include that as part of the pilot report that'd be helpful.
[12:47] Samir: Yes, send the prompt set and we'll run the throughput/latency bench and include token-level cost breakdown.
[12:55] Alex: Ok going to wrap. Thanks everyone for time. We'll follow up with the materials and the redline.
[13:02] Dana: Thanks.
[13:04] Ravi: Thanks all.

End of call.

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcription cut some proper nouns (KMS sometimes transcribed as K M S), occasional speaker attribution swapped during crosstalk.
