document.content:
Open-model Exit & Compatibility Audit - Heliotrope Systems

Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-28
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 54 minutes (scheduled)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (CTO, Heliotrope), Luca Romano (ML Infra), Sara Kim (SRE), Tom Erickson (Product)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be rough):
Heliotrope is evaluating an exit from their current managed provider stack toward a mix of hosted and private Redwood deployments. Key concerns: eval parity (quality differences across OpenAI/Anthropic and self-hosted vLLM/TGI), tokenization and embedding divergence, latency vs cost tradeoffs, and compliance (KMS, audit logs, region). Agreed next steps: run parity eval with Heliotrope prompts, share security/compliance docs, schedule deep-dive for private deployment architecture.

Topics: evaluation parity, quantization and KV cache behavior, dedicated vs private hosting, streaming/function calling compatibility, compliance/KMS, benchmark runbook

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for carving out time, um we wanted to kick off a short audit to understand where Heliotrope is today and what the migration constraints are. Aisha, do you want to open with current state?
[00:12] Aisha Patel: Sure yeah, thanks Maya. So we've been on a managed stack — some mixing of OpenAI and Anthropic APIs — and more recently experimenting with vLLM hosts for cost reasons. Our driver is predictability and control; we need lower unit costs but can't regress on answer quality for our core summarization and retrieval tasks.
[00:28] Luca Romano: To add, our infra has a vLLM fleet behind TGI for some lightweight inference. It's fine for batch but we're seeing tokenization differences and, uh, embedding drift between providers which breaks downstream similarity searches.
[00:42] Diego Morales: Makes sense. When you say tokenization differences — are you seeing consistent length inflation or are prompts being split differently?
[00:48] Luca Romano: Mostly inflation; for certain models the token counts go up 10-18% compared to OpenAI, which throws off our promt-ratelimit calculations and cost estimates. Also embedding vectors from Anthropic have a different normalization which affects our cosine thresholding.
[01:02] Tom Erickson: And function calling — we've architected product features around tool-calling from the model, so the semantics need to be close. We've had to write provider-specific glue which is becoming a maintenance burden.
[01:12] Maya Chen: That's exactly the kinds of gaps Redwood tries to address at the runtime and API abstraction layer. Quick question: for the vLLM/TGI pieces, are you running quantized models or FP16?
[01:23] Luca Romano: Mostly 4-bit quantized on commodity GPUs to save cost; occasional FP16 on p4s for latency-sensitive endpoints.
[01:30] Diego Morales: Noted. So two immediate risk vectors: quality parity (tokenization, embeddings, decoding/formats) and perf parity (KV cache behavior, batching, cold-start latency on quantized stacks).
[01:42] Sara Kim: Also SRE perspective — we need audit logs, KMS integration, and the ability to lock down egress to specific cloud regions. We have regulatory needs for EU residency for a subset of customers.
[01:52] Maya Chen: Good — Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem, and our private control plane can be co-located in EU regions. We have KMS and HSM options plus audit log exports. I'll share the compliance packet after the call.
[02:02] Aisha Patel: Great. Can you walk through what parity evaluation looks like from Redwood's side? How invasive is it?
[02:10] Diego Morales: Yeah so we typically ask for a representative prompt set — ideally a few hundred prompts across the primary use-cases (summarization, retrieval-augmented generation, code-gen, classification). We run those prompts across the candidate models and variants: hosted redwood catalog models, reserved Dedicated variants, and your on-prem vLLM/TGI configs if you provide artifacts or container images.
[02:31] Diego Morales: We'll produce metrics: token counts, latency p50/p95, exact/soft match scores against your golden outputs, and embedding cosine distributions. We'll also run structural checks for function calling and streaming behavior — e.g., whether chunked streaming reassembles into identical outputs.
[02:49] Luca Romano: For the on-prem side we can give Docker images and a small sample of our vLLM config; there's some custom kernel flags in our fork though, hope that's okay.
[02:58] Diego Morales: Usually fine; we can run parity in a customer-provided environment or in our lab if we need to instrument. For private deployments we can mirror your kernel flags to reproduce behavior.
[03:07] Tom Erickson: What about model variants? We sometimes use a smaller Mistral variant for cost. How granular are your rollouts?
[03:15] Maya Chen: You can pin endpoints to model versions, do canary rollouts, and set automated fallback policies. For Dedicated we also give capacity pools so you can reserve throughput. For private you keep control of the images but Redwood's control plane can orchestrate rollouts.
[03:29] Aisha Patel: One of our immediate fears is hallucination increase after quantization. How do you quantify that?
[03:35] Diego Morales: We'll use a mix of automated NLI-based hallucination detectors, prompt-specific heuristics, and manual spot-checks for high-risk categories. We'll tie regressions back to prompts so you can decide to pin to alternative variants or apply different quantization profiles.
[03:49] Sara Kim: From ops, we need to know the rollback path. If a canary shows regressions, how quickly can we flip back?
[03:55] Maya Chen: Rollbacks are immediate at the routing layer; in Dedicated and Hosted we maintain fallbacks to a compatible model family. In Private, the control plane supports quick reconfigure but exact time depends on your deployment topology — Diego can follow up with a runbook.
[04:10] Diego Morales: Yep I'll write a rollback playbook. Also, we often see subtle divergence from tokenizers; one mitigation is to add an SDK shim that normalizes tokenization and prompt pre-processing across providers. That reduces surprise token inflation.
[04:24] Luca Romano: That could help. Our stack is already doing whitespace normalization and some prompt templating, but not a full shim.
[04:30] Tom Erickson: Can you speak to pricing expectations for Dedicated vs Hosted for our traffic profile? We're heavy on inference for summarization with spikes at EOD.
[04:38] Maya Chen: We'll do a sizing exercise after you share representative traffic. Hosted tends to have faster time to value and lower ops overhead, Dedicated gives predictable per-token economics at a commit, and Private gives the most control but with higher runbook/ops overhead. We'll model a 3-month and 12-month cost projection for the prompt set you share.
[04:55] Aisha Patel: On the legal side, we'll need data retention, audit trail, and the ability to egress logs. Can you export audit logs to our SIEM?
[05:02] Maya Chen: Yes, audit logs are exportable to Splunk/Datadog or via S3 on a schedule; Redwood's Private can also stream logs to your SIEM through secure connectors.
[05:12] Sara Kim: KMS / HSM — do you have integrations with major providers? We want to use our existing AWS KMS keys.
[05:18] Diego Morales: We integrate with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and customer-managed HSMs. We also support BYOK flows for private deployments.
[05:25] Luca Romano: Fine. A few technical nitty-gritty things: how do you handle KV cache persistence across restarts? In our vLLM fleet we lose warm caches on node churn which spikes latencies.
[05:36] Diego Morales: Redwood runtime keeps an LRU-backed KV cache and can optionally shard persistent caches to local NVMe for warm-starts; for Dedicated we can provision sticky worker pools or stateful pods to preserve hot caches. For Private you can opt into the same persistence layer.
[05:52] Tom Erickson: Are embeddings stable across quantization? We rely on embedding similarity for reranking.
[05:57] Diego Morales: Quantization can affect embeddings. We compare embedding cosine distributions and if we detect drift we recommend either post-hoc re-normalization, using a float-embedding-only pipeline, or a retrain of the reranker thresholds. We'll surface per-model guidance in the benchmark report.
[06:12] Aisha Patel: What's the timeline for an initial parity run? We want results before our budget meeting mid-Feb.
[06:18] Maya Chen: If you can deliver the prompt set and traffic profile by end of this week, Diego can start and deliver a first pass in 7-10 business days. That should put you before mid-Feb.
[06:27] Luca Romano: We can do that. We'll redact PII from the prompts but keep representative structure.
[06:32] Diego Morales: Perfect. For instrumentation we'll capture p50/p95, tokens per response, embedding cosine histograms, and a small human review sample for edge cases.
[06:42] Tom Erickson: Any gotchas with function calling? We've seen mismatch in argument encoding with Anthropic vs OpenAI.
[06:49] Diego Morales: Yeah function-call semantics differ; Redwood's SDK normalizes the call/response shape and can wrap provider-specific quirks. For Private setups, you can maintain your own runtime hooks to keep the exact contract.
[06:59] Sara Kim: We also need SLA language and uptime targets for Dedicated.
[07:04] Maya Chen: Our Dedicated contracts include SLA tiers; I'll include draft SLA language in the packet. For Private deployments we offer enterprise support levels but SLA specifics depend on the support package.
[07:14] Aisha Patel: One more thing — data residency. Some EU customers require model inputs not leave region at any point. Can Redwood enforce strict regional routing?
[07:22] Maya Chen: Yes, you can set routing policies by region and customer tier; for the strictest case we recommend Private in-region with local KMS so data never leaves the EU.
[07:33] Luca Romano: Ok that's helpful. Are there any reference customers who've done a similar transition from Anthropic/OpenAI to Redwood Private?
[07:40] Maya Chen: We have a few enterprise case studies; I'll anonymize and share them, and include a short architecture diagram showing the private control plane.
[07:48] Tom Erickson: Regarding benchmark artifacts, what format will you share results in? We prefer a spreadsheet so we can slice by prompt type.
[07:54] Diego Morales: We'll produce a spreadsheet plus a short summary deck. The spreadsheet will include per-prompt rows with tokens, latency, score, embedding vector hash, and drift metrics.
[08:05] Aisha Patel: Sounds good. Any questions from your side, Luca?
[08:08] Luca Romano: Not right now — Diego, we'll send the prompt set and a docker tarball of our vLLM config. Keep in mind there are kernel-level flags.
[08:16] Diego Morales: Got it — we'll treat it as a customer-hosted environment if you prefer.
[08:20] Maya Chen: Quick recap before we close: Luca will share prompt set and traffic profile by 2027-01-31; Diego kicks off parity run and delivers results within 7-10 business days; Maya to send compliance and SLA materials by 2027-01-31; schedule private-deploy deep-dive week of 2027-02-07. Anything else?
[08:37] Aisha Patel: That covers it. Appreciate the clarity.
[08:40] Tom Erickson: Thanks everyone.
[08:42] Maya Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up via email with links to the shared spreadsheet and a calendar invite for the deep-dive.

(ends at approx 15:54 PST)

References shared during call:
- parity-runbook.xlsx (will be created by Redwood)
- security_compliance_packet_v2.pdf (Redwood)
- demo-sprint-runbook.md (link to internal doc)

Notes about transcript: occasional transcription artifacts, speaker labeling approximated, and timestamps are coarse.

document.content:
Audit pathing and hosting fit discovery with Weston Asset

Intro discovery to validate Weston Asset's hosting needs vs residency and audit constraints. Covered tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, and Private; log retention/redaction options; KMS and key residency, and evidence pathing for audits. Agreed next steps: send security pack, propose pilot for Dedicated with region locking, schedule compliance deep dive.
Meeting header: 2026-11-10 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~52m | Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Mark (Weston CTO), Jenna (Weston Compliance), Samir (Weston Cloud)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick intro — im Alex on the account team, priya is our solutions eng, we'll cover hosting options and the audit/evidence questions you sent over. how's that sound?
[00:18] Mark: Yep this works. Jenna and Samir are here to talk compliance and infra. our main thing is residency and what shows up in logs when we call models, so we can map to our audit pipeline.
[00:30] Jenna: And just to flag, we have an upcoming regulator review in Q1 so we need to validate traceability, retention windows, and proof of key residency if data is in euro regions.
[00:44] Priya: Great, we'll run through Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. quick note — transcription might mess up acronyms, but platform features are: hosted api with multi-tenant, dedicated reserved capacity, and private (VPC or on-prem).
[00:58] Samir: First question: if we use hosted, can we guarantee that logs and request payloads never leave eu data centers? we have concerns about cross-border flows for certain PII.
[01:12] Priya: For hosted, region-locking is available for EU — requests are routed to eu clusters. however we still have a shared control plane in our control region; metadata for billing/usage may traverse us-west for the control plane unless you go dedicated or private. we do offer options to limit metadata export, but note: Hosted won't give you full control-plane isolation.
[01:36] Jenna: When you say metadata for billing, what exactly goes out? audit timestamps? request ids? anything that could be considered personal?
[01:46] Alex: Good callout. Typically the billing metadata is aggregated tokens/usage, invoice-level metadata, and request id hashes. We don't store prompt contents for more than 30 days in hosted by default, but retention is configurable on dedicated/private.
[02:02] Mark: 30 days default is...maybe not enough for us, we need 7 years for certain audit trails for financial products. so retention config is a hard requirement.
[02:12] Priya: Understood. Dedicated and Private both allow you to set retention windows and export raw logs to your S3 or GCS for archival, which can then be fed into your legal hold/archival system. We also support redact-on-ingest to remove detected PII from logs — but more on that in a sec.
[02:28] Jenna: redact-on-ingest sounds promising but we need deterministic proof that the redaction happened. our auditors want a chain of custody: where a blob lived, when, who had access. how does Redwood provide that evidence?
[02:40] Priya: We provide audit logs for control-plane actions and access events — MFA logins, role changes, who pulled exports. For data plane, for dedicated/private with customer-managed keys, you can get key usage logs from your KMS, plus object-level access logs from your storage. Redwood can surface those links in the Console and we can package a zip of evidence.
[02:58] Samir: Customer-managed keys — is HSM supported? we can't have keys in a Berkeley-grade soft keystore.
[03:06] Alex: Yes, we integrate with AWS KMS, Cloud HSM, and bring-your-own-key models. For private on-prem we can plug into an HSM. for dedicated we support CMKs with HSM-backed KMS in region.
[03:18] Mark: Ok, so thematic question: from a region/residency standpoint, what are the real tradeoffs if we choose Dedicated vs Hosted? we want the operational simplicity of hosted but need auditable separation.
[03:30] Priya: Hosted is easiest to stand up and cheaper. Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and stronger isolation — it's single-tenant at the serving layer and you can ask for region-locking and control-plane features — but Dedicated still uses Redwood control plane unless you purchase the private control plane add-on. Private gives you the most isolation: private control plane and on-prem options. So tradeoff: cost/ops vs separation and evidence granularity.
[03:54] Jenna: Would Dedicated satisfy auditors if we can show region locking, CMK logs, and log forwarding to our archive? or do they insist on private control plane?
[04:05] Priya: Many financial customers have passed audits with Dedicated when they have CMKs, log forwarding, and contractual data residency guarantees. However, certain regulators prefer private control plane — e.g., when they require that the vendor cannot access tenant metadata at all. We can help scope that in a compliance deep-dive.
[04:24] Mark: Another angle — legal hold. Suppose there's litigation and we get a legal hold for specific customer records. Can Redwood run targeted retrievals or preserves for specific prompts?
[04:36] Alex: Yes, with Dedicated/Private we can preserve object-level snapshots and export them. Hosted is trickier because of multi-tenant storage and retention windows, but we have options to capture session-level artifacts for a contractual period.
[04:50] Jenna: How do you handle log redaction accuracy? our compliance team wants false negative rates and evidence that PII patterns are redacted.
[05:00] Priya: Our redaction uses hybrid rules + ML detectors. We can share metrics from evaluation sets — false negative/positive rates — and run a sample evaluation against a sanitized prompt set you provide. We'll include the evaluation in the security pack.
[05:16] Samir: About telemetry — what's included in request logs? token counts, latency buckets, model version, prompt IDs, KV cache warms?
[05:26] Priya: Request id, model, model version, latency, token counts, and optional prompt hash. We don’t log full prompts to long-term logs unless you opt-in. KV cache internal metrics are not surfaced to customers but are part of the runtime telemetry.
[05:40] Mark: We need a very strict map: prompt origins -> user id -> timestamp, for regulator traceability. can Redwood attach our user ids to requests in a way that's immutable?
[05:52] Alex: You can pass an external_id field with each request that Redwood persists as part of the request metadata. For Dedicated/Private it can be persisted for longer and exported. For Hosted, you'd have to accept the standard retention policy or contract a custom retention.
[06:06] Jenna: Are there encryption-in-transit and at-rest guarantees for hosted? and where are the keys?
[06:14] Priya: TLS in transit for all. At-rest uses provider encryption by default; with CMKs you control the key used to encrypt model cache and storage. For hosted, the ciphertext keys are managed by Redwood unless a CMK is provisioned. region of key storage follows the KMS region.
[06:30] Samir: What about SSO and RBAC? auditors will ask to see role separation and admin logs.
[06:38] Alex: We offer SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and role-based roles in the Console. Access logs for admin actions are retained in our audit log and can be exported. For private control-plane, those logs can be fully retained under your control.
[06:52] Mark: Are there SLA differences between hosted and dedicated for latency and uptime? we run customer-facing features, so SLA matters.
[06:59] Priya: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed latency and throughput targets. Hosted has best-effort tiers; high-tier hosted customers get better SLOs but not the same contractual guarantees as Dedicated. Private may carry enterprise SLAs depending on deployment.
[07:12] Jenna: Another requirement: pseudonymization and masked logs for EU personal data. what tools do you provide?
[07:20] Priya: We provide regex-based and ML-based masking, tokenization modules, and can implement a preprocessor in your VPC for additional pseudonymization before data hits Redwood. That preprocessor can be customer-managed.
[07:34] Samir: On compute isolation — in Dedicated, are kernels co-located with other tenants' kernels on same GPUs? we want physical isolation for certain workloads.
[07:44] Priya: Dedicated gives dedicated GPU pools that aren't shared at the serving layer. There may be multi-tenant control-plane components unless you opt for private control-plane. For Private on-prem, you get full physical isolation.
[07:58] Mark: Any prior examples of proof bundles you provided to financial auditors?
[08:05] Alex: Yes, we've packaged SOC2 reports, key usage logs, redaction evaluations, and export bundles for a couple of banks — happy to share a redacted example.
[08:14] Jenna: Please do. also need to know your retention policy for raw prompts in hosted again — you said default 30 days but can it be shortened to zero?
[08:24] Priya: Default is 30 days with options to shorten. You can request zero retention but that impacts debugging and model quality analysis. For regulatory needs, Dedicated/Private where you manage exports is more common for zero-retention requirements.
[08:38] Mark: Pricing is always relevant. high-level question — what's the delta between hosted and dedicated for our scale? we're estimating a few hundred requests per minute in peak.
[08:48] Alex: We'll follow up with a cost model. high level: Dedicated has a committed monthly cost plus usage; it's typically 2-3x the hosted pure usage cost at small scale but provides predictability. We'll send a sizing/pricing workbook.
[09:00] Samir: On the subject of data subject requests — if an EU user requests deletion, can Redwood help identify and remove all traces in logs and models?
[09:10] Priya: For request logs and archives, yes — we can identify external_id traces and delete exported objects if you control the archive. For model-internalization (like training leakage), we don’t retrain on customer prompts in hosted; model weights aren't altered by runtime requests. For models with longer-term fine-tuning that ingest prompts, you'd need to ensure that pipeline is separate.
[09:34] Jenna: That helps. we still need to understand your legal posture if we ask for contractual data residency guarantees. do you offer addendums?
[09:44] Alex: Yes, we have Data Processing Addendums and SOC2 packages; for enterprise contracts we include residency clauses and breach obligations. We'll attach the DPA template.
[09:54] Mark: ok practical pilot idea: we'd like to run a scoped pilot on Dedicated with region-locking to eu-west-1, CMKs in our account, and log-forwarding to our archive for 6 weeks to capture evidence. Is that feasible?
[10:06] Priya: That is feasible. We'll need to size capacity (gpu type), onboard your KMS, and set up the S3/GCS export. minimal lead time is ~3 weeks for provision + security review.
[10:20] Jenna: 3 weeks is ok, as long as you can provide initial evidence artifacts for the first week so compliance can preview the outputs.
[10:30] Alex: We can provide initial evidence snapshots within the first 10 days. we'll commit to weekly check-ins during the pilot.
[10:36] Samir: Who will own the pilot runbook? Redwood or Weston?
[10:40] Priya: Joint ownership. Redwood will provide an onboarding doc and a runbook template; your Cloud team will supply the CMK and storage.
[10:48] Mark: Any known limitations around model variants and quantization — if we use quantized models to save cost, does it change log visibility or cache behavior that affects audits?
[10:58] Priya: No change in audit logs; quantization is an execution detail. The model version is still recorded. however latency and tokenization behavior might differ slightly; we'll surface the model variant in logs.
[11:10] Jenna: Final compliance question: can you support a dedicated evidence S3 bucket that only our auditors can access, and will Redwood ever write keys or have access to that bucket?
[11:22] Alex: We can write to your audited bucket; Redwood won't retain persistent access unless you grant it. typical pattern is short-lived write credentials during onboarding, then you rotate those keys. We can also set up a signed write-only endpoint.
[11:36] Priya: Ok switching gears, quick checklist of docs we'll share: SOC2, DPA, redaction eval, the example evidence bundle, and the pricing workbook + pilot runbook.
[11:48] Jenna: Good. one more small ask — can you include a diagram showing data flow for hosted vs dedicated vs private? auditors like visuals.
[11:58] Alex: Absolutely. We'll include architecture diagrams and an annotated evidence map.
[12:06] Mark: timeline-wise, after you send docs we can get legal + security review in two weeks, and if all good we'll kick the pilot.
[12:15] Alex: Sounds good. I'll summarize next steps.
[12:18] Priya: Anything else from your side?
[12:22] Jenna: not from me, thanks.
[12:24] Samir: No, that's it. thanks both.

Meeting recap snippet (auto): prioritized Dedicated pilot w/ CMK and eu-west-1 locking; Redwood to supply SOC2/DPA and redaction eval; onboarding lead time ~3 weeks; initial evidence snapshot within 10 days; weekly pilot check-ins.

Alex - Send SOC2, DPA template, redaction evaluation and example evidence bundle by 2026-11-12
Priya - Share pilot runbook and sizing workbook by 2026-11-13
Mark/Jenna - Confirm legal/security reviewers and provide CMK contact by 2026-11-17
Schedule compliance deep dive (30-45m) week of 2026-11-22
Alex: package SOC2 + redaction eval + evidence sample (due 2026-11-12)
Priya: sizing and pilot runbook (due 2026-11-13)
Mark: confirm pilot scope and internal reviewers (due 2026-11-17)
Samir: provision CMK and prepare destination S3 for log forwarding (target 2026-11-20)

2027-09-21-horizon-gauge-and-execution-pledge

Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-21 10:00 PT | Duration: 1:12 | Location: Zoom Town Hall
Attendees: Evelyn Park, Raj Patel, Lena Ortiz, Tom Nguyen, Marta Silva, ~140 watchers (company-wide)

Summary:
Evelyn opens with company pulse: revenue growth steady, churn low, cost pressure increasing; proposes temporary headcount pause and refocus on execution; Raj reviews reliability incidents and next actions; Lena outlines three product bets for Q4; Tom lists infra optimizations; Q&A follows with many live questions; meeting ends with clear next steps and action owners.

Topics:
- Company pulse and headcount guidance
- Reliability and Dedicated capacity incident review
- Q4 product bets and measurable outcomes
- Cost optimization (infra + model serving levers)
- People and hiring cadence
- Open Q&A and anonymous questions

Transcript body:
[00:00] Evelyn: good morning folks thanks for joining, sorry we pushed it to the late slot but wanted to make sure leadership could be here, um this is a short, but slightly heavier than usual all hands so i'll lead with the headline.
[00:12] Evelyn: revenue is — month over month growth is healthy, usage is up, customers using Dedicated more — so thanks to product and se for that, however cost per token / infra spend is outpacing net revenue growth this quarter.
[00:28] Evelyn: so after a review of hiring and runway, we are instituting a temporary hiring pause for all non-customer-facing IC roles, there will be a narrow set of exceptions for critical hires. i know this is a, uh, tough thing so marta will walk through the rationale and the exception process.
[01:02] Marta: thanks ev, quick note — this is a two-week pause to give us time to evaluate open reqs, re-prioritize, and make sure we staff the most mission-critical work; managers will hear more in the handbook post and there will be an exceptions form.
[01:20] Raj: ok jumping into reliability — we've had two P1 incidents in the last 6 weeks, both related to Dedicated autoscaler edge cases and one due to a failing kernel upgrade on a subset of instances. the good news is no data leakage, customer traffic rerouted; the bad news is latency SLO misses for some enterprise routes which is unacceptable.
[01:44] Raj: action items — runbook updates, change windows tightened, and an osc (ops) postmortem; i'm assigning myself to lead the SLO adjustments and a Dedicated capacity postmortem.
[02:02] Tom: hi this is tom — on infra, quick wins we found: reclaim stuck gpus from stranded pods, reduce cross-region replication for low-value logs (shorter retention), and tweak the scheduler to favor low-latency pools for hot routes. these are small perf wins with immediate cost upside.
[02:25] Tom: also, we validated a quantization rollout for a non-sensitive model family that drops token cost by ~28% in our staging benchmarks, we need more canaries but promising.
[02:44] Lena: product — we propose three Q4 bets: 1) Project Lighthouse: small-batch latency-critical offering for fintech/enterprise with tighter SLOs and premium pricing; 2) Private First: a push for more VPC/on-prem sales enablement and hardened compliance bundles; 3) Optimize-as-a-Service: automated cost tuning + suggested quantization/caching profiles for customers. each bet has owners and a 'must move the needle' metric.
[03:20] Lena: for lighthouse we will aim for 6 pilot customers by EOY and 95th percentile latency under 100ms for short requests, that's ambitious but necessary.
[03:34] Evelyn: quick context — these moves are to align org around revenue quality and defensibility. i want us to be a company that ships and measures outcomes not just features.
[03:47] Audience Q: (anon chat) will layoffs happen?
[03:52] Evelyn: no, we're not doing layoffs; the hiring pause is to preserve runway while we optimize spend. we will be careful to protect customer engineering and sales hiring.
[04:06] Audience: (raised hand) question about SOC two and audit timeline
[04:12] Raj: yes SOC 2 Type II is on track, audit window scheduled for late october, engineers should expect some compliance questionnaires. we'll publish a checklist. apologies if the earlier doc said 'SOC two' in the wrong font — that's on me.
[04:29] Lena: on Private First, we've closed two small pilot deals already in europe with finance customers who need VPC and KMS integration; we will invest more in sales enablement and a hardened onboarding pack.
[04:44] Evelyn: we also confirmed a new channel partner in APAC that helps with sales presence there; logistics and legal still sorting the resale agreement but it's a meaningful signal.
[04:56] Raj: back to technical ops — we noticed the KV cache behavior under high burst; small bug in prefix eviction logic caused some cache thrashing, patched in staging. i'll coordinate a controlled rollout and more extensive load tests.
[05:18] Tom: small note on benchmarks — our internal latency numbers speak to a wide distribution; some traffic patterns still see 150-300ms tails for certain long-turn chat sessions, so the Lighthouse product will require kernel tuning and possibly different routing.
[05:36] Evelyn: on the financial front, cfo sent a note: burn is up vs forecast. we are not in panic mode but need to show a path to better unit economics. hence product bets with near-term monetization and tech work to reduce per-token cost.
[05:50] Evelyn: we will not change the pricing publicly today, but sales will see an updated packaging preview and a pilot pricing for Lighthouse.
[06:03] Q: (someone) are we going to cut R&D?
[06:06] Evelyn: not cut R&D, we will re-prioritize roadmap and slow down some exploratory projects. this is about focus, not killing innovation.
[06:16] Marta: people stuff — i know hiring pauses cause anxiety; we're committed to transparency. managers please schedule 1:1s this week to talk about near-term impact. we will set up an AMA with people ops on wednesday.
[06:32] Audience: (chat) request for bump on parental and medical leave policies

Infra Gate & Credentialing Sync — Redwood POC

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-14 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (BlueRiver Platform Eng), Diego Morales (BlueRiver SRE), Hannah Li (BlueRiver Security)

Summary:
Quick sync to unblock infra gating and credentials for the POC. Covered outstanding access (service accounts, keys), network (VPC peering, egress NAT), security requirements (KMS/HSM, audit logs, SSO), and planned staging benchmark to validate latency SLO. Agreed on concrete next steps and owners. Shared artifacts: infra runbook (link), benchmark sheet (link).

Resources referenced:
- Infra runbook (placeholder): https://redwood.internal/poc/infra-runbook-bridger
- Benchmark spreadsheet: https://sheets.redwood/BR-poc-benchmarks
- Security pack (SOC2 + KMS notes): https://redwood.internal/compliance/small-biz-pack

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: okay everyone, thanks for joining on time, we only have 45 minutes so we'll keep tight. I'm Maya from Redwood, Liam's on the call for the infra checks. Uh, Priya, Diego, Hannah, great to see you. Can we do a quick round of status?
[00:22] Priya: yeah thanks. On our side, we've provisioned the staging VPC, but peering hasn't been accepted yet from the infra team. So that's the main blocker. We also need a list of exact ports and IPs to allow for the gateway.
[00:40] Liam: got it. We published a minimal firewall matrix in the runbook but I can call that out: outbound to 52.14.x.x on 443, and inbound for callbacks to your webhook on port 8443 if you enable streaming. Also note there are optional ports for metrics scraping, 9100 if you want Prom exporter.
[01:05] Diego: do we need dedicated NAT or can we use the shared egress? The compliance folks prefer dedicated egress for auditability.
[01:18] Hannah: yes, on security we prefer dedicated egress + VPC flow logs retained for 90 days. Also KMS control — keys must be customer-managed K M S or HSM-backed, we can't have provider-managed keys for PII inference traffic.
[01:35] Maya: understood. For the POC we typically support customer-managed KMS. There is a small setup step to grant Redwood service principal decrypt permission; we'll spell it out. I'll add a snippet to the runbook.
[01:50] Priya: perfect. Also on credentials: do we do API keys, or service account with short-lived tokens? We want short-lived if possible.
[02:01] Liam: we can support OAuth-backed short-lived tokens via our token-exchange flow, or API keys for simpler setups. For BlueRiver I'd recommend service account + short-lived tokens, because you already have automation for rotation. We do have examples in the runbook.
[02:20] Diego: are there any SAML/SSO hooks needed for the console access? We might have non-dev folks that need to peek at dashboards.
[02:31] Maya: yes console SSO we support SAML. SSO setup is a separate step; for initial POC the AE and SE can share read-only links but we can switch to your SAML provider before any demos.
[02:45] Hannah: we also need to validate audit logs go to our SIEM; can you confirm the format and fields?
[02:55] Liam: logs are JSON lines with event_type, request_id, model_id, timestamp, and redacted_input flag. We'll provide a sample schema. For PII, we have redaction toggles and a separate audit export.
[03:12] Priya: on the network side, firewall rules are simple, but peering is stuck because our infra ticket didn't include the CIDR for the instanced nodes — do you have that?
[03:25] Liam: yes currently the POC nodes are in 10.40.32.0/24; I'll paste that into the shared ticket. We can also provide a NAT gateway IP for allowlist.
[03:38] Priya: great. Add that to the ticket. Also, one more question: latency targets. Our product SLO is 95th percentile <= 300ms for small prompts, what's realistic here?
[03:51] Liam: for hosted infra with our smallest-medium model we see 95th around 120-180ms for single-turn 128-token requests in our benchmarks. For dedicated GPU pools it depends on sequence length and batching. For your concurrency pattern (you said 6 req/sec steady), we would expect to be in the 150-250ms 95th pctl range. We should run a baseline in staging to be sure.
[04:20] Diego: okay baseline please. We can ramp load gradually, maybe 1, 3, 6 req/s and capture p95, p99 and token cost.
[04:33] Maya: we'll do that. Liam will own the test and upload results to the benchmark sheet.
[04:40] Hannah: on cost and data residency, we need confirmation data isn't stored beyond the configured TTL and that logs don't contain raw user input.
[04:50] Maya: by default we keep inputs for 7 days for debugging, but for enterprise POCs we can set retention to 0 (no retention) and enable strict audit-only logging to your SIEM. We'll note that in the security pack.
[05:03] Priya: thanks. About model variants — do we have fallback to a smaller quantized model if capacity is constrained? We plan to test failover.
[05:15] Liam: yes we support automatic fallback rules: for example primary model rdx-large, fallback to rdx-medium-8q. There are slight quality regressions — we'll show you a quick prompt set to compare. We also can pin versions to avoid drift during the POC.
[05:35] Diego: on pinning, we need an immutable endpoint for load testing. How do we ensure the model doesn't switch mid-test?
[05:45] Maya: during the POC we recommend pinning a model version on the route — that'll prevent automatic upgrades. We'll document how to do that and include the API curl.
[05:55] Priya: security question: do you support customer-managed HSM for key wrapping? Hannah asked about HSM-backed KMS earlier.
[06:05] Liam: yes, we integrate with AWS CloudHSM and external HSM via our KMS adapter. There is an initial handshake and IAM roles to grant. It usually takes a day to set up on your side.
[06:20] Hannah: okay please share the exact IAM policy.
[06:23] Maya: noted, I'll include the policy snippet in the runbook.
[06:30] Liam: quick note on monitoring — we can stream metrics to your Prometheus via pushgateway or expose scrape endpoints. For low-latency metrics we suggest scrape interval 10s.
[06:45] Priya: we'll use scraping. Can you give the port and path?
[06:50] Liam: /metrics on port 9100 by default; again optional but recommended.
[07:00] Maya: let's run through the unblock list quickly: 1) VPC peering accept + CIDR (Priya), 2) service account provisioning (Priya), 3) KMS policy (Hannah), 4) baseline latency run (Liam). Any additions?
[07:15] Diego: add a security review of data retention and redaction rules before demo.
[07:20] Hannah: yes, please. We'll need the SOC2 attestation and proof of encryption in transit + at rest.
[07:28] Maya: we'll share the SOC2 summary and the KMS attestation doc in the security pack.
[07:35] Priya: timing: we need the infra gate cleared by 2026-05-21 to stay on our sprint. Is that feasible?
[07:44] Maya: yes, if peering and service account are done by 2026-05-17 we can run baseline and clear gates by 2026-05-21. Liam, do you agree?
[07:51] Liam: yes, with the caveat that our baseline run might reveal small tuning (batch size, kv cache warmup) but we can iterate quickly — should be within the window.
[07:59] Diego: if we see tokenization cost spikes, can we test quantized variants?
[08:06] Liam: absolutely — we'll include cost-per-1k-tokens estimates in the benchmark sheet for each variant.
[08:15] Maya: last logistic: I'll send a follow-up email with the runbook, the exact IAM snippet, and the shared spreadsheet link. Also I'll create the ticket in your tracker with the NAT IP and CIDR info.
[08:29] Priya: thank you. Anything else?
[08:33] Hannah: just one small ask — can you include a sample request/response showing redaction flag so our SIEM knows to ignore raw input fields?
[08:42] Liam: yes I'll paste a sample JSON in the sheet.
[08:47] Maya: perfect. We'll recap next steps in the follow-up. Thanks everyone.
[08:53] (meeting ends)

Meeting recap (end):
- Infra gating items: VPC peering, service account, KMS policy, NAT IP allowlist.
- Security docs to be shared: SOC2 summary, KMS/HSM attestation, sample audit log format.
- Baseline tests: Liam to run p95/p99 latency runs at 1/3/6 reqs/sec and upload results.
- Owners/persons of contact: Maya (runbook + follow-up), Liam (benchmarks), Priya (VPC + creds), Hannah (security artifacts), Diego (SRE coordination).

Notes about transcription: there are occasional mis-heard acronyms (K M S sometimes transcribed as kay-em-ess), and a few speaker overlaps. Natural filler words retained for authenticity.

Private deployment inference networking runbook review

Runbook-focused technical deep dive to validate Copperline's network diagram and constraints for a private VPC deployment of Redwood Inference. Discussed NAT hairpinning, PrivateLink endpoints, route tables, DNS resolver placement, KV cache affinity, benchmarking approach, and compliance touches (KMS/audit). Agreed on runbook edits and a benchmark window next week.
Redwood: update runbook with border-router NAT recommendations and share by 2026-07-24
Customer: confirm maintenance window for benchmark (preferred 2026-07-29 02:00-05:00 UTC)
Both: agree on a 90-minute benchmark script (p95 latency, throughput ramps, cold vs warm KV cache)
Redwood: provide sample iptables/eBPF hint for hairpinning and egress health checks
Priya - update runbook and diagram, include PrivateLink vs TGW notes - due 2026-07-24
Ibrahim - confirm border router/NAT appliance model and rules, share config snippets - due 2026-07-25
Alex - send benchmark harness repo and example loadfile - due 2026-07-23
Leah - provide list of compliance requirements (KMS, audit retention) to Redwood - due 2026-07-26
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-22
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Luis (Redwood SRE), Jordan (Copperline CTO), Maya (Platform Eng), Ibrahim (Network Lead), Leah (Security)

00:00 Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll do a runbook review for Copperline's private deployment. I pulled the diagram you shared, Ibrahim, and there are a couple spots we want to call out around egress and DNS.
00:18 Jordan: Thanks Alex. We're mostly focused on keeping traffic internal to the VPC and limiting public egress. The app team also asked about cold-starts for inference and the KV cache warmup.
00:33 Priya: Cool, we'll step through the runbook section by section. First up, PrivateLink endpoints and how the inference runtime reaches our control plane and model artifacts. Your diagram shows a VPC Endpoint in the workload subnet, right?
00:50 Ibrahim: Correct. We put an Interface endpoint in the app subnet, tied to the ENIs on the subnets where the pods run. We plan to NAT from a border appliance in the transit VPC for any external egress.
01:06 Priya: Two quick clarifications: 1) When you use an interface endpoint for the control plane, traffic should not hairpin out via NAT — it should go to the ENI->endpoint path. If DNS is resolving to the public hostnames for Redwood, hairpinning crops up. 2) KV cache affinity: we prefer the KV cache to sit in the same AZ or in a colocated subnet to reduce cross-AZ latency.
01:28 Ibrahim: On hairpinning, we're running an on-prem border router that does SNAT for internet-bound flows. I worry about cases where a request to the Redwood control plane hits the NAT because the VPC resolver returns a public IP.
01:40 Luis: That's a common trap. Our recommended runbook step is to pin the private DNS via the VPC endpoint, and enforce route table entries so the internal ENI is preferred. If you must use split-horizon DNS, ensure the VPC DNS resolver rewrites the name to the endpoint IP.
01:58 Maya: Quick question: what about egress for the model artifact pull? The image repo is in a private S3 bucket accessed via VPC endpoint, but the checksum server is external. We can't allow arbitrary outbound to the internet.
02:13 Priya: For artifact pulls, we see two patterns: 1) Use a proxy in the transit VPC that allows outbound to specific hostnames/IP ranges, with strict TLS cert pinning for vendors. 2) Mirror artifacts to an internal bucket behind the endpoint — that removes the need for NAT at runtime. Both are in the runbook notes.
02:31 Ibrahim: If we mirror artifacts, that's preferred. But mirroring adds storage ops. We can do it for production.
02:40 Alex: Let's call out an explicit runbook flow: bootstrapping hosts only contact internal endpoints; artifact pulls from internal S3 endpoints; control plane only reachable via Interface PrivateLink; egress only for metric/ops to allowed destinations via transit proxy. We'll add that.
02:56 Jordan: Nice. Can we discuss KV cache placement? We're expecting model context KV cache to be hot for chat workloads, p95 token latency target is ~120ms.
03:09 Priya: Sure. For p95 120ms you need KV cache <5ms round-trip inside the same AZ if possible. If the cache is cross-AZ you add 2-15ms depending on provider, and that eats into CPU plus batching windows. So runbook says: co-locate cache pods on same AZ and use pod anti-affinity to keep caches near inference workers. Also configure continuous prefix caching to warm cache when you ramp.
03:34 Maya: Any specific recommendations on cache types? In-memory vs managed Redis?
03:40 Luis: In-memory local KV inside the inference pod gives best latency, but you lose shared warm-state. Managed Redis (or elasticache) is fine, but pick the shortest network hop. We recommend our runtime to use a small local L1 cache and use a managed L2 for cross-instance sharing — that hybrid is in the docs.
03:58 Ibrahim: How about memory footprint? Our nodes are GPU-heavy, but limited RAM per pod. Is the hybrid approach memory efficient?
04:06 Priya: You can keep L1 small (evict hot prefixes only) and rely on L2 for larger state. We'll provide sample configs showing L1=128MB per pod and Redis maxmemory-policy=allkeys-lru tuned to expected prefix cardinality. We'll add that sample to the runbook.
04:25 Jordan: Good. Let's move to batching and latency tradeoffs. We're sensitive to tail latencies because customers interact in real time.
04:34 Priya: Right. For interactive chat you want small batch sizes (2-8) and more aggressive latency SLOs. For background embeddings jobs you can batch higher. Our runtime supports dynamic batching where we set a max batch size and a max wait (ms). Runbook suggests starting with max batch 8 and max wait 30ms for p95 120ms target, then iterate with the benchmark harness.
04:58 Maya: What about quantization? We want to use int8 to save memory, but worried about latency jitter.
05:05 Luis: Quantization reduces model footprint and allows higher throughput per GPU. For latency, quantization tends to reduce per-token compute, so p95 improves; but you must run accuracy/regression evals. Runbook includes a quantization checklist: run eval suite on the model, A/B test in canary, enable fallback to float if quality regresses.
05:25 Ibrahim: On the network side, anything special with quantized models? Not really, but model size means different artifact pull strategies. Smaller models reduce cold-start time on disk.
05:36 Alex: Good point. We'll add cold-start measurements pre/post-quantization to the benchmark plan.
05:42 Jordan: Let's pivot to NAT hairpinning specifics and route table recommendations. Ibrahim can you sketch your current architecture?
05:50 Ibrahim: Sure. We have a transit VPC with a border router. Workload VPCs peer to transit via TGW. The border appliance sits in a public subnet in transit and handles SNAT for outbound. Interface endpoints are in each workload VPC. DNS is AmazonProvided resolver; split-horizon is not set up currently.
06:08 Priya: The runbook step: don't rely on NAT for interface endpoint traffic. Add explicit endpoint DNS entries or host overrides so that the service CNAME resolves to the private endpoint IP. At the route table level, ensure the ENI subnet has a route to the endpoint and not to 0.0.0.0/0 for that prefix.
06:27 Ibrahim: If a host resolves to a public IP and hits the border router, do we get asymmetry?
06:32 Luis: Yes, you can get asymmetry and TCP resets because source IPs will be SNATed. We recommend: 1) enforce VPC resolver to return the endpoint IP 2) add iptables on the border router to block hairpinned flows for known Redwood FQDNs as extra safety. We'll provide the iptables snippet.
06:50 Maya: How about TLS termination? We must ensure client certs validate to our gateway.
06:54 Priya: We recommend mTLS between the runtime and control plane (mutual TLS) where possible; PrivateLink provides the secure channel, but mTLS adds defense-in-depth. We'll include cert rotation notes tied to your KMS.
07:11 Leah: On KMS and audit: our security team needs to know how Redwood stores keys and what audit logs we get for model loads and inference requests.
07:20 Alex: For Private deployments you run a customer-controlled KMS/HSM; Redwood can integrate to customer KMS via standard APIs. We stream audit events to your S3 (or your SIEM) with configurable retention. Runbook will include sample audit events and a mapping table.
07:36 Leah: Great. For SOC2 we need 12 months of certain logs. Can we get line items?
07:41 Luis: Yes, we'll add an appendix showing log types (auth events, model-load, artifact pull, rollout changes, user access) and retention options.
07:52 Jordan: Back to benchmarking — what metrics should we collect in the run?
07:57 Priya: Collect: p50/p90/p95/p99 token latency, end-to-end request latency, GPU utilization, batch sizes distribution, KV cache hit ratio, cache RTT per AZ, network RTT, DNS resolution times, artifact pull times for cold starts, memory/swap metrics. We'll provide a Prometheus job and Grafana dashboard template in the repo.
08:21 Ibrahim: For the benchmark harness, do you recommend synthetic traffic or replaying production traces?
08:26 Priya: Both. Start with synthetic steady-state ramps to validate SLOs, then run a replay of a sanitized production trace to check hotspots. We have a script that replays user traces with preserved inter-arrival timing. We'll share it.
08:44 Jordan: About failover: if an AZ goes down, what happens with KV cache warmness?
08:50 Luis: If an AZ fails we recommend a two-tier strategy: 1) allow cross-AZ cache fetches but expect higher latency; 2) on failover, pre-warm caches in the target AZ using predictive prefix lists so cold-start penalty is reduced. Runbook includes pre-warm hooks during autoscaling events.
09:09 Maya: I saw mention in the runbook of egress health checks. What do those look like?
09:15 Priya: Egress health checks are lightweight probes from the workload subnet to allowed external endpoints via transit proxy, validating SNI/TLS and firewall rules. Also probes to the PrivateLink endpoint IPs to validate interface ENI reachability. We'll include a Kubernetes liveness probe example.
09:34 Ibrahim: Anything special for the on-prem link? We have an IPsec tunnel to the transit VPC.
09:40 Luis: Over IPsec you'll want to ensure MTU accommodations (don't fragment NVMe transfers), and we recommend jitter tests during the benchmark to measure tail latency. If the tunnel adds >10ms, that affects p95. We'll add the MTU and MSS clamping hints.
09:58 Jordan: Can we get an example runbook excerpt for the border-router NAT rules?
10:03 Priya: We'll paste an excerpt but high level: deny hairpin flows for Redwood FQDNs, allow only proxy egress to specific nets, and implement stateful inspection for long-lived streaming connections. Also provide an iptables/eBPF config for performance.
10:20 Ibrahim: Good. Let's touch on PrivateLink vs TGW choice for endpoint exposure. We're leaning TGW for centralization.
10:28 Priya: TGW centralizes connectivity but increases the chance of cross-AZ hops depending on attachment AZs. PrivateLink keeps traffic to the local ENI in the same AZ and often gives lower latency. Runbook has a table: if low-latency interactive is primary -> prefer Interface Endpoint per AZ; if centralized management and cost is priority -> TGW with colocated caches.
10:54 Jordan: That table will be helpful. Also want to discuss routing policies for session stickiness during canaries.
11:02 Alex: For canaries we suggest a 5-10% traffic split with a route policy that pins session cookies or connection hashes to the canary. We also support canary rollouts in the control plane that coordinate model versions and fallback rules.
11:18 Maya: One more networking nuance: DNS caching on nodes might collide with split-horizon changes. How do we mitigate TTL issues?
11:25 Luis: Lower TTLs for the private entries and run a DNS flush job on DST changes; include a systemd-resolved restart snippet for nodes. Also add an endpoint healthcheck before you flip TTLs.
11:41 Ibrahim: When we do the benchmark, what's the expected fallout window? We want to avoid impacting prod.
11:47 Priya: We recommend a maintenance window in a staging-like environment or a production canary with rate-limiting; the planned window you suggested 2026-07-29 02:00-05:00 UTC works. We'll run gradually and monitor for packet drops, error rates, and SLO regressions.
12:03 Jordan: Good. Any guidance on firewall appliance connection limits? The border router we have supports X concurrent connections but we need to know expected ephemeral port consumption with thousands of clients.
12:15 Luis: We'll model ephemeral port consumption in the benchmark; typical inference flows use long-lived streaming connections which conserve ports, but bursty REST traffic consumes ports. Runbook includes formulas and a calculator spreadsheet. We'll send that.
12:33 Maya: About TLS cert rotation: who rotates and how do we automate for PrivateLink?
12:38 Alex: For Private deployments customers manage certs. Redwood supports cert rotation hooks in the deployment agent and consumes certs from your KMS. We'll include an automation example using HashiCorp Vault and KMS-backed secrets.
12:58 Leah: For audit ingestion, we need a near-real-time pipeline to our SIEM. Is that supported?
13:04 Luis: Yes, Redwood can stream audit events to your HTTPS sink or push to S3 then ingest; the runbook describes both patterns and pros/cons. We'll add message schemas and throughput expectations.
13:26 Jordan: Anything else on quantization and model rollout?
13:31 Priya: One more item: when you test quantized models include mixed-precision fallback paths and tune the runtime kernel selection for int8 on your GPU family. Different kernels may have different latency characteristics; we have a kernel profiler that records per-layer timing.
13:49 Ibrahim: Will you share the profiler output format?
13:52 Priya: Yes, the benchmark repo includes a sample profiler output and a small parser to aggregate layer-level latency into per-token estimates.
14:06 Alex: Looks like we're coming up on the top of the hour. Quick recap of agreed edits: runbook NAT/hairpin section, KV cache affinity examples, benchmark harness and schedule, iptables snippet, audit/event mapping, and cert rotation examples.
14:19 Jordan: That matches our notes. Any final questions?
14:24 Leah: Just one — retention of audit logs. Make sure 12 months retention is doable and documented.
14:28 Luis: We'll include exact retention configs and the cost estimates for S3 lifecycle.
14:38 Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll expect the updated runbook by Friday and confirm the benchmark window.
14:44 Alex: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the repo link and schedule.
14:50 (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcription had garbled some proper nouns (e.g., "Redwood runtime" sometimes transcribed as "red wood runtime") and occasional speaker flips. We preserved the conversational flow and added timestamps for reference.

Optimize workshop: quant sweep and operational risks (INT8 vs FP8)

Redwood Optimize walkthrough focused on quantization sweep (INT8 vs FP8) and the operational tradeoffs. SE demo'd Console metrics, q-profiles, and live latency/quality curves. Customer cares about latency SLOs for customer-facing features and strict PII handling; discussed Dedicated vs Hosted and fallback policies. Agreed next steps: share benchmarks, get prompt corpus, and schedule a short Dedicated pilot.
Header: 2025-06-18 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~57 mins | Recording: yes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Ellen (Redwood SE), Marcus (Product), Joanna (Solutions), Diego (AvaBank Head ML), Priya (Platform), Liam (CTO), Noah (SRE)

[00:00] Samir: All right folks, thanks for hopping on. We wanted to do an Optimize workshop — take you through a quant sweep, show INT8 and FP8 q-profiles in the Console and call out operational risks. Quick intro round, then Ellen will share her screen.

[00:18] Diego: Hey thanks, Diego here. We're mostly focused on latency for our front-end insights pipeline, and also we have pretty strict data retention and KMS requirements.

[00:30] Priya: And we need to understand what success looks like — like fidelity thresholds and regressions. We run a mix of closed-book and retrieval-augmented prompts.

[00:44] Ellen: Cool. I'll share my screen — just to set expectations, this is a demo environment not your account, but the q-profiles are the same format you'll see in Optimize. We'll run a sweep across FP16 baseline, INT8 quant, and FP8 microformat for one of the LLaMA-derived models you referenced.

[01:12] Ellen: (screen) Here is the Console -> Optimize tab. On the left is the q-profile manager, you can define per-model profiles: block size, per-channel vs per-tensor, and the aggressive clipping thresholds.

[01:35] Ellen: We have a pre-made profile called "avabank-int8-conservative" and "avabank-fp8-balanced" for today's demo. I'll kick off a 5k-sample eval that runs the internal fidelity tests and latency probes.

[01:52] Liam: Quick question — when you say FP8, do you mean the newer hybrid FP8 kernels on A100s or is this a generic 8-bit floating point format?

[02:05] Ellen: Good call-out. In our runtime FP8 here maps to the hardware-accelerated bfloat-ish FP8 path on Ampere and Hopper where supported. If hardware lacks native FP8 we emulate with optimized kernels — throughput goes down but you still get numeric benefits versus INT8.

[02:32] Noah: And for INT8, is calibration required per model snapshot? We have many pinned versions.

[02:40] Ellen: Yes, INT8 typically needs a small calibration corpus. We provide automated calibration in Optimize, but if you pin a model version you'd want to run a short calibration job per checkpoint — that job is small, usually a few hundred example prompts.

[02:55] [02:57] Speaker 1 (Marcus): One thing to flag — INT8 yields much better throughput on current GPUs because kernels are mature, but you can see quality regressions on edge-case reasoning prompts we call out in the eval.

[03:20] Ellen: Kicking off the sweep now. You'll see three live charts: latency distribution (p99/p95), token-per-second, and a delta in fidelity (we surface straightforward metrics like exact-match and an embedding-similarity score).

[03:40] [04:00] Ellen: (pointing) Here's the first run: FP16 baseline p95 latency ~120ms with our sequence length (approx 512 tokens). INT8 conservative profile drops p95 to ~90ms and tokens/sec up ~1.4x. FP8 balanced hits p95 ~78ms and tokens/sec ~1.6x.

[04:32] Priya: That 78ms seems optimistic — what's the tail like? p99?

[04:40] Ellen: p99 for FP8 is at ~220ms in this synthetic run; INT8 p99 ~180ms; FP16 p99 ~300ms. The Console shows tail histograms and the request-level traces if you want to inspect particular slow requests.

[04:58] Diego: And how about quality — what's the delta for our critical customer answer set?

[05:06] Ellen: For the closed-book eval we ran: FP16 baseline exact-match 0.82, INT8 conservative 0.79 (delta -0.03), FP8 balanced 0.80 (delta -0.02). Embedding-similarity stays high (cos sim ~0.985 -> 0.98). For reasoning prompts we saw a higher variance; INT8 degraded on some multi-step reasoning by up to 6% absolute on our metric.

[05:39] Liam: Is that 6% consistent across seeds or just one-off?

[05:44] Ellen: It's repeatable on the flagged prompts, so we treat those as regression risk. That's why we recommend a small focused eval set — which you have to provide — and to run regression alerts in Optimize.

[06:00] Samir: Quick pause — this is a typical tradeoff: INT8 gives steady throughput gains and lower cost, FP8 can be faster but sometimes has a longer tail and hardware constraints. Our Optimize product surfaces these tradeoffs and gives rollback options.

[06:18] [06:40] Ellen: Now switching to the Console's per-route SLO UI. You can pin a model variant to a route and set a latency SLO and a quality guardrail. If a quantized variant crosses the guardrail we auto-fallback to a safer variant or to the baseline FP16.

[06:55] Priya: How is the fallback triggered? Do you do per-request scoring or batch windows?

[07:02] Ellen: It's configurable — you can use sliding-window metrics (e.g., p95 over last 5 minutes) or per-request checks for things like low-confidence tokens. We also support canary percentages.

[07:20] Diego: About safety and PII — when we run calibration corpora we have to ensure no customer data leaves our VPC. Can that be done inside our Private deployment?

[07:33] Joanna: Yes — in Redwood Private you run the control plane inside your VPC and calibration jobs can be run on-prem or inside your VPC. All KMS interactions remain under your key. We also export audit logs for SOC2.

[07:50] Diego: Good. Also curious about memory — INT8 reduces RAM but how about KV cache with quant?

[07:58] Ellen: Quantization reduces model weight memory; KV cache is typically still full precision for stability. But we have experimental KV-cache compression that can help memory, it adds a small CPU compression/decompression cost.

[08:18] [08:40] Ellen: The sweep completed for our 5k items. I'm pulling up the report. Here is a ranked list of prompts with biggest fidelity drop. You can click into each and see token-level diffs.

[08:52] [09:10] Ellen: For prompt ID 237 (a multi-hop finance summarization) INT8 changed the chain-of-thought and gave a hallucinated company name — that's flagged as high severity. FP8 preserved the chain better but still had slight numeric differences.

[09:35] Priya: How do we set alerting thresholds? For example we want to allow <=2% drop on closed-book answers, and <=5% for retrieval-augmented summaries.

[09:44] Ellen: In Optimize you define evaluation policies and severity levels. You can set thresholds per-route. When thresholds are crossed we can open a ticket, trigger a webhook, and optionally pause low-latency variants.

[10:05] [10:20] Marcus: Walkthrough of cost estimates — in this synthetic run INT8 reduced token compute cost by ~40% vs FP16; FP8 saved ~48% but had marginally higher operational overhead due to fallback. We present unit economics and cumulative cost curves in the Console.

[10:42] Diego: What about night/day traffic variance? We have bursty peaks. Does the autoscaler handle model-variant cold starts, especially with FP8 kernels?

[10:56] Ellen: Yes autoscaling includes warm pools and fast-scaling policies. For FP8, if you rely on specialized hardware, cold start can be slower if the runtime has to provision specific instances. We recommend a warm-min and burst-bucket for safety.

[11:18] [11:40] Priya: Can we do a canary of INT8 on 5% of traffic and run A/B evaluation on the same prompts?

[11:47] Samir: Absolutely. You can route a percentage in the Console and capture diffs. We also provide side-by-side token deltas for canaries.

[12:05] Diego: Let's talk about the calibration corpus size — you said a few hundred prompts. That sounds small; how representative does it need to be?

[12:16] Ellen: It needs to cover token distributions and corner cases. For most model families 500-1k diverse prompts gives good calibration. For finance datasets, include multi-step reasoning and numeric-sensitivity prompts.

[12:35] [13:00] Ellen: I'm going to export the benchmark CSV. Here you can filter by severity and by model variant. I'll open the top-20 regression list and show how to attach comments to each item.

[13:20] Priya: If we see persistent regressions on key prompts, can Optimize automatically revert the route?

[13:28] Ellen: Yes — we call it "auto-fallback policy". You can choose immediate auto-fallback or require a human in the loop. Policies are versioned so you can audit who changed them.

[13:45] Liam: From infra side — if we run Dedicated, what does the SLA look like for latency and throughput?

[13:53] Samir: For Dedicated we offer capacity SLAs and target latency tiers; specifics depend on reserved pool size and hardware family. We'll share a sample SLA in the follow-up.

[14:08] [14:30] Diego: Are there known corner cases where FP8 is worse than INT8? I would've thought FP8 is always better numerically.

[14:40] Ellen: FP8's numeric range can help but it can also amplify certain instabilities in layernorm or attention if kernel implementations differ. INT8 sometimes preserves behavior more predictably for some architectures because the quant strategy is per-channel and less lossy for weights. It's model-dependent.

[15:05] [15:30] Samir: We also discussed behavioral differences on instruction-following vs open-completion tasks — FP8 seems to be slightly better on short completions, INT8 is consistent on long-form generation in some families.

[15:48] Priya: Could you show us the API snippet for switching q-profiles programmatically? We want to tie that into our deployment pipeline.

[15:58] Ellen: Sure. (types) Here's an example curl/SDK: set route -> model_variant -> q_profile = "avabank-int8-conservative". You can change on the fly and the runtime will apply the new kernel within seconds for hot workers and on next bootstrap for new ones.

[16:25] [16:50] Ellen: Note: we also surface per-token cost breakdown in the API response when you enable debug tokens, so you can estimate cost for a request. That is off by default for performance reasons.

[17:05] Diego: For compliance we need to ensure logs are redacted. What's the level of control?

[17:12] Joanna: Full control — you can set token redaction policies, disable full request logging, and stream only hashed metadata. All logs stored in your account can be configured to use your KMS.

[17:35] [18:00] Ellen: I want to call out one recommended q-profile pattern — conservative int8 (higher precision for attention/ln layers, asymmetric quant for dense layers) gives most of the throughput gains with modest quality loss. Aggressive int8 (per-tensor) saves more memory but increases regression risk.

[18:22] Priya: Do you support mixed profiles where embeddings are INT8 but head layers stay FP16?

[18:30] Ellen: Yes, Optimize supports hybrid profiles. You can customize layer groups (embedding, transformer body, lm head) and set quant per-group. This is a common pattern.

[18:50] [19:10] Marcus: We're seeing a frequent customer ask — how to validate hallucination changes after quant. We recommend a test harness with known-answer prompts and an embarrassment-of-exact-match metric plus embedding similarity and human spot checks.

[19:34] Diego: Let's pivot to pilot scoping. We'd like a 2-week pilot on Dedicated with a small pool and both INT8 and FP8 variants in canary. The goals: 1) verify latency SLOs in real traffic, 2) run our regression suite, 3) measure cost delta.

[19:55] Samir: Sounds good. We'll propose a pilot plan — sample pool size, cost estimate, and success criteria. We'll also include rollback runbooks.

[20:10] Priya: On security docs — we need SOC2, ISO attestation, and details on KMS integration and audit logs.

[20:20] Samir: We'll attach our security whitepaper and a vendor package with SOC2 certs and integration guides in the follow-up.

[20:33] [21:00] Ellen: Running another small live test — this time with our per-request confidence check enabled. If confidence falls below threshold we tag the request and don't count it for canary rollouts.

[21:18] Priya: How are confidence scores computed?

[21:24] Ellen: We compute a token-level perplexity proxy and an embedding-cluster distance from reference responses. It's heuristic but useful to catch token-level weirdness.

[21:40] [22:00] Diego: You mentioned KV cache compression earlier — what effect does that have on latency?

[22:10] Ellen: Compression reduces memory footprint at the cost of a small CPU decompress per request; it's worth it when memory is the limiter. We measure an added 6-12ms in our tests depending on sequence length.

[22:32] [23:00] Marcus: Let's look at a specific regression item. Ellen opens prompt 237 and steps through token diffs.

[23:15] Ellen: You can see INT8 swapped a named entity phrase; the console highlights token replacements and confidence drops. You may choose to whitelist that prompt from quant use or pin that route to FP16 for that prompt class.

[23:40] Priya: We have a policy that financial entity names must be exact; can the Console enforce a strict-match guardrail for certain tokens?

[23:50] Ellen: We support token-level guardrails via post-processing hooks; you can add exact-match constraints for sensitive fields. That action will force fallback if violated.

[24:08] Samir: Time check — we've gone ~24 minutes, great discussion. Any other deep infra questions?

[24:20] Noah: On autoscaling, do you support GPU type mixing? We sometimes want cheaper instances for background jobs and higher-power for real-time routes.

[24:32] Ellen: Yes — routing policies can be hardware-aware; you can route low-priority requests to cheaper GPUs and reserve premium GPUs for high-priority routes. Optimize's cost estimator will reflect that.

[24:55] Diego: About metrics export — can we stream traces to our Datadog?

[25:02] Joanna: Yep — we have integrations for Datadog, Prometheus, and BigQuery. Traces include request IDs for correlating with your logs.

[25:20] [25:40] Ellen: Demo: switching the route to avabank-int8-conservative on 5% traffic. Starting canary now. You can watch real-time deltas.

[26:00] Priya: Let's hold — we want to ensure the calibration job can be run inside our VPC. Diego will coordinate a sample data transfer.

[26:12] Diego: Yes I'll drop a short list of prompts into secure storage and Priya will reference it.

[26:22] Samir: Great — officially logging next steps. Ellen will package the benchmark CSV and q-profiles; I'll send the pilot proposal and security docs.

[26:40] Ellen: One last note on model rollouts — you can schedule staged rollouts with ramp percentages and auto abort on quality breach. This is how many customers safely adopt INT8.

[26:56] Priya: If we do the pilot on Dedicated, do we need to provision a Private control plane?

[27:04] Samir: Not immediately — Dedicated includes a managed control plane by default. Private is recommended when you need stricter network/VPC control or air-gap requirements. We can discuss which fits your compliance bar.

[27:20] [27:40] Liam: Can you share cost curves for the pilot? Rough monthly estimate for a small pool?

[27:49] Marcus: For a small 4-GPU pool on Ampere with INT8 we estimate ~X (we'll put real numbers in the pilot doc). The Console's cost estimator will give scenario baselines once we link your traffic profile.

[28:10] Priya: Anything else on tooling? We'll want webhook support for regression alerts to our internal ticketing flow.

[28:18] Ellen: Webhooks and Slack integrations available. We'll include templates in the follow-up.

[28:32] Diego: Quick clarifying question — if we detect regression on a small subset of prompts, can you auto-exclude those from the quantized route rather than fallback all traffic?

[28:42] Ellen: Yes — you can create prompt classes or fingerprints and route them to different model variants. It's fairly granular.

[29:00] [29:20] Samir: We're about halfway through; let's move to an operational checklist for the pilot.

[29:30] Samir: Checklist items: security review, calibration run inside VPC, pilot Dedicated pool size, eval criteria, rollback runbook, and cost estimate. We'll propose dates.

[29:50] Diego: For timelines, we'd like to start pilot in the first week of July.

[29:58] Samir: We'll propose July 1 start with a 2-week window.

[30:10] [30:40] Ellen: One more technical note: some models respond better to quant-aware fine-tuning. If you need peak fidelity with quant, fine-tuning with a quantization-aware loss can recover some of the drop. We offer guidance but typically customers run this if the regression risk is unacceptable.

[31:00] Priya: Do you support running that fine-tune within our Private deployment?

[31:08] Joanna: We can enable training ops in Private, but it's a separate engagement. We'll outline options and costs.

[31:22] Liam: Any examples of customers who regressed on INT8 but resolved with hybrid profiles?

[31:30] Marcus: Yes — financial SaaS typically used hybrid profiles: keep attention/head layers FP16, quantize bulk dense layers. That preserved named-entity fidelity while giving 30-40% cost savings.

[31:50] [32:10] Ellen: wrapping up the live metrics view — here's the perf vs quality scatter plot. You can click any point to open the detailed trace.

[32:25] Diego: This is helpful. For the pilot we'll supply three prompt cohorts: short queries, long multi-hop, and RAG summaries. Please run the regressions and produce per-cohort results.

[32:40] Samir: Noted. We'll put that in the pilot doc.

[32:54] Priya: A few quick follow-ups: 1) share scripts for auto calibration, 2) sample q-profiles, 3) pilot SLA estimates.

[33:04] Samir: We'll deliver those.

[33:20] [33:50] Ellen: Quick demo of the API for programmatic rollback. This is a small SDK snippet that calls the route update endpoint.

[34:10] Priya: Security question again — where are your audit logs stored and how long?

[34:18] Joanna: Logs are stored in customer buckets by default with retention configurable; for Hosted we keep short-term logs unless you opt-in for longer retention. For Dedicated/Private we can align with your retention policy.

[34:40] Diego: OK. I think we're good on policy.

[34:52] [35:10] Samir: Any final technical questions?

[35:20] Priya: One last: what happens if an FP8 kernel is not available on a region? Do you auto-fall back to INT8?

[35:28] Ellen: We can auto-fallback to a compatible variant. Smart routing can send requests to a region with FP8 if latency budget allows, or to INT8 in same region. It's all policy-driven.

[35:48] Samir: Great — time to recap.

[35:55] Samir: Recap: 1) We'll share benchmark CSV, q-profiles, and pilot proposal. 2) Customer will share prompt corpus and infra constraints. 3) Pilot: 2-week Dedicated run starting around July 1. 4) Security docs and SLA will be attached.

[36:18] Priya: Perfect. We'll also confirm the specific success metrics for the pilot in our reply.

[36:28] Diego: Thanks everyone. A couple of smaller questions we'll send via email to Samir.

[36:36] Samir: Sounds good. Thanks all — we'll follow up with the materials and a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff.

[36:50] [37:10] (small wrap-up chatter, people saying thanks, goodbyes)

[37:30] End of recording.

Notes: Transcription includes occasional speaker label errors and timestamps are approximate. Some technical terms were abbreviated (q-profile vs qprofile). The demo values are synthetic and for planning purposes only.
Demo used synthetic 5k eval set; numbers not final for production
Conservative INT8 recommended starting point; FP8 good for throughput but check tails
Pilot scope: Dedicated small pool, canary both INT8 and FP8, 2-week run
