POC weekly - eval crosstalk and guardrail tuning with Lodestar Security

Weekly POC sync focusing on recent eval score regressions and guardrail behavior. Went through failing prompt set, discussed scoring thresholds, proposed prompt surgery and rerun cadence. Agreed on a short benchmark run on Redwood Dedicated with KV cache toggled and quantization profile v2, plus security checklist follow-up.
Meeting header: 2026-01-15 14:00 UTC / Duration ~48 mins / Attendees: Maya (AE), Ravi (SE) - Redwood; Ari (Head of ML), Samir (CTO), Nia (DevOps), Jules (Product) - Lodestar.

Summary snippet: quick review of yesterday's eval drop, walked through guardrail false positives on the taxonomy prompts.

[00:00] Maya: okay everyone, thanks for joining, we got about 45 minutes, quick agenda - regression triage, prompt surgery, inference config, and next steps.
[00:18] Ari: uh thanks Maya, quick note - we saw a jump in false negative on the phishing-detect set after the last rollout, so that's what we want to dive into.
[00:30] Ravi: yeah we pulled the logs, it looks like the new prompt ensemble amplified a rare tokenization edge. there are some prefix interactions with the context that make the model more conservative.
[00:47] Samir: conservative meaning it's rejecting things it used to accept? can we quantify, like how many percent change?
[00:55] Ari: roughly FP stayed same but FN up about 7 points on the 5k holdout, precision stayed fine.
[01:12] Maya: ok that's consistent with what we saw in the heatmap - the score distribution slid left a bit. also note the scoring threshold was bumped to 0.78 last week during canary.
[01:30] Nia: I can share the canary logs but remember we had the KV cache enabled for faster responses; could that be influencing context propagation?
[01:45] Ravi: yes KV cache can change the prompt/state alignment; in our experiments caching sometimes masks prompt collisions, so we want to run a test matrix with cache on/off.
[02:05] Jules: also curious about quantization - we switched to q4_0 for cost but maybe that increased conservatism?
[02:14] Ravi: q4_0 can increase hallucination in certain instruction colors, but usually it affects token probabilities subtly. recommended to try quant v2 with per-channel calibration.
[02:32] Maya: action item for Redwood - run a 6k sample benchmark on Dedicated with two runs: kv cache off + quant v2, and kv cache on + baseline quant. we also want the raw token-level logits if possible.
[02:50] Ari: that'd be great. we can provision a small VPC endpoint for the run.
[03:05] Nia: I'll stand up a temp endpoint and give access - but we need an access window and creds management - we prefer short-lived tokens.
[03:18] Maya: we'll take that, short-lived creds only; send the details and we'll coordinate.
[03:28] Samir: timeline - when can Redwood run the bench? we have a release gating on 1/22 so need results earlier.
[03:40] Ravi: we can queue it and run by Mon 1/19, assuming endpoint is ready. gives 3 days to analyze.
[03:50] Ari: perfect.

[04:10] Maya: let's go into the prompt set - Ari you flagged 40 edge examples where the model flipped from accept to reject. did you label them with expected outcome?
[04:20] Ari: yes we labeled FP/FN and gave short notes; many are truncated email bodies or abbreviated domains, so the model misinterprets intent. transcription of some token like 'svc' got tokenized oddly.
[04:35] Ravi: that might be a tokenization artifact with the model/vocab combo. which model variant are you on in the pilot?
[04:45] Ari: currently pointing at 'open-guest-1.2' from the catalog; we tried the newer 'open-guest-2.0-fast' for latency but rolled back due to scoring drift.
[04:58] Maya: got it - we'll test both variants in the bench. also we'll test a trimmed prompt template that removes some leading micro-instructions to reduce collision.
[05:12] Samir: when you say 'trim' do you mean removing role descriptions? some of those lines are important for policy enforcement.
[05:22] Ravi: we mean removing redundant system-level fluff that duplicates content in the user message; small changes can reduce entity overlap and improve sensitivity.

[05:45] Ari: one weird thing - guardrail flagged a lot more 'sensitive-data' alerts after we changed the template, even on obviously safe examples.
[05:55] Jules: are the guardrails externalized or in-prompt heuristics? last time we discussed a mixed approach.
[06:05] Maya: currently Lodestar runs a hybrid: a model-based in-prompt safety shim plus a rules engine downstream. the rule engine hasn't changed, so we suspect the in-prompt signals got amplified.
[06:20] Nia: rule-engine logs show the same rules fired but with higher confidence scores, so the model shim likely bumped scores above rule thresholds.
[06:30] Ravi: we should consider lowering the shim's internal thresholds or moving certain checks fully downstream to avoid overblocking.

[06:58] Samir: cost question — if we revert to non-quantized or a higher param variant, cost will rise. what's the tradeoff?
[07:10] Maya: Redwood can provide cost delta estimates for Dedicated vs Hosted for the benchmark run. we'll include per-token and per-prediction averages.
[07:18] Ari: also want latency breakdown - the user experience team is sensitive to added latency beyond 200ms median.
[07:28] Ravi: on Dedicated with burst sizing and small batch config we should be able to keep p50 under 180ms for the 1k prompt size distribution; we'll measure p95 too.

[07:52] Maya: let's note success criteria: FN reduction to within 2 points of baseline and no >5% increase in guardrail false positives, with p95 latency under 500ms. agree?
[08:06] Ari: yes that's reasonable.
[08:10] Jules: + stakeholder sign-off if sample pass rate >= 93% on the curated set.

[08:28] Maya: ok moving on - scoring thresholds, currently you have a hard cutoff 0.78 - consider a sliding window / adaptive threshold during peak times.
[08:40] Ravi: adaptive thresholding can help when distribution shifts, but adds complexity: need drift detectors and a safe fallback. Redwood can instrument a drift monitor and auto-fall back to baseline model variant.
[08:55] Samir: fallback is important - we can't have silent degradation in prod. can we do canary + automatic rollback?
[09:05] Maya: yes, Redwood supports canary rollouts with automatic rollback if quality metrics drop below thresholds. that's part of Dedicated rollout config.

[09:25] Ari: a note on eval tooling - our scoring scripts produce macro F1, but we should look at per-class PR curves. some classes get crushed and pull global metric down.
[09:40] Ravi: agreed, per-class heatmaps are more actionable. we'll push a heatmap with clusters, and also a diff of token-level logits for the 40 flagged examples.

[10:05] Nia: on security items - we need to confirm KMS integration for keys, and confirm audit log retention policy, also SSO SAML for Redwood console.
[10:18] Maya: I'll share SOC2 summary and the KMS integration guide. For audit logs we can export to your SIEM; retention configurable per plan.
[10:30] Samir: data residency — some of our logs must stay within EU region, can you guarantee that?
[10:38] Maya: yes for Dedicated in EU region we can keep inference logs and meta in region; for Hosted we have region options but need a contract clause for enforced residency.

[10:58] Ari: ok back to guardrail FP cases - I can give 10 representative examples right now: (reads) 'confirmation token: 0x92', 'svc-listing' etc. some tokens are parsed as patterns and flagged.
[11:12] Ravi: those look like pattern match bleed-through. we can add negative examples into the prompt shim to de-amplify those triggers. that's low risk.
[11:25] Jules: prefer prompt-based softening over rules changes if possible because rules are widely used across products.

[11:40] Maya: let's talk rollout plan after bench: if bench shows fix, we do a canary 10% traffic for 48 hours, monitor guardrail and FN, then ramp. if regression shows up we auto rollback.
[11:55] Samir: sounds fine. Who will own monitor alerts during canary?
[12:02] Ari: Lodestar will own, Redwood will get the webhook alerts.
[12:10] Maya: we'll configure webhook, and set up a Slack bridge for paging on metric breaches.

[12:30] Ravi: technical detail - for the Dedicated benchmark we'll run two kernel profiles, default and optimized-attn; can you accept slightly longer p95 in exchange for better FN?
[12:42] Ari: yes if it's a few 10s of ms we can accept. UX team sets the cap.

[12:55] Nia: about the temp VPC creds - we need Redwood's IPs whitelisted, I'll send the CIDR ranges and a short TTL for the keys.
[13:06] Maya: fine, send to security@redwood.com and we'll coordinate.

[13:20] Samir: circling back on scoring thresholds: can we run a small A/B inside the bench where we compare 0.78 vs 0.74 cutoffs and see operating points?
[13:31] Ravi: yes we'll do a ROC analysis and return suggested thresholds per class.

[13:48] Ari: one more ask - can Redwood capture example-level explanations (saliency) for the 40 flagged items? we want to triage root cause quickly.
[13:58] Ravi: we can attach attention-weight proxies and token gradient approximations — will include as separate artifact in the bench output.

[14:12] Maya: logistics - recap of who does what and due dates. Ravi will run bench by 1/19 and share raw logs + heatmaps. Ari will curate 40 examples by 1/18. Maya sends security docs by 1/16. Nia stands up temp VPC by 1/17. Jules will reconfirm success metric owners by 1/20.
[14:35] Samir: quick question on cost: Maya can you ballpark cost delta for Dedicated runs?
[14:42] Maya: estimate in the notes - likely a few hundred to low thousands depending on runtime; we'll send a short pricing sketch with the bench results.

[14:58] Ari: excellent. anything else?
[15:02] Jules: just that once we have bench results we might want a focused session on adaptive thresholds and drift hooks.
[15:10] Maya: we'll schedule a follow-up post-benchmark - propose 1/21 afternoon?
[15:18] Ari: works.

[15:30] Maya: ok thanks everyone, we'll follow up with meeting minutes and artifacts.
[15:36] Ravi: thanks, logging action items now.
[15:40] Nia: thanks all.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription quality: medium — a few proper nouns and model names may be slightly off (e.g., q4_0 vs q4o), some timestamps approximate.

Ravi Patel | Run Dedicated benchmark with KV cache off/on, quant v2 | due: 2026-01-19
Ari Romero | Curate and tag 40 edge-case prompts + label FP/FN examples | due: 2026-01-18
Maya Chen | Send SOC2 summary & KMS integration notes + pricing sketch | due: 2026-01-16
Nia Brooks | Provision a short-lived VPC endpoint, share creds for benchmark (temp) | due: 2026-01-17
Jules Park | Confirm product-level success metrics and internal stakeholders for sign-off | due: 2026-01-20
Redwood to run 6k sample benchmark on Dedicated + send raw logs (Ravi) by 2026-01-19
Customer to prune prompt set and flag 40 edge examples (Ari) by 2026-01-18

Schedule rollback drill with Nia and Redwood for 2026-01-22

document.content:
POC playbook timeline and risk triage with Apollo Systems

Header:
Date: 2026-03-05
Start Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Lena Morales (Redwood AE), Omar Patel (Redwood SE), Diego Santos (Redwood CSM); Mark Jensen (CTO, Apollo), Priya Rao (Head of ML), Ben Cho (Infra), Sara Liu (Product)

Summary: Kickoff-style scoping for a 4-week POC focused on retrieval-augmented generation for Apollo's customer support assistant. Discussed success criteria, access gating, benchmark metrics, timeline with kickoff, access, mid-point, and exec readout. Identified security/SSO/KMS questions and initial risk triage. Agreed deliverables and owners.

Topics: POC goals and success criteria; dataset and workload sizing; benchmarking plan (throughput & latency targets); access and security checklist; timeline and milestone cadence; risk & fallback plan; exec readout prep.

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena: Hi everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Lena from Redwood, AE on this account. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Mark: Mark Jensen here, CTO at Apollo Systems.
[00:11] Priya: Priya Rao, Head of ML.
[00:13] Ben: Ben Cho, infra engineer.
[00:15] Sara: Sara Liu, PM for support assistant.
[00:17] Omar: Omar Patel, solutions engineer, Redwood.
[00:19] Diego: Diego Santos, CSM.
[00:22] Lena: Great. Goal for today is to align on a concrete 4-week POC plan, what success looks like, and what access we need. We'll propose a kickoff tasks timeline and agree on midpoint and exec readout. Sound good?
[00:30] Mark: Yeah, makes sense. We're hoping to validate latency under realistic load and see qualitative answer quality compared to our current model. Also cost modeling.
[00:38] Priya: And security — we need to confirm SOC2 posture and that logs are handled in our VPC.
[00:43] Omar: Totally. We'll cover both. Quick question on scope: are you planning a retrieval augmented pipeline with your vector DB, or a closed model approach?
[00:50] Sara: RAG — we have an existing vector store (Pinecone) and S3 for attachments. We want the assistant to reference internal KB and attachments.
[00:57] Omar: Good. For benchmarking we'll need a sample set of queries and golden-label answers if you have them, or we'll do blind human eval.
[01:04] Priya: We have a few thousand annotated tickets, not full labels but we can surface a 300-case subset for eval.
[01:11] Lena: OK that's perfect for initial quality gates. Let's walk through a proposed milestone map.

[05:12] Omar: Week 0 (kickoff & access): we need read-only S3, vector DB credentials (readonly), account ID, and an IP allowlist for our integration agents or a VPC peering option. We'll also request sample traffic profile — average QPS, burst, typical prompt lengths (tokens). Typical POC footprint for this use case is 1-4 GPU instances, but depends on concurrency.
[05:40] Ben: For infra we're fine opening an allowlist and adding a service account with read-only S3. VPC peering might take longer — open to allowlist for POC.
[05:48] Lena: Great. We generally recommend allowlist in early POCs, unless you require private-only. We'll note that as a risk.

[08:20] Omar: Benchmarks: we propose the following metrics — throughput (qps), latency p50/p95/p99, token cost per response, and qualitative accuracy scored by your SMEs. For SLOs what are you expecting?
[08:35] Priya: We'd like p95 under 800ms for typical tickets and p99 under 2s. For accuracy, intent/answer correctness should be at least parity with our baseline, ideally +5% F1 on retrieval answers.
[08:47] Lena: Those are reasonable. We'll highlight that the p95/p99 will vary with sequence length and whether KV cache warming is used. For cost we can provide a delta comparing Redwood-hosted vs dedicated capacity.
[09:01] Mark: Can you also show us a worst-case fallback plan if latency spikes? We can't have timeouts during peak mornings.
[09:08] Omar: Yes — typical Redwood pattern is multi-variant routing: if a large model is slow, request can fall back to a smaller variant or to a cached response. We'll demo fallback policies in the mid-point.

[12:33] Priya: Security — SOC 2, SAML/SSO, KMS integration for key management, and audit logs. We need to know what Redwood retains in hosted mode.
[12:43] Diego: We have an enterprise package for Private deployments and VPC options. For hosted, we can provide an org-level retention setting and customer-managed KMS on Dedicated/Private. I can follow up with our security pack PDF.
[12:57] Ben: For the POC we'll need specifics on log redaction and whether PII can be filtered before hitting Redwood.
[13:05] Omar: We can add a pre-processing hook to scrub PII; alternatively you can send a de-identified dataset. We'll include both options in the runbook.

[16:02] Lena: Let's set milestones: Kickoff (this week) — access & runbook; Week 1 — baseline runs and quick throughput baseline; Week 2 — tuning (quantization/ batching, caching), Week 3 — increased concurrency and mid-point review; Week 4 — exec readout prep and final report. Does that align?
[16:17] Sara: Yes but we need a mid-point demo to product leadership — can we lock the date now?
[16:21] Diego: We suggested 2026-03-19 for midpoint; does that work for you?
[16:24] Priya: That works.
[16:26] Mark: We'll reserve the exec readout week of 2026-03-30 with 30-60 minute slot.

[19:40] Omar: On workload sizing — please confirm expected concurrent users and average tokens per conversation. Example: if you expect 50 concurrent at peak with avg 600 tokens per exchange that's higher GPU time than 10 concurrent with 200 tokens.
[19:54] Priya: Typical peak is 40-60 concurrent during business hours; median session is 3 back-and-forth turns, average token per turn is about 250. So planning for 50 concurrent with bursts to 120 for 30s is good.
[20:08] Omar: Noted — that will push us to target batching strategies and maybe 2-medium model replicas for burst handling. We'll put concrete instance recommendations in the runbook.

[24:20] Lena: Success criteria spelled out: 1) p95 latency < 800ms on target traffic profile; 2) human-eval quality >= your baseline or +5% F1; 3) cost per conversation within agreed threshold (we'll model); 4) infra & security gating satisfied (SAML/KMS/logs). If these pass, move to exec readout.
[24:40] Mark: Agree. Also include a risk gate for PII handling — if we can't guarantee scrub then we need Private deployment.
[24:49] Diego: We'll list that as a hard gate.

[29:12] Sara: For the human eval — can Redwood run blind A/B tests between our current system and the Redwood-backed model?
[29:20] Omar: Yes — we can implement a shadow evaluation and A/B traffic split. For the POC we usually do offline blind eval on the 300-case subset, then a small online experiment if infra supports it.
[29:31] Priya: We'll budget resources for annotators to do the initial 300-case labeling.

[33:50] Ben: Networking question — is there a small agent to push inside our VPC or do you require open egress?
[33:56] Omar: We support both patterns. For most POCs an allowlist + TLS egress is simplest. For air-gapped or strict networks we can use CSC-connector or private deployment but that adds setup time.
[34:07] Ben: Ok allowlist it is for now. We'll provide IPs.

[37:10] Priya: On benchmarks, can you produce a cost per 1M tokens estimate and a modeled monthly cost at our traffic profile?
[37:18] Lena: Yes — we'll include tokenized cost modeling and options: hosted (with dynamic scaling), reserved dedicated GPUs, and approximate savings from quantization/batching.
[37:27] Mark: We also want to see failure modes and monitoring dashboard examples.
[37:31] Diego: We'll share screenshots of the Redwood Console and trace examples, plus the runbook's observability checklist.

[41:00] Omar: Proposed POC deliverables: runbook + SOW, initial benchmark report (week 1), tuning notes & intermediate report (week 2), mid-point demo + ops checklist (week 3), final report + exec slide deck (week 4).
[41:15] Priya: Can you make the exec deck digestible for engineering + revenue folks?
[41:19] Lena: Absolutely — we'll prepare a 10-slide readout focusing on metrics, risks, costs, and recommended next steps.

[44:40] Mark: One last item — competitors. We're evaluating Anthropic and Bedrock too. How do you recommend we benchmark fairly?
[44:48] Omar: We'll run identical prompt sets and traffic profiles across model endpoints where possible, normalize for temperature/ prompts, and show token & latency deltas. If you want we can include a small table with known caveats.

[47:10] Lena: Ok to recap and next steps: Lena will send runbook + SOW draft by Monday (2026-03-09). Omar will share the benchmark template and initial instance recommendations by Sunday (2026-03-08). Ben will provision allowlist and sample dataset by 2026-03-10. Diego will calendar midpoint and exec readout invites. Priya will finalize the 300-case eval set by 2026-03-12.
[47:42] Mark: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[47:45] Sara: Thanks.
[47:46] Lena: Thanks all — we'll follow up in email with links to the security pack and benchmark sheet.
[47:52] Diego: End recording.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-hearings (K V cache vs KV cache, SAML sometimes transcribed as sample), some speaker overlaps.

References shared during call: Redwood POC runbook (link unspecified), security_pack_redwood_enterprise.pdf (will be shared), benchmark_template.xlsx (to be shared), sample eval set link (to be provided).

End of transcript.

Uniform Token Governor & Prefetch Policy Deep Dive

Deep technical session focused on tuning the scheduler's token governor and prefetch window for mixed-shot workloads on a Stratos VPC/on-prem deployment. We walked through continuous batching behaviors, the interplay between max_num_seqs and token ceilings, KV cache warmup strategies, and tradeoffs with quantization. Agreed next steps: Redwood will send knob JSON and prefetch suggestions; Stratos will run a multi-day stress test and share logs.
[00:00] Sophie (Redwood AE): Hi everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda: walk through a recommended token governor approach, prefetch window profiles, and then review the scheduler knobs for your on-prem VPC tests.
[00:18] Daniel (Stratos): Yep, thanks. we've been hitting some weird tail latency at peak. average p50's fine but p95/p99 spikes during larger multi-turn chats.
[00:30] Arun (Redwood SE): Cool, can you remind us of your workload mix? earlier you said ~70% short completions (<64 tokens) and 30% multi-turn where sequences can go to 800 tokens, is that still accurate?
[00:44] Priya (Stratos): That's right-ish. median seq len is actually closer to 48, but we have a fat tail from a small set of agents doing long dialogs.
[00:55] Speaker 2: and the long dialogs are batched with the short ones currently?
[00:58] Maya (Redwood SRE): Right now the scheduler is doing continuous batching without strict seq caps, so long requests can cause batch bloat and push latency. that's where max_num_seqs helps.
[01:12] Daniel: We tried bumping max_num_seqs up to 64 to improve throughput but saw worse tail latency.
[01:18] Arun: yeah, that matches expectations. raising max_num_seqs increases packing density but increases latency for the short requests in the same batch — they wait for the long ones. The trick is to pick a governor and token ceilings that protect short tails while still allowing high throughput.
[01:35] Sophie: let's talk concrete knobs. We'll propose a 'uniform token governor' — basically cap per-request token accrual and enforce soft preemption if a request exceeds a window.
[01:48] Priya: soft preemption? do you mean interrupt and requeue?
[01:51] Arun: more like slice and continue: split a long request into multiple scheduling quanta so it doesn't block a slot for too long, this is scheduler-level slicing, not model-level. It keeps KV cache locality but prevents head-of-line blocking.
[02:05] Daniel: Will that increase overall compute because of more context switches?
[02:08] Arun: marginally, yes. there's some overhead to more smaller dispatches, but in our tests the throughput loss is offset by reduced tail latency and better utilization across tenants.
[02:19] Liam (CTO): how does this interact with KV cache warmup? we saw cold cache penalties on first long requests after evictions.
[02:27] Maya: Good point. our recommendation is to combine a prefetch window with a warmup policy: when a long request is detected we prefetch the KV shards for the next N tokens into the local GPU cache (or pre-warm across the pool) and mark the request as 'warm' in the governor so subsequent slices read cached KV.
[02:45] Priya: sounds good; what's N typically?
[02:48] Arun: depends. for your model and quantization profile, we often use prefetch windows between 64-256 tokens. for int8 quantized runs we've seen 128 be a sweet spot. for int4/qat variants you might do a bit lower, like 64.
[03:05] Daniel: we run Q4_0 on some envs, and int8 on others — any guidance?
[03:10] Sophie: quantization lowers memory and can increase throughput but can alter kernel selection and kv cache size. Q4_0 often reduces KV per token which helps cache hit rate, but int8 with different kernels may have different warmup profiles. we'll include model-specific prefetch profiles.
[03:29] Speaker 1: can you explain how the 'uniform token governor' enforces fairness across tenants?
[03:33] Arun: Sure. it's like a token bank per request with a per-tenant weight. Each request accrues budget up to a ceiling; if the request exhausts budget, it's paused and requeued. the scheduler ensures no single request consumes >X% of GPU time in a rolling window. We also do priority windows for enterprise tiers so you can allow larger headroom for reserved capacity.
[03:56] Priya: are these ceilings expressed in tokens or in token-time (token*seq_len)?
[03:59] Arun: tokens. but we map tokens to estimated exec time using a small model of kernel latency per token for the current model/quant; that helps make ceilings meaningful across different models.
[04:12] Daniel: interesting. about KV eviction — we noticed aggressive eviction during bursts; our eviction threshold is basically LRU with size limits. recommendations?
[04:21] Maya: We prefer a two-tier policy: keep a hot set pinned for a short TTL, evict least-recently-used outside that. Also use a small async prefetch thread to pre-warm items based on request patterns. Set eviction threshold to keep hot-set hit-rate >85% for your trace.
[04:36] Liam: how do we measure hit-rate easily? the console has token-level breakdowns?
[04:40] Sophie: Yes, Redwood Console exposes per-prefix KV hit-rate and per-route latency splits. we'll point you at the dashboards and the sample queries to compute a rolling hit-rate.
[04:50] Speaker 3: you mentioned splitting requests into quanta, what about model state across slices?
[04:54] Arun: We maintain KV across slices so long as the request id persists; slices are contiguous in time and the runtime stitches outputs. model's attention state (KV) is preserved in the runtime's cache; prefetch ensures the next slice's KV is resident.
[05:07] Priya: network implications for on-prem VPC — prefetch generates additional egress between control plane and workers?
[05:13] Maya: Prefetch is internal to the serving cluster if you're on dedicated/dedicated private. For VPC/private deployments we do recommend colocating KV shards with GPUs or using a high-bandwidth fabric. we will provide a recommended NIC and MTU config.
[05:27] Daniel: we use 100GbE between NVLink boxes; is that sufficient?
[05:30] Arun: yes, but watch congestion; prefetch spikes can saturate fabric so use a smoothing window and rate-limit prefetch per node.
[05:39] Sophie: let's walk the exact knobs we'll propose: suggested max_num_seqs per slot, token_ceiling per request, prefetch_window tokens, warmup threshold, and eviction_ttl.
[05:51] [screen share: scheduler-knobs.json referenced]
[05:54] Sophie: sample: max_num_seqs: 16 for mixed workloads, token_ceiling: 256 for enterprise reserved, token_ceiling: 128 for shared, prefetch_window: 128, warmup_threshold: 64, eviction_ttl_secs: 600.
[06:10] Priya: why 16? we thought 8 looked safer earlier.
[06:13] Arun: 16 is a starting point when your median seq len is 48 and you have modest tail. 8 will be safer for latency but lower throughput. we recommended testing [8,16,32] to map the throughput-latency curve for your traffic.
[06:27] Daniel: ok. what about continuous batching parameters — batch_timeout and batch_size?
[06:31] Arun: use adaptive batch_timeout that shrinks when latency SLO is tight. for your P95 SLO of 250ms for short completions, set batch_timeout to 10-15ms and batch_size to max_num_seqs*1.25.
[06:45] Speaker 2: and token guards?
[06:47] Maya: token guards cap cumulative tokens per tenant per window. set a per-tenant soft limit and a hard limit to prevent noisy neighbors. soft triggers a downward weight adjustment, hard rejects or routes to a lower-priority tier.
[06:59] Priya: any gotchas with quantization + prefetch? we saw perf regressions on int4 in some kernels.
[07:05] Arun: yes, some int4 kernels are slower for short sequences because of kernel launch overheads; quantization is not universally faster. recommended approach: benchmark the model in each quant profile with the real seq distribution and capture kernel selection. we'll include profiler output and recommended model-specific prefetch sizes.
[07:23] Daniel: what's the impact on billing/metrics? more slices means more requests counted?
[07:28] Sophie: Billing counts tokens and GPU time; more slices add small overhead in GPU time but tokens are same. we'll show you cost delta for a sample 48h run.
[07:39] Liam: security — prefetch touches KV for upcoming tokens; any data residency issues?
[07:44] Maya: Prefetch only pulls encrypted KV shards; in Private/VPC we use customer-managed KMS keys and HSM integration is possible. we record audit logs for prefetch access.
[07:55] Daniel: ok, timeline — can you send the knobs and a sample prefetch profile?
[07:59] Sophie: yes, we'll send scheduler-knobs.json and prefetch profiles by Friday (that's 2026-12-18).
[08:06] [cross-talk] Priya: also want the stress harness you mentioned earlier.
[08:10] Arun: we'll share the harness and an example runbook for the 48h mixed workload.
[08:16] Daniel: last question — how do we safely roll these changes on our private cluster without impacting prod?
[08:20] Sophie: do a canary: apply knobs to 5% of traffic or run a 2h isolated canary on a reserved pool. we recommend using the console's rollout feature with automatic fallback if P95 increases >20% vs baseline.
[08:36] Liam: perfect. thanks everyone.
[08:39] Sophie: recap in chat, action items and knobs. we'll follow up with the scheduler JSON, prefetch profile, and the stress harness.
[08:48] [end recording]

document.content:
Vector fanout latency & cost pilot scoping - CedarPulse

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-02
Start time: 15:32 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Park (Redwood AE), Daniel Romero (Redwood SE), Marta Lopez (CedarPulse Head of Search), Ethan Wu (Platform), Ravi Patel (ML)

Summary:
CedarPulse is evaluating Redwood for a rerank-heavy retrieval stack. Primary concerns: tail latency at high fanout, cost per query (esp. during peak), and ability to run in VPC/private for PHI-sensitive docs. They want a short pilot to compare hosted vs dedicated vs private with particular focus on fanout sizes and quantization effects on recall/latency.

Topics covered:
- Current vector store + neural reranker pipeline
- Fanout sizing (k candidates) and rerank cost model
- Dimensionality & quantization tradeoffs (float16 vs int8/4bit)
- Dedicated capacity and VPC/private deployment questions
- SLAs, security (SOC2, KMS), and next steps for pilot

Action items (quick in-meeting list):
- Redwood to share benchmark sheet and suggested test configs
- CedarPulse to share telemetry and sample documents
- Schedule pilot kickoff and align success criteria

Transcript body:
[00:00] Sophie Park: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:04] Marta Lopez: yeah we can hear you, hey Sophie. thanks for taking the time.
[00:07] Sophie Park: awesome. quick intros, i'm Sophie, AE at Redwood, daniel here is our SE who will own the perf plan.
[00:13] Daniel Romero: hi all, hi Marta, hi Ethan, ravi. excited to dig in.
[00:16] Ravi Patel: hey all.
[00:18] Ethan Wu: morning.
[00:20] Marta Lopez: so high level — CedarPulse is a clinical knowledge search product, a lot of short queries, sometimes long documents, we do a vector retrieval then small neural rerank. our current infra is Milvus on k8s + a python reranker running on a few CPU boxes.
[00:33] Marta Lopez: main pain is p95 is spiky during morning peaks and our cloud cost for rerank is killing us when fanout is large.
[00:39] Sophie Park: makes sense. can you give us a sense of fanout sizes you typically use? like k=...
[00:44] Ethan Wu: typical live traffic uses k=200 for recall, but for some queries we go up to k=800 in nightly tasks. our p50 is fine but p95 goes to 1.2s on the full pipeline.
[00:54] Daniel Romero: helpful — thank you. so the pilot we usually do is set up three configs: 1) hosted - Redwood hosted API with our recommended model and default quantization 2) dedicated - reserved capacity with tuned batching and kv cache tuned for your workload, 3) private - VPC or on-prem if you need network isolation and KMS. we measure throughput and p95 at several fanouts.
[01:16] Marta Lopez: can Redwood actually run the reranker in the same flow or do we need to call out to our existing service?
[01:21] Daniel Romero: good question. two main patterns: i) do vector retrieval from your DB (we can plug into Milvus/SSF/whatever) and call Redwood for rerank as a second step — that is easy. ii) full pipeline in Redwood where retrieval and rerank happen inside our runtime with prefix caching, which reduces RPC overhead and can lower p95. the latter is available for dedicated/private pilots.
[01:41] Ravi Patel: are there published numbers for the cost delta when you move rerank into the runtime vs calling out?
[01:45] Sophie Park: we'll share a benchmark sheet but rough rule of thumb: removing one network hop + combining batching can cut per-query token cost by 15-30% depending on fanout and model size.
[01:55] Ethan Wu: your benchmark vs pinecone — we evaluated pinecone earlier and weaviate but their rerank integration was clunky, we ended up shipping a bunch of glue.
[02:04] Sophie Park: yea Pinecone is oriented at vector store, not rerank-in-runtime. Redwood's different because the runtime is model-first and we can do continuous batching + KV cache for generative steps.
[02:13] Marta Lopez: ok hypothethically, if we do k=200, what's p95 on hosted vs dedicated?
[02:19] Daniel Romero: depends on model choice and quantization. for a medium-size cross-encoder reranker (around 220M parameters) with int8 quantization on A100/gpu-ish hardware we typically see p95 of 120-180ms for the rerank step at k=200 in dedicated; hosted numbers are similar but we keep conservative limits on concurrent sessions so tails can blow up under burst. hosted p95 might be 180-300ms under burst unless we add burst capacity.
[02:44] Ethan Wu: interesting. and the dedicated option — is that physically separate GPUs for us? we need data isolation for PHI.
[02:50] Sophie Park: yes Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and data isolation; Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you full control of network and KMS. both options meet SOC2 but private has extra controls for compliance.
[02:59] Ravi Patel: any support for quantization beyond int8 — we tried 4bit at dev and accuracy dropped but cost saved was nice.
[03:04] Daniel Romero: we support 4-bit/qlora-like routes and mixed precision. for rerankers, sometimes 4-bit is fine; you should validate your eval set. in the pilot we'll test float16, int8 and 4-bit dtypes and measure Recall@10/20 and MRR.
[03:18] Marta Lopez: about hybrid search — we still want BM25+vector blending for certain queries. how do you recommend integrating?
[03:24] Daniel Romero: two patterns: 1) blend at retrieval time in your vector db (score combine), return top-K hybrid candidates to rerank; 2) return two lists (bm25 top 50 and vector top 200) and let reranker dedupe and score. The second gives better control but more work; the first is simpler and often fine. We'll test both in the pilot.
[03:45] Ethan Wu: latency impact of fanout — if we increase k to 500 for recall improvement does rerank cost scale linearly?
[03:51] Daniel Romero: rerank cost is roughly linear in k for cross-encoders, but batch scoring and tensorized rerank on GPU can amortize some overhead. beyond a certain k you hit memory limits and need sharding. for k=500 you should expect roughly 2.5x the compute of k=200, but with optimized batching and kv/prefetch you can get better throughput.
[04:12] Marta Lopez: we also need to think about cold start spikes, our morning window is 8–9am with 5x baseline qps for 20 minutes.
[04:19] Sophie Park: for spikes we recommend a mix: reserved baseline in Dedicated + burst capability in Hosted or burst nodes within Dedicated. Also aggressive caching of popular prefixes and storing rerank outputs for frequently repeated queries helps a lot.
[04:31] Ravi Patel: can Redwood rerank outputs be cached? what about staleness concerns — our docs update daily.
[04:36] Daniel Romero: yes caching works at the prefix/embedding level; TTL controls let you tune staleness. for daily updates we usually set TTLs of a few hours and have a cache invalidation hook from your pipeline.
[04:47] Ethan Wu: on private deployment, what's install complexity? we have an air-gapped site option for PHI workloads.
[04:52] Sophie Park: Private has two modes: customer-managed VPC deployment (we provide images + helm charts) or full on-prem package for air-gap. On-prem requires a short professional services engagement for install and entitlements; we can supply an installer and a runbook.
[05:04] Marta Lopez: security checklist — SSO, SAML; audit logs; KMS; can you support our KMS?
[05:09] Sophie Park: yes we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for private, support SAML/SSO, RBAC, and rich audit logs. we'll attach SOC2 and pen test reports in the follow-up.
[05:17] Ethan Wu: pricing — we need a cost per query ballpark for each config, especially for heavy fanout rerank.
[05:23] Sophie Park: we'll put a sample cost sheet: hosted per-token + compute; dedicated reserved monthly with utilization assumptions; private more licensing + infra. We'll provide modeled examples for k=50/200/500 with medium reranker.
[05:35] Marta Lopez: one more technical: are you doing any kernel-level optimizations for attention? we saw some vendors mention fused kernels.
[05:41] Daniel Romero: yes our runtime picks kernels based on sequence length and model, we have fused attention and KV cache optimizations, and we can tune sequence length cutoff to minimize unnecessary compute. All that helps with the rerank generation steps and reduces cost.
[05:55] Sophie Park: ok let's outline measurable success criteria for the pilot so we can make the vendor decision quickly — what's your bar?
[06:00] Marta Lopez: target p95 end-to-end (retrieval + rerank) < 500ms at production fanout k=200 and cost per request no more than 1.5x our current spend. Also maintain privacy controls.
[06:12] Daniel Romero: great, we'll design tests to measure end-to-end p95 and cost-per-query at k=50/200/500 and test quantization.
[06:18] Ethan Wu: timeline — we want to decide by mid-Sept. can you get a pilot plan and cost in the next week?
[06:23] Sophie Park: yes we'll send pilot plan + pricing in 48-72 hours and propose a kickoff the following week.
[06:28] Ravi Patel: any gotchas we should be aware of? like sharding vector DBs when you pass big k's?
[06:32] Daniel Romero: when k grows you may need to shard retrieval across nodes, or do layered retrieval (first narrow with smaller k then expand). We'll include those architectural options in the plan. Also monitor GPU memory when using large batch rerank.
[06:44] Marta Lopez: ok that sounds good.
[06:46] Sophie Park: quick recap of next steps: sophie sends pricing + benchmark sheet, daniel sends test configs, ethan shares telemetry, we schedule kickoff.
[06:55] Ethan Wu: yep i'll get the telemetry exported.
[06:57] Marta Lopez: thanks everyone.
[06:59] Sophie Park: thanks all, talk soon.

End of transcript.

document.content:
Vendor governance, usage commitment & SLA handoff

Kickoff between Redwood AE/SE and Orchid procurement/legal to align on MSA/DPA redlines, committed usage pricing, SLA targets, and security controls. Key asks: dedicated capacity for PHI-adjacent workflows, KMS integration, SSO with SAML, SOC 2 evidence, and clear overage billing paths. Agreed next steps: Redwood to send redlines and pricing worksheet; SE to provide performance docs for Dedicated and on-prem options; Customer to confirm committed token volumes and legal requirements.
MSA redlines and DPA exceptions
Committed usage and overage pricing
Dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs
KMS & key management / encryption
SSO and RBAC for Console
Audit logs and retention
Support SLAs and escalation paths
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hi everyone, thanks for taking the time. We'll do a short agenda run, then Tom will go through the capacity and performance bits, and then we'll land on contract asks. Jill, thanks for organizing this with procurement.
[00:12] Jill (Orchid, Procurement): Thanks Maya. Yep, we've got legal and security on. We want to walk away with a clear path for MSA/DPA, pricing for committed usage and clarity on SLA and support.
[00:23] Tom (Redwood SE): Hey all. Quick note — I'll try to keep the deep perf numbers high level, but happy to deep dive afterwards. We ran the Dedicated cluster tests on 8xA100 equivalent and on the Quantized Llama-ish model family, which showed predictable p99 latencies when token lengths are under 1k.
[00:40] Rajesh (Head of Cloud): Quick clarifying Q — when you say Dedicated is predictable, do you mean reserved VMs in our VPC or your Dedicated managed pool? We need to understand network egress, private peering, and egress billing.
[00:52] Tom: Good question. Two flavors: Redwood Dedicated (we allocate a physical pool in our data plane for your tenancy, optional VPC peering) vs Redwood Private (we can ship a control plane but you run inference in your VPC/on-prem). The Dedicated offering can be VPC peered so traffic stays within your networking and egress billing is managed per our contract. Note: in a true on-prem Private deployment, you control all egress.
[01:15] Morgan (Legal): On the DPA side we have a short list: data residency for PHI-adjacent logs, KMS/HSM key custody, and an audit trail with immutable logs for 7 years. Is that supported out of the box?
[01:28] Tom: KMS integration is supported — we integrate with customer KMS for model ingest and keys at rest. HSM-backed KMS is possible via our KMS connectors. Audit logs exist in the Console, and we can extend retention as an add-on. I will caveat that the default retention is 90 days in hosted consoles.
[01:46] Samir (Security): That default retention is a problem for us. We need at least three years on audit logs and tamper-evidence. Also, can you sign a clause for data subject access requests that routes through our SOC?
[01:58] Maya: We have enterprise add-ons for extended retention and tamper-evidence. For DSAR we typically map request flows in the DPA so we can do that. We'll note Morgan and Samir's ask in the redlines.
[02:08] Jill: Another legal ask — indemnity carve-outs around model hallucinations that lead to patient harm. We understand that Redwood can't promise content accuracy, but we need clear limits and incident response commitments.
[02:21] Maya: Understood. We usually include a standard Warranties and Liability section, and we can add an incident response SLA and an obligation to cooperate on investigations. We should log that for legal redlines.
[02:32] Ivy (Finance): Pricing — we need committed discounts vs pay-as-you-go. What's the typical commitment tiers and overage rates?
[02:40] Maya: Typical is a 12-month committed tokens model with tiers — e.g., 0–1B tokens, 1B–5B, 5B+. Discounts increase with commitment. Overage billing is typically at a blended rate slightly above the committed unit price; we can provide an exact worksheet.
[02:55] Rajesh: For our forecasting we need committed units per month and peaking profile. If we underutilize, is there a carryover or true-up?
[03:04] Maya: We offer two constructs: a smoothing true-up where unused committed tokens can be carried forward for a short window, or a firm reservation with lower unit cost but no carryover. We'll include both options in the pricing worksheet.
[03:16] Tom: Also for cost control we have config knobs — batching, KV cache, sequence-length caps — that materially affect unit cost. For example, enabling prefix KV cache reduced token cost by ~18% in our internal bench on stateful chat patterns.
[03:30] Rajesh: What's the latency impact of batching? Our clinical UI is latency-sensitive.
[03:35] Tom: You can target latency SLOs by configuring max batch latency, and Redwood's smart batcher will prioritize low-latency queues. With our Dedicated SLOs we can guarantee p95 ≤ 220ms for <512 token responses in typical setups; p99 depends more on sequence length and KV hits. We'll include the SLI/SLO language for contract.
[03:53] Morgan: On the MSA redlines: we flagged export control and crypto clauses. We need clarity on who is the data processor vs controller for different flows — e.g., telemetry for model improvements.
[04:05] Maya: We can set telemetry to off for your tenant, or configure it so data used for model improvements is anonymized and requires explicit opt-in. We'll mark that as an available setting in the DPA.
[04:16] [crosstalk] Jill: And HIPAA— are you willing to sign a Business Associate Agreement?
[04:21] Maya: We have customers under HIPAA; we can sign a BAA but that does come with additional controls. Tom, can you speak to redwood's approach to PHI?
[04:29] Tom: Yes. For PHI workflows we recommend either Dedicated with VPC peering or Private. The key is to keep token payloads inside the private network and to enable KMS where only the customer's KMS holds the encryption keys for stored artifacts. Also we offer logging to a customer-managed S3 for audit retention.
[04:46] Samir: We will need to run a security questionnaire and have an onsite (or virtual) security review. Do you have a standard questionnaire or attestation pack?
[04:54] Maya: We maintain an Infosec pack: SOC 2 report, pen test summary, architecture diagrams, and a security questionnaire template. I will share the folder link after the call.
[05:03] Tom: To call out a small nuance — when we talk about KV cache and prefix caching, the cache is encrypted at rest and scoped per-tenant. However, for token-level dedup caching there are operational considerations if you want zero-sharing between tenants on the same physical host; Dedicated gives that guarantee.
[05:21] Jill: Can you summarize the difference again between Hosted with VPC peering and Dedicated? Legal just wants to understand risk surface in the MSA.
[05:30] Maya: Sure. Hosted with VPC peering — we still operate the inference plane, but network peering reduces public internet egress. It's still in our multi-tenant control plane but with tenant isolation at app-level. Dedicated is a reserved pool for your account and we can enforce physical separation of GPUs and host OS as an option. Private means you run the inference plane in your environment and we provide a control plane or software.
[05:50] Morgan: For indemnity and liability, our counsel asked about caps tied to fees and carve-outs for willful misconduct. Is your standard cap 1x ARR?
[05:59] Maya: Standard is 1x fees in the past 12 months, but enterprise customers sometimes negotiate higher caps or carve-outs for certain liabilities. We'll note Morgan's ask.
[06:08] Ivy: For accounting, we need to know whether commitment counts as OPEX vs CAPEX for our financials. Do you provide invoicing monthly? Quarterly? Annual?
[06:16] Maya: We typically invoice monthly for usage and can do monthly or quarterly invoices for committed contracts. We can accommodate preferred billing cadence; we'll reflect options in the pricing worksheet.
[06:26] Tom: One more technical item — support tiers. We offer Standard (business hours email), Premium (24/7 on-call with guaranteed response times), and Enterprise (dedicated CSM + priority escalation). SLAs for platform availability are included in Dedicated agreements; the Hosted default is best-effort unless you buy an SLA addon.
[06:46] Rajesh: For PII and PHI we need 24/7 support with a 1-hour response for Sev1 incidents. Is that part of Enterprise?
[06:54] Maya: Yes, that's Enterprise. We'll include a proposed Sev matrix in the SLA section and map target response/resolution times.
[07:02] Jill: About termination — if we decide to stop the contract mid-year, what's the run-out and data return policy? We want guaranteed deletion and proof-of-deletion.
[07:12] Maya: Our standard is a 90-day run-out for data handoff; we can extend to an agreed period and provide signed proof-of-deletion and a downloadable archive. I'll capture that.
[07:20] Morgan: Also, can you commit to scope-limited subcontractors? We need to list any third-party subprocessors and have a notification period for new ones.
[07:29] Maya: We maintain a subprocessors list and provide 30 days' notice for changes; we can also include subprocessors in the DPA appendices.
[07:39] Tom: I'll flag the required appendix template for subprocessors and the cryptographic key custody language.
[07:46] [08:00] Maya: Switching to pricing specifics — for a 12-month firm commit of 3B tokens/month, here's an example: base unit price X with a 22% discount versus PAYGO, overage billed at 1.25x unit price. We can also offer a smoothing true-up where unused tokens can be carried forward up to three months.
[08:17] Ivy: If we go for the smoothing option, and we underutilize by 30% for two months, does that affect our quarter-end all-in cost modeling? We need predictability.
[08:26] Maya: Smoothing helps predictability; however, finance typically models committed spend as the minimum. We'll put both firm reservation and smoothing cashflows in the worksheet.
[08:36] Rajesh: A technical follow-up — for VPC peering, do you support AWS PrivateLink or just standard VPC peering?
[08:42] Tom: We support VPC peering and PrivateLink in most regions; for sensitive deployments we recommend PrivateLink as it reduces cross-subnet exposure. We'll note region constraints in the runbook.
[08:54] Morgan: Regarding the DPA, we also require breach notification within 48 hours on incidents affecting PHI. Is that acceptable?
[09:01] Maya: We commit to 72-hour notification in standard DPAs, but for enterprise we can negotiate 48 hours with the right controls. We'll surface that as a redline.
[09:10] Samir: On pen tests, do you provide test windows and coordinate with your infra team? We need to run auth-proxied tests against the console and private endpoints.
[09:20] Tom: Yes, we coordinate pen-test windows; our infra team provides guidance. For Private deployments you can run tests directly. For hosted instances we require an approved scope and timeslot.
[09:29] Jill: Can we get the MSA track with inline comments? Our counsel prefers markups rather than a list of asks.
[09:36] Maya: Absolutely — we'll send a redline of the MSA + DPA and also a tracked changes version for ease.
[09:42] [crosstalk] Ivy: On the point of tax and geo billing, are EU customers billed VAT-inclusive? We have entities in both US and EU.
[09:50] Maya: We handle region-based billing and can invoice either entity depending on the contract. We support VAT handling; we'll align with your finance contact.
[09:58] Rajesh: Any blockers for storing tokens or models in EU-only regions for GDPR?
[10:03] Tom: No blocker — we can pin inference and log storage to EU-West region in both Dedicated and Private. For Hosted, we have region footprint and can allocate capacity in EU region under your tenancy.
[10:13] Morgan: Sequence control — we need a provision that restricts Redwood from training models on customer-provided prompts unless explicitly authorized.
[10:18] Maya: That's standard. We'll add an explicit clause that customer data won't be used for model training or improvement unless opted in.
[10:26] Tom: Quick perf nuance — when you enable quantized weights some long-tail token patterns can increase inference jitter; we usually recommend a small canary before broad rollout.
[10:35] Rajesh: Sounds fair. We'll plan a canary pilot.
[10:38] Jill: For signoff path — procurement wants to know the timeline for approvals. We are aiming to have procurement sign by end of March, assuming no major redlines. Is that reasonable?
[10:47] Maya: That's reasonable. If we turn around redlines this week and have parallel legal reviews, late March is feasible.
[10:53] Ivy: Finance will need a SOW or order form that maps to our PO process. Do you template that?
[10:58] Maya: Yes, standard order form to capture committed tokens, billing cadence, billing entity, and SLAs. We'll include that in the package we send.
[11:05] Morgan: One open item — export controls. We flagged encryption export control language that may block some regions. How do you manage that?
[11:13] Tom: We follow export compliance; if a dataset or usage falls under controlled crypto/export restrictions we will highlight and propose mitigations. Usually this is handled in a DPA appendix.
[11:21] [pause, paper shuffling]
[11:30] Maya: OK let's recap quickly: Redwood to send MSA/DPA redlines + pricing worksheet + perf/runbook links. SE to attach Dedicated perf spreadsheet and canary guidance. Customer to confirm committed token volume and preferred billing entity, and legal to return DPA addendum items.
[11:45] Jill: We'll aim to have legal comments back within 7 business days.
[11:49] Rajesh: We'll scope the canary with Tom — looking for a small 2–3 node footprint in US-EAST to start.
[11:56] Maya: Great. Anybody else have burning questions?
[12:00] Samir: One last sec — will you allow our security team to onboard to the Console in read-only to validate audit logs?
[12:06] Maya: Yes, we can provision RBAC roles (read-only auditor) for your team. We'll include that in the onboarding checklist.
[12:12] Ivy: Thanks all.
[12:14] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts.
[12:18] [call ends]

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings: "K V" for KV cache, "redwood dedicated" lowercase or split in audio; some speaker labels merged (Morgan / Maya overlap) — verified by attendees in follow-ups. Links shared: (1) Redwood Dedicated perf spreadsheet — link to be sent, (2) Infosec pack (SOC2 + pen test) — folder link to be shared, (3) draft MSA/DPA redline — to be delivered with pricing worksheet.
Maya to send draft MSA/DPA redlines and pricing worksheet by 2027-02-10
Tom to share Dedicated capacity perf spreadsheet and runbook link by 2027-02-09
Customer to confirm expected monthly committed tokens and pilot start date by 2027-02-14
Maya Patel | Send MSA/DPA redlines and pricing worksheet | 2027-02-10
Tom Hargreaves | Share dedicated perf benchmark and runbook link | 2027-02-09
Rajesh Patel | Confirm committed monthly tokens and regions (US-EAST, EU-WEST) | 2027-02-14
Morgan Lee | Provide list of required contractual controls for DPA addendum | 2027-02-12

POC architecture sprint, access plan & exec readout cadence - Meridian Bio

Meeting header: 2027-03-03 14:00 UTC | Duration: 58m | Location: Zoom
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Claire Nguyen (Redwood SE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Dr. Miguel Alvarez (Meridian CTO), Jenna Park (Meridian PM), Ravi Shah (Meridian SRE), Tanya Li (Meridian Security)

Summary: Quick scoping for a 3-week POC focused on latency/throughput benchmarks across hosted vs dedicated deployment, access gating for VPC tests, success criteria definition (latency p95 / quality threshold), and scheduling of kickoff / midpoint / exec readout.

Topics: scope, success criteria, workload sizing, access plan, benchmark matrix, timeline & milestones, compliance notes

Action items (captured above)

00:00 Samir: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're going to run through the POC plan, make sure we align on what success looks like and what access we need. can folks hear me okay?
00:06 Miguel: yes loud and clear, thanks Samir. we have about an hour, hope that's enough to cover gating and the timeline.
00:12 Claire: quick intro from me, i'm Claire on the SE team, i'll lead the benchmark plan and run the initial perf sweeps. Luis will help with the environment and dedicated sizing notes.
00:22 Jenna: quick context — product team's primary goal is to replace an internal heuristic summarizer with a more robust LLM pipeline; latency is important because the feature is user-facing. budget is limited so cost/unit is a hard constraint.
00:34 Ravi: on infra — we're AWS, VPC-only for prod, can open a test VPC peering or we can run traffic from Redwood's hosted endpoints; security will require audit logs and SAML SSO for the control plane.
00:46 Tanya: also need to validate KMS integration before we allow any private model artifacts; SOC2 scope will be relevant but we can share a compliance contact later.
00:55 Samir: great, that aligns with our common patterns. so talking success criteria — what would you call a pass/fail for the exec readout?
01:03 Miguel: p95 latency under 350ms for typical 256-token payloads, p50 around 120ms. and output quality measured by our QA set: rouge-L > 0.65 and precision/recall-ish metric equivalent — we have a small labeled dataset. cost target is less than $0.045 per 1k tokens across expected usage.
01:25 Claire: ok noted. we usually run three model variants for benchmarks: an open 7B, a quantized 4-bit variant, and a larger 13B with reduced context kernels. we'll measure p50/p95, throughput QPS, memory usage, and KV cache hit characteristics.
01:40 Luis: can you explain the 'reduced context kernel' comment? i'm not familiar with that notation.
01:45 Claire: sorry, bunker phrase — some runtimes use attention-kernel FastPath for long sequences; for our 13B we pick a kernel that favors throughput on 512 tokens. it may introduce a small perf tradeoff on 64 token workloads.
01:58 Ravi: for sample workload, we have bursty traffic — concurrency peaks at 120 concurrent sessions but median is 18. monthly tokens ~90M. important to size for burst headroom not just median.
02:10 Samir: good, so POC should validate two operating points: median steady-state and burst peak. we'll plan a baseline run at 18 concurrent and a stress run targeting 120 concurrent. what about token distribution — mostly short/medium?
02:22 Jenna: ~70% short (<64 tokens), 25% medium (64–256), 5% long (>512).
02:29 Claire: perfect, that informs batching and KV cache testing. for throughput targets we'll measure sustained tokens/sec and cold-start latency with/without cached prefixes.
02:40 Miguel: security gating — we will only allow dedicated testing in our VPC if Redwood can sign a data processing addendum and we can provide a customer-managed KMS key. if not, we'll accept hosted but only with obfuscated payloads for early runs.
02:58 Tanya: also need to log all admin activity, so Redwood console audit hooks need to be documented.
03:05 Samir: we'll send the DPA and the security checklist. Claire, can you capture the required audit log fields?
03:10 Claire: yes, i'll attach the doc. quick note on observability — the Redwood console can show token-level cost and latency by route, we'll enable a demo dashboard for the POC.
03:22 Miguel: timeline question — we want a 3-week pilot window. kickoff as soon as we have access, mid-point after week 2 for a 15-min readout, and an exec readout following completion. does that match your plan?
03:35 Samir: it does. proposed dates: kickoff 2027-03-08, mid-point 2027-03-24, exec readout 2027-03-31. those are placeholders pending access. are those feasible?
03:44 Jenna: kickoff 3/8 works if access is ready by 3/7. we need at least service account + s3 samples + allowlist.
03:52 Ravi: we can do the allowlist quickly, i'll coordinate with security.
03:56 Samir: great. on benchmarks — here's the matrix we propose: 1) Baseline throughput (hosted) on 7B; 2) Dedicated reserved runtime on same 7B; 3) Quantized 4-bit variant on Dedicated; 4) 13B reduced-kernel variant for quality comparison. Metrics: p50, p95, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens, failure rate, avg memory. we'll also run a quality eval against your labeled set and produce a small ROC-like table.
04:28 Claire: for the stress test, we'll replay a 10-minute burst trace derived from your production 95th percentile and measure tail latency and retry behavior. any rate-limiting policies we should respect?
04:38 Miguel: we do have rate-limits on the backend but the feature sits in a frontend proxy — we can remove the proxy for the POC and replay directly to the Redwood endpoints from our runners.
04:48 Luis: for dedicated sizing, do you have expected RPS or tokens/sec target? that will determine whether we need 1 or 2 GPUs in the pool for this POC.
04:55 Ravi: target peak tokens/sec ~ 2.5k, sustained ~400; that maps roughly to 1-2 A100 equivalents depending on model variant.
05:04 Claire: ok we will include a sizing recommendation in the kickoff doc. likely a single GPU for 7B, dedicated with burst policy for the 13B runs.
05:12 Samir: testing plan: week 0 (access & provisioning), week 1 (baseline hosted runs + perf tuning), week 2 (dedicated runs + quantized test), week 3 (midpoint readout and buffer for follow-ups and exec prep).
05:25 Miguel: curious about cold start behavior — if we do dedicated with KV cache warmup, what should we expect on the first requests?
05:33 Claire: cold-start on an idle node can add 80–200ms depending on model size; with warmed KV cache the first few related requests are faster. we'll measure cold vs warm latency as part of the baseline.
05:46 Tanya: on compliance, can we get a list of where logs are stored and retention window? we have to show legal how long traces are retained.
05:53 Samir: yes, we'll include the console retention settings and a recommended retention plan for the POC — default is 30 days but we can adjust retention for the pilot.
06:00 Jenna: success gating for the exec readout — what are the qualitative and quantitative checks?
06:06 Miguel: quantitatively: p95 <350ms for 256 tokens on the chosen model variant, cost <= $0.045 per 1k tokens when amortized across median workload, error rate <0.5%. qualitatively: model outputs must not introduce hallucination patterns flagged by our QA rubric; we will run a 200-sample blind eval.
06:26 Claire: we'll run the blind eval and produce side-by-side examples for the readout. we'll also capture metrics for reranking when applicable.
06:34 Luis: one operational question — if we hit a perf regression mid-POC, what's the rollback behavior?
06:39 Samir: we can pin to a previous model or throttle to a smaller variant; Redwood has automated fallback to a compatible model with controlled rate-limiting to preserve latency SLOs. we'll document the automatic fallback policy in the runbook.
06:53 Miguel: ok noted. any blockers on our side?
06:55 Ravi: i'll need the exact IPs for allowlist, and i'll need a test IAM role. i can have those by 3/5.
07:02 Samir: perfect. i'll send the access checklist and the POC workbook after the call. Claire, anything else for the benchmark plan?
07:08 Claire: i'll prepare a spreadsheet with the matrix and expected measurement windows; also include a sample JMeter/locust script we use for replay.
07:16 Jenna: can you also include cost breakdown templates so we can show finance?
07:19 Samir: yes, pricing estimate will go with the workbook.
07:22 Miguel: one more question — are there known differences between hosted and private (VPC) regarding observability or is it parity?
07:30 Claire: near parity for metrics. private deployments have additional network isolation and customer-managed KMS but the console still surfaces the same latency/cost breakdowns; certain audit hooks differ because of VPC egress limitations, we'll call that out.
07:47 Miguel: ok. to recap, kickoff 3/8 pending access, mid-point readout 3/24, exec readout 3/31. success criteria as discussed; Redwood to send workbook, DPA, and allowlist IPs.
08:02 Samir: thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs.
08:07 Jenna: thanks, bye.
08:09 Claire: thanks everyone.

References and artifacts mentioned: POC workbook (link: https://redwood.example.com/poc-workbook/meridian-bio), Security checklist (doc link), Benchmark spreadsheet (will be attached by Claire)

Meeting end.

Harborline Renewal: staggered uplift & SLA walkthrough

Quarterly renewal/check-in focused on a staggered capacity uplift across US-East and EU-West, feasibility of VPC activation for private traffic, and locking SLA targets. Customer is leaning toward a mixed approach (hosted + dedicated reserved capacity) with a private VPC gateway for sensitive workloads. Action items: pricing & canary plan, latency benchmark, and security/KMS confirmation.
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-04
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Avery (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (CSM), Evelyn (Harborline VP Eng), Marcus (SRE), Lena (Procurement), Samir (Security)

Summary (auto): quick check-in ahead of renewal to align uplift phasing, confirm VPC onboarding constraints, and agree next steps for benchmarks and pricing.

[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Evelyn: Evelyn here.
[00:09] Marcus: Marcus - SRE.
[00:11] Lena: Lena from procurement.
[00:13] Samir: Samir, security.
[00:15] Avery: Great, Diego and Priya here on the Redwood side. The goal for today is to align on the renewal window, the uplift sequencing (we heard you wanted a phased increase across US-E and EU-W), and the VPC activation for a subset of traffic. We'll also touch SLA numbers and any blockers.
[00:34] Marcus: Sounds good. We've got projected volume increases starting mid-March, Q1 to Q2 ramp, but we want to stage it to validate latency and cost.
[00:42] Diego: Cool. When you say 'stage' — do you mean split by route/namespace or split by traffic percentage?
[00:48] Evelyn: Prefer percentage, initially 10% canary, then 30, then full. But some endpoints are sensitive and must go through our VPC.
[00:57] Samir: Right, the sensitive endpoints need a private channel and KMS-backed encryption. We can't have DB keys in a vendor-managed KMS without approval.
[01:06] Avery: Understood. We can do a VPC private gateway for those routes; that would keep traffic on a customer-managed VPC and we integrate with your KMS/HSM for key wrap. There are some options — Diego, do you want to outline?
[01:18] Diego: Yeah. The two main patterns we've seen: 1) Redwood Private in-customer VPC with a private control plane and customer-managed KMS — full sovereignty but more provisioning lead time, or 2) Hosted with VPC peering and a customer egress path for the KV cache and sensitive calls — faster but slightly less isolation. The performance delta depends on region egress and whether you need on-prem onramp.
[01:42] Marcus: Latency is the key metric for us. For session-based routing we need p95 under 220ms for the main endpoints. Right now with a standard hosted route we see ~160ms p95, but when we tested the EU/W region under load it crept to 260ms.
[01:58] Diego: Were those tests using continuous batching turned on? That matters a lot for p95 versus cost.
[02:03] Marcus: I think batching was default - we ran the standard SDK. We can re-run with explicit config.
[02:08] Priya: Note: we can instrument per-route batching suggestions from Redwood Optimize to see what balance hits your SLA.
[02:16] Evelyn: Ok, so sequence: 10% canary in US-E first, validate p95 and token-cost, then bring EU-W 10% and run a cross-region failover test. We'll need pricing for the staggered uplift and a canary runbook.
[02:32] Avery: I'll put together a staggered pricing schedule — we can show per-token blended rates for hosted vs reserved Dedicated vs private host-combo. We'll also include expected cost delta from increasing batch sizes and from different quantization profiles.
[02:45] Lena: From procurement, the schedule is important. We have internal approvals that align with quarter ends. If there are big bumps in committed spend, we'll need to tee up contract amendments before March 15.
[02:58] Avery: Good to know, we'll target docs before March 10 to give you buffer.
[03:02] Samir: On encryption: we need to know if Redwood will hold any unwrapped customer secrets. We have a policy: no persistent plaintext keys in third-party control planes.
[03:12] Diego: For the VPC Private option, keys remain customer-managed in your KMS; Redwood supports envelope encryption so we don't store unwrapped keys. For Hosted, we use customer-supplied keys via a HSM integration but there are limits with our hosted telemetry. We'll get you a short tech note.
[03:28] Samir: Please make sure the tech note covers audit logs and retention — we also need an example audit sampling.
[03:34] Priya: We'll attach our audit log spec and a sample retention policy.
[03:38] Marcus: About benchmarking — we need a reproducible harness that hits your public endpoint and also the VPC route. Diego, can Redwood provide the script?
[03:46] Diego: Yes. We'll provide a benchmark script and a test plan. It will include continuous batching on/off toggles, token-length profiles, and concurrency curves. We'll also add a KV cache warm-up phase.
[03:57] Marcus: Perfect. If we can measure p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1k tokens, that will help our capacity planning.
[04:05] Diego: We'll produce a spreadsheet with run outputs and cost model assumptions.
[04:09] Evelyn: On SLAs — our legal wants availability numbers tied to credits and latency windows. What are typical Redwood SLA options for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[04:19] Avery: For Dedicated we offer stronger SLOs — typically 99.9% uptime with defined latency baselines per model and region. Hosted is slightly lower but still enterprise grade. We can propose a blended SLA for the phased rollout: baseline on hosted routes and a stricter target once Dedicated/Dedicated pool is live for core traffic.
[04:35] Lena: We need the SLA language to be explicit on credits and on time-to-failover for cross-region fallback.
[04:42] Priya: We can include our automatic fallback policy in the doc — Redwood supports policy-defined fallback to a cheaper model or a different region, with an SLO for automatic fallback time (usually sub-2s for routing config, but depends on KV cache rehydrate).
[04:58] Marcus: Rehydrate is the tricky part — if fallback incurs KV cache misses, it can add tens of ms per token and sometimes more. We'll need a plan to prime caches for failover nodes.
[05:08] Diego: Agreed. Our standard approach is to pre-warm caches for canary nodes during rollout windows and to have a 'soft-fallback' policy that degrades model size before switching region — that can keep latency acceptable.
[05:20] Evelyn: Good. Procurement will want to see a cost comparison: immediate hosted uplift vs reserved Dedicated commit plus private gateway ops.
[05:28] Avery: I'll include a 12-month cost model with a break-even analysis at different usage tiers.
[05:33] Lena: Also include billing cadence, invoice line items for Dedicated pools, and any one-time provisioning fees.
[05:40] Samir: On compliance, we do want to review the SOC 2 Type II evidence and penetration test cadence. Is Redwood SOC 2 now?
[05:48] Priya: Yes, Redwood is SOC 2 Type II — we'll attach the attestation and the whitepaper on penetration testing. Samir, we'll also include our KMS/HSM integration spec and sample audit logs.
[05:59] Samir: Great. If possible, include a redaction template for logs (PII masking) — that's a blocker for us.
[06:06] Diego: We have a log-redaction config that can mask known fields and also a post-processing hook for additional patterns. We'll share an example config.
[06:16] Marcus: Back to technical: when we did the EU load test, the token CPU utilization spiked and we saw throttling upstream. Can Redwood throttle at the model route level or is it global?
[06:27] Diego: We support per-route rate limits and token-level quotas. For Dedicated you can also configure guaranteed throughput per pool. Throttling behavior can be tuned—either queueing with timeout or rejecting at the edge.
[06:38] Marcus: We prefer queueing with backpressure headers so we can shed gracefully in the app.
[06:44] Diego: That's supported; we'll include sample response headers and backpressure handling guidance.
[06:50] Evelyn: One more on timeline: given provisioning lead times for Dedicated capacity and VPC peering, what do you think is realistic to have both live for a partial subset of traffic?
[07:00] Avery: If we start provisioning next week, Dedicated pool availability in US-E could be 4-6 weeks, EU-W a little longer (6-8 weeks) depending on capacity. VPC peerings typically 2-3 weeks if there's no network ACL complexity. So a staged plan through April is realistic.
[07:16] Lena: That works with our internal procurement windows if we get the proposal in two weeks.
[07:21] Avery: We'll aim for docs by 2026-02-06.
[07:24] Marcus: For the benchmark, we'd like to run a first pass next Thursday.
[07:27] Diego: I'll create the benchmark ticket and share the harness by 2026-02-05.
[07:30] Samir: I may have follow-ups after reviewing SOC2 and KMS specs — expect questions.
[07:34] Priya: We'll be available to fast follow.
[07:37] Evelyn: On the commercial side — if we commit to a 12-month reserved pool with a staged uplift, can we get a mid-term true-up option? We want flexibility if usage grows faster.
[07:48] Avery: Yes, we can include a flexible true-up clause — usually 30 days notice and prorated adjustments. We'll draft options: standard commit, commit + buffer, and commit + burst credits.
[07:59] Lena: Also need cancellation terms for unused reserved capacity — typically we ask for a minimum notice and a reduced refund schedule.
[08:08] Avery: We'll include sample amendment language.
[08:12] Marcus: Anything else on the technical front?
[08:14] Samir: Just to reiterate that any logs shipped to Redwood must have PII masked and we need sample evidence.
[08:21] Diego: We'll add the masking template and a short redaction test you can run.
[08:25] Evelyn: Ok, sounds like we have alignment. Let's recap next steps — can someone do a recap?
[08:31] Avery: Sure. Recap: 1) Redwood to send staggered pricing and canary playbook by 2026-02-06. 2) SE to ship benchmark harness by 2026-02-05 and coordinate test next Thursday. 3) Security to review SOC2/KMS artifacts and confirm redaction/KMS constraints by 2026-02-10. 4) Procurement to review contract amendment window; Redwood to include flexible true-up language. Any additions?
