Threshold tuning and fallback playbook sync - ValenceAI POC Week 3

Date: 2026-11-26 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~48m | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes
Redwood: Maya (AE), Jonas (SE) | ValenceAI: Samir (Head ML), Elena (Platform), Marco (CTO)
Week 3 POC sync focused on tuning latency thresholds and finalizing a fallback playbook vs incumbent. Redwood presented tuned configs showing p50/p95 improvements vs baseline but persistent p99 tail at peak. Agreed next steps: share artifacts, run p99 tail with burst credits + prefix caching, customer to share traces, schedule canary rollout and security review.
Benchmark diff: Redwood tuned vs IncumbentVendorX baseline
Tail latency (p99) behavior during 95-100% load
KV/prefix caching and impact on live traffic
Burst credits / QoS slots and dedicated reservations
Fallback playbook: model variant swap, regional reroute, degrade-to-embeddings
Security/VPC implications for private connector
[00:00] Maya (AE): ok hi everyone, thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, jonas is with me, we wanted to walk through the week 3 tuning and the fallback playbook, um we'll start with the numbers we ran overnight.
[00:22] Jonas (SE): yeah hey, quick note, the bench harness we used is the same request shape you shared but we enabled prefix cache and slightly higher batch timeout, so you'll see lower p50/p95 but tail still shows jitter.
[00:45] Samir (ValenceAI): hey thanks, I saw the summary you sent in the deck, the p95 look great but p99 is concerning, are we seeing spikes only at sustained 90% load or at short bursts?
[01:10] Jonas (SE): mostly short bursts combined with KV cache cold-starts, when the KV cache miss rate rises above ~18% we see tail degrade, and that aligns with your traffic traces where you have spikey bursts at 11:00 and 14:00.
[01:35] Elena (ValenceAI): yeah those are our peak periods, also we have a lot of >2k token requests that lock up the GPU longer.
[01:50] Maya (AE): ok back to the baseline comparison: IncumbentVendorX was at p50 38ms, p95 210ms, p99 490ms in your demo harness; our tuned runtime hit p50 32ms, p95 160ms, p99 420ms — so improvement but not yet the margin you need at tail.
[02:20] Marco (CTO): those numbers look promising, will the tuned profile require dedicated slots or is it achievable on shared?
[02:33] Jonas (SE): good question, the tuned profile in the spreadsheet used dedicated QoS slots with a small reserved pool (2 slots) plus burst credits. On shared, you'd see similar p50/p95 with more variance at p99. We can replicate on shared but we recommend reserved for production SLOs.
[03:00] Samir: their incumbent had a placeholder for reserved throughput; they promised consistency but we saw those p99 spikes during deployment windows. How do you handle graceful degradation?
[03:20] Maya: that's the fallback playbook we wanted to lock down today — high level: 1) auto-fallback to a quantized model variant (lower mem/compute), 2) regional reroute to secondary pool, 3) degrade to cached embeddings for non-critical requests. We have a doc draft and a runbook.
[03:45] Elena: can you walk through quantized variant latency tradeoffs? I worry about hallucination/regression risk.
[04:05] Jonas: sure — quantized variant we used is 4-bit with per-channel scales; in the tests we saw 15-20% token latency reduction, sometimes 30% cost savings. Quality regressions were minimal on your eval set but we'll need your acceptance tests in CI to guard. There is a tiny increase on rare edge prompts.
[04:40] Samir: ok acceptable if we gate by QA. What about KV/prefix cache warmup? Is there a way to avoid cold-start misses during sudden bursts?
[04:58] Jonas: yes, two levers: proactive warmup (pre-warm common prefixes at expected peak times) and adaptive prefetching based on request telemetry. We demonstrated both in the lab; prefetch reduced cold miss by ~60% in our run.
[05:25] Maya: we added the prewarm hook in the runtime config we shared, see the link in the notes (links: /redwood/benchmarks/valence-2026-11-24.csv and /redwood/configs/valence-prewarm.yaml).
[05:45] Marco: network-wise, will VPC private connector add latency? our infra team is sensitive to any extra hops.
[06:05] Elena: we measured on our side a few ms overhead with the private connector, but if it buys security we can accept it as long as p99 meets SLO.
[06:25] Jonas: private connector adds minimal ms on average, but can add jitter if egress path is saturated; Elena we'll need confirmation on egress bandwidth and NAT pooling.
[06:40] Elena: noted, will validate and send config.
[07:00] [brief silence, rustling papers]
[07:12] Samir: earlier you mentioned burst credits — explain how that works operationally.
[07:20] Jonas: burst credits are reserved transient capacity we can allocate to a customer for short periods; operationally they come from a capped pool and are applied automatically when queue depth spikes. They reduce queueing and lower p99 for short windows. For guaranteed behavior we suggest reserved dedicated slots.
[07:45] Maya: and if dedicated isn't possible, we can throttle non-critical routes, e.g., background enrichment can be deprioritized or routed to embeddings fallback.
[08:05] Samir: ok good. about the benchmark harness, you said there was a small change to batch timeouts that helped p95, what did you change?
[08:20] Jonas: we increased batch wait from 8ms to 12ms under low-latency workloads to allow slightly better packing without hurting p50. That helps throughput and p95 but can worsen tail if queue bursts are large; tradeoff must be tuned to your max inflight.
[08:45] Marco: are those knobs accessible to our SEs? we'd like to run a couple of permutations ourselves.
[08:55] Maya: yes we'll supply the harness and a runnable RBAC token for the bench scripts, plus a short how-to. Action: Maya will send artifacts.
[09:10] Samir: one more question — how do you ensure deterministic fallback so we don't flip-flop during a spike?
[09:25] Jonas: we use circuit-breaker thresholds with time windows, and a hysteresis period before reverting back. Also the playbook has a staged rollout (canary) with metrics monitoring and rollback rules. We'll share the playbook draft.
[09:50] Elena: that addresses my ops concern. For legal/security, if we failover to a different region, are there data residency issues?
[10:05] Maya: good flag — the playbook includes residency constraints; if a request touches personal data flagged by your policy we will not reroute cross-region unless permitted. We'll need your data classification to enforce this.
[10:25] Samir: ok we'll provide that.
[10:40] [fast forward conversation covering small config points and a brief silence]
[18:10] Jonas: returning to p99 numbers — in the tuned run (sheet v3) under a synthetic ramp to 95% sustained, p99 plateaued at ~420ms with prefix prewarm, without prewarm it hit 540ms. With dedicated 2-slot reserve and burst credits we saw p99 drop to ~380ms.
[18:40] Samir: so dedicated really buys you tail consistency. Do you have cost delta estimates vs incumbent?
[18:55] Maya: yes we added per-request cost delta in the sheet; rough ballpark is 12-18% higher for reserved capacity but you get 30-40% less user-visible errors and better p99. We can optimize further with quantization and route-level caching.
[19:20] Marco: acceptable if we can prove SLO; what's a reasonable pilot scope to validate?
[19:30] Jonas: single region, canary traffic at 5-10% for 48-72h with real traces and monitoring hooks. If p99 holds, expand to 25% and then full.
[19:45] Samir: done, we'll run canary after we receive the tuned artifacts.
[20:00] Elena: small ops ask — we need the exact runtime images and config hashes to feed into our IaC pipeline.
[20:10] Maya: yes we'll provide container digest, config hash, and deploy scripts.
[20:25] [several quick clarifications about logs and observability]
[25:00] Jonas: regarding observability, the console exposes per-route token-level latency, KV hit rates, and can emit traces to your tracing backend. We can correlate p99 spikes with KV miss rate and GPU stalls.
[25:40] Samir: good, can you also push alerts for p99 > 450ms for 5m?
[25:55] Maya: yes will configure.
[26:10] Marco: last big one — fallback to embeddings for non-critical requests, how do you detect these?
[26:25] Jonas: either by route tag or by request header; your app can mark low-confidence/low-importance calls and those can be routed automatically to an embeddings-only path which is far cheaper and faster.
[26:40] Samir: ok we'll annotate a few routes for the pilot.
[26:50] [longer block of cross talk as folks review notes]
[35:00] Maya: recap quick — action items we listed, we'll share tuned CSV, bench harness, config, run the p99 tail test, and you will send traces and validate VPC. We proposed security review the week of 2026-12-08 and a canary rollout target 2026-12-10 pending results.
[35:30] Elena: fine by us; small ask, please also include a failure-mode doc for legal so we can forward to compliance.
[35:45] Maya: sure, we'll add a one-page failure-mode summary.
[36:00] Samir: any other blockers?
[36:05] Jonas: none from our side; just need the traces and you'll need to decide on reserved slots vs shared.
[36:20] Marco: decision timeline — we should aim to decide by 2026-12-03 to hit the canary date.
[36:34] Maya: noted.
[36:45] [wrap up pleasantries]
[37:00] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with the files and next steps.
[37:10] Samir: thanks, appreciate the thoroughness.
[37:20] [call ends]
Maya Patel - send tuned benchmark CSV and patched runtime config - Due: 2026-11-30
Jonas Schmidt - run head-to-head p99 tail test with burst credits enabled and send results - Due: 2026-12-01
Samir Rao - provide 48h request trace and peak hour SLO definition - Due: 2026-11-29

Ops runway SLO refresh & stability deep-dive

Quarterly check-in focused on SLO alignment and runway stability. Customer is seeing intermittent p99 latency spikes on checkout-related calls, wants updated SLOs tied to cost impact, and is evaluating a small Dedicated pool for latency-sensitive traffic. Action items center on benchmark runs, traffic profile sharing, and a revised SLO/pricing proposal.
p99 latency spikes and root-cause hypotheses
Dedicated vs Hosted routing policy for checkout flow
Cost modeling for mixed workload (low-latency + batch embeddings)
Security/compliance asks (audit logs, KMS, SSO)
Pilot amendment and next milestones
[00:00:00] Sofia (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick check — audio ok?
[00:00:06] Alex (Peregrine): Yeah, loud and clear. We have Jordan and Priya on from infra.
[00:00:12] Sofia: Great, today's goal: walk SLO options, surface the p99 behavior you saw, and line up the bench so we can quantify cost/latency tradeoffs. Marcus will lead the technical bit.
[00:00:24] Marcus (Redwood SE): Hi all. Priya, can you give a quick recap of the symptomset so we align on what to measure?
[00:00:32] Priya (Peregrine): Sure — so since launch month we been mostly fine but last two weeks we've had intermittent spikes on our checkout endpoint; p50 is fine, p95 okay, but p99 jumps to 1.6s sometimes 2.2s when concurrency hits around 80–90 requests. It's not consistent, seems correlated with longer prompt sequences and when third-party enrichment calls return slowly.
[00:00:55] Marcus: That's helpful, thanks. Couple immediate Qs: are you sending full context each time or relying on prefix/KV cache?
[00:01:03] Priya: We do a full context send for simplicity — we've not integrated Redwood's prefix caching yet. We were worried about cache invalidation with user-specific context.
[00:01:13] Marcus: Got it. Two levers then — caching and routing to a dedicated low-latency pool for checkout. Both have costs.
[00:01:22] Jordan (CTO): Can you ballpark the incremental cost of a small Dedicated pool? We're trying to compare against rewriting to reduce prompt length which also has engineering time.
[00:01:31] Sofia: We can. We'll include that in the SLO/pricing doc. For rough sense, a dedicated 1–2 GPU pool for heavy tail traffic can be more predictable but shows up as committed capacity with monthly cost. Hosted routing with a model variant can be cheaper but less predictable for p99.
[00:01:46] Alex: Also, we'd like to keep data in our VPC for regulatory reasons — is the Dedicated option the same as Private? I thought Dedicated was still Redwood-hosted.
[00:01:56] Marcus: Good call-out. Dedicated offers isolated GPU pools but runs in Redwood regions; it isn't the same as Private (VPC). If you need customer-managed VPC, that's Redwood Private. Dedicated gives data isolation at rest and strict tenancy but network egress still goes through Redwood infra unless you choose Private.
[00:02:13] Priya: Ok, so Dedicated gives tenancy and capacity guarantees, but not full VPC control. That might be fine for now. We need to check the audit log retention and KMS integration — legal asked.
[00:02:23] Hannah (CSM): We can share the SOC 2 and KMS integration docs — I'll ping them after the call. Also note there's an add-on for longer audit retention if you need.
[00:02:33] Jordan: Good. Back to latency — do you think quantization or model variant selection could materially change p99? We're currently using redwood/gpt-small-1 (example name, actual model varies).
[00:02:45] Marcus: Two pieces — model architecture and serving configuration. Quantization often reduces throughput cost but can slightly change token times; it won't magically fix a tail caused by concurrent KV cache eviction or blocking third-party enrichment. For model choice, a lower-parameter variant with consistent decoding might reduce per-token latency but at some quality cost.
[00:03:04] Priya: The enrichment calls are external and sometimes add 200–600ms. We are considering pre-fetching, but that adds complexity.
[00:03:12] Marcus: For the bench we want to reproduce the composite flow: enrichment + full prompt + model decode. If we can get a traffic histogram and a few representative prompt sets (top 10 prompts by volume), we can replay with similar concurrency and measure p50/p95/p99 and KV cache hit rates.
[00:03:29] Priya: We can do that. We'll share a CSV with token counts distribution and concurrency traces.
[00:03:34] Sofia: Excellent. One thing customers often miss — batching behavior interacts with concurrency. If you have bursty traffic, continuous batching can help cost but might increase tail. We'll include recommended batch/window settings in the doc.
[00:03:46] Alex: We already have a short internal SLA with product — trying to keep checkout under 800ms p99. That's tight.
[00:03:54] Marcus: 800ms p99 is tough at your current traffic patterns without Dedicated and prefix cache. Two paths: 1) invest in prefix/KV cache + shorter prompts so hosted infra meets 800ms most of the time; or 2) route checkout traffic to a small Dedicated pool with pinned GPUs and smaller batching window for strict latency.
[00:04:14] Jordan: What's the measurable delta? Like expected p99 and monthly cost?
[00:04:18] Sofia: We'll put numbers in the proposal. Example: with dedicated 1-GPU pool and optimized routing, you may get p99 ~650–850ms for that flow at expected concurrency; hosted mixed-traffic might be 900–1.6s depending on bursts. But we'll confirm with the bench.
[00:04:34] Priya: Also curious about fallbacks. If dedicated is down, can we auto-failover to hosted without double cost?
[00:04:41] Marcus: Yes — we can configure smart routing with automatic fallback to a compatible model variant in hosted. The objective is graceful degradation, but during failover you might see higher latency and different cost profile. We can set up A/B routing or canary so you don't route all traffic immediately.
[00:04:54] Alex: Ping — curious about cache invalidation approaches for user-specific context. Any patterns you've seen?
[00:05:00] Marcus: Common pattern: prefix cache for static parts of the prompt (product descriptions, business rules) and per-user ephemeral data appended at decode time. That reduces serialized tokens and KV reuse while keeping personalization. There's some engineering work, but it's usually the best cost/latency win.
[00:05:16] Priya: That would require app changes; timeline unknown. Jordan is worried about engineering bandwidth.
[00:05:21] Jordan: Right, we have a rewrite sprint next quarter. If Dedicated can buy us time and meet 800ms, it might be cheaper than a full rewrite now.
[00:05:30] Sofia: That aligns with what other customers choose — Dedicated as a bridge while app changes are scheduled. We'll model the cost of that bridge.
[00:05:37] Hannah: Quick note on observability — Redwood Console can show route-level token breakdown, model-specific latency histograms, and per-token cost. Marcus, can you add screenshots to the proposal so they see the per-route view?
[00:05:48] Marcus: Yep, I'll export the dashboard and include a sample. Also I'll annotate where to look for KV cache hit ratio and continuous batching windows.
[00:05:57] Priya: About security — our security team asked if we can use their Key Management Service for encryption at rest. Is KMS integration available for Dedicated?
[00:06:06] Marcus: KMS/HSM integrations are supported for Private deployments; for Dedicated we offer customer-managed keys in supported regions — there's a short onboarding checklist. I'll include the exact steps and caveats.
[00:06:19] Alex: Great. One more — audit log retention: we need 2 years for compliance. Is that an extra cost?
[00:06:26] Hannah: We have an add-on for extended retention. I'll add pricing to the SLO/pricing doc and include the retention SLAs.
[00:06:33] Jordan: Ok — on contracting: if we go Dedicated for the next quarter as a trial, what's the process to convert to a longer reserve?
[00:06:41] Sofia: We can do a pilot term with month-to-month commitment on a small Dedicated pool and then convert to a 3–12 month reserved contract for discounts. Hannah will draft the amendment.
[00:06:52] Priya: For the bench, can Redwood simulate network variance for enrichment calls so we see composite tail?
[00:06:58] Marcus: Yes, we can add latency injection to the enrichment mock and run the replay. That'll show composite p99.
[00:07:05] Alex: Perfect. Anything else on the technical side?
[00:07:08] Jordan: I'm worried about model drift when we switch variants for latency. How do you monitor quality regressions?
[00:07:15] Marcus: We recommend a small eval set tied to your core checkout prompts — we run automated quality monitoring and set regression alerts. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization/model knobs but quality signals are always tied to your domain test prompts.
[00:07:29] Priya: We'll include a list of 50 critical prompts for eval.
[00:07:33] Sofia: Awesome. Quick recap and owners then next steps.
[00:07:37] Sofia: Action items — Marcus will run the p99 bench (owner Marcus), Priya will send traffic histogram (owner Priya), Sofia/Hannah will draft SLO/pricing and pilot amendment. We agreed target dates on the follow-up email.
[00:07:49] Alex: Sounds good. One tiny thing — competitor question: we are also talking to Anthropic — they quoted lower per-token during the demo but had less mature routing. Any advice?
[00:07:58] Sofia: Price isn't the only angle — look at p99 under realistic traffic, fallback strategies, and operational observability. We'll include a side-by-side in the doc with known tradeoffs.
[00:08:10] Jordan: Ok, thanks everyone.
[00:08:14] Hannah: I'll share SOC 2 and KMS checklist after the call.
[00:08:18] Marcus: I'll propose two bench windows (one for heavy-burst and one steady) and include instructions for the CSV.
[00:08:25] Sofia: Great. We'll follow up with a single-threaded doc and email. Thanks all.
[00:08:30] Alex: Thanks.
[00:08:33] [meeting end — recording stops]

Segregated Node Reservation & Burst Sizing Discovery

Discovery focused on dedicated reserved GPUs with isolation requirements for PHI workloads. Customer wants a mixed model: base reserved capacity for steady inference, isolated tenancy per environment, and controlled burst to a shared pool. Key concerns: deterministic latency SLOs, data residency, KMS/HSM integration, and cost predictability. Agreed to run a benchmark and share security docs and pricing.
Meeting header: 2025-12-02 10:00 AM PT | Duration: 73 min | Recording: Fireflies auto
Attendees: Sahir Patel (Redwood AE), Elena Morales (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Aurelia CTO), Rajiv Kapoor (Aurelia Platform Eng), Lena Ortiz (Aurelia SRE)

[00:00] Sahir: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm sahir from redwood, and with me is elena who will cover the perf/infra bits. how's everyone doing?
[00:15] Maya: good thanks, a little early for us but all good. appreciate the time.
[00:23] Elena: morning — quick agenda, we want to understand your steady-state, peak bursts, isolation needs for PHI, and then talk about how dedicated reserved capacity maps to that. then next steps around bench and security.
[00:39] Rajiv: yeah that's right. we run inference for several EHR normalization and triage models, roughly 150ms p50 now on our in-house cluster, but the throughput patterns are spiky. we need predictable latency under load.
[00:55] Lena: and from SRE perspective, we need tenant isolation between prod / staging / internal research — can't have cross-tenant noisy neighbor for PHI workloads.
[01:10] Sahir: got it. quick qualification: are you evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private? where's your preference?
[01:18] Maya: priority is dedicated — security & compliance reasons. hosted api is attractive for dev but prod must be in a dedicated pool or a private vpc.
[01:28] Rajiv: also want to avoid single-tenant hardware per environment for cost reasons; a model where we reserve a pool with logical isolation is preferred.
[01:40] Elena: ok so mixed approach: reserved capacity with node-level isolation (affinity/taints) plus a burst pool that can be shared across customers but with encryption in transit at rest. any hard constraints on region or data residency?
[01:53] Maya: data at rest stays in our VPC, and keys managed by our KMS/HSM. so we need Redwood to support BYOK and bring-your-own-kms integration.
[02:05] Sahir: yes we support KMS integrations and HSM options in the Private/Dedicated offering — we'll share the KMS doc.
[02:12] Rajiv: another thing — can we get strict CPU/GPU isolation so noisy neighbor isn't an issue? We've had contention when other jobs schedule on same host.
[02:22] Elena: on dedicated we can pin workloads to physical GPUs and nodes, plus node isolation (dedicated tenancy) with reserved slots per pool. that prevents co-located tenant jobs. for the burst pool we use work-sharing, but there are controls: concurrency caps, preemption priority, and fallback to smaller quantized models.
[02:44] Maya: fallback to quantized model — interesting, but can that break quality? we need a cutoff threshold.
[02:51] Elena: yes you can configure a quality budget — if primary model out of capacity, route to a quantized variant only if confidence scores above threshold, otherwise queue or fail with graceful degradation.
[03:05] Lena: what's the typical latency hit when moving to 4-bit quantization?
[03:10] Elena: rough ballpark depends on model; for LLM-style decoders, p50 might increase a bit but cost per token drops significantly. we'll include model-specific numbers in the perf matrix.
[03:22] Rajiv: ok can you explain burst sizing? we have 2.5M tokens/day average but 80% of traffic in 4 hours a day.
[03:33] Sahir: common pattern. recommended is base reserved capacity sized for steady-state 95th percentile, plus a burst pool sized to handle X additional concurrent sessions based on your peak qps. do you have concurrency and per-request token estimates?
[03:45] Rajiv: average session ~600 tokens, peak concurrent sessions around 350 today, baseline 80 concurrent.
[03:53] Elena: quick calc: if baseline 80 concurrent mapped to N GPUs for your chosen model, to absorb 350 you'd need about 4-5x capacity during peaks. with reserved + burst we can reserve enough to handle baseline and allow bursts up to commit levels with throttles.
[04:10] Maya: how are costs modeled? are burst hours billed at higher rate?
[04:15] Sahir: pricing model: reserved monthly commit covers base capacity at discounted rate. burst usage beyond commitment billed on-demand; we can also do committed burst blocks for predictable billing if you prefer.
[04:27] Rajiv: what's the minimum commitment? we need to understand financial exposure.
[04:31] Sahir: typical starting point is 3-month commit for a minimum set of GPUs, sliding scale discounts at 6/12 month. i'll send the tier sheet.
[04:39] Lena: we need SLA for latency as well — can you guarantee p95 under X ms?
[04:45] Elena: we can commit to infra-level latency SLOs per model family and sequence length. important note: application-level p95 includes prompt variability and network; we provide token-level latency breakdowns in the Console. for firm guarantees we recommend Dedicated with pinned nodes.
[04:59] Maya: can we pin specific models to nodes? e.g., smaller Llama variant on a different pool?
[05:06] Elena: yes, model pinning and rollout controls are supported. you can create routes so certain calls go to specific pools or model variants, and use canary/AB rollouts.
[05:16] Rajiv: failure modes — if dedicated pool is saturated, what's fallback?
[05:20] Sahir: two options: automatic fallback to hosted-compatible model in another region, or queueing with exponential backoff. we can also define strict rejects if you prefer not to touch hosted resources for PHI.
[05:33] Maya: prefer reject > fallback for PHI unless it's encrypted end-to-end and KMS managed by us.
[05:40] Elena: noted. we'll show config for reject vs fallback and policy toggles.
[05:47] Rajiv: on the network side — VPC peering or private link? we need private connectivity with enforced egress rules.
[05:54] Sahir: Redwood Private offers VPC connectors and private link. for Dedicated we can do customer-managed VPC attachments and strict egress control.
[06:02] Lena: any audit/logging we can export? we need immutable audit logs for inference requests tied back to request ids.
[06:09] Elena: yes, request-level audit logs, model versioning metadata, and trace hooks. logs can be exported to your SIEM and retained per your retention policy.
[06:18] Maya: to move forward, we want a bench run. what do you need from us?
[06:23] Elena: ideally a representative prompts set (10-50 prompts), expected concurrency, max sequence length, and a brief corpus to emulate typical token distribution. Rajiv, you mentioned heatmaps — that will help.
[06:36] Rajiv: i'll export heatmaps and attach. we can provide 30 sample prompts and a synthetic load profile.
[06:42] Sahir: great. we'll do a 2-hour run that includes baseline reserved capacity sim and burst spike test. we'll test both A100 and H100 configs if you want.
[06:54] Maya: yes please include H100, we want to compare perf/cost. also need to test encrypted key performance with BYOK.
[07:02] Elena: BYOK perf test requires a KMS proxy in the loop; small latency added but measurable. we'll include that path.
[07:10] Rajiv: how long to provision a dedicated pool for benchmark?
[07:13] Sahir: for a test lab we can spin ephemeral capacity within 48 hours depending on queue; for Reserved production it's lead time 2-4 weeks for dedicated capacity provisioning.
[07:24] Lena: can we simulate noisy neighbor effects? we want to see worst-case tail latencies.
[07:29] Elena: yes we can run synthetic co-tenancy experiments and show isolation behavior; for dedicated with pinned GPUs you'll see minimal cross-talk.
[07:38] Maya: what's the upgrade rollback story? if a model rollout causes regressions in quality we need auto rollback.
[07:44] Elena: rollouts support canary + thresholds on quality metrics. if regression detected against eval prompts we auto rollback and route to previous model. you can configure detection sensitivity.
[07:56] Rajiv: ok this is useful. question from procurement: what about contract terms on data retention and incident response?
[08:04] Sahir: we'll share the standard enterprise contract and the data processing addendum. we typically allow custom terms for PHI customers; we'll loop in legal if needed.
[08:15] Maya: please include indemnity and breach notification windows.
[08:19] Sahir: noted.
[08:22] [08:22] Lena: small callout — we want to avoid cold starts for large models; does Redwood keep KV cache warm across requests?
[08:30] Elena: yes continuous KV cache and prefix caching are supported; we also have warm pools that keep activations in memory for low-latency paths. that can be part of your reserved footprint.
[08:42] Rajiv: and autoscaling — how quick? we need scale-up under sudden spikes but not let cost explode.
[08:48] Elena: autoscaling has configurable cooldowns, prioritization and rate limits. for burst we use classified priority queues and can spin up extra nodes within minutes depending on hardware availability; faster if you commit reserved burst blocks.
[09:02] Maya: can we set hard caps to prevent runaway cost?
[09:05] Sahir: yes, budget caps and alerts, plus forced rejects. we can also do pre-commit billing so bursts are in a prepaid block to avoid surprises.
[09:14] Rajiv: any partner integrations we should know? monitoring, prometheus exporters etc?
[09:18] Elena: we have prometheus metrics, traces (open-telemetry), and plug-ins for Datadog/Databricks. we'll share samples.
[09:27] Sahir: quick recap and proposed next steps — i'll send pricing + commitment tiers and contract template; elena will produce perf matrix and bench plan; rajiv will send heatmaps and sample prompts; maya will identify compliance contact. then we schedule the 2-hour benchmark week of 12/08. anything else?
[09:47] Maya: sounds good. please also include SOC2 and ISO docs and KMS integration guide.
[09:52] Sahir: will do. last question: timeline to production if bench looks good?
[09:57] Elena: typical ramp: bench + security review 2-3 weeks, procurement + contract 2-4 weeks, provisioning dedicated capacity and initial rollout 2-4 weeks after that. total 6-10 weeks typical.
[10:09] Maya: ok that aligns with our target window. thanks everyone.
[10:15] Sahir: thanks all — we'll follow up with notes and items.
[10:20] [END TRANSCRIPT]

document.content:
Deployment model evaluation & residency check - Arcadia Mutual

Introductory residency and compliance discovery to map Arcadia Mutual's requirements for handling PII/PHI and financial data. Discussed Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment trade-offs, logging retention rules, encryption/KMS, SOC2/HIPAA overlap, and pilot next steps. Agreed to run a short on-prem simulation and a hosted token-scrubbing test; Redwood to share security pack and tentative pricing for Dedicated with regional locking.
data residency requirements (EU/US split)
HIPAA vs financial controls overlap
logging and audit retention policies
KMS and key residency
hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
pilot and benchmarking plan
Redwood to send security & compliance package (SOC2, HIPAA addendum, data flow diagrams) by 2027-02-18
Evan to run deterministic benchmark using Arcadia anonymized sample dataset and share latency/cost numbers by 2027-02-23
Arcadia to confirm internal list of stakeholders for pilot and legal touchpoints by 2027-02-19
Schedule technical POC kickoff (private deployment checklist) for week of 2027-02-28
Evan Ruiz - spin up a hosted token-scrub test with sample logs and report findings - due 2027-02-23
Maya Patel - send Dedicated pricing tiers and regional lock options + security pack - due 2027-02-18
Liam O'Connor - provide anonymized sample with schema and retention rules - due 2027-02-19
Priya Menon - provide Arcadia's minimum audit log retention policy doc and list of regulators of concern - due 2027-02-19
Meeting header:
- Date: 2027-02-16
- Time: 15:00 EST
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Evan Ruiz (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Arcadia Head of Eng), Priya Menon (Arcadia CCO), Nadia Ruiz (Arcadia Cloud Architect)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
We did a residency and hosting model intake with Arcadia to map their constraints. Main asks: EU customer data must stay in EU regions, certain logs must be retained for 7 years, HIPAA-ish requirements for some broker-sourced medical claims (edge case), and need for KMS keys to be customer-managed. They are evaluating Dedicated vs Private but want quick benchmark data first.

Topics covered:
- Residency boundaries and geofence needs
- Logging: ingestion, raw transcripts, sanitized versions, audit trails
- KMS/HSM and key escrow preferences
- SSO/SAML and RBAC mapping for ops
- Pilot criteria and success metrics (latency percentiles, token cost, audit completeness)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Speaker 1: okay good afternoon everyone thanks for joining, uh this is Maya from Redwood, I'll hand over to Evan for a quick tech intro then we'll hear from Arcadia about the compliance boundaries
[00:12] Evan R: thanks Maya yeah hi all Evan Ruiz here, solutions engineer. We'll cover how Redwood's hosting modes map to residency, what stays in region, and the logging controls. I'll also flag where we typically see friction.
[00:25] Liam O: thanks Evan, quick context - Arcadia Mutual handles life insurance and some claims that have accompanying medical notes. We're moving to embed LLM features into our claims triage flow but legal wants absolute clarity around where data lives and what logs are kept.
[00:40] Priya P: (Priya) yes hi, from compliance side we need to know — if we use Hosted Redwood API, does any PII cross borders? Also HIPAA equivalence - some of our records are health-adjacent.
[00:52] Evan R: good q. Short answer: hosted can be regionally restricted, but there are caveats. For Redwood Hosted we have region endpoints and we can ensure processing occurs in a given cloud region, however some non-production telemetry or control-plane metadata may be centrally processed unless you opt for Private/Dedicated with regional control. So for strict EU residency we often recommend Redwood Dedicated with regional lock or Private deployment.
[01:10] Nadia N: and with Dedicated, where do KMS keys live? do we get customer-managed keys?
[01:18] Evan R: yes, Dedicated supports BYOK (bring your own key) integrated with the cloud KMS — Google KMS, AWS KMS, and HSM options for private. For Private deployments on-prem, keys never leave your vault. There's a small ops overhead for rotation.
[01:31] Liam O: okay, good. For our regulators we need proof that raw transcripts are not kept longer than 30 days unless explicitly chosen. We also need an immutable audit trail of inference requests for at least 7 years for certain audit events. Is that doable?
[01:46] Maya P: that's a common ask. We can configure logging retention per customer on Dedicated and Private. Hosted has default retention windows but we can propose extended retention as an enterprise add-on — but that may change cost.
[02:00] Evan R: to add — we can offer two-tier logs: raw ingestion (can be auto-redacted) and audit-event logs (immutable event log pointers). For the 7-year requirement we usually recommend exporting audit events to customer-managed storage (S3/GCS) with immutability settings turned on, or we can stream to your SIEM.
[02:18] Priya P: is the raw ingestion the same as the KV cache? i'm worried about forgotten prefixes in cache or model context that might leak PHI.
[02:28] Evan R: good callout: KV cache is in-memory only and ephemeral — we don't persist KV cache to disk in the runtime. But session transcripts and optional debug dumps are stored in logs. We recommend enabling in-flight redaction and token-scrubbing. For our pilot we'll demonstrate the scrub step.
[02:45] Liam O: what's token-scrubbing look like? do you do regex or ML-based PII detection?
[02:52] Evan R: currently it's a hybrid. We do pattern-based redaction for obvious identifiers plus an entity classifier for less structured PHI. It's configurable — you can choose to strip full identifiers or replace with stable tokens. Note it's not perfect so for regulated data some customers prefer Private.
[03:10] Speaker 3: (crosstalk) sorry quick — how about backups, are inference logs included in backups that could be replicated across regions?
[03:18] Evan R: backups are region-scoped; for Dedicated we can disable cross-region replication by default. For Hosted there's a default replication for high-availability but we can negotiate region-locking as part of a contract.
[03:32] Priya P: we need SSO — SAML with SCIM user provisioning and role-based access for ops. Can Redwood integrate with Okta?
[03:40] Maya P: yes Okta is standard, we support SAML and SCIM and can map roles (admin/operator/read-only). For Private deployment you can keep the control plane in your VPC and integrate with your IdP directly.
[03:52] Liam O: on the subject of regs — HIPAA. Our legal says we need a Business Associate Agreement for anything that might touch protected health info. Do you support that?
[04:02] Maya P: yes Redwood has a HIPAA addendum we can sign for Dedicated/Private. For Hosted we can often add the addendum but we need to inspect the integration and data flow with your lawyers. We'll share the standard BAA text in the security pack.
[04:16] Nadia N: any certifications we can use in procurement? SOC2 Type II, ISO27001, something like that?
[04:22] Evan R: SOC2 Type II is available, ISO27001 is in progress for certain parts. We'll include current certs and scope in the pack. Also we provide penetration test reports under NDA.
[04:36] Priya P: auditability - we need sequence numbers or unique request IDs for every inference for chain of custody. Is that built-in?
[04:44] Evan R: yes every request is stamped with a UUID and trace header. On Dedicated/Private we can guarantee those are persistent and stream them to your SIEM; on Hosted we still generate them but control plane hooks may be less direct.
[04:58] Liam O: ok good. Cost question — we have to make a business case. How big is the cost delta between Hosted and Dedicated? Also performance implications — we need p95 latency under 350ms for triage calls at our median sequence length of 128 tokens.
[05:13] Evan R: typical delta depends on throughput. For light throughput Hosted is cost-effective. Once you need region isolation and strict key management the Dedicated baseline is higher (monthly reserved GPU capacity) but unit token cost may drop at scale. For latency p95 350ms depends on model chosen and batching; for sequence length ~128 we can hit that on Dedicated with the recommended model. We'll benchmark with your sample.
[05:35] Maya P: I'll share a spreadsheet of example cost models mapping expected qps and 99th percentiles — but we'll need Evan's benchmark numbers.
[05:45] Priya P: one more on retention — if we export audit events to our S3 bucket, does Redwood keep an index? can we purge from Redwood side but keep the exported copy as the canonical audit?
[05:56] Evan R: yes you can have Redwood retain minimal operational metadata and push full events to your canonical storage. Purging Redwood-side logs is part of the contract and we can automate lifecycle policies.
[06:08] Liam O: about private deployment — what's the deployment packaging? container images? AMIs? appliance?
[06:14] Evan R: we ship an on-prem bundle (containerized runtime) with orchestration instructions. For VPC deployments we have cloud templates (Terraform & CloudFormation). There's an ops checklist and preflight script.
[06:24] Nadia N: ok, if we do a Private/air-gapped install, will there still be any call-home? we cannot allow outbound control-plane connections without sign-off.
[06:33] Evan R: Private can be fully air-gapped; we have a control-plane option that runs in your environment with no outbound, but the trade-off is you lose Redwood-hosted telemetry and auto-update paths. We provide an update bundle you can apply manually.
[06:46] Priya P: question on legal hold — if a regulator asks for a snapshot of all inference logs for a given period, can Redwood produce that in an auditable format?
[06:55] Evan R: yes, audit export in CSV/NDJSON with request IDs, user IDs, and hashes of content for integrity. For long-term archival we recommend customer-managed buckets with immutability locks.
[07:08] Liam O: okay. I'd like to talk about data minimization — best practice seems to be pre-scrubbing at source before sending to inference. Would Redwood support a sidecar or client-side lib to do that?
[07:20] Evan R: absolutely. We provide lightweight client SDK hooks and a scrubbing sidecar for common platforms. For customers that need extra assurance we recommend client-side redaction plus server-side tokenization so both ends have double protection.
[07:34] Maya P: let's align on pilot scope: Arcadia will provide anonymized sample logs, Redwood will run a hosted token-scrub test and a Dedicated benchmark. If results are within thresholds, Arcadia will greenlight a Private pilot or Dedicated reserved capacity. Sound right?
[07:47] Liam O: yes that sounds right. Priya anything else from compliance?
[07:51] Priya P: need the SOC2 report and BAA text. Also please include a short note about our ability to delete logs on demand and the SLA for deletion requests.
[07:59] Maya P: noted. we'll include deletion SLA options.
[08:03] Speaker 4: may I ask about data residency mapping when a single customer has EU and US customers? how do we partition tenant data?
[08:12] Evan R: we partition by tenant ID: routing rules send EU tenant traffic to EU-region instances. For multi-tenant companies we can also offer tenant pinning so a tenant's data is always processed in a single region and its logs export to region-specific storage.
[08:26] Nadia N: how are IP and derivative data handled? if a model used training that included public data, any downstream derivative IP issues?
[08:33] Evan R: Redwood doesn't mix customer corpora into shared training. For hosted models we provide model provenance and usage guidelines; if you have stricter IP requirements we recommend Dedicated/Private where you can pin a frozen model and track all inputs/outputs for IP review.
[08:48] Liam O: one more procurement note — we need an RPO for logs and a max RTO for the service in contracts, and a proof of disaster recovery. can Redwood provide standard SLO language?
[08:58] Maya P: yes we'll include standard SLOs and propose targets in the contract. Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime.
[09:06] Evan R: small technical caveat — for p95 latency under 350ms we need to tune batching and kernel selection; we'll test with your typical prompt distribution. If you have a mix of long and short prompts we may have to serve different model sizes and route accordingly.
[09:22] Liam O: routing by policy — could Redwood route lower-risk requests to hosted cheaper model and high-risk to Dedicated?
[09:30] Evan R: yes that's exactly a common pattern: smart routing by sensitivity label. You can specify policies that route to different model tiers or deployment modes.
[09:41] Priya P: who within Redwood will be our point of contact for security questions during legal review?
[09:46] Maya P: I'll be primary for commercial and coordination, Evan is SE lead for tech questions. For deeper security we have a security liaison (we'll share contact in the pack).
[09:55] Speaker 2: okay what's the immediate timeline? we want to complete pilot approval within 2 weeks of receiving the security docs.
[10:01] Maya P: we can get the security pack out in 48 hours, bench results in about a week after we receive samples, and then a POC kickoff the week after that.
[10:10] Liam O: perfect. let's wrap with a recap and next steps.
[10:15] Maya P: recap: Redwood to send security pack + SOC2/BAA, Evan to run token-scrubbing hosted test and Dedicated benchmark, Arcadia to provide anonymized logs and retention policy. Follow-up call scheduled after Evan's benchmark.
[10:30] Priya P: sounds good. thank you all.
[10:34] End of meeting.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker labeling errors (Speaker 1/2/3 used where names would be). Some technical terms spelled phonetically (K M S sometimes K-M-S), small pauses and crosstalk not fully captured.

Axiom Transport - Peak Tokenflow & Concurrency Discovery

Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-04-11
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Recording ID: fireflies-20270411-axiom-001-bk7

Summary (auto):
Customer evaluates Redwood for low-latency streaming inference for conversational routing and telematics summarization. Primary concerns: p95 token latency targets during streaming, sustained concurrency during morning peaks, data residency and private deployment for PII in logs. Discussed Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs and benchmarking plan.

Topics:
- p95 streaming token latency targets
- concurrency & burst sizing
- token/sec throughput and batching tradeoffs
- KV cache and cold-start impacts
- security/SOC2 & VPC option for logs

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Ramos: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, and with me is Priya, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Marcus Li: Hey Alex, good thanks. A busy day but ready to dig in.
[00:09] Jenna Ortiz: Hi all. I'm Jenna, we'll probably ask a lot about network egress and how logs are handled.
[00:13] Priya Nair: Great, Jenna. We'll cover both infra and security. I'm Priya, I'll take the technical parts.
[00:18] Samir Patel: Samir here, ML eng, I own the prompt infra and model experiments. We have a couple of real-world prompt shapes to run.
[00:25] Alex Ramos: Awesome. Quick agenda: we want to understand your p95 goals for streaming, concurrency needs, and then map Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private options and next steps.
[00:35] Marcus Li: High level — our app is voice -> transcription -> LLM streaming for intent detection and short summary sent back to driver. We have two windows: morning surge 07:00-09:00 and evening 17:00-19:00. Peak concurrency around 120-180 streams concurrently, average session 30s but we stream tokens continuously. P95 latency target is tough: we want token-to-token latency under 80ms p95 ideally, 150ms max.
[00:59] Priya Nair: 80ms p95 token latency is ambitious for streaming; depends on model size, sequence length, and whether you use hosted low-latency variants or dedicated GPU pools. For context, our smallest low-latency variants on hosted can hit ~60-120ms p95 for small-medium LMs at 512 token context when optimized. Larger 13B+ tends to be higher unless you pin dedicated capacity and tune batch sizes.
[01:24] Jenna Ortiz: When you say "pin dedicated capacity", do you mean reserved GPUs that always run our model? What are the failure modes when load spikes?
[01:32] Priya Nair: Yes. Dedicated means you get reserved workers — consistent KV cache residency and predictable per-token compute. During spikes, we offer burst capacity (optional) that can spin up additional instances but with some cold-start penalty. Hosted has autoscaling, but during a huge spike you may see brief increases in p95 as requests get routed to warm-up workers or smaller quantized variants as fallback.
[01:52] Marcus Li: Could you ballpark throughput? If we have 150 concurrent streams and each produces say 10 tokens/sec on average, that's 1500 tokens/sec sustained. What GPU profile do we need?
[02:03] Priya Nair: Roughly, if you're using a 7B model with optimized kernels and 4-bit quant, a single A100 (or equivalent) in our Dedicated pool can sustain ~2k-3k tokens/sec for autoregressive workloads with moderate batching. For 13B it's lower, maybe 1k-1.5k tokens/sec. The streaming token-to-token latency is influenced by micro-batching windows — we can configure a small continuous batching window to keep per-token latency low.
[02:32] Alex Ramos: Also consider prefix caching and KV cache warmness: if many sessions reuse similar prompts (like standard instruction + small user context), caching reduces work. If every session is unique, your token/sec demands increase.
[02:46] Samir Patel: Our prompts are mostly templated with a few driver-specific fields — so there is some prefix reuse. We also do short summaries every 10-15s which adds extra tokens. So maybe 12 tokens/sec average.
[02:58] Jenna Ortiz: On private deployment: we have regulatory constraints around PII in telematics logs — would Redwood Private let us keep logs on-prem and only use control plane? How does billing work?
[03:10] Priya Nair: Private allows control plane to be customer-managed; you can configure local log sinks and HSM/KMS integrations. Billing typically is enterprise license + infra. We can also run a hybrid where model inference runs in your VPC (private) while Redwood manages orchestration.
[03:25] Marcus Li: That sounds promising. Cost-wise for Dedicated vs Hosted, do you have numbers for our expected sustained 1.5k-2k tokens/sec?
[03:33] Alex Ramos: I'll share a detailed cost matrix after this call, but high-level: Hosted per-token is simplest for eval — but for sustained high throughput Dedicated reserved capacity often becomes cheaper and more predictable. For 24/7 sustained load, Dedicated with reserved commits usually wins. We can run a cost proforma tailored to your prompt shape.
[03:50] Speaker 1: (unintelligible)
[03:53] Priya Nair: One planning detail — p95 token latency target of 80ms means we should optimize for micro-batch size of 1-2 tokens and tune kernel paths; that increases per-token overhead but keeps latency tight. There's a cost tradeoff: smaller batches reduce throughput efficiency.
[04:12] Samir Patel: If we accept 150ms p95, does that change hardware needs?
[04:16] Priya Nair: Yes, 150ms p95 is more forgiving — you can allow slightly larger micro-batches and higher accelerator utilization, needing fewer GPUs. We'll model both SLO bands in the benchmark.
[04:27] Marcus Li: Any notes on tokenization or tokenizer overhead? Our voice pipeline emits subword tokens — we saw in prior infra tests tokenizer can add 10-30ms at scale.
[04:35] Priya Nair: Good callout. Redwood can host the tokenizer close to the model execution path; in Dedicated setups we can colocate tokenizer service on the same node to reduce RTT. We'll include tokenizer profiling in the benchmark script.
[04:47] Jenna Ortiz: Network egress — during peak we saw spikes in RTOs when egress limits were hit. For hosted, how do you guarantee throughput to regions?
[04:56] Alex Ramos: We have regional endpoints. For strict egress and residency controls, Private with VPC peering is recommended. For Hosted we can prioritize routes by region and fall back across adjacent regions, but that's subject to cloud bandwidth limits. We'll surface documented throughput baselines per region in the follow-up.
[05:14] Marcus Li: What about fallback policy — say one model variant is overloaded, can Redwood route to a smaller quantized model automatically?
[05:20] Priya Nair: Yes, smart routing supports fallback chains by policy: latency-first, cost-first, or custom. For latency SLOs you'd pick latency-first and the system will fallback to a compatible model variant with a similar API. You can control fallback order.
[05:33] Samir Patel: For benchmarking, we'd want to replay a 1-hour morning surge with real traffic. Can Redwood replay traffic into Dedicated test workers?
[05:41] Priya Nair: Absolutely. We have a benchmark harness that replays traffic, records per-token latency (p50/p95/p99), concurrency profiles, and token/sec. We'll run an initial smoke test on Hosted for quick intel, then a Dedicated run with pinned capacity to validate steady-state.
[05:56] Alex Ramos: Priya, maybe outline the benchmark steps?
[05:58] Priya Nair: Sure. Step 1: ingest the prompt set and traffic profile from Axiom. Step 2: smoke run on Hosted low-latency to validate functional correctness and gather baseline. Step 3: Dedicated run with configs: micro-batch window 10-15ms, KV cache warm-up period 10 minutes, quantization Q4_optimized for 7B or Q8 for 13B. Step 4: measure p95 token latency, tail latency, and cost per 1k tokens; run several scenarios: 120 concurrent, 180 concurrent, and 240 burst. We'll also measure cold-start behavior and burst ramp.
[06:38] Jenna Ortiz: Can we get telemetry at token granularity? We need that for some audit requirements.
[06:42] Priya Nair: Yes, we can instrument token-level traces in the Dedicated and Private deployments; for Hosted we provide aggregated token latency histograms and per-request traces on demand. Private gives you full raw traces that you can ship to your logging stack.
[06:56] Marcus Li: Security: SSO, RBAC, KMS?
[07:00] Alex Ramos: We support SAML SSO integrations, fine-grained RBAC, and KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS) for key management. Private deployments can be configured to use your HSM if needed. We'll include the SOC2 docs and our security whitepaper.
[07:14] Samir Patel: One tricky piece — we run summary generation at end of session that sometimes requires 1-2k tokens. How does that affect KV cache and concurrency?
[07:22] Priya Nair: Long-form summaries can be batched differently; they usually increase memory pressure on KV cache and increase per-request compute significantly. We'll model a mixed workload where some sessions trigger long-form jobs. That will affect peak GPU utilization and might push you to a larger Dedicated footprint or offload long-form to separate instance pool.
[07:45] Jenna Ortiz: For cost modeling, do you show cost per active seat or per-token estimates?
[07:50] Alex Ramos: Both. We'll produce a per-token estimate and a per-concurrent-stream cost for your peak windows, plus recommended commit levels for Dedicated.
[07:59] Marcus Li: Timeline — we want a pilot before Q2 end. Is that realistic?
[08:03] Alex Ramos: Yes, pilot within 4-6 weeks is doable: we need your prompt set and a traffic dump, Redwood sets up a Dedicated trial pool for 1-2 weeks, run benchmark, then iterate.
[08:12] Samir Patel: A note on evals — we'll want to compare quality delta if you fallback to smaller quantized models. Does Redwood provide regression tooling?
[08:20] Priya Nair: Redwood Optimize includes regression alerts tied to prompt sets. We'll run the same prompts across variants and capture quality metrics and examples. We'll include that in the benchmark report.
[08:33] Alex Ramos: Anything else on architecture?
[08:35] Jenna Ortiz: Autoscaling cooldowns — we need deterministic behavior during our surge, not oscillation.
[08:40] Priya Nair: We can tune autoscale policies and use pre-warming/burst reservations to avoid oscillation. Dedicated is best when you need deterministic behavior.
[08:48] Marcus Li: Ok, action items?
[08:50] Alex Ramos: I'll send the SOC2 and security docs, Priya will send the benchmark plan, Samir will drop the prompt set. We'll schedule the benchmark run next week.
[08:58] Samir Patel: I'll aim to get the S3 link by Thursday.
[09:00] Jenna Ortiz: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:03] Alex Ramos: Thanks, we'll follow up with the plan and pricing. Bye.

End of Transcript.

document.content:
Oxford Labs - marketplace connector certification & ops playbook review

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-03
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 64 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Ramakrishnan (Oxford Head of Cloud), Liam O'Connell (Oxford Lead DevOps), Sara Nguyen (Oxford Security), Ethan Moore (Oxford SRE)

Summary:
Quick alignment on marketplace certification steps, operator/helm packaging compatibility, KMS integration expectations, and an ops/runbook sketch for the joint listing. Agreed to run an end-to-end staging validation and a focused performance run with quantized model variants.

Topics covered:
- Marketplace packaging checklist and required metadata (screenshots, icons, billing metering hooks)
- Helm operator compatibility and upgrade path for on-prem customers
- VPC peering, private deployment and KMS/HSM requirements
- Benchmark plan: quantization profiles, batching, KV cache behavior, latency SLOs
- Security gating: SOC2 evidence, audit log retention, SSO/SAML and RBAC mapping

Action items (recap): see action_items field.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll do a quick run through the marketplace cert path then dive into the operator/helm questions. Priya, thanks for coordinating on Oxford's side.
[00:19] Priya (Oxford): thanks Maya. we want to make sure the listing can be consumed by our customers who run in VPC and also on-prem, so packaging and the operator story is the top thing.
[00:34] Daniel (Redwood SE): yeah totally. the short version: we have a helm chart plus a lightweight operator that handles lifecycle hooks for model assets, and a connector to the marketplace metering API. the operator supports upgrade hooks and pre/post deploy migrations.
[00:51] Liam (Oxford): quick question — does your operator need cluster-admin? our security team is twitchy about broad perms.
[01:02] Ravi (Redwood): good call. by default the operator requests cluster scoped RBAC for node-level provisioning, but we have a restricted mode that uses a delegated service account and a small set of CRDs only in the target namespace. most customers use the restricted mode for marketplace installs. i'll send the exact role bindings.
[01:22] Sara (Oxford): can you make that role binding example explicit? we need to run it past our infosec team. also how does KMS integration look? we can't have keys managed by the vendor.
[01:36] Maya (Redwood AE): absolutely. Redwood supports both customer-managed KMS (Cloud KMS, AWS KMS, or on-prem HSM) and bring-your-own-key patterns. we integrate via envelope encryption and the runtime keeps only encrypted model artifacts and wrapped keys. we'll share the KMS playbook.
[01:55] Ethan (Oxford SRE): is there any secret that lives unwrapped in the pod? like a plain text token?
[02:03] Daniel (Redwood SE): no, we never persist raw model keys. the operator will mount a KMS agent that fetches wrapped keys at boot; tokens can be short-lived and rotated. i will note that our earlier internal docs had a miss where the var name was REDWOOD_KMS_KEY but in the operator manifest it shows as RW_KMS_KEY - sorry for the confusion, that's a docs bug we'll fix.
[02:28] Priya: perfect. on marketplace metadata — what do we need for the listing tile? screenshots, support contact, billing metered hooks?
[02:39] Maya: on the marketplace side we need: product icon, 3 screenshots, a short blurb, pricing tiers (metered + subscription options), and the metering webhook integration details. our marketplace connector expects an event POST to the metering endpoint with usage deltas in the standard schema (we'll attach spec).
[02:58] Liam: about metering — our finance team needs to reconcile usage with our billing. do you support offline metering for air-gapped installs?
[03:10] Maya: yes — for private/offline installs the operator writes compact usage logs to a signed ledger file that can be pulled and ingested via the marketplace back-office. it's not real-time but suitable for monthly reconciliation.
[03:23] Speaker 1 (contractor): sorry can i ask about quantization? we saw notes that Redwood recommends 4-bit on Ampere but that impacts latency variance — is that accurate?
[03:34] Daniel: yeah quantization tradeoffs. 4-bit int quant gives big cost wins on token throughput, but you can see some tail-latency variance depending on the prompt length and KV reuse. our Optimize team recommends profile-driven selection: e.g., short chat paths use Q4 and aggressive KV caching; long-context embeddings prefer Q8 or unquantized for fidelity.
[03:58] Priya: can we run a short benchmark to validate those numbers on our hardware profile? we use mixed T4 and A100 pools.
[04:08] Ravi: absolutely. we'll prepare a perf harness and tokenized scripts — Daniel will share the harness repo link and a sample runbook. we suggest a baseline test: 1k short prompts (avg 40 tokens), 1k long prompts (avg 1024 tokens), 3 quant profiles (fp16, q8, q4).
[04:31] Sara: retention and audit logs — what's the retention by default in hosted vs private? and can we forward audit logs to our SIEM?
[04:42] Maya: hosted keeps audit logs 90 days by default; Dedicated and Private we allow configurable retention and log forwarding via syslog/ELK/Kinesis. for marketplace listing we need to surface those options in the ops playbook.
[04:57] Ethan: about VPC peering — will your connector require open egress to the internet? some of our customers have strict egress controls.
[05:07] Daniel: the connector has two modes: direct egress, where the operator reaches the Redwood control plane for updates and metering, or an air-gapped mode where you run a small reverse-proxy bundle that pulls updates over an authorised proxy. we'll document both flows.
[05:26] Liam: sounds good. on the upgrade path — if a customer installs via the marketplace and then wants to move to a dedicated Red wood reserved pool, how stateful is the transition?
[05:36] Ravi: we designed the flow to be state-light: model artifacts are stored in the customer's object store (S3/GCS/MinIO) by default, so migrating compute is mostly a routing and credentials update. the operator handles pinning model versions and a canary rollout pattern for traffic.
[05:53] Priya: are there compatibility notes for MinIO? we run MinIO on-prem for many clients.
[06:01] Daniel: yes MinIO is supported; there is an S3-compatible manifest and a small shim for listing/ACLs. we'll include the MinIO example values in the helm sample.
[06:12] Maya: quick housekeeping — we'll attach the packaging checklist and the marketplace schema in the followup. any blockers from your side?
[06:20] Priya: infosec will want to see penetration testing history and the SOC artifact list. also the KMS integration details.
[06:29] Maya: we can share SOC2 Type II report redacted, and a high level of recent pen test notes. for KMS we'll share the playbook and sample IAM policies.
[06:38] Sara: one more sec — when you say 'audit logs' is that the model request payloads too? we have PII concerns.
[06:47] Daniel: by default request payloads are redacted in hosted mode for PII-sensitive fields; on Private, customers control the logging level. we recommend scrubbing sensitive fields at the operator ingress and we can provide a reference sanitizer filter.
[07:02] Ethan: what about the runtime's prefix caching — if two different deployments share a similar workload, can cached KV slices be exported or is it local to the node?
[07:13] Ravi: caches are local to the serving cluster. we support a shared KV cache in dedicated deployments via a best-effort replicator, but we don't recommend cross-tenant sharing for security reasons. the replicator is per-tenant.
[07:29] Speaker 1: timing on the benchmark and a rough estimate of how many GPU hours we should allocate?
[07:36] Daniel: for the suggested runs (3 profiles x 2 prompt sets x 1k each) you'd need roughly 6-8 hours on an A100 or about 18-24 hours on a T4 cluster to get stable tail-latency numbers. we'll tailor the harness to parallelize across GPUs.
[07:55] Priya: good. I'd like us to schedule that next week — Liam, can you get staging creds?
[07:59] Liam: yes we'll spin up a staging VPC and share kubeconfig and peering details by Sep 8.
[08:08] Maya: i'll also note that for marketplace listing we need one UAT run where our cert team installs the operator in Oxford staging — that's the gating step before publish.
[08:19] Ravi: small note on packaging: make sure your OCI image manifest includes the SBOM artifact; the marketplace will flag missing SBOMs during preflight.
[08:30] Sara: do you have a preferred SBOM format? cyclonedx or SPDX?
[08:36] Daniel: we accept CycloneDX, v1.4 preferred. we'll include an example.
[08:44] Priya: is there any certification cost or fee on Redwood side for marketplace listing?
[08:50] Maya: no listing fee from Redwood; marketplace takes a commission per their standard terms. we'll connect you to the marketplace ops contact if you want detailed commission numbers.
[08:59] Ethan: can we have a short bulleted runbook in the followup? like install, configure KMS, run test workload, validate metering, escalate.
[09:08] Maya: yes we'll send a 1-page ops playbook plus a 10-step install guide.
[09:14] Priya: last question — any known regressions with function/tool calling in quantized runs? a few of our ML folks worry that structured output gets more brittle.
[09:24] Ravi: fair point. in our internal tests we saw some structured-output variance at Q4 for very long sequences; for function-calling we recommend Q8 or baseline fp16. but that’s workload dependent — part of the benchmark we'll include schema-based correctness checks.
[09:42] Speaker 1: random nit — earlier you said REDWOOD_KMS_KEY vs RW_KMS_KEY, will that be fixed in the operator?
[09:49] Daniel: yes, i'll push a patch to the operator examples and update the doc.
[09:53] Maya: okay let's recap next steps: we'll send packaging checklist + helm values, Daniel sends harness repo + SBOM example, Ravi prepares perf harness, Oxford provides staging creds and compliance questions. we'll aim to reconvene after the staging validation.
[10:09] Priya: thanks everyone, this was helpful. 
[10:12] Maya: thanks all. we'll follow up with the artifacts and calendar invites. end.

Notes on shared artifacts referenced:
- Packaging checklist (link to be shared)
- Helm chart values example (repo link: github.com/redwood-inference/marketplace-helm)
- Perf harness (repo link: github.com/redwood-inference/perf-harness — internal)
- Marketplace metering schema (attached in followup)

End of transcript.

document.content:
Security intake / deployment readiness - Orion Analytics

Discovery focused on security posture and deployment options. Customer is security-first and wants SOC2 + ISO attestations, SSO/SAML, RBAC details, audit log retention, and KMS integration. Team is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Next steps: send compliance docs, schedule infra deep dive, provide pricing and pilot scope.
SOC2 / ISO attestation
SSO / SAML and SSO provisioning
RBAC and tenant isolation
Audit logs and retention policy
Encryption at rest / KMS / HSM
Data residency and retention
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
Pilot scope and performance targets
Send SOC 2 + ISO27001 attestation PDF and pgp link to Priya
Schedule infra deep dive with Orion platform team (Ethan + Samir) week of 11/10
Provide a rough pricing sheet comparing Hosted vs Dedicated by 11/07
Share private deployment network diagram + sample KMS integration notes
Priya Mehta - review SOC2 report and list any gaps - due 2025-11-12
Ethan Park - draft VPC peering network diagram and KMS integration example - due 2025-11-07
Maya Thompson - send pricing deck and pilot contract template - due 2025-11-07
Samir Kapoor - provide sample workload (qps, seq len, perf targets) for bench - due 2025-11-10
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-05
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Jared (CTO - Orion), Priya (Head of Security), Samir (Platform), Lina (Procurement)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be rough): Customer wants to understand Redwood security controls, compliance artifacts, and how keys/data are handled in Hosted vs Dedicated and Private deployments. Also asked about SSO/SAML flows and audit log retention.

[00:00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you taking the time. Quick intros?
[00:00:07] Jared (Orion): Jared here, CTO, I'll lead on architecture but Priya is our security owner.
[00:00:11] Priya (Orion): Hey all, Priya, Head of Security. Main topics: SOC2 / ISO, SSO, RBAC, auditability, KMS.
[00:00:17] Maya (Redwood): Great. Ethan from our infra team will cover the technical pieces.
[00:00:21] Ethan (Redwood): Hi, thanks. I'll jump in on the deployment options and KMS bits.

[00:00:35] Priya: Big one for us is whether using Hosted means we lose control of keys. We need to know about encryption at rest and if Redwood manages keys or if we can bring our own.
[00:00:50] Ethan: Short answer: Hosted uses Redwoods managed keys by default; we also support customer-managed keys via KMS integrations for Dedicated and Private. For hosted we can do a bring-your-own-key (BYOK) flow through cloud KMS with additional contract terms — but caveat, the private control-plane pattern is strongest for key ownership.
[00:01:12] Priya: When you say BYOK for hosted, is that envelope encryption or full disk? What's the model?
[00:01:20] Ethan: It's envelope encryption. We store model artifacts and KV caches encrypted using a data encryption key (DEK) wrapped by your KMS CMK. So you can rotate keys on your side and we respect that. There are some service account perms we need.
[00:01:33] Priya: Okay, can you show an IAM policy sample?
[00:01:37] Ethan: I'll include a sample in the follow-up — it'll show the minimal permissions we request for key use.

[00:01:55] Samir (Orion): On Dedicated vs Private: what's the difference for audit logs and retention? We need logs retained for 7 years for some data flows.
[00:02:04] Maya: Right — hosted has standard log retention windows (configurable up to 90 days by default for our analytics console) but for longer-term retention you can export audit logs to S3 or your SIEM. Dedicated gives you greater control and we can set longer retention or ship directly to your logging infra. Private (on-prem/VPC) keeps logs in your environment entirely.
[00:02:26] Priya: So with Hosted we rely on Redwood to ship logs to S3? Is that push or can Orion pull logs?
[00:02:31] Ethan: Both patterns exist. We typically offer push exports to your storage via a signed role; you can also query via API and pull. For compliance we recommend push to your vaulted S3 with lifecycle rules.

[00:02:55] [Minor crosstalk] Lina (Orion): sorry - procurement note - are there extra charges for log exports?
[00:03:01] Maya: There can be egress/storage costs depending on volume; we'll include a sizing/pricing estimate.

[00:03:20] Priya: On SSO — we use Okta and SCIM provisioning. We need SAML for SSO and SCIM for group sync to enforce RBAC. How do you support groups mapping?
[00:03:30] Ethan: We support SAML 2.0 and SCIM 2.0. You can map Okta groups to Redwood roles. We support custom roles — so you can have least-privilege roles and map them via SCIM group attributes.
[00:03:41] Priya: Is there an audit trail when an admin changes role mappings?
[00:03:45] Maya: Yes — admin actions are logged in the audit trail with actor identity, timestamp, and the change payload. Those logs are available in the Console and can be exported.

[00:04:02] Jared: What's the model for data residency? Our EU customers' PII must stay in EU. Can Redwood ensure model inference for those requests stays in-region?
[00:04:12] Ethan: We support region routing. For Hosted we run in multiple regions; you can mark requests to route to eu-west-1 endpoints or restrict model serving to regional pools. Dedicated gives you region isolation for committed capacity. Private is fully in your VPC/region.
[00:04:28] Priya: If we route to EU region, are backups replicated elsewhere? That's an issue for our policy.
[00:04:36] Ethan: By default we replicate for HA within the region. Cross-region replication is opt-in and we can disable cross-region backups for EU-only datasets in a Private or Dedicated setup. Hosted default may replicate within the same geo-cluster; we'll include specifics in the compliance doc.

[00:04:58] Samir: For RBAC and multitenancy — we plan to host multiple internal teams and want strict isolation per tenant. Is tenant data logically separated?
[00:05:06] Maya: We have both logical multi-tenancy with strict scoping via namespaces and physical isolation options in Dedicated/Private. For strict regulatory needs, Dedicated with tenant-level VLANs or Private on-prem is recommended.

[00:05:28] Priya: Audit logs — retention, immutability, and ability to prove non-repudiation?
[00:05:34] Ethan: Audit logs have write-once semantics in our internal pipeline and we can provide signed hash chains for attestation upon request under enterprise contracts. For full non-repudiation we recommend shipping logs to your own immutable storage (S3 with Object Lock) — we can automate that export.

[00:05:58] [00:06:00] Priya: SOC2 — is Redwood SOC2 Type II? Can we get the report under NDA?
[00:06:07] Maya: Yes, Redwood has SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certifications. We'll send the attestation and the certs post-call.
[00:06:14] Priya: Any outstanding exceptions in the latest report we should know about?
[00:06:19] Maya: No major exceptions — we'll share the cover letter and summary. If you want specifics we can schedule a doc walk.

[00:06:36] Jared: For legal — data retention policies in the contract — can we set deletion windows per dataset?
[00:06:43] Maya: Yes, you can set retention and we support TTLs and explicit deletion APIs. For Hosted, deletion requests go through our pipeline; we provide deletion confirmations and audit entries. For Private, it's fully in your control.

[00:07:05] Samir: Technical deep dive request: we want to run a bench with a 512‑token average sequence, 150 qps, 99th-p95 latency SLO of <200 ms for small models. Is that realistic on Dedicated?
[00:07:17] Ethan: Sounds doable with Dedicated and right GPU profiles; we'll need model details and warm KV cache expectations. We'll scope a pilot with those numbers.

[00:07:33] Priya: KMS rotation process — if we rotate keys, what's the exposure window? How fast can you swap wrapped keys?
[00:07:40] Ethan: Key rotation is immediate for new writes; for existing encrypted artifacts we rewrap lazily or you can trigger a rewrap job. We provide migration tooling; speed depends on dataset size. For KV cache keys it's a smaller surface.

[00:07:58] Lina: procurement: do we need a separate addendum to enforce key control?
[00:08:03] Maya: Typically for BYOK and certain data residency requirements we sign a security addendum (SDA) or bring-your-own-key addendum. I'll surface a template.

[00:08:20] [00:08:22] Priya: About pen tests — does Redwood run annual pen tests? Can we see results or a summary?
[00:08:28] Maya: Yes, annual third-party assessments; we can share the summary report and remediation timelines under NDA.

[00:08:40] Samir: Regarding network topology for Private — can we do direct fiber / cross connect or is it just VPC peering?
[00:08:47] Ethan: Private supports VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink, and in some regions partner direct connect options. Cross-connects to co-lo sites are possible with our private deployment package.

[00:09:05] Priya: Can we have a dedicated control plane but still have inference in our VPC? We want control plane logs not to leave our tenancy.
[00:09:13] Ethan: We offer a private control plane option that can be customer-hosted; that keeps control-plane metadata in your environment. For hybrid we can run the data plane in your VPC and the control plane in a restricted customer-managed tenancy. We'll include diagrams.

[00:09:32] Jared: Any downtime SLA for Dedicated?
[00:09:36] Maya: Dedicated comes with an SLA, typically 99.9% based on reserved capacity; enterprise tiers can go higher. We'll share the SLA table.

[00:09:50] Lina: procurement follow-up: what's typical commitment length for Dedicated?
[00:09:54] Maya: 12 or 36 month commitments are common; we offer monthly burst capacity.

[00:10:10] [A few clarifying q's and some small interruptions omitted for brevity]

[00:12:14] Ethan: I'll call out one nuance — hosted BYOK has more limited guarantees around key escrow since Redwood still runs the control plane. For full key sovereignty we recommend Dedicated with CMK integration or Private where the control plane is on-prem.

[00:12:40] Priya: What about data plane logs for inference prompts — we have regulatory restrictions on PII; can you redact or avoid storing prompts altogether?
[00:12:50] Maya: We support prompt redaction at ingestion and selective logging. For strict PII scenarios we can turn off request logging for specific routes and only keep aggregate metrics. This is easier on Dedicated/Private.

[00:13:06] Samir: Schema: do you log full prompts for analytics or just token counts?
[00:13:12] Ethan: By default we keep request/response traces for debugging with redaction rules; you can configure to store only metadata. We'll provide the default schema and fields.

[00:13:35] Priya: Are audit logs tamper-evident? You mentioned signed hash chains — can you automate verification?
[00:13:43] Ethan: We can produce signed digests on a cadence and you can verify them. For automated continuous verification we'd recommend shipping to your S3 with Object Lock and running your verifier.

[00:13:58] Jared: Onboarding timeline — if we choose Dedicated, how long to provision capacity?
[00:14:04] Maya: Usually 4–6 weeks for baseline capacity (procurement/contracting dependent). Private on-prem depends on your infra readiness — often 6–12 weeks. Hosted is immediate.

[00:14:20] Priya: For compliance we'd like a pre-demo security workshop where we go through the SOC2 controls mapped to our internal control IDs. Can we do that?
[00:14:27] Maya: Absolutely — that's a reasonable request. We'll schedule a controls-mapping session with our compliance lead.

[00:14:40] [00:15:00] Action recap from Maya: I'll send SOC2/ISO certs, share the KMS/IAM sample, and pricing. Ethan will set up the infra deep dive.

[00:15:15] Priya: One last question: do you support HSM-backed keys (Cloud HSM or external HSM)?
[00:15:21] Ethan: Yes — we integrate with cloud HSM (e.g., AWS CloudHSM) and external HSM via key wrapping; for Private you can use your own HSM.

[00:15:32] Jared: Great — sounds good. We'll review docs and come back with a prioritized list of must-haves.

[00:15:40] Lina: Procurement will want the pricing doc and contract template before 11/07.

[00:15:45] Maya: We'll get that out. Thanks everyone.

[00:15:50] [Call winds down with a few technical clarifications off-line] 

Closing notes (auto): Next steps and action items captured. Red flags: customer insistence on long-term log retention (7 years) and strong key sovereignty; requires Dedicated/Private conversation.

References mentioned (to be attached in follow-up): SOC2 report (link), ISO 27001 cert (link), KMS integration sample policy (link), pricing deck (link), pilot scope template (link).

End of transcript.
