document.content:
VesperCloud x Redwood — channel / reseller alignment (intro)

Introductory call to evaluate reseller/channel partnership between VesperCloud and Redwood. Discussed go-to-market motion (APAC focus), technical compatibility for dedicated and private deployments, partner economics and margin expectations, and next steps to run a joint tech workshop and exchange architecture docs.
Meeting header: Recorded 2026-03-09 15:30 UTC | Duration 46m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Anika (Redwood Partner Ops); Alan (VesperCloud Partnerships), Priya (BD APAC), Ethan (Cloud Arch)

[00:00:03] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya Thompson, AE at Redwood. Quick round robin?
[00:00:10] Alan: Alan Chu here, Head of Partnerships at VesperCloud. Glad to meet you all.
[00:00:13] Priya: Priya Nair, BD focused on APAC channels.
[00:00:16] Ethan: Ethan Park, cloud architecture.
[00:00:18] Diego: Diego Ramos, solutions engineer on Redwood's partner integrations.
[00:00:23] Maya: Great. High level agenda — intro to Redwood, how our partner/reseller program works, technical compatibility check, and explore go-to-market in APAC. Sound good?
[00:00:30] Alan: Yep, let's go.

[00:02:05] Maya: To start, VesperCloud — give us a few bullets on what you do and why you're interested in an LLM inference partner.
[00:02:15] Alan: Sure. VesperCloud is a managed multi-tenant cloud provider focused on regulated customers in APAC and EMEA. We run bare-metal GPU pools and have a reseller arm for SaaS partners. We're exploring adding managed inference capabilities to sell to regulated verticals — primarily fintech and health — and we need a partner who can do private/VPC deployments and also support a hosted offering we can resell.
[00:02:45] Priya: Key for us is being able to offer this through our channel quickly, have a predictable margin, and preserve data residency.
[00:02:53] Maya: Understood. On Redwood's side we have hosted API, Dedicated reserved capacity, and Private (VPC / on-prem) deployments. For channel partners, we offer partner pricing tiers and an enablement pack. Diego, quick on tech fit?
[00:03:10] Diego: Yeah. We support a unified runtime that can be deployed into customer VPCs or on-prem. Important bits from your side are networking (eg ingress NAT, peering), KMS/HSM for key management, and the size of GPU pools. Any constraints there?
[00:03:25] Ethan: We run a mix of NVIDIA and custom accelerators. Most customers expect strict egress rules — no outbound to public internet unless explicitly allowed — and HSM integration for encrypted keys. Also, many want SOC2-level audit logs.
[00:03:40] Diego: That aligns with our Private option. We can integrate with customer KMS/HSM (we've seen some variation in terminology in transcriptions...), and we ship audit logs plus role-based access control that maps to SAML/SSO. There may be some kernel tuning for custom accel but we've partnered with several infra vendors for that.

[00:05:12] Alan: From a commercial perspective we want to understand margin bands — what's resale pricing look like, and are there co-sell rebates?
[00:05:20] Maya: We typically have tiered margins based on committed monthly spend. For Dedicated we can do capacity commitments with reseller discounts; hosted has per-token margins. We don't have a rigid cookie-cutter model — we usually do an initial pilot and then a committed capacity contract if both sides are happy. I'll send a sample partner pricing grid after this call.

[00:07:00] Priya: Timeline is tight. We have a few customers in APAC ready to pilot in Q2. We need to know if Redwood can onboard a pilot in 4–6 weeks.
[00:07:10] Diego: 4–6 weeks is aggressive but doable if we scope the pilot — usually a small Dedicated pool or Private deployment with limited tenants. We'll need the network diagrams and expected QPS and concurrency.
[00:07:25] Ethan: Expect around 200–500 QPS for a medium customer with burst patterns. Token consumption varies. We'll share more numbers.

[00:09:40] Alan: Security questions: SOC2? ISO? Data residency? Do you store payloads?
[00:09:47] Maya: We have SOC 2 Type II and ISO certifications; we can provide attestation. Hosted API retains logs for a configurable retention window but for Private deployments data can remain in-customer VPC with no outbound storage by Redwood. KMS/HSM integration means customers manage keys.
[00:10:12] Priya: Important — many APAC customers require encryption-at-rest with HSM and audited key rotation.
[00:10:18] Diego: We support HSM integration and can provide audit traces for key rotation events. There are some onboarding steps for HSM trust and certificate exchange, which we can do in a workshop.

[00:12:05] Maya: On the product side, quick callout — we provide features that help partners reduce unit cost: automatic KV/prefix caching, batching controls, and quantization options for supported models. That can materially change unit economics for resellers.
[00:12:20] Ethan: Can you quantify that? Our finance folks will want a sample TCO impact.
[00:12:25] Diego: Roughly, depending on workload shape, caching and batching can reduce per-token cost 20–40%. Quantization and smaller model variants can further drop cost but with some quality tradeoffs. We can run a short benchmark if you provide a representative prompt set.

[00:14:30] Alan: What about support SLAs for partners? If we resell to a regulated customer, we need 24/7 escalation and agreed uptime.
[00:14:40] Anika: For Enterprise partners we offer tiered SLAs — can be part of the Dedicated contract. For Private deployments, uptime is typically the customer's responsibility for infra, but Redwood can provide an enterprise support add-on and optional SRE-run managed services.
[00:14:58] Alan: Good.

[00:17:05] Priya: On the GTM side, how do you do enablement — training, co-marketing, sales materials?
[00:17:12] Maya: We have a partner enablement pack (sales playbook, demo scripts, technical primers), monthly partner office hours, and co-marketing funds for strategic partners. We can co-run webinars targeted at APAC fintech.
[00:17:30] Priya: That would help. Localized materials in APAC markets are critical.

[00:19:00] Ethan: Tech-specific: how do you handle autoscaling for Dedicated GPU pools? Some of our customers want predictable latency for inference spikes.
[00:19:10] Diego: Our Dedicated runtime supports autoscaling policies with reserved minimum capacity and burst capacity. We can target latency SLOs by pinning model variants with lower memory footprints or enabling more replicas. There is a trade-off: more aggressive autoscaling can increase cost. We usually tune policy per workload during pilot.
[00:19:35] Ethan: And does autoscaling happen at model-level or node-level? Any warmup issues with KV cache?
[00:19:41] Diego: Both. We can scale models across nodes and we keep a KV cache that is replicated to improve warm-starts; however very cold starts can still incur higher latency — caching reduces that for common prefixes.

[00:22:50] Alan: Competitors question — our execs asked about differentiators vs HeavyCloud and LambdaGrid. What's Redwood's positioning for partners?
[00:22:58] Maya: We position as production-first inference — unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private, strong observability and rollout controls, and cost-performance tooling. For partners we emphasize predictable economics and SRE-friendly integrations.
[00:23:14] Anika: Also, our rollout features (canary, A/B) and token-level cost breakdowns are helpful for customers trying to reduce spend during pilots.

[00:26:40] Priya: We need an idea of legal terms — is there a partner MSA or reseller agreement template? How do you handle indemnities and data processing addendum (DPA)?
[00:26:50] Maya: We have a partner MSA and a DPA. Typically we use a template and negotiate a few clauses. For high-regulation customers we can add clauses around data residency and audit rights. I'll attach the template.

[00:29:00] Ethan: Network: we will want to see how Redwood deploys agents in our VPC and whether outbound egress is required for telemetry. Some customers disallow any outbound.
[00:29:10] Diego: We can run with fully isolated Private — telemetry can be forwarded to customer-owned logging endpoints or disabled. For hosted we need outbound to Redwood endpoints. We'll detail the required ports and peering steps in the tech workshop.

[00:32:20] Alan: From business ops — do you provide metering/billing endpoints so we can invoice customers? We want to re-bill usage to our downstream customers.
[00:32:29] Maya: We expose usage APIs and monthly usage reports. Partners can choose whether to white-label billing or have Redwood bill end customers directly and bill the partner. There are multiple options; we can include in the commercial appendix.

[00:35:00] Priya: Example case — we have a healthcare customer in Singapore, data never leaves region. Would Redwood be able to run inference inside their VPC?
[00:35:08] Diego: Yes, that's exactly the Private option. It would be deployed into the customer's VPC or your VPC depending on the contractual setup, with KMS integration and no outbound logging unless requested. We'll need to validate GPU compatibility.

[00:38:10] Maya: Next steps — we'll run a technical workshop to scope a pilot, we'll share partner pricing grid and MSA, and VesperCloud will share network diagrams and sample throughput. Anything else?
[00:38:22] Alan: Can we also get a short benchmark run for a small prompt set to understand latency and cost?
[00:38:28] Diego: Yes — send the prompt set and expected payload size; we can run a short benchmark on a hosted or dedicated variant and share numbers.

[00:41:00] Priya: One more — channel enablement timelines. If pilot goes well, we want to onboard 3 customers in Q3. Is that feasible?
[00:41:08] Maya: Feasible, assuming pilots are successful and we agree on margin and enablement. We'll plan a phased enablement calendar.

[00:44:05] Alan: Thanks everyone — useful call.
[00:44:10] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up with the deck and draft MSA. Diego will reach out about the tech workshop.
[00:44:18] Diego: I'll schedule the workshop for next week; will include checklist for HSM keys and network ports.
[00:44:25] Maya: Meeting notes will be uploaded.
[00:44:30] Alan: Bye all.

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect): Partner intro; agreed to pilot and tech workshop; Redwood to send pricing and MSA; VesperCloud to share architecture and throughput; security and HSM integration are primary constraints.

Offsite recap and org reset

Cost optimization & headcount tradeoffs

Marcus Lee - publish prioritized bets doc (due 2026-03-25)

Header:
Date: 2026-03-18
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~1h15m
Attendees (as listed on calendar): Alex Rivera (CEO), Nina Gupta (CTO), Marcus Lee (Head of Product), Jasmine Ortiz (People Ops), Avery Chen (Head of GTM), Samir Venkatar (Platform), Leah Park (Finance), plus company-wide All-Hands connection

Summary: Leadership after-offsite briefing; focused on next-quarter priorities and immediate people/hiring decisions.

-- Auto-generated Topics (may be imperfect) --
1) Org reset and tactical priorities
2) Cost savings and hiring posture
3) Product bets and timelines
4) Customer impact and comms

Action items (read out): see action items section above.

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Alex (CEO): hey everybody thanks for joining, I know this is a busy week after the offsite so appreciate you carving time. we'll get through the key decisions and then open for q and a.
[00:18] Nina (CTO): yeah, and quick heads up i'll run through runtime perf notes after Alex, we had a few infra, infra— uh anecdotes from the offsite that we need to fold in.
[00:30] Speaker 1: Apologies, mic fuzz for a sec— but ok go ahead.
[00:38] Alex: high level first — two things changed for me at the offsite: one, the market is compressing on price, and two, customers are asking explicitly about private options and auditability. so we need a tighter list of bets. not 100 things, 3 big bets.
[01:05] Marcus: to be clear, are we saying 3 product bets for the company or 3 per department?
[01:12] Alex: three company-level bets — like the pillars. Marcus: serving runtime (latency and cost), Optimize (cost/perf toolkit), and Private (enterprise foot in the door).
[01:25] Marcus: ok that helps. i'll draft the bets and include measurable success metrics.
[01:31] Jasmine (People Ops): on hiring, leadership agreed to a temporary hiring posture shift — not a full freeze — we'll prioritize mission-critical roles and pause non-essential reqs pending the rubric from finance.
[01:45] Leah (Finance): right, we need a clear hiring rubric so managers know which reqs get greenlit. the objective is cost containment without crippling product velocity.
[01:55] Samir: and on the infra side, there's a short-term optimization: more aggressive batching and KV cache configs for high-volume customers, which buys us runway on GPU spend.
[02:10] Nina: small note — some of the kernel selections we prototyped at the offsite didn't generalize yet; we need a perf gate for release. otherwise we risk customer regressions.
[02:25] Speaker 2 (Engineering): does that perf gate mean delaying the dedicated rollout?
[02:30] Nina: possibly for the broad rollout; we can still do targeted pilots with specific customers. the rollout strategy becomes canary-first rather than big-bang.
[02:40] Alex: i want to emphasize customer trust. if we move slower but keep SLAs intact, that's better than pushing out something that's cheaper but unreliable.
[02:51] Marcus: on timeline — Q2 objectives will reflect two parallel streams: ship the Dedicated broader but with canary policies; and accelerate Private for two verticals (finance and healthcare) where compliance buys premium.
[03:12] Jasmine: quick people note — there's some churn risk in mid-senior eng; we need retention plans, comp band clarifications, and manager check-ins.
[03:25] Audience: [crosstalk] please clarify comp band timeline.
[03:30] Leah: finance will run comp band updates but it's going to take 2-3 weeks to map to budgets.
[03:36] Alex: okay next, GTM posture — Avery do you want to walk through enterprise asks?
[03:42] Avery (Head of GTM): sure. in short, customers want clear SLAs, private deployment options, and predictable pricing. we're working a 3-tier enterprise motion: self-serve hosted, dedicated reservation, private deployment with revenue guarantees. we'll pilot new pricing with two existing logos.
[04:05] Marcus: are we pricing Private as a platform fee plus support? or usage-based?
[04:11] Avery: hybrid — platform seat + committed usage. Leah, finance is building models.
[04:18] Leah: yes hybrid appears to maximize revenue predictability. we'll share sample TCOs.
[04:25] Speaker 3 (Product): any decisions on open-source models vs curated internal models for hosted?
[04:31] Alex: continue to curate. we don't have the scale or appetite to host every OSS variant. focus on a few verified families and give devs clear guidance.
[04:40] Nina: also we should make model quantization profiles first-class in our docs — that reduces customer questions and support load.
[04:48] Marcus: note taken — docs + runtime defaults are on the bet list.
[04:55] [05:00] Q&A start — (employees ask live questions, some mic dropouts, slight transcription glitches)
[05:12] Employee (Taylor): hey — are we doing any immediate org moves? like, will teams be reorg'd?
[05:18] Alex: no immediate mass reorgs. we'll make targeted moves to align with the three bets. some pod consolidations might happen.
[05:30] Jasmine: we'll be engaging managers tomorrow to discuss headcount decisions and one-on-ones with impacted ICs.
[05:36] Employee (Priya): can we get more detail on the perf gate Nina mentioned? what metrics?
[05:42] Nina: p95 latency delta under 5% vs baseline on standard sequences, and token throughput within 10% of current for the same GPU config. if either fails, escalate to platform and product for triage.
[05:54] Speaker 1: note — those thresholds may be tuned after early pilots.
[06:00] Marcus: on customer comms — we'll draft a short FAQ and a customer-facing roadmap slip explanation for customers in Dedicated piloting. Avery will coordinate.
[06:12] Avery: yep we'll have a template and internal slack channel to surface redlines.
[06:18] Alex: hiring posture — main point: we will continue to hire for revenue generating and critical infra roles; pause others pending the rubric. Leah and Jasmine to lock the rubric.
[06:33] Leah: finance will also reforecast ARR assumptions to check runway sensitivity for two scenarios.
[06:40] Employee (Omar): will this impact our conference presence this quarter?
[06:44] Alex: smaller presence — focus on high-value events and partner meetups. cut the broad lower-ROI sponsorships.
[06:52] [07:00] Short silence and then more questions — occasional background noise, someone shuffling papers.
[07:08] Marcus: ok — next, product shipping cadence. we'll shift to 3-week sprints for the next two months to increase cadence on bet validation.
[07:16] Speaker 2: will that change sprint planning overhead?
[07:19] Marcus: some overhead yes, but each 3-week increment is a rapid experiment. teams should prepare A/B prompts and evals in each sprint.
[07:27] Nina: on infra cost — Samir will share a config recommendations sheet for batching, kv cache TTLs, and quantization defaults to reduce immediate spend by mid Q2.
[07:38] Samir: noted. i'll publish it with expected savings and risk matrix.
[07:44] Jasmine: people question — severance / support for impacted roles? we'll follow standard policy and offer placement support where feasible.
[07:53] Alex: thanks. last piece — transparency. leadership committed to weekly updates for the next 6 weeks. we'll host a short check-in every Tuesday to report progress against the bets and hiring rubric.
[08:08] Alex: ok, we'll open to broader q's for the last block — please be concise.
[08:15] Employee (Maya): how do we handle support load if we shift pricing and reduce some headcount?
[08:22] Avery: triage — increase self-serve docs, push better onboarding, and prioritize high-touch customers. Support will get augmented playbooks.
[08:31] Employee (Taylor): will managers get autonomy to backfill critical roles quickly?
[08:36] Jasmine: yes, for critical roles aligned to bets, there's a fast path approval. details in the rubric.
[08:44] [09:00] Alex: quick recap — three company bets, hiring rubric, perf gate for kernels, canary-first rollout, updated enterprise pricing pilot, weekly updates. action owners: Marcus, Leah, Avery, Nina, Samir, Jasmine.
[09:18] Alex: anything else? otherwise i'm going to hand off to Nina for the perf deep dive scheduling.
[09:25] Nina: i'll set Doodle for next week and share an agenda.
[09:30] Alex: thanks everyone. meeting adjourned.

POC hosting rundown - WillowCare pilot criteria

MEETING HEADER
Date: 2025-01-14
Time: 11:00 AM PST
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Sofia Alvarez (Redwood SE), Dr. Aisha Khan (WillowCare Head of ML), Marcus Lee (CTO), Rita Patel (Platform Engineer), Samir Gupta (Security)

SUMMARY: Short scoping to align on POC success criteria (latency SLOs, throughput), sizing and benchmark plan comparing Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, data residency/SOC2 questions, and timeline for a two-week pilot. Agreed next steps and owners.

TOPICS: success criteria; workload sizing; p95 latency vs cost; bench plan; security; timeline and pilot cutover.

TRANSCRIPT:
[00:00] Ethan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Ethan from Redwood, AE on the account. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Aisha: Aisha here, head of ML at WillowCare.
[00:10] Marcus: Marcus, CTO.
[00:12] Rita: Rita, platform.
[00:14] Samir: Samir, security.
[00:16] Sofia: Sofia, Redwood SE, hi all.

[01:05] Ethan: Cool. High level — the reason for the call is to scope the POC: what success looks like, what benchmarks you want us to run, and to pick a hosting mode for the pilot — hosted API, dedicated reserved capacity, or private (VPC/on-prem). We're expecting this to be a two-week technical pilot once we sign off on the pilot plan.
[01:25] Aisha: Yep that's right. From our side the primary use case is clinical-note summarization and triage prioritization. Key stakeholders are product and compliance, we're sensitive to PHI and run in AWS us‑east‑1. So data residency and audit logs matter.
[01:40] Marcus: Also we need predictable latency for triage — p95 under 300ms ideally for short notes (~150 tokens) for the UX path, and with bursts up to 200 qps during spikes. Cost is a concern but second to reliability.
[01:55] Sofia: Good, that helps. Quick clarification — when you say p95 300ms for 150 tokens that's end-to-end user facing latency including our routing and network, right?
[02:04] Marcus: Correct. From app to model response and back to user.

[02:40] Ethan: Right, so this drives whether Hosted is sufficient or Dedicated/Private is needed. Hosted usually achieves lower time-to-value and is fine for 95% of workloads, but for guaranteed p95 SLOs at spikes, Dedicated or Private with reserved capacity is typical. We'll capture concrete numbers in the bench.
[03:02] Aisha: If we go Dedicated, what granularity of reserved capacity — GPU counts, and do you have autoscale for bursts?
[03:12] Sofia: Yes, Dedicated is a reserved GPU pool. We size by tokens/sec and concurrency. Autoscale can be configured with burst capacity but there is a warm-up for extra nodes — so we recommend configuring a small burst band or pre-warming around expected traffic windows. We'll propose a sizing model after we see sample traffic.

[03:50] Rita: We are also evaluating Private VPC because our compliance team prefers customer-managed networking and KMS. Is on‑prem necessary? We're mostly fine with VPC endpoints, but if we need air‑gapped that's heavier.
[04:05] Ethan: Understood. Private VPC gives you the control and KMS/HSM integration and audit logs. On‑prem is an option but it's a larger project. For the pilot we can do a VPC-connected Private deployment if you can open peering/privatelink — otherwise Hosted may be acceptable with encryption and SOC2 but less network control.

[04:40] Samir: We need to see SOC2 report, key rotation details, and an audit log sample. Also data retention policy — do you persist inputs/outputs in Hosted?
[04:52] Sofia: Good call. For Hosted we have retention defaults but can disable retention for enterprise customers; Dedicated and Private give you full control. We'll attach our SOC2 and a sample audit log. Note: sometimes filenames or acronyms transcribe weirdly, e.g., our 'KV cache' notes might show up as 'key view cache' in exports, so apologize in advance for transcript noise.

[05:30] Ethan: For the benchmark plan we propose a 48-hour run that exercises three modes: Hosted (our standard production tier), Dedicated (reserved capacity sized to match expected qps), and a simulated Private (VPC with same instance types) — measure p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, steady-state throughput and cold-start behavior. Sofia will run this and share results.
[05:55] Aisha: For data we'll provide 5000 synthetic notes and a set of 200 critical 'edge' prompts. We want pass/fail thresholds: p95 < 300ms for the short path, p95 < 800ms for long summaries (~600 tokens), and throughput sustaining 150 qps with spikes to 200 qps with < 10% error rate.

[06:30] Sofia: Sounds reasonable. We'll instrument with tracing and show breakdowns: model compute time, network, and our routing overhead. We also include token-level cost estimates — that's helpful for your finance team.
[06:45] Marcus: Cost estimates are important. Can you show a delta between Hosted per-token and Dedicated amortized GPU cost for our expected burn rate?
[06:54] Ethan: Yes, Sofia will provide a cost model: per-token hosted vs amortized GPU cost with utilization assumptions (we'll include a 60–80% utilization band). Also quantization suggestions — smaller models on Dedicated can be cheaper while meeting quality.

[07:20] Aisha: Quality — we also need regression checks. If you recommend quantized 4-bit models, can we run a small eval set to confirm no drop in clinical accuracy?
[07:30] Sofia: Absolutely. We'll run the evaluation harness on your supplied prompts and report metrics (precision/recall-ish metrics for triage labels plus ROUGE for summarization). We'll flag any regressions.

[08:02] Rita: Network-wise, for VPC we'd want private endpoints. How long to set up Private VPC pilot? Our infra team usually needs a week to grant peering/logs.
[08:13] Ethan: If you can provision peering and shared subnets within 5 business days, we can do VPC pilot same week. On‑prem requires longer (multi‑week) and an operations checklist.

[08:40] Samir: On encryption, KMS integration is a must. Shared keys or customer keys only? Also SSO/SAML for access?
[08:50] Sofia: We support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM in Private and Dedicated; Hosted supports BYOK for enterprise if needed. SAML SSO is supported in the Console for RBAC.

[09:10] Ethan: To recap success criteria proposed by WillowCare: (1) p95 < 300ms for short notes, (2) p95 < 800ms for long summaries, (3) <10% error rate at spikes up to 200 qps, (4) no regression on the evaluation set, (5) compliance checklist satisfied (SOC2, KMS, audit logs). Are we missing anything?
[09:30] Aisha: Also include sustained throughput test for at least 1 hour at target qps to validate thermal/perf stability.
[09:39] Marcus: And a rough cost projection for 6 months at expected burn.

[10:00] Sofia: We'll add a 1-hour soak test at target qps in the bench run.
[10:05] Ethan: OK, next on timeline. We're proposing bench results in one week (Sofia), security packet and SOC2 by Ethan in three business days, and pilot kickoff the week of 1/27 if all good.
[10:18] Aisha: That timeline works but product wants to see a demo before pilot kick; can we schedule a short demo of the Console and rollout features?
[10:25] Ethan: Yes, we can do a 30-minute demo. How about next Tuesday?
[10:28] Marcus: That works.

[10:45] Sofia: Quick note on Dedicated sizing methodology — we estimate required GPU based on tokens/sec * average tokens per request * model throughput (tokens/s per GPU). Example: at 150 qps with 150 tokens avg that's 22.5k tokens/s; if a single A100 can do ~150k tokens/s for the target model with batching, you'd need the corresponding fraction of a GPU, so we choose a configuration that avoids high tail latencies. We'll show a sizing spreadsheet.
[11:10] Rita: The math helps. Also please include fallback strategy — if Dedicated capacity spikes, can requests fall back to Hosted or lower-cost variant?
[11:20] Sofia: Yes, smart routing supports fallback to compatible model variants or Hosted fallback. We'll include policy examples for canary A/B and automatic fallback rules.

[11:48] Aisha: One more thing — our legal team asks about data deletion SLA for Hosted. Do you have a documented process?
[11:56] Ethan: We do; we'll include a deletion SLA and process map in the security packet.

[12:10] Samir: Any competitors mentioned in our evaluation? We're also comparing Anthropic's endpoints and OpenAI, primarily for latency and cost. We may ask for a side-by-side latency/cost note.
[12:20] Sofia: We'll include competitor context at a high level but won't do direct benchmarking without permission.

[12:37] Marcus: Final recap and owners?
[12:40] Ethan: Sure. Action items — I'll send SOC2 and network diagram; Sofia runs the 48-hour bench and 1-hour soak across Hosted, Dedicated and VPC; Aisha sends prompt set; Marcus and Rita coordinate VPC peering; Samir reviews security docs. We'll aim to review bench results and demo next week and, if green, kick pilot week of 1/27.

[13:10] Aisha: Sounds good. Minor point — in previous transcripts some names were butchered, so apologies if that shows up.
[13:17] Ethan: No worries. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with an email summarizing next steps.

[13:30] (Meeting ends)

NOTES AND LINKS: Security packet (link to internal doc), sample benchmark spreadsheet, Console demo recording (to be scheduled).

TRANSCRIPTION NOTES: Some words transcribed imperfectly (e.g., 'KV cache' -> 'key view cache'), slight speaker overlap around 06:45-07:30.

POC Provisioning & Governance Weekly - SynapseHealth

Weekly POC sync focused on Dedicated capacity sizing and governance. Redwood reviewed autoscale windows, pre-warm options and cost guardrails; Synapse raised concerns about unpredictable surge billing and KMS integration for PHI. Agreed to run controlled bursts and share telemetry to finalize commit sizing.
Meeting header: 2027-01-12 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~52m | Attendees: Maya, Jon (Redwood) -- Priya, Marco, Lena (SynapseHealth)

[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, hope you all had a good week. Today we're going to zero in on the dedicated sizing ask and the governance around burst and pre-warm. Jon from infra will walk through the test plan.

[00:28] Jon (SE): Hi all. Quick agenda: review last week's run, propose autoscale windows, show pre-warm options (instant vs queued), then map to cost impact. I have the results slide deck here: https://redwood.example.com/poc/synapse/benchmark-deck

[00:52] Priya (Eng Mgr): Quick context — our production has spiky traffic, sometimes 10x baseline for 20-30 minutes, and if we go with hosted we need clear caps. We also have PHI concerns so KMS + audit logs are non-negotiable.

[01:15] Marco (SRE): Also we run nightly batch jobs that touch the same models, so KV cache behavior during bursts is important, we saw cache thrash in the last sim which bumped latencies.

[01:40] Jon (SE): Right, so two takeaways from last run: 1) with baseline of 4 Dedicated units and autoscale up to 12 we saw tail latencies at 95th of ~420ms for 1k concurrent users; 2) when a sudden 3x surge hit, cold start caused a 2.3x token cost bump because kernels recompiled and KV missed. Note — some of the log labels in the run had the model name spelled "redwood-dediate-v1" in telemetry, small transcription in the logs.

[02:20] Lena (Product): Are we able to pin a warm pool that survives for X minutes? Our compliance team wants determinism.

[02:37] Jon (SE): Yes, pre-warm pool with configurable TTL — options: keep-warm (minutes) or keep-warm-on-traffic (adaptive). Keep-warm adds fixed hourly cost; pre-warm-on-demand has a small per-burst ramp fee. We showed the math on slides 6-8.

[03:00] Priya (Eng Mgr): Concern is opaque surge cost. If your autoscaler spins up GPUs and we get charged per token at higher rate, how do we cap that?

[03:18] Maya (AE): Good point — we recommend committed burst units as part of the Dedicated contract. That caps per-burst rates and gives predictable invoicing; after committed burst is exhausted there's a throttled fallback and a notification policy.

[03:44] Marco (SRE): Can we set hard budget caps or a fail-open to lower-tier model to avoid runaway cost?

[03:52] Jon (SE): Yes, two mechanisms: budget guardrail (hard stop) and graceful fallback to smaller model variant. Also route-by-policy so latency-critical paths prefer pre-warm nodes.

[04:10] Priya: And KMS? We need to know if keys stay in our HSM and whether the audit logs capture per-token access.

[04:22] Maya: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and per-request audit logs. We'll share SOC2 + KMS integration docs after this call.

[04:40] Jon: For the upcoming controlled burst test — plan is: 2-hour window, step up concurrency 1x -> 3x -> 5x at 20 minute intervals, include KV cache warm and cold variants. We'll collect latency, token rate, pre-warm hit rate, OOM events.

[05:05] Marco: How will you simulate our prompt distribution? Our average prompt length is variable, around 120 tokens but long tails to 1k.

[05:19] Jon: Please send us the histogram CSV (top 100) and we'll seed the generator. If you can't share real prompts because PHI, provide anonymized token-length distribution.

[05:35] Priya: We'll anonymize and share by Friday.

[05:40] Maya: Cost calc — for a 3x sustained burst with pre-warm pool set to 30 minutes, estimated incremental monthly cost is shown on slide 9. There's also a burst add-on that gives discounted pre-warm rate.

[06:05] Lena: What's the SLA impact if we fallback to smaller model?

[06:15] Jon: Latency increases roughly 30-60ms depending on model. Quality regressions are minimal for our reranker style prompts but for critical flows we'd prefer to avoid fallback. We can add canary routing — only non-critical traffic falls back.

[06:45] Marco: Operationally, I want a single place to see token spend by route and a signal when pre-warm is consumed. Does console do token-level tracing?

[06:57] Maya: Yes — Redwood Console gives per-route token and latency breakdowns with a threshold alerting UI. We'll set up a dashboard for Synapse pilot.

[07:15] Priya: On retention and cache: if we evict KV cache after X minutes we saw cold starts in the last sim. Can we make eviction policy sticky for named tenants?

[07:30] Jon: Tenant pinning for KV is supported in Dedicated. You can set tenant-specific TTL and pin certain keys — useful for low-churn prompts.

[07:48] Priya: Great. For compliance, can we prove deletion and data residency per request?

[07:55] Maya: Audit logs + request-level metadata recorded, with optional longer retention for enterprise. We'll include retention SLAs in the Private contract.

[08:10] (short crosstalk) Marco: timestamps in logs are slightly skewed in last run (clock drift) — we'll ensure NTP sync before next test.

[08:32] Jon: On autoscale windows, recommendation is: keep a warm baseline sized to 95th of typical traffic, autoscale headroom of 2-3x for normal surges, and define an emergency burst pool for 5x spikes (pre-warmed at low cost). We'll show policy YAML after call.

[08:58] Priya: Can you show the policy examples?

[09:05] Jon: Sure. Example snippet: scalePolicy: {type: "incremental", step: 2, coolDownSeconds: 120}. Apologies if transcription mangles brackets. We'll push the real YAML to the shared folder.

[09:28] Lena: Any thoughts on multi-region? Our users are global and a regional outage is a risk.

[09:37] Maya: Multi-region routing is supported. We recommend primary in us-east-1 + failover replica in eu-west-1 for latency-sensitive endpoints. Cross-region cache warming can be expensive — better to replicate model weights and warm separate pools.

[10:05] Priya: Ok. Last week's run indicated a weird spike in tokenization time — could be tokenizer implementation mismatch.

[10:18] Jon: We'll validate tokenizer versioning in the runtime and include the exact model+tokenizer hash in telemetry. Expect that in the run logs.

[10:35] (silence)

[10:47] Maya: Recap of decisions: run controlled 2-hour burst, Redwood shares pricing variants with committed burst units and pre-warm add-on, Synapse shares traffic histogram and KMS details. We'll aim to finalize commit sizing after the run.

[11:12] Marco: One operational ask — can Redwood surface estimated bill impact in real-time so we can abort a test if cost delta exceeds X%?

[11:24] Jon: Yes, we'll enable a live estimate feed in the dashboard for the test run. It hooks into the same accounting pipeline.

[11:35] Priya: Thanks — that helps. Any blockers on Redwood side?

[11:40] Maya: None, just need the histogram and KMS provider. We'll also need a short window to run the dry run; Marco and Jon to coordinate via Slack.

[11:55] Lena: Let's schedule the engineering dry-run early next week.

[12:05] Maya: Great — we'll follow up with invite. Thanks everyone.

[12:15] (meeting ended)
Redwood to provide YAML policy examples and pricing variants
Synapse to anonymize prompt length distribution and verify KMS/HSM details
Plan a dry-run between Marco and Jon to validate NTP sync and tokenizer versions
Jon to run a 2-hour simulated 3x burst in us-east-1 and share telemetry CSV by 2027-01-14
Maya to share updated pricing sheet with committed burst units and pre-warm rates by 2027-01-13
Synapse to confirm retention window for KV cache and whether PII flows will require on-prem deployment by 2027-01-19
Schedule engineering-only dry-run for warp-start pre-warm script (Marco/Jon) in next 7 days
Jon Ruiz (SE): Create load script that simulates 80/60/30 concurrent users and attach kpis - due 2027-01-14
Maya Chen (AE): Update commitment options spreadsheet, include pre-warm and burst add-on pricing - due 2027-01-13
Priya Nair (Eng Manager): Provide sample traffic histogram and top-100 prompt length distribution - due 2027-01-15
Marco Diaz (SRE): Provide SOC2 scope questions and current KMS provider details - due 2027-01-18

Aurora Health - Embeddings & Rerank: Dimensionality, Batching & KVCache Deep Dive

Technical deep dive on embeddings dimensionality, batching strategy, KV cache relevance for reranking, and quantization tradeoffs for Aurora Health. Discussed latency SLOs (target 120ms p95 for rerank path), cost estimates across dims (128/256/512/1024), and on-prem/VPC constraints. Agreed next steps: run targeted benchmarks (Redwood), share query distributions (Aurora), and scope pilot for Dedicated/on-prem evaluation.
Vector dimension tradeoffs (128 / 256 / 512 / 1024)
Batch sizing and continuous batching impact on p95 latency
KV cache relevance for rerank vs LLM scoring
Quantization profiles (q8_0, q4, int8, GPTQ) and kernel impacts
Private deployment constraints (VPC, KMS, offline on-prem packaging)
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Dana (Aurora): Hey, Dana here. Samir and Priya on my side.
[00:08] Samir: Samir present.
[00:10] Priya: Priya — SRE/security.
[00:12] Maya: Great — Liam from Redwood will lead perf. Liam?
[00:17] Liam (Redwood SE): Yeah hi all, thanks. Goal for today: walk through embeddings/rerank performance tradeoffs — dims, batch sizes, kv cache question, and quantization effects.
[00:30] Dana: Topline — we want p95 under ~120ms for rerank on clinical search use cases. Throughput is bursty but median qps is low ~15 qps, tail matters. Also must meet data residency for PHI.
[00:48] Liam: Okay got it. Quick clarifying Qs: is rerank a two-stage pipeline (ANN candidate retrieval followed by embed scoring) or are you calling a cross-encoder LLM for scoring?
[00:58] Samir: Two-stage. We do ANN (Milvus today) -> embed similarity rerank using cos-sim on GPU. But we're considering switching to a denser/or larger-dim embed for better recall.
[01:12] Liam: Good. So the key knobs: vector dim (d), embedding model latency/cost, batch size at embed generation and at rerank scoring (matrix ops), and whether we quantize vectors on disk/compute.
[01:28] Ravi (Redwood): Also note continuous batching in our runtime can aggregate small requests to keep GPU utilization and unit cost down, but that affects tail latency. We'll discuss balancing micro-batches vs SLOs.
[01:40] Dana: Walk us through a concrete example — what if we move from 256 -> 512 dims?
[01:44] Liam: Rough numbers: doubling dims roughly doubles embedding memory (and disk if stored dense) and increases per-cosine compute proportional to d. On a single rerank call for k=50 candidates, compute ~ O(k*d) vec-ops. So 256->512 roughly doubles CPU/GPU flops for the scoring step and increases transfer costs. In practice we measured p95 impact of ~1.6x for scoring stage due to better kernel utilization.
[02:10] Samir: Do you have cost numbers?
[02:12] Liam: Short answer: token-generation cost isn't relevant here unless you're generating embeddings from a decoder model. For embed inference: per-request runtime cost for 256 dims on a T4-class GPU is X (we shared a spreadsheet), for 512 it's ~1.9x. I'll send the spreadsheet.
[02:28] Maya: (interrupting) we'll attach that benchmark sheet after the call. Note these are ballpark — exact depends on batching and quantization.
[02:35] Priya: On kv cache — I thought kv cache helps generative contexts. Do you use it for rerank?
[02:42] Liam: Good callout. KV cache is mainly for autoregressive generation. For pure embeddings and cos-sim rerank, KV cache isn't used. However, if you add a small LLM scoring pass (e.g., prompt-based re-scoring, or a cross-encoder) the KV cache matters for repeated contexts and can lower token latency. For rerank stage that is vector-only, focus on matrix throughput and memory bandwidth.
[03:05] Dana: We're exploring a hybrid: ANN to retrieve 200 candidates -> embed re-score to top 50 -> optional LLM-based final check for top 5. So yeah both types matter.
[03:18] Liam: Then we should split pipeline SLOs: embedding generation (if doing on-the-fly for new docs), rerank scoring, and LLM final check. Each has different latency/cost profile.
[03:27] Samir: For embed storage — we store vectors in Milvus and use float32 today. Thoughts on storing quantized vectors (int8 or PQ)?
[03:34] Liam: Quantized on-disk is fine — PQ or int8 reduces storage and I/O; search accuracy tradeoff depends on quantization scheme. For compute-time quantization (loading into GPU as q4/8) you save memory and sometimes increase throughput but must watch accuracy. We recommend benchmarking with your recall set.
[03:48] Dana: Any recommended default dims for clinical search? 256 vs 512?
[03:53] Liam: Many customers start at 256 for a good cost/recall sweet spot; 512 helps recall but cost rises. For sensitive domains where recall is critical, 512 can be justified. 1024 is usually overkill unless doing large multi-modal or very nuanced semantics.
[04:10] Maya: I'll note that for Aurora's dataset size (~2M docs) storage and retrieval cost is material; we can run cost sims for 256 vs 512.
[04:20] Samir: Batching — what's a good batch size in production? We can't introduce per-request tails.
[04:25] Liam: Two things: batch used at embed generation (if you generate embeddings for queries in realtime) and batch in scoring (matrix multiply across k candidates). For query-time embeddings of single queries, batching with continuous batching can group requests to batch sizes 8-32 without much extra latency if you accept a 10-40ms queuing delay. For scoring stage, scoring k=50 is effectively a small matrix multiply; optimal single-op batch sizes vary by GPU and kernel. We often see best throughput at microbatch sizes 16-64 depending on d.
[04:58] Ravi: Example: with d=256 and batch=32, p95 was 85ms on our infra for the scoring step; reduce batch to 8 -> p95 60ms but cost per query rises due to lower GPU utilization.
[05:12] Priya: How does quantization affect tail latency?
[05:15] Liam: Quantization often improves memory footprint and can reduce kernel runtime, lowering p99 in some cases. But some library kernels for q4 are less mature and you can see jitter. We advise running three profiles: float32 baseline, int8/PQ on-disk + float compute, and q4 runtime. Liam: We'll provide these runs.
[05:36] Samir: Any pitfalls moving to on-prem Dedicated? We care about KMS, audit logs, and network egress.
[05:41] Maya: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM, audit log exports, and can run behind VPC with no external egress if required. On-prem package is more involved — we do an appliance-style install and help with certs.
[05:55] Priya: We need SOC2 artifacts and details about encryption-at-rest for vectors. Also want to know how RBAC works.
[06:02] Maya: We'll share the security pack in Confluence and schedule a follow-up security-only session.
[06:07] Dana: For a pilot, what's a minimal test to validate latency and recall?
[06:11] Liam: Minimal pilot: 1) supply 100k sample docs & 24h query traces; 2) Redwood runs embeddings for 3 dims (128/256/512) with quant profiles and returns recall metrics and p95 latencies; 3) run a small Dedicated instance or hosted stress test simulating your burst pattern. That should give clear cost/latency tradeoffs.
[06:31] Samir: Sounds good. Do you have real numbers for p95 at various dims?
[06:34] Liam: From internal tests on A30-class GPU: embedding generation latencies per query (single) — d128 ~18ms, d256 ~28ms, d512 ~48ms. Rerank scoring for k=50: d128 ~30ms, d256 ~55ms, d512 ~92ms (p95-ish). These vary by batch strategy.
[06:58] Samir: If we allow 20ms queueing for batching could we hit p95 120ms budget for rerank + final LLM?
[07:05] Liam: Possibly. Example path: ANN retrieval 30ms, embed rerank 55ms, small LLM final 20-30ms with q8 quantization — totals in the 120-140ms window. With tuning and dedicated capacity, you can compress that.
[07:20] Dana: Are there infra differences between hosted vs dedicated that materially change p95?
[07:24] Ravi: Hosted has multitenant queuing and smart routing; Dedicated gives you pinned GPUs with less noisy neighbors and deterministic scheduling — tail tends to be lower on Dedicated. For strict SLOs we recommend Dedicated or Private.
[07:38] Priya: License and support questions — what's included in Private on-prem?
[07:41] Maya: Platform software, runtime, support tier per contract. For on-prem we do an engagement to set up monitoring and patches.
[07:48] Samir: A few random notes — does Redwood do automatic prefix/KV caching for repeated queries?
[07:53] Liam: We do prefix caching for short-term repetition (helps generative workloads). For embedding rerank the primary optimizations are vector caching at the ANN/disk level and warm-hot vector caches (in-memory) to avoid cold loads.
[08:06] Dana: We'll need to see how our Milvus setup could be replaced or integrated.
[08:09] Liam: We have connectors and have done Milvus customers; it's usually an index migration or proxy layer.
[08:15] Priya: On encryption: if vectors stored in customer infra, we want envelope encryption and audit logging.
[08:21] Maya: Noted — will include KMS/HSM options doc.
[08:24] Dana: OK recap and next steps before we wrap.
[08:27] Maya: Recap: Redwood to run targeted benchmarks for d=128/256/512 with quant profiles, attach perf logs and cost sim; Aurora shares query histograms and sample docs; security follow-up for on-prem compliance.
[08:40] Samir: Thanks — we'll prioritize sending the traces.
[08:43] Priya: I'll compile SOC2/ISO checklist we need.
[08:46] Maya: Great. I'll send calendar for pilot kickoff and include the benchmark spreadsheet.
[08:50] Dana: Great, thanks everyone.
[08:52] Maya: Thanks, bye.

Redwood: send benchmark spreadsheet + livebench run instructions (Maya)
Aurora: share typical query distribution and SLA combos (Samir)
Schedule on-prem/priv pilot kickoff (calendar invite from Maya)
Redwood SE to provide q4/q8 quantization whitepaper and kernel notes (Liam)
Maya Chen: email cost/latency spreadsheet and sample request trace (2025-05-22)
Liam O'Connor: run 3 model + quantization profiles and attach perf logs (2025-05-26)
Samir Khan: export 24h production query histogram and sample doc sizes (2025-05-23)
Priya Iyer: list compliance artifacts needed for on-prem (SOC2/ISO scope) (2025-05-27)
Benchmark spreadsheet: (sent post-call) — placeholder link in notes
Quantization whitepaper (q4/q8/GPTQ) — will attach
Action: pilot kickoff calendar invite

Heron Data - renewal / capacity & failover playbook

Quarterly renewal check-in focused on capacity uplift for peak traffic, adding EU private nodes, and a failover / fallback playbook. Customer asked for SSO/KMS details, a short benchmark plan for latency vs cost, and an updated SOW. Agreed next steps: pricing sheet, security pack, and a 2-hour onprem pilot planning session.
capacity uplift and burst planning
EU private / on-prem pathway
failover and cross-region fallback
security: SOC2/KMS/SSO/RBAC
benchmarking latency vs cost
contract extension terms
Redwood: Send refreshed pricing sheet with dedicated vs hosted cost delta by 2025-05-12
Redwood: Share SOC2 / ISO docs and KMS/HSM integration notes by 2025-05-09
Heron: Confirm list of 3 most critical endpoints for latency benchmarks by 2025-05-10
Schedule 2-hour onprem pilot planning workshop w/ infra + security (target week of 5/19)
Rachel Kim (AE): Update pricing + include reserved capacity ramp options (due 2025-05-12)
Tom Serrano (SE): Draft pilot benchmark plan and latency vs cost spreadsheet (due 2025-05-09)
Ivy Chen (CSM): Coordinate onprem planning session invites and prep checklist (due 2025-05-14)
Maya Patel (Heron): Provide the three sample endpoints and traffic pattern CSV (due 2025-05-10)
Priya Shah (Heron Security): Send current SSO/OAuth config and KMS provider details (due 2025-05-09)
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-07
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Rachel Kim (Redwood AE), Tom Serrano (Redwood SE), Ivy Chen (Redwood CSM), Maya Patel (Heron Head of Infrastructure), Luca Romano (Heron Platform), Priya Shah (Heron Security), Jonas (Heron SRE)

[00:00] Rachel Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:04] Maya Patel: Hi — Maya here.
[00:06] Luca Romano: Luca.
[00:07] Priya Shah: Priya.
[00:08] Jonas: Jonas.
[00:09] Rachel Kim: Great, Rachel here, Tom and Ivy from Redwood as well. We're here for the renewal and capacity check-in, and to talk through the EU private pathway and failover playbook.
[00:18] Tom Serrano: Hi team. I put the agenda in the calendar note — ramp options, onprem pilot plan, security questions, and a short benchmarking approach.
[00:25] Maya Patel: Sounds good. Our CDP traffic has been spiking — we've seen a 3x daytime burst the last two weeks and last week we had a sustained peak that hit our SLA cushions. We're evaluating either a capacity bump or routing some EU traffic to a private cluster.
[00:40] Luca Romano: Also curious about the failover behavior. We had a region outage in March and the fallback increased latency a lot. Does Redwood have an automated fallback to a lower-latency hosted variant without dropping connections?
[00:52] Tom Serrano: We do have smart routing policies — you can set policies by region, latency threshold, and cost band. When you mark a model variant as fallback, requests will be routed to a compatible variant. There's a short KV-cache cold start hit for new sessions if the KV cache isn't warmed, which adds some tokens latency, but you can mitigate with prefix caching.
[01:12] Maya Patel: Right, the KV cache cold-start is our worry because our customers are latency-sensitive. How big is that hit typically?
[01:19] Tom Serrano: Depends on session length and how warm your cache is. With our Continuous Batching + prefix caching set, we've measured 20-80ms extra for typical gen calls; for large LLM sessions it could be 200-400ms if the KV cache is fully empty. We recommended proactive warming and sticky routing for session-affine workloads.
[01:40] Jonas: That aligns with what we saw in our logs. Is sticky routing supported for Private deployment?
[01:44] Tom Serrano: Yes, Private supports session-affinity. For onprem/VPC you can pin model versions and maintain KV caches per node. The main ops overhead is keeping your warmers running during low traffic windows.
[01:56] Priya Shah: Security first — we need details on key management. Do you support external KMS/HSM and customer-managed keys? Also SOC2 and audit log retention?
[02:06] Rachel Kim: Yes — Private supports customer KMS integration (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault, HSM gateways). We also have audit logs that can be exported to your SIEM. I'll add SOC2 and ISO docs to the packet.
[02:16] Priya Shah: Great. Also need SSO/SAML config and RBAC for operator roles.
[02:20] Ivy Chen: We typically map Redwood roles to your IdP via SAML and support SCIM provisioning. We'll include a sample RBAC mapping and an example SAML metadata file.
[02:29] Maya Patel: For the renewal terms — we have an annual renewal coming up in June. If we commit to a six-month ramp of reserved capacity, what pricing delta are we looking at vs hosted burst?
[02:40] Rachel Kim: Roughly speaking, reserved committed capacity saves ~25-35% on per-token cost compared to pure hosted for steady-state volume. There's also tiered discounts if you commit to multi-region reserved nodes. We'll send a refreshed pricing sheet showing dedicated reserved vs burst usage.
[02:54] Luca Romano: Can you show an example cost for our baseline: 2.5 billion tokens/month steady with 4x peak spikes to 10B tokens/day in bursts?
[03:03] Rachel Kim: We'll run that in a spreadsheet — Tom, can you own the model of cost/latency tradeoffs and add quantization/throughput recommendations?
[03:10] Tom Serrano: Yep, I'll put together latency profiles: hosted low-latency variant, dedicated with 8-bit quant, and private onprem with 4-bit quant options and expected throughput. Include sequence length assumptions.
[03:21] Maya Patel: For EU onprem, timeline is tight. We need EU residency by July for a new product. Is a Private VPC deployment feasible in that window?
[03:29] Tom Serrano: It's feasible but aggressive. Typical timeline for EU private node setup: 4-6 weeks for infra and network prep, plus 1-2 weeks for model onboarding and testing. So to hit July we'd want to kick off infra prep mid-May. There are options for an interim hybrid: provision dedicated EU capacity in our hosted fleet while we stand up your private cluster.
[03:49] Maya Patel: Hybrid sounds promising. What about latency for EU users if we route to hosted EU while private is warming?
[03:55] Tom Serrano: Hosted EU region will have comparable latency to a private EU node but the difference is in data residency and audit control. Latency-wise, hosted EU is fine as a short-term fallback.
[04:05] Priya Shah: For compliance we need proof of data flow boundaries and the ability to purge data. How long do you keep logs and input data in hosted vs private?
[04:14] Rachel Kim: By default, hosted retains logs for 90 days; we can configure retention and purge policies for enterprise plans. Private gives you full control and no retained request payloads unless you enable them for debugging. We'll surface exact retention options in the security pack.
[04:29] Maya Patel: Okay. Let's talk failover playbook specifics — we want an automatic failover to a lower-cost variant only if latency stays below a threshold; otherwise circuit-break.
[04:40] Tom Serrano: That's doable. You can set a policy: if p95 > X ms for > Y seconds route 30% traffic to fallback model, increase over 60s. If latency continues to degrade, failover entirely and trigger an A/B test for output quality. Also automatic rollback if quality regressions exceed a threshold.
[04:59] Luca Romano: Sounds good. We'll need a test harness for those policies — can Redwood simulate region outage and run chaos tests?
[05:06] Tom Serrano: We have a staging tool that replays traffic and simulates latency; for Private we can run a chaos test plan together. We'll give a playbook with steps and expected metrics to watch.
[05:17] Jonas: On the bench side, we want to measure latency distribution at 50ms granularity and token cost. Can you provide client-side instrumentation examples?
[05:24] Tom Serrano: Yes, we instrument token-level timings in SDKs and provide token + cost breakdown per request. We'll share example dashboards and a Prometheus exporter for onprem.
[05:33] Maya Patel: One other ask: we want to quantize some models to 8-bit to lower cost. What's your recommendation?
[05:39] Tom Serrano: 8-bit is a good starting point for many workloads. For the hallucination-sensitive flows we recommend evaluating quality regressions with A/B tests. We can recommend quantization profiles per-model in Redwood Optimize.
[05:53] Rachel Kim: Quick check — renewal paperwork: are you looking to extend current contract or add an amendment for the next quarter?
[05:58] Maya Patel: Probably amend for July private pilot and then extend the annual contract in August. We need flexible accrual for the pilot.
[06:05] Rachel Kim: We can draft an amendment with a short pilot addendum and a path to a full renewal. We'll include options for reserved ramp.
[06:12] [10-minute silence covering deeper technical questions and jitter adjustments — transcript jumps ahead] 
[16:13] Tom Serrano: Back to benchmarking specifics — I'm thinking of a three-step plan: 1) baseline latency & token cost on current hosted for your endpoints, 2) dedicated reserved run with batching and caching enabled to show cost delta, 3) private onprem pilot with KV cache warmers and 24-hour soak. Each step will include synthetic load and replay traffic.
[16:35] Luca Romano: For the soak, do you recommend a rolling warm-up to avoid cold-start storms?
[16:40] Tom Serrano: Yes, warmers + staggered prefetch. Also set request throttles and circuit breakers to avoid overwhelming the cold cache.
[16:48] Maya Patel: For the onprem network topology — do you need direct peering or just VPC endpoints?
[16:54] Tom Serrano: VPC endpoints are sufficient for most customers; direct peering helps in some low-latency use cases. We'll capture network diagrams in the runbook.
[17:02] Priya Shah: Any encryption-in-transit specifics? TLS mutual auth?
[17:06] Ivy Chen: We support mTLS for Private clusters and always-encrypted TLS for hosted. mTLS can be enforced per-route with client certs.
[17:13] Jonas: Storage for logs — do you offer S3-compatible export for audit logs?
[17:17] Rachel Kim: Yes, logs can be exported to S3 or pushed into your SIEM. We can also set up a dedicated logging bucket with lifecycle policies.
[17:24] Maya Patel: Pricing question again — if we take a six-month ramp to a committed tier starting in July, is there a minimum commit?
[17:31] Rachel Kim: Minimums vary by region; typical minimum is 3 reserved nodes for EU private, but we can model smaller commitments depending on expected throughput. We'll outline scenarios in the pricing sheet.
[17:41] Luca Romano: For the pilot, who from Redwood will be hands-on?
[17:45] Rachel Kim: Tom will lead the SE work, Ivy will coordinate ops and CS, and I'll handle contract/pricing.
[17:51] Tom Serrano: We'll also bring an infra specialist for network/hardening during the pilot.
[17:56] Maya Patel: Good. On the SLA side, what uptime do you guarantee for Private versus Dedicated?
[18:02] Rachel Kim: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; Private SLAs are negotiated in the enterprise package and depend on your infra operating window. Typical targets are 99.9% for Dedicated and we can discuss custom SLAs for Private.
[18:14] Priya Shah: We need auditability — who can access logs, operator audit trails?
[18:18] Ivy Chen: We provide token-level access logs, operator activity logs, and RBAC. We can map to your least-privilege roles and provide an audit exporter.
[18:27] [brief crosstalk]
[18:30] Rachel Kim: Ok let's capture decisions so far: 1) Heron wants a hybrid approach for July to meet residency while private is provisioned, 2) run a 3-step benchmark plan, 3) pilot scheduling, 4) Redwood to provide security pack + pricing.
[18:45] Maya Patel: Yes that's correct. Also want a documented failover playbook with specific thresholds.
[18:49] Tom Serrano: We'll draft a playbook with threshold examples and rollback criteria.
[18:54] Luca Romano: One more question — do you support canary rollouts on model changes? We need to avoid regressions in production.
[18:59] Tom Serrano: Yes, Canary rollouts and A/B testing are supported. You can do a percentage rollout and monitor quality regressions. We can integrate with your eval framework.
[19:08] Jonas: For the onprem pilot, will you require root-level access or just a service account?
[19:12] Tom Serrano: Service account and admin privileges for the installer are typically enough; we don't require persistent root. Installer runs as root initially, but runtime uses lower privilege.
[19:22] Priya Shah: Anything else on security before we wrap?
[19:25] Maya Patel: I want to confirm data purge API — is there a manual and programmatic purge?
[19:29] Rachel Kim: Yes, both. We'll add API docs.
[19:31] [meeting moves into scheduling logistics] 
[20:05] Ivy Chen: For scheduling, does the week of May 19 work for a 2-hour planning session?
[20:09] Maya Patel: Yes, that should work. We'll confirm by Friday.
[20:12] Rachel Kim: Great. We'll send invites pending Maya's confirmation.
[20:15] [wrap-up recap]
[20:20] Rachel Kim: Quick recap: Redwood action items — pricing sheet (Rachel), security pack (Rachel + Ivy), benchmark plan (Tom). Heron action items — endpoints list (Maya), SSO/KMS details (Priya). We'll aim to reconvene after the pilot planning session.
[20:35] Maya Patel: Thanks all. Appreciate the clarity.
[20:38] Luca Romano: Thanks.
[20:39] Tom Serrano: Thanks everyone.
[20:40] Rachel Kim: Bye.

[End of meeting — total recorded 58:00]

document.content:
BlueFjord Therapeutics — reserved node surge evaluation

Meeting header: 2026-09-07 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~52m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Head of ML, BlueFjord), Owen Park (Platform Eng), Dr. Lena Moreno (CTO)

Summary:
- Intro + quick qualification of burst patterns and isolation needs.
- Discussed dedicated (reserved) node options, warm-pool/burst credits, and VPC/private control plane tradeoffs.
- Agreed pilot: 2 reserved nodes + warm pool for 2 weeks, Redwood to run benchmark template.
- Action items: send security docs, pilot template, traffic trace.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, really appreciate it. quick round robin — Maya here on Redwood, I'm the AE. Diego's our solutions engineer.
[00:15] Diego: Hi all — Diego Ramos, SE. I typically focus on runtime behavior, warm pools, prewarm timing and kernel selection stuff, so happy to dig in.
[00:25] Priya: Hey, Priya Singh — BlueFjord, head of ML. We run a few large LLM features for our drug discovery UI and internal batch scoring.
[00:33] Owen: Owen Park, platform. I'll be the one running infra, hooking up VPCs, KMS, that sort of thing.
[00:40] Dr. Lena: Lena Moreno, CTO. I'm mainly here to understand failure modes and compliance boundaries.

[01:05] Maya: Cool. We wanted to start with a quick overview of what your current shape is, and then map to reserved GPUs. Priya, can you say peak QPS and typical payloads?
[01:20] Priya: Sure — typical inference is two buckets: interactive UI chat at low token lengths, say 60–150 tokens, latency target sub 300ms p95; then batch scoring where we send larger sequences, sometimes up to 2k tokens, but that's async. Peak concurrent interactive sessions right now hit about 220 qps during med spikes, but sustained is more like 40–60. We saw one incident where a partner demo spiked to 900 qps for about 7 minutes — that was painful.
[02:05] Diego: Okay that's helpful. 900 for 7 minutes suggests burst tolerance is important. Do you want guaranteed isolation? e.g., dedicated reserved nodes for absolute tenant isolation, or is logical tenant fencing (soft isolation) acceptable?
[02:25] Priya: We need hard isolation for our regulated workloads — can't share customer data with other tenants. So dedicated reserved GPUs or an on-prem/private deployment are on the table.
[02:38] Dr. Lena: And from a compliance POV we need audit logs, KMS integration, and we have a SOC2 report requirement. Also data residency — most of our EU trials must keep data in EU region.
[02:55] Maya: All of that is doable on Redwood Dedicated and Private. We have a Dedicated offering with reserved GPU pools and VPC peering for private traffic. We can also do a private control plane for on-prem. Diego, maybe you can explain warm-pools and burst credits?
[03:15] Diego: Yeah, quick overview: we offer reserved nodes: these are physical or logically dedicated capacity and you get a steady baseline throughput. On top of that, we have a warm-pool mechanism (we call it "hotpool" internally) that keeps a small number of instances pre-warmed with the model KV caches to reduce cold-start latencies. Burst credits are a separate bucket that lets you exceed baseline for short windows — we predefine a burst budget in tokens/minute or GPU-seconds. The warm pool addresses the latency hit when scaling up; the credits address brief throughput overshoots.
[04:00] Owen: How do prewarms handle KV cache for big models? Our models are heavy — 70B and some loRA finetunes — the KV cache warm time can be minutes if cold.
[04:15] Diego: Right — for large context and 70B, warm times are non‑trivial. With hotpool we keep the KV cache loaded in GPU memory for the specific model variants you want. There is also a technique where we keep prefix caches for the most frequent prompts to shave off first-token latency. But it's memory-heavy. For some customers we recommend a small dedicated warm pool sized to hold the most common model variants.
[04:45] Priya: That sounds promising. In the demo we ran with MegaCloud AI their warm pool still had a 400–500ms tail, which frustrated the front-end product team. Is your p95 number usually lower?
[05:00] Diego: It depends on the model and GPU type. For L4 or A10-like class we generally see sub-200ms p95 for small contexts, and for 70B on H100-class, with hotpool primed, you can be around 250–350ms p95. We'll need to benchmark your exact model + prompt shapes.
[05:25] Priya: What's the minimum reserve? We don't want to overcommit financially.
[05:30] Maya: Our reserved units are offered in blocks, you can reserve 1, 2, 4 GPU node blocks depending on instance type. For initial pilots we often recommend 2 nodes sized at about 2x expected load to give headroom and to validate warm-pool effectiveness. That pairs with on-demand burst credits.
[05:50] Owen: For us, the finance team is sensitive to sustained monthly charges. How are burst credits billed? Is it a separate overage at a higher rate?
[06:05] Maya: Burst credits are charged at a premium over the reserved rate — think of them as short-duration metered usage. We can model estimates once we have your traffic profile. For the pilot we can provide capped burst allowances so costs are bounded.
[06:25] Dr. Lena: We also need to understand failure modes. If a reserved node fails, what's the fallback path? What if capacity is exhausted across a region?
[06:40] Diego: Good Q. For Dedicated, we have automatic failover policies: requests are routed to other reserved capacity in the same pool if available, or to preconfigured fallback model variants (smaller quantized model) if you opt in. We also support cross-region fallback but that's a latency tradeoff. We can set a safe degrade path — e.g., fallback to a 8-bit quantized 13B variant during shortage.
[07:10] Priya: Would fallback spill logs or payloads out of region that would violate residency?
[07:20] Owen: That's our fear.
[07:22] Diego: If you enable cross-region fallback, yes it would cross boundaries. For strict residency, we'd lock fallbacks to the same region or to Private (on-prem) so that it never leaves the EU.
[07:35] Priya: Good. On encryption — we use customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). Can we integrate with our KMS?
[07:45] Maya: Yes, Redwood Dedicated and Private both support CMK integrations and HSM-backed keys for encryption at rest. We'll share the KMS integration guide in the security packet.
[07:58] Priya: Great.

[09:00] Owen: About traffic shaping — do you have preemption or eviction policies if warm pool fills up? We saw preemption on another vendor where long-running batch jobs got killed when interactive spiky traffic showed up.
[09:15] Diego: We provide tenant fencing and priority queues. You can mark interactive traffic as high priority and batch as low — Redwood runtime will pause or throttle low-priority batch errands rather than evict the reserved node owner, depending on policy. But if you're in a shared Dedicated cluster with multiple tenants on the physical node, hard isolation avoids that entirely.
[09:40] Priya: So if we choose reserved nodes, would we still have noisy neighbor issues?
[09:48] Diego: Not if you choose dedicated physical nodes (we offer single-tenant reserved nodes). If you pick shared reserved pools, then there's logical isolation; noisy neighbors are less likely but possible. Single-tenant reserved nodes cost more but they guarantee isolation.

[11:00] Maya: Let's talk numbers briefly — what's an acceptable p95 latency vs cost tradeoff for you?
[11:10] Priya: We want sub-300ms p95 for interactive, ideally 200ms. If we have to sacrifice some cost, fine, but under 400ms is hard to accept.
[11:22] Diego: For 70B that's ambitious but doable on H100-like hardware with hotpool. We'll model with your traffic to see exact GPU counts.

[12:00] Dr. Lena: We also need audit logs with token-level redaction and long retention for 12 months. Is that supported?
[12:12] Maya: Yes, we can provide audit logs and token-level metadata. For sensitive data we recommend redaction at the ingestion layer and storing only hashed references, but we can meet 12-month retention as an add-on.

[13:30] Priya: On private deployment — if we go private control plane in our VPC, what's the ops burden? Do you manage the runtime or we do?
[13:45] Maya: With Private deployments we offer a managed runtime option where Redwood operates the serving layer inside your VPC with access controls, or a self-hosted distribution where your team operates it and we provide support. Managed private is more common for customers wanting minimal ops friction.
[14:05] Owen: If managed, what's the network pattern? VPC peering or private link?
[14:12] Diego: We typically do VPC peering or AWS PrivateLink depending on the cloud. For on-prem we can expose a secure tunnel to the control plane or operate with a customer-managed control plane. We'll include both patterns in the architecture doc.

[15:00] Priya: For the pilot you mentioned — what's the instrumentation we should send? Are there standard samples you need?
[15:10] Diego: We'll send a benchmark template: request/response payloads, concurrency profile, and a 72-hour trace would be ideal. We'll also include prompts and model checkpoints info. That lets us simulate both interactive and batch flows.
[15:28] Maya: To add — we'll cap burst credits during the pilot and provide a cost estimate so finance is comfortable.

[17:00] Priya: A question on SSO — we use Azure AD SAML. Can we do SAML SSO for console access and RBAC?
[17:10] Maya: Yep, SAML/SSO and SCIM provisioning for user management are supported. We'll include a sample SAML metadata in the pack.

[18:30] Owen: On the model side — we run open weights with custom finetunes. Do you support customer-supplied model artifacts and LoRA layers?
[18:45] Diego: We do; Redwood Dedicated can load your model artifacts. We have a verification step for binary compatibility and will suggest quantization profiles if you want to reduce footprint. Note: some quantization paths can change output fidelity; we'll run evals against your golden prompt set.

[20:10] Priya: About quantization — we need to preserve certain medical entity detection fidelity. Are there guarantees?
[20:22] Diego: We can't promise identical outputs after aggressive quantization, but our Optimize team runs quality monitoring and regression alerts for prompt sets. For mission-critical detectors we usually keep full precision or conservative quantization.

[22:00] Priya: Can you walk through a failure scenario — e.g., region outage in EU -- what happens to requests?
[22:12] Diego: If it's a region-level outage and you haven't set up cross-region fallback, requests will fail. If you have cross-region fallback enabled, replication and routing will shift but you'll see higher latency. For strict residency, we recommend multi-AZ within region but not cross-region fallback.

[24:00] Dr. Lena: Does Redwood provide traceability for model versions and rollout history? We need to tie output changes to a model rollout for audits.
[24:12] Maya: Yes, rollout history, model versions, and per-route tracing are in the Console. We also support tagging rollouts with change notes for audit trails.

[26:00] Owen: What's the onboarding timeline for a Private managed instance? Weeks or months?
[26:10] Maya: Typically 4–8 weeks depending on compliance and network approvals. For Dedicated reserved nodes it's faster — often 2–3 weeks to provision reserved nodes and set up warm pool configs. Pilot timelines are usually shorter — we like to get a pilot running in 10 business days.

[28:00] Priya: On cost forecasting — will you help model cost per 1M tokens for our particular mix of interactive vs batch?
[28:12] Diego: Yes, once we have your trace we'll run the pilot sim and provide a per-token and per-request breakdown (including warm pool amortization). That's part of the pilot deliverable.

[30:00] Priya: Any security gotchas we should be aware of when we supply traffic traces?
[30:08] Maya: Please scrub PII before sharing, or we can set up a secure transfer and do the scrub on your behalf under an NDA. We'll coordinate offline on the preferred method.

[31:30] Owen: A technical nit — how do you handle KV cache invalidation for model updates? We occasionally roll new weights mid-day.
[31:40] Diego: Cache invalidation can be staged — you can do canary rollouts where we warm a fraction of pool with new weights, then switch traffic. We support automated rollout policies to minimize cold starts.

[33:00] Priya: What's your SLO for warm pool availability?
[33:08] Diego: For Dedicated customers with warm pool we commit to hotpool warm coverage of 95% during expected windows as part of our operational runbook; specifics are contractable.

[35:00] Dr. Lena: For eventual production, we'll need an SLA with uptime and latency targets. Are those negotiable?
[35:10] Maya: SLAs are part of the Dedicated enterprise contract. We can discuss latency SLOs tied to node sizing and instrumentation.

[37:00] Priya: Any limitations on model size for Private on-prem?
[37:10] Diego: On-prem hardware will dictate it — Redwood runtime itself supports large models up to multi-100B with model sharding, but you'll want the appropriate GPU memory and NVLink topology. We'll provide a sizing guide.

[39:00] Owen: We also have a legal checklist — data processing agreement, subprocessing, liability caps. Can you share a redline-friendly contract?
[39:12] Maya: Yes, we'll share a standard ELA and a redline-enabled contract and involve legal as needed.

[41:00] Priya: I'm worried about token-level logging — do you ever store full prompts in cleartext in logs?
[41:10] Diego: By default we store metadata and optionally the prompt, but for regulated customers we recommend prompt redaction or hashing. We can configure logs to never persist raw prompts.

[43:00] Maya: Ok, circling back — agreed immediate deliverables: security packet + SAML doc, pricing for 2-node reserved pilot with capped bursts, and the pilot benchmark template. We'll also need the 72-hour trace from Priya.

[43:25] Priya: Sounds good. One more question — latency SLO testing: will you run against our EU region?
[43:35] Diego: Yes, we'll provision pilot nodes in your EU region for realistic latencies.

[45:00] Owen: For the pilot run, do you expect us to provide load generation or will Redwood simulate traffic?
[45:10] Diego: Either works. Usually teams provide a representative trace and we replay it; we can also provide load agents if you prefer.

[47:00] Priya: Can we get a quick estimate now for 2 H100-equivalent nodes with hotpool? Even rough.
[47:10] Maya: Very rough — for reserved H100-equivalent nodes with hotpool and pilot burst caps, expect in the ballpark of X — we'll replace X with detailed pricing in the follow-up. (laughter) We'll send a concrete quote.

[49:00] Dr. Lena: Do you have references in biotech? It helps with our procurement.
[49:10] Maya: Yes — we'll include anonymized references and a short case study for a regulated customer in the pack.

[50:00] Priya: Ok that's it from me, thanks.
[50:05] Maya: Great — recap next steps: Maya sends security packet and pricing; Diego sends pilot template; Priya shares traffic trace. Schedule pilot kickoff next week.
[50:20] Owen: I'll coordinate calendar invites.
[50:30] Dr. Lena: Thanks everyone.
[51:00] Maya: Thanks all — we'll follow up in email.

End of transcript.
