POC pivot readout & routing triage - Nightingale Labs weekly sync

Weekly POC readout comparing Redwood inference results to incumbent baseline. Key wins on p95 latency and tail behavior; throughput comparable after batching improvements. Discussed routing/fallbacks, quantization artifacts on long-context prompts, and next steps to run a 99th-percentile load test and share raw logs and benchmark CSV.
latency/throughput comparison vs baseline provider
routing and fallback policy adjustments
quantization artifacts and knob tuning
dedicated slot request and pilot timeline
Jordan Miles: Send raw benchmark CSV, consolidated latency histograms, and comparison sheet (due 2026-06-05)
Priya Desai: Prepare a short checklist for routing fallback configuration and sample policies (due 2026-06-06)
Maya Singh: Share sample traffic profile and top-10 prompt set used in production (due 2026-06-06)
Dr. Aaron Kline: Confirm success criteria for 99th percentile latency and max acceptable cost per req (due 2026-06-09)
Schedule 2-hour lab window for 99th-percentile load run (proposed dates 2026-06-08 or 2026-06-10)
Redwood to provision a temporary dedicated slot for spike testing during lab run
Customer to provide representative prompt set and traffic mix by 2026-06-06
Follow-up sync to review lab run results and make routing/quantization changes (target 2026-06-11)
Meeting header
Date: 2026-06-03 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Miles, Priya Desai (Redwood); Dr. Aaron Kline, Maya Singh, Liam O'Connor (Nightingale Labs)

Summary: Quick readout on POC benchmark comparing Redwood runtime to incumbent baseline. We go through p50/p95/p99, talk about throughput with batching, routing fallbacks, and a strange quantization artifact on long clinical notes. Action items and lab scheduling at end.

[00:00] Jordan Miles: Hey everyone, thanks for joining on a Wednesday afternoon. Quick sanity check — audio ok for folks?
[00:05] Maya Singh: Yep can hear you, loud and clear.
[00:08] Jordan Miles: Great. I'll kick us off with a short agenda: readout of the latest bench numbers, discuss routing/fallback changes we proposed, dig into quantization artifacts Dr. Kline mentioned, and align on next steps. Priya will cover the more technical bits.
[00:22] Priya Desai: Hi all. I pulled the run from yesterday's lab. We ran the same prompt set the customer provided and matched request concurrency to the baseline test as close as possible. Two variants from Redwood: a default FP16 path with KV cache enabled and a quantized int8 path we tested for cost delta.
[00:40] Dr. Aaron Kline: Quick needed context — baseline is CloudGen AI with their managed endpoints, we see p95 around 230 ms and p99 spikes to ~580 ms on our production mix. Cost per 1k reqs is about $12 on their pricing.
[01:05] Priya Desai: Thanks Aaron. Our summarized numbers: p50 ~35 ms, p95 ~120 ms, p99 ~340 ms on the FP16 path when using Redwood hosted runtime with continuous batching tuned to your observed seq lengths. Throughput in the steady-state test was ~280 reqs/sec for the 2xA100 equivalent config we simulated locally.
[01:30] Liam O'Connor: So p95 is roughly half of baseline, p99 still high but better. What's the delta that causes the p99 spikes?
[01:40] Priya Desai: The main contributors are cold KV cache misses when requests land on different workers and occasional kernel fallbacks on long prompts that exceed the fast path. We saw about 12% of requests crossing the long-seq threshold which pushes execution to a slower attention kernel.
[01:58] Jordan Miles: To clarify, long prompts are primarily clinical notes that run past 2k tokens, right Aaron?
[02:05] Dr. Aaron Kline: Correct. Many discharge summaries and multi-section notes go 2k–4k tokens. Those are nontrivial and are where we saw the quantized int8 artefacts — some hallucination-like truncation on the final lines in the int8 runs.
[02:25] Priya Desai: Right, on int8 we saw a small increase in token error rate on the generation tail for >3k contexts. We've got a few mitigations: prefix KV caching pinned to session affinity, or routing long-context requests to the FP16 variant to avoid the int8 fast-path artifact.
[02:45] Maya Singh: Session affinity — what are the tradeoffs? We care about horizontal scale and not losing throughput.
[02:53] Priya Desai: Affinity reduces cache misses and dramatically lowers p99, but it reduces the global packing opportunities for batching across sessions. So p50/p95 improves for those long sessions, but overall throughput can drop if too many workers are pinned. We can implement heuristics: affinity only for requests exceeding 2.5k tokens and with a TTL of 10 minutes. That way bursts get benefit but normal short requests still pool.
[03:20] Jordan Miles: We tested that heuristic in sandbox and saw p99 drop from 340 ms to ~220 ms with affinity on long sessions, while overall throughput fell only 7% in our synthetic mix.
[03:33] Dr. Aaron Kline: That sounds promising. What about cost implications between FP16 and int8?
[03:40] Priya Desai: In our runs, int8 reduced average token compute cost by roughly 35% but introduced the tail risk on very long contexts. Mixed policy — route short/medium contexts to int8 and long contexts to FP16 — achieves about 20% cost savings overall vs baseline while keeping p99 within your target range.
[04:03] Liam O'Connor: Would that be automatic routing on our side or policy we set in Redwood?
[04:09] Jordan Miles: We can push a routing policy template and you can operate it from the console. It supports conditions: token_count > X, model_variant = int8, fallback = FP16, and region preference. Priya can show an example.
[04:24] Priya Desai: I'll share a sample policy after the call. Quick demo: it's a JSON-like policy but for the console we have a UI. You can set priorities and a weighted fallback.
[04:35] [05:00] (brief cross-talk, jam with screen)
[05:10] Maya Singh: On throughput — your 280 reqs/sec baseline, how does that scale if we add more workers or change batching windows? We can't afford latency regressions during peak bursts.
[05:25] Priya Desai: Batching window tuning is key. For your median token lengths (about 120 tokens), we get high packing and near-linear throughput scaling. If we increase batching window by 10 ms, throughput improves ~8% but p50 increases ~5 ms. We can expose a safe envelope so you can trade latency for throughput.
[05:50] Jordan Miles: We also tested an autoscale policy for dedicated slot that adds temporary burst capacity; Redwood's dedicated slot can be configured to add 1.5x burst capacity for up to 10 minutes. That keeps tail under control during spikes.
[06:06] Dr. Aaron Kline: Ok — one odd thing: in one of the int8 runs we saw truncated outputs where the final sentence got cut mid-word about 2% of the time. Is that a quantization glitch or a decoder timeout?
[06:20] Priya Desai: Our hypothesis is that it's a combination of two things — slight divergence in logits due to quantization rounding in the attention kernel, and a tokenization boundary mismatch in the prompt preprocessor for very long contexts. We reproduced it locally and added a guard to force FP16 on sequences that hit the boundary; that eliminated the truncation in our test run.
[06:41] Maya Singh: That will probably be fine as long as it doesn't change semantics. We need to see examples. Can you share 10 failure cases?
[06:48] Jordan Miles: Yes — ACTION ITEM: we will export the 10 failure transcripts and include model outputs across FP16 and int8 for comparison.
[06:55] [07:00] Jordan Miles: Next, a quick look at the raw numbers I sent in the sheet. (screen share) p50/p95/p99 table: Baseline (CloudGen) — p50 45 ms, p95 230 ms, p99 580 ms. Redwood FP16 — p50 35 ms, p95 120 ms, p99 340 ms. Redwood int8 mixed policy — p50 30 ms, p95 140 ms, p99 410 ms. Throughput: baseline steady 260 reqs/sec, Redwood 280 reqs/sec on our config.
[07:30] Liam O'Connor: These are encouraging. How confident are you these numbers map to our prod traffic, not just the synthetic bench?
[07:38] Priya Desai: We ran two validation passes: 1) replay of a day of production traffic with exact traffic mix and sticky sessions, 2) a stress run with amplified concurrency to test tail behavior. The replay matched the p95/p99 deltas within ~10%. Stress run exposed the quantization edge cases.
[07:58] Dr. Aaron Kline: Good. What's the plan to validate cost assumptions? We need ledger-level numbers for finance.
[08:06] Jordan Miles: We'll include estimated cost per 1k requests for each config in the sheet. For Redwood mixed routing we estimate $8.5 per 1k requests compared to CloudGen at $12 per 1k (approx). That's before reserved capacity discounts.
[08:24] Maya Singh: If we go to Dedicated, what pricing floor can we expect? Our procurement wants ballpark numbers for a 6-month pilot with expected 25M requests/month.
[08:33] Jordan Miles: I'll follow up with a ballpark: dedicated reserved nodes would drop unit cost significantly; I'll include a 6-month reserved quote in the pricing doc — ACTION ITEM: Jordan to send a pilot quote.
[08:45] Priya Desai: On the routing technical side, one more recommendation: enable per-route prefix caching for high-volume patient lookup prompts. That reduced repeated prefix recomputation and improved throughput for those routes by ~18% in our tests.
[09:03] Maya Singh: That is interesting — can that be applied selectively per route via the console?
[09:08] Priya Desai: Yes, you can apply cache hints on a per-route basis. We'll share a route config example.
[09:15] [09:30] (short pause while exchanging links)
[09:40] Dr. Aaron Kline: Let's talk acceptance criteria. For us, primary metrics are: p95 < 200 ms for standard workflows, p99 < 400 ms for long-context workflows, and no more than 0.5% quality regressions observed by our clinical review. If you can hit that, finance will be happy.
[10:02] Jordan Miles: That seems achievable with the mixed routing + affinity heuristic. We'll aim for p95 < 180 ms in the lab run.
[10:10] Liam O'Connor: One operational ask — audit logs for inference calls. We need request-level metadata in a format we can ingest.
[10:18] Priya Desai: Redwood can export request traces and per-token cost breakouts to your S3. We can provide a streaming audit log or daily batch. We'll include a sample schema in the security packet.
[10:31] Maya Singh: Also need SSO SAML integration and RBAC so only certain teams can access the dedicated slot.
[10:38] Jordan Miles: Yep — we have an integration guide. Jordan to attach the security and SSO instructions after the call.
[10:45] [11:00] (customer side background noise, brief interruption)
[11:15] Maya Singh: For the 99th percentile lab run, what's the recommended setup? We want to reproduce worst-case tails.
[11:22] Priya Desai: Two-phase test: A replay phase that uses your actual session affinity and prompt set at production concurrency, then a stress phase where we amplify concurrent short bursts and long-context interleaving. We'll provision a temporary dedicated slot equal to the pilot target capacity and run for 90 minutes. This will surface p99 and resource contention.
[11:45] Dr. Aaron Kline: Good. If we see regressions, do you have a quick rollback plan?
[11:50] Priya Desai: Yes — automatic fallback to baseline model variant or to FP16 within the same runtime. Console allows immediate rollback of routing and quantization policies. We'll test rollback in the lab window.
[12:04] Jordan Miles: Ok let's lock dates. Maya, Aaron — does 6/8 morning US time work for a 2-hour block?
[12:12] Maya Singh: 6/8 morning works for me. Aaron and Liam confirm?
[12:18] Dr. Aaron Kline: Works for me. Liam O'Connor: fine, set it up.
[12:22] Jordan Miles: Great. Actions recap: Jordan send benchmark CSVs, failure cases, pricing/quote; Priya send routing and policy examples plus route config; Maya provide prompt set and production profile. Then lab on 2026-06-08.
[12:40] Maya Singh: Quick question — can we get a temporary test token with increased rate limits to run the stress pass?
[12:46] Jordan Miles: Yes we can provision that; I'll include token and dedicated slot details in the email.
[12:52] Dr. Aaron Kline: Cool, thanks. Anything else before we wrap?
[12:56] Priya Desai: I'll attach the short checklist for the lab run and sample JMeter script we used.
[13:05] Jordan Miles: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in the email with attachments and schedule.
[13:10] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional timestamps every 20–60s; minor speaker attribution noise; disfluencies present.

document.content:
Evidence packaging and audit snapshot workshop

Redwood walked Helios through what admin and audit telemetry we capture, export options (S3 export, syslog, webhook streaming), and retention/rotation patterns. Helios clarified required retention windows and legal-hold needs for financial records. Action items: Redwood to send SOC2/ISO evidence pack and sample export manifest; schedule pilot to validate streaming exports to Helios S3/syslog; customer to confirm retention matrix.
1) What admin events are captured (user logins, role changes, API key ops, workspace/model changes, system-level errors)
2) Export mechanisms (S3 batch export, continuous syslog, webhook, CDC Kafka)
3) Retention/archival and legal hold (90 days default vs 7-year regulatory needs)
4) Encryption and KMS/HSM options (customer-managed keys, rotation, dual control)
5) RBAC/SSO audit trails and identity mappings
6) Evidence packaging for auditors (samples, formats, hashes, chain-of-custody)
[00:00] Jamie: Okay thanks everyone for joining, we should be able to run about 50 minutes today, thanks for carving the time. I'm Jamie from Redwood, with Riley on the call, that's our solutions engineer.
[00:08] Aisha: Hi all, Aisha here, security owner for Helios. We're mainly focused on what you retain, how we can pull it out, and proof for audits, like chain of custody and integrity.
[00:20] Riley: Great, thanks Aisha. Quick agenda: capture surface, export options, retention & legal hold, encryption/KMS, and then we close with next steps. Sound right?
[00:28] Darren: Yeah that's right, we have auditors in December so we're trying to lock the playbook.
[00:34] Marta: plus we need to be explicit about evidence formats, CSV vs JSON, checksums, that kind of thing.
[00:40] Riley: Perfect. So first, what we capture — high level — admin actions: user account creates/deletes, role assignments, SAML SSO sessions, token and API key creation/deletion, model publish/rollback, configuration changes to routing/policies, and escalation events. Also system events: scheduler/autoscale failures and node reboots — those are captured but labeled as infra telemetry.
[01:05] Aisha: When you say 'token ops' does that include full token content or just metadata? We cannot have full secrets in logs.
[01:12] Riley: Good point, we never store secret tokens. It's metadata only — actor, operation type, timestamp, request ID, resource id. If a token value is present in an incoming request, it's redacted server-side and we only log a hash for linkage.
[01:28] Aisha: okay that's fine. How long are these retained by default?
[01:31] Jamie: Default retention for admin events in hosted is 90 days, with options to push to your own long-term storage. Dedicated/private can be configured to respect customer retention SLAs.
[01:41] Darren: Our compliance requires 7 years for certain transaction-related admin ops. That means we need export and archiving, and immutable storage with checksums.
[01:50] Riley: Yep, we support a couple of export mechanisms: periodic batch exports to your S3 or GCS bucket (daily/weekly), continuous streaming to syslog/ELK via our syslog forwarder, and webhook/Kafka CDC style pushes for real-time ingestion. There is also a log-archive snapshot we can produce on demand — basically a time-limited snapshot with manifest and SHA256 checksums.
[02:11] Marta: Tell me more about the manifest and chain-of-custody. Auditors want proof the logs weren't tampered with.
[02:17] Riley: For each snapshot we produce a manifest (JSON) that lists files, sizes, sha256 hashes, a signed metadata file using Redwood's internal signing key, and optionally we can provide a signed timestamp from an external timestamper. If you'd prefer, we can encrypt the archive with your KMS key and provide the key wrap metadata so you have exclusive decrypt.
[02:40] Aisha: Signing with your key is fine but we prefer customer-managed keys where possible, especially for older archives — can Redwood support CMK or HSM integration?
[02:48] Jamie: Yes, for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) and HSMs for on-prem. For Hosted we offer a bring-your-own-key flow for snapshot encryption — the archive is encrypted client-side using a key you rotate; Redwood never sees plaintext. We also support envelope encryption when pushing to S3.
[03:10] Darren: How about key rotation — do you rotate the signing keys? What's your retention of the signing key history for verification in future audits?
[03:16] Riley: Redwood rotates internal signing keys on a regular schedule (annually or on-demand for incidents). We keep an archived chain-of-trust mapping so when we sign a manifest we also include the signing key ID and certificate chain. If you bring your own keys, you manage rotation and we store only the wrapped key metadata.
[03:33] Marta: Are audit exports tamper-evident if sent to our S3? If someone deletes files from the bucket accidentally, what's the recovery model?
[03:40] Riley: For S3 we strongly recommend using immutable object lock / retention policies and cross-region replication for durability. On top of that, we provide manifests and checksums so you can detect deletion or modification. If you use Glacier-like storage, we can provide a rehydration playbook. For accidental deletes, typical recovery is via your cloud provider's object versioning or backup. Redwood can also keep an internal cold snapshot for a limited window upon request.
[04:06] Aisha: Okay good. On the RBAC/SSO side, we need to map Redwood roles to our internal roles so auditors can see who had what permissions when an action occurred. How granular are your role change events?
[04:16] Riley: We log role change events with before/after state, actor, and request ID. The logs include human-readable role names and internal role IDs. We also capture role inheritance events, e.g., when a team inherits model access through a policy.
[04:28] Aisha: Do you capture the SAML assertion id so we can tie a login to an external identity provider?
[04:33] Riley: We capture assertion id and the issuer field, but not the full SAML payload. We can store the assertion id and the subject name id to link back to your IdP logs.
[04:42] Darren: For our legal hold workflows, we need the ability to flag a stream and prevent automatic purging. Does Redwood support an immutable hold flag per-resource?
[04:50] Jamie: Yes, in Dedicated/private we can set retention windows per workspace and support legal hold — preventing automated deletion until release. In hosted we offer a hold workflow via customer support request and an API to tag artifacts for hold; depending on plan we can automate that as well.
[05:05] Marta: If we ask for a snapshot for an audit, how quickly can we get it? We might need a same-day extraction with checksums.
[05:12] Riley: For standard requests, we can produce a snapshot within 24 hours. For expedited requests there's a rush option — depends on the size but often same-day for small-to-medium footprint customers. We'll include a manifest and signed metadata.
[05:24] Aisha: Are there PII redaction features or field-level filters? Some events include user-provided content pointers and we need to avoid capturing PII in logs.
[05:33] Riley: We have configurable scrubbing filters that can redact or hash specific fields in events before they're stored. You can supply a list of fields or regex patterns. For higher-sensitivity tenants we recommend private deployment or dedicated which keeps the runtime isolated and gives you more control over scrubbing rules.
[05:48] Darren: On the exports side, what's the throughput and cost considerations if we stream every admin event in real-time to our SIEM?
[05:56] Riley: Admin events are generally low-volume compared to application logs, but throughput depends on activity level. For continuous syslog streaming we support batching and backpressure — if your SIEM gets overwhelmed we can buffer and publish in bursts. We can also do a filter layer so only high-priority events stream in real time and lower-priority ones go to batch export. We'll share config suggestions based on your event profiles.
[06:18] Aisha: For the evidence pack, auditors will want policy docs: retention policy, change control, key rotation policy, access logs for the signing keys. Can you include those?
[06:29] Jamie: Absolutely, we'll include SOC2/ISO artifacts: access control policies, key mgmt SOPs, change control logs for the service, and sample audit exports. We'll redact anything customer-specific unless you authorize sharing.
[06:39] Marta: I want an example of the JSON manifest format. Does it have a version? We need reproducibility for future audits.
[06:46] Riley: Yes manifests are versioned. We'll attach a schema and an example with the evidence pack. Each manifest includes schema version, generated_at, files listing with hashes, signing metadata (key id, signature), and optional encryption metadata if archived with a customer key.
[07:02] Darren: How do you handle cross-account access for the S3 export? We need to minimize access footprint — ideally Redwood writes into a pre-signed bucket path without assuming a role indefinitely.
[07:11] Riley: Common pattern is either Redwood assumes a short-lived role in your account or we do customer-side pull via pre-signed URLs. For push model we prefer assuming a role with limited time-bound permissions and audited role usage; for pull, we create a pre-signed manifest URL you can fetch. We'll show both options in the runbook.
[07:29] Aisha: Regarding GDPR and data residency, some of our records must reside in EU for EU customers. Can you scope exports by region or tenant?
[07:38] Jamie: Yes. Exports can be region-scoped; we support exporting only EU-region logs and we can place archives in your EU bucket. For Private deployments you control region and physical location. We'll need a mapping of which tenants/organizations require EU residency.
[07:52] Marta: Does Redwood provide proof of deletion for purged records? We need an auditable trail when data is destructed.
[07:58] Riley: We emit deletion events with before/after metadata and a deletion manifest that includes the deleted file/object names and deletion timestamps. If you use immutable object lock we can also include retention-release evidence.
[08:12] Aisha: On the SSO audit side, auditors often ask for a chain showing when admin privileges were granted and used. Can you show a timeline for a principal: when granted, when elevated, and when used?
[08:22] Riley: We can generate a timeline view. Because we log role change events, token generation, and action events with request IDs, we can link and produce a human-readable timeline for a principal over a given window. We'll provide an example in the evidence pack.
[08:36] Darren: For long-term archival we may want to keep an offline signed copy. Is Redwood willing to sign and hand over a copy for retention in our vaults?
[08:44] Jamie: Yes, we can provide signed archives for you to store in a vault. For hosted customers we sign with our certificate; for Private customers you can sign with your own KMS prior to upload.
[08:55] Marta: A nit: audits often want to see who accessed signing key metadata. Is that protected?
[09:00] Riley: Access to signing key metadata is limited; it's part of our control plane audit. We can include the control plane access logs as part of the evidence pack, with role-scoped redaction if needed.
[09:12] Aisha: Okay, let's walk through a hypothetical: auditor requests admin logs for user X between Jan 1 and Jan 31, 2025 — what do you deliver?
[09:20] Riley: We generate a snapshot for that date range, include a manifest, signature, and optionally encrypt with your CMK. We also include the timeline view for the user, raw event files in compressed JSONL, and a verification script to run sha256 checks.
[09:37] Darren: Great. Anything we should be aware of for latency when exporting large ranges?
[09:42] Riley: For large date ranges it's a heavy IO job — time depends on size. We recommend doing incremental exports (weekly) for normal ops and ad-hoc snapshots for audits. For the pilot we'll scope a small window to measure throughput.
[09:54] Jamie: Quick recap then: Redwood to share evidence pack + manifest example and runbook, set up a pilot streaming to Helios S3/syslog, Helios to share retention matrix and list of audit timelines. Any other open questions?
[10:08] Marta: One more: SLA around export availability — if you promise a 24-hour snapshot window, what's the SLA and remediation?
[10:16] Jamie: We'll include SLA language in the evidence pack; typical enterprise SLA includes a 24-hour fulfillment target and credits for missed commitments. We'll surface exact terms in the contract addendum.
[10:27] Aisha: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[10:29] Riley: Thanks, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[10:32] Jamie: End meeting.

Notes on transcription: occasional words garbled (e.g., 'timestamper' sometimes transcribed as 'time stamper'), speaker turns compressed in a few places, natural filler words left intact.
Mentioned export patterns: S3 push (assume role or pre-signed), continuous syslog, webhook/Kafka CDC. Discussed manifests with sha256, signing metadata, signed timestamps, CMK envelope encryption. Discussed legal hold, immutable S3 object lock, role mapping, SAML assertion ids, redaction filters, retention windows (90 days default vs 7 years required), evidence pack deliverables and a pilot for streaming exports.
Redwood to share SOC2/ISO evidence pack and audit export sample (S3 + syslog) by 2025-11-10
Customer to provide list of required retention windows and legal hold scenarios by 2025-11-12
Schedule a short pilot to validate live admin event streaming to Helios S3 on 2025-11-18

Syntara Health POC — security KPIs and benchmark scope

Discovery and POC scoping between Redwood and Syntara Health focused on security/compliance gates, SSO/SAML integration, RBAC and audit log export, plus performance targets for a 6-week pilot. Agreed success criteria include SOC 2/ISO evidence, SSO via SAML with SCIM provisioning, audit log export to Splunk, dedicated or Private deployment for EU data residency, throughput and latency benchmarks, and an acceptance plan driven by a canonical prompt set. Next steps and owners assigned.
Samira Patel | Send security whitepaper, SOC 2 Type II attestation, and network diagram | Due 2026-12-10
Lina Gomez | Upload sample traffic CSV and canonical prompts to shared drive | Due 2026-12-13
Jordan Lee | Share Dedicated pricing and draft SOW for 6-week pilot | Due 2026-12-11
Marco Ruiz | Complete and return security questionnaire and confirm SIEM endpoint | Due 2026-12-15
Samira to send SOC 2 Type II report, recent pen-test summary, and network diagram (by 2026-12-10)
Lina to share daily traffic profile, sample payloads, and canonical prompt set (by 2026-12-13)
Jordan to provide Dedicated pool pricing, pilot SOW and onboarding runbook (by 2026-12-11)
Schedule on-prem/Private deployment tech deep dive with infra team if needed (target week of 2026-12-14)
Meeting header: 2026-12-08 16:00 UTC | Duration: 57 minutes | Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Marco Ruiz (CISO, Syntara Health), Lina Gomez (Platform Engineer), Priya Nair (Product), Alex Chen (SRE)

Summary (auto-gen, may be partial): Syntara is evaluating Redwood for inference serving for clinical notes summarization and triage. Primary constraints: EU data residency for EU patients, SOC 2/ISO evidence, SSO via Okta, RBAC for audit sensitivity, and integration with existing Splunk SIEM. Pilot scope is 6 weeks with agreed test harness and acceptance criteria.

00:00 Jordan (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll run 50 minutes or so, quick intros, then Samira will walk the tech plan and we can map security gates and perf goals
00:28 Marco (Syntara CISO): thanks jordan, quick note, we're here mostly to validate controls—SOC two, ISO 27k evidence, and our legal will want auditable logs exported to our splunk cluster
01:04 Samira (Redwood SE): totally, we have the SOC2 Type II packet and pen test summary, we'll share them after this call. For the pilot we usually do a dedicated pool or private VPC if residency is required
01:39 Priya (Product): our primary use-case is note summarization and triage prioritization, about 30% of traffic is short prompts, 70% are mid-length, expect bursty spikes during morning rounds
02:05 Alex (SRE): just to flag, we need syslog/JSON audit events exported to our splunk forwarder, retention policy is 1 year and we need a near real-time stream for alerts
02:44 Samira: ok noted, syslog export and S3 retention options are available. question on identity—are you using Okta or Azure AD for SSO?
03:10 Lina (Platform): Okta with SCIM for provisioning, we want SAML assertions to carry role claims, RBAC mapping on Redwood side should enforce least privilege, e.g., dev vs security vs analytics roles
03:47 Jordan: we support SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning, RBAC can be configured per tenant and per-route, we also have KMS integrations for customer-managed keys (HSM option)
04:18 Marco: does Redwood provide audit log tamper evidence or hashes? our compliance team expects immutable audit trail or proof of integrity
04:44 Samira: we write append-only logs and you can stream them to your SIEM; we can also provide checksums on log batches, but full WORM storage would be via your S3 + object lock on the customer side for Private deployments
05:12 Marco: good. about penetration tests—any recent third party? we need a summary and any open findings
05:36 Samira: we had a third-party red team last quarter, low severity findings only, we'll redact details and share the summary doc after sign NDA if needed
06:02 Priya: performance goals—what can you promise for p99 and sustained throughput? We have a service-level bar for triage where p99 should be sub-250ms for short outputs
06:30 Samira: depends on model size and deployment. For our recommended config (Redwood-optimized M-Large equivalent quantized) we can aim for p99 <250ms for short prompts at 100 rps with continuous batching and KV caching tuned. For longer outputs (200-400 tokens) p99 can be up to 450ms in worst case, but we can tune batch windows and warmups
07:12 Alex: our baseline traffic for the pilot will be 100 rps sustained for 1 hour in the load test, and a separate 5 minute spike to 400 rps, we need to see graceful degradation and fallbacks
07:38 Samira: ok we can run a load-plan: step test to 100 rps sustained for an hour, then spike test, and an overnight soak. We'll instrument token-level costs and latency percentiles.
08:05 Marco: data residency—EU patient data must stay in eu-west-1 and not be cached offsite, does Redwood offer region pinning or on-prem?
08:33 Jordan: yes, we offer Dedicated pools in eu-west and Private (VPC) with customer-managed control plane for full isolation. For EU-only tenancy we recommend Private so logs and keys remain in your VPC
09:00 Lina: for pilot we prefer Dedicated in eu-west first, then discuss Private if SSO or KMS requirements force it. Also need SCIM provisioning to mirror our Okta groups into Redwood roles
09:30 Samira: SCIM is supported, group-to-role mapping is configurable. For SAML attributes, we support custom role claims and can map them to RBAC rules on resource paths
09:56 Priya: success criteria question—beyond security sign-off, what are Redwood-specific acceptance tests?
10:20 Samira: we propose acceptance criteria: 1) security checklist complete (SOC2 + ISO evidence + pen-test summary), 2) SSO + SCIM working with at least one test user, 3) audit logs exported to Splunk with retention 1 year, 4) performance: p99 <250ms for short prompts at 100 rps sustained for 1 hour and spike handling demonstrated, 5) model fidelity: canonical prompt set accuracy/acceptance > 95% on quality review, 6) cost report and runbook delivered
11:02 Marco: the fidelity metric—what does acceptance mean? is product team human-review threshold?
11:25 Priya: yes we'll sample 500 outputs from the canonical set, and the clinical reviewers will accept/reject, target >95% acceptable with no high-severity hallucination incidents
11:48 Samira: we can run automated evals and human review; we'll integrate with your eval harness or provide ours. Also will include drift monitoring and alerting for quality regressions
12:12 Alex: about keys and encryption—we must use our KMS, rotate keys every 90 days, and ensure the model cache isn't persisted outside the region
12:36 Jordan: we support CMK via AWS KMS and HSM-backed keys in Private deployments. KV cache is ephemeral within the region by default; for Private we can guarantee no cross-region replication
13:05 Marco: retention and deletion—data used for inference must be deletable on request, and logs must be retained per policy
13:24 Samira: we have deletion APIs, and we can zero out KV caches; logs can be purged or exported to your archive for long-term retention
13:50 Priya: timeline then—what does a 6-week pilot timeline look like?
14:08 Samira: suggested plan: week 0: kickoff and security review, week 1: env setup + SSO/SCIM integration, week 2: test harness and canonical prompt upload, week 3: functional runs and short load tests, week 4: sustained load and spike tests, week 5: human-in-the-loop evals and quality review, week 6: follow-up, final report and decision meeting
14:44 Jordan: we can compress if Syntara wants earlier decision, but 6 weeks gives us time for security sign-offs and human review
15:10 Marco: who signs the pilot SOW and who has approval? our security team needs to review SOW with redlines for data residency and indemnities
15:30 Jordan: AE will draft the SOW, legal will accept redlines; we'll mark data residency and KMS clauses explicitly. We'll push draft by end of week
15:55 Lina: for benchmarking, what metrics will you collect and share? and are raw logs available for us?
16:15 Samira: we'll collect token counts, per-route latency percentiles, gpus utilization, batch sizes, cache hit rates, and model version. Raw request/response bodies will not be shared unless redacted; audit logs and anonymized telemetry can be provided
16:50 Alex: need to ensure PII is not retained in training/logging—are there guarantees?
17:05 Samira: we don't use customer data to train models unless there's an explicit opt-in. For logs we have redaction options and can hash identifiers; we'll note that in the data handling doc
17:30 Priya: one more on fallback—if Dedicated capacity drops, do you have automatic fallback to hosted or smaller model? we need graceful degradation path for the triage flow
17:58 Samira: yes routing policies can fallback to compatible model variants in same region; you can configure priority: Dedicated -> Hosted compatible -> Smaller quantized model. Fallback preserves functionality but may change latency and fidelity; that's part of acceptance testing
18:25 Marco: ok. For compliance, we'll need a SOC2 attestation, ISO 27001 scope and the red team summary. Please include exact dates of the reports
18:44 Jordan: yes we'll include report dates and scope in the packet we send. any other blockers?
19:02 Lina: network firewall rules—we need ip ranges and cert pins so we can whitelist them in our proxies
19:22 Samira: we'll send the ingress egress IP CIDR list and public cert fingerprints. For Private, we can hand off a network diagram for your infra team
19:45 Alex: also we want to run an initial benchmark on our staging data set, can we get a harness or script to reproduce tests locally?
20:03 Samira: yes we'll share the benchmark harness (jq scripts, locust scenario, and a small python runner) and sample terraform for spinning test infra
20:30 Priya: cost expectations for pilot—rough estimate? we need to budget internally
20:46 Jordan: rough ballpark: a 6-week dedicated pilot with reserved capacity and some burst allowances probably in the low tens of thousands USD, exact depends on model variant and sustained throughput; we'll itemize in the SOW
21:15 Marco: who will be our day-to-day contact for escalation?
21:25 Jordan: Jordan for commercial and Samira for tech and runbook. We'll include CSM contact if pilot goes live on Dedicated
21:40 Priya: ok let's confirm acceptance checklist and timelines in the follow up email
22:02 Jordan: will do. quick recap and then we can open for any quick Qs
22:15 Jordan (recap): deliverables — security packet from Samira, traffic and prompt share from Lina, pricing and SOW from me, benchmark harness and runbook, pilot kickoff next Tuesday if all agree
22:48 Marco: sounds good. small Q: does Redwood keep an immutable change log for RBAC policy updates? we need admin audit trail
23:09 Samira: yes change events are logged with actor identity; we can export those as part of the audit stream
23:35 Alex: and can we enforce 2FA for all admin roles?
23:50 Jordan: 2FA via SAML-provider enforced policy is supported; we can make it a required admin control
24:10 Priya: any blockers on our side? we need legal to sign NDA before detailed pen-test findings are shared
24:30 Jordan: able to do that, we'll attach a mutual NDA in the follow-up
24:50 Marco: perfect. thanks everyone.
25:05 [CROSSTALK] brief side discussion about test datasets and redaction details, some names mis-spoken (red team vs red team report)
26:20 Samira: note on telemetry—we can provide token-level cost breakdown to help your finance model the per-call cost during pilot
26:45 Priya: great, also please include worst-case cost modeling for spikes
27:02 Jordan: will add to SOW appendix
27:35 Lina: timeline questions, if we hit blocker on SAML attributes mapping, can we do manual onboarding for pilot?
27:55 Samira: yes we can do manual user creation and RBAC assignment to unblock the pilot while SCIM is configured
28:18 Marco: last item—incident response, does Redwood provide an incident timeline and post-incident report for severity 1s?
28:42 Samira: yes we provide an incident report and a post-mortem with timeline, root cause and corrective actions; SLA for incident ack is per SOW
29:05 Jordan: OK we'll close here. thanks all, follow-up email will have attachments and next meeting invite
56:30 [Meeting end]

Auto sections (optional):
Action items recap: Samira to send security packet; Lina to share traffic and prompts; Jordan to send SOW and pricing; Marco to confirm legal sign-off schedule.
Questions raised: data residency, KMS/CMK, SCIM group mappings, audit export format, p99 latency targets, fallback model fidelity.

Notes on transcription quality: speaker overlaps possible, some product names transcribed imperfectly (e.g., 'K-V cash' for KV cache, 'SOC two' for SOC 2).

Runtime alignment & token economics workshop — OpenAI/Anthropic/Together -> Redwood

AE + SE demo focused on runtime parity and token economics when migrating endpoints from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood. Covered API mapping, batching, KV/prefix cache, quantization tradeoffs, routing/fallbacks, security asks (KMS, SSO), and next-step benchmarks and docs to validate parity.
API parity mapping (endpoints/params)
Console demo: rollouts, model pinning, tracing
Redwood Optimize: batching, cache, quantization recommendations
Latency vs cost tradeoff and dedicated vs hosted
Security/compliance: SOC2, KMS, SSO, audit logs
Header:
Date: 2026-08-05 16:00 PDT
Length: 62 minutes
Meeting started on Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Riley Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Gupta (Redwood Optimize PM), Evan Morris (LuminaBio Head of ML), Sofia Alvarez (LuminaBio Infra), Priya Nair (LuminaBio Security)

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. quick intro, I'm Jordan, AE on this account, Riley is our solutions engineer, Maya runs the Optimize product and will talk about token economics and recommendations. Evan, Sofia, Priya, thanks for joining.

[00:18] Evan Morris: Hey, thanks. we're short on time but excited. main goal here is to understand how close Redwood gets to our current latencies on OpenAI and Anthropic, and how the cost math changes once we switch. Also we have to make sure nothing in the pipeline breaks — model outputs parity, tokens cost, and security.

[00:35] Riley Chen: Awesome. we'll start with a quick mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together APIs to the Redwood API — basically, call shapes are similar but there are some parameter name differences, and we have a couple of Redwood-specific knobs like continuous batching and KV prefix cache.

[00:54] Sofia Alvarez: can you show how streaming works? we rely on streaming right now for our chat UI to hit p95 under 300ms for short responses.

[01:10] Riley Chen: yeah absolutely. quick demo — I'm in the console, hitting the same prompt we've been using. On OpenAI you have chunked events, on Anthropic too; Redwood streams via chunked HTTP and supports function/tool calling. watch the console trace — you can see per-token latency, and if you look at the tracing panel you get per-request breakdown (kernel time, queue wait, kv cache hit).

[01:42] (screen shared) Riley Chen: So here the console shows a 120ms token generation p50 and p95 around 350ms for long responses; that's with hosted config and our default batching. For your short chat responses we can tune batch windows down, or use a dedicated allocation with lower queueing.

[02:10] Priya Nair: Quick security question — what's the story for KMS and customer-managed keys, we need envelope encryption and key rotation logs.

[02:18] Maya Gupta: We support KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS) for Private deployments and Dedicated customers. For hosted we have a managed key but enterprise customers can opt for BYOK and you get audit logs, and we surface key rotation events in the console's audit view. we'll share our SOC2 pack and an excerpt of KMS integration docs after this call.

[02:45] Evan Morris: Great, that's promising. on parity — we've seen subtle output differences when swapping models; we need to know if Redwood can serve the same model weights or if we need to switch to a Redwood-verified equivalent.

[03:02] Riley Chen: For most workloads you can bring the same open model weights (we support common HF-compatible formats) or use the Redwood-curated catalog which includes verified performance profiles. When exact identical weights are available we can run bit-for-bit validation but more often we run output parity tests: same prompts, compare top-n completions and eval metrics.

[03:28] Evan Morris: ok so what's the typical delta on latency/cost when moving from OpenAI to Redwood hosted? ballpark.

[03:36] Maya Gupta: Ballpark depends on model size and context. For shorter contexts, Redwood's continuous batching and KV cache usually give you 10–40% token-cost savings, sometimes more with quantized variants. Latency can be within 5–15% of OpenAI p95 for comparable configs on hosted; dedicated can bring latency below or equal depending on GPU type. we'll put concrete numbers in the parity workbook.

[04:02] Sofia Alvarez: we have a mixed workload — some short chat, some longer completion/generation at 2k tokens. how do we tune batching so that short chats don't get stuck waiting on long requests?

[04:15] Riley Chen: good Q. we recommend request partitioning and route by SLO. Redwood supports policy-based routing: route chat endpoints to low-latency pool with small batch windows, route long generations to separate pools with larger batching to improve throughput. plus prefix/KV cache helps the chat case by returning cached continuations very quickly.

[04:44] Evan Morris: you mentioned KV cache — can you explain possible cache poisoning or data residency concerns? we sanitize everything but security needs to be clear.

[04:55] Riley Chen: KV cache stores model key-value cache for in-flight contexts and optional prefix caching for repeated prompts. for Hosted we encrypt caches at rest; Dedicated/Private gives you data isolation and optional customer-managed keys. cache keys are ephemeral by default; we also provide TTLs and ability to disable prefix caching. we'll add a short doc on cache guarantees and retention.

[05:20] (crosstalk) Priya Nair: so for us, Private is the preference but we need a sense of complexity to run it on prem versus VPC.

[05:28] Jordan Lee: Right, Private means customer-managed control plane, and we have a prebuilt on-prem appliance for high-reg workloads; it's more effort than hosted but we provide an install guide and runbooks. If you don't want on-prem, VPC-hosted private plane is the middle ground. we'll include our network/topology diagram in the follow-up.

[05:48] Riley Chen: back to parity testing — we propose a three-step plan: 1) small sample parity run on hosted (same prompts) to surface behavioral diffs, 2) tune model params + Optimize recommendations (batching/quantize/cache), 3) run dedicated benchmark with your SLOs.

[06:10] Evan Morris: sounds reasonable. what about quantization — we use fp16 on some endpoints. does Redwood support int8/int4? does it change output quality?

[06:22] Maya Gupta: yes we have quantized variants (int8, int4) and Redwood Optimize gives model-by-workload guidance on when quantization is safe. usually int8 is safe for many LLM workloads with minimal degradation; int4 can be hit or miss depending on model. Optimize will flag risky prompts and propose rollback policies.

[06:44] Sofia Alvarez: will running quantized models reduce cost linearly?

[06:48] Maya Gupta: Not perfectly linear, but you see a noticeable reduction in GPU consumption and per-token cost, sometimes 30–60% depending on baseline. we include effective dollars per 1k tokens in the workbook.

[07:05] Riley Chen: quick demo shift — I'm going to show the API mapping doc in the console and a short snippet of code. On OpenAI you'd call completions/chat with model, messages, temp; on Redwood you call /v1/generate or /v1/chat with similar fields. There's a few param rename cases — e.g., "max_tokens" is the same but "stream" behavior and function calling have slightly different markers. we provide adapter snippets for node/python that are drop-in with minimal change.

[07:45] (screen) Riley Chen: showing Node example — we replaced openai.ChatCompletion.create with Redwood.chat.create. adapter handles streaming events and emits the same shape for your front-end. for Anthropic it's similar; we have an Anthropic->Redwood mapping sheet.

[08:10] Evan Morris: If we need to keep both vendors for failover, how does Redwood handle routing and fallback?

[08:18] Jordan Lee: Redwood supports multi-backend routing policies: you can prefer Redwood-hosted, then fallback to a cheaper model or even to another vendor via a routing rule; we also have automatic fallback when a model's p95 exceeds threshold. important note: if you route to other vendors you'll need to handle data residency and contract terms.

[08:42] Priya Nair: our procurement team will want to know retention and audit logs — is there per-request identity and a trace id?

[08:50] Riley Chen: yes every request has a trace id, you can export logs to your SIEM, and audit events are visible in the console. We'll attach a sample log export format.

[09:05] Evan Morris: can we see a cost example for one of our endpoints? we have a customer support chat that averages 20 tokens per user turn and about 5 turns.

[09:14] Maya Gupta: sure, quick calc: with current vendor cost assumptions and your traffic, Redwood's recommended config (dedicated small-pool + prefix cache + int8 for long jobs) reduces the per-convo token cost by roughly 35% in the model we simulated. i'll put the exact spreadsheet with assumptions.

[09:40] Sofia Alvarez: how do we test regressions for output quality? we need an eval harness.

[09:48] Riley Chen: we recommend a prompt set of 500–5k examples, automated diffing for ngram/semantic metrics, and human spot checks for critical flows. Redwood has an eval runner you can use; we'll include a quickstart.

[10:05] Evan Morris: ok, let's talk scheduling — we'd like a short hosted parity run first, then a week later a dedicated benchmark. is that workable?

[10:12] Jordan Lee: totally. timeline: parity run within 48–72 hours if you share the prompt set; benchmark on dedicated within 7–10 days depending on pool provisioning.

[10:24] (pause) Priya Nair: on compliance again, for logs - does Redwood redact PII automatically or provide hooks for us to strip before logs leave our VPC?

[10:33] Maya Gupta: We provide post-processing hooks and redaction options; for Private you can keep logs entirely under your control. hosted has customizable redaction rules and we can do contract-level commitments. i'll include the policy doc.

[10:50] Riley Chen: demo wrap-up — console preview of rollout/canary. you can pin a model version, do a canary traffic split at route-level, and set automatic rollback if error rate or latency exceeds thresholds. here's the trace where we did a 10% canary and then rolled back automatically.

[11:12] Evan Morris: nice. I noticed the console traces kernel time vs queue wait — what's the main contributor for our workload spikes?

[11:20] Riley Chen: usually queue wait from batching. spikes happen when long-gen jobs join the pool. route separation and smaller batch windows on the low-latency pool keep your chat p95 stable.

[11:38] Sofia Alvarez: about telemetry — can we ingest those traces into Datadog?

[11:42] Jordan Lee: yes, we have integrations; you can forward spans and metrics. we'll include sample config.

[11:58] Evan Morris: any gotchas on the code adapter? I worry about subtle function-calling differences breaking our orchestration.

[12:06] Riley Chen: adapters aim to preserve function-call shape. for edge cases we recommend an automated test that runs the function call examples and asserts json shape equivalence. we'll provide the adapter test harness.

[12:28] (fast forward, mid-call discussion of benchmarks and config specifics)

[32:14] Riley Chen: benchmark plan details — we'll test 512 and 2048 context lengths, measure p50/p95, token throughput, and cost per 1k tokens. For dedicated we'll test different GPU types; for hosted we'll test default and a higher-performance instance.

[33:01] Evan Morris: Are there any known incompatibilities with Together models?

[33:08] Riley Chen: Together uses some custom tokenizers and sometimes model packaging that needs conversion; we have an adapter step in our onboarding to normalize tokenization. occasionally there are subtle detokenization differences; those are usually fixable with a pre/post-tokenization shim.

[33:35] Priya Nair: procurement question — do you have enterprise terms for data residency and deletion upon contract termination?

[33:43] Jordan Lee: yes standard enterprise addendums include data residency commitments for Private and Dedicated and deletion escrow provisions for hosted. we'll share the legal pack.

[34:00] Sofia Alvarez: one more infra Q — how long does dedicated capacity provisioning take?

[34:06] Riley Chen: depends on zone and GPU type; typically 3–7 business days for reservation. if you need immediate we can use hosted burst capacity during the wait.

[34:20] Evan Morris: okay good. last thing — what's the rollback story if we see a quality regression in production after swap?

[34:28] Maya Gupta: you can pin your previous vendor as a fallback or keep a shadow route; Redwood's canary + auto-rollback will pull traffic back. Optimize will also monitor quality regressions on your eval set and trigger alerts.

[34:50] (wrap) Jordan Lee: to recap quickly — action items: LuminaBio shares sanitized prompt set; Riley runs the hosted parity run + uploads results; Jordan sends the cost parity workbook; Maya shares Optimize config suggestions and KV/cache docs; Priya gets SOC2/KMS docs. we'll reconvene after the parity run to review the numbers.

[35:15] Evan Morris: that works. thanks everyone, appreciate the thoroughness.

[35:22] Sofia Alvarez: thanks, bye.

[35:25] (meeting ends)

Notes: transcription has minor errors and occasional missed words. Refer to attached assets: parity_workbook.xlsx (link), console-screencast.mp4 (link), security_pack.pdf (link).

Montrose Biologics — Sandboxed Inference Readiness & Update Workflow

Meeting Header:
Date/Time: 2025-03-17 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Olivia Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Nguyen (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Redwood Solutions), Dr. Elena Ruiz (Montrose CTO), Samir Patel (Montrose Infra), Lucia Gomez (Montrose Compliance), Ravi Menon (Montrose Data Ops)

Summary: quick discovery for an on-prem, air-gapped style deployment — Montrose wants a sandboxed inference node for regulated assay data, strict offline update policy, hardware constraints (older single-socket hosts), and auditability. Main risk areas: update channels, signed packages, KMS/HSM access, and fallback to hosted in emergencies.

Topics: deployment topology, offline updates, signed images, hardware compatibility, maintenance windows, compliance evidence, pilot scope, timeline

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Olivia Park: Hey everyone thanks for joining. I'm Olivia from Redwood, Marcus and Priya are with me on the call. Could we do quick intros?
[00:08] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Yeah hi I'm Elena, CTO at Montrose — we run a set of diagnostic models against protected assay data, must stay inside our network, no outbound to the internet.
[00:15] Samir Patel: Samir here, infra, I manage the racks and the air-gapped sites. We have a couple of single-socket 32GB GPU hosts and some older 16GB cards.
[00:22] Marcus Nguyen: Marcus, Redwood SE. I'll focus on the deployment architecture and the offline update mechanisms.
[00:27] Lucia Gomez: Lucia, compliance — I review audits, we need audit trails, SAML SSO, and evidence for auditors.
[00:33] Olivia Park: Great. High level, Montrose is looking at Redwood Private — either fully air-gapped on-prem or a hybrid with dedicated reserved capacity. Today's call is discovery for the on-prem, sandboxed node case, correct?
[00:42] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Correct. We need to validate feasibility and get a pilot plan. Important: updates must be manual, cryptographically verified, and deployed during a monthly maintenance window.
[00:52] Marcus Nguyen: Understood. A couple clarifying q's — when you say manual updates, do you mean bring-your-own media (USB / physical) or an internal signed repo accessible from the closed network?
[01:02] Samir Patel: Mostly bring-your-own media for the sterile sites. We have a process where security team signs images offline and transfers via encrypted USBs. No outbound connectivity allowed.
[01:12] Priya Shah: Ok that impacts how we deliver the runtime. Redwood Private supports an offline image bundle and signed artifacts — we can produce a tarball with the runtime, model weights, and a signed manifest. The host can verify signatures via a local HSM or a KMS shim.
[01:26] Lucia Gomez: HSM is interesting — are you talking about an HSM appliance or software HSM? We need FIPS validated crypto for certain data types.
[01:34] Marcus Nguyen: We support both integrations. For strictly offline sites, common pattern is using an HSM appliance or an on-prem KMS that can validate signatures locally. If HSM isn't available we support a signer that runs in an approved FIPS mode — but we need to map that to your compliance requirements.
[01:48] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Also model lifecycle — we can't allow model pulls from the cloud. We will want to pin model versions and have an internal approval step before any model swap.
[01:57] Marcus Nguyen: Absolutely, model pinning + rollout guard rails are part of the Private offering — you can pin a model digest, require an approval token for rollouts, and maintain versioned artifacts. The image manifest includes SHA256 checksums.
[02:09] Samir Patel: Quick question on hardware — some of our hosts are older and only have 16GB VRAM GPUs. Can Redwood runtime operate in quantized mode or smaller memory footprint?
[02:18] Marcus Nguyen: Yes, we have quantized runtime builds and memory-optimized kernels — but throughput will vary. For small VRAM, we can recommend CPU+NVMe KV-cache offload or lower-precision weight formats. We'll put recommended profiles in the pilot BOM.
[02:31] Ravi Menon: Are there any network requirements for initial provisioning? Even for air-gapped sites?
[02:36] Priya Shah: For pure air-gapped provisioning you can bring the node image and model artifacts on media. For integrity checks we provide deterministic manifests and a signing key. For the first boot you might run a local verification process that checks the manifest with the signer public key. No external access required.
[02:50] Olivia Park: Let's walk through a hypothetical update flow so we're aligned — Marcus?
[02:55] Marcus Nguyen: Sure. Step 1: Redwood generates a signed artifact bundle (runtime + model + manifest) and hands it to your security team via a secure channel. Step 2: Your security team validates signatures with their private HSM or signs it themselves after inspection. Step 3: Physical transfer into the sterile network. Step 4: Local verification on the node ensures checksum and signature match before activation. Step 5: Rollback option — if verification fails the node retains the previous pinned model.
[03:25] Dr. Elena Ruiz: That fits our compliance needs. What's the support model if something goes wrong in the sterile site? We can't give remote shell access.
[03:33] Marcus Nguyen: Support model for air-gapped is commonly a runbook + remote-assisted troubleshooting via recorded logs — you produce sanitized logs via a secure handoff and we review. For critical failures we can ship a bootable rescue image for on-site application. We can also set up an emergency escalation where a vetted engineer is authorized to review signed logs.
[03:53] Samir Patel: Logs are tricky — they contain PII-ish assay IDs. We need log redaction. Can Redwood support granular audit log settings that remove sensitive fields?
[04:02] Priya Shah: Yes, logging configuration is configurable at token/model level. You can redact or exclude fields before logs are written. Also we can create a curated log export that strips assay identifiers and only includes stack traces and performance counters.
[04:15] Lucia Gomez: On the audit front, we need proof of key management, proof of image signing, and traceability for model changes. Will you provide artifacts auditors can consume?
[04:24] Olivia Park: Yes, we can provide a compliance package: SOC 2 Type II reports, an architecture whitepaper describing the private deployment, and a manifest audit trail for each rollout with timestamps and signer identities. We'll put that in the package I send.
[04:37] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Are there latency implications if we use quantized models or KV cache over NVMe? Our inference latency wall is tight for some assays — sub 80ms 95th percentile ideally.
[04:47] Marcus Nguyen: Sub-80ms on 16GB GPUs is challenging for large-context models. For short prompts and trimmed sequences it's feasible with careful batching and prefix caching. We'll run a benchmark during pilot using your sample payloads to generate a latency profile. If needed we recommend a small pool of larger VRAM cards for the strict SLO routes.
[05:04] Samir Patel: Benchmarks — we can provide representative payloads, but they contain PHI. How do you handle that?
[05:10] Priya Shah: For benchmarking we accept sanitized or synthetic payloads. If you need Redwood to run on real data, that would have to be inside your environment using the offline bundle during pilot and logs/artifacts remain on-prem.
[05:22] Ravi Menon: On the lifecycle side we need to know image composition — what parts are Redwood-controlled vs customer-controlled? We want minimal third-party code in the sterile image.
[05:32] Marcus Nguyen: The standard private image has three layers: boot image (OS and security patches), Redwood runtime (inference engine, launcher), and model artifacts. We can produce a customer-only variant where the customer builds the OS layer and we deliver only runtime and model bundles. The manifest will show exact package versions.
[05:48] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Good. About fallback — in case of resource exhaustion or a failed local model, can the node return to a safe degraded response instead of sending data out?
[05:57] Marcus Nguyen: Yes, the runtime supports graceful degradation policies. It can return predefined canned responses, an error code, or queue requests for later processing. No automatic outbound failover unless you explicitly enable a managed fallback (which you wouldn't do for an air-gapped environment).
[06:12] Samir Patel: Security controls — SSO, RBAC, and audit trails. We use SAML with our IdP. Can Redwood integrate?
[06:19] Olivia Park: Redwood supports SAML SSO for the control plane. For the private offline control plane we have a local SAML assertion proxy pattern or token-based RBAC mappings. We'll include the integration patterns in the playbook.
[06:30] Lucia Gomez: Data residency — some models can be sensitive even as embeddings. Are we able to prevent any telemetry from leaving the node?
[06:37] Priya Shah: Yes, telemetry is optional. For private, air-gapped deployments telemetry is disabled by default; any export must be explicit and packaged as a signed artifact.
[06:46] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Pricing — high level, how do you price a pilot for one node vs a dedicated reserved pool?
[06:52] Olivia Park: For pilots we typically offer a time-limited seat or reserved node pricing with a pilot discount. Dedicated reserved pools are contracted monthly. I'll follow up with a pilot quote that includes the single-node BOM and optional on-site assistance.
[07:04] Samir Patel: BOM — for the older servers do you have minimal PCI/driver requirements? Our nodes are old gen — limited NVLink, older CUDA.
[07:14] Marcus Nguyen: We'll list supported CUDA/drivers and recommended kernel flags. For GPUs with older drivers we may need a slightly older runtime build. That is fine for pilot — we support multiple runtime builds and can coordinate driver compatibility.
[07:26] Olivia Park: Let's cover timeline. Montrose would like to run a pilot in April if possible?
[07:31] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Yes, target April pilot. We have a compliance window the second week of April.
[07:36] Olivia Park: Action items and deliverables — we'll send the compliance pack and whitepaper, Marcus will deliver a BOM and an offline image signing proposal, and we'll propose pilot dates.
[07:46] Marcus Nguyen: One more technical note — model quantization and activation caching require a local NVMe with adequate IOPS for best throughput. For NVMe-less hosts we can fallback to in-memory but that increases memory pressure. I'll include a tradeoff table.
[07:59] Ravi Menon: Ok. Regarding emergency patches — how do we patch the runtime without risking integrity?
[08:04] Priya Shah: Patch flow: build signed patch artifact, provide patch manifest, customer verifies signatures and applies during the maintenance window. For hotfixes we can provide a signed rescue image and clear rollback instructions.
[08:15] Lucia Gomez: Will you supply an evidence bundle for each patch — e.g., who approved, hash, and when applied?
[08:21] Marcus Nguyen: Yes, the rollout manifest includes signer identity, timestamp, and hash; we can also include an approval comment field that maps to your change control ticket.
[08:30] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Anything else from Redwood?
[08:33] Olivia Park: Just that we'll avoid any default outbound fallbacks and treat the environment as fully isolated. We'll follow up with the docs pack and pilot quote.
[08:41] Samir Patel: Sounds good. We'll gather inventory and provide maintenance windows and stakeholders.
[08:46] Olivia Park: Great. We'll wrap with a short recap and next steps.

Recap / Next steps (verbatim):
- Redwood to send SOC2, ISO, architecture whitepaper and private deployment playbook (Olivia)
- Redwood to send pilot BOM and offline image signing workflow (Marcus)
- Montrose to share inventory, maintenance windows, and compliance contacts (Samir / Lucia)
- Schedule pilot kickoff (target week of 2025-04-07)

Links referenced: private deployment playbook: https://redwood.ai/private-deploy-playbook (access controlled)

Notes on transcription: some proper nouns and acronyms may be mis-transcribed, e.g., HSM vs HMS, NVMe spelled NVM-E, small filler words omitted.

End of transcript.

Mid-Q4 Health & Efficiency Check-in - Cerulean Health

Quarterly health check focused on usage trends (spike in embeddings), cost drivers, a reliability incident triage, and roadmap alignment for Q4. Discussed options for short-term cost controls (burst vs dedicated), rectangular caching improvements and a pilot for Redwood Dedicated capacity. Agreed on next steps: share usage export, security package, run small dedicated pilot benchmark, and schedule follow-up deep-dive on SSO/KMS integration.
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-05
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Dr. Maya Grant (Cerulean Head of AI), Eli Torres (Cerulean Platform), Samir Banerjee (Cerulean SRE), Hannah Cole (Finance)

Auto-generated summary: mid-quarter health, cost spike on embeddings, reliability incident on 10/28, roadmap ask for dedicated pilot.

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick roll call — we got Maya, Eli, Samir, Hannah?
[00:06] Dr. Maya Grant: Hi, Maya here. Sorry running a little late, thanks for doing this.
[00:09] Eli Torres: Eli, on platform.
[00:11] Samir Banerjee: Samir.
[00:12] Hannah Cole: Hannah, finance.
[00:13] Jordan Lee: Awesome. Priya from our infra team is here too — Priya, do you want to intro?
[00:18] Priya Patel: Yeah hi all, Priya Patel, Redwood SE. I'll be the main technical point for the dedicated pilot and the benchmarks.
[00:24] Jordan Lee: Great. Agenda — usage/cost trends, reliability incident brief, Q4 roadmap alignment, next steps. Sound good?
[00:29] Dr. Maya Grant: Yes.

[00:32] Jordan Lee: Ok, first slide — usage. We've noticed an embeddings spike in mid-October, Eli I know you were digging in. Can you summarize?
[00:38] Eli Torres: Sure, so we saw tokens up about 48% the week of Oct 12, but the big increase was embeddings volume — that's the recall microservice we rolled out. Our queries per minute doubled for 10 to 16 seconds windows — uh, sorry 10 to 16 days — and that drove cost up. It was mostly small vectors but lots of parallel requests.
[00:54] Priya Patel: That aligns with what our routing logs show. Lots of parallel short sequences don't batch well, so you hit per-request overheads. We suggested prefix caching and small-batch pooling to help.
[01:05] Samir Banerjee: Right, and for us the problem was the concurrency in the ECS tasks — we over-provisioned to meet latency SLOs and that cost scaled.
[01:12] Hannah Cole: So bottom line, what did that cost us month over month? I need the Finance view.
[01:17] Jordan Lee: We prepared a cost snapshot — month-over-month bill jumped about 22% compared to September after the recall rollout. We can send the detailed export.
[01:25] Hannah Cole: Please. Also can you show the per-route token breakdown?
[01:28] Jordan Lee: Yep, we'll include token-level CSV.

[01:32] Dr. Maya Grant: A question — is the spike primarily due to model choice? We're on a mid-sized open model, some quantization.
[01:38] Priya Patel: It's a mix. Model selection matters but the key is workload shape — lots of small embedding calls. Quantization helps CPU/memory for large batches but doesn't reduce per-call RPC overhead. Batching and a global cache for embeddings reduce cost significantly.
[01:50] Eli Torres: We tried the lightweight cache the week after and saw about 12% reduction in embeddings cost, but it caused a slight increase in tail latency for cold keys.
[01:58] Jordan Lee: That's expected tradeoff — can configure TTLs and warming policies.

[02:05] Jordan Lee: Moving to reliability — I know there was an incident on 2026-10-28 where a region failover affected 3 endpoints. Samir, can you walk through impact?
[02:13] Samir Banerjee: Yeah, so at 02:07 UTC our primary region hit an autoscaler bug, which caused a slow scale-up. The requests routed to fallback region but we didn't have the same model pinned there, so fallback used a larger-latency variant and latency spiked above our 200ms SLO for about 27 minutes. A few customers saw degraded p95.
[02:32] Priya Patel: From Redwood's side we saw the routing policy fall back to the regional variant — we flagged the model mismatch during the failover window. We recommend pinning compatible model variants across regions to guarantee consistent tail latency.
[02:44] Dr. Maya Grant: We did have different pinned variants — guess that was the issue. We need to understand automatic fallback behavior better.
[02:51] Jordan Lee: We'll send the failover timeline and the routing logs. 

[02:56] Jordan Lee: Quick question for SREs — are you comfortable with Dedicated capacity if we offered a small reserved pool for Cerulean to avoid cross-region fallback?
[03:04] Samir Banerjee: Sounds good in principle, but we need to see the economics. Hannah, from finance?
[03:09] Hannah Cole: If it reduces surprise overage and improves p95, yes it's promising, but we need hard numbers: commitment price, burst pricing, and expected ROI from lower overages.
[03:18] Priya Patel: We can propose a 3-month pilot on Redwood Dedicated with a small GPU-backed pool. We'll include autoscale policies and burst caps — the pilot includes a benchmark run to estimate token cost delta.
[03:29] Eli Torres: Ok that pilot would also help for private deployment questions we're getting from compliance.

[03:34] Jordan Lee: Speaking of compliance, any outstanding security controls Cerulean needs?
[03:38] Dr. Maya Grant: SOC 2 Type II is table stakes, but we also need KMS integration, audit logs retention for 13 months, and SAML SSO. We may also need VPC peering for the pilot.
[03:49] Priya Patel: We support Customer-managed KMS via HSM/KMS integrations, and audit logs — Redwood Console can export logs for retention. SAML SSO we support, and VPC peering is available for private deployments. There may be some network setup lead time.
[04:01] Samir Banerjee: Lead time how long? We have a freeze mid-November for network changes.
[04:06] Priya Patel: For VPC peering and KMS config for a pilot, estimate 2–3 weeks including security review; we can accelerate but that is realistic.
[04:14] Hannah Cole: Ok timeline noted.

[04:18] [04:18] Jordan Lee: Let's do a quick cost optimization checklist — Priya, walk us through low-hanging fruit.
[04:22] Priya Patel: Sure. 1) Batch embeddings where you can — use the batching client or queue small calls for 500ms and group them. 2) Enable prefix/KV cache for repeat queries. 3) Use model-family routing to route non-critical traffic to cheaper variants. 4) Tune autoscaler to avoid sustained over-provisioning. 5) Consider quantized variants for background jobs.
[04:41] Dr. Maya Grant: For #3, how risky is routing to cheaper model for synthesis tasks where quality matters?
[04:47] Priya Patel: You can do canary routing — split 10% cheap model and compare outputs using our quality monitors. If quality regressions are detected, it auto-rolls back.
[04:56] Eli Torres: We want the quality monitor to tie into our tests. Can Redwood send their evaluation hooks?
[05:01] Priya Patel: Yes, we'll share the eval webhook and a sample prompts set.

[05:06] Jordan Lee: Incidently finance — Hannah, any questions about the current invoicing cadence?
[05:11] Hannah Cole: Yes, can we get line-item detail per team and export in CSV? Also, can we get forecasted monthly spend if we move 20% of inference to Dedicated?
[05:19] Jordan Lee: We can provide both — we'll model a 20% shift scenario in the cost deck.

[05:24] [05:24] Dr. Maya Grant: A roadmap ask — Q4 is packed but we'd like Dedicated pilot first week of December, then roadmap review mid-December for next year. Is that feasible?
[05:34] Priya Patel: Pilot first week of December is tight but feasible if we start network/KMS work this week.
[05:40] Samir Banerjee: We'll prioritize the network ticket.

[05:44] Jordan Lee: Ok let's capture concrete next steps.
[05:47] Jordan Lee: Action items in chat — I'll read them out.
[05:50] Jordan Lee: 1) Jordan to share month-to-date usage export and per-route token CSV.
[05:55] Jordan Lee: 2) Priya to send security package (SOC2, KMS integration guide, SAML steps).
[05:59] Jordan Lee: 3) Priya to propose Dedicated pilot config and cost model for a 3-month pilot.
[06:05] Jordan Lee: 4) Cerulean (Eli + Samir) to open network change ticket and confirm freeze constraints.
[06:10] Jordan Lee: 5) Schedule follow-up deep-dive on quality monitoring and canary routing (Priya + Maya + Eli).

[06:16] Dr. Maya Grant: One more thing — we noticed occasional transcription artifacts in the logs, like model name spelled weird — not urgent but make sure diagnostic IDs are stable for postmortems.
[06:28] Priya Patel: We'll include stable request IDs and span traces in the logs export.

[06:33] Jordan Lee: Anything else from Cerulean?
[06:35] Hannah Cole: No, just make sure the cost scenario is clear.
[06:38] Eli Torres: No, good.
[06:40] Samir Banerjee: All good.
[06:42] Jordan Lee: Great, we'll follow up — expect the usage export and security package by EOD Nov 10, and a pilot proposal by Nov 12.
[06:51] Dr. Maya Grant: Thanks everyone.
[06:52] Jordan Lee: Thanks, bye.

End of transcript.

Notes: there are a few small transcription artifacts in the recording (model names and some numeric timing). Redwood to provide exact routing logs and timeline.

Priya Patel - Send security package (SOC2, KMS guide, SAML SSO steps) - Due: 2026-11-10
