Instrumentation strategy + KV/batching + OTLP integration sync - Meridian Vision

Deep dive on hooking Redwood runtime token-level and KV cache telemetry into Meridian's OpenTelemetry stack. Discussed OTLP exporter options, span semantics for per-token traces, sampling strategy to control cardinality, dashboards in Redwood Console vs Grafana, and constraints for VPC/on-prem deployment. Agreed on a short tracing spike and on-prem POC kickoff timeline.
Meeting header: 2025-10-30 16:00 PST | Duration: ~62 minutes | Recording: on
Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Noah (Redwood SRE advocate), Liam (Meridian Head of ML Infra), Priya (Platform Eng), Miguel (SRE), Anita (Security)

[00:00] Samira: All right folks, thanks for joining — we wanted to focus today on how you can ingest Redwood runtime telemetry into Meridian's OTEL stack and then visualize token-level and KV cache metrics, plus any constraints for your VPC/on-prem setup. Quick intros?
[00:18] Liam: Yeah hi I'm Liam, we run infra for Meridian's transformer services, running mostly on-prem in our colo. We've got Prometheus/Grafana and a Tempo instance for traces.
[00:32] Priya: And I'm Priya, platform; our big ask is getting per-request token latency and KV cache hit rate into our dashboards without exploding cardinality.
[00:45] Ethan: Great — that's exactly what we see a lot. Quick note, Redwood has a couple of exporters: hosted direct ingestion, and an OTLP/gRPC exporter you can run to your collector. We'll go through both.
[00:58] Miguel: Quick Q: will the exporter run inside our VPC without opening outbound ports? We have strict egress rules.
[01:10] Noah: Short answer: yes. For private (VPC) deployments we typically recommend a sidecar collector pattern, or using our local collector binary which writes to your internal OTLP gateway. You don't have to punch public egress.
[01:25] Anita: On compliance: we need to ensure token-level telemetry doesn't include raw prompt text or PII. How does Redwood handle scrubbed telemetry?
[01:38] Samira: Good point. We emit aggregated token metrics and hashed identifiers; by default we do not include full prompt text in spans unless you opt in for debug mode. We can show the scrub rules.
[01:51] Liam: Perfect. Can we talk about the span model for token-level traces? We want to maintain a single root span per request and sub-spans for heavy operations.
[02:05] Ethan: Sure — our recommended model is: root span = request lifecycle; child spans for model token generation loops and KV cache lookup spans. Token-level timing is recorded as attributes on generation spans rather than thousands of individual spans to avoid cardinality explosion. We can also emit per-token histogram metrics if you want per-token latency distributions.
[02:35] Priya: Histogram metrics sound promising. How do you correlate a cache miss to a specific token generation step?
[02:45] Ethan: We include attributes like cache.hit=true/false, cache.layer=prefix/kvcache, batch.size, seq.len. Then in OTLP you can filter by cache.hit==false and inspect associated latency histograms. The link between token position and cache event is done via an attribute token.index, but that's optional — we recommend sampled token.index only for debug traces.
[03:10] Miguel: Right, we don't want token.index in prod traces because of cardinality. What about sampling strategy?
[03:20] Ethan: We suggest hierarchical sampling: 1) low-rate full-trace sampling for debug (e.g., 0.1%), 2) event sampling for cache misses (always sample cache.miss), and 3) metric aggregation for p50/p90/p99 per model/route. Most teams rely on metrics for SLOs and sampling for investigatory traces.
[03:45] Liam: How does batching affect observed per-token latency? We need to ensure our SLOs reflect user-facing latency, not batched amortized latency.
[03:55] Ethan: Key point: batching reduces cost but masks tail latency. We provide both 'per-invocation' and 'per-token' metrics. For SLOs tied to interactive latency, use per-invocation p99; for throughput tuning, look at token/sec and batch.size distributions.
[04:20] Priya: Is batch.size exposed as an attribute?
[04:25] Ethan: Yes, batch.size and batch.queue_time_ms are attributes, plus kernel selection id and quantization profile (e.g., fp16, int8-q4).
[04:36] Miguel: Speaking of quantization — we saw different per-token CPU / GPU times across int8 vs fp16. Can Redwood emit the kernel-level timings?
[04:47] Ethan: We can emit optional performance counters: kernel.exec_ms, kv.lookup_ms, kv.deserialize_ms, kv.cache_hit_ratio. For on-prem you can enable more granular counters, but they increase metrics volume.
[05:05] Liam: Can we wire those into Prometheus? We have a pushgateway and long-term storage.
[05:12] Samira: Absolutely. The collector can translate OTLP metrics to Prometheus exposition; we also provide example prometheus.yml and Grafana dashboards. We'll share the dashboard json.
[05:24] Priya: When you say "token-level metrics" — are we talking one metric per token? That's unmanageable.
[05:30] Ethan: No — avoid one metric per token. We provide histograms and aggregated counters keyed by model, route, quantization, and logical features like user_tier. Token index is optional and only used in debug. The normal flow is aggregated histograms for token latency and counters for cache hits/misses.
[05:52] Miguel: How do we correlate Redwood Console traces and our Tempo traces?
[05:58] Noah: Use a shared trace_id propagated through OTLP. Redwood can inject a trace_id into our request headers so your collector and Redwood Console can correlate. We'll also export span links if you prefer to stitch.
[06:14] Priya: What about volume — if we sample every 1% but still produce many metric labels per model, what's the recommended retention/rollup?
[06:26] Ethan: Typical pattern: keep high-cardinality data for 7–14 days in raw form, then roll up to 1h buckets for 90 days. Token histograms are expensive; we pre-aggregate on the host and export summaries to reduce cardinality.
[06:45] Liam: Let's go through a concrete pipeline: Redwood runtime -> OTLP (local collector) -> Tempo/Prometheus -> Grafana. Any gotchas?
[06:58] Ethan: Watch for batching at the exporter layer. The collector will batch metrics/traces for efficiency; adjust exporter batch sizes so latency-sensitive traces flush quickly. Also ensure your OTLP receiver is sized for peak token throughput — many teams underestimate token/sec spikes.
[07:20] Priya: Is there an example OTLP config?
[07:24] Ethan: Yes — we'll send a minimal collector config: otlp receiver grpc, prometheus exporter, tempo exporter, and a tail-based sampling processor for cache.miss attributes.
[07:38] Miguel: Tail-based sampling — that means we buffer traces to see whether they contain a cache.miss before deciding to keep them? That adds memory overhead.
[07:47] Ethan: Correct; tail-based buys you better decisioning (e.g., keep traces that have errors or cache misses) but requires memory. We usually cap buffer size and fallback to probabilistic sampling under pressure.
[08:05] Liam: For VPC/on-prem restrictions, anything special about certs/KMS?
[08:12] Noah: For private deployments we integrate with your KMS for artifact signing and we support mTLS to your OTLP endpoint. No public keys need to be exposed. We can also run the entire collector inside your subnet.
[08:25] Anita: Will any telemetry include user tokens or PII? We need assurance for SOC2.
[08:32] Samira: By default no PII in metrics. Traces can include hashed ids but not raw prompts. We also provide an option to scrub by regex at the runtime exporter. We'll provide the scrub rules doc.
[08:48] Priya: Let's talk alerting: what alerts do you recommend for KV cache regressions?
[08:55] Ethan: Alerts we recommend: sudden drop in cache.hit_ratio by >10% over baseline, spike in kv.deserialize_ms, and increases in batch.queue_time_ms. Also correlate increases in per-invocation p99 with cache misses.
[09:12] Liam: Can Redwood Console surface these alerts or do we need to do this in Grafana?
[09:18] Samira: Both. Redwood Console can emit events to your pager or slack and we can forward to your alert manager. Many enterprises prefer central alerting in Grafana/Alertmanager.
[09:30] Priya: For the POC, we'd like a dashboard showing: p50/p90/p99 per invocation latency, token histograms, cache.hit_ratio, batch.size distribution, quantization profile usage.
[09:40] Ethan: That's straightforward. We'll share a template Grafana dashboard and a Redwood Console panel mapping.
[09:48] Miguel: Any recommendations on instrumentation libraries? We use java/kotlin for orchestration and python for model wrappers.
[09:55] Ethan: Use the OTEL auto-instrumentation for Python and Java, plus a small Redwood runtime shim that emits the model-specific attributes. We provide shims in python and java; the shim is a 2–3 file integration you can drop in.
[10:12] Liam: About cost — will exporting token-level histograms drive cloud ingress costs?
[10:18] Samira: Potentially if you route to hosted storage. For on-prem with your own collectors, you avoid egress. Also, using pre-aggregation and histograms reduces payload size.
[10:30] Miguel: Can we do derived metrics like tokens_per_user_per_minute?
[10:36] Ethan: Yes, either at the collector or in PromQL using rate() and grouping by user_id (but watch cardinality). We typically recommend grouping by user_tier rather than raw user_id for dashboards.
[10:50] Priya: Let's switch briefly to quantization telemetry — we want to ensure int8 models don't regress for specific prompts.
[10:58] Ethan: We emit quantization.profile and quality.regression_count attributes tied to evaluation prompts. For heavier regression detection we integrate with Redwood Optimize which runs evals and can trigger alerts when quality dips relative to a baseline.
[11:18] Liam: Does that eval data touch production prompts?
[11:22] Samira: No — evals are run on synthetic or recorded prompt sets; production prompt data never leaves your cluster unless explicitly permitted.
[11:33] Priya: OK. Can we see a quick walkthrough of the sample spans and metrics?
[11:38] Ethan: (screen share) here's a root span for request id abc123, we have child spans: token-gen-loop (with token_latency_histogram attr), kv-lookup span with cache.hit=false, and kernel.exec span with kernel.exec_ms=2.4. The trace has links to a prior warmup span. Note the names are semi-structured — some transcriber noise might call kernel "car nel" — sorry pasting note, bad auto-caption.
[12:10] Miguel: That sample's helpful. I see the token_latency_histogram buckets — how big are they by default?
[12:17] Ethan: We use exponential buckets tuned for typical transformer token latency (0.1ms to 500ms) but you can override.
[12:25] Priya: Anything else we should watch for in an on-prem POC?
[12:30] Ethan: Right-sizing the collector memory for tail-based sampling, ensuring OTLP endpoint scaling for token/sec peaks, enabling pre-aggregation for histograms, and firewall rules for the sidecar. Also coordination on kernel selection flags if you want lower latency at cost of throughput.
[12:48] Liam: Good. Let's recap concrete next steps.
[12:52] Samira: Recap: we'll send OTLP config example and Grafana + Redwood Console dashboard jsons; Ethan will run a 1-hour tracing spike with a test model to produce sample traces and demonstrate tail-based sampling and cache.miss capture; we'll schedule the on-prem POC kickoff with infra teams.
[13:08] Priya: And security docs.
[13:10] Anita: Yes please include KMS and SAML/SSO notes.
[13:14] Samira: We'll include SOC2 report and KMS integration notes.
[13:18] Liam: Sounds good. Anything else?
[13:22] Miguel: No, thanks — excited to move forward.
[13:26] Samira: Great thanks everyone. End.

Notes / artifacts referenced: "OTLP-collector-example.yml" (shared in chat), "grafana-dashboard-meridian.json" (shared), "redwood-scrub-rules.md" (link), "redwood-soc2-kms.pdf" (shared)

Sealed deploy checksum, driver provisioning and KV warmup sync

Meeting header: 2026-02-27 16:00 UTC | Duration: 72 minutes
Attendees: Jared Lin (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marco Rivera (Redwood CSM); Elena Mora (Granite Lead Infra), Tomás Ruiz (Granite ML Platform), Hiro Tanaka (Granite SecOps), Leila Ahmed (Granite SRE)
Shared links: internal doc - sealed-bundle-checksum (redwood-internal link), offline-license-playbook.pdf (shared after)

[00:00] Jared Lin: OK hi everyone, thanks for making time, quick intro — Jared from Redwood, Priya our SE, Marco on CSM side. Elena, Tomás, hi — want to surface the on-prem sealed deploy details today.
[00:12] Elena Mora: Hi all, yes we pulled together engineers from infra and sec. Primary goal is zero-network-install for both artifacts and license so we can validate drivers and perf before we flip prod.
[00:22] Priya Shah: Got it. We'll walk through checksum/GPG approach for artifact bundles, offline license flow and then deep dive into kernel/driver compatibility and KV warmup recommendations.
[00:30] Tomás Ruiz: Quick ask up front — we care most about tail latency at p95/p99 for chat workloads, but also throughput for batch embeddings. We'll be testing both.
[00:38] Priya Shah: Perfect, we'll call out config knobs — batching window, continuous batching, and prefix cache warmup steps. Also talk quant profiles - int8 vs int16 and perf/quality notes.

[00:52] Speaker 1: (mumble) are you going to provide the signed bundles as tar gz or rpm?
[00:56] Priya Shah: We provide tar.gz sealed bundles plus an envelope that contains signed SHA256 sums and a detached GPG signature. For customers who want packages we can produce .deb/.rpm but for air-gapped installs tar.gz is simpler.
[01:08] Hiro Tanaka: How do we validate offline? We can't egress to the internet for key lookup.
[01:12] Priya Shah: Good Q. We provide the public GPG key in the install media and the verification script. The flow is: vendor-signed bundle.tar.gz, "manifest.sha256" and "manifest.sha256.sig"; run gpg --verify with the provided public key. The installers we hand over include the pubkey pinned to the bundle so no external lookup.
[01:28] Leila Ahmed: Is there any HSM involved for license activation? We use an internal HSM cluster to ensure activation keys are not exfiltrated.
[01:35] Jared Lin: Yes, for enterprise we ship an encrypted offline license blob. The blob is signed by Redwood and encrypted with a customer public key (or wrapped for the customer's HSM). Activation is done locally by the license-manager service which talks to the on-host HSM or a customer KMS proxy. We'll share our recommended HSM integration patterns.
[01:50] Elena Mora: We need to see the license rotation and revocation story — if we rotate keys how do we update offline systems?
[01:56] Marco Rivera: Good point — our offline playbook covers periodic mailboxed rotation. We produce short-lived activation tokens that can be reissued via new sealed blobs delivered via the same offline channel. We also log revocation events in the audit bundle shipped to the customer — that can be imported into their SIEM.
[02:12] Tomás Ruiz: On the driver side — which NVIDIA driver/CUDA combos do you guarantee? We run R770 and R515 depending on node class. Also CUDA 11 vs CUDA 12.
[02:22] Priya Shah: We certify across a matrix. For 80xx/40xx GPUs we test on driver family 535+ with CUDA 12; for older Ampere/RTX classes we have validated 510/515 lines on CUDA 11. We'll send an explicit compatibility matrix. Note that NCCL versions matter for multi-GPU; we recommend matching our runtime image with NCCL version in the sealed bundle.
[02:44] Hiro Tanaka: Does your installer modify kernel modules via DKMS? Some hosts have immutable kernels in our fleet.
[02:50] Priya Shah: The sealed bundle contains prebuilt kernel modules for the exact kernels you list, plus a DKMS hook if you allow kernel module builds. For locked-down kernels we provide signed kernel modules and an installation path that uses kmodload with the module signature verified by the customer's keyring. If DKMS isn't permitted we can coordinate to push prebuilt modules compiled against the target kernel.
[03:08] Elena Mora: What about PCI firmware/BIOS requirements? We've run into performance cliffs when firmware mismatch and the NVLink topology changed.
[03:16] Priya Shah: We request a hardware manifest: kernel version, PCI firmware, BIOS, microcode. Our preflight script checks for required firmware and warns if incompatible. We also include an optional NV peer mapping script to validate NUMA and PCIe topology.
[03:30] Speaker 2: (crosstalk) and grub entries?
[03:33] Priya Shah: We don't touch GRUB by default — only for customers who want kernel cmdline tweaks to enable large page mappings or isolate CPUs. That step is explicitly documented and customer-controlled.

[03:48] Priya Shah: Switching to runtime perf — KV cache warmup. For chat workloads the biggest p99 wins come from preloading KV caches for common prefixes. We recommend a two-stage warmup: (1) synthetic prefix replay to populate LRU caches and page mapping; (2) targeted warmup of hot prompts extracted from your logs.
[04:06] Tomás Ruiz: How do you run synthetic prefixes offline?
[04:10] Priya Shah: We build a small warmup harness that runs tokenized prefixes through a headless runtime. It replays prefixes in random interleaving with adjustable concurrency to prime KV shards. It emits CSV with first-token latencies and token-per-second throughput. We'll share the harness as part of the sealed bundle.
[04:26] Tomás Ruiz: Are there special flags for KV cache prefetch to avoid cache churn?
[04:29] Priya Shah: Yes, set aggressive cache TTL for warmup, and run a low-overlap schedule to avoid evicting hot entries. In practice: 1) set prefix_cache_multiplier=2 for warmup run, 2) run at 0.25x expected QPS for 10-30 minutes; 3) after warmup revert TTL to normal. These keys are in our runtime config file.

[04:48] Speaker 3: (mumbled) quant stuff?
[04:51] Priya Shah: We recommend starting with int8 quant on non-critical models — it's a good cost/latency tradeoff but watch degradations in some QA benchmarks. For customer models we supply a quant profile (per-layer sensitivity) and a validation harness. For latency-sensitive chat models, int8 reduced token latency by ~15-25% in our tests but increased nll on rare tokens; for embeddings we prefer fp16.
[05:17] Elena Mora: If int8 causes accuracy drift, can you fallback to a float variant automatically?
[05:20] Priya Shah: Yes — our smart routing supports per-request model variant selection. In Dedicated/on-prem you can set a policy: if quality metrics exceed threshold in monitoring, switch traffic to a non-quantized variant or route low-risk traffic to int8. We also support canary rollouts of quant profiles.

[05:40] Jared Lin: Let's talk observability in an air-gapped site — how do we get traces and token-level cost telemetry back to Redwood?
[05:47] Hiro Tanaka: We will not allow telemetry egress. We need audit logs and traces locally.
[05:51] Marco Rivera: Understood. We have an on-host collector that stores metrics in local object store (S3 compatible) and produces a signed bundle you can export. For support cases we ask customers to upload signed bundles to a staging bucket via a secure transfer process; alternatively we can accept encrypted bundles on a USB or a courier.
[06:08] Leila Ahmed: Any concern about replay attacks on the license blob if someone grabs it physically?
[06:12] Jared Lin: The offline license blob is single-use and contains a nonce tied to the host's attestation machine-id. Our license-manager validates TPM/HSM attestation on activation. If someone copies the blob it won't activate on another host. We also include a time-bound window in the activation metadata.

[06:32] Tomás Ruiz: For multi-GPU perf — is NVLink required or can you run over PCIe and still keep throughput?
[06:38] Priya Shah: PCIe is OK for many workloads but for large context models NVLink reduces inter-GPU allgather cost a lot. Our recommendation: for >100k token cache footprints or very large KV shards prefer NVLink; otherwise optimized NCCL over PCIe works if PCIe gen is high and topology is balanced.

[06:58] Speaker 1: (laughter) can you give a sample preflight checklist?
[07:01] Priya Shah: Sure — preflight includes: hardware manifest, kernel versions, available DRAM, swap disabled, hugepages config, PCIe topology, driver version, CUDA version, NCCL version, thermal throttling checks, existing cgroup config. We'll attach the checklist.

[07:20] Elena Mora: About driver signing — if our fleet enforces module signature checks, will Redwood-provided modules be individually signed?
[07:28] Priya Shah: Yes, modules are signed using a key we co-manage or you can provide the signing key. We can either sign modules with our vendor key or provide unsigned modules plus instructions and a proxy key-signing workflow you run internally.

[07:40] Tomás Ruiz: On the install day, who will lead the handshake? We want an on-call SE.
[07:44] Jared Lin: Priya will lead runtime and driver install, Marco will coordinate logistics, and Jared will be on standby for licensing/audit. We'll provide a runbook and a checklist.

[07:56] Speaker 4: (brief pause) any gotchas on udev rules and device permissions?
[07:59] Priya Shah: Yes, ensure nvidia udev rules are present and the runtime user is in the video/dri groups. We also recommend isolating nodes via systemd cgroups and reserving CPU isolates for kernel threads to avoid jitter.

[08:15] Tomás Ruiz: We also saw tokenization mismatches when runtime Python/tokenizer pip versions differ. How do you lock those?
[08:20] Priya Shah: The sealed bundle contains a pinned runtime image and a tokenizer binary snapshot. We ship checksums for each binary. The runtime enforces tokenizer version at startup and will fail if mismatch to prevent silent drift.

[08:36] Elena Mora: If we need to patch drivers after install, what's the update path in air-gapped mode?
[08:41] Priya Shah: We support two update modes: replace+verify (deliver new sealed bundle, run verification, install), or patch module path for urgent security fixes. All updates go through the same GPG verification and produce an audit bundle. For large fleets we recommend an internal package repo behind your firewall and we provide signed packages to seed it.

[08:58] Jared Lin: Quick perf note — batching windows: for chat we see sweet spot ~30-50ms collection window for low-latency interactivity with batching; increasing to 80-100ms gives better throughput but adds latency. We expose batching.ms and max_batch_tokens in runtime config.
[09:16] Tomás Ruiz: And what about continuous batching / async tokens?
[09:19] Priya Shah: Continuous batching (streaming) reduces latency variance; we use a hybrid: prefer eager token emit once first token ready, while collecting subsequent tokens for batch compute. That setting is tunable per route.

[09:33] Speaker 2: (static) can you re-mention the checksum algorithm?
[09:35] Priya Shah: SHA256 with a detached GPG signature. We also include an incremental Merkle manifest for large artifact sets so you can verify partial transfers without rehashing the whole tarball.

[09:48] Hiro Tanaka: Are there PoC sized license terms? We need to trial for 2 weeks with limited tokens.
[09:54] Marco Rivera: Yes, we'll issue a timeboxed trial license blob that enables limited token budgets. We add telemetry to the audit bundle but it never egresses without your consent.

[10:04] Tomás Ruiz: For KV warmup benchmark you mentioned CSVs — can you share expected columns?
[10:08] Priya Shah: Columns: prefix_id, tokens_replayed, first_token_latency_ms, mean_token_latency_ms, tokens_per_second, cache_hit_rate. We'll include sample results.

[10:20] Elena Mora: Any known perf regressions when enabling large page support?
[10:24] Priya Shah: Large pages help reduce TLB pressure but can cause higher memory fragmentation; in our tests large pages improved p95 for long contexts but required tuning of slab allocators. We'll share recommended vm.nr_hugepages and libc tunables.

[10:38] Jared Lin: Quick recap before close — Priya will share the signed-bundle verification script, compatibility matrix, runtime preflight checklist, and the KV-warmup harness. Jared will ship offline license packaging docs and HSM integration notes. Elena will confirm install window and kernel/firmware list. Tomás will run initial warmup test post-install and share CSVs.

[10:58] Leila Ahmed: One last sec — what if we need emergency rollback during seaside? (laughs)
[11:01] Priya Shah: We include a fail-safe: each sealed bundle includes a rollback marker and we keep the previous runtime image available. Rollback is a mapped switch and will not require license reactivation if host-id unchanged.

[11:10] Jared Lin: Great thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the docs and runbook.
[11:14] Elena Mora: Thanks all.

[11:18] End of Call

Notes: transcription includes small speech artifacts; some proper nouns may be slightly off (e.g., "K-V cash" instead of KV cache in a couple spots). See attached: redwood/internal/sealed-bundle-checksum (shared after meeting).

POC: model evaluation & scoping - ZenWell shortlist

Discovery/POC scoping focused on selecting an open-model shortlist for a medical note summarization POC. Discussed success criteria (accuracy, hallucination rate, latency SLO), workload sizing, benchmark design, multilingual needs (EN + ES + PT), and operational constraints (VPC, SOC2, KMS). Agreed next steps: Redwood to run benchmarks on 4 candidate models and share results by 2025-05-17; customer to provide 2k de-identified sample notes and a priority eval rubric.
success criteria
workload sizing & qps
benchmark design & eval sets
open-model shortlist
multilingual/domain needs
security & deployment constraints
timeline & next steps
Redwood to run latency + generation-quality benchmark on shortlist and deliver spreadsheet by 2025-05-17
ZenWell to upload 2,000 de-identified clinical notes and priority rubric to shared S3 by 2025-05-13
Schedule a follow-up to review results and pick model for 4-week POC (target week of 2025-05-19)
Aisha Kapoor: send SOC2 + security checklist + example SSO SAML flow by 2025-05-12
Marco Diaz: prepare benchmark harness (latency, top-k hallucination probes, rouge/bleu-ish automatic metrics) and baseline scripts by 2025-05-16
Priya Raman: produce de-identified sample set (2k notes) and target labels + evaluation rubric by 2025-05-13
Sam Ortiz: confirm network/VPC peering feasibility for private deployment by 2025-05-14
[00:00] Aisha Kapoor: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:03] Priya Raman: Priya here – Head of ML at ZenWell.
[00:05] Sam Ortiz: Sam, backend.
[00:06] Lena Cho: Lena, PM.
[00:08] Marco Diaz: Marco from Redwood (SE).
[00:09] Aisha Kapoor: Great. Goal for today: scope the POC and pick a small open-model shortlist. We want to confirm success criteria, dataset, and timeline.
[00:20] Priya: Cool. High level — use case is clinical note summarization: take visit notes and produce SOAP-friendly summaries and patient-facing lay summaries. Must be accurate, low hallucination, support English and Spanish, possible Portuguese later. Latency target 99th <= 1s for interactive editor, and throughput about 10 qps during business hours, burst to 50.
[00:40] Sam: Also important — data can't leave our VPC for the Dedicated/private POC. We'll need to evaluate private deployment or at least VPC peering.
[00:48] Marco: Ok noted. We can do Dedicated or Private (VPC). We'll scope both options in parallel but the initial benchmark can run on hosted infra then port to private.
[00:56] Lena: Timeline — we'd like to pick the model in two weeks, run a 4-week POC after that.
[01:02] Aisha: Makes sense. Let's talk success criteria. Marco — from an SE perspective?
[01:06] Marco: For summarization we'd look at: automated metrics (ROUGE-L or adapted ones), but more importantly an hallucination rate measured by targeted probes, factuality checks against patient fields, and human acceptability. Target numbers: automated metric bump vs current baseline (we'll need baseline numbers — Priya?), and hallucination under 2% on our probe set for the POC to be compelling. Latency: p50 < 150ms token generation and 99th under 1s as Priya mentioned, cost per 1k tokens comparable to X (we'll show numbers).
[01:36] Priya: Our current baseline is an internal seq2seq model — roughly ROUGE-L 32 on our dev set, hallucination probes around 8-10%. Latency for our self-hosted model is erratic at scale.
[01:48] Aisha: Ok so we need models that increase quality and drop hallucinations. Now model shortlist. We recommend open models to start: Mistral-7B-Instruct, Falcon-40B-Instruct, Llama2-70B (if licensed), and MPT-30B-Instruct. Any constraints on size?
[02:10] Priya: We prefer smaller if they meet quality because infra cost matters. But accuracy and hallucination reduction is primary. Spanish support is a must.
[02:19] Marco: Quick notes on tradeoffs — Mistral 7B is very cost-effective and good on code/structured tasks but sometimes underperforms on nuanced clinical reasoning. Falcon-40B tends to be good for instruction-following, but historically shows more hallucinations unless tuned. Llama2-70B generally strong but heavier infra; licensing for commercial use needs to be checked. MPT 30B is a wildcard on clinical.
[02:45] Priya: What about 4-bit quantized int4 runs? We want to see latency/cost tradeoffs.
[02:51] Marco: Yes we'll run quantized runs (int8/int4) in the benchmark; expect some quality delta with int4 on some models. We'll include CPU fallback numbers too for cost comparison.
[03:00] Sam: Any mention of Red- uh Redwood's own optimizations e.g., KV cache improvements?
[03:04] Marco: Yeah we have continuous batching and KV cache strategies; note the transcript auto-gen sometimes shows K V cash — (laughs) — but yes those optimizations reduce per-token latency and cost in production.
[03:16] Lena: For the benchmark, what metrics do you plan to run?
[03:18] Marco: We'll do: ROUGE-L, ROUGE-1, a bespoke clinical factuality probe suite (we'll design ~300 targeted questions that check attributes like med lists, dosages, medications present/absent), hallucination scoring, latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) under our target loads, throughput at batch sizes 1/4/8, and memory footprint. We'll also do multilingual quality slices: EN, ES, PT where present.
[03:45] Priya: About the clinical probes — we'll need to map what counts as hallucination vs acceptable paraphrase. We'll provide a rubric with categories: hallucination (adds wrong med), omission (drops key med), paraphrase acceptable, privacy redaction.
[03:58] Aisha: Great. Data handling — Priya, can you confirm samples will be de-identified?
[04:03] Priya: Yes will be de-identified. We'll use our internal masker and then give synthetic IDs. We'll still want to ensure Redwood's handling is compliant with our DPA.
[04:10] Aisha: We'll send the security pack, SOC2 evidence, KMS options.
[04:14] Sam: For the private deployment, we need KMS integration (we use AWS KMS) and audit logs to S3 with retention policy.
[04:22] Marco: We support KMS and can stream logs to your S3 with configurable retention. We'll include that in the security checklist.
[04:30] Priya: Back to model shortlist — could we include a fine-tuned variant candidate? Maybe open instruction-finetuned Llama2 or a Llama-based tuned checkpoint?
[04:40] Marco: We can bench vanilla checkpoints and also a tuned lightweight LoRA-style candidate if you want to include a small supervised fine-tune step during the POC. That adds time (1 week) but often helps hallucination.
[04:51] Lena: That sounds interesting. Our product team might prefer a small supervised fine-tune if it reduces hallucinations.
[04:56] Priya: What's the expected compute footprint for a 4-week POC if we run a 2-model pilot at ~10 qps?
[05:03] Marco: Rough estimate: for a dedicated private pool for 2x 40B-ish models, you'd want 8x A100-80GB equivalents for steady 10 qps and burst to 50 with headroom; or we can do shared hosted dedicated with autoscaling. For smaller 7-30B models, you can get away with 2-4 GPUs depending on quantization. We'll provide a sizing spreadsheet.
[05:26] Sam: Cost estimates please — we need to present to execs.
[05:29] Aisha: We'll include ballpark numbers for hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[05:32] Marco: For the benchmark we'll provide normalized cost per 1k tokens and cost per inference at observed latency.
[05:37] Priya: Multilingual support — how do you surface language-specific regressions in the dashboard?
[05:42] Marco: Console can slice evals by language; we can add custom tags for your samples (en_es_pt). Also we support per-model per-route dashboards with token-level cost.
[05:50] Lena: Any concerns around HIPAA?
[05:53] Aisha: We have enterprise compliance options, SOC2, and contractual DPA — we'll send legal templates. For PHI in the POC, private deployment is the safest path and avoids egress issues.
[06:05] Priya: Regarding benchmarks — can we include a human evaluation slice? Maybe a small panel to rate 300 summaries for factuality and usefulness?
[06:12] Marco: Yes. We'll set up a human evaluation workflow and can run an initial 300-sample panel. Cost is separate but reasonable.
[06:19] Sam: For tooling — do you provide a harness to reproduce the test locally?
[06:23] Marco: We'll provide a reproducible harness (scripts + docker images) that you can run in your env or ours. Also we'll share seed prompts, sampling configs (top-p vs top-k), temperature sweeps, and deterministic eval settings.
[06:39] Priya: On prompt design — we have two output formats (clinical SOAP and patient-facing). Will that require separate evals?
[06:44] Marco: Yes, we recommend separate eval buckets per output format and treat them as distinct tasks because the constraints differ (length, tone, precision).
[06:52] Lena: Any immediate red flags on our side?
[06:54] Marco: None besides licensing checks for Llama2-70B for commercial use and the VPC network questions Sam raised. We'll clarify both.
[07:03] Aisha: Model shortlist we'll test: Mistral-7B-Instruct, Falcon-40B-Instruct, Llama2-70B (license permitting), MPT-30B-Instruct. We'll also include a tuned LoRA candidate for one of them if Priya's team approves.
[07:20] Priya: Sounds good. Can you rank them for multilingual capability quickly?
[07:24] Marco: Quick verbal rank: Llama2-70B > Falcon-40B > MPT-30B ~ Mistral-7B for Spanish, but this changes with finetune. We'll validate in the bench.
[07:35] Sam: Will you test hallucination probes that check for fabricated medications? That's our main worry.
[07:40] Marco: Absolutely — we'll create probes that obfuscate some fields and check if models invent data. We'll instrument precision/recall metrics for entity mention.
[07:50] Priya: We care about deterministic behavior — e.g., same prompt should yield same med list. How will you control randomness?
[07:55] Marco: We'll run deterministic decoding for evaluation (greedy or low-temp beam) and controlled sampling for production-like outputs. We'll record seeds and sampling settings so results are reproducible.
[08:06] Aisha: On deployment modes — initial bench on hosted infra is fastest. Then port winning model to your VPC for a private POC. Does that align?
[08:12] Sam: Yes but network policies must be validated first.
[08:15] Priya: Also license: if Llama2-70B commercial license is an issue, we may deprioritize it.
[08:20] Marco: We'll check licensing and present alternatives (e.g., Llama 2 via appropriate license or MetaContact).
[08:26] Lena: Any performance tradeoffs with LoRA?
[08:29] Marco: LoRA adds small runtime overhead for adapters but usually negligible; it can dramatically reduce hallucinations if trained well. Training time is short for a few epochs on 2-4 A100s.
[08:40] Priya: What about evaluation throughput — we have 2k samples, how long will the bench run?
[08:44] Marco: Depends on model and batch size. Rough estimate: for a 40B model at batch 8, the full run across metrics and language slices might take 6-8 hours on adequate infra. For multiple models plus quantizations maybe a day. We'll parallelize.
[08:58] Sam: Can you commit to finishing the bench in one week?
[09:01] Marco: We'll aim for a prioritized bench within 5 business days for the four models in the shortlist (hosted runs). Full swept runs (quantization + human eval) might extend to two weeks.
[09:11] Aisha: Ok targets: Redwood delivers initial bench spreadsheet by 2025-05-17. Customer provides the de-id dataset and rubric by 2025-05-13. Follow-up meeting week of 2025-05-19 to choose the POC model and deployment approach.
[09:27] Priya: Agreed. A couple of quick technical Qs — does your runtime support fused attention kernels and custom CUDA ops for Mistral?
[09:33] Marco: Yes we have kernel selection and compile-time optimizations. We'll test kernel set per model in the bench.
[09:39] Lena: Anything else on compliance?
[09:41] Aisha: We'll get legal templates. Also we'll include an SOC2 attestation excerpt.
[09:47] Sam: Network — we'll share our VPC CIDR and networking contact, but need to know what open ports Redwood needs for peering.
[09:53] Marco: We'll send a short network checklist.
[09:56] Priya: One last thing — can you include an evaluation of the models on redaction safety (PII/PHI leakage)?
[10:00] Marco: Yes we'll include probes that check for hallucinated PHI and verify model doesn't introduce specific PII.
[10:06] Aisha: Perfect. Any other questions? (brief silence)
[10:10] Lena: No.
[10:11] Sam: Not for now.
[10:12] Priya: Thanks.
[10:13] Aisha: Recap: Redwood to run host bench across four models and quant configurations, share spreadsheet by 2025-05-17; customer to provide de-id samples + rubric by 2025-05-13; next meeting week of 2025-05-19. Action items and owners on the recap email after this call.
[10:30] Marco: I'll put the benchmark plan and initial config in the shared drive and tag Priya.
[10:36] Aisha: Thanks everyone. Meeting adjourned.

Tail surge mitigation: streaming vs buffering deep dive

Deep dive on p95/p99 tail behavior during policy-search surge. Covered differences between streaming and buffered (non-streaming) response modes, network hop contribution, KV cache hotkeys, batching strategies, and quantization trade-offs for Aurora's VPC deployment. Agreed to run a controlled 24-hour soak with synthetic surge and share dashboard + traces.
--- Meeting Header ---
Date: 2026-03-28
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Claire N. (Redwood), Marcus L. (Redwood SE), Asha P. (Redwood SA), Priya K. (Aurora Head of Platform), Jamal W. (Aurora SRE), Elena S. (Aurora ML), Tom B. (Aurora CTO)
Recording ID: ff-20260328-aurora-td-07

Summary (auto): Deep technical session to isolate sources of tail latency during policy-search surge for Aurora Insurance. Focus on streaming vs buffered response modes, network hops, KV cache behavior, batching, and quantization.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Claire Nguyen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. um, we'll go through the p95/p99 behavior you saw in staging last week, and dig into streaming vs buffering strategies and where the tail actually comes from. Marcus, do you want to start with the observed numbers?
[00:18] Marcus Lee: Yeah, sure. So Aurora sent a sample trace last Friday, it showed median ~70ms but a p95 of 210ms and p99 spiking to 520ms during a brief 10-minute surge. That was with buffered responses (non-streaming) and 2 replicas behind the LB.
[00:36] Priya Kapoor: Right, and to add context, our users do a policy-lookup flow that fans out to 3 prompts in parallel and then we do a final ranking call, so bursts concentrate at about 1.2x normal QPS during peak times.
[00:51] Jamal Wright: We also observed that the p99 correlates with NAT gateway scaling events in our VPC - when a new NAT pair spins up, connections get rebalanced and some requests add an extra 30-80ms.
[01:07] Marcus Lee: That's a good callout. Network hops are often under-estimated in latency budgets. For the Redwood side we instrument at request ingress, kernel selection, kv cache checks, and token generation. The traces you sent show a few rows where the KV cache lookup was fine but the first token suffered a ~120ms wait.
[01:30] Elena Soto: Is that the "KV cash" you said earlier? sorry, I wrote kv cash in notes, clearly transcribe...
[01:36] Marcus Lee: (laughs) kv cache, yup. sometimes whispered as kv cash in the transcript.
[01:42] Tom Becker: Can you unpack streaming vs buffered for us? If we flip to streaming, does that change p99 significantly?
[01:50] Asha Patel: Short answer: sometimes yes, sometimes no. Streaming reduces tail impact from token-by-token generation because you start delivering earlier, but it can surface jitter if network hops add per-chunk latency. Buffered (non-streaming) can hide that jitter until finalization, so you might see worse p95/p99 at end but fewer incremental delays. There's also a CPU and context switching tradeoff on the server side for many concurrent streaming connections.
[02:18] Priya Kapoor: So streaming could make intermediate latencies visible to our frontend, but overall p99 for the end-to-end call might improve?
[02:25] Marcus Lee: Exactly. In our internal tests we saw streaming reduce p95 by ~20% in steady-state for 2-3 token chunk sizes, but when there's a network flake in the middle of a chunk, the perceived latency jumps for that user.
[02:41] Jamal Wright: Our firewall team asked about keepalives and TLS session reuse because we see session renegotiation during NAT rebalances. Does Redwood support long-lived connections from the VPC to reduce that?
[02:53] Claire Nguyen: Yes, for Dedicated and Private we recommend persistent connections and pinning to dedicated gateways. For your VPC setup, we can provide a private peering option to reduce NAT bounce and you can also use connection pooling at the LB layer.
[03:07] Elena Soto: On the ML side, how much does quantization change the tail distribution? We were worried that int8 or llama.cpp-like quant could increase variance.
[03:15] Marcus Lee: Good question. Quantization reduces median token latency because the kernel runs faster, but it can increase jitter in rare cases where fallback to higher precision happens (e.g., for custom ops or attention patterns). In our tests quantized fp8/int8 variants had a slightly higher p99 tail on very long sequences unless KV caching absorbed most of the repeated tokens.
[03:38] Priya Kapoor: Hmm ok. We run a lot of short prompts (average 24 tokens) with a few longer ranking calls. Would KV caching help more for the short ones or the ranking ones?
[03:47] Marcus Lee: KV caching helps for continuation/refixing patterns – so the ranking call that fans out then continues will benefit if you can cache the initial prefix. Short one-off queries less so. But there's a big win if you pre-warm the cache for the top N hot prefixes; that reduces both median and tail since cold starts are often the worst offenders.
[04:05] Jamal Wright: We're seeing hotkeying on two templates: "policy_search_v1" and "entity_expand_v2". Can Redwood automatically shard or TTL those keys differently?
[04:13] Asha Patel: We have config for key TTLs and hotkey isolation. For example, you can route heavy hitters to a small warm pool so they don't evict general cache entries. Also prefix partitioning helps. But if a single tenant floods one key you'll still see contention unless you apply per-key rate limits.
[04:31] Tom Becker: What about batching? Our instinct is to increase batch size to improve throughput, but we worry about added latency for small urgent calls.
[04:39] Marcus Lee: Dynamic batching with adaptive timeouts is the usual pattern: you set a max batch delay (say 8-12ms) and a max batch size. For latency-sensitive routes keep the timeout short and accept lower throughput. For backend ranking where throughput matters more you can increase window. Redwood Optimize can recommend per-route batch config based on your observed seq length distribution.
[05:00] Priya Kapoor: Any quick math you can show for effect on p99 if we go from batch delay 5ms to 15ms?
[05:07] Marcus Lee: Roughly, added batching delay is added to every request in the batch, so worst-case p99 can increase by that window. If your p99 was 520ms because of sporadic kernel scheduling, adding 10ms might be negligible. But if your baseline is tight, it can push you over SLOs. We'll produce a sensitivity spreadsheet.
[05:27] Claire Nguyen: (interruption) Also remember network hop + NAT jitter compounds with batching delay, so it's multiplicative in the tail.
[05:34] Jamal Wright: On instrumentation — the traces you sent were great but we need span-level breakdowns we can correlate with our VPC subnets. Can you attach span IDs to your traces?
[05:44] Marcus Lee: Yes we can include full span traces and also export them to your OTEL collector. We'll annotate the spans with kernel type, quantization variant, and cache hit/miss flags.
[05:56] Elena Soto: About streaming chunk sizes — you mentioned 2-3 token chunks earlier. Is there a sweet spot?
[06:02] Marcus Lee: Empirically 2-4 tokens per chunk balances start-of-response latency and network overhead. If you go 1 token chunks you pay more overhead per chunk; if you go >6 tokens you start to increase first-byte latency. Also chunking interacts with chunk reassembly on the client and your frontend timeouts.
[06:21] Tom Becker: If we enable streaming for the ranking flow, would that break any existing front-end logic?
[06:26] Priya Kapoor: Our frontend expects a single JSON response now. Switching to streaming would require changes to the aggregator to accept partials. That's non-trivial.
[06:33] Asha Patel: If changes are hard, consider hybrid: deliver a small 1-2 token preview stream to improve perceived latency while still finalizing a single JSON body at the end. That gives perceived snappiness without re-architecting too much.
[06:50] Jamal Wright: One specific concern: TLS renegotiation during NAT rebalancing caused a batch of requests to stall ~120-150ms. Would private peering eliminate that?
[06:59] Claire Nguyen: Private peering or a dedicated gateway eliminates the NAT hop and should remove that class of 30-150ms spikes. We recommend that for Dedicated customers with strict tail SLOs.
[07:12] Priya Kapoor: Great. Can you outline the concrete experiment? We want to see numbers for streaming vs buffered and q8 vs fp16.
[07:19] Marcus Lee: Proposed experiment — we'll run three variants across identical traffic: (A) buffered fp16, (B) buffered quantized (q8), (C) streaming fp16 with 3-token chunks. Each run 6 hours stable then 18 hours soak including synthetic 1.5x surge. We'll capture p50/p95/p99, top 50 slowest traces, and network hop counts.
[07:40] Tom Becker: Also make sure to include spike scenarios where we tear down a NAT and re-establish to simulate real infra churn.
[07:47] Asha Patel: We'll add that. Claire will share the benchmark doc and the orchestration playbook.
[07:52] Claire Nguyen: I'll drop links in the follow-up: perf spreadsheet (https://redwood.example/reports/aurora-p99), tracing dashboard sample, and a short runbook for peering.
[08:03] Priya Kapoor: Anything else on quantization safety? We need to be sure there are no regressions for our regulated policy text outputs.
[08:10] Marcus Lee: We'll include a quality eval set — ~200 prompts with golden outputs and measure rouge/bertscore and human-inspected diffs for top 20. If quantization shows >2% regression on critical prompts we won't recommend it for those routes.
[08:26] Jamal Wright: On the cache side, if we isolate hotkeys to a warm pool, what does that cost look like?
[08:33] Asha Patel: Cost depends on the size of warm pool and hit ratio. Warm pools are just reserved memory on the serving nodes; we can give an estimate after we see your prefix distribution.
[08:42] Elena Soto: Could you also include a run with pre-warming the cache for top 500 prefixes? We want to know cold-start impact.
[08:49] Marcus Lee: Yep, we'll include pre-warm vs no-prewarm in the plan.
[08:54] Tom Becker: Ok sounds actionable. Any blockers from Redwood side to run the tests in our staging VPC?
[09:00] Claire Nguyen: We'll need your staging network map and an API key for a dedicated test account. We'll also need permission to accept a small NAT peering for the duration if you want to test private connectivity.
[09:10] Priya Kapoor: We'll provide that by Tuesday.
[09:14] Claire Nguyen: Great. To recap: Redwood will run the 3-variant experiment, attach full spans to OTEL, include quant evals, and recommend batching/streaming configs. Aurora will provide topology, traceroutes, and approve staging connectivity. Follow-up on 2026-04-06.
[09:30] Jamal Wright: Thanks, that was super helpful.
[09:33] Claire Nguyen: Thanks everyone. I'll send the notes and the plan shortly.
[09:36] (call ends)

--- References / Artifacts mentioned ---
- Perf spreadsheet: https://redwood.example/reports/aurora-p99
- Tracing dashboard sample (will be shared)
- Security docs link (SAML/SOC2) requested by Aurora - to be attached

--- End transcript ---

Prefix Coherence & Long-Context Paging runtime triage - BlueHarbor Systems

Header:
Date: 2026-05-20 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya (AE), Sanjay (SE), Lina (SE), Jordan (Head of ML), Priya (Infra), Tomás (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto):
- Deep dive into unexpected eviction/paging behavior when serving long user sessions; focus on prefix reuse across customers and how prefetch heuristics interact with KV cache TTL and quantized model memory footprints.
- Agreed next steps: share prefetch heuristics, run benchmark, provide security docs for VPC/on-prem staging.

Topics:
- KV cache eviction patterns
- Paging spillover under long-context workloads
- Prefix reuse vs. prefix hotspotting
- Batching interplay and quantization memory changes
- VPC/on-prem deployment constraints (disk/IO, NVMe spillover)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (AE): All right everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to get into the weeds on the prefix coherence issue you reported where after about 20k tokens the latency spikes and you see a lot of spill/paging activity. Jordan, do you want to quickly frame the problem?
[00:18] Jordan (Head of ML): Yeah, sure. So we run multi-turn assistants with long session history, sometimes 10k to 30k tokens. After steady state, the p99 latency climbs, we see eviction logs and then more KV loads, it almost thrashes. We suspect some prefix reuse across different user sessions but not sure why eviction seems correlated with certain quantization settings.
[00:40] Sanjay (SE): Okay, got it. When you say "eviction" are we seeing full KV eviction events or small per-shard TTL expiries? Can you show a snippet of logs?
[00:52] Tomás (SRE): We have a sample in the ZIP we uploaded, but here's an excerpt: "kv-evict: shard-7 prefix=usr_47abcd evict_count=120 spike_ms=900" and then later "page-out: nvme0n1: 3.4GB". There's also a line where the runtime says "prefetch miss" a bunch.
[01:14] Priya (Infra): Important detail: our private deployment is on the VPC appliance - not fully air-gapped but the NVMe backing is a 1.6TB local pool, we configured quantized weights to int8. We also had a model variant with Q4_0 for one lane.
[01:32] Lina (Solutions Eng): That mix—int8 and Q4_0—can change the memory profile per instance which affects how the KV cache fills. We usually see more frequent prefix evictions when per-model KV footprint fluctuates.
[01:45] Jordan: Interesting. I thought the KV was independent of quantization? The cache stores KV keys/values for past tokens; why would quant change that?
[01:55] Sanjay: Two things: model quantization changes per-layer activation sizes and sometimes changes KV element packing (we've seen the runtime pack kv entries differently when the kv-value dtype changes). Second, the allocator and GC heuristics depend on resident memory pressure—so if the quantized model is using a bit more scratch or the model memory isn't aligned with our prefetch assumptions, the cache will see earlier eviction.
[02:20] Maya: Let's walk through the high-level architecture here so everyone's on the same page. Redwood serving runtime keeps a per-prefix KV in RAM up to a TTL or until memory pressure triggers eviction. We also do prefix-aware prefetch: when a request for prefix P arrives and we've seen a reuse pattern, we try to prefetch the likely next KVs into a hot store. If prefetch guesses are wrong, prefetch blobs can push memory high and force eviction of other prefixes.
[02:48] Jordan: In our case, I think prefix reuse across tenants is high—users frequently share similar system prompts and templates. Is there mitigation around prefix isolation?
[03:00] Sanjay: We provide namespace isolation options (per-tenant prefix namespaces) but for your workload you had enabled prefix pooling to boost cache hit rates across tenants. That pooling increases chance of hotspots because shared prefixes become "hot" and then eviction ripple effects occur for long tail prefixes.
[03:18] Tomás: So turning off pooling would increase miss rate for shared prefixes but might reduce tail thrash. Tradeoff, got it.
[03:26] Priya: We did try toggling pooling earlier, it helped a little but not enough—latency still increases at ~20k tokens. Also noticed a correlation with batching: when we raise batch size throughput increases but latency spike frequency also increases.
[03:42] Lina: Right—that's because larger batches cause more concurrent KV accesses and increase working set temporally. Our continuous-batching mechanism aggregates across requests and can hold KV references longer inside the runtime. If the batch contains many different prefixes, you get a temporary combined working set that outstrips available hot memory and triggers eviction/paging.
[04:05] Jordan: That aligns with our telemetry. We saw p50 still good; p95/p99 drifted once concurrency hits ~180 reqs/sec sustained.
[04:16] Sanjay: A few immediate debugging checks: 1) confirm per-shard resident set size, 2) check prefetch hit/miss ratio over time, 3) compare quantization profiles across instances. Priya, can you dump the runtime metrics for a problematic window?
[04:30] Priya: Yes, will share traces. We have histogram outputs and slab occupancy metrics.
[04:36] Maya: Let's talk about paging details—your logs showed NVMe page-out. Our runtime will spill cold KV pages to local SSD if RAM pressure crosses threshold. Paging works but it's slower and increases token latency. We need to know whether the paging was sustained or bursty.
[04:55] Tomás: From the sample, it was bursty: a big spill then repeated small writes while the eviction rate climbed. Not continuous.
[05:03] Sanjay: Bursty spills typically mean a misaligned prefetch window: the prefetch influx created a spike and then the runtime tried to spill the least recently used prefixes. If spills are asynchronous it's okay but repeated spill+read cycles cause thrash.
[05:18] Jordan: Any heuristics you can recommend for prefetch sizing?
[05:22] Sanjay: We've had success with adaptive prefetch: start conservative—prefetch the top 2 most likely continuations, monitor hit ratio; if hit ratio > 0.7 for 30s window, increase. For your workload—because prefix reuse is high—set initial concurrency-safe prefetch to 4 with strict upper bound memory caps. We'll share a config.
[05:42] Maya: Also consider eviction policy tuning: default is LRU per-shard. For your workload we can shift to a frequency-based policy (LFU-ish) to keep stable shared prefixes resident. That helps when a small set of prefixes dominate traffic.
[05:58] Priya: If we move to LFU does that complicate multi-tenant fairness? We worry hot tenants starving other customers.
[06:06] Lina: Good point. We support hybrid policies: primary LFU weight on pool-level but with per-tenant fairness quotas. You can cap the max resident prefixes per tenant to avoid starvation.
[06:18] Tomás: One more question: when you say "prefix"—how granular is that? Is it per prompt template or per conversation id?
[06:25] Sanjay: Can be either, configurable. For your setup you used conversation-id grouping but many customers opt for prompt-hash grouping. If you hash too coarsely you create bigger hot groups; too fine-grained and you lose hit rate. There's a sweet spot depending on reuse patterns.
[06:42] Jordan: Our reuse is mostly prompt-template based across users, so maybe we should move to prompt-hash grouping.
[06:48] Maya: Let's also talk about quantization interaction—Priya you mentioned int8 and Q4_0 mix. The runtime's memory accounting currently approximates KV footprint using a per-model factor. If models change dtype mid-flight (e.g., canary deploys), accounting lags and can under- or over-provision hot store. We recommend uniform quant profile across a deployment pool.
[07:10] Priya: We had a canary lane for Q4_0 for cost reasons. Do you recommend stopping that?
[07:15] Sanjay: For production long-context workloads it's safer to maintain a consistent quant profile for the serving pool. If you need mixed precision, isolate them into separate pools with separate cache caps.
[07:26] Jordan: That makes sense.
[07:29] Maya: Another angle is batch shaper and KV pinning—if you can pin critical prefixes (system prompts) into a tiny persistent hot slab, those won't be evicted except under extreme pressure. We can configure pin lists via the console or via API.
[07:44] Tomás: Pinning looks promising. Is pin size small?
[07:47] Lina: Pins are small; they use reserved hot memory and are accounted separately. You set a pin quota per pool.
[07:53] Priya: Regarding disk IO—our NVMe configuration is default smoothed lz4 compressed spill files. Do compression settings affect spill/read latency much?
[08:03] Sanjay: Yes. Compression lowers dump size but increases CPU cost on spill/read. If your NVMe is the bottleneck, reduce compression to minimize CPU overhead; if network/IO is the limit, compress more to reduce bytes written. We'll correlate your CPU vs IO metrics.
[08:19] Jordan: There was a mention in our logs about "kv prefix shadowing" – what does that mean?
[08:24] Sanjay: Shadowing is when two prefixes hash-collide in the small fast-access index and the runtime keeps one hot copy shadowed while the other is in cold store. It's rare but when it happens under heavy churn you can get unexpected misses. We can increase index size or change hash function, at cost of memory.
[08:41] Maya: Ok let's list immediate mitigations: 1) isolate quant profiles into separate pools, 2) enable prefix pinning for system prompts, 3) adopt adaptive prefetch with conservative starting window, 4) consider LFU hybrid policy with per-tenant quotas, 5) tune compression settings for spill files.
[09:01] Priya: For testing, we'd like a controlled benchmark. We usually replay 1000 sessions with avg 15k tokens and vary concurrency. Can Redwood run a 30-min bench to reproduce the spike?
[09:12] Lina: Yes we can run a benchmark using your traces if you provide them. We can do it on a staging VPC with identical NVMe and model config.
[09:21] Jordan: We'll upload the traces.
[09:23] Sanjay: A few more notes on telemetry you should include in the logs: per-prefix reuse heatmap, slab occupancy over time, per-shard eviction timeline, prefetch hit/miss timeline, and per-instance resident set snapshot. Those help us pinpoint whether it's a single shard or cross-shard correlation.
[09:41] Tomás: We'll add those metrics.
[09:43] Maya: Question from my side—do you need us to change anything in your VPC config?
[09:48] Priya: We have 16GB reserved per runtime container for hot memory and 256GB NVMe. Is that small?
[09:55] Sanjay: 16GB hot is modest for 30k token sessions when multiple prefixes are hot. You might benefit from bumping hot memory to 24GB or more depending on resident slab size. But that depends on cost and instance type.
[10:08] Jordan: If we bump hot memory, do we need different instance types?
[10:12] Lina: Typically yes; more RAM per GPU node or use nodes with more host memory. We can recommend instance families.
[10:19] Priya: For the on-prem box we have constraints on RAM; NVMe is the preferred buffer. Is there a recommended spill strategy for memory-constrained boxes?
[10:29] Sanjay: For low-RAM boxes, be conservative on prefetch and pin only the top-critical prefixes; also increase spill throttle so it batches writes rather than many small writes. Use async read-ahead to minimize read latency.
[10:40] Jordan: Any thoughts on batching strategy — should we throttle batch size instead of concurrency?
[10:45] Sanjay: Throttle both. Use a batch shaper that caps effective concurrent working set: limit the number of distinct prefixes per batch and set batch timeout so you don't accumulate widely diverse prefixes into a single big batch.
[10:57] Maya: There's a question that often comes up—fallback to smaller model variants when memory pressure is high, does Redwood support automatic fallback?
[11:02] Lina: Yes, runtime supports routing rules to fallback to a smaller model variant or to an approximate quantized variant. But fallback changes the token output quality and you should test it.
[11:12] Jordan: We might consider fallback as last-resort.
[11:15] Sanjay: Also worth noting—if you fall back mid-session you may break KV compatibility (kv layout differences) unless you use a migration shim. We can configure session pinning to avoid mid-session fallback or have a warm-up path.
[11:28] Priya: Good to know.
[11:30] Maya: Let's recap the root cause candidates we agreed on: mixed quant profiles causing accounting variance, prefetch surge creating burst working set, prefix pooling hotspotting, and batch concurrency increasing transient working set. Any others?
[11:44] Jordan: Maybe hash collisions and NVMe IO contention.
[11:47] Tomás: Also our custom plugin for session stitching—it may create extra temporary prefixes per request.
[11:54] Sanjay: Right – if you generate ephemeral prefixes per request that will blow up the unique prefix count. Consider collapsing ephemeral tokens into a single conversation-level prefix to reduce cardinality.
[12:05] Maya: Action items we captured: Sanjay to draft heuristics doc, Priya to upload logs, Maya to send security + deployment checklist, Redwood to run benchmark once traces are uploaded.
[12:18] Jordan: Timeline is tight; we'd like the bench by end of next week.
[12:21] Maya: We'll aim for that.
[12:23] Tomás: Quick question—do you have any tooling to visualize prefix heatmaps?
[12:28] Lina: Yes, Console has a prefix telemetry view; we can share a link to a demo dashboard.
[12:33] Priya: Please share.
[12:35] Maya: I'll send the dashboard link and the security pack.
[12:38] Jordan: Thanks everyone, that was helpful.
[12:41] -- End of recording --

Post-call notes:
- Customer to provide traces and expanded logs (per action item).
- Redwood will stage a replicate bench and share prefetch heuristics + LFU hybrid config.
- Security materials: SOC2, network diagram for VPC, and on-prem checklist to be shared by Maya.

References mentioned during call:
- link: staging-bench-playbook (we referenced the playbook on internal console)
- link: prefix-telemetry-dashboard (console demo link)

Verdant Systems POC - weekly performance sync

Weekly POC sync reviewing benchmark delta vs Verdant's incumbent provider. Redwood reports strong median throughput improvements but a small P95 latency regression on long-tail conversational requests. Agreed next steps: instrument trace for cold KV misses, try tuned quantized variant for throughput, provide dedicated slot estimate, and share updated benchmark spreadsheet and security docs.
Luca Moretti: add distributed trace tags for KV miss path and push new logs (due 2027-12-05)
Aisha Khan: send updated benchmark sheet with per-route p50/p95 and unit-cost calc (due 2027-12-06)
Redwood/SE: run quantized model variant A/B for 24h window and report throughput gains (due 2027-12-09)
Redwood to publish updated benchmark sheet: https://redwood.app/sheets/VDNT-bench-v3
Customer to whitelist Redwood IPs and enable longer trace window for next run
Schedule dedicated-slot pricing review call (AE+Finance) week of 2027-12-13
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-12-03
Time: 14:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Khan (Redwood AE), Luca Moretti (Redwood SE), Rhea Patel (Verdant CTO), Miguel Santos (Verdant ML Eng), Dana Lee (Verdant Infra), Oliver Grant (Verdant Product)

Summary (auto-gen, may be noisy):
Redwood: median throughput up ~2.6x vs incumbent for our streaming workload; p95 for longer ctx requests drifting 30-120ms higher on certain keys. Work to instrument KV cache misses and test quantized variant. Discussed dedicated slot ask and security artifacts (SOC2 scope, KMS).

Transcript:
[00:00] Aisha Khan: hey everyone thanks for jumping on, quick round robin who we got real quick?
[00:06] Rhea Patel: hey, Rhea here, CTO at Verdant. Miguel and Dana joining too.
[00:09] Miguel Santos: Miguel, ML. Morning for you all.
[00:12] Dana Lee: Dana infra. we'll be the one flipping the firewall switches.
[00:15] Aisha Khan: awesome, Luca will run the bench readout, i'll cover business items. Luca over to you.
[00:20] Luca Moretti: ok, cool. so the main thing we ran overnight was a 6hr steady-state against the real traffic replay you shared. baseline was IncumbentCloudAI's endpoint configured with your current batching and caching. Redwood ran with the recommended batch size and prefix/KV caching enabled. results — median tokens/sec up about 2.6x, average latency lower on p50 by ~18ms overall.
[00:40] Luca Moretti: but on the tail — p95 on longer contexts (requests > 1.5k tokens) we saw a regression, roughly +80 to +130 ms compared to baseline on a subset of calls hitting cold KV paths. that lines up with a couple of the sequences that do dynamic retrievals.
[01:05] Miguel Santos: hmm, that's interesting. was cache miss rate higher on your side?
[01:09] Luca Moretti: preliminary look, yeah we saw a slightly higher miss amplification for those sequences — likely due to the different prefix canonicalization; your replay has lots of near-duplicate prefixes which under our continuous-batching heuristic leads to splitting into separate KV entries at times.
[01:28] Dana Lee: can you explain the canonicalization bit — is it something we change on our side?
[01:32] Luca Moretti: short answer: we can tune it. currently Redwood normalizes whitespace and punctuation, but your customer app has many small template variations — e.g., extra newline before patient note — that cause separate cache keys. we can implement a lightweight normalization layer or we can adjust the cache TTL to be more aggressive for near-duplicates.
[01:52] Rhea Patel: we don't want to change app code if possible. a normalization layer in the serving path sounds better. what kind of risk / perf hit does that add?
[01:59] Luca Moretti: minimal; it's a micro transform, a few CPU cycles per request pre-tokenize. cost-wise negligible, latency add is sub-5ms for prep on our infra.
[02:08] Oliver Grant: are we sure the baseline provider doesn't already be doing something similar?
[02:11] Miguel Santos: baseline had a custom preprocessor we built months ago; might be why it's better on those tails — we hadn't realized.
[02:16] Aisha Khan: ok so action: Luca will prototype a normalization shim and run targeted replay to see KV miss delta.
[02:23] Luca Moretti: yes, i'll put a small patch in the bench harness and rerun a selective 2hr test.
[02:28] Aisha Khan: on the quantization side — you mentioned trying the int8 variant?
[02:31] Luca Moretti: yeah, we spun up the quantized v1 variant overnight. throughput improved another ~20% in tokens/sec but interestingly p95 on those long-tail requests didn't improve much — because quantization helps per-token throughput but doesn't eliminate the KV miss wall time.
[02:52] Miguel Santos: so we'd get lower unit cost per token but still see tail spikes when retrievals miss. is the cost math still favorable vs baseline?
[02:58] Aisha Khan: in our model yes — even if p95 is slightly higher in a few buckets, unit cost drops 18-23% depending on request mix. i'll share a per-route cost table.
[03:12] Dana Lee: Can you share the workbook with the exact p95 and unit cost numbers?
[03:16] Aisha Khan: yes sending after this: Benchmark sheet link — https://redwood.app/sheets/VDNT-bench-v3 (read-only for now).
[03:23] Miguel Santos: noted, i'll look after. one more thing — how reproducible was the p95 regression? is it noisy day-to-day?
[03:30] Luca Moretti: it's somewhat stable across replays that include those specific long dialogues. if we remove retrieval events it disappears. so it's tied to the KV path.
[03:38] Rhea Patel: ok, sounds like root cause. any ideas about mitigation besides normalization? maybe prefetching?
[03:44] Luca Moretti: prefetching helps if you can predict keys; we can also increase the cold-cache parallelism — we currently throttle concurrent cold fetches to protect the DB behind the KV layer. we could relax that for your POC to measure impact.
[03:58] Dana Lee: that sounds risky for our DB, we need to keep throttles. could you instead use a short-lived local in-memory LRU to catch immediate replays?
[04:06] Luca Moretti: yeah a tiny LRU at the edge is feasible — we can deploy per-instance with a small memory cap and TTL 30s to 5m. it'd catch hot replays without hitting your backing storage.
[04:17] Miguel Santos: that could work. what's the memory impact?
[04:19] Luca Moretti: couple hundred MB depending on key size, we can cap to 128MB and tune.
[04:27] Aisha Khan: next topic — dedicated slot ask. Rhea flagged predictable throughput needed. Rhea, can you outline target QPS and SLO?
[04:35] Rhea Patel: we're aiming for sustained 120 QPS with p95 < 350ms for short-medium queries and < 700ms for our long dialogs. also a failover SL: if latency breaches 1.2s more than 3x/hour we want auto-fallback to incumbent for that route.
[04:50] Aisha Khan: ok, Luca, based on today's bench can Redwood meet that with dedicated reserved capacity?
[04:55] Luca Moretti: yes. for 120 QPS sustained we'd recommend 4 dedicated slots on our m-series GPU profile with autoscale headroom of +1 for bursts. expected p95 is ~280ms on short queries with caching; long dialogs will be variable until we fix KV misses but can target sub-650ms with the edge-LRU + normalization.
[05:15] Aisha Khan: i'll get finance to send a pricing estimate, but rough numbers now would be helpful — Aisha to send rough monthly reserved estimate later today.
[05:25] Oliver Grant: one more security question — we need KMS integration details and audit log retention options. SOC2 attestation too.
[05:32] Aisha Khan: docs are in the security pack: https://redwood.app/sec/verdant — includes KMS/HSM options, log retention tiers, SAML/SSO support, and our SOC2 report. if you want we can set up a security-only call with our compliance lead.
[05:47] Rhea Patel: yes please, that will be needed for procurement.
[05:50] Aisha Khan: great. back to tuning — Luca will run normalization shim + edge-LRU + quantized variant A/B for a 24h window and we'll compare p50/p95 and unit cost.
[06:02] Luca Moretti: i'll also add trace tags for KV cold path and increase trace retention on your cluster to 72h so we can correlate.
[06:09] Dana Lee: we'll enable the longer trace window and whitelist Redwood IPs tonight.
[06:12] Miguel Santos: timeline for the updates?
[06:14] Aisha Khan: Luca to run by 2027-12-09 and send results, Aisha to send bench sheet by 2027-12-06, security call to be scheduled for week of 2027-12-13.
[06:24] Oliver Grant: any blockers from procurement we should flag?
[06:26] Aisha Khan: main one is SOC2 + KMS alignment, we'll surface that in the security call; finance quote will help procurement start the SOW review.
[06:35] Rhea Patel: ok, looks good. small ask — can we get a short write-up on fallbacks and the automatic reroute behavior? our product team wants to understand how automatic fallback works in case of regional degradation.
[06:45] Aisha Khan: yes, i'll include a one-pager on fallbacks and routing policy examples in the follow-up email.
[06:50] Miguel Santos: thanks, appreciate it.
[06:52] Aisha Khan: cool, thanks everyone, we'll recap and follow up with the artifacts.
[06:55] Rhea Patel: thanks all.

End of transcript.
