document.content:
Bridgewell Console Playbook: usage analytics & cost attribution demo

Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood Product), Aisha Patel (Bridgewell Head of ML), Roberto Diaz (Platform Eng), Ellen Kim (Director Product), Samir Vohra (Security), Speaker 6
---
Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete): Quick console walkthrough focused on per-route usage analytics, cost attribution, and playbook for reducing unit costs. Customer wants clarity on cost per route, per-environment tagging, how to link SLOs to routing & fallback, and options for Dedicated vs hosted for predictable spend. Agreed next steps: send recording + pricing scenarios, run sample cost export for Bridgewell routes, schedule VPC technical deep-dive.
Topics: 1) Per-route dashboards and top-level metrics 2) Cost breakdown by model/route/token/embedding 3) Attribution and tagging (env, feature flag) 4) SLO/routing policy and canary rollouts 5) Dedicated vs Hosted economics 6) Security/compliance notes
Action items (recap in transcript): see metadata
---
Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, i'm the AE on this account, quick intro?
[00:07] Aisha Patel: hi, i'm Aisha, Head of ML at Bridgewell, we run a few user-facing assistants and some internal summarization pipelines. we want to understand cost attribution per feature basically.
[00:15] Liam Ortega: cool, hi all, Liam on the infra SE side, i'll do the console walkthrough and show the per-route dashboards and the cost playbook.
[00:22] Roberto Diaz: morning — afternoon for some, Roberto here, we're most worried about seeing spike costs from a broken prompt or model drift.
[00:30] Priya Rao: i'll jump in on product questions, especially around the analytics retention and custom metrics.
[00:36] Samir Vohra: Samir, security; we'll ask about KMS, SAML, audit logs.
[00:40] Maya Chen: perfect, ok we'll start with the console, then show how Optimize recommendations tie into cost, and end with Qs and next steps.
[00:48] Liam Ortega: sharing screen, give me one sec, windowing... all right, you're seeing the Redwood Console home — there's the top nav: Routes, Models, Billing, Optimize.
[00:59] [01:00] Liam Ortega: we'll jump to Routes. so this is Bridgewell's demo org — you can see the left filters, env tags, and a route list with traffic. note that this is a demo dataset so numbers are synthetic.
[01:18] Ellen Kim: quick question — can we map our internal feature flags to Redwood routes? we have a lot of microfeatures.
[01:24] Liam Ortega: yeah you can tag routes with arbitrary labels — env:prod, feature:quick-summarize, team:chat — and those tags show up across all analytics panels and cost breakdowns.
[01:33] [01:35] Liam Ortega: okay, clicking into route 'patient-summary-v2' — new panel shows recent latency p50/p90, token breakdown, model used, and cost-per-minute curve. see the top-right KPI: total tokens, est cost for period, and effective cost-per-1k-tokens.
[01:51] Aisha Patel: how's the 'est cost' calculated? is it per-token plus model multiplier or does it include infra overhead?
[01:58] Liam Ortega: good question — it's model-specific token cost + a small infra allocation — for hosted it's a token-based price, for Dedicated we compute based on capacity footprint (GPU-hours) and amortized tokens. the console shows both views: token-unit and capacity-attrib. sometimes the wording in the UI says 'estimated billing' because of rounding and attribution heuristics.
[02:22] [02:25] Liam Ortega: here is the cost waterfall: model inference costs, cache savings, batching gains, and routing overhead (like cross-region). you can toggle to show costs normalized by requests, by tokens, or by session.
[02:36] Roberto Diaz: do you have an export? i want to run this with our cost model in BigQuery.
[02:40] Liam Ortega: yes there's a 'Export CSV' button and a scheduled export API — we can create a daily/weekly dump to your S3/GCS with route-level granularity, and it's columned by timestamp, route, tags, model, tokens_in, tokens_out, est_cost, backend_capacity_hours.
[02:55] [03:00] Liam Ortega: toggling to the 'Attribution' tab — here you can select primary and secondary tags to attribute cost: e.g., by feature then by environment. we'll show a stacked bar and a latency scatter to find expensive outliers.
[03:17] Ellen Kim: neat — can we surface which prompts are causing high token usage?
[03:21] Liam Ortega: there's a 'Top prompts' view that samples request inputs (PII redaction optional) so you can see the average tokens per prompt and examples. we do sampling to avoid storing all raw prompts unless you enable request logging.
[03:33] [03:40] Aisha Patel: sample — okay that's good. our product team needs examples to iterate on prompt tuning.
[03:44] Liam Ortega: moving to 'Optimize' suggestions — this panel runs a lightweight analysis of routes and suggests batching thresholds, cache prefixes, and model quantization profiles that reduce spend with minimal quality loss.
[03:55] [04:00] Liam Ortega: for the 'patient-summary-v2' route it suggests enabling prefix cache for the 50% of requests that share the same patient context, and drop the model from the 8-bit float to a 4bit quantized variant for non-sensitive fields.
[04:12] Samir Vohra: pause — quantization, is that allowed for PHI or is that a no-go?
[04:17] Maya Chen: good callout — for PHI you'd default to Dedicated or Private where you control the keys and can enforce HSM-backed KMS. quantization itself is an inference optimization and doesn't change data residency, but whether you allow it on PHI needs cross-org policy.
[04:35] [04:40] Liam Ortega: switching to 'Billing > Route Breakdown' — the UI has a scatter of routes sized by total spend; click a route to see hourly burn and the spike detector. you'll also see a 'Why did cost spike' panel that tries to correlate spikes with recent rollouts, model swaps, or unusual prompt lengths.
[04:58] Roberto Diaz: that spike detector — is it rule-based or ML?
[05:02] Liam Ortega: hybrid — we run heuristic checks (sudden token length increase, new model variant) and a light anomaly score based on historical median absolute deviation. it's not heavy ML, so it's explainable in the UI.
[05:16] [05:25] Liam Ortega: demoing 'SLO routing' — you can set an SLO at the route level (p99 latency target, error budget), then link a routing policy. if latency breaches, the policy can fallback from a high-cost model to a cheaper variant automatically, or route to Dedicated reserved capacity.
[05:38] Aisha Patel: so we could have patient-facing assistant route to the highest-quality model, but burst to dedicated cheaper variants under heavy load?
[05:45] Liam Ortega: yes, you can tier: gold (quality model), silver (quantized variant), bronze (cached or embedding-based). Redwood supports automatic fallbacks and sticky session logic so you don't disrupt ongoing conversations.
[05:58] [06:00] Priya Rao: how do rollouts look? can we canary a model and see cost delta during canary?
[06:06] Liam Ortega: canary shows a side-by-side cost/time series — you can pick a percent of traffic for the canary and the console shows projected cost delta plus observed quality metrics if you attach eval test sets.
[06:18] [06:25] Roberto Diaz: we'd like to project what a monthly commit to Dedicated would look like. can the console simulate commit math?
[06:31] Liam Ortega: there's a 'Capacity Planner' in the Dedicated tab — you can input target RPS/latency and it suggests GPU pool size, monthly cost, and break-even point vs hosted. we'll include sample numbers in the export.
[06:46] [06:50] Liam Ortega: quick note on tagging best-practices — we recommend: env, team, feature, data_sensitivity. the attribution engine can roll-up by those tags or by custom user property.
[06:58] Aisha Patel: about retention — we need 13 months of audit-level usage for compliance, can the console keep that?
[07:04] Maya Chen: yes, we have configurable retention tiers; audit logs and aggregated metrics can be kept longer under enterprise retention add-on. detailed request logs are opt-in.
[07:15] [07:20] Samir Vohra: KMS question — we use AWS KMS and have HSM-backed keys in some projects. can Redwood integrate?
[07:25] Liam Ortega: yes we support customer-managed keys (CMKs) and HSM through our Private deployment and certain Dedicated setups; hosted can integrate via an encrypted link but for HSM-backed you usually pick Private or Dedicated with KMS peering.
[07:40] [07:50] Liam Ortega: moving on — i'll show a short 'playbook' sequence for cost incident response: 1) identify route with spike, 2) check top-prompts and recent rollouts, 3) apply temporary routing policy to fallback to cached responses or cheaper model, 4) roll back last model change if needed, 5) run Optimize recommendations for long-term fix.
[08:08] Ellen Kim: can that playbook be run as an automated runbook? so a button to 'apply mitigation'?
[08:13] Liam Ortega: yes, we have an 'Auto-mitigate' toggle that can apply pre-approved policies when certain thresholds are hit; it requires RBAC and signed approvers for production use.
[08:26] [08:30] Aisha Patel: is there a Slack/PagerDuty integration for alerts?
[08:33] Liam Ortega: yep — webhook, Slack, PagerDuty, and email alerts, and you can attach a short remediation script or runbook link.
[08:42] [08:50] Maya Chen: let's jump to a live example — Liam can you show a real export sample from a week so they can see the CSV structure?
[08:55] Liam Ortega: okay pulling a one-week export, give me a sec — here's the CSV preview: columns: timestamp, route_id, route_name, tags, model_id, tokens_in, tokens_out, est_model_cost, infra_alloc, total_est_cost, latency_ms_p50,p90,p99,request_count. downloadable link shown in chat.
[09:18] Roberto Diaz: perfect. can we add an extra column for session_id and request_prompt_hash?
[09:23] Liam Ortega: we can add request-level columns if you enable request logging, which we usually avoid for PII reasons, but prompt_hash and anonymized session_id are doable.
[09:33] [09:40] Aisha Patel: about the Optimize suggestions — are those suggestions backed by historical AB tests or just static heuristics?
[09:47] Liam Ortega: currently it's a combination: heuristics plus historical sim runs on sampled traffic. we also provide a confidence score and an estimated cost-savings percentage.
[09:58] Priya Rao: can we preview the expected quality delta?
[10:01] Liam Ortega: if you attach an eval set, we can show predicted metric changes pre/post optimization; otherwise we provide a conservative estimate.
[10:09] [10:20] Maya Chen: Samir, any other compliance asks?
[10:22] Samir Vohra: audit trail granularity, user access control mapping to our IdP, and data residency for EU patients — we'll need those docs.
[10:28] Maya Chen: noted. we'll include SOC 2 and data residency docs in the follow-up.
[10:35] [10:40] Liam Ortega: small demo of model swap — switching a route from 'redwood-llama-13b' to 'rdw-qlite-13b-4bit' and you can see immediate estimated cost drop and a simulated QA diff using attached eval set.
[10:56] Aisha Patel: that simulated QA diff — is it reflective of conversational quality or just static metrics?
[11:02] Liam Ortega: it's mainly static eval metrics (ROUGE, BLEU, and some instruction-following pass rates) tied to your eval prompts; for conversations we recommend synthetic convo evals.
[11:14] [11:25] Roberto Diaz: how does prefix/KV cache interplay with stateful sessions? we have multi-turn conversations per patient.
[11:30] Liam Ortega: KV cache is per-session and can be preserved across requests if you set sticky routing; prefix cache is separate and caches common prefixes like repeated instructions. for PHI you'd use Dedicated and ensure the cache is stored in encrypted storage with retention policy.
[11:48] [12:00] Liam Ortega: question from chat: 'Does the console show model warm-up costs after scaling events?' — yes, warm-up GPU-hours are accounted and visible in infra_alloc column.
[12:15] Priya Rao: how often are Optimize suggestions recomputed?
[12:19] Liam Ortega: daily for active routes, weekly for low-traffic routes. you can also trigger an on-demand analysis.
[12:27] [12:35] Maya Chen: this is really helpful — could we talk about an implementation timeline, roughly how long to onboard routes and get 90-day historic attribution?
[12:42] Liam Ortega: initial onboarding (routes + tags + exports) typically 1–2 weeks; full historical backfill depends on retention and whether you want request-level logs — for aggregated metrics we can backfill up to 3 months automatically; for full 90-day request logs you'd enable logging and we can import if you provide the data.
[12:59] [13:05] Aisha Patel: we don't want all raw request logs; can you do aggregated at 5-minute rollups?
[13:09] Liam Ortega: yes, aggregated rollups are default and sufficient for most cost analysis.
[13:16] [13:25] Ellen Kim: one more product question: can we build custom dashboards on top of the data?
[13:30] Liam Ortega: yes we have a dashboard builder and a public metrics API. many customers pipe exports into BI tools.
[13:37] Roberto Diaz: about Dedicated economics, can the console simulate mixed deployment — e.g., host critical low-latency routes on Dedicated and keep burst on hosted?
[13:46] Liam Ortega: yes the Capacity Planner supports hybrid configs and will show combined cost and break-even.
[13:54] [14:00] Aisha Patel: timeline-wise, we have a Q1 procurement window — we need a pilot that proves cost savings. what would you recommend as an initial pilot?
[14:07] Maya Chen: start with 2–3 high-spend routes, enable Optimize suggestions, run a 4-week canary with cost/quality tracking, and then evaluate Dedicated commit numbers. we'll help instrument the evals.
[14:21] [14:30] Liam Ortega: demoing 'quality vs cost' chart — here's a route with measured quality on y-axis and cost on x-axis; you can see points for each model variant and quantization level. this helps select pareto-optimal models.
[14:42] Priya Rao: can we export that view as a PDF for the execs?
[14:45] Liam Ortega: yes there's export as PNG/PDF and a short slide deck generator.
[14:50] [15:00] Maya Chen: we're ~15 minutes left, let's open the floor for any final technical deep questions.
[15:06] Samir Vohra: two quick ones: 1) Can we do per-tenant encryption keys? 2) Are audit logs tamper-evident?
[15:12] Liam Ortega: per-tenant keys are available in Private and certain Dedicated setups; for hosted we offer envelope encryption with customer keys. audit logs are append-only and we can provide signed log digests for tamper evidence.
[15:25] Aisha Patel: on the cost side, what levers do you most see customers using to reduce spend?
[15:30] Liam Ortega: top levers: batching (for short calls), prefix caching, model quantization for non-critical paths, routing policies (SLO-based fallbacks), and schedule-based scaling for predictable nightly jobs.
[15:42] [15:50] Ellen Kim: any gotchas when using tagging heavily? we've had tags be inconsistent across teams.
[15:55] Priya Rao: good governance question — we recommend an enforced tagging schema and a pre-commit hook or CI job to validate route creation metadata; Redwood supports enforcement policies.
[16:05] [16:10] Maya Chen: ok recap and next steps: Maya to send recording + pricing scenarios, Liam to run sample export and simulated Dedicated commit math, Aisha to provide traffic patterns and SLOs, Samir to follow-up on KMS questions.
[16:24] Aisha Patel: that works, thanks — this was very helpful.
[16:29] Roberto Diaz: thanks everyone.
[16:31] Maya Chen: we'll follow up in email with the links and the CSV. thanks y'all.
---
Post-call notes (manual):
- Customer is focused on clear cost attribution across features; wants sample CSV with route-level columns to run internal ROI modeling.
- Sensitivity: PHI across many routes, so they'll likely evaluate Dedicated or Private for HSM/KMS controls.
- Pilot recommended: 2–3 high-spend routes, 4-week canary with Optimize suggestions enabled.
- Follow-ups: pricing scenarios, SOC2/KMS docs, scheduled VPC deep-dive.

document.content:
Crestline - Semantic Search Workshop

40min product walkthrough of Redwood hosted embeddings + reranking endpoints. Focus on integration patterns, latency vs. cost tradeoffs, Console walkthrough for Optimize suggestions, and a short live demo sending batch queries. Customer wants pilot for 100k docs and strict PII redaction needs. Agreed to run a small benchmark and follow up with pricing and security docs.
Architecture: embedding + kNN retrieval + reranker flow
API endpoints: embeddings, search/recall, rerank
Console: per-route latency/cost dashboards and Optimize suggestions
Quality vs cost: quantization and batching tradeoffs
Security: PII redaction, KMS, audit logs, SOC2
Pilot scope: 100k documents, 2 region latency targets
Meeting header: 2026-05-14 16:00 PDT | Duration: ~54m | Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Rachel Gomez (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Mark Huang (Crestline HoS), Lina Torres (Eng Mgr), Devon Price (ML Eng), Priya (Intern)

[00:00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for taking time, um, from Redwood side it's Samir and Rachel and Jordan. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:06] Mark: Good, thanks. Excited to see how this could help our search stack.
[00:00:10] Samir: Awesome. Quick agenda — we'll do a brief recap of your goals, then a walkthrough of the embeddings + reranker flow using the hosted endpoints, show the Console Optimize suggestions, and finish with a short live batch demo and next steps. Any additions?
[00:00:22] Lina: Maybe if we have time, could you show how prefix caching or batching affects latency? We've been tripping over tail latency spikes.
[00:00:28] Rachel: Absolutely we'll cover KV caching, batching, and tip on sequence lengths.
[00:00:33] Samir: Cool, Mark — can you quickly restate the success criteria? I have a note but want to confirm.
[00:00:38] Mark: Yeah so primary is relevance uplift — we want +10 to click-through on top-3 results on content search. Secondary is latency under 150ms p95 for our public web queries, and third is data safety — anything with PII needs to be redacted and not leave our tenant. We also want a clear unit-cost estimate for 100k docs.
[00:00:54] Jordan: Thanks. A couple clarifying Qs from our side: What's your current vector store and retrieval stack?
[00:00:59] Devon: We're running FAISS on-prem for embeddings store, nightly re-embeds with a transformer from last year, and the reranker today is a lightweight in-house BERT for reordering top-20. We tried a dense-rerank but it was too slow.
[00:01:12] Rachel: Great context. Today's demo assumes using Redwood hosted embeddings to reduce embedding ops cost and the reranker hosted too, so you'd keep FAISS or swap to a cloud-managed vector DB — both are supported.
[00:01:24] Samir: Ok jumping into the flow — slide 4 of our deck, but I'll also show the Console. The simple flow: client calls /embeddings to index documents, store vectors in your vector DB, then at query time call embeddings for query, run approximate kNN, then call /rerank endpoint with top-K candidates. The reranker returns scores and optionally a final result list.
[00:01:44] Mark: Quick question — can we use Redwood embeddings but keep vectors in our on-prem FAISS? We have to keep primary copy local for compliance.
[00:01:51] Rachel: Yes, you can. Many customers do that: use hosted embeddings, stream vectors to on-prem FAISS. For privacy, you can use Redwood Private or dedicated tenancy; hosted API also supports VPC peering for private network setups but for strict isolation we'd recommend Private.
[00:02:05] Lina: And are embeddings exempt from being logged? We need to ensure PII is not retained.
[00:02:09] Samir: Good point — we have redaction guidance. For hosted, you can enable request-level retention controls and automatic PII redaction upstream; we also have KMS controls and an option to disable retention entirely per customer. We'll send the security brief after the call.
[00:02:24] Mark: Appreciate that.
[00:02:27] [00:03:00] Jordan: Switching to the Console — I'm sharing my screen. You should see a per-route dashboard with tokens, latencies, and cost breakdown. Over here is Optimize suggestions for reranker — it recommends quantization to int8 for that model class, and shows predicted token cost savings.
[00:03:16] Lina: That prediction looks optimistic. How accurate are those savings?
[00:03:19] Jordan: It's a heuristic based on similar workloads; we run a short profiling job on your corpus during pilot and give a tailored estimate. In our experience it's within 10-20% of actuals.
[00:03:30] Rachel: Also worth noting quantization impacts output slightly — we show a quality delta metric with example outputs so you can verify.
[00:03:37] Devon: How is batching handled? We have spikes with 20k qps in marketing campaigns, but typical is low.
[00:03:42] Samir: The runtime supports continuous batching with request shaping. For spikes we recommend autoscaling and burst capacity; you can also set per-route max batch sizes in the Console. That controls latency vs cost.
[00:03:53] Mark: Can the reranker operate synchronously with top-K = 50 within 150ms p95?
[00:03:58] Rachel: Depends on model choice and hardware. For a mid-sized reranker on our hosted tier, top-K=50 is borderline. We typically recommend retrieving top-100 with a cheap scorer and then rerank top-20 with the stronger model. Or using a lighter reranker architecture.
[00:04:14] Samir: We'll include a latency profile with recommended K values in the follow-up.
[00:04:18] [00:05:00] Jordan: Time for a quick live demo — I'm going to run a batch of 25 sample queries against a sandbox dataset of news articles similar to Crestline's corp. Running /embeddings for index is already done for the sandbox. Now I'll call /search-recall (client-side kNN) and then /rerank.
[00:05:16] [00:05:30] Jordan: (typing) Ok, calling /rerank with top_k=20, scoring model named 'redwood-rerank-v2'. Response coming back...
[00:05:45] Speaker 3: Uh the console is a bit laggy on my side, but I see the request and response times.
[00:05:50] Rachel: The sample shows p50 ~ 70ms, p95 ~ 130ms for the reranker on these inputs, memory usage moderate. You can also enable streaming to see partial scores as they come.
[00:06:02] Mark: Those numbers look promising. What's the per-query cost?
[00:06:06] Samir: Rough ballpark on hosted gen + rerank small model — think on the order of single-digit cents per heavy search if you do per-query rerank; embeddings per-query are a few tenths of a cent if you're batching. We'll run exact pilot numbers.
[00:06:20] Devon: We definitely need concrete pricing for 100k doc pilot and projection to 10M.
[00:06:24] Samir: Understood, will include cost spreadsheet.
[00:06:28] [00:07:00] Rachel: Switching to edge cases — how do you handle query paraphrases and long queries? We often have long product descriptions as queries.
[00:07:06] Jordan: For long queries we recommend truncating or using cross-encoder rerankers which can handle longer context. We also have specialized embedding models tuned for long docs — embedding length affects memory and cost.
[00:07:18] Lina: Any tooling in Optimize to detect regressions? We run A/B tests and need alerts when relevance drops.
[00:07:23] Rachel: Yes, Console has eval set integration. You can upload test prompts and expected answers; metrics are tracked and we send regression alerts when score falls beyond thresholds. We can wire that into your Slack.
[00:07:34] Mark: On compliance: SOC2 + ISO?
[00:07:36] Samir: Redwood is SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001 compliant. For audit trails we provide per-request audit logs and optional immutable retention. We'll share the compliance pack.
[00:07:46] Devon: For PII redaction, is there an on-the-fly scrub option? We tried regexes but it's brittle.
[00:07:52] Rachel: We have an optional preprocessor that runs a token-level PII detector and can either redact or hash detected spans before sending to embeddings. For highest assurance customers we recommend Private with customer-managed KMS.
[00:08:07] Lina: If we use hosted embeddings but store vectors on-prem, are embeddings ever materialized in logs?
[00:08:12] Samir: Not if you opt out of retention and enable the no-logs flag. For pilot we'll set that up.
[00:08:18] [00:09:00] Jordan: A brief note on model selection — we have a catalog; for embeddings we recommend mid-sized contextual embeddings for news content (they capture semantics better). For rerankers, we have a family of distilled cross-encoders. The Console shows a quick compare plot of nDCG vs cost.
[00:09:15] Mark: Can we A/B test two models and have Redwood route 10% traffic to a new variant?
[00:09:19] Rachel: Yes. Rollouts in Console support canary and A/B routes, automatic fallback, and experiment metrics.
[00:09:27] [00:10:00] Jordan: Ok running the next demo: I'm toggling quantization suggested by Optimize to int8 on the reranker sandbox to estimate quality delta. This will take a few sec — I'll run a small eval set of 200 queries.
[00:10:18] [00:11:00] Jordan: Results — quality delta shows a 2% nDCG drop but cost savings ~32%. You can inspect individual failure cases; here's a couple where int8 dropped the rerank order.
[00:11:13] Lina: 2% might be acceptable depending on business impact, we need to see top-3 CTR impact.
[00:11:18] Samir: Right, that's why we couple eval sets with real traffic tests during pilot.
[00:11:24] Mark: About scale — for 100k docs what's the onboarding process? How long to index?
[00:11:29] Jordan: Typically indexing 100k documents with embeddings takes a few hours depending on doc size and batch parallelism. We provide ingestion templates and a small SDK script. For larger corpora we recommend a streaming pipeline with checkpointing.
[00:11:41] Devon: Do you have examples or templates for FAISS import?
[00:11:44] Rachel: Yes, we have a repo with sample code to push embeddings to FAISS or other vector DBs. We'll share the link in the notes.
[00:11:51] [00:12:30] Mark: Any competitors we should be aware of for this space? We've looked at some managed vendors and open self-hosted stacks.
[00:12:34] Samir: Customers often compare us with Anthropic/Embeddings vendors and folks who piece together self-hosted runtimes. Key difference is our integrated Console and Optimize with production-grade serving.
[00:12:45] Priya (intern): Quick question — is there a quota for model versions?
[00:12:49] Jordan: You can pin model versions per-route; we support many versions and keep a short retention of old artifacts. For private deployments you control model binaries.
[00:12:58] [00:13:30] Rachel: Ok we have about 15 minutes left — let's capture action items and next steps.

[00:14:11] Samir: Great. Any final questions?
[00:14:15] Mark: No, that covered it. Good demo.
[00:14:19] Samir: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the materials and proposed pilot plan.

[00:14:26] Mark: Bye.

Arcadia Health POC - Week 4 Rollout & Cutover Planning

Week 4 pilot sync focused on rollout/go-live planning. Reviewed canary and A/B rollout options, monitoring and alerting needs, cutover dry-run schedule, and security gating (KMS, audit logs, SSO). Agreed next steps: Redwood to share runbook and canary checklist; Arcadia to provide gating metrics and on-call details; schedule a dry-run before production cutover.
Canary rollout strategy
A/B routing and traffic split
Cutover dry-run and rollback plan
Monitoring, SLOs, and alerting
Security gating: KMS, audit logs, SSO/SAML
Maya Chen: Share cutover runbook draft and canary checklist by 2025-03-14
Ravi Patel: Run 2x latency + throughput benchmarks with target batch sizes (8/16) and share CSV by 2025-03-16
Samir Gupta: Provide current on-call escalation matrix and primary PagerDuty rotation by 2025-03-14
Ellen Park: Confirm required audit log retention policy and KMS/HSM key ownership constraint by 2025-03-15
Redwood to send cutover runbook draft and canary checklist
Customer to confirm go/no-go gate metrics and A/B cohorts by 2025-03-14
Schedule 2-hour dry-run for cutover 2025-03-19 (tentative)
SE to deliver latency/cost benchmark CSV and sample traces
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Maya from Redwood here, we'll kick off. We have Ravi (SE) and Olivia on the line as well. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Jonas (Arcadia): Good, Maya. Morning — afternoon for some of us. Quick note: Priya had to jump to another meeting but will dial back in at ~15 minutes.
[00:20] Maya: Totally fine. This call is the week 4 POC sync, main goal is cutover/rollout planning - canary vs A/B, monitoring and runbooks. We want to agree on next steps so the dry-run goes smoothly.
[00:31] Ravi (Redwood SE): I'll cover the canary checklist and what metrics we recommend measuring during the canary window — latency p50/p95, token cost, error rate, and some qualitative checks on hallucination rate using your eval set.
[00:45] Priya (Arcadia): (joins) Sorry, was on the sales planning sync, I'm here now.
[00:49] Priya: Quick signal: we need near-zero data exfil risk and we must keep keys customer-managed due to compliance, so KMS/HSM ownership is a hard requirement. Ellen will cover the exact policy.
[01:02] Ellen (Arcadia Sec): Yep. For SOC2 and our internal audits, we require customer-managed keys for model prompt payload encryption at rest and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. Retention must be 7 years for certain records.
[01:15] Maya: Understood. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS in the VPC deployment and we can forward audit logs to your SIEM via secure collector. We'll put specifics in the security appendix of the runbook.
[01:28] Samir (SRE): From an on-call perspective, we need a clear escalation path during the canary. Who's primary SE to ping if we see token throttles or OOM?
[01:36] Ravi: That would be me first-line; we'll include a 24/7 escalation contact in the runbook, plus a fallback policy to the hosted model variant if dedicated nodes degrade.
[01:47] Jonas: Let's talk canary sizing. We were thinking a 5% traffic slice for 6 hours, then expand to 20% if metrics look good. Thoughts?
[01:58] Ravi: 5% for 6 hours is conservative and reasonable. During that window we want to validate latency SLOs (target p95 < 600ms for typical prompts), error rate < 0.5%, and no regression in embedding similarity drift for your reranker. We'll instrument traces.
[02:15] Aisha (PM): For A/B we plan to measure conversion and downstream task accuracy. If we do canary + A/B, how does routing work? Can Redwood route by user cohort or session?
[02:25] Maya: Yes — Redwood routing supports traffic by route, header, or user_id hash. We can do a hybrid: canary on 5% of traffic system-wide, and an A/B experiment within that slice if you want to run different prompts or model variants.
[02:38] Priya: We have two cohorts: clinical-facing users and patient-facing. We want the clinical cohort to be first; can we prioritize them in the canary?
[02:46] Ravi: Absolutely — we can scope the 5% to only the clinical cohort using header-based routing. We'll include the exact routing rules in the runbook.
[02:55] Jonas: On rollback: what's the quickest path? Back to previous model on Dedicated or fallback to hosted?
[03:03] Ravi: Fastest is automatic fallback to a warm-hosted variant in a different region; cutover back to previous dedicated snapshot requires model pin rollback which takes a bit longer but is safe. Runbook will document both automated and manual rollback steps.
[03:15] Samir: We need to rehearse the rollback in a dry-run. Not just read steps — actually execute them in a staging window.
[03:22] Maya: Agreed. We're proposing a dry-run on 2025-03-19 where we perform a simulated cutover with test traffic, validate monitors, and exercise rollback. Does that date work?
[03:32] Priya: Tentatively yes, pending calendar approvals.
[03:35] Ellen: Back to security — audit logs: what events do you surface by default and can we add custom event hooks?
[03:44] Ravi: By default we capture request metadata, token counts, model version, errors, and routing decisions. We can add custom hooks to emit application-level events — we'll need a small integration for your SIEM collector.
[03:56] Ellen: And retention? You said you can forward, but retention on your side for the control plane logs — is there a configurable retention window?
[04:04] Maya: Yes, control plane logs default to 90 days but for Private deployments you can configure longer retention or opt to export all logs to your S3 bucket where you control retention. We'll note that in the security appendix.
[04:18] Jonas: Monitoring: which dashboards should we have live during canary? We want token-level cost, per-route latency p50/p95, request QPS, error counts, and a metric for quality/regression based on eval prompts.
[04:33] Ravi: We'll provision dashboards in the Console: per-route latency histograms, token-cost breakdown per-request, and an eval pipeline that replays your prompt set and emits a quality score in near-real-time. Also we'll push traces to your tracing backend.
[04:45] Aisha: For the quality metric, how fast can we get numbers? We need near realtime during the canary (within 10 minutes).
[04:54] Ravi: If the eval harness is set up to run on a sliding window it can produce rolling metrics within 5-10 minutes. We'll walk through the eval config during the dry-run.
[05:06] Priya: What about cold start and KV cache warming? If we cutover at 2pm PDT and we have long-tail session lengths, will token latencies spike?
[05:18] Ravi: There's always some initial KV cache warm up, but Redwood supports prefix caching and progressive pre-warm strategies. For the canary we recommend a 30-minute warm-up with synthetic traffic to populate KV and prompt caches — included in the runbook.
[05:33] Samir: Can your synthetic warm-up be replayed from our anonymized traces? We want realistic tokens.
[05:39] Ravi: Yes, we'll take a sampled set of historical requests (anonymized) and replay them in a staging job. We'll need permission and a brief script to scrub PII first.
[05:51] Ellen: KMS question — customer-managed keys: will Redwood ever be able to decrypt payloads?
[05:57] Maya: No. With customer-managed KMS/HSM the keys remain under your control; Redwood can’t decrypt without your authorization. We'll include the detailed flow in the security appendix for sign-off.
[06:11] Jonas: A little bit about SLOs: we want p95 latency < 600ms most of the time, but more importantly we need a user-facing availability SLO of 99.9% for the clinical cohort. How does Redwood expose SLO burn rate and alerting?
[06:27] Ravi: Console supports SLO dashboards and burn-rate alerts. You can configure thresholds that trigger PagerDuty via the alerting integrations. We'll provide a recommended alerting policy in the runbook: p95 breach >2 min => P1; error rate spike >0.5% => P1; sustained cost anomaly >15% => P2.
[06:45] Samir: Make sure the alert integrates with our PagerDuty team and we need quiet hours for noncritical alerts.
[06:52] Olivia (CSM): We'll collect the on-call roster, and set the PagerDuty integration to route to the provided rotation. Quiet hours can be configured.
[07:00] Aisha: For A/B metrics, what's the plan to ensure statistical significance? We don't want to flip based on noise.
[07:08] Ravi: We'll recommend cohort sizing and minimum exposures for statistical tests; typically for conversion we want at least N requests per cohort to reach 80% power. We'll share a sample calculation and the tooling we use to compute uplift and p-values.
[07:21] Priya: Okay — back to the runbook contents. Can we get a short checklist in the first page: go/no-go gates, who signs off, key metrics, rollback steps?
[07:31] Maya: Yes — runbook will start with an executive checklist: pre-cutover validations, go/no-go metrics, primary contacts, cutover window, step-by-step. We'll attach the canary checklist as an appendix.
[07:42] Jonas: Also include a communication plan — internal comms and user-facing messaging in case we need to throttle patient traffic.
[07:50] Maya: Noted.
[07:52] Ellen: On the compliance side, we need to run a short pen-test on the Private control-plane endpoints before cutover. Timeline?
[07:59] Maya: We can accommodate a light scope pen test, but it needs to be scheduled at least 10 business days in advance. If you want results before the dry-run, we should start that immediately.
[08:11] Ellen: We'll open a ticket to Redwood security to scope the test.
[08:14] Priya: Can we talk about cost during canary? If token cost spikes unexpectedly, what's the control?
[08:21] Ravi: There are throttles and cost guardrails — you can set per-route rate limits and token budget alerts. If we detect cost anomaly we can automatically reroute to a lower-cost quantized variant. That will be in the rollback/mitigation section.
[08:36] Samir: We want a rehearsed mitigation where we cut traffic by 50% and route to quantized variant under 5 minutes. Is that feasible?
[08:44] Ravi: Yes — we can pre-warm the quantized variant and keep it warm so the switch is sub-5 minutes; we'll document exact steps.
[08:52] Jonas: Let's pin the success criteria for go-live: 1) p95 latency < 600ms for clinical cohort; 2) error rate < 0.5%; 3) quality regression delta < 1.5% on your eval metric; 4) no P1 alerts for 24 hours post-cutover. Agree?
[09:11] Priya: Sounds good. One addition: audit logs exported and accessible in SIEM within 10 minutes.
[09:19] Ellen: Yep that's critical.
[09:22] Maya: We'll add that as a hard gate.
[09:25] Olivia: Quick note on runbook ownership — Redwood provides the baseline, Arcadia owns the final sign-off and you control the gating.
[09:34] Aisha: What's the expected time to restore to previous behavior if we rollback?
[09:39] Ravi: Auto-fallback to hosted variant is minutes; full rollback to previous dedicated snapshot and re-sync takes longer (maybe 20–40 minutes depending on state). We'll put RTO estimates in the runbook.
[09:50] Jonas: For metrics collection, do you stream raw traces or summaries? We prefer both.
[09:55] Ravi: We stream summarized metrics but can configure traces export for sampled requests to your tracing backend (e.g., Jaeger/Tempo). We'll include sampling rules.
[10:05] Priya: Any further infra needs from our side for the dry-run?
[10:09] Maya: We need a staging API key, a sanitized sample trace set for warm-up, and your PagerDuty rotation. Also confirm who will be the production sign-off authority during the canary window.
[10:20] Jonas: I'll be on the hook for sign-off for the clinical cohort, Priya will coordinate exec approval for full roll.
[10:28] Maya: Great. Wrap-up — I'll list the deliverables: runbook draft, canary checklist, latency/cost benchmark CSV, and sample traces scrub script. Ravi will run the benchmarks and start the synthetic warm-up script.
[10:41] Ravi: FYI from the benchmark runs yesterday: median token latency improved ~12% with batching 8 vs 1, but p95 didn't shift as much because of long tail. We'll test batch sizes 8 and 16 and share raw CSVs.
[10:55] Samir: Make sure the bench includes a simulated multi-tenant load spike to observe autoscaler behavior.
[11:02] Ravi: Will do.
[11:06] Maya: Any blockers?
[11:09] Ellen: We need to confirm the KMS flow and pen-test schedule; once those timelines are clear we can lock the dry-run date.
[11:18] Maya: We'll send the runbook and security appendix by 2025-03-14; pen-test ticket requested by Arcadia to start ASAP.
[11:25] Priya: Sounds good.
[11:28] Maya: Ok that's it. We'll follow up in email with the artifacts and the calendar invite for the dry-run. Thanks everyone.
[11:36] Jonas: Thanks all.
[11:40] End of recording.

Redwood Optimize walkthrough focusing on batching, prefix/KV prefetch strategies, and cost models for Nimbus Health patient-assist virtual agent. Discussed latency vs cost tradeoffs, sessionization, VPC/private deployment considerations, and next steps to run a throughput pilot and security review.

Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Sara Patel (Redwood AE), Markus Chen (Redwood SE), Janelle Ortiz (Head of ML, Nimbus), Arjun Mehta (Platform Eng), Priya Rao (Security)

Auto-summary (auto): Redwood Optimize demo focused on batching/prefetch. Customer cares about latency at 95/99, data residency, KMS integration. Next steps are data sample, cost model share, security review.

Topics covered: batching/concurrency, prefix vs KV cache, sessionization heuristics, quantization and model variants, private/VPC considerations, pilot scope.

--- Transcript (selected, automated timestamps every ~30s, transcription imperfect) ---
[00:00] Sara Patel: Hey everyone, welcome, thanks for joining. I'm Sara, AE on the account, and with me is Markus, our SE. We're going to run through an Optimize-focused walkthrough — batching, prefix and KV prefetch, and a cost model that maps to Nimbus's virtual patient assistant workload.

[00:18] Janelle Ortiz: Thanks Sara. We've been getting push from product — latency needs to be under 300ms p95 ideally, and cost needs to be within our existing inference budget. We also have compliance constraints on PHI handling, so anything that touches patient data needs to be under our VPC or customer-managed KMS.

[00:35] Markus Chen: Totally. We'll cover both the hosting options. For the Optimize recommendations, key knobs are batching size vs concurrency, sessionization (how you group prefixes), and whether you use prefix cache vs the KV (key-value) prefetch approach. I'll start with a quick sketch of the cost model and trade-offs.

[01:00] Markus Chen: So at a high level, batching gives you token throughput wins because GPU amortizes the model's fixed cost. But batching increases tail latency when requests arrive sparsely or when you wait to fill a batch. Redwood Optimize suggests dynamic batching with latency SLOs so you only batch up to a certain hold time. For Nimbus, we tuned the sim for 300ms p95 target.

[01:28] Arjun Mehta: Quick question — when you say "hold time" are you implying you always delay at the front end? We can't add more than 50ms average additional latency into our pipeline.

[01:37] Markus Chen: Great question. The hold time is a tuning parameter. For example, 10ms hold + larger batch size might be net positive because you reduce per-token cost a lot. In the sim we ran, a 10ms hold with expected concurrency of 4 saved ~35% token cost while keeping p95 within 280-320ms depending on sequence length distribution. We'll send the spreadsheet after the call.

[02:05] Janelle Ortiz: Can we see that sim? Also, our prompts vary — some sessions are short context (one-turn triage) and others are long multi-turn threads (prep notes). How do you handle mixed distributions?

[02:20] Markus Chen: That's where sessionization + prefix cache comes in. For short sessions, prefix cache isn't helpful. For multi-turns, if you can prefix the conversation — e.g., patient metadata and recent exchanges — a prefix cache avoids recomputing early layers. Prefix cache is great when the same prefixes repeat across requests (like standardized intake prompts). KV prefetch is slightly different: you store key/value attention caches per session and prefetch them on next request so you avoid rerunning earlier tokens. It's more storage heavy but yields bigger latency wins for deep multi-turn sessions.

[03:00] Priya Rao: We need to be careful with cached PHI. If you store KV state, how is that encrypted and who has access? We can't keep patient data in an external managed cache unless it's under our KMS and audit logs.

[03:15] Markus Chen: Absolutely. For Redwood Private / VPC deployments we support customer-managed KMS (HSM/HSM-backed keys) and detailed audit logs. KV state can be stored only inside your VPC and encrypted with your keys. For hosted API we have encryption at rest but for PHI-sensitive ops we recommend Private deployment. We'll schedule a security deep dive for that.

[03:38] Janelle Ortiz: Good. From a costing perspective — I want to understand marginal token cost vs sessionization savings. Do you have a simple per-1000-turns cost delta?

[03:50] Sara Patel: We prepared a simplified example in the sheet. Roughly, for a standard 2k-token model: pure stateless calls at low concurrency cost X per 1k requests. If you employ prefix cache/prefetch with average reused prefix of 200 tokens across sessions, the per-request token compute drops by ~10-25% depending on reuse. If you use KV prefetch for long sessions, savings can be 30-60% but with added state-storage cost.

[04:25] Arjun Mehta: What's the storage overhead look like for KV? If we have 100k active sessions, is the storage footprint huge?

[04:33] Markus Chen: KV entries are proportional to sequence length times model KV size per token. For a 2k-token context, an active session might be a few megabytes. For 100k sessions that becomes sizable. So we typically recommend TTL and LRU eviction policies, and offloading older sessions to encrypted blob storage if you need retention. The cost model includes storage cost vs compute savings.

[05:05] Janelle Ortiz: Can Redwood Optimize propose TTLs automatically? We don't want to guess.

[05:12] Markus Chen: Yes — Optimize has workload-aware TTL suggestions. It looks at session access patterns and suggests TTLs and prefetch thresholds that maximize cost savings for a given latency SLO. We'll show the Optimize console view in a second.

[05:28] Sara Patel: Quick aside: do you currently run on cloud-managed GPUs or on-prem?

[05:34] Arjun Mehta: We're mixed — dev on cloud, production expected to be Private VPC due to PHI. We'll likely start a Dedicated reserved pool for baseline throughput.

[05:45] Markus Chen: Good — Dedicated + Private combo is common. Dedicated capacity gives predictable throughput for steady-state, and Private gives control over KMS and network. That also factors into the cost model because Dedicated commits change per-token effective price.

[06:05] [Screenshare starts - Markus walks through the Optimize console and a cost spreadsheet]

[06:15] Markus Chen: On the left you can see the traffic histogram and session-length heatmap. This is a mocked import of Nimbus sample traffic. The model of interest is "redwood-2k-v1" (note: model names may appear slightly different in transcript). On the right is the cost-sim. We model three strategies: stateless baseline, prefix caching with modest TTL, and aggressive KV prefetch with 60s session affinity.

[06:48] Janelle Ortiz: In the aggressive KV scenario what happened to p99?

[06:52] Markus Chen: The p99 increases slightly during cold starts or when cache misses occur, but overall p95 improved. We also model fallback to a smaller quantized model variant if SLOs are at risk — that keeps availability high while capping cost.

[07:10] Arjun Mehta: Can Redwood route to a cheaper variant on overflow automatically? We want graceful degradation rather than errors.

[07:18] Markus Chen: Yes — in Smart Routing you can set policy to route by latency or cost budget. For example, 95% of requests go to the top-quality model, overflow goes to a quantized variant with lower cost and slightly lower quality. That routing is in the same config layer and the console surfaces expected quality delta.

[07:40] Priya Rao: On the KMS question — if we bring our own key, does Redwood still see plaintext?

[07:46] Markus Chen: With Private install in your VPC and customer-managed KMS, Redwood does not have access to your keys. The control plane can be customer-managed depending on the deployment model. We'll put together the architecture diagram for the security review.

[08:05] Janelle Ortiz: I like the idea of TTL based per-session savings. How do you recommend we set TTLs for a health chat where users come back days later? We can't keep everything forever.

[08:18] Markus Chen: Two patterns: short-lived session cache (minutes to hours) for active conversations, and archival strategy for long-term retention. For rehydration after days, we often store a compact semantic embedding of past important snippets (not full KV) that can be prefixed to the prompt. That reduces KV storage cost but preserves context. Optimize can recommend which conversational tokens to compress into embeddings.

[08:48] Arjun Mehta: Interesting. About concurrency — you mentioned autoscaling and burst — what's the typical concurrency per GPU you recommend for 2k-token model?

[08:58] Markus Chen: It depends on model and GPU. For an A100-like class for 2k tokens, concurrency of ~6-10 per GPU can give high utilization. For quantized variants on newer hardware, concurrency can be 12-20. Optimize sim accounts for kernel performance and selects optimal concurrency, but we always recommend real benchmark runs. We'll provide a k6 script and the runbook.

[09:26] [Brief cross-talk about exact GPU types and cost numbers]

[09:44] Janelle Ortiz: Can you show how the console explains the cost per 1k requests when you change TTL?

[09:50] Markus Chen: Sure. Changing TTL from 60s to 600s in the sim increased average hit rate from 18% to 54% given the traffic distribution, which reduced compute token cost by ~22% but increased storage by about 4% — net savings are obvious on 1k scale in the spreadsheet. We'll attach the exact numbers.

[10:18] Priya Rao: Are audit logs detailed enough for HIPAA audit? We need per-request tracing and retention of logs for 6 years in some circumstances.

[10:29] Markus Chen: For Private we can extend log retention; logs can be stored in your S3 with encryption under your KMS. Per-request tracing and token-level timings are available and can be exported to SIEM. We'll include a sample log schema and retention options.

[10:46] Arjun Mehta: One more on the pilot: what telemetry do you need from us to run an accurate sim?

[10:53] Sara Patel: Best is a 24h sample of requests with timestamps, prompt length distribution, concurrency peaks, and a mapping of latencies you currently observe. If you can include user session IDs (hashed is fine) that helps with sessionization analysis.

[11:10] Janelle Ortiz: We'll get that. Also, can we set up a 2-week pilot against a Dedicated pool to measure real savings?

[11:18] Sara Patel: Absolutely. Typical pilot is 2-4 weeks with a small Dedicated pool and a KB of instrumentation. We'll propose target throughput, acceptance criteria (e.g., p95 < 300ms and cost reduction > 20%), and a rollout plan.

[11:35] Markus Chen: Quick demo note: in Optimize you can run synthetic sims and then an "apply" that generates recommended server configs (batch sizes, TTLs, prefetch thresholds). Those configs can be exported as IaC snippets for your infra team.

[11:52] Arjun Mehta: Will those IaC snippets work with our cloud setup and private VPC? We use Terraform and some internal modules.

[11:58] Markus Chen: We output Terraform-friendly snippets and also a simple YAML manifest for the Private agent. There may be minor glue work on your side. We'll include a short integration checklist.

[12:12] [30 minutes into the call — jump to questions and concerns] 

[12:20] Priya Rao: Two final security things: SSO/SAML integration for console access and role-based access controls for seeing KV content. We need to ensure only service accounts can rehydrate full context.

[12:32] Markus Chen: Yes we support SAML/SSO and fine-grained RBAC. For KV access we can enforce encryption scopes and only give decryption permission to a limited set of service principals inside your VPC.

[12:45] Janelle Ortiz: One more practical question — when you estimate "savings", how much is theoretical vs empirically observed?

[12:53] Sara Patel: Our numbers are a combination — the sim uses empirical kernel throughput and historical traffic patterns, but we always validate with pilot benchmarks. We present both simulated and pilot-measured deltas to set expectations.

[13:07] Markus Chen: Also note that cost savings are sensitive to hit rates. If reuse is lower than expected, prefix cache ROI falls. That's why we include a sensitivity analysis in the spreadsheet: best/median/worst-case scenarios.

[13:22] Arjun Mehta: Ok, that sounds reasonable.

[13:26] Sara Patel: Quick recap and next steps: We'll send the cost-model spreadsheet and the optimize export examples (Sara), Markus will send the benchmark runbook and k6 scripts, Nimbus will provide a 24h sample and session histograms (Arjun), and Nimbus security will schedule a separate deep-dive (Priya + Markus).

[13:45] Janelle Ortiz: Sounds good. When can we expect the docs and sim?

[13:50] Sara Patel: I'll email the spreadsheet and console export by Monday 2026-08-17. Markus will include the runbook by Thursday 2026-08-20.

[14:05] [Closing remarks]

[14:10] Priya Rao: Thanks, appreciated. We'll review and get the sample data uploaded to the shared S3.

[14:18] Sara Patel: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with attachments and a calendar invite for the security deep-dive.

[14:25] Call ended.

--- Notes on transcription quirks: the transcript has some mis-hears: model name rendered as "redwood-2k-v1" but in console it may show as "rdw-2k-opt"; KV is sometimes transcribed as "K V" or "kay-vee"; SLO spelled S-L-O in the transcript occasionally.

References shared during call (links noted in transcript):
- Cost model spreadsheet (link shared in chat)
- Optimize console export (config yaml)
- Benchmark runbook + k6 script (attached later)
- Security architecture diagram (to be scheduled)

Request replay & error-paths demo — Skyward Health platform team

Meeting header:
Date/Time: Thu, 29 Jan 2026 — 15:00 PST (scheduled 45m)
Duration: 48 minutes (recording)
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Pierce (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Liam Park (Redwood SE), Elena Torres (Skyward), Marcus Liu (Skyward SRE), Priya Raman (Skyward SecOps), Noah Kim (Skyward Eng)

Summary:
Quick console-focused demo to show request replay (playback), error path analysis, request logs with correlation ids, and how Redwood handles fallback to smaller quantized variants when a GPU pool runs low. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC for regulated PHI-like workload; main concerns: audit logs, KMS, data residency, retention, and predictable 99th percentile latency.

Topics covered:
- Request replay / playback flow in the Console
- Tracing: how request spans are captured and stitched to tokens
- Error triage: identifying model vs infra vs prompt issues
- Logs & download: exporting request logs for SOC-2 audit
- Fallback policies: model variants / KV cache miss handling
- Pilot and next steps: security docs and pilot scope

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everybody, thanks for joining, this is Jordan from Redwood, um I'm gonna hand over to Maya to drive the console demo, show the request replay, error paths and then we'll leave time for Q&A.
[00:18] Maya: thanks Jordan, hi Elena, Marcus, Priya — hi team, quick agenda, I'll show a live request replay, then we'll step through traces and error analysis, and then show how you can download logs for audits. Note recordings will include some nudges cause the demo environment has slightly smaller load than your production.
[00:36] Elena: sounds great, we interested in like how much we can reproduce problems and what we can hand to our auditors.
[00:45] Maya: perfect. Starting in the Console, here's the request table. I'll filter by project and then by route name. You can see request IDs, timestamps, model variant, latency, tokens and status code.
[01:02] Noah: a quick question, are those request IDs correlated with our app trace id or are they Redwood-only?
[01:10] Liam: good one — we support passing a customer request id header (x-cust-request-id) so you can correlate. We also ingest OpenTelemetry spans if you push them, so stitching is possible.
[01:25] Marcus: we push OTLP to our collector, so that's helpful. What about the kv cache — sometimes our assistant returns earlier cached prefix and that confuses the logs.
[01:36] Maya: yeah so KV cache is surfaced as a span in the trace, but FYI the transcription sometimes renders KV as K V or kv-cash in exports, so if you search CSV watch both.
[01:47] Priya: ha, noted.
[01:50] Maya: I'm going to pick a failed request here, status code 502, and click 'Replay'. The replay opens a stepper: it shows original input, the model variant used, the kernel selection hints, and the token-by-token playback.
[02:10] [02:10] Speaker 1: the playback is a bit jumpy, I think network on demo VM...
[02:18] Maya: yes, playback uses streaming websocket to show tokens; sometimes demo infra drops frames, but the token timeline is preserved. Here you can scrub to the time the error happened.
[02:30] Marcus: can you show how we identify if failure was model capacity versus a runtime OOM?
[02:35] Maya: sure — check the trace timeline: infra-level spans are labeled with GPU id and kernel reason, so an OOM in the serving runtime will have a kernel error and the span includes memory metrics. Model capacity exhaustion or queued time shows up as scheduler queue spans.
[02:50] Maya: see here, there's a long queue span before the final error; that indicates we batch and then the request timed out.
[03:00] Noah: and the console shows the per-token latency histogram?
[03:05] Maya: yes, per-request token histogram + a breakdown: model compute, scheduling, and serialization. You can click to expand per-kernel traces.
[03:15] [03:15] Marcus: are compute kernel names human readable? Sometimes our infra team needs to map to driver traces.
[03:22] Maya: we try to map kernels to friendly names where possible — but note, in some builds they show internal identifiers, so you might see something like cu-matmul-v3 in the trace; we add mapping tables in the debug export.
[03:36] Elena: about security — how do you handle logs containing PHI-like prompts? We need controls for redaction and KMS.
[03:44] Jordan: great question, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and optional on-the-fly redaction before logs land in long-term storage. We can also configure retention windows and PII scrubbing rules.
[03:56] Priya: can we get an SSO / SAML audit trail for who viewed a request?
[04:02] Jordan: yes, Console access logs tie into SAML/SSO and we surface per-user access events in the audit trail; that's part of our enterprise package.
[04:12] Maya: back to demo — I'm toggling to the error-analysis panel. There's an auto-classifier that suggests root cause categories: model, prompt, infra, network. It's not perfect but it surfaces likely suspects.
[04:30] [04:30] Speaker 2: classifier pulled from past incidents, right?
[04:33] Maya: yeah it's trained on past debug labels; you can override or add your own labels.
[04:38] Marcus: if we want to run this on-prem, does the auto-classifier still work?
[04:44] Maya: for Private deployments we ship the classifier as part of the control plane; inference for the classifier runs in your environment. There may be small config differences but functionally similar.
[04:55] Noah: show the trace export flow for auditors.
[04:58] Maya: sure — click export on the request group, pick time range and scrubbing options. You can choose full raw trace, redacted trace, or summarized CSV. The export is a signed URL and can be pushed to your S3-compatible bucket with SSE-KMS.
[05:16] Elena: will that include stable identifiers or will IDs be rotated? We need stable ids for incident correlation but rotated for public share.
[05:25] Maya: export options include 'anonymize' which replaces PII and rotates user ids, and 'preserve correlation' which keeps request ids. You choose per-export.
[05:35] Marcus: performance question — if we enable continuous request logging for all requests, what is the cost/throughput impact?
[05:42] Liam: continuous logging adds metadata overhead; on our side we stream lightweight spans and then, based on sampling you can retain full token payloads only for errors or sampled sessions. For cost we provide a unit estimate: delta tokens stored and egress.
[05:58] [05:58] Marcus: okay send the cost model.
[06:01] Jordan: will do.
[06:05] Maya: next, fallback behavior — here's a failure policy: if a primary model variant is unavailable, Redwood can route to a quantized variant or a smaller model pinned in the route. The console shows the policy order and you can simulate fails.
[06:20] Noah: do we lose output quality when fallback triggers?
[06:23] Maya: usually yes a bit; Optimize gives suggested quantization profiles to reduce quality drop. You can set a SLO that prefers latency over absolute quality.
[06:34] Priya: and what's the rollback / canary story?
[06:37] Maya: Console supports canary rollouts across model versions and region-aware routing. If latency regressions exceed thresholds, automatic rollback can trigger.
[06:47] Elena: about pilot scope, we want to test producer endpoints for triage and see how long we can keep logs. Also need to validate private deployment network setup.
[06:56] Jordan: for the pilot we recommend: 1) 2-week running of 5 endpoints with tracing enabled, 2) run synthetic load to exercise queueing paths, 3) a security review with Priya's team and our compliance engineer.
[07:10] Priya: okay we'll want SOC2 and encryption detail before we sign off.
[07:15] Jordan: fine, I'll share the security whitepaper and SOC2 attestation.
[07:18] [07:18] Speaker 3: can we do a short backlog of acceptance criteria?
[07:21] Jordan: yes, we'll add to next steps.
[07:25] Maya: one last pro tip — if you have recurrent flakiness, set up synthetic golden prompts and a periodic regression check; Optimize will highlight token-level regression and suggest model/quantization swaps.
[07:38] Marcus: that could help. also curious about telemetry retention — can we keep 180 days for audit?
[07:44] Jordan: retention is configurable; long-term retention is an add-on. For Private deployments you can manage the retention in your storage.
[07:55] Elena: thanks — that was helpful.
[07:58] Jordan: ok, quick recap of next steps: Jordan will send pricing + security docs; Maya will anonymize and send the demo trace clips and how-to GIFs; Marcus will supply example request IDs and retention needs; schedule follow-up 2/5. Anything else?
[08:15] Priya: please include a short checklist of network ports and IP allowlists for VPC deployment.
[08:20] Jordan: noted, will include.
[08:24] Elena: thanks everyone, appreciate it.
[08:27] Maya: thanks team, we'll follow up.

End of recording.

Peregrine dev sandbox SDK sprint walkthrough

Intro + live SDK walkthrough (Python + TS) for sandbox environment, auth options (API key, SSO, service accounts), env setup, quickstart run. Discussed Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs for Peregrine's latency and PHI constraints. Agreed on sandbox provision, share security pack, and schedule POC benchmark.
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-04 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Lena Morris (Redwood AE), Carlos Vega (Redwood SE), Ava Patel (Peregrine Lead ML Eng), Marcus Lin (Peregrine Infra Eng), Nina Cho (Peregrine PM)

Summary: quick hands-on SDK walkthrough, auth patterns, environment setup and sandbox run, alignment on POC and security questions.

[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intros?
[00:05] Ava: Ava here, lead ML, mainly build inference pipelines for clinical summarization, hi.
[00:09] Marcus: Marcus infra, I'll own network and security bits.
[00:12] Nina: Nina product, timeline and success metrics.
[00:15] Carlos: Carlos, infra/SE at Redwood, I'll run the demo and the benchmark runbook.
[00:18] Lena: Great. Objective today is a hands-on SDK sprint: python + typescript quickstarts, auth options, environment setup and a sample run in your sandbox. We'll cover caveats around PHI and private deployment too.

[02:12] Carlos: Alright I'm going to share my screen — starting with repo layout. We keep two tiny samples: quickstart_py and quickstart_ts. The py one uses our redwood SDK pip package, ts one is from npm.
[03:01] Carlos: Example env vars: REDWOOD_API_KEY or for service accounts REDWOOD_SA_KEY, plus REDWOOD_ORG if you have multiple. For local dev we recommend dotenv for secrets, for CI use secret manager.
[03:27] Marcus: Quick Q — are API keys long lived? We want rotation policies.
[03:30] Lena: API keys can be short lived if you mint them via our control plane; we also support OIDC/SSO and service account keys with rotation. Carlos will show the workflow.

[05:05] Carlos: Showing python sample: pip install redwood-inference (note: pkg name may be slightly different in registry, transcriber: package name spelled as "redwood inference" here), then set REDWOOD_API_KEY. Code snippet — client = Redwood(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')) then client.generate(...).
[06:18] Carlos: Running the sample now — hitting hosted endpoint in us-west1, streaming output. (audio: keyboard clicks) 
[06:45] Speaker 1: mm-hmm
[07:01] Ava: The streaming looks good. What's the default model?
[07:05] Carlos: Default is a curated open model alias we call rdx-small in hosted, but you can pin specific model versions like rdx-2.1-fp16 or a quantized variant. We recommend starting with mid-sized for latency tests.

[09:00] Carlos: For TS example: npm install @redwood/inference, then set env REWOOD_API_KEY — actually typo in example, should be REDWOOD_API_KEY, noted. Then new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }). Generate call similar.
[10:20] Nina: Any CI pattern for key rotation?
[10:25] Carlos: We recommend using short-lived service account tokens minted via our control plane + your identity provider; otherwise use vault + periodic rotate. We have a sample GitHub action in the repo.

[12:40] Marcus: On networking: will we need VPC peering for private deployment or for dedicated? If we do hosted can we restrict by IP?
[12:48] Lena: Hosted supports IP allowlist for egress and inbound webhook callbacks; Dedicated and Private support VPC peering and private connectivity. For PHI workloads, many customers choose Redwood Private (VPC or on-prem) with KMS integration.
[13:30] Marcus: KMS — can we use our AWS KMS?
[13:35] Carlos: Yes, KMS/HSM integration supported. For Private we can integrate with your KMS; for Hosted we can bring your CMKs in some enterprise packages. We'll send the exact notes in the security pack.

[15:05] Carlos: Back to code, showing how to stream and handle tokens. We show the continuous batching example: set batch_size in client config or use the platform auto-batching. Remember batching trades latency for throughput.
[16:10] Ava: Our SLO is 300ms median for 512 tokens — does that seem attainable?
[16:17] Carlos: For hosted with a mid-sized model and low sequence length yes, but depends on concurrency. You may prefer Dedicated to get predictable p95s. We'll propose a baseline during the POC.

[18:55] Carlos: Now demoing prefix caching and KV cache usage — caching helps for chat history reuse. Note: demo artifacts contained some transcriber typos e.g., KV cache referred to as KV cash earlier.
[20:00] Lena: Security checklist — SOC 2 present, we also have ISO readiness for some customers. For audit logs, Console surfaces token-level cost and latency breakdowns, and we retain logs per contract.
[20:45] Nina: For compliance, we need data residency in eu-west. Is that available?
[20:50] Carlos: Yes EU regions supported in our hosted plane; for strict residency customers often choose Private.

[23:10] Alex? (unlabeled):
[23:22] Marcus: (interrupt) do you have a sample perf test we can run locally?
[23:28] Carlos: Yes, benchmark runbook in repo. It's a python script that fires variable concurrency and reports latency percentiles to stdout and CSV. We'll run a small one now against the sandbox. 
[25:05] (sound of commands)
[25:30] Carlos: Results coming in — warm tokens, cold start penalties small. Remember quantization reduces memory and can improve throughput but may affect quality. We'll attach quantization profiles and recommended model variants.

[28:12] Ava: On quality — we need to ensure summarization accuracy isn't degraded. How do you guard against regressions during rollouts?
[28:20] Lena: We have Redwood Optimize: eval sets tied to changelogs, automatic regression alerts when quality drops. You can pin models and run canary traffic. Carlos: we'll show a brief screenshot in the pack.

[30:40] Carlos: Quick note on cost: per-token pricing for hosted, plus reserved capacity tiers for Dedicated. We can run cost estimates with your throughput numbers. There is also intelligent batching/caching that lowers per-token costs.
[31:10] Nina: Who typically owns the Dedicated purchase — infra or procurement?
[31:14] Lena: Usually procurement signs the reserved capacity; infra sponsors technical requirements. We'll coordinate with your procurement if you move forward.

[33:00] Marcus: Networking again — for Private we need to know firewall rules and egress constraints, we'll share a diagram.
[33:07] Lena: Yes please add that to Marcus' action item. We'll review.

[34:20] Carlos: Back to quickstarts: demo shows both py and ts samples running against sandbox and streaming. Also showed postman/curl examples. Note: cURL sample uses Authorization: Bearer <REDWOOD_API_KEY>.
[36:45] Ava: Can we embed Redwood SDK in our microservices? Any notable language limitations?
[36:52] Carlos: No, SDKs are lightweight; just ensure you manage keys via environment or service accounts. For high throughput we suggest using the HTTP2 streaming path or gRPC if you're on Private.

[39:00] Lena: Ok let's surface open questions from your side.
[39:06] Nina: Timeline — we want a 6 week POC, success is meeting median latency <350ms and cost per call under $0.08 for our summarization workload.
[39:17] Lena: Noted. We'll shape the POC to that.
[39:25] Marcus: Security: need SOC2 report, encryption at rest, and KMS notes. Also legal will want data deletion SLA.
[39:35] Lena: We'll share the security pack and legal checklist.

[41:00] Carlos: One thing to watch: if you enable aggressive prefix caching and re-use, throughput is great but you have to be careful about state size. We'll add recommended TTLs.

[43:12] (brief silence, typing)
[43:25] Lena: Recap: Redwood will provision a sandbox, send quickstart links, share security docs and benchmark runbook. Peregrine will share prompt set and confirm networking constraints. Schedule benchmark with Carlos for week of 11/17.
[44:00] Nina: Sounds good. Any blockers?
[44:05] Marcus: Only confirming VPC peering options — I'll get that doc to you.
[44:10] Ava: I'll pull together a 100-example prompt set for summarization.
