2026-06-15-harlequin-health-latency-econ-discovery

Initial latency and throughput discovery for Harlequin Health's real-time clinical summarization feature. Customer evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for p95 latency <= 300ms on streaming responses, concurrency targets ~200 simultaneous users, and token/sec throughput for 2k concurrent chats. Discussed VPC/KMS requirements, SOC2, and benchmarking approach; agreed to run a streaming token/sec microbenchmark and share security pack.
p95 latency targets for streaming generation
concurrency and multiplexing strategy
hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
token/sec microbenchmarking plan
security: SOC 2, KMS, SSO, audit logs
Meeting header
Date: 2026-06-15 09:00 PDT | Duration: 44m | Recording: On
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Sarah (CTO), Rajesh (Lead ML), Jenna (Infra), Omar (PM)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you carving time. quick round intro?
[00:08] Sarah: Hi I'm Sarah CTO at Harlequin, we run a clinical notes product for hospitals.
[00:12] Rajesh: Rajesh, lead on ML infra and production models.
[00:15] Jenna: Jenna on infra, mostly networking and security.
[00:18] Omar: Omar product, driving timelines.
[00:20] Maya: Great. Liam and Carlos from our side, SEs who will nerd out on perf stuff.
[00:26] Liam: hey all, will dive into latency and throughput.

[00:34] Maya: To set context, Harlequin wants real-time summarization of patient-provider chats, streaming token output to the front end. Target p95 latency is pretty tight right? Sarah you mentioned ~200-300ms p95 per token?
[00:46] Sarah: yeah, on live streams we need p95 for user-visible tokens under 300ms ideally. for shorter prompts maybe lower. otherwise clinicians notice lag and UX drops.
[00:57] Rajesh: our peak concurrency estimate is about 150 to 250 active streams during morning rounds, but bursts hit about 2k concurrent short-lived sessions across the org — those are lighter. We're mostly worried about sustained concurrency of ~200.
[01:12] Jenna: and we have strict networking: private VPC peering, no public egress for PHI at rest. KMS must be customer-managed.

[01:22] Liam: okay good. quick framing — we support three deployment modes: Hosted API for quickest time-to-value, Dedicated reserved capacity for predictable throughput, and Private (VPC/on-prem) for strict compliance. Each has tradeoffs for p95, cold starts, and token/sec economics.
[01:40] Carlos: for streaming, the p95 you see in-hosted will depend on model choice and prefix lengths; smaller context and quantized models help. dedicated tilts predictability — consistent p95 under load. private gives full network control but you manage GPUs.

[01:58] Sarah: can you give us numbers? like realistic p95 and tokens/sec per GPU for the popular open models?
[02:05] Liam: sure. rough numbers — for a 13B-ish model on NVidia A100 with our runtime, sustained streaming token generation (greedy) p95 per token under low-latency config can be around 80-120ms; for 70B models it's more like 180-350ms depending on optimization and quantization. those are ballpark and vary by prompt length and kv cache reuse.
[02:28] Rajesh: when you say kv cache reuse, does that mean sessions with similar prefixes get faster?
[02:32] Liam: yes, our prefix/KV caching improves steady state. for conversational flows where the prompt is shared you often see token/sec improve by 20-40% after warmup.

[02:45] Jenna: about concurrency — if we need 200 concurrent steady streams, how many GPUs for dedicated?
02:50] Carlos: depends on model/sequence length. Example: 13B with batch multiplexing and small window might serve ~30-40 concurrent streaming users per A100 with our config. So 200 concurrent would map to ~6-7 GPUs with headroom. For 70B you'd need ~3-4x that.

[03:09] Sarah: and burst to 2k short sessions — do you recommend autoscaling or a hybrid?
[03:14] Liam: hybrid works: Dedicated for steady sustained capacity, hosted burst to handle spikes, or reserved capacity with burst credits. Automatic fallback policy can route to cheaper model variants or hosted pool.

[03:28] Omar: latency across region? our primary is us-west and some east coast hospitals. We need < 50ms network RTT ideally.
[03:35] Liam: network RTT is key. hosting region in the same cloud region reduces network tail. For Private, you'd be on-prem or VPC — network controlled.

[03:45] Sarah: security — SOC2, encryption, audit logs — do you provide SOC 2 docs and customer-managed KMS?
[03:51] Maya: yes, we have SOC 2 Type 2. Customer-managed KMS for Private and Dedicated options; Hosted also supports envelope encryption with customer keys on request (needs paperwork). Audit logs and token-level tracing available in Redwood Console. we'll send our security pack after the call.

[04:10] Rajesh: okay good. can we talk about benchmark methodology? we'd like to run token/sec streaming microbenchmarks that mimic our muxing and input lengths. what's the recommended harness?
[04:19] Liam: recommended approach: 1) start with a microbenchmark using short prompt lengths representative of clinician queries (avg 40 tokens in prompt, outputs 100 tokens), 2) measure cold start and steady state, 3) run multiplexing tests with your concurrency distribution, 4) measure p95 and tail. We'll provide a reference client open-sourced and an nginx-like load generator.

[04:40] Jenna: what about measuring p95 at token level vs response level? we care about token latency for streaming — the initial token matters for perceived latency.
[04:49] Carlos: agree. measure both: initial token latency and per-token steady state p95. streaming can show lower per-token once kv warmed. We'll instrument with per-token timestamps.

[05:03] Sarah: our tolerance for errors: occasional 400ms spikes okay but not above 600ms frequently. how do you handle graceful degradation?
[05:11] Liam: multiple levers — model fallback to smaller variant, turn on more aggressive quantization, or route to hosted fallback with higher latency but guaranteed availability. Also we can shape traffic at the edge to prioritize critical clinician sessions.

[05:28] Omar: cost question — which is more economical for our profile? heavy steady 200 concurrent plus bursts.
[05:35] Maya: Dedicated with reserved GPUs usually gives best unit economics for heavy steady usage. Hosted is more expensive per token for sustained volumes but lower ops. Private has higher upfront but good long-term if you want control. We'll run a cost model.

[05:48] Rajesh: can you quantify tokens/sec per A100 for our 13B baseline in your runtime?
[05:54] Liam: ballpark: for 13B we often see ~2500-4000 tokens/sec per GPU sustained in non-streaming generation when maximizing throughput. For streaming per-token latencies, the tokens/sec metric is less straightforward — because of tail and multiplexing overheads. But you can think of effective user streams: ~30-40 concurrent streams per GPU if outputs are ~100 tokens at interactive latency targets.

[06:18] Sarah: hmm ok. We need to validate with our prompt mixes. Can Redwood run a benchmark on our behalf in hosted and dedicated to show comparatives?
[06:26] Maya: yes we can run a joint benchmark. For hosted we'll run against the hosted pool with your prompts (sanitized). For Dedicated we'll provision a reserved pool and run identical load. For Private we'd provide a reference runner you can run in your env or a partner can run on-prem.

[06:42] Jenna: network constraints — we need traffic to stay inside our VPC, no internet egress. For Dedicated can you do VPC peering?
[06:49] Carlos: Dedicated and Private both support VPC peering. For Hosted we can do private link-ish setups in some clouds via marketplace, but hosted by default goes through Redwood endpoints — would need an architecture review.

[07:02] Rajesh: any caveats with streaming and TLS handshake overhead? we aim for long-lived websockets.
[07:08] Liam: websockets/socket streaming is the best for token-level latency. TLS handshake overhead is only at session start; long-lived sessions amortize that cost. Our runtime supports persistent connections and multiplexing for efficiency.

[07:20] Sarah: do you have any customer references in healthcare who run streaming clinical flows?
[07:24] Maya: yes, a couple—can't share PII on call but we'll include redacted references in the security pack.

[07:33] Omar: timeline — we want to pilot Q3, production by Q4. Anything that would block?
[07:38] Maya: typical next steps are security review, run benchmarks, and pilot contract for Dedicated or Hosted pilot. Should fit Q3 if security review finishes in 2–3 weeks.

[07:50] Rajesh: technical nit — how do you handle KV cache persistence across failover? if a worker dies mid-session do we lose context and does that spike latency?
[07:59] Liam: KV cache is in-memory on the worker for fastest access. We support sticky routing to keep sessions on the same worker; for failover we rehydrate from the request context which adds overhead. In Dedicated we can configure cross-worker checkpointing at some cost; we'll show your options in the benchmark.

[08:19] Jenna: audit logs — do you provide immutable append-only logs that we can ingest into our SIEM?
[08:25] Carlos: yes, audit logs with different retention tiers; we can push to your cloud bucket or stream to SIEM. That's configurable per account.

[08:36] Sarah: let's talk SLOs. We likely need an SLA for p95 targets and uptime. What's Redwood's standard SLA for Dedicated?
[08:44] Maya: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency SLOs in enterprise contracts; exact wording is negotiated. Hosted has standard availability guarantees. We'll introduce legal and SRE in the next meeting to iron SLA specifics.

[08:58] Omar: okay can we get a simple test plan and a price estimate for a 3-month pilot (Dedicated with 8 GPUs + hosted burst)?
[09:06] Maya: yes we'll produce a pilot proposal with cost and test plan.

[09:10] Carlos: on benchmarking specifics — we'll need a representative prompt set, concurrency distribution, and a script for token-level timestamps. If you can share a sanitized sample dataset we can run realistic tests.

[09:24] Rajesh: shareable, yes. We will sanitize. we have a set of 500 prompts typical of morning rounds.

[09:30] Liam: perfect, that will give us a good distribution. We'll run cold-start, steady-state, and burst tests. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 at token-level and response-level, plus token/sec.

[09:43] Sarah: question on function calling and structured outputs — we rely on deterministic JSON chunks. Does streaming split JSON objects mid-token and how to guarantee parsing?
[09:52] Liam: we support structured streaming with chunk boundaries and heuristics to avoid breaking tokens in the middle of JSON. Also function calling can be done server-side and we can return structured deltas. We'll demo that if needed.

[10:05] Omar: any pitfalls you've seen with hospital networks (TLS proxies, deep packet inspection) that affect websockets?
[10:12] Carlos: enterprise middleboxes sometimes terminate websockets or inject delays. Long-lived TLS is best and for worst-case we support fallback to short-polling, albeit with increased latency. Work with your infra to allow persistent websockets to Redwood endpoints over TLS.

[10:28] Rajesh: ok. can you summarize the concrete deliverables after this call?
[10:33] Maya: yes — we'll send: (1) security pack (SOC2, encryption, KMS details, audit logs), (2) pilot proposal w/ cost for 3 months Dedicated 8 GPUs + hosted burst, (3) benchmark plan and runner repo, (4) contract/SLAs template to review.

[10:49] Sarah: timeline for these?
[10:51] Maya: security pack and pilot proposal within 3 business days; benchmark runner and instructions within 5; set up architecture review meeting next week.

[10:58] Jenna: one more: SSO — we use SAML and SCIM for provisioning.
[11:03] Carlos: supported. We'll include SAML/SCIM docs.

[11:10] Omar: ok that's the gist. any final questions?
[11:14] Rajesh: one micro thing — tokenization differences matter for token/sec. which tokenizer are you using in the hosted models?
[11:19] Liam: we track model tokenizer, which can be GPT-like BPE or custom. We'll align on tokenizer in the benchmark to avoid mismatches.

[11:29] Sarah: great thanks.
[11:31] Maya: thanks all. we'll follow up with the pack.

[11:36] [Meeting end]

Notes on transcription quality: occasional speaker mislabels and a couple of word swaps (KV cash vs KV cache) — see "transcription_quality" field.

Redwood to send security pack (SOC2 + KMS + audit logs) within 3 business days
Redwood to deliver pilot proposal for 3-month Dedicated (8 GPUs) + hosted burst within 3 business days
Customer to sanitize and share 500-prompt sample set by 2026-06-22
Schedule architecture review with Redwood SEs next week (proposed: 2026-06-22)
Run joint streaming token/sec benchmark (hosted vs dedicated) once prompts received
Maya Patel: Send security pack and pilot cost estimate (due: 2026-06-18)
Rajesh Patel: Sanitize and upload 500-prompt sample (due: 2026-06-22)
Liam O'Neil: Prepare benchmark runner and instructions (due: 2026-06-20)
Jenna Morris: Confirm VPC peering constraints and share network diagram (due: 2026-06-19)
Carlos Ruiz: Schedule architecture review meeting (due: 2026-06-17)

Vendor gate and onboarding checklist — Citrine Commerce kickoff

Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-07
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Evan (Redwood SA), Marta (Citrine Head of Procurement), Liam (Citrine Security), Sara (PM), Rajesh (Finance)
Shared links: Deck: https://redwood.ai/decks/onboarding-checklist.pdf , Security pack: https://redwood.ai/security/citrine-pack.pdf , Benchmark sheet: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/citrine-pilot.xlsx

Summary (auto): high-level procurement intake and technical preflight. Discussed MSA/DPA redlines, SLA targets (p99 and availability), KMS integration options, on-prem vs VPC private control plane, pricing bands for pilot and committed capacity, and next steps to run a pilot.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh wanted to kick off — we have about an hour — so the goal is align on procurement asks and technical preflight for Citrine, and make sure legal has what they need for MSA/DPA, and then get pilot timing.
[00:12] Marta: thanks Jordan, appreciate it. quick note — procurement, legal and finance on this call, we need to understand the path to approval. main sticking points for us are data residency, KMS integration and the SLA for latency, especially for peak shopping hours.
[00:25] Priya: understood. hi all, Priya from Redwood engineering — i'll walk through technical constraints, and then we can map to legal. maybe i should start with our deployment options: hosted API, dedicated reserved pools, and private (VPC or on-prem) — each has tradeoffs for egress, kms, and performance.
[00:40] Liam: quick q, does private mean customer side control plane or is control plane still hosted by Redwood? that impacts our compliance.
[00:48] Evan: good question. for our private offering we provide a private control plane option where the control plane can be deployed in the customer's VPC — so config and audit logs stay in your environment. there's also a hybrid where we host the control plane but we provide strong network isolation and customer-managed KMS. sometimes the wording in the dpa confuses folks, happy to clarify.
[01:05] Sara: can you describe the KMS options? we currently use HashiCorp Vault + AWS KMS for key wrapping.
[01:11] Priya: yep we support customer-managed KMS via standard KMIP and cloud provider KMS APIs — we can do envelope encryption, and we also have an HSM-backed option for dedicated Private installs. in Hosted API, we offer bring-your-own-key via a customer-managed KMS key for data at rest, but key usage patterns differ so we'll need to validate with your security team.
[01:32] Liam: and are audit logs available for all modes? we need per-request logging for model invocations for three months.
[01:38] Evan: yes, audit logs are available. in Private control plane, logs can be stored in your S3 or Splunk. in Dedicated we stream to customer endpoints; for Hosted we provide exportable logs and a 90-day retention option — we can extend retention as an add-on.
[01:51] Marta: ok good. procurement will want to review SLA language around uptime and response times — specifically p99 for inference under an agreed traffic profile.
[01:59] Jordan: right — typical enterprise SLA we can commit to availability (monthly) and support window. the tricky part is the p99 latency target — we usually tie that to configured dedicated pools or reserved capacity. Priya, maybe you can sketch typical numbers for a 4k token sequence and a 2k token sequence?
[02:16] Priya: sure, rough ballpark — on our dedicated GPU pool with 8xA100 equivalent, p50/p90/p99 for a 2k request is about 60/120/250 ms for generation-only workloads. at 4k, add another 70–120ms across percentiles due to attention scaling; these numbers vary with model family and quantization. for hosted api (shared) expect higher p99 due to multi-tenant queueing. we'll include a perf profile in the benchmark sheet.
[02:47] Rajesh: for finance we need to see cost impact — can you provide example of committed monthly commit bands and an example bill for a 1M token/day workload?
[02:55] Jordan: yes, i'll send a pricing band PDF. quick note — committed capacity reduces per-token price by about 30–45% depending on the model and quantization. i'll include examples for hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[03:06] Marta: on the legal side, our counsel flagged two DPA items: subprocessors list and data deletion/return language post-termination. can you confirm subprocessors for hosted?
[03:15] Evan: we'll provide the subprocessors list. hosted uses cloud infra providers for compute and object storage, but we can provide attestations. for private on-prem, no external subprocessors for compute if you run it fully air-gapped.
[03:27] Liam: also need clarity on model provenance and logging for prompt/response retention — can we disable retention for prompts in the hosted mode?
[03:35] Priya: yes — we support per-customer retention policies. by default we store prompts for debug and quality monitoring for 30 days; we can opt-out or set shorter windows. for the pilot we'd recommend enabling short-term retention to capture regressions, but we can guarantee deletion on a schedule and supply audit manifests.
[03:55] Sara: this is good — one of our product goals is consistent latency during flash sales — what does burst capacity look like?
[04:02] Jordan: we have burst capacity options on Dedicated — can configure autoscale and guaranteed baseline. the SLA ties to baseline capacity; burst is best-effort unless you buy a dedicated burst band.
[04:13] Marta: procurement will likely want the MSA to include a clear escalation path and a penalty structure if SLOs aren't met. are you flexible on that?
[04:20] Jordan: we have standard and enterprise SLA tiers — enterprise can include credits or service level credits. we try to avoid heavy monetary penalties but will do credits and remediation commitments; that tends to be the negotiation point.
[04:33] Liam: from a security review perspective, we need SOC2 Type II report and pen test summary. do you have the latest reports?
[04:40] Evan: yes, we'll share the latest SOC2 and a pen test summary. for private installs, we can run additional attestations if needed. links in the security pack above.
[04:51] Sara: what about data residency — we operate EU and US storefronts; we need EU-only processing for EU customer traffic. can routing be region-specific?
[04:59] Priya: yes — smart routing policy supports region pinning. requests can be routed to EU-only serving tier, and we can ensure model artifacts stay in region if you choose private control plane in EU region.
[05:10] Marta: great. procurement will ask for an implementation timeline — what's realistic to get to pilot with a basic model and routing in place?
[05:18] Priya: technically, if we get network access and KMS details, a basic dedicated pilot can be stood up in about 2–3 weeks. private control plane in your VPC is about 4–6 weeks given infra approvals. pilot tests and tuning add another 1–2 weeks.
[05:32] Rajesh: i need those timelines in writing for our internal gating.
[05:35] Jordan: absolutely, we'll follow up with a one-pager.
[05:37] Marta: a few specific redline asks: 1) change the DPA deletion clause to 30 days post-termination for customer data, 2) limit subprocessors to named list and prior notice for new ones, 3) explicit SSO/SAML support for SSO integration.
[05:52] Evan: deletion clause — we can accommodate 30 days in Private but hosted has nuances since logs may be aggregated for a period; we can commit to deletion of customer-stored data within 30 days and provide attestations. subprocessors — we can provide notice and a 30-day objection window; for cloud infra sometimes we ask for carveouts. SSO — we support SAML and OIDC, yes.
[06:12] Liam: can we get an example of the SAML metadata flow and the SCIM provisioning capabilities? we use SCIM to provision roles.
[06:19] Priya: yes, SCIM v2 supported for user provisioning and role mapping; we'll provide our SAML metadata and a short integration guide.
[06:26] Sara: i want to confirm that function/tool calling and streaming responses are supported for our chat experiences.
[06:32] Priya: supported — streaming, tool-calling, structured outputs — those are in the hosted API and available in Dedicated/Private as part of the runtime. function calls that reach out to external systems will be executed in the same network context as the runtime, so for private you have full control.
[06:48] Marta: procurement is also looking at governance — is there an authorized user list and RBAC support for the console?
[06:55] Evan: yes RBAC support, SSO-backed roles, and token-management. we can require MFA via your identity provider.
[07:03] Rajesh: one more finance question — what's escrow or continuity path in case Redwood stops supporting a particular model? we need code or model artifacts to be exportable.
[07:12] Jordan: standard approach: we provide model checkpoints and a runtime compatibility migration guide for your private deploy; for hosted we offer an export of logs and data and a migration assist clause in enterprise agreements. we can discuss escrow for critical models.
[07:29] Marta: counsel asks for a clause on audit rights — can internal auditors run a read-only audit of logs?
[07:36] Evan: we can provide an auditor access window and export snapshots under NDA; for Private you can run your own auditors directly against your logs.
[07:47] Liam: about compliance — do you support customer-managed keys for log encryption as well?
[07:53] Priya: yes we can wrap logs with customer keys in Private and Dedicated. for hosted logs we can support envelope encryption with BYOK.
[08:02] Sara: if we run a pilot, is there a non-prod environment for integration? we need a staging cluster identical to prod behavior.
[08:09] Priya: we stand up a dedicated staging cluster for pilots so you can run end-to-end tests; sometimes it's a smaller footprint but behaves the same.
[08:17] Jordan: ok we're near time — let's recap actions and owners. Jordan to send pricing bands and sample bill; Priya to send pilot runbook and perf-test checklist; Evan to send security artifacts and MSA/DPA templates; Liam to send KMS and egress policy; Marta to confirm procurement redline list.
[08:33] Marta: yes i'll consolidate legal redlines and share with Jordan by 2027-04-12.
[08:36] Rajesh: finance will review sample bills once received.
[08:38] Jordan: great — we'll schedule the pilot kickoff tentatively 2027-04-20 pending docs. thanks everyone.
[08:44] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription quality: speaker overlaps at times; some product names transcribed loosely (e.g., 'KV cache' as 'k-v cash' in earlier auto transcripts), adjusted manually where obvious.

Jordan: Send pricing band and committed capacity options with examples of cost impact by 2027-04-09
Liam: Provide current KMS/HSM vendor and network egress policy doc by 2027-04-12
Priya: Prepare pilot runbook & perf-test checklist and link to benchmark sheet by 2027-04-13
Redwood to share redlined MSA and standard DPA by 2027-04-12
Customer to confirm required SLA thresholds and list of systems for private deployment by 2027-04-14
Schedule technical pilot benchmark with 1mln token/day profile w/ Priya week of 2027-04-19

Orchard Systems Q4 Health & Roadmap Check-in

Meeting header:
Date: 2028-12-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~49 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording ID: ff-2028-12-05-orchard-q4
Attendees: Maya, Luis, Priya (Redwood); Samir, Aisha, Noah, Eleni (Orchard)

Summary: Quick Q4 health check focused on cost drivers (quantization + batching), reliability incidents in November, and next quarter rollout/roadmap. Agreement to run a short synthetic load test and share pricing scenarios. Security follow-up requested.

Topics: usage trends, tail latency spikes, dedicated vs hosted runway, model variants and quantization, SSO/KMS/data residency, pilot scope and metrics for success.

Action items (recorded above)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everybody, thanks for joining, quick intro from our side, um this is Maya (AE) with Luis (SE) and Priya (CSM), how're we all doing?
[00:08] Samir Kapoor: good thanks, busy quarter. We wanted to focus on the November spike and planning for the Q1 rollout.
[00:14] Maya Chen: perfect, goal is to surface what happened, get to root causes, and align on next steps — cost, reliability, and security.
[00:22] Aisha Mbatha: quick note — we got the usage/export you asked, there was a missing bucket so some minutes were double counted, we cleaned that up.
[00:29] Luis Ortega: ok thanks, helpful. I'm going to run through the latency profile we pulled from the shared runbook, and then we can talk cost levers.
[00:37] [00:37] Luis Ortega: (screen share) so this is the 95/99 tail for token generation, you can see the jump on Nov 18th during the batch job; the 99 went from about 480ms to 1.6s, and that matched a background retrain triggering high prefix cache churn — or at least the logs suggest the KV cache got thrash.
[00:57] Noah Greene: hmm yep that aligns with the deploy window, we had a heavy retrain cluster that pulled data and I think the autoscale didn't catch up for short lived spikes.
[01:06] Eleni Park: small thing — the transcript of the incident said "V K cache" which made it confusing, but yes cache churn.
[01:13] Luis Ortega: lol yea auto transcript :), but the technical bit is the cache TTLs and our batching behaviour — when you get intermittent high prefix diversity batching becomes suboptimal.
[01:24] Samir Kapoor: can you remind us how Redwood routes to hosted vs dedicated? We may want to shift some high-volume routes to dedicated pools on peak windows.
[01:32] Maya Chen: sure — routing policy can be by customer tier, latency SLO, or cost. For Orchard we'd recommend keeping critical low-latency routes on Dedicated (if you have reserved capacity) and non-critical async tasks on hosted cheaper endpoints.
[01:45] Aisha Mbatha: cost question: our token bill jumped 28% month-over-month. How much of that is model choice vs inefficient batching?
[01:54] Luis Ortega: rough split from our preliminary look: ~45% model size/sequence length, ~30% lack of KV cache hits due to prefix variability, ~25% suboptimal batching and retry storms. Quantization profile would reduce model cost by ~20-30% for your typical traffic.
[02:12] [02:12] Samir Kapoor: what about quality? We can't have a hallucination regression when we quantize.
[02:17] Luis Ortega: yes, you need to validate on your eval set. Our Optimize toolkit can produce candidate quantized variants and run your prompt families through them; we also score behavioral regressions and surface diffs. Typically 8-bit quant works with minimal quality loss on these models but we want to run your prompts to be sure.
[02:34] Eleni Park: we'll need the tooling integrated with our CI; can Redwood's eval hooks run in our pipeline?
[02:39] Priya Rao: yes, we have an API to push prompt sets and get regression alerts; Luis can show a demo but the integration is straightforward — it's an HTTP webhook and S3-compatible results.
[02:52] [02:52] Aisha Mbatha: security follow-up — we need assurance around KMS and key rotation, plus SOC 2 scope.
[02:58] Maya Chen: understood — Priya will set up a security deep-dive; we support KMS integrations and can provide our SOC 2 report and audit logs. For private deployments you can bring your own KMS in the VPC.
[03:11] Noah Greene: do you support HSM or is it just cloud KMS?
[03:14] Luis Ortega: we can integrate HSM via customer network for Private deployments; hosted supports cloud KMS with customer-controlled keys in many regions. We'll clarify exact HSM options in the follow-up.
[03:24] [03:24] Samir Kapoor: timeline — we want to pilot Q1, ramp mid-Q1 into prod. What are realistic guardrails and milestones?
[03:31] Maya Chen: pilot scope suggestion: 2 weeks of shadow load on dedicated instance, 24-72h peak soak, then ramp to 20% traffic for 2 weeks, check metrics (99 lat, error rate, cost per 1k tokens) and then full roll. We'll align on observability dashboards and alert thresholds.
[03:48] Luis Ortega: and we'll run a synthetic 24h test to simulate your traffic shape (Luis to own), that will show batching behaviour and tail latency under sustained load.
[03:57] [03:57] Aisha Mbatha: great — what's the expected cost delta if we go dedicated reserved vs hosted pay-as-you-go for our forecasted volume?
[04:05] Maya Chen: depends on commitment length; rough math: for your projected Q1 volume a 3-month commit on Dedicated gives ~18-24% lower unit cost after accounting for throughput efficiency; we'll send a trimmed pricing sheet with scenarios.
[04:18] Samir Kapoor: and bursting? We still need burst to hosted when dedicated saturates.
[04:22] Luis Ortega: yes that's standard — routing policy supports burst to hosted with fallback model variants; that lets you keep a low-latency core while absorbing spikes.
[04:33] [04:33] Eleni Park: question on model variants — if we pin a model, can Redwood automatically fallback to a quantized variant if the primary is unavailable?
[04:39] Luis Ortega: yes you can configure a compatible fallback chain — e.g., full-precision -> 8-bit quant -> smaller architecture, and you can set thresholds for quality/regression alerts.
[04:50] Priya Rao: also note we can run canary rollouts by route so you can gate new models on small traffic slices.
[04:58] [04:58] Samir Kapoor: about the November incident, do you have a concrete remediation suggestion?
[05:03] Luis Ortega: operationally: increase cache TTLs for stable prefixes, add a pre-warm step when a retrain kicks, and set autoscale faster on short pulses; plus route long-running batch jobs to a separate pool so they don't evict hot KV cache used by low-latency routes.
[05:20] Noah Greene: that sounds doable, we'll need runbook changes.
[05:23] Maya Chen: we can help with runbook templates and alert thresholds — Priya will share the templates.
[05:30] [05:30] Aisha Mbatha: small nit — can you ensure logs include request IDs so we can reconcile with our service logs? Our compliance team demands traceability.
[05:38] Luis Ortega: yes, request IDs and per-token tracing are available; there's a opt-in payload field for you to send a correlation ID.
[05:45] [05:45] Samir Kapoor: success metrics for pilot — what should we measure?
[05:49] Maya Chen: agreed pilot metrics: 99p latency < target, error rate < 0.1%, cost per 1k tokens within agreed delta, no regression in hallucination rate on sampled prompts, and successful SSO/KMS integration.
[06:03] Eleni Park: can we get a dashboard template for those KPIs?
[06:06] Priya Rao: yes — we'll provision a shared dashboard and set up alerts; you get token-level breakdowns and per-route tracing.
[06:15] [06:15] Aisha Mbatha: about data residency — some of our EU customers require EU-only model execution. How does Redwood enforce region pinning?
[06:22] Luis Ortega: route policy supports region pinning by model and by route; you can restrict certain routes to EU regions and disable cross-region fallback for those routes.
[06:30] [06:30] Samir Kapoor: any gotchas with VPC on-prem customers? We may eventually move sensitive pipelines on-prem.
[06:36] Maya Chen: on-prem requires additional setup (private control plane, network extents), longer lead time for upgrades, and different upgrade windows. We'll map that if you decide.
[06:46] [06:46] Noah Greene: ok noted.
[06:49] [06:49] Luis Ortega: quick run-through of the synthetic test plan: we'll replay representative prompts at actual concurrency, track batching stats, KV hit rates, token throughput, and tail lat. We'll share raw logs and a summary workbook.
[07:05] Samir Kapoor: sounds good — we'll provide prompt families and representative traffic histogram.
[07:10] [07:10] Aisha Mbatha: the prompts include some long sequences (700-1k tokens) — is that supported without degrading other routes?
[07:17] Luis Ortega: longer sequences cost more CPU and memory; best practice is to route long sequence workloads to a separate pool or schedule them during off-peak; we can also recommend a quant/profile that handles long context more cheaply.
[07:30] Priya Rao: I'll add that as a risk to pilot scope.
[07:34] [07:34] Maya Chen: quick commercial note — there is a small onboarding credit for pilot customers that run through our Optimize program; Maya will include that in the pricing note.
[07:44] [07:44] Eleni Park: nice, every bit helps.
[07:47] [07:47] Samir Kapoor: any known regressions with the latest model family you surfaced? We saw one thread about increased repetitions on a few prompts.
[07:55] Luis Ortega: some small distributional shifts, but we can evaluate; that's why we'll run the eval hooks on your prompts. We'll also monitor for latent regressions post-rollout.
[08:06] [08:06] Aisha Mbatha: logistics — who will be the day-to-day contact during the pilot?
[08:11] Priya Rao: Priya will be the CSM and Luis will handle SE tasks; Maya will be Exec sponsor. We'll include contact details in the follow-up.
[08:21] [08:21] Samir Kapoor: ok good. Next — procurement timing: we need standard T&Cs and an example SOW for Dedicated pilot.
[08:29] Maya Chen: I'll loop in legal but we'll send an example SOW and standard terms; for enterprise we can do a streamlined addendum for pilot.
[08:36] [08:36] Aisha Mbatha: can you include a clause about data deletion timelines?
[08:40] Maya Chen: yes, deletion and retention are negotiable in the enterprise SOW — we'll propose standard 30-day soft-delete plus enterprise options.
[08:49] [08:49] Eleni Park: please add audit log retention windows to that doc too.
[08:52] Priya Rao: will do.
[08:55] [08:55] Luis Ortega: one more technical suggestion: enable prefix dedupe at the client side for high-cardinality prompts — we've seen big wins where customers do lightweight canonicalization before calling the API.
[09:07] Samir Kapoor: good call, we'll prototype that.
[09:10] [09:10] Maya Chen: ok wrapping up, quick recap: Redwood runs synthetic load (Luis), Orchard provides prompts and histograms (Samir), Redwood sends pricing and SOW (Maya), security deep-dive scheduled (Priya/Noah).
[09:25] [09:25] Aisha Mbatha: timeline check — can we get the pricing and synthetic test plan this week?
[09:30] Maya Chen: we'll aim for pricing by Friday and synthetic test kickoff early next week.
[09:34] [09:34] Eleni Park: thanks all, this was productive.
[09:36] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with notes and links (pricing spreadsheet, test plan, runbook templates).
[09:43] [09:43] Meeting end

Shared artifacts referenced:
- Deck: "Orchard Q4 Review" (link: drive.google.com/orchard-q4-deck)
- Pricing spreadsheet (internal link will be shared by Maya)
- Runbook templates and Eval hooks docs (link: redwood.com/docs/eval-hooks)
- Incident logs (shared in workspace)

Notes about transcript quality: speaker labels sometimes generic; some proper nouns mis-transcribed (KV -> V K, HSM -> H S M), occasional run-on sentences.

End of transcript.

PolarityMesh gateway listing + on-prem quantization lab sync

Technical sync to align Redwood and PolarityMesh for marketplace listing and an on-prem quantization pilot. Covered helm packaging, networking/VPN and VPC-like constraints on customer side, KMS/HSM integration, telemetry/OTel tradeoffs, and benchmark plan for 8-bit quantized runtime. Agreed actions and schedule for lab runs and security artifact handoff.
Meeting header: 2027-03-17 15:00 UTC | Duration: 78 min
Attendees: Ethan (Redwood AE), Nora (Redwood SE), Jamal (Redwood SA), Priya (Redwood Product) — Marco (PolarityMesh CTO), Tanya (Lead Platform Eng), Samir (Security Architect), Aisha (SRE)

[00:00] Ethan: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, um we'll kick off, quick agenda — marketplace listing checklist, on-prem connector packaging, quantization pilot and perf benchmarks, and security artifacts. any additions from the PolarityMesh side?
[00:12] Marco: nope that looks good, uh big thing for us is the onprem installer and KMS workflow — we have strict HSM boundaries, can't export keys.
[00:21] Tanya: also interested in how your kv cache behaves with our streaming gateway, we do a lot of prefix reuse so cache hit patterns matter for cost.
[00:30] Nora: yeah, good call. the runtime has some heuristics for prefix caching and continuous batching, but when you run on smaller nodes the batch windows can change latency. we'll show some profiles.
[00:45] Jamal: quick intro to our helm chart approach — the partner listing uses a values-overlay model, so you can pin node pools, kms config, and quant profiles per environment. we'll attach a sample values.yaml.
[00:58] Samir: security question off the top: do you support in-cluster KMS or do you rely on external HSM endpoints? our compliance needs require HSM-backed envelope keys and audit trails.
[01:12] Priya: we support both; we have integrations for cloud KMS (AWS/GCP/Azure) and customers can point to customer-managed HSM endpoints. audit logs are exportable to S3 or our observability collector. we'll share the exact artifact.
[01:27] Marco: ok good, can you share the retention/rotation details? we have legal asking for 7-year auditability for certain logs.
[01:36] Priya: we'll check policy but we can surface log retention controls and long-term export. expect a doc link.

[01:55] Ethan: shifting to quantization — PolarityMesh mentioned interest in 8-bit int quant and how it impacts latency and rightness. Nora, can you walk through tradeoffs?
[02:05] Nora: yeah so, short answer: 8-bit and Q4 variants reduce memory and throughput cost but can slightly change token probabilities. our optimize tool suggests quant profiles by workload. for chat workloads with long contexts the KV cache behavior becomes critical — quantized kernels can change per-token latency a bit. we should run a small pilot with your sample prompts.
[02:32] Tanya: are you doing per-layer quant or whole-model? we have concerns about hallucination regressions.
[02:40] Nora: we do mixed strategies; the pilot will compare full 8-bit vs hybrid 16/8 on last n layers. we'll capture eval set passed from you and compute regression metric.
[02:51] Samir: what's your eval infra? do you keep PII when running pilots? we need assurance that sample data isn't stored outside our control.
[02:58] Jamal: good point — on-prem pilot will run fully in your cluster, no outbound model artifacts; logs can be configured to not send prompt text upstream. we'll provide a privacy-mode helm overlay.

[03:20] Marco: networking — our infra is air-gapped-ish, but we can open a controlled VPN for the lab. how do you handle catalog updates and model downloads in that scenario?
[03:32] Ethan: two modes — vendor-pulled images via internal registry (you push the image) or we provide an offline bundle that you can scp into your cluster. for cloud parts we can mirror.
[03:45] Aisha: for ops, we need to verify healthchecks, liveness/readiness and canary rollback hooks in your operator. can these be tuned?
[03:53] Nora: yes, our operator has hooks for rollout gates, automatic fallback to lower-capacity variants, and route-level SLOs. you can wire in your canary metric (p50/p95 latency or error rate) to trigger rollbacks.

[04:12] Ethan: let's talk telemetry — we recommend OTel for traces, and we can forward traces to your existing backend or to Redwood's console with tokens. what's your current observability stack?
[04:22] Tanya: we run a hosted OTLP collector to Splunk, and also push metrics to Prometheus. we prefer local sampling before export to reduce egress.
[04:30] Nora: our runtime supports OTLP and can run local sampling and batching; we can also emit structured per-request metadata (model_id, sequence_length, quant_profile, route). note that structured tokens can be large so there's a privacy/size tradeoff.

[04:54] Samir: about billing and metering — for marketplace listing we need to map usage to our product metering. how does Redwood expose token/embedding counts?
[05:03] Jamal: we have token-level metering and per-model counters; the partner listing connector can expose a usage webhook or push to your billing pipeline. works offline too via periodic reconciliation.
[05:15] Marco: perfect, important for revenue share.

[05:26] Ethan: let's kick off a concrete pilot plan — proposed: week 1: you provide representative workloads and deploy test cluster; week 2: Redwood runs baseline with FP16, week 3: run quant profiles, week 4: joint analysis and canary run. sound reasonable?
[05:40] Tanya: yes but we need to compress timeline if possible — our Q2 roadmap wants listing live by mid-April. can we move the pilot earlier?
[05:49] Nora: we can parallelize baseline and quant runs if you can provide infra access earlier. Nora: (laugh) if you push the cluster this week we can start benchmark jobs asap.

[06:05] Ethan: action items recap — I'll send the listing checklist and helm values, Priya will send the security packet, Nora & Jamal will prep quant scripts. anything missing?
[06:14] Marco: please include an example values.yaml for kms pointing to HSM endpoints and a sample for offline image bundle instructions.
[06:22] Ethan: noted.

[06:30] Tanya: one small deep point — our gateway uses a fan-out pattern with short sequential requests; we worry about KV cache fragmentation on per-request basis. how to avoid poor cache locality?
[06:42] Nora: good question — best practice is to coalesce prefixes and use session affinity for chat flows so the same worker keeps KV cache warm. we can add affinity hints in the request headers and we have a session pinning option in the operator. we'll demonstrate in the lab.

[07:00] Samir: compliance again — can you provide an example audit event for model inference that includes user_id hash but not the prompt text? we need to show auditors what we store.
[07:12] Priya: yes we will produce a sample audit schema; it includes request metadata, model_version, latency, non-PII hashed user id, and a flag for prompt retention set to false by default.

[07:25] Ethan: competitors — Marco asked earlier about alternatives, any concerns?
[07:30] Marco: we looked at ApexAI and FastServe; main reason to work with Redwood is your deployment flexibility and the prebuilt listing path. just need to prove perf on our long-tail workloads.

[07:38] Nora: we'll focus the benchmark on throughput at p95 under simulated burst traffic and on-chat quality regression using your eval prompts.

[07:50] Aisha: ops question: how are upgrades handled for models pinned in listing — can we freeze a model version while still getting security patches for runtime?
[07:59] Jamal: yes, the operator allows you to pin model artifacts and runtime separately; you can opt into security-only updates for the runtime while keeping the model version pinned. we'll show the helm flag.

[08:15] Ethan: anything else before we wrap?
[08:18] Marco: can you include estimated infra cost delta for quant vs fp16 in the pilot report? procurement will need that.
[08:24] Nora: yes we'll include per-token cost and estimated monthly spend with sample traffic profiles.

[08:33] Ethan: okay, recap of next steps and owners — I'll send checklist and images; Priya sends security assets; Tanya stands up cluster; Nora/Jamal prepare quant pilot and benchmarks; schedule canary run in next two weeks. thanks everyone.
[08:47] Marco: thanks all.
[08:50] (meeting ends)
PolarityMesh has strict HSM/KMS requirements and air-gapped constraints
Redwood to provide offline bundle and helm overlay for privacy-mode
Pilot to measure quantization impact on latency, throughput, and quality with PolarityMesh eval set
Ethan Brooks - Send marketplace checklist and helm sample values (due: 2027-03-22)
Priya Singh - Pull SOC2 summary and KMS integration notes, share doc link (due: 2027-03-20)
Tanya Liu - Stand up on-prem test cluster and provide access details (due: 2027-03-24)
Nora Patel - Prepare quantization pilot script and baseline token-per-second benchmark (due: 2027-03-28)
Marco Rivera - Confirm performance acceptance criteria and list of representative workloads (due: 2027-03-25)
Redwood to share marketplace listing checklist + example helm values (Ethan) by 2027-03-22
PolarityMesh to provision onprem test cluster and share VPN details (Tanya) by 2027-03-24
SE-led lab: run quantization pilot using 8-bit profile and baseline benchmark (Nora/Jamal) week of 2027-03-29
Security packet: Redwood to send SOC2/ISO artifact links and KMS integration notes (Priya) by 2027-03-20
Schedule canary routing test and failover runbook review (joint) - propose times 2027-03-30 to 2027-04-02

document.content:
NorthStar AI - POC interop & benchmark sprint kickoff

Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-03-30
- Start: 15:00 PDT
- Duration: 62 minutes (approx)
- Attendees: Avery Collins (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Lina Romero (Redwood SE), Dr. Mei Chen (NorthStar Head of ML), Omar Ruiz (NorthStar Platform), Priya Singh (NorthStar PM)

Summary:
- Kickoff to scope POC for integrating Redwood inference into NorthStar AI's assistant product.
- Primary goals: validate OpenAI-compatible endpoints, function/tool calling, structured output accuracy; measure latency/cost at 50 req/s baseline with bursts to 200 req/s; determine hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs and timeline for 4-week benchmark sprint.
- Success criteria drafted: p95 latency < 350ms for short prompts, structured output schema F1 > 0.92, acceptable unit cost delta vs current provider, end-to-end failure < 0.5% for 24h run.

Topics covered:
- Integration approach: SDK vs raw OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoints
- Tool/function calling support and best practices for action grounding
- Structured output verification and eval metrics
- Workload sizing, KV cache and batching expectations
- Deployment options: hosted, dedicated, private VPC and SOC2/compliance needs
- Benchmark design, timelines, and deliverables

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery (Redwood AE): alright thanks everyone for joining, appreciate you making time. quick roll call?
[00:08] Mei (NorthStar): hi hi Mei here, thanks.
[00:10] Omar: Omar on platform.
[00:12] Priya: Priya, product.
[00:14] Avery: and from our side Samir and Lina are on the technical tracks, we'll run through the POC plan. rough agenda: success criteria, workload/trace, integration touch points, benchmarks, timeline, next steps.
[00:30] Samir (Redwood SE): cool, I'll start with the baseline ask. NorthStar said earlier you see about 50 requests per second steady with occasional bursts up to 200/sec during peak. is that correct?
[00:38] Priya: yes that's the ballpark for chat assistant front door, the heavy ops are usually between 11am-1pm PST.
[00:44] Mei: i want to validate structured output mostly — the assistant returns a JSON action schema that triggers downstream tools, so schema correctness is critical.
[00:52] Lina (Redwood SE): understood. do you have example schemas and some canonical prompts we can run? even a small set of 5-10 will help craft the eval.
[00:58] Priya: we'll share 8 examples and the schema, aim to get those by Friday.
[01:05] Samir: great. for benchmarking we'll test three configs: hosted Redwood API (fastest onboarding), dedicated pool with reserved GPUs, and a private VPC deployment if security requires. we'll measure latency (p50/p95/p99), token cost, and structured output accuracy.
[01:18] Omar: what's our current latency with provider X? p95 is around 280ms for short form prompts, p99 occasional spikes to 800ms. cost is... we're trying to trim 15% overall.
[01:26] Avery: helpful. we'll aim to show parity or improvement on latency and a clear map to cost per 1k tokens for each config.
[01:34] Mei: security questions — we need SOC2 docs, audit logs, SSO and KMS integration details for key material. also data residency notes.
[01:42] Avery: yes we'll share SOC2 and private deployment docs today; KMS integrations supported for Private and Dedicated, hosted supports customer-managed keys in some regions — we'll include specifics.
[01:50] Samir: about the OpenAI-compatible endpoints — Redwood exposes an OpenAI-like HTTP surface for generation and function calling, plus SDKs that add retries, streaming, and a structured output helper. if you use the OpenAI path things like function call semantics map but there are some field name differences (we'll document).
[02:05] Mei: can we do function/tool calling end-to-end? like have the model return a tool invocation that our orchestrator picks up?
[02:10] Lina: yes, function calling is supported. two options: 1) use OpenAI-compatible function calling and our SDK does automatic parsing and validation against the JSON schema, or 2) use the SDK's structured-output helper that enforces schema at generation time and runs quick heuristics for fallback partial outputs.
[02:24] Omar: curious about KV cache and prefix caching — our assistants often reuse conversation context which matters for cost. how does Redwood cache keys across requests?
[02:31] Samir: we have prefix caching and multi-request KV cache to reuse transformer KV state; for chat you can pass a cache key and Redwood will keep the KV between tokens to reduce full recomputation. caching reduces cost but adds some staleness complexity for multi-user sessions.
[02:45] Mei: ok good. on metrics, we need structured output F1 and exact match thresholds; for the POC we propose F1 > 0.92 across the canonical set and for the 24-hour run, failure rate less than 0.5%.
[02:58] Priya: timeline idea? we were thinking 3-4 week sprint to validate.
[03:02] Avery: we usually run a two-week benchmark sprint plus a one-week integration/validation phase; total 3 weeks feels reasonable. schedule: week 0 prep (workload traces + schema), week 1 baseline runs hosted + small dedicated sample, week 2 full load dedicated vs hosted comparisons, week 3 structured output validation and wrap.
[03:20] Omar: do you need us to spin up any infra?
[03:23] Samir: for hosted no, but for dedicated we'll ask you to allow incoming test traffic from Redwood test harness and possibly open a peering/VPN if you want private deploy. for an initial dedicated eval we can run from our sandbox using your credentials or a short-lived VLAN — we'll detail options in the SOW.
[03:40] Mei: latency SLOs are important. what about p99 under load? we need predictable tail behavior.
[03:44] Lina: we'll collect p50/p95/p99 and show resource utilization. dedicated typically gives tighter p99, hosted has multi-tenant variations but we can enable reserved slots for burst protection.
[03:55] Samir: also we'll test quantized model variants if you care about cost tradeoffs — 4-bit/8-bit quantization to see MME (model mean error) impact on structured output.
[04:05] Priya: yes cost is a big factor, if quantization impacts schema accuracy it's a no-go.
[04:10] Avery: we'll include quality regressions in the eval and flag any quantized config that drops below the F1 threshold.
[04:16] Mei: what about model versioning and rollouts? if we do a canary we want auto-fallback if quality dips.
[04:22] Lina: Redwood supports canary rollouts per route, and automatic fallback to a pinned model variant if quality checks fail. we can wire simple eval hooks into your CI to auto-promote.
[04:33] Omar: for the benchmark inputs, we can provide a 24-hour anonymized log and note peak concurrency windows. is that enough?
[04:38] Samir: perfect — we'll replay traces using the same temporal distribution so burst patterns are realistic. also please include distribution of prompt lengths and percentage of tool-calling events.
[04:50] Priya: the assistant triggers tools about 12% of the time. most prompts are short, median prompt length 90 tokens, 95th percentile 450 tokens.
[04:59] Samir: that's great context. for cost modeling we'll estimate token footprint including response sizes. do you have average generated tokens per request?
[05:06] Mei: average response is 160 tokens. long tails to 1200 tokens but rare.
[05:12] Samir: noted. for benchmarking we'll run canonical prompts, synthetic bursts, and a 24-hour replay. the 24-hour run will detect skews and tail behavior.
[05:22] Avery: let's capture success criteria clearly: 1) latency: p95 < 350ms for <512-token sequences; 2) structured output F1 > 0.92 on canonical examples; 3) end-to-end error/failure rate < 0.5% during 24-hour replay; 4) unit token cost within X% of current provider — we'll compute exact numbers once Samir has cost baseline.
[05:40] Mei: that seems reasonable. for compliance, we'll need audit logs — retention 1 year, and SSO with SCIM or SAML.
[05:47] Avery: both supported, we'll include SSO/SCIM flow and example audit log formats in the docs pack.
[05:54] Priya: schedule the canary for 2026-04-08, leave a week to iterate.
[05:57] Lina: I'll create a calendar invite for 2026-04-08 10am PDT for the canary / benchmark session.
[06:04] Omar: one practical question — SDK languages? our stack is Go + Node.
[06:09] Samir: we have official SDKs for Node and Python; Go SDK is community maintained but supports core flows including streaming and function calling. we can provide a thin Go wrapper or some examples.
[06:20] Mei: would prefer official Go support before full pilot, but can use Node for early runs.
[06:26] Samir: we'll prioritize Go examples in the repo for this POC and include snippet for function calling and structured output validation.
[06:33] Priya: how do you handle retries and backpressure? in peak we saw dropped requests with our current provider.
[06:38] Lina: our SDK has built-in retry with jitter, and the serving runtime supports request queuing with prioritized routes; backpressure metrics surfaced in the console. we'll include suggested policies for retry/backoff.
[06:50] Mei: okay. can we get a short runbook for failure modes? like when KV cache misses spike or when model runs out of memory?
[06:57] Samir: yes we'll include an operations runbook with mitigation steps: scale up dedicated pool, enable prefix-only caching, fall back to smaller model, etc.
[07:08] Avery: to recap action items: Samir runs latency/cost baseline (due Apr 6); Avery shares SOC2 + private deploy docs (due Apr 2); Priya supplies canonical prompts and schema (due Apr 3); Omar provides anonymized 24h trace (due Apr 4). Lina will invite the canary benchmark for Apr 8.
[07:27] Priya: that works. any blockers on Redwood side?
[07:30] Avery: none immediate. we'll flag if we need additional creds or a short onboarding token.
[07:35] Mei: one more item — our legal team will want a data-processing addendum for the POC.
[07:40] Avery: we can share a POC-level DPA and SOW template today.
[07:44] Omar: great.
[07:46] Priya: thanks all, looking forward.
[07:48] Avery: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the doc pack and invite.

End of transcript.

Referenced artifacts/links:
- Redwood POC SOW template (link shared via email)
- SOC2 report & Private deploy guide (link)
- Benchmark spreadsheet template (will be filled by Samir)

Notes on transcription quality: medium — occasional mis-attributions and minor word swaps (e.g., 'MME' vs 'mean model error'), timestamps approximate.

POC success criteria (as recorded):
- p95 latency < 350ms for <512 token prompts
- structured output F1 >= 0.92 on canonical eval set
- end-to-end failure rate < 0.5% during 24-hour replay
- unit token cost within agreed delta vs current provider (to be quantified)

document.content:
Governance activity streams & retention planning - Halo Insurance

Security review focused on audit log fidelity, export paths (S3/GCS/Kafka), retention options, and KMS integration for Halo Insurance. Discussed RBAC/SSO implications and SOC 2 evidence needs. Agreed next steps include sample export, log schema, and a short POC to validate retention and access controls.
Meeting Header
Date: 2025-06-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Maya Lin (Redwood SE), Priya Menon (Halo - Head of Security), Ben Ortiz (Halo - Cloud Architect), Sara Lu (Halo - Compliance Manager)

[00:00] Jordan: Thanks for carving out time, everyone. We're here to walk through audit and admin activity capture options for Redwood — especially export and retention that your compliance team needs. Maya and I will take you through current capture surface and then we can deep dive into KMS and SSO stuff.
[00:14] Priya: Thanks Jordan, appreciate it. Just to set context — we're doing internal SOC 2 readiness and Palo Alto asked about offsite retention of admin trails. We're looking for immutable export and evidence that keys are customer controlled where necessary.
[00:28] Maya: Yep, totally — good starting point. Quick run-through of what Redwood captures by default: admin console logins, API key lifecycle events (create/rotate/revoke), model route changes, rollout events, RBAC grant/revoke, SSO logins (SAML/assertions), and operator actions like scale-up, drains, and config changes. We also capture request-level metadata for inference calls: timestamps, model ID, tokens counted, but not PII by default unless you've sent it in prompt — we'll talk about redaction later.
[00:54] Ben: How granular are the admin logs? Like do we get the before/after of a configuration change or just the event that it happened?
[01:05] Maya: We capture both the event and a JSON patch in most cases — so you can see old vs new for things like rollout thresholds or model pins. Occasionally the patch may be truncated for very large blobs — UX thing — but we include a reference to the full artifact stored in the internal log store. That's the part some customers choose to export off-platform for long-term legal retention.
[01:29] Priya: Ok. For SOC 2 we need immutable evidence for a 12 month window with restricted access. How do we support that?
[01:38] Jordan: Two patterns we recommend: short-term retention in Redwood with role-based access and audit policies, and long-term export to your own cloud bucket (S3/GCS/Azure) with server-side encryption and bucket locking enabled. For immutability we support S3 Object Lock-compatible exports. We can also stream logs to your SIEM via Kafka or syslog if you want near-real-time ingestion.
[02:03] Sara: Does Redwood sign the logs or provide a tamper-evidence checksum?
[02:09] Maya: We compute and store SHA-256 digests for log batches and persist them with the event header. If you export them, the digests are included so you can verify integrity after transit. We're working on HSM-backed signing but currently digests plus S3 Object Lock is the common compliance pattern.
[02:26] Ben: On encryption, do we manage keys or can we use customer KMS/HSM?
[02:31] Jordan: Both. Hosted mode has Redwood-managed keys by default. For Dedicated/Private or enterprise customers you can bring your own key (BYOK) via KMS integration — we support AWS KMS (multi-region), GCP KMS, and on-prem HSM via PKCS#11 for private deployments. We key-wrap the log encryption keys with your KMS so Redwood doesn't have plaintext key material for long-term exports.
[02:57] Priya: And rotation? We need quarterly rotation and a documented rotation history.
[03:02] Maya: Our KMS integration supports automatic key rotation. Rotation events are logged with key IDs and timestamps, and we store the previous key metadata so you have a clear chain of custody.
[03:13] Priya: Good. Now about access controls — we have multiple teams and need fine-grained RBAC, especially for who can request exports.
[03:22] Jordan: Redwood's RBAC maps to roles and policies. You can separate export privileges into a specific role. We also support SCIM provisioning so your identity provider can centrally manage group membership. Exports require a multi-step approval flow if enabled — the request shows up in an approval queue and approvers get email/SMS notifications.
[03:44] Ben: Is approval flow customizable? We might want 2 approvers for production exports.
[03:48] Maya: Yes. Approval policies are templated and can enforce n-of-m approvers, timeouts, and audit comments. Everything about who approved is part of the audit trail.
[03:58] Priya: In terms of what's actually in the exported artifact, can we tailor fields? Our legal folks want certain fields and to redact others.
[04:08] Maya: Export templates let you pick a schema. Default includes timestamp, event_type, actor (user id & email), resource, action, before_state (if present), after_state, request_id, and origin IP. You can add custom metadata like correlation_id. For redaction we offer post-ingest processors to mask PII — or you can use pre-export hooks to transform fields. We recommend keeping unredacted logs in your own bucket if you need full fidelity but redacting copies for business use.
[04:40] Sara: If we redact for business use, how do we keep an unredacted canonical for audits but still limit access?
[04:46] Jordan: Keep canonical in a separate bucket with restrictive IAM and S3 Object Lock, and create a derived redacted view in a different bucket or attach a lifecycle that limits read access. We can automate that via the export job, and we can include a manifest with checksums for the canonical copy.
[05:03] Ben: How about retention policies? We need rolling retention: operational logs 90 days, audit evidence 3-7 years depending on region.
[05:13] Maya: The platform supports per-stream retention. You can set short retention for inference telemetry and longer for admin trails. For long-term, we strongly suggest exporting to your archive bucket with lifecycle rules to Glacier/Coldline. We also support configurable deletion windows and legal hold flags.
[05:30] Priya: Data residency — can we force logs originating from EU regions to stay within EU endpoints?
[05:36] Jordan: Yes — region routing policies can pin storage to specific regions. When you provision export targets, you select the target region and Redwood will only write to endpoints in that region. For cross-region replication you'd need explicit approval.
[05:49] Ben: On the streaming side, if we feed logs into our SIEM, do we need to run agents or is it push from Redwood?
[05:56] Maya: Redwood can push via HTTPS/webhook, Kafka, or forward via syslog. We do offer a lightweight agent for edge cases, but push-based integrations are more common. All pushes are authenticated via signed tokens and optional mTLS.
[06:16] Priya: Any SLA around export jobs? For example, guaranteed delivery within X hours?
[06:21] Jordan: For hosted customers we provide best-effort, typically minutes for near-real-time streams, and export jobs for larger historical snapshots run in batch and we provide delivery windows based on size — we'll commit specifics in the Dedicated contract. For compliance POCs we usually run a sample job and confirm end-to-end within agreed window.
[06:42] Sara: We need evidence for the last 6 months — how much data volume should we expect? Our ingress is fairly heavy during policy updates.
[06:49] Ben: Our ops team does a lot of model pinning and config changes, maybe several thousand events a month.
[06:55] Maya: We can estimate. Admin events are low-volume compared to inference tokens — usually tens to hundreds of KB per event. I'll run an estimate off your projected event count and send a sizing doc.
[07:08] Priya: On the topic of dashboards and evidence collection, do you provide pre-built SOC 2 evidence exports?
[07:15] Jordan: We ship a SOC 2 pack — a set of evidence artifacts including config snapshots, rotation logs, export manifests, and selected audit intervals. For the auditor you usually provide the canonical logs and the manifests verifying tamper-evidence.
[07:30] Sara: Great. Any limitations on filters when exporting? e.g., can we export by user or action type?
[07:36] Maya: Yes filters are flexible: time-range, user_id, event_type, resource_id, region, and custom tags. Exports can be incremental (only appended events) to minimize data transfer.
[07:49] Ben: About retention enforcement — suppose a user asks to delete an event under GDPR. If an event is in a write-once bucket with Object Lock, how do you reconcile that with erase requests?
[07:59] Jordan: Good question. For EU data subject requests we recommend storing replicates for audit in an internal legal hold that is separate from personal-data copies. If an erase is required, we will provide an export that omits the subject's personal identifiers and mark the canonical with an access restriction. This is an area we consult on per-case, and it's why many customers keep PII out of logs or tokenize it at ingestion.
[08:29] Priya: For our purposes we want a POC: 1) export admin trails for last 30 days to our S3 with Object Lock enabled and KMS key, 2) show proof of digest/checksum verification, 3) show RBAC controlling who can request the export. Can you do that?
[08:45] Maya: Yes — that aligns with a standard POC. We can run it against a test bucket in your AWS account; we'll need cross-account role details or a pre-signed bucket policy.
[08:57] Ben: I'll set up a test bucket and send role arn to Maya. Any specific IAM permissions you need?
[09:03] Maya: Minimal: s3:PutObject, s3:PutObjectAcl (if needed), kms:Encrypt/kms:GenerateDataKey (for key wrap), and s3:PutObjectTagging if you want manifest tags. We'll send a sample policy.
[09:16] Priya: One more thing — we use Okta for SSO. How does session mapping appear in the logs?
[09:22] Jordan: We ingest SAML attributes like email, subject, groups, and session id. The logs will include assertion_id and the raw assertion reference. Note SAML raw assertions are sensitive, so we redacted full assertion by default but include assertion_id for traceability.
[09:41] Sara: For retention lengths in different jurisdictions, can you make export lifecycle be conditional on region?
[09:47] Maya: Yes, export jobs can be configured per-region and lifecycle rules follow the bucket’s configuration. We can orchestrate per-region export tasks.
[09:56] Priya: Any gap windows where logs are buffered but not yet exported — we need to demonstrate no blind spot.
[10:01] Maya: Buffering exists for retry resilience — default is low minutes, and we surface queue depth metrics in the console. For the POC we'll set low buffer TTL and show the metrics to prove there’s no significant blind spot.
[10:15] Ben: Are there e2e encryption examples we can show to auditors? A document or a diagram?
[10:19] Jordan: Yes — we'll attach an encryption flow diagram, key rotation history sample, and the digest verification steps in the POC pack.
[10:29] Priya: Okay, let's recap next steps.
[10:32] Jordan: Recap: Jordan will send the audit log schema, export policy options, and a sample S3 bucket policy by 2025-06-05. Maya will run the POC export into Halo's test S3, configure KMS wrap, and provide checksum verification steps by 2025-06-09. Sara will confirm required audit fields and any regulatory hold rules by 2025-06-06. We'll schedule a follow-up POC review week of 2025-06-16.
[10:57] Sara: Sounds good, thanks.
[11:00] Ben: Thanks everyone.
[11:03] Jordan: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links to the docs.

Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect):
- Focus: admin activity capture, export, and retention for SOC 2 readiness.
- Key features discussed: export to S3/GCS, Object Lock, KMS/BYOK, SHA-256 digests, SSO attributes in logs, RBAC & approval flows, region-specific exports.
- POC requested: export 30 days admin trails to Halo S3 with Object Lock + KMS; verification of digests; demo of RBAC/approval flow.

Notes on transcription quality: some proper names and acronyms may be mis-transcribed (e.g., "Object Lock" spoken fast appears as "object locke", KMS as "K M S").

End of transcript.
