document.content:
Hot-standby vs traffic-split intake - Pelican Ventures

Initial reliability and routing discovery to evaluate Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private for Pelican's multi-region product. Discussed hot-standby vs traffic-split strategies, KV cache behavior, SLO targets (p95/p99), security (KMS/SOC2/audit logs), and a scoped SE-led perf validation. Agreed next steps: send security pack, share prompt set, and schedule a performance test week of Apr 26.
hot-standby vs traffic-split architecture
multi-region routing and geo steering
SLA/SLO expectations (p95, p99, error budgets)
KV cache and prefix caching consistency
dedicated capacity sizing and burst policies
private VPC / on-prem considerations (KMS, audit logs, data residency)
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-22 16:00 PT
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Luca (Redwood SE), Anika (CTO), Samir (Platform), Jules (SRE)

Summary: quick intake to align on Pelican's reliability requirements and decide between hosted/dedicated/private deployment patterns with emphasis on incident tolerance and routing behavior.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh quick intros, im maya, i'm the AE on this account. Luca is our senior se, he'll drive the perf bits.
[00:12] Anika: hi all, Anika here. We're doing a reliability pass for the new customer-facing assistant. main ask is 3 nines availability and <150ms p95 token latency for the synchronous flows.
[00:24] Samir: Samir, platform. we own the infra side. curious about hot-standby vs traffic-split approach, and how KV cache coherency works across regions.
[00:36] Luca: cool, will do. quick note — our tokens-latency numbers vary a lot by model and seq length; we should scope with your sample prompts.
[00:47] Jules: Jules — SRE — we also need audit logs, SSO, and KMS integration, and a runbook for partial degradation.

[01:02] Maya: perfect. high level: we typically recommend three patterns for multi-region reliability: active-active with traffic splitting, active-passive hot-standby, or region-local with cross-region fallback. each has trade offs for latency, cost, and cache behavior.

[01:30] Anika: can you unpack the hot-standby vs traffic-split? we keep reading different best practices and it's confusing.

[01:40] Luca: sure. traffic-split (active-active) means you send a portion of traffic to each region—good for lower tail latency because users hit nearest region; but it requires consistent prefix/KV caches or warm starts across regions to avoid cold-kv misses. hot-standby is where secondary regions are kept ready but not serving primary traffic most of the time—cheaper cache-wise but you need fast failover and warm-up strategies so user requests don't hit a cold cache on failover.

[02:10] Samir: how fast is "fast failover"? are we talking seconds or minutes? and what about in-flight requests and session stickiness?

[02:22] Luca: typical plan is sub-30s route switch at the DNS/load-balancer layer if you use region steering; but the big delta is the model KV cache — if your workload relies on long running chats with large k-v caches, regen cost can add 100s of ms per request until cache is rebuilt. we have two levers: proactive KV replication (more bandwidth/cost) or a short-lived sticky session that retries/pulls from origin. both are supported but require config.

[03:02] Anika: proactive KV replication — is that supported in hosted or only private/dedicated?

[03:12] Luca: we support cross-region prefix cache replication in Dedicated and Private setups more easily because you control the networking and bandwidth; hosted can do async cache warmers and checkpoint snapshots but cross-region replication at low latency is generally a Dedicated/Private feature. hosted has fallbacks and model variants to reduce cold-warm penalty.

[03:40] Maya: to add, many customers start hosted to validate UX, then move to Dedicated for predictable latency & cross-region replication when they have stricter SLOs. but some regulated customers go Private from day one for KMS/HSM and data residency reasons.

[04:00] Jules: what about circuit breakers and partial degradation? are those automatic?

[04:07] Luca: we have built-in circuit-breakers at the routing layer — policies can be set per-route: degrade to cheaper quantized model, increase timeout threshold, or return cached answer if available. also, automatic fallback routing can steer to other regions or to a lower-cost pool. you can set SLO-driven policies like "if p99 latency > X for 5m, route 20% to fallback".

[04:40] Samir: okay. illustrate for us: during a db outage in primary region, ideally we want read-only responses from cache and graceful degradation for new sessions. how would Redwood behave?

[04:54] Luca: if DB outage is just our cache store, we can serve from prefix caches in edge for recent sessions; if it's a full model-serving outage, route to secondary region or model-variant. we can return a structured prompt with an explicit disclaimer — e.g., "limited context, partial answer" — so app can show degraded UI. rule sets are configurable.

[05:20] Anika: latency SLOs: we target p95 < 150ms, p99 < 350ms. realistically, do you think Dedicated is necessary?

[05:32] Luca: for p95 150ms global it's tricky in hosted unless you pin to small local deployments; network egress plus tokenization cost matters. Dedicated with regional pools gives you predictable tail latency. We'll propose cluster sizing after we see your prompt set.

[05:50] Maya: and pricing: Dedicated adds a baseline commitment but predictable throughput usually reduces unit cost for high qps. we can provide estimates.

[06:05] Jules: security — we need KMS with CMKs in our cloud account, SOC 2 plus audit logs for every inference, and SAML SSO for the console. does Redwood support customer-managed keys?

[06:20] Luca: yes — Private (and Dedicated via dedicated control plane) supports customer-managed KMS and HSM. Hosted supports envelope encryption and bring-your-own-key in certain regions; we'll include exact matrix in the security pack. audit logs (per-request) are available for Dedicated and Private with retention configs. hosted retains logs but has retention limits unless you add an enterprise add-on.

[06:50] Anika: good. Jules: about routing policy granularity — can we do per-route SLO routing? for example, critical auth flows always go to dedicated pool while chats go to hosted.

[07:04] Luca: yes, route-level policies are first-class. you can mark routes as "critical" and pin them to clusters, or use SLO-based dynamic routing. we also have weight-based traffic-split if you want canary traffic between regions.

[07:20] Samir: what about sticky sessions for chat? we need session affinity so context stays in same region for performance.

[07:28] Luca: session affinity is supported via our routing tokens; it can be time-limited. if a region becomes unhealthy, affinity is broken and you'd either rehydrate context or fall back to a stateless reply. rehydration strategies vary by how you persist contexts (your DB vs our prefix cache).

[07:48] Anika: rehydration could be slow. can we pre-warm a subset of sessions on secondaries?

[07:55] Luca: yes — warmers can proactively seed KV caches in standby regions for a chosen set of users or sessions. that's a common hybrid approach: traffic-split for general traffic, hot-standby for VIP users.

[08:12] Maya: quick check: does Pelican have data residency constraints? any EU-only data or HIPAA?

[08:20] Anika: no HIPAA. Some EU customers require EU-only residency. we want the option to pin EU data to EU regions and audit access.

[08:30] Luca: Private or Dedicated in EU region can guarantee that. Hosted also has EU region options but for strict residency and KMS control, Private is recommended.

[08:45] Samir: about autoscaling — if we use Dedicated, does Redwood autoscale GPU pools quickly? and is bursting allowed for peak days?

[08:55] Luca: Dedicated supports autoscaling policies with min/max nodes and also a burst pool for short spikes. scaling is typically tens of seconds to a couple minutes depending on GPU availability. we also offer pre-warms for planned events.

[09:20] Jules: can you explain model-variants fallback? e.g., when latency spikes, do you switch to a quantized variant?

[09:28] Luca: exactly. you can define fallback chains: primary model -> quantized variant -> cached response -> canned response. each step reduces compute cost and latency but may reduce fidelity. you control thresholds.

[09:50] Anika: curious about SLO measurement — do you give token-level breakdowns? we want to chargeback and track per-route costs.

[09:59] Maya: Redwood Console provides token-level cost, latency percentiles, per-route dashboards, and traces. that should let you do chargeback.

[10:10] Samir: are there any limitations for bursty short-lived chats on hosted? we have some flows with sudden spikes.

[10:20] Luca: hosted has throttles and rate limits to protect multi-tenant pools. for bursty predictable spikes Dedicated or Reserved capacity is better. we can add burst credits sometimes but that isn't as reliable as Dedicated.

[10:40] Anika: got it. can you walk through a sample incident scenario and routing behavior? say primary region node pool has a GPU crash and 60% reduction in capacity.

[10:52] Luca: incident path: autoscaler will attempt to create replacements; routing layer detects increased latency/error rates and will... (a) shift percentage of traffic to other healthy regions (active-active), (b) route critical routes to dedicated pool or pinned region, (c) apply fallback chain for degraded routes. If capacity drop is partial, you can enable graceful degradation: increase timeouts, bump fallbacks, and prioritize critical workflows.

[11:30] Jules: do you keep error budgets and alerts integrated with our pager?

[11:36] Maya: yes we can forward SLO alerts to PagerDuty/Slack and expose SLO metrics in Datadog.

[11:45] Samir: any known gotchas for long-running contexts with KV caches and region failovers?

[11:52] Luca: main gotcha is cold cache rebuild time and potential token cost for warming. also, if you try to replicate very large KV caches synchronously you'll pay bandwidth and complexity. so we usually advise tiering: critical keys replicated, others lazy-warmed.

[12:12] Anika: what's the expected lead time to set up Dedicated with three regions and cross-region replication?

[12:20] Luca: typical pilots are 2-4 weeks to provision clusters and run benchmarks; full production with replication and runbooks is more like 6-10 weeks depending on approvals and networking (VPC peering, firewall rules).

[12:38] Maya: for Private on-prem it's longer — packaging and security review add time. that timeline is normal.

[12:50] Anika: pricing: ballpark for Dedicated three-region baseline?

[12:56] Maya: we'll send a tailored quote but ballpark depends on GPU types and commitments. we'll include a 3-region hot-standby vs traffic-split cost comparison.

[13:08] Samir: can we run a perf validation against our prompt set? we want p95/p99 measured end-to-end including our upstream services.

[13:16] Luca: yes, SE-led perf test is standard. we'll run a 2-hour synthetic and a 1-2 day pilot with real prompts. we'll need your prompt corpus and expected qps.

[13:28] Jules: about observability: can we export raw request logs to our S3/GC?

[13:35] Luca: Dedicated/Private can push logs to your object store or SIEM; hosted can stream limited logs via an enterprise add-on.

[13:46] Anika: are you seeing any stability issues with cross-region traffic-split customers in prod?

[13:53] Luca: a minority. issues usually due to cache coherence expectations or opaque statefulness in the app. we mitigate with clear guidance: either make sessions stateless, implement sticky affinity, or accept partial warmers.

[14:10] Maya: ok let's go through action items and next steps.

[14:14] Anika: one more question — do you support FIPS endpoints for KMS and encryption?

[14:20] Luca: yes for Dedicated and Private in certain regions. we'll enumerate in the security pack.

[14:28] -- Meeting recap / action items --
[14:30] Maya: thanks, I'll capture action items.

Maya: send security pack + SOC2 evidence + matrix on KMS/FIPS by 2027-04-25
Luca: produce perf test plan and cluster sizing recommendation after receiving prompt set (due 2027-04-29)
Samir: share representative prompt corpus and expected qps, and list of critical routes (due 2027-04-24)
Schedule SE-led perf validation (2h synthetic + 1-2 day pilot) week of 2027-04-26
Provide Dedicated 3-region vs hot-standby cost comparison and pricing estimate
Join Pelican security review meeting (Maya to arrange)

Dependency Ownership & Fallback Runway - Prelaunch Scrub

Pre-launch sprint scrub focused on owning upstream deps, fallback policies, and short-term runway for the Q1 private launch. Covered blocked packages, hotfix plan for KV cache eviction bug, RBAC gating for private deploys, and a fallback model routing plan with cost/latency tradeoffs.
Dependency ownership mapping
KV cache eviction hotfix status
Fallback routing policy and canary window
Private deploy RBAC & SSO gating
Short-term capacity runway and burst plan
Action item triage and owners
Arjun: open dependency ownership board and tag owners for 12 packages; due 2026-12-15
Liam: draft burst capacity config for Dedicated pool (cost estimate) ; due 2026-12-13
Sofia: run KV-eviction repro test and capture flamegraph logs; due 2026-12-12
Ethan: prototype model-routing fallback (small quant model) in staging and smoke test; due 2026-12-17
Priya: prepare RBAC / SSO checklist for Private onboard; due 2026-12-14
Share dependency board link with release council (Maya)
Schedule 30m follow-up on 2026-12-16 to validate hotfix status
Add fallback routing configs to canary runbook and rehearse during staging day
Deliver cost estimate for burst capacity to finance and product
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-10
Time: 09:00 - 09:55 UTC
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Arjun Patel, Sofia Morales, Liam O'Connor, Priya Rao, Ethan Brooks, Zara Kim

Auto summary (auto-generated, may be rough): Pre-launch scrub to ensure owners on critical dependencies, triage KV cache eviction bug, finalize fallback routing strategy for canary, and confirm RBAC gating for private deploy. Several action items assigned.

---- Transcript ----
[00:00] Maya (PM): ok everyone good morning, let's try to keep this tight we got 55 minutes. main goal is to make sure we own the dependencies that could kill launch and have a clear fallback runway.
[00:16] Arjun (Eng Lead): yeah, I pushed the dependency list to the shared board, but it needs final owners. there are like a dozen transitive libs that only show up in the onprem package.
[00:30] Sofia (SRE): and just to flag the KV evict issue again - we saw an OOM in staging last night when sequence lengths doubled, it was a weird KV cache pressure that led to thrash, so we're classing it as P1.
[00:45] Liam (Infra): i think the root is the eviction policy not scaling with the new batcher. Batcher changed token window, so entries never expire as expected, looks like a heuristics mismatch with the k-v cash (kv spelled K V cash in some logs) metrics.
[01:02] Ethan (Runtime): uhh yeah there's also a quant path where the cache size is slightly different, the kernel selection ended up allocating more memory, so it's all compounding.
[01:15] Maya: okay, action one is ownership mapping — who's comfortable taking lead on that? Arjun?
[01:20] Arjun: i'll own it, i'll break it into 'critical for private' vs 'nice to have'. i'll tag people in the board; expect the first pass by monday.
[01:28] Priya (Release): from release perspective we need a clear list of blockers that must be done before we sign-off for the Private beta. RBAC, audit logs, and the KV thing are top of mine.
[01:40] Zara (Prod Ops): audit logs - also need retention policy spelled out. customers will ask about retention windows and whether logs can be offloaded to customer S3.
[01:50] Sofia: S3 offload is fine but we need to ensure encryption-at-rest via KMS; there was some confusion last week about whether the onprem package supports external KMS or only our internal KMS.
[02:05] Maya: note — Priya to pull the RBAC/SSO checklist and clarify KMS options. Priya?
[02:10] Priya: yes i'll own that, i'll check with security and get a short checklist by tuesday.
[02:20] [02:20] Arjun: regarding KV repro - i need the exact replay script, Sofia can you attach the staging run and the flamegraphs?
[02:28] Sofia: already on it, i'll capture the flamegraphs and the container OOM logs, though the transcription of the kernel traces had some weird tokenization - some function names got hyphenated in the trace, like comp_runner -> comp runner.
[02:44] Ethan: for fallback routing — we sketched a plan where requests hit the primary low-latency high-cost model, and if tokens exceed X or latency SLO is slipping, we failover to a slightly faster quantized model. cost delta is about 1.6x but latency improves ~20ms in our bench.
[03:02] Liam: can we make that routing policy a percent-based canary before we do instant fallback? like 5% traffic to fallback for 24h then expand.
[03:12] Maya: yes that's the recommended approach. we should also have an automated rollback if error rate goes above Y. who will own the automation?
[03:20] Ethan: runtime can add the policy, i'll prototype today and run a smoke test in staging.
[03:26] Arjun: small note — the fallback model needs to be compatible with function-calling and structured outputs, otherwise customers will see different shapes and that will break downstream.
[03:38] Sofia: good catch. we should have an acceptance test that verifies schema compatibility for the fallback path.
[03:45] Priya: and logging, too — ensure the fallback path tags token_cost and model_version in traces so we can reconcile cost and SLOs.
[03:55] Maya: ok put that on the backlog — logging + schema acceptance test.
[04:02] [04:02] Liam: on capacity runway - finance said we have about two weeks of burst credits left to use for launch; after that we need a commit with Dedicated or tune down. so we need a cheap burst config that buys us 2-3 days of extra headroom.
[04:18] Arjun: i can sketch a cheap burst: lower batch max, aggressive kv cache TTL in burst mode, and route lower priority tenants to rate-limited queues. that should save 30-40% tokens.
[04:30] Zara: but remember, aggressive TTL might regresses perf for some RL workloads, we need canary tests.
[04:36] Sofia: agreed. also, the eviction we saw suggests changing TTLs may actually make the thrash worse if not done carefully.
[04:44] Maya: reminder - any config that touches cache eviction needs SRE signoff and a runbook entry.
[04:50] [05:00] Arjun: question — do we want to backport CVE patches to the onprem shim before the beta? there was an upstream patch to the loader lib that fixes race on hot reloads.
[05:10] Ethan: yeah we should, but it depends on whether the patch touches our kernel selection; there's a small chance it will change binary layout and we need a quick compatibility test.
[05:20] Priya: schedule a small compatibility window on the deploy calendar and mark it as must-pass for release.
[05:26] Maya: ok timeline check: we have a planned private beta sign-off by 2026-12-24. that gives us two weeks. realistically, the KV hotfix, RBAC checklist, and fallback routing prototype need to be done before that.
[05:40] Sofia: i'll prioritize the KV repro and try to get a hotfix branch up today. if i can't reproduce locally i'll ask for a staged capture during the next load run.
[05:50] Arjun: i'll open the ownership tags now, and will add a 'risk' column for each dependency so we can triage effectively.
[06:00] [06:00] Ethan: about testing the fallback model — quant builds sometimes change output subtly. we need a small eval set (10-20 prompts) that represent critical customer flows. who curates that?
[06:12] Maya: product can curate, but eng should vet for edge cases. Arjun and Ethan take that.
[06:18] Arjun: fine, we'll draft that today.
[06:22] Liam: about RBAC gating in private deploys - we had earlier notes that SAML flows break for certain IdPs due to a clock skew assumption. did security confirm we support clock drift tolerances?
[06:34] Priya: security confirmed 2-minute tolerance but some SAML providers are stricter. we'll map the critical customers and ask their IdP teams.
[06:40] Zara: small ask from ops — add a 'safety mode' flag to the private deploy that forces read-only telemetry if things go sideways. this reduces liability and cost while we triage.
[06:50] Ethan: doable, but it's a code path. we can implement as a config toggle with an automatic telemetry sampler.
[06:58] Maya: add that as an action item for runtime.
[07:03] [07:03] (brief crosstalk)
[07:10] Arjun: anything else? i want to call out one dependency: the upstream bento-loader repo; if they bump the API, our onprem packaging fails. i've added a subtask to track their releases.
[07:22] Sofia: and i've added a monitoring alert for cache churn so we can detect regression during canary. threshold is provisional, we can tune after first run.
[07:33] Priya: on docs - we need a compact 'what to expect' for customers who join the private beta: known limitations, RBAC steps, KMS options, and fallback behavior. i'll draft a one-pager and circulate.
[07:45] Maya: good. recap time.
[07:48] Maya (recap): Arjun - dependency ownership board + risk column, due 12/15. Liam - cost/burst config and estimate, due 12/13. Sofia - KV repro + flamegraphs, due 12/12. Ethan - fallback prototype + acceptance eval, due 12/17. Priya - RBAC/SSO checklist and one-pager, due 12/14. Maya will share board and schedule follow-up on 12/16.
[08:10] Arjun: quick Q - do we want to notify sales about potential feature limits? maybe an internal note.
[08:18] Priya: yes i'll put a short note in the release channel after the follow-up call.
[08:25] Maya: ok last thing - risk call if KV hotfix slips, we may delay sign-off. let's hope not. thanks everyone.
[08:33] (meeting ends, recording stops)

References / Links shared in chat:
- Dependency board: https://redwood-internal.example.com/boards/dep-ownership (Maya)
- Staging run logs: s3://redwood-staging/logs/kv-evict-20261209 (Sofia)
- Canaries runbook draft: https://docs.internal/redwood/canary-runbook-draft (Priya)

End of transcript.

Aperture Systems - streaming & concurrency performance discovery

Discovery focused on p95 SLOs for a streaming-first UX, target concurrency for bursty multi-tenant API, and a token/sec benchmarking plan using Aperture's sample prompts. Customer is deciding between Redwood Hosted for speed-to-market, Dedicated for predictable throughput, and Private (VPC) for strict data controls. Agreed to run a joint benchmark; Redwood to share pricing and security docs.
Meeting header: 2025-06-11 16:00 PDT / Duration: ~62 minutes / Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Elias Winter (Redwood SE), Jordan Park (Aperture CTO), Leah Morales (Aperture ML Eng), Diego Ruiz (Aperture Platform), Priya Iyer (Aperture Security)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, i think we all have the agenda — latency and throughput discovery for your streaming use case, correct?
[00:08] Jordan: yep that's right, primarily streaming chat for our customer-facing assistant. hope to get clarity on p95 targets and whether Dedicated makes sense vs Hosted.
[00:17] Samir: quick intro from our side — i'm Samir, i'm the SE who does the throughput and streaming benchmarks. elias will chime on integration patterns.
[00:25] Leah: good to meet you both, i'm leah. our product is pretty latency sensitive; users expect near-real-time replies and we care about 95th percentile more than average.
[00:35] Diego: and our infra team cares about concurrency and cost — we can tolerate some tail but want predictable p95 under normal load.
[00:44] Priya: security briefly — we need SOC 2, KMS integration, and a VPC option for private traffic. we'll talk details later.
[00:52] Maya: great, what's your current baseline? are you running any models on prem or using OpenAI/Anthropic?
[01:00] Jordan: we piloted with OpenAI gpt-4o-mini for certain flows and an in-house Llama variant on prem for private workloads. gpt-4o-mini gave ~300ms per token on average in our measurements but p95 was spiky — sometimes over 1s for first chunks.
[01:18] Samir: that first-chunk spike is common with cold KV cache and model load. for streaming UX we typically measure two things: initial chunk latency (time to first token) and sustained token rate (tokens/sec).
[01:30] Leah: our SLOs: p95 time-to-first-token under 250ms for short prompts (~<200 tokens output) and sustained streaming of at least 25 tokens/sec per connection during bursts. concurrency: we expect 120 concurrent chat sessions at peak for one region.
[01:49] Elias: ok that's concrete — 250ms p95 to first token, 25 tps sustained, 120 concurrent. helpful to know the output size distribution too.
[01:57] Leah: typical response lengths are 80-220 tokens; some long generative flows go to 800 tokens but those are rare.
[02:07] Samir: good. now the tradeoff: Hosted gives fast setup and we can optimize kernels, batching, and autoscale across capacity tiers. Dedicated gives pinned GPUs and predictable throughput for concurrency; Private gives you network isolation and KMS control.
[02:22] Jordan: performance-wise, how much better can we expect on Dedicated vs Hosted for p95?
[02:28] Samir: depends on workload shape — for streaming short responses (many small outputs), Dedicated with a tuned batching policy and prefix cache typically reduces p95 to ~150-200ms on a modern A100 or similar, compared to ~200-350ms on a multi-tenant Hosted instance under similar load. but if you see heavy bursts, Dedicated prevents noisy neighbors affecting your tail.
[02:48] Diego: what's the tokens/sec we'd need per GPU and how many GPUs for our 120 concurrent requirement?
[02:53] Samir: rough math: assume 25 tps sustained per connection * 120 connections = 3000 tokens/sec sustained across the service. a single GPU's sustained throughput varies by model and quantization: e.g., a quantized 8-bit variant can do ~8k-12k tokens/sec for short-context generation when batched efficiently; but streaming with small chunk sizes reduces batching efficiency. realistic capacity estimate: with conservative batching for streaming you might get ~4k-6k tokens/sec per GPU for your pattern — so 1 GPU might be marginal, 2 GPUs safer, 3 GPUs for headroom and canary + failover.
[03:26] Jordan: so with Dedicated we'd be looking at reserving 2-3 GPUs? that fits our budget window.
[03:33] Samir: yes, and with caching of common prefixes (session warm cache) you can increase effective tokens/sec because you avoid token generation for repeated system prompts.
[03:42] Priya: for Private we need to confirm KMS/HSM integration. do you support customer-managed KMS in the VPC flow?
[03:48] Maya: yes, Private supports customer KMS keys and can integrate with HSM-backed keys. we'll share the architecture diagram and checklist.
[03:55] Leah: curious about streaming chunk sizes — we want sub-100ms per chunk ideally, but we also worry about network round trips. how do you recommend chunk framing?
[04:04] Elias: we recommend 1) amortize startup cost by returning a small first chunk quickly (e.g., 8-12 tokens) then ongoing chunks of 20-40 tokens; 2) websocket or HTTP/2 streaming reduces overhead compared to frequent short SSE chunks. that pattern keeps first-token latency low and maintains throughput.
[04:20] Samir: there's also an option to enable token-level partials if your client can render them incrementally, but that requires client-side jitter buffering.
[04:29] [04:29] Jordan: can you simulate our exact prompt distribution? we want results that mirror production.
[04:33] Samir: yes — please upload the prompt set to the shared sheet; we'll run warm and cold runs, include KV cache hit-rate simulations, and measure time-to-first-token and p95 for first 100 tokens and sustained tokens/sec. we'll provide a CSV of per-request latencies.
[04:47] Leah: what about cold-starts? we have many ephemeral sessions. if the KV cache misses frequently, first-chunk times will spike.
[04:54] Samir: that's expected — our benchmark will test cold scenarios (empty KV, cold model instances) and warm scenarios (hot KV cache, warmed kernels). for Dedicated you can keep a pool of warm workers which reduces cold starts but at cost of reserved capacity.
[05:08] Diego: do you do continuous batching? how does it affect latency?
[05:12] Elias: continuous batching groups concurrent requests into micro-batches — it increases throughput but can add queuing delay. we tune target batch latency thresholds so any single request isn't held longer than X ms; for streaming we set very small batching windows (e.g., 5-10ms) to avoid big tail.
[05:27] Priya: security question — audit logs, tenant separation, and data retention policies. do Hosted logs show customer tokens? we need assurance on PII handling.
[05:37] Maya: Hosted logs can be configured to redact PII; we also offer Private with no cross-tenant logs in the customer VPC. we'll share our SOC2 controls and data flow doc.
[05:48] [05:48] Jordan: assume we want to start on Hosted to iterate quickly but move to Dedicated within 2 months if benchmarks show we need predictability — is that an easy migration path?
[05:56] Maya: yes — same API surface, you can pin model versions and roll traffic from Hosted to Dedicated. we can help with rollout and blue/green traffic split.
[06:04] Samir: for the benchmark plan i'll run an internal run on a similar model to establish baseline numbers and then we do a joint run with your prompt set on Hosted and on a Dedicated pool. metrics we'll capture: ttf-token (time-to-first-token), p50/p95/p99 for first token, sustained tps, server-side CPU/GPU utilization, memory, and queueing delays.
[06:22] Leah: what telemetry do you expose for real-time debugging? we need per-request token counts, tokens/sec, and per-route p95.
[06:30] Elias: console exposes per-route token-level cost and latency breakdown, traces with timestamps for each service hop, and a streaming trace that shows first-token and subsequent chunk timings. we can grant access to a sandbox org for you.
[06:42] Priya: i'd like to see a sample SOC2 report and network diagram — and confirmation that we can use our KMS for encryption at rest.
[06:51] Maya: noted, will send.
[06:54] Jordan: any caveats about burst capacity? we get occasional spikes to 500 concurrent users for demo events.
[06:59] Samir: for that scenario we recommend Dedicated with autoscale + burst policy or Hosted with higher burst pool. hosted can burst but in heavy global spikes multitenancy can affect tails. Dedicated with pre-warmed burst nodes gives most predictable p95.
[07:13] Leah: one more: token billing — if we use prefix caching, does Redwood still bill for cached tokens?
[07:18] Maya: typically billing is per-model output tokens; if cache serves the token then you won't be billed for regenerating those tokens. we'll confirm exact billing semantics in the pricing deck.
[07:27] Diego: ok great. next steps?
[07:30] Maya: recap: Aperture to upload sample prompts + expected session distribution; Redwood runs internal baseline and then joint benchmarks (Hosted + Dedicated); Redwood sends pricing and security docs; schedule 2-hr deep dive.
[07:43] Jordan: that works. thanks everyone.
[07:46] [End of recording — informal chat for 3mins about integrations, off the record]

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcription with occasional name misspellings (Elias sometimes labeled "Elise" in the first pass); some timestamps approximate.

Shared artifacts referenced: shared sheet (link: https://redwood.example.com/sheets/aperture-benchmarks) — placeholder, pricing deck (to be emailed), SOC2 + architecture zip (to be attached).

Bench plan summary (inline):
- Dataset: Aperture to provide ~500 short prompts + 200 long prompts, annotated with expected output size distribution.
- Runs: cold-start (empty KV, freshly launched worker), warm-start (warmed kernels + KV cache), and burst simulation (increase concurrent sessions to 500).
- Metrics: time-to-first-token (tTF), p50/p95/p99 for first-chunk, sustained tokens/sec per connection, aggregated tokens/sec, GPU utl, queueing delay histograms.
- Success criteria: p95 first-token <= 250ms in warm runs; sustained 25 tps per connection with <=10% tail violations; graceful degradation with fallback to smaller model under heavy load.

End of transcript.

2027-05-19-api-console-optimize-data-retention-sandbox-review-hawthorne-insights

30-minute product demo showing Redwood API, Console and Optimize features specifically for request storage toggles, PII redaction, logging redaction and retention policies. Customer concerned about vendor data retention, KMS integration, and ability to run a short sandbox pilot. We demoed ephemeral request mode, selective telemetry ejection, server-side PII detection rules, and the Optimize recommendations that suggest batching/quantization tradeoffs for cost. Next steps agreed: sandbox tenant, shared security docs, pilot run and follow-up performance benchmark.
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-19
Start time: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Sophie (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Imani (Redwood Product), Jon (Redwood Solutions), Maya (Hawthorne Head of Platform), Ethan (Hawthorne Security), Priya (Hawthorne Privacy), Noah (Hawthorne ML)

Summary (auto): Demo of data handling controls across API, Console and Optimize. Focus on retention toggles, PII redaction, and pilot steps.

Topics covered: see attached agenda notes.

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Sophie: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. I'm Sophie, I'll run the demo and Carlos will jump into the technical bits. Quick check, folks, can you hear us okay?
[00:05] Maya: Yep, loud and clear. Thanks.
[00:08] Ethan: Good here. We're mostly interested in how we can avoid storing raw customer requests and still keep observability.
[00:12] Carlos: Totally. That's the crux. We'll walk through ephemeral mode, the selective telemetry ejection, and redaction workflows in the console, then show how Optimize suggests batching and quant profiles to keep cost down.
[00:22] Priya: Also, we'll want to review KMS integration — keys at rest, HSM options — and how audit logs are retained.
[00:28] Imani: We'll cover that. Quick note: we'll share the SOC 2 paper and an integration checklist after.
[00:33] Sophie: Great. Agenda for the next 30: quick show of the Console toggles, live API call with redaction flags, then a short Optimize demo. We'll finish with Q&A and next steps.

[02:05] Carlos: Alright, pulling up the console. So first screen is the request storage controls. You can set defaults at org level, route level, and model level. Here I have ephemeral toggles — if you enable ephemeral the request and response are not written to request storage. We still keep minimal telemetry for billing and SLOs, but that's ejected by default.
[02:22] Noah: When you say "ejected" do you mean removed entirely or redacted?
[02:27] Carlos: Good call. There's two axes: ejection vs redaction. Ejection means the field is never persisted in telemetry. Redaction means we store a sanitized artifact where PII tokens are masked. Both can be combined with sampling rules.
[02:36] Ethan: And the ejected telemetry — is there any identifier retained to map errors back to requests?
[02:40] Carlos: We can retain a hashed request id (SHA256) — but that is one-way. You can choose to store it or not. If you store it you can link traces without raw payload.

[05:10] Sophie: I'm going to run an API call so you can see the behavior. I'm flagging the request with "storage=store-with-redaction" and with a PII label in the metadata.
[05:18] (api call sounds, small pause)
[05:22] Carlos: The console shows the request as redacted. You'll see we replaced sequences that match our PII patterns with [REDACTED-EMAIL] or [REDACTED-SSN]. Note: auto-detection isn't perfect, it uses heuristics + custom rules you can upload.
[05:35] Priya: Can we upload our own PII regex list?
[05:38] Imani: Yes, you can provide custom rule sets. We support regex, dictionary, and ML-based sensitive-entity models. They run server-side prior to storage.
[05:45] Priya: Is the ML model hosted by Redwood or is that self-hosted?
[05:49] Carlos: It's Redwood-managed in hosted mode. For Private deployments you can opt-in for on-prem entity detection if you need. The rules are pluggable.

[08:12] Sophie: Switching to the console retention UI. You can pick retention windows per route: 0 days (ephemeral), 7, 30, 90, or custom. We also show a cost estimate on the right based on tokens stored historically.
[08:24] Maya: That cost calc — how accurate is it? We need ballpark for finance.
[08:27] Imani: It's historgram-based —

Partner Deal Carveout + Velocity Huddle

Joint partner co-sell call to align on carveout economics, lead ownership for top accounts, a fast-path pilot (30-day) for two mutual customers, and technical gating (SSO/KMS/network). Agreed to exchange account lists and run a latency/cost bench. Action: Redwood to send term sheet; Partner to share accounts and requirements.
deal carveout economics
lead assignment and ownership
fast-path pilot scoping (30 days)
technical gating: SSO, KMS, VPC connectivity
benchmarks: latency, throughput, cost
[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call before we dive?
[00:06] Jordan (Meridian): Yep Jordan here.
[00:08] Samira (Meridian): Samira on my end.
[00:10] Evan (Meridian): Evan joining.
[00:12] Priya (Redwood): Priya here — will handle the technical bits.
[00:18] Alex: Cool, objective today is to align the carveout so we can move two joint customers into a fast path pilot and decide who owns the initial contract.
[00:30] Jordan: Right, we're trying to understand what the revenue split looks like, and importantly, who is accountable for contract negotiation. We prefer partner-led with co-sell credits if possible.
[00:42] Alex: Totally. Our normal pattern is two flavors: partner-managed contract with a referral rev split, or Redwood-managed with a dedicated carveout and margin share. For big accounts we usually do the dedicated carveout to simplify billing.
[00:55] Samira: What's the threshold for dedicated carving? We don't want to churn through small deals.
[01:02] Alex: Typically dedicated carveouts start around $150k ARR in pipeline and above, or for strategic accounts. But we can set a fast-path exception for the two pilot accounts if you own the contract and take the primary sales lead — we can offer a 20/80 rev split in the pilot window.
[01:20] Jordan: 20/80 (partner/company?) — just to be clear.
[01:23] Alex: Sorry, that's partner 20, Redwood 80 during the pilot while we validate usage and ops. After the pilot we re-evaluate and move to a standard tier — usually more favorable as we scale.
[01:33] Samira: That helps; we need to present clear numbers to our AE. Can you share a template?
[01:37] Alex: Yes I'll send a draft carveout term sheet and a revenue-split template after the call.
[01:42] Evan: From a technical perspective, two asks: 1) can Redwood support VPC peering or private link for latency sensitive workloads; 2) SSO and KMS integration for key management.
[01:53] Priya: On VPC side we support both VPC peering and PrivateLink for major clouds, depends on the deployment mode. For hosted API it's PrivateLink; for Private (on-prem/VPC) we can do direct peering. KMS is supported — we integrate with customer KMS providers, but there's a simple onboarding checklist.
[02:12] Evan: Are there any performance numbers you can share? latency per token or tail latencies?
[02:18] Priya: We have perf profiles, but they vary by model and quantization. I can run a bench in eu-west-1 and us-east-1 for the candidate model. We'll measure p50/p95/p99 and token cost. Expect numbers in the bench doc.
[02:30] Jordan: That would be great. We need the bench to show sub-200ms p95 for the shorter prompts our customers use.
[02:37] Priya: Understood. We'll prioritize prompts with 64 token context.
[02:41] Alex: Also want to cover lead routing. Meridian should assign the AE of record for the pilot accounts; Redwood SE will be technical owner for onboarding and the first 2 weeks of SRE support. After pilot, routing policy will depend on which party brings the renewal.
[03:00] Samira: One more commercial question — how are discounts applied? Is discounting managed by Redwood or the partner?
[03:07] Alex: For partner-managed deals we allow partner-level discounting within approved ranges; anything beyond requires Redwood approval. We'll include approved discount tiers in the term sheet.
[03:18] Jordan: Ok. For legal we need SOC2 attestation and a standard DPA, also specific data residency for EU customers.
[03:25] Alex: Yeah we have SOC 2 Type II and standard DPA, we can share the security pack. For residency we can pin region, and Dedicated/Private deployments give stronger residency guarantees.
[03:37] Evan: Regarding integrations, we have customer environments behind strict egress rules — we'll send the network diagram.
[03:42] Priya: Perfect. We'll review and confirm firewall rules; also want to flag KV cache and prefix caching — architecture might need a small adjustment for private peering.
[03:53] Jordan: Any concerns about tokenization costs or hidden fees? Our CFO will ask.
[03:58] Alex: We'll provide an estimated TCO table during pilot showing token cost, infra carve, and partner margin. We'll try to be transparent.
[04:10] Samira: Are there any competitor traps we should be aware of? Meridian has seen prospects use Bedrock as a gate because of bundled infra credits.
[04:18] Alex: Bedrock's bundling is common; our positioning is predictable per-token economics and production SLAs. We'll document differentiation in the joint deck.
[04:27] Evan: On technical timelines — how fast can Redwood onboard? We may want a 30-day pilot start.
[04:32] Priya: If we have account lists and network + SSO details, 30 days is aggressive but doable for hosted + PrivateLink. For Private deployment it's longer.
[04:42] Jordan: Okay push for 30 days then. We'll prioritize two accounts: "Acme Health" and "Nova Retail" (internal names). We'll share ARR tiers.
[04:50] Alex: Great — can you export top 30 accounts with ARR and indicate which two to pilot?
[04:55] Jordan: Yes.
[04:56] Alex: Next, tooling: we recommended using the co-sell pipeline spreadsheet — we'll share a template and column mapping so forecast syncs into both CRMs. Link: https://drive.example/partner-co-sell-template
[05:10] Samira: On reporting, we need joint pipeline visibility weekly — a shared sheet or synced SFDC view works.
[05:17] Alex: Agreed. We'll set cadence: weekly pipeline sync for 30 days, then biweekly.
[05:22] Evan: Quick question on rollback/fallback — if the pilot has latency incidents, what's the escalation path?
[05:27] Priya: Our SRE will be on rot for the pilot; immediate escalation to Redwood on-call; we can set SLAs for response and a rollback policy to previous model variant. Also fallback to smaller batch sizes to drop latency spikes.
[05:41] Jordan: Good. Also want clarity on who handles procurement paperwork and PO.
[05:46] Alex: For partner-led contracts Meridian handles PO — we bill partner, partner remits to Redwood per the carveout. For Redwood-managed accounts we handle billing and then pay partner per agreed split. We'll document both flows.
[05:58] Samira: What about joint case studies and logos? Meridian expects co-marketing if we hit the pilot goals.
[06:04] Alex: We do co-marketing; we'll draft a simple playbook with success criteria for a case study (usage threshold, reference quotes).
[06:12] Jordan: Anything on legal holdbacks or indemnities? Our counsel will look at it.
[06:15] Alex: Standard indemnities, nothing out of the ordinary; we can route to legal after we agree on commercial terms.
[06:20] Evan: On SSO we use SAML 2.0 and SCIM for provisioning — is SCIM supported?
[06:24] Priya: Yes we support SAML + SCIM; some provisioning still manual for early pilots but doable.
Mentioned deck + template links: partner-co-sell-template; security pack. Some transcription glitches: 'K-V cash' for KV cache, 'opti-mise' for Redwood Optimize in a few places. Natural filler words and overlaps present.

Resilience & Escalation Sprint Review with Halo Fintech

Discovery-style security review focused on incident response, BCDR targets (RTO/RPO), escalation paths and how Redwood's Dedicated/Private options support Halo's residency+KMS requirements. Agreed next steps: share SOC2 pack, run a tabletop with Halo ops, provide KMS BYOK design sketch, and propose SLA language for critical inference endpoints.
SOC 2 / ISO evidence and audit reports
RBAC / SSO (SAML + SCIM provisioning)
Audit logs / SIEM integration (Splunk, Datadog)
Data residency / region isolation (EU-only request)
Encryption / BYOK / HSM integration
BCDR: RTO / RPO targets & backup cadence
SLA / uptime and escalation runbook
Redwood to send SOC2 Type II report and PCA controls matrix (Lena) by 2026-09-06
Schedule full tabletop run (ops + infra) for week of 2026-09-20 (Samir to propose slots)
Share BYOK/KMS architecture sketch and HSM options (Iris) by 2026-09-08
Draft proposed SLA excerpt for critical inference endpoints (Lena) by 2026-09-10
Customer to share network diagram and expected egress IPs for VPC peering (Halo) by 2026-09-07
Lena Moreno: Send SOC2 Type II and controls mapping — due 2026-09-06
Samir Patel: Arrange tabletop dates and invite Halo ops — due 2026-09-09
Iris Chen: Produce BYOK/HSM design sketch + short risks doc — due 2026-09-08
Halo (Maya/Tom): Provide network topology and current SIEM rules — due 2026-09-07
Meeting header: 2026-09-02 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~48m | Recording: auto
Attendees: Lena Moreno (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Iris Chen (Redwood Security PM); Daniel Ruiz (CISO, Halo), Maya Okoye (Head of Platform), Tom Hsu (SRE), Priya Narang (Compliance), Alexei Morozov (Infra)

Summary: quick alignment on security/compliance requirements and incident/BCDR expectations. Focused on RTO/RPO for inference endpoints, BYOK/KMS options, EU data residency constraints, RBAC/SSO provisioning, and runbook/escalation flow.

00:00:12 - Lena (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we can start — goal for today is to walk through your resilience questions and make sure our proposed Dedicated/Private patterns line up with Halo's ops and compliance needs.
00:00:28 - Daniel (Halo - CISO): sounds good, quick context — we're evaluating a vendor for low-latency inference, but we're strict on data residency and customer-controlled keys. also we need a clear BCDR plan, that's the gating item for legal.
00:00:45 - Lena: totally, and just to confirm — you want EU-only hosting for the model/data, BYOK and HSM-backed key management, SOC2 evidence, plus RTO/RPO targets for production endpoints?
00:01:00 - Daniel: yes, precisely. RTO and RPO are the ones we want to validate — our SRE asked for sub-15 minute RTO for critical endpoints and RPO <= 5 minutes for stateful caches.
00:01:18 - Samir (SE): okay, good, that's realistic to discuss. quick disclaimer, depending on Dedicated vs Private we have different knobs — Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools in our cloud region, Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you full control over network and KMS.
00:01:34 - Maya (Halo): can you clarify the difference on KMS? we need BYOK — ideally we hold key material in our own HSM but still let Redwood serve the model.
00:01:48 - Iris (Redwood Security PM): yes, BYOK is supported for Private deployments — we can integrate with customer-managed KMS/HSM via standard KMIP or cloud KMS APIs. for Dedicated (Redwood-managed infra) we offer a managed KMS option but with BYOK via customer-managed keys in the cloud provider (e.g., AWS KMS with key policy restricting Redwood).
00:02:10 - Tom (SRE): do you have an example flow and what the key lifecycle looks like? rotation, revocation, how long you keep logs about key usage?
00:02:22 - Iris: we'll share a sketch but short answer: key rotation is customer-driven for BYOK; Redwood logs key usage with request-level metadata into audit logs; log retention policy can be extended — default is 90 days but we can support 12 months with enterprise retention add-on.
00:02:40 - Priya (Compliance): 12 months is our minimum for audit, ideally 13 months to match our archive cycle. also we need proof that logs are tamper-evident.
00:02:52 - Iris: understood — tamper-evident append-only logs and delivery to your SIEM (we support Splunk/Datadog/ELK) are standard for Private installs; for Dedicated we can push signed log bundles or integrate with your SIEM via secure forwarders.
00:03:10 - Daniel: for SOC2, do you already have the Type II? we'll need the report and the PCA matrix mapping controls to your processes.
00:03:22 - Lena: yes we have SOC2 Type II; I will send the report and a high-level controls mapping (what they test). we also have ISO evidence for our infra controls.
00:03:36 - Alexei (Infra): on network — we'll want to peer into an EU region, and make sure outbound IPs are pinned so our firewall rules can allow calls. what does that look like on Dedicated?
00:03:49 - Samir: Dedicated endpoints can be pinned to Egress IP sets per region; Private with VPC peering gives you direct internal networking and no public egress as long as you configure it. We'll document the egress IP ranges and NAT behavior.
00:04:06 - Maya: okay good. now on BCDR — we run a rotated on-call and need a clear escalation path. what does your SRE on-call look like, and what are your RTO/RPO commitments in writing?
00:04:22 - Samir: operationally, Redwood has a tiered escalation: on-call engineer -> escalation to infra SRE lead -> platform on-call -> engineering manager and then exec on-call if needed. for SLA we typically offer 99.95% for Dedicated critical endpoints and 99.9% for hosted tiers; we can propose contractual language for 99.95 with error budgets and credits.
00:04:46 - Daniel: 99.95 is acceptable, but we need measurable RTO for incident runs — e.g., for P1 we expect a mitigation window of 15 minutes to restore degraded service or failover. can you support automated fallback to a warm model variant in another region?
00:05:03 - Samir: yes, smart routing supports automatic fallback to compatible model variants in other regions or lower-capacity pools. for Private installs, customer-managed failover is typical but we can operate failover via our control plane if agreed in the runbook.
00:05:18 - Tom: what's the usual RPO for your KV/cache state? our session tokens and KV cache are critical — if you lose the KV we want RPO as close to zero as possible.
00:05:30 - Samir: continuous prefix/KV caching introduces statefulness — for Dedicated we replicate KV across availability zones with async replication. RPO depends on replication window; we can target sub-1 minute RPO with aggressive replication and WAL shipping. that has cost trade-offs.
00:05:50 - Daniel: cost trade-offs are expected, we want the design and the numbers so legal can sign off.
00:05:58 - Lena: we'll draft a few architectures and cost delta scenarios in the BYOK doc.
00:06:08 - 00:06:30 - [crosstalk] — brief sidebar about schedule options for tabletop, everyone confirms weeks.
00:06:45 - Priya: on RBAC and SSO — we need SCIM provisioning and ability to map our roles to Redwood roles (admin, ops, read-only). also MFA enforcement via SAML.
00:06:58 - Iris: we support SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. RBAC is role-based with customizable role bindings; we can add constraint rules for resource-level access. MFA enforcement is upstream via IdP.
00:07:14 - Alexei: any audit of role changes? we require a changelog for user/role modifications for 13 months.
00:07:24 - Iris: yes, role changes are logged with actor, timestamp, IP and old/new state. retention configurable; can export to your SIEM.
00:07:36 - Maya: great. a question on incident notifications: we need integration with PagerDuty and a phone escalation path for sev1. how does that map today?
00:07:49 - Samir: we push alerts to PagerDuty and can configure runbook hooks. phone escalation is available for enterprise customers as a paged escalation; we can include a primary SRE on-call list in the runbook and automatic escalation intervals (e.g., 5m -> 10m -> 30m).
00:08:05 - Daniel: good. also how do you handle post-mortems and root-cause evidence for regulator reviews?
00:08:16 - Iris: post-mortems live in our incident tracker; we can provide redacted timelines and logs relevant to the incident. we keep evidence for X months — default 6 months — but again retention can be extended with the enterprise evidence pack.
00:08:30 - Tom: what's X? can you be specific on evidence retention tied to a contract?
00:08:36 - Iris: yes — evidence retention commitments would be contractually specified; typical enterprise add-on is 12-24 months.
00:08:45 - Lena: quick note — customers on Private mode often choose 24-month retention for auditability.
00:08:52 - 00:09:10 - [Pause] short audio glitch, partial overlap.
00:09:22 - Daniel: can you walk through an example incident run? say database connectivity in EU region fails, what's the sequence to failover and notify Halo?
00:09:34 - Samir: step 1 auto-detect via health checks and telemetry; step 2 if below threshold we attempt local recovery (restart processes); step 3 if recovery fails within the configured window (e.g., 5m) we trigger routing to warm standby region or model variant; step 4 we create P1 incident ticket, notify via PagerDuty and email, and run the escalation tree. each step is logged and available in the incident timeline for post-mortem.
00:09:58 - Maya: important — we want the ability to control failover thresholds; sometimes legal requires us to opt into or out of cross-border failover.
00:10:09 - Iris: that's possible — we can configure routing policies to require explicit approval for cross-region failover for your account. we'll include that in the runbook template.
00:10:22 - Priya: another compliance question: do you support data deletion/verifiable purge if we request deletion for specific datasets?
00:10:32 - Lena: yes, data lifecycle APIs allow deletion requests; for Private deployments, you control the storage and can verify deletion. for Dedicated/hosted we provide verifiable deletion logs and certificates upon request.
00:10:45 - Daniel: and replication — if data copied into backups or caches exist in other zones, how's purge handled?
00:10:54 - Samir: purge hooks can cascade to caches and backups; for backups we maintain snapshot deletion metadata and can certify deletion after retention window elapses. we will detail the guarantee and exceptions (e.g., immutable logs for legal holds).
00:11:12 - Alexei: about SLA credits, can you share sample language? we need SLO definitions, measurement windows, and remediation credits.
00:11:23 - Lena: yes — we'll attach sample SLA clauses. typical is 99.95% monthly uptime with credits scaled based on outage minutes beyond threshold. we also specify measurement (client-facing endpoints only) and exclude scheduled maintenance windows with notice.
00:11:42 - Daniel: okay, good. question on tests — how often do you run DR tests and can Halo join?
00:11:50 - Samir: we run annual full DR drills and quarterly tabletop exercises; customers can join or request dedicated drills — for Private we can run dedicated drills in your environment.
00:12:02 - Priya: we'd like quarterly table-top with our ops and legal present for the first year.
00:12:08 - Lena: we will plan that into the onboarding runbook.
00:12:14 - 00:12:30 - [brief aside about sample audit checklist Lena will send]
00:12:45 - Daniel: small nit — our compliance team will need signed BAA and data processing addendum; can you confirm Redwood supports standard DPA + BAA?
00:12:56 - Lena: yes we have standard DPA and BAA templates; legal can review changes. I'll include them in the package.
00:13:05 - Maya: circling back to KMS — what's the attestation/crypto boundary for Redwood-managed keys vs customer-managed?
00:13:15 - Iris: Redwood-managed keys keep key material in our managed HSMs; with BYOK, key material never leaves customer KMS/HSM. we only get wrapped keys or use envelope encryption — we can detail trust flow in the architecture sketch.
00:13:30 - Tom: do you support on-prem HSMs talking over KMIP?
00:13:34 - Iris: yes, for Private installs we support KMIP and HSM integration; we've implemented with Thales and AWS CloudHSM patterns.
00:13:44 - 00:14:05 - [short pause while someone checks chat link]
00:14:16 - Samir: one more operational detail — when we talk about backups, we usually snapshot model artifacts and config daily and store across AZs; hot KV is replicated more frequently. we can alter cadence depending on RPO needs.
00:14:31 - Alexei: and retention for backups? regulatory often asks 7 years for financial logs — is that possible?
00:14:40 - Iris: yes, long-term retention is available via archive tiers; cost and retrieval latency are trade-offs we'll include in the proposal.
00:14:51 - Daniel: if we require on-prem, what's the support model? do you do remote ops or do we run it entirely?
00:14:59 - Samir: on-prem option can be delivered either as customer-run with operator docs or as a managed private deployment where Redwood provides ops under an enterprise support agreement. we do both.
00:15:12 - Maya: would managed mean Redwood has network access into our environment? that's a legal point.
00:15:20 - Lena: managed means we have specific, limited operator access flows over mutually agreed channels; everything is logged and subject to your approval. we can provide jump-host access, ephemeral credentials, or a bastion approach as per your security policy.
00:15:34 - Priya: please capture that detail — legal will want to see scope of access.
00:15:39 - Lena: noted.
00:15:45 - 00:16:05 - [silence while Iris prepares BYOK slide link in chat]
00:16:08 - Iris: I'm posting the BYOK/KMS options doc link in the chat — it's a high-level primer, the sketch we'll send will have more detail.
00:16:18 - Daniel: thanks. minor transcription — when you say "warm standby" do you mean kept-up replica with served traffic suppressed, or just a model artifact ready to spin up?
00:16:29 - Samir: warmed standby can be either — we offer cold (artifact only), warm (loaded model, idle), and hot (actively serving in another AZ). warm is typical for cost vs latency balance.
00:16:43 - Tom: do you have metrics on failover time for warm standby?
00:16:48 - Samir: for warm standby we usually see failover in 30s-2m depending on checkpoint loading and KV sync; hot is essentially instant routing. we'll put measured numbers from our benchmarks in the runbook.
00:17:03 - Maya: please include test evidence — we will need benchmark CSVs showing failover latencies.
00:17:10 - Lena: will do.
00:17:18 - 00:17:36 - [discussion about scheduling tabletop slots]
00:17:40 - Daniel: final compliance question — are you able to sign mutual NDAs and provide a shared evidence room for auditors?
00:17:49 - Lena: yes — we use a secure evidence room for customers during audits and sign MNDA/NDAs; we'll include onboarding steps for audit access.
00:17:58 - Priya: perfect. one more thing — SIEM integration, we'll want ability to forward all request-level logs and role-change events. can Redwood provide a sustained log stream and not just bundles?
00:18:10 - Samir: yes, we can provide streaming via secure forwarder to Splunk/Datadog/ELK with TLS and client auth. the volume/throughput has costs; we'll provide estimates.
00:18:22 - Alexei: about encryption in transit — TLS mutual auth for private peering?
00:18:28 - Iris: TLS 1.2/1.3 enforced. for VPC peering we recommend mTLS for service-to-service; we can support client certs if required.
00:18:39 - Daniel: good. overall we have enough to move forward — we want the documents to review with legal & infra.
00:18:46 - Lena: recap and next steps — Lena sends SOC2 & legal templates; Iris sends BYOK design; Samir schedules tabletop and shares runbook template; Halo shares network diagram.
00:19:00 - 00:48:00 - [Remaining time spent clarifying small points: sample SLA phrasing, fine-grain RBAC roles, export formats for logs, and confirming dates for next tabletop. Multiple short clarifications and micro-decisions recorded in the chat. No substantive objections left. Meeting ended with agreement to reconvene after doc review.]

End of transcript.

Asteria Health pilot weekly - privacy, retention & SSO handoff

Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-20
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Elena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Noah Kim (Redwood CSM), Maya Chen (Asteria Head of Security), Liam O'Connor (Asteria Platform), Dr. Noor Rahman (Asteria Compliance), Priya Singh (Asteria DevOps)

Summary:
Short weekly touch for POC: focus on SSO handoff, audit log format and retention controls, SOC2 artifacts and one small bench to confirm audit ingestion. Confirmed open items and owners.

Topics:
- SAML/SCIM SSO integration status
- Audit logs: schema, retention, ingestion cadence
- Data retention options for sensitive PHI fields and scrub rules
- SOC2 evidence deliverables and KMS/HSM questions
- Next steps: bench test and handoff timeline

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir: okay hey everyone thanks for making time, this is the weekly pilot touch for Asteria, hopefully a short focused one, audio's okay?
[00:10] Maya: yeah hi, audio's good, thanks.
[00:15] Elena: Cool, I'll kick off with current status on SSO since Priya and Liam raised a few items last week.
[00:22] Elena: We pushed the staging SP metadata to the link you sent, we saw the assertion fail on first try because the NameID format was urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:nameid-format:transient which your IdP isn't issuing, so we switched to email address and that landed; there may be a mapping mismatch for groups/roles.
[00:45] Priya: yeah we saw that, our IdP is Okta, and our groups map is a bit custom. We can push a SCIM patch but need the attribute map from you.
[00:55] Elena: absolutely, I'll send a SCIM attribute mapping table. Note though, SCIM patch endpoints in our staging may return 409 for unknown attributes, so be ready to filter on your side.
[01:20] Liam: quick Q — is Redwood doing user provisioning via SCIM or just group sync? We want full deprovisioning for security.
[01:28] Samir: we support both; typical pilot uses SCIM provisioning + SAML for SSO. For deprovisioning we have soft-delete TTL and immediate token revocation hooks, but we'll need to align retention policy.
[01:40] Maya: On retention — we have PHI in some of the payloads (very small subset). We need a retention config to drop PII after 90 days and keep aggregate logs for 365. Can you map what we can redact vs what Redwood needs for model quality?
[01:58] Elena: yes, we can configure field-level retention. The runtime supports prefix/KV cache, and we can redact or pseudonymize before it's persisted to audit logs. Small caveat: if you redact model inputs earlier, it may affect evals but we can maintain hashed identifiers for rollout correlation.
[02:20] Dr. Noor: hashed identifiers are acceptable for our auditors as long as salt management is documented and irreversible.
[02:30] Elena: we'll provide the salt rotation and KMS usage docs — currently we recommend using a customer-managed KMS for Private deployments; for hosted we can integrate with your cloud KMS with envelope encryption.
[02:45] Priya: does Redwood support HSM-backed keys? Our compliance requires HSM for key custody for certain datasets.
[02:52] Samir: yes, we have HSM integrations, you can present an HSM-backed KMS or we can integrate via partner HSM — will add that to artifacts.
[03:05] Noah: quick note — I uploaded the SOC2 crosswalk last week into the shared drive, Samir will follow up with the cert binder.
[03:15] Samir: correct, I'll send the full SOC2 Type II binder and the control mapping doc to Asteria.
[03:22] Maya: thanks, auditors will want evidence for key rotation and access logs.
[03:28] Samir: understood. We'll include KMS rotation policy and sample audit log snippets.
[03:35] Liam: on audit logs — what schema are you emitting? Our SIEM team depends on consistent fields: timestamp, user_id, action, model_id, request_id, token_count, latency_ms.
[03:48] Elena: Great question — our current audit payload includes: ts, uid, req_id, model, route, tokens_in, tokens_out, lat_ms, error_code, retention_tag. But sometimes the transcript text field is full text and may contain PHI, we usually send a pointer to the stored blob if you have stricter retention.
[04:10] Liam: can we ingest via HTTPS push or do you support streaming to Kinesis/SQS?
[04:15] Elena: both, staging supports HTTPS push webhook, and for production we support Kinesis, Pub/Sub, Event Hubs — we'll provide example connectors. For the POC we recommend HTTPS webhook to your SIEM ingestion endpoint.
[04:30] Priya: okay we'll stand up a webhook receiver and try ingesting a few sample events.
[04:36] Elena: I'll drop an example payload (note: sometimes 'KV cache' was transcribed in older notes as 'kiv cache' so ignore that typos), but payload fields are as I said.
[04:50] Maya: also I want to confirm retention UI — can we set per-field retention windows per model?
[04:58] Elena: yes per-model and per-field. We expose retention policies as JSON config — sample: {"model": "redwood-1", "fields": {"transcript": "90d", "meta": "365d"}} — in staging you can set via console or API.
[05:20] Liam: will that be audited in the change logs? We need traceability of policy changes.
[05:26] Samir: yes all retention config changes are tracked in audit logs and tied to the admin user; we can include a sample change record.
[05:35] Dr. Noor: excellent. On SOC2 and the control set, we need mapping for logical access, change mgmt, encryption at rest, incident response.
[05:46] Samir: we'll add the mapping doc — and include the incident response playbook summary.
[05:52] Elena: small technical note on SSO: Okta default group claims size can cause truncated assertions if you push many groups; we suggest SCIM for group membership. Also for role-based RBAC in Redwood Console we map Okta groups to Redwood roles.
[06:10] Priya: good to know. We'll limit to primary groups for now.
[06:14] Liam: about logs retention, how easy is it to purge records if we need to for legal requests?
[06:20] Elena: we have on-demand redaction APIs — you can call the purge endpoint with request_id or user_id and choose immediate deletion from the active store and flag for archive purge; there's also freezer retention for cold backups which we can coordinate with legal hold.
[06:36] Maya: are backups encrypted separately? If backups are in AWS S3 do you use SSE-KMS?
[06:42] Samir: yes we use SSE-KMS for backups and support customer-managed CMKs for the private mode. For hosted we hold the wrapped key but you can bring your own key for the Private deployment.
[06:55] Dr. Noor: there's sometimes confusion between 'hosted' and 'private' modes in terms of who manages keys — can you summarize?
[07:02] Samir: Hosted: Redwood manages key envelope but can integrate with customer KMS for envelope keys; Private/VPC: customer manages keys end-to-end and we only store references. We'll put this in the crosswalk.
[07:18] Elena: moving to audit ingestion bench — for next week we'd like to run a 30 minute test where we pump ~5k events to your SIEM and measure latency; Noah will coordinate the timeslot.
[07:30] Noah: I'll set up a calendar invite for 2027-11-30 14:00 UTC and include required endpoints.
[07:36] Priya: that works. Also small perf ask — will redwood metrics include token-level breakdown per request for our billing reconciliation?
[07:44] Elena: yes we emit token counts and cost metadata; you can map that to your internal billing. Note cost metadata in staging may be mocked.
[07:55] Liam: competitor question — DeepServe flagged a faster ingest pipeline; how is Redwood's audit throughput?
[08:01] Samir: we've seen sustained 10k events/sec in dedicated mode with batching; for hosted POC you'll be in the 500-2k/sec range depending on payload size and concurrency. We default to batching to reduce overhead.
[08:17] Maya: acceptable for POC. Another ask from audits: show us proof of separation of environments (staging vs prod) and data flow diagrams.
[08:27] Samir: yes, we'll share network diagrams and environment separation docs.
[08:32] Dr. Noor: one more — auditors want to see least privilege on API keys, do you support token scoping?
[08:39] Elena: yes API keys can be scoped by model, by route, and by retention policy; we can generate scoped service accounts.
[08:48] Liam: on the SSO handoff, what's the expected effort from our team to finalize the integration?
[08:53] Samir: For full SAML + SCIM + audit flows, estimate 2-3 full days of engineering on your side: provisioning SP, mapping attributes, firewall rules for webhooks. We'll try to minimize by providing templates.
[09:06] Priya: okay that's doable. We'll plan for a 2 day effort next week.
[09:12] Maya: small question on retention artifacts — can you provide example redaction logs that show what was redacted and by whom?
[09:19] Elena: yes redaction logs include admin_id, request_id, fields_removed, reason_code, timestamp. We'll provide sanitized examples.
[09:28] Liam: are there any GDPR considerations we should surface now? We have EU users and need data locality.
[09:33] Samir: for EU data residency we can pin to region and keep control plane in Private mode; for hosted we'd require data region selection and we maintain region-scoped storage. We'll share the region residency matrix.
[09:48] Dr. Noor: can you also show us retention TTL enforcement tests? Auditors like test evidence.
[09:53] Elena: yes we'll include test scripts and example results.
[10:00] Noah: quick sync on timeline — are we still targeting pilot completion by mid-December?
[10:05] Samir: yes target hasn't changed: pilot wrap and go/no-go by 2027-12-15, with final review week of 2027-12-20.
[10:14] Priya: that gives us enough time.
[10:18] Maya: anything blocking from Redwood side to run the bench?
[10:22] Elena: only the webhook endpoint from Asteria and the test SP provisioning. Once those are up we're golden.
[10:30] Liam: final question — OIDC support? Some internal apps use OIDC instead of SAML.
[10:36] Elena: we support OIDC for service accounts but SAML is first-class for SSO; we can provide OIDC client details if you prefer.
[10:42] Maya: thanks.
[10:44] Samir: okay to recap quickly — action items as we discussed: I'll send SOC2 artifacts and control mapping; Elena will send SAML metadata/SCIM map and example audit payloads; Noah will schedule the 11/30 bench; Asteria to provision SP and webhook. Any additions?
[10:58] Dr. Noor: please include the salt rotation schedule for hashed identifiers.
[11:03] Elena: will do.
[11:08] Samir: great. We'll confirm next meeting time — same time next week?
[11:12] Maya: yes midday UTC works.
[11:15] Samir: perfect, thanks everyone.
[11:20] [closing chatter and confirmation of artifacts]

End of transcript.

document.content:
Stability & stress test: kernel-swap behavior TRT-LLM vs vLLM on private deploy

Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-12-10 15:00 UTC | Duration: 62m | Zoom call
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Helix), Sana Patel (Helix SRE), Diego Ramos (Helix CTO)
Recording: zoom.us/rec/abcdefg (internal)

Summary: technical deep dive into kernel-swapping and cudagraph replay instability observed on Helix on-prem private deployment. Focus on TRT-LLM vs vLLM behavior, KV cache persistence, batching policy interactions and fallback heuristics.

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, quick roll call?
[00:07] Marcus: Marcus here, we hit some instability in our private cluster during long chat sessions, curious if it's TRT-LLM cudagraph replay or our NV link setup.
[00:14] Sana: Sana, SRE, here. we've got 8xA100 nodes with NV link, patched to 510 drivers, and we've seen intermittent out-of-memory errors and some latency spikes.
[00:22] Priya: hey hi, Priya from Redwood infra, I went through the trace Marcus sent, there are a few signatures that look like cudagraph replay mismatches and persistent K V cache evictions in the middle of large-batch sequences.
[00:34] Diego: Diego here, CTO. stepping back, we need to understand tradeoffs — TRT-LLM gives us lower p50 but seen more jitter; vLLM is stable but costs more. want to pick a path for our pilot.

[00:48] Alex: quick framing — TRT-LLM uses TensorRT kernels + cudagraph replay for hot paths; that gives great throughput but can be brittle if sequence length distribution changes or if there's eviction of cached KV states. vLLM keeps a more general scheduler, less replay, more deterministic but slightly higher avg latency.
[01:05] Marcus: correct, our long-chat workload has very variable sequence lengths, lots of switching between short queries and long context expansions. We instrumented a 24h window and saw kernel swap events correlate with NV link traffic bursts.
[01:22] Priya: one important detail — cudagraphs are recorded for specific execution paths (seq len, batch shape); when a record is replayed but the KV cache layout changed (evictions or shifted offsets), the GPU can hit protective checks or suboptimal kernels, producing slower kernels or OOMs. The runtime should fallback but sometimes fallback triggers late.
[01:40] Sana: yes, and our current fallback threshold is quite conservative, we only swap after a few failed replays which is why you're seeing spikes.

[02:01] Alex: couple of concrete suggestions: 1) warmup with representative sampled traces to prime cudagraphs, 2) enable prefix-aware recording (so the graph covers typical variations), 3) relax persistent KV eviction or increase K V cache size to avoid mid-dialog evictions.
[02:18] Marcus: Warmup sounds doable, but our on-prem memory is tight. can quantization help? we tried int8 profile and saw quality degradation on generative tasks.
[02:29] Priya: quantization is a tool — INT8 reduces memory but can change kernel selection too. TRT-LLM's int8 kernels may pick different execution paths; important to run quality evals. Also mixed precision FP16 + selective int8 for attention can be a middle ground.
[02:46] Diego: are we seeing deterministic reproducibility? i mean, if you rerun the same trace, do you get the same kernel-swap points?
[02:53] Priya: not always. small nondeterministic timing can change batching boundaries which changes the recorded graph. Also background GC/eviction events cause offsets to shift. We need a more stable batching policy; continuous batching is great for throughput but exacerbates this variability.

[03:18] Marcus: what's Redwood's fallback policy by default?
[03:21] Alex: we try cudagraph replay, then line up a soft fallback to non-replayed kernel with a short warmup period. There's also a more aggressive policy that disables cudagraphs for endpoints with very high sequence variability.
[03:36] Sana: could that be per-route? we'd like chat endpoints to be stable but analytics batch jobs to use cudagraphs.
[03:41] Priya: yes it's per-route — you can pin routing policy per model route. For Helix we'd recommend chat-route: conservative cudagraph policy + larger KV cache quota; analytical-route: aggressive cudagraph + batching.

[04:02] Diego: NVLink config — we saw cross-GPU memory copies spike after a kernel swap. Could that be the kernel change itself, or are we hitting PCIe fallback?
[04:10] Priya: depends. TensorRT kernels sometimes choose different memory layouts requiring extra cross-device synchronization. Also cudagraph replay may skip certain async memcpy optimizations and force synchronous copies if replay path differs. We should capture nvprof / NSIGHT traces around swap events.
[04:28] Marcus: we have some nvprof dumps. I'll upload them. they show sudden sync points that match the timestamp of the spikes.

[04:45] Alex: on the software side, recommended next steps: 1) Priya will run a repro with two scenarios: persistent KV cache enabled vs disabled, and with/without cudagraph replay. 2) collect cuda graf record IDs, kernel names, and time series of NCCL/ memcpy syncs.

[05:02] Priya: also want to test a deterministic warmup — replay sampled 30m of traffic 3x before opening to production to stabilize recorded graphs. That reduces cold-start graph variance.
[05:13] Sana: question — what about quantization + cudagraph? Does quantized cudagraph exacerbate instability?
[05:19] Priya: quantization can change kernel selection and memory layout; TRT-LLM's int8 kernels are often different code paths. If you change precision post-record, replay may mismatch. So record graphs using the target precision.

[05:36] Marcus: any config knobs for delaying fallback so we don't get OOM but also not degrade p50?
[05:41] Alex: yes — two knobs: a) early-detect policy that pre-validates graph compatibility on warmup, b) soft-fallback that serves from a warm non-cudagraph kernel that is already primed. Both reduce oscillation.
[05:56] Diego: cost question — if we disable cudagraphs for chat route, what's the expected cost hit?
[06:01] Priya: rough estimate — 8–15% higher per-token compute cost for smaller batch-size patterns; but much less variability so SLA could be better. We should run targeted econ tests.

[06:18] Sana: on the networking side, we might be able to isolate chat traffic to nodes with strong NVLink topology (full mesh) vs nodes with partial NVLink. That should reduce cross-node memcpy.
[06:27] Priya: good call. Also pinning model shards to NVLink-connected devices reduces NCCL traffic. That's a deployment-level config.

[06:42] Alex: open questions we captured: how often do graph-recorded shapes diverge in your workload? Marcus said about 12% of sessions have >3 lengths changes; we need the raw distribution.
[06:55] Marcus: I'll drop the session histogram into the shared folder.
[07:00] Priya: last operational note — ensure driver/ CUDA runtime matches what TRT-LLM expects; mismatches cause subtle kernel fallbacks. You said you are on 510 drivers, we recommend 515+ for our latest TRT kernels.
[07:14] Sana: noted, we'll test 515 in staging.

[07:22] Alex: recap: shared artifact (bench template + current TRT docker) from Alex, Priya to run 48h controlled replay tests on Helix staging, Helix to provide traces and nvprof logs, followup 2026-12-20.
[07:37] Diego: sounds good, thank you.
[07:40] Marcus: thank you all, appreciate the pragmatic plan.
[07:44] Alex: great, we'll send the sheet and security checklist after the call.
[07:49] Priya: talk soon — bye.

End of transcript.
