CobaltBeam — Channel reseller compatibility & SLA framing

Intro call to evaluate mutual fit for CobaltBeam becoming a Redwood channel reseller. Covered deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs private), SLA expectations, routing and capacity guarantees, security/compliance (SAML, KMS/HSM, audit logs), and a pilot framing for a 6-week technical validation. Action items and next steps agreed: pricing matrix, security pack, pilot scope doc, and a joint tech benchmark window.
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-08-14 15:00 PDT
- Duration: 48 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Kate Lin (CSM), Noah Patel (Solutions); Samir Rao (Head of Partnerships, CobaltBeam), Eve Trent (Platform Eng), Derek Holmes (Security), Lina Park (Product)

Summary: Intro + mutual discovery to scope reseller integration. Focus on technical compatibility, SLAs, and compliance gating. Agreed to pilot and exchanged docs to align commercial and technical requirements.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intros? I'm Maya, AE on the channel partnerships team, with Luis our SE. Um, we wanted to walk through how Redwood surfaces reseller partners and what the technical bar looks like.

[00:28] Samir Rao: Thanks Maya, Samir on my side. We're exploring channel partnerships, specifically resellers who can embed a managed inference stack for our MSP customers. We want to understand latency guarantees and where Redwood sits on hosted versus dedicated vs private.

[01:10] Luis Ortega: Great, so to frame it, Redwood runs three primary modes - hosted API, Dedicated reserved capacity, and Private (VPC/on-prem). For resellers, we typically see a mix: hosted for small customers, dedicated or private for regulated customers. Our dedicated pools give predictable throughput and burst options.

[01:42] Eve Trent: Quick clarifying question — when you say 'dedicated' do you mean single-tenant GPU pools or logically isolated? We have a few finance vertical customers that will require physical isolation.

[01:58] Noah Patel: It's physical isolation at the worker level, yes. Dedicated is reserved GPU capacity which can be tenant-isolated; private is the full on-prem/VPC control plane option.

[02:18] Derek Holmes: Security wise we care about SSO, SAML, audit logs, and keys. Does Redwood support customer-managed KMS or HSM integrations?

[02:32] Luis Ortega: Yes — we support KMS integration and we can plug into customer-managed KMS/HSM for private deployments. For hosted, we offer encryption at rest and customer keys via a managed KMS integration pattern. We'll follow up with specific diagrams.

[03:00] Samir Rao: Cool. Commercially, what's the reseller margin model look like? Is there an MSP pricing tier?

[03:12] Maya Chen: We have tiered partner discounts based on committed reserved capacity. For a reseller program we can do margins + referral ppm, and there's a partner SOW template. Maya: I'll share the initial pricing matrix after this call.

[03:40] Eve Trent: On the technical side, two immediate blockers: 1) routing and fallbacks — can requests be routed to a cheaper model when capacity is constrained? And 2) caching — we rely heavily on prefix caching and re-use patterns. How does Redwood handle KV cache across deployments?

[04:02] Luis Ortega: For smart routing, yes — we have policy-based routing that can route by latency, cost, or region and can fallback to compatible model variants. For caching, we have automatic KV cache and prefix caching in the runtime; note that the K-V cash makes a big difference on token cost — sorry, K-V cash, I mean KV cache — but caching behavior and persistence vary by mode. In a private/on-prem setup you get more control for persistent caches.

[04:40] Lina Park: When you say fallback to compatible variants, how do you manage quality regressions? Our product needs predictable semantic output for certain prompts.

[04:56] Luis Ortega: We tie rollouts to eval sets and have canary deploys. Redwood Optimize also suggests quantization and model variants per workload. We recommend a short canary and an eval set covering the customer's critical prompts to detect regressions.

[05:20] Samir Rao: Timeline wise, our partners often want a fast path to pilot within 2–4 weeks. Is there a light pilot we can run, and what would be included?

[05:34] Kate Lin: From CSM perspective, typical pilot: 6 weeks, includes integration support, sandbox tokens for dedicated nodes, and a joint benchmark window. We'll help define acceptance criteria.

[05:50] Eve Trent: We'll need a benchmarking window where CobaltBeam supplies two representative workloads — one short chat-style, one long-form summarization. We want to measure P50/P95 latency and per-token cost.

[06:12] Luis Ortega: Perfect. We usually run a 60m technical benchmark with the partner, capture token distribution, latency percentiles, and memory/kv cache hit rates. That feeds recommendations: batching, quantization, and kernel selection.

[06:36] Derek Holmes: On compliance, our legal asks for SOC 2 type II evidence and an audit log export pattern. Also need a contract-level SLA for uptime and latency. Can Redwood commit to a 99.9% uptime on Dedicated?

[06:56] Maya Chen: We have SLA tiers for Dedicated and for Private enterprise. 99.9% is feasible for higher tiers with reserved capacity and a commercial SLA. We'll send the detailed SLA doc.

[07:14] Samir Rao: Any channel/distribution mechanics we should know about? Do you handle white-labeling or co-branded experiences?

[07:25] Noah Patel: We support reseller APIs and white-label endpoints for partners; the UX is often handled on the partner side, but we can provide SDKs and example integrations.

[07:40] Eve Trent: A couple of edge questions — data residency: can you pin inference traffic to EU regions for some customers?

[07:52] Luis Ortega: Yes, regional routing is supported. For private deployments we'd recommend colocating the control plane and inference nodes in the customer's region to meet residency.

[08:10] Lina Park: How do billing and metering work for resellers? Do you provide token-level exports?

[08:20] Kate Lin: We provide token-level billing, per-route breakdowns, and usage analytics. For resellers we can provide aggregated billing or per-customer line-items depending on the contract.

[08:40] Samir Rao: Any notable integration pitfalls other partners have hit?

[08:50] Luis Ortega: The usual: underestimating KV cache hit patterns (so initial cost spikes), and not accounting for cold-starts on long contexts. Also SSO configuration for multiple sub-tenants can be finicky; we'll share our SSO runbook.

[09:12] Eve Trent: For the pilot, what level of access will we have to logs and traces? We need request-level traces for debugging.

[09:22] Luis Ortega: The Redwood Console exposes per-request traces, token-level latency breakdowns, and model-level dashboards. For private deployments we can extend retention. We'll include sample screenshots in the security pack.

[09:40] Samir Rao: Competitor question — our procurement asked if Redwood has better unit economics than MajorCloudAI for typical summarization workloads.

[09:52] Maya Chen: We usually show cost comparisons after we get the workload token histogram; without the data it's noisy. That benchmark window will make it concrete.

[10:10] Derek Holmes: On the KMS/HSM note — we need to run a short review to validate your KMS key rotation and HSM attestation process. Can you support an external audit request?

[10:24] Luis Ortega: Yes, we can support SOC2 artifacts and have an attestation flow for HSM integrations in our private deployments. We'll list the exact artifacts in the security pack.

[10:40] Maya Chen: Let's align on pilot success metrics: latency P95 below X ms, cost per 1k tokens below Y, and no functional regressions on the eval set. Kate will draft an initial success criteria doc.

[11:00] Kate Lin: I'll take that. Also propose weekly syncs during the pilot with an AE+SE touchpoint.

[11:12] Samir Rao: Sounds good. A couple more questions from product: Lina — are they going to commit to supporting tool-calling and structured output?

[11:28] Luis Ortega: Yes we support function/tool calling and structured output guidance. Implementation details will depend on the model and the SDK version.

[11:44] Eve Trent: For the technical benchmark, can you surface kernel selection and quantization recommendations per-model? We want to know if quantized models will impact quality for our prompts.

[11:58] Luis Ortega: We'll produce a recommendation sheet: model variant, quantization profile, expected latency delta, and observed quality deltas from the eval set. For the pilot we can test a quantized candidate versus FP16 baseline.

[12:20] Maya Chen: Great. Operational question — what does on-call / escalation for a reseller customer look like?

[12:32] Noah Patel: Partners get a dedicated onboarding channel plus a 24/7 escalation path for production incidents depending on the SLA tier. We'll outline the support playbook.

[12:48] Derek Holmes: Do you log request payloads? We need to know redaction options and retention periods.

[12:58] Luis Ortega: Request payloads can be redacted; retention windows are configurable for private deployments and for Dedicated we have retention tiers. We'll include config knobs in the security pack.

[13:16] Samir Rao: Okay, high level looks promising. Let's lock the next steps: 1) Redwood to send pricing and security docs; 2) CobaltBeam to share workloads and compliance checklist; 3) schedule benchmark window.

[13:32] Maya Chen: Yep, I'll circulate a meeting summary and the action items. Any final quick asks?

[13:40] Eve Trent: Please include any sample SAML metadata and a runbook for multi-tenant SSO.

[13:46] Luis Ortega: We'll include that.

[13:52] Samir Rao: Thanks everyone, excited to run the pilot.

[13:56] Maya Chen: Thanks team — we'll follow up on the docs and set the benchmark calendar.

[14:00] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings around acronyms (K-V cash -> KV cache) and Redwood product names are present. Occasional overlapping talk at ~05:30.

Maya Chen - Share reseller pricing matrix and SOW template - due 2026-08-21
Luis Ortega - Export security pack: SOC2 summary, SAML flow doc, KMS/HSM integration notes - due 2026-08-19
Eve Trent (CobaltBeam) - Share 2 representative workloads for pilot (latency & token profile) - due 2026-08-18
Derek Holmes (CobaltBeam) - Send compliance checklist and PII data flow for review - due 2026-08-20
Kate Lin - Draft joint pilot success metrics doc - due 2026-08-25
Redwood: Share reseller pricing matrix and margin tiers (Maya) - due 2026-08-21
Redwood: Send security pack (SOC2 summary, SAML docs, KMS integrations) (Luis) - due 2026-08-19
CobaltBeam: Provide example customer SLA and deployment targets (Samir) - due 2026-08-20
Schedule 60m technical benchmarking window (week of 2026-08-24) (Maya+Eve)
Draft pilot scope (6-week) & acceptance criteria (joint) - initial draft by 2026-08-25
Partner expresses high interest in a white-label reseller flow and wants a narrow pilot with two workloads. Key gating items: SOC2 artifacts, SAML runbook, and clear SLA for Dedicated. Pricing matrix will determine commercial fit.

2026-12-28 Pilot flow surge tuning review

[Meeting Header]
Date: 2026-12-28
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Noah Ruiz (Redwood CSM); Jared Mills (Crestline), Priya Rao (Crestline), Samantha Cho (Crestline), Diego Alvarez (Crestline)

[Summary]
Quick sync on pilot throughput: reviewed last week's steady-state run, discussed continuous batching behavior under spike patterns, tuned concurrency targets and queue depth, agreed next steps to validate in dev and surface traces/latency buckets. Some audio mis-reads on the auto-transcript; see timestamps.

[Topics]
- steady-state throughput results
- continuous batching dynamics
- per-GPU concurrency and p95/p99 latency tradeoffs
- queue depth / backpressure behavior and fallbacks
- telemetry needed (token-level timing, KV hit rates)

[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep to about 45 minutes, we wanted to go over the throughput runs from last thursday and then push some tuning recs, is that ok?
[00:18] Jared Mills: yes, sounds good, quick note, sorry my mic's a bit low, but i can share the numbers from our run, we did three 30 minute intervals at target load
[00:35] Priya Rao: just to set context we are running the rlhf-model-1 variant — it's a 13B-ish open model quantized to 4-bit but i think the runtime shows some variance around dense attention ops, sometimes the word "quantize" came out wrong in the logs as "quantwise" so ignore that
[01:05] Liam O'Connor: got it, thanks, so we pulled out the per-shard p95 and p99, i'll share a chart afterwards, but headline: at concurrency 8 per GPU we get steady 780 rps aggregate with p95 ~210ms, p99 ~520ms, continuous batching avg batch size 12 tokens, occasional spikes to 24 during bursts
[01:42] Diego Alvarez: that's helpful, our initial target for production is 1k rps with p95 < 250ms, p99 we can tolerate ~700ms for now — what's the gap to 1k?
[02:05] Maya Patel: the primary lever is concurrency + queue depth shaping; we saw diminishing returns after 12 concurrency per GPU because KV cache thrashing started showing up and batching efficiency worsened
[02:33] Priya Rao: when you say KV thrash, are you referring to the KV cache hit-rate drop that was in the telemetry? our logs showed about 18% miss during the second interval
[03:01] Liam O'Connor: yes exactly, miss-rate rose when we pushed concurrency beyond 10, because many requests have different prefixes so KV reuse drops; continuous batching helps when prefixes are shared, but with more diversity you lose the prefix coalescing benefit
[03:28] Jared Mills: I remember in the config you suggested a short prefix cache TTL and a slightly larger batch-window to let more requests join the batch, is that still recommended?
[03:45] Maya Patel: recommend increasing batch window from 8ms to 12ms for this workload and lower the queue depth cap to avoid large tail latencies — basically a throughput smoothing play: more consistent medium batches rather than big swings
[04:12] Priya Rao: ok, we can try window=12ms; curious about queue depth cap, what numbers should we set for our cluster of 4 GPUs?
[04:30] Liam O'Connor: empirically for 4 gpus we set queue depth per-gpu to 48 to limit in-flight requests that cause KV eviction; also set soft concurrency target 10 and hard cap 14 — that gave us 920 rps with p95 ~230ms in the lab
[05:02] Diego Alvarez: can you clarify soft vs hard caps? our infra team wants predictable memory usage
[05:18] Liam O'Connor: soft concurrency is the target the scheduler tries to maintain — it can float a bit for batching optimization; hard cap is absolute maximum concurrency to protect memory/KV state. So set soft=10, hard=14 for now
[05:36] Samantha Cho: procurement question — if we move to Dedicated, is burst capacity automatic or do we need a commit? also curious how pricing will change if we run longer soak tests
[05:55] Maya Patel: Dedicated has reserved pools and optional burst credits; we'll send the pricing tiers. For soaking tests we can grant extended test credits under the pilot clause — i'll follow up with exact limits
[06:20] Jared Mills: back to metrics — liam mentioned p99 was still a bit high, what's causing the p99 tails?
[06:35] Liam O'Connor: p99 usually correlates with two things here — cold KV misses and large single-request sequences that exceed token-length assumptions; we saw a handful of long-context requests in the trace which pushed CPU and then the queue stack
[06:58] Priya Rao: can we surface token-level timings? our APM doesn't break that down
[07:12] Maya Patel: yes, redwood can emit token-timing traces and per-request kv hit flags; we'll attach sample traces. they are a bit noisy but will show if the tail is KV/skew or model compute
[07:35] Jared Mills: perfect. also we saw downstream retries from our side that compounded the queueing — Diego noted a retry storm when p95 slipped
[07:54] Diego Alvarez: yeah that was our client-side retry backoff being too aggressive, we have default 200ms retry which is too low for these loads — we'll increase jitter and backoff
[08:12] Maya Patel: good call, reduce retries and add jitter; in parallel we'll add a server-side short-circuit fallback to a smaller model for sub-100 token completions to protect tail
[08:40] Priya Rao: smaller model fallback is interesting, how seamless is it? do we lose embeddings or certain structured outputs?
[08:57] Liam O'Connor: fallback can be configured as a route with compatible output schema, for short completions quality difference is small; we'll annotate responses with model source so you can audit
[09:13] Samantha Cho: also need to confirm logs and audit for compliance — SOC2 is a must for our procurement — do you have SOC2 docs?
09:25] Maya Patel: yes we have SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 summaries, i'll drop the security packet after this call
[09:42] Jared Mills: thanks. switching to tuning results, priya do you want to walk through the three intervals?
[09:52] Priya Rao: sure, interval one steady at 650 rps, p95 180ms, p99 420ms. interval two we pushed burst pattern for 5 minutes and saw batching increase avg batch size to 18 but with p99 spikes ~900ms. interval three we applied queue cap and soft concurrency 10 and got 820 rps, p95 220ms, p99 560ms
[10:38] Liam O'Connor: those numbers line up with what we expect — burst increased batch sizes but also introduced KV churn; the queue cap smoothed the tail at cost of a small drop in throughput
[10:56] Diego Alvarez: for planning purposes, can you give us a cost estimate per 1M tokens at these settings vs the smaller fallback? procurement needs ballpark
[11:12] Maya Patel: yes we'll include cost per token table in the follow-up; ballpark, using quantized 4-bit runtime and batching improvements, the variable inference compute cost decreased ~18% vs naive single-request serving
[11:33] Jared Mills: on instrumentation, can you send a sample of the trace format so our observability team can ingest it into our datadog? we prefer JSON lines
[11:50] Liam O'Connor: we'll send a sample that includes per-token timing, kv_hit boolean, batch_size, concurrency snapshot and route id
[12:05] Priya Rao: when you say route id, is that per-model or per-customer route? we have multiple product routes
[12:16] Liam O'Connor: per-route (your route config) which maps to model variant + decoding settings, so you can separate econ routes from high-quality routes
[12:33] Maya Patel: quick question on canary rollout: you wanted to run canary on dev 20% then prod 5% is that right?
[12:44] Jared Mills: yes dev 20% first to validate no regressions in throughput, then prod ramp 5% steps
[12:53] Noah Ruiz: i'll coordinate the canary schedule and invite the SRE folks, also capture rollback triggers
[13:07] Diego Alvarez: what are rollback triggers? high p99, error rate thresholds? we need clarity
[13:18] Noah Ruiz: standard triggers: error rate > 0.5% sustained 5 minutes, p99 increase > 2x baseline, or KV miss rate > 30% for 5 minutes
[13:35] Priya Rao: good. can we get a sample helm values or docker env vars to copy? we want to replicate the pilot config
[13:48] Liam O'Connor: yes sample helm + values will be in the repo, includes queueDepth, softConcurrency, hardConcurrency, batchWindowMs, fallbackRoute
[14:05] Jared Mills: when you run the 3-hour steady-state, what telemetry should we collect? full traces or sampling?
14:16] Liam O'Connor: capture full per-request traces for 1% sampling and aggregated histograms for all requests (p50/p90/p95/p99), plus kv hit-rate by prefix bucket
[14:32] Priya Rao: we can do that but our storage budget is limited — what's the typical footprint for the full traces at 1%?
[14:45] Maya Patel: depends on token length, but ballpark a few GB per hour for a 1k rps workload at 1% sampling; we'll provide guidance on retention and compressed export
[15:03] Jared Mills: ok, action items recap? priya will run the soak, maya send configs and pricing, liam send helm template and sample traces
[15:15] Maya Patel: yep, and we'll schedule the next sync after the soak results, target wednesday 2027-01-06, same time
[15:31] Samantha Cho: from procurement i'll review the pricing tiers, and i'll need a vendor security packet and contract template
[15:43] Maya Patel: noted, we'll include that packet
[15:50] Jared Mills: last thing, we briefly chatted about alternatives earlier — did anyone mention Anthropic or bedrock, we want a quick comparison on latency + price
[16:05] Maya Patel: we'll include a short note with the tradeoffs; in our internal bench Anthropic had slightly higher latency on this workload, bedrock has regional advantages but higher per-token list price — we can provide a 2-slide comparison
[16:24] Noah Ruiz: ok thanks all, i'll circulate meeting notes and jira tickets
[16:33] Maya Patel: thank you everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts, see you on the 6th
[16:40] Jared Mills: thanks

[Action items listed above]

[End of transcript]

Interop harness handshake and SLO synthesis

POC scoping focused on integrating Arcadia's customer scripts with Redwood's benchmark harness. Discussed streaming fallbacks, warmup and KV/prefix caching expectations, success criteria for throughput and p99 tail, and an initial timeline for a 2-week benchmark window. Action items include sharing adapter template, running a baseline non-streaming pass, and scheduling a live streaming acceptance run.
Maya: Share adapter template + sample config and env var list (due 2026-11-13)
Priya: Convert 2 canonical customer scripts to harness adapter; upload to Arcadia S3 share (due 2026-11-18)
Tom: Provide recent production traffic slice and 95/99 token length distribution (due 2026-11-15)
Samir: Draft live-stream acceptance test plan and failure-mode doc (due 2026-11-16)
Maya to share harness adapter template and README (by 2026-11-13)
Priya to onboard two representative customer scripts to the adapter and return logs (by 2026-11-18)
Schedule baseline non-streaming benchmark with 48-hour window (target week of 2026-11-22)
Book 1-hour live streaming acceptance run with Redwood SE present (tentative 2026-12-01)
Samir to provide fallback policy examples and canary rollout checklist (by 2026-11-16)
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-11
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Iris Gomez (Redwood CSM); Jordan Lee (Arcadia CTO), Priya Nair (Lead ML Eng), Tom Ruiz (SRE)

Auto-summary: Quick scoping for benchmark harness integration. Focus on making Arcadia's scripts run in Redwood's harness, defining success: throughput buckets, p99 tail, failure tolerances, streaming fallback behavior, warmup/kvcache expectations, and a realistic timeline for a two-week acceptance window.

--- Transcript (timestamps approximate) ---
[00:00] Maya (AE): Alright everyone thanks for joining, quick intro then we'll get into the stic— the script handoff and SLOs. Jordan, Priya, Tom, can you confirm audio?
[00:12] Jordan (CTO): Yep, loud and clear. Thanks, Maya.
[00:16] Samir (SE): Cool, I'll jump into the adapter details later, but first can you tell us what you mean by "customer script" in your workflow? Full end-to-end? pre- and post-processing?
[00:25] Priya (Lead ML Eng): Yeah it's the whole shebang — prompt building, a retry wrapper, some local caching for session state, and we do token-level post-filtering for PII. Mostly python.
[00:36] Maya: Perfect, that maps well. Our harness accepts a small adapter shim, we call it the harness-adapter, that wraps your script and handles streaming vs chunked cases. We'll send the template.
[00:48] Tom (SRE): Quick Q — does the harness expect requests to be idempotent? We have some side-effecting calls in our pre-hook.
[00:55] Samir: Good question. Ideally the adapter should isolate side-effects; for load runs we recommend a dry-run mode or mocking those external calls. The harness can also emit per-request metadata so you can correlate, but side-effects during a synthetic run will skew results.
[01:12] Jordan: Makes sense. On success criteria — we want <= 150ms median, p95 under 400ms, p99 under 900ms for 90% of the traffic slice. Is that realistic?
[01:26] Samir: It's tight depending on model size and streaming. For a 13B model with quantization and prefix cache warmed, median 150ms is plausible, but tail will depend on cold starts and concurrency. We should define the traffic slice.
[01:40] Priya: We'll provide a 10% representative slice — shorter prompts, interactive chat patterns. Also we'll include a longer 2–3% tail with 1k+ token sequences for stress.
[01:52] Maya: Good. We'll capture token length distribution and report SLO windows. Also want to call out K V cache behavior — our prefix cache drastically reduces repeated prefix cost, but the harness needs to populate warmup keys.
[02:07] Tom: How do you handle KV warmup on streaming? We sometimes see big spikes at warmup windows.
[02:14] Samir: For streaming, warmup is trickier. We have two modes: continuous warmup where we replay representative traces so the KV gets populated, or staged warmup where the first N requests in a window are treated specially. For acceptance you can run a warmup ramp for 10–20 minutes before measuring.
[02:33] Priya: That ramp time — do you account for it in the report? We need raw numbers excluding warmup as well as system-stable numbers.
[02:41] Maya: Yes, baseline and stable windows. Baseline for raw cold-starts; stable for steady-state SLOs.
[02:48] Jordan: We're concerned about streaming fallbacks — if streaming stalls do you switch to non-streaming automatically? We can't accept large partial responses.
[02:56] Samir: We support fallback policies: automatic fallback from stream to chunked non-streaming, or an immediate error depending on your policy. We can set thresholds like 'if client ack latency > X then fallback'. We'll share example policies.
[03:12] Tom: Any differences in harness metrics for streaming? We need per-chunk latencies and end-to-end deliver times.
[03:20] Samir: Yup, harness emits per-chunk timing, first-byte/last-byte, plus callback ACKs. It's a lot of telemetry; we can push to your S3 or cloud storage.
[03:30] Priya: About determinism — our scoring pipeline needs consistent outputs during regression checks. Does the harness pin RNG seeds or quantization jitters?
[03:38] Samir: We can pin seeds and use deterministic kernels for the test runs. Quantization introduces small differences but we log similarity metrics and embed a delta threshold.
[03:47] Maya: Let's talk timeline: we propose a 2-week window. Week 0: adapter onboarding + smoke; Week 1: baseline non-streaming runs + analysis; Week 2: streaming acceptance and fallbacks. Does that fit your release calendar?
[04:02] Jordan: That aligns, though we might need an extra day for internal sign-off.
[04:07] Maya: Fine. We'll pad a couple days.
[04:10] (--- quick micro break, 03:50 mins in ---)
[04:15] Priya: On harness infra, do we need to provide keys or tokens? We prefer not to put prod data in the run.
[04:22] Iris (CSM): We recommend obfuscated or synthetic data. For any secrets we support short-lived tokens and you can run in a VPC/hybrid.
[04:31] Tom: VPC — can the harness talk back to our private endpoints?
[04:35] Samir: For Private customers yes. For hosted benchmarks we proxy via a secure tunnel or you can bring a private instance. We'll note options in the adapter README.
[04:47] Jordan: Competitor note — we trialed ModelServeX last year; their streaming chops were okay but they fell over on long token sequences. Hoping this is better.
[04:58] Maya: We'll make sure to include long-tail stress tests.
[05:03] Priya: For the scripts themselves, we have a retry wrapper that does exponential backoff. How will that interact with harness concurrency?
[05:12] Samir: Retries need to be controlled at the adapter layer, otherwise you double-count requests. The adapter should surface a retry policy that the harness can respect. We'll add a sample.
[05:22] Tom: Anything special about batch vs streaming with your runtime? Our traffic is a mixture.
[05:27] Samir: Streaming favors low-latency interactive flows; batch is efficient for throughput and cold-batch inference. The harness supports mixed-mode runs, you can tag traffic and we'll run a blended profile. Important to report per-mode unit economics.
[05:43] Jordan: On metrics we need cost-per-1k-tokens estimates too, during the benchmark.
[05:48] Maya: We'll include cost proxies and a token accounting CSV.
[05:52] Priya: Can we run an initial non-streaming baseline at lower QPS to validate correctness before load spike?
[05:59] Samir: Absolutely — smoke tests at 1-2 qps, then ramp. We'll provide ramp templates.
[06:06] (--- timestamps skip forward, mid-session notes, some cross-talk) ---
[25:10] Samir: ...so sample adapter code — you'll see an ENV var to toggle streaming true/false, and a handler that yields chunks. We recommend architecting the script so chunk emission is a single generator.
[25:25] Priya: That will be fine. We'll need to refactor one of our legacy handlers which currently writes to disk mid-request.
[25:33] Tom: Disk writes — not great during high-concurrency. We'll mock those out.
[25:40] Maya: For SLO synthesis, can we agree on acceptance gates? I propose: 1) Baseline correctness pass (100% success on 200 sample requests), 2) Stable window SLOs: median/p95/p99 thresholds, 3) No more than 0.5% request failures due to harness errors, 4) Streaming fallback success for any degraded stream under policy.
[25:58] Jordan: Agree with those gates, though 0.5% might be tight — maybe 1% tolerated?
[26:06] Priya: Can we define what counts as a harness error vs model error? We need clarity for RCA.
[26:13] Samir: We'll tag errors. Harness errors are transport/adapter/runtime errors. Model errors are generation anomalies. We'll attach logs and correlation IDs for RCA.
[26:25] Tom: We'll need the raw traces for 100 failing requests for analysis.
[26:29] Maya: Noted.
[26:33] (--- later: deep-dive on telemetry schema ---)
[39:20] Samir: Telemetry payload includes request_id, start_ts, first_byte_ts, last_byte_ts, model_variant, quantization_flag, kv_hit_ratio, chunks_emitted, client_ack_latency. We'll provide schema and a sample parquet.
[39:36] Priya: kv_hit_ratio — how is that computed?
[39:39] Samir: It's the fraction of predicted prefix keys that were served from cache vs recomputed. Rough proxy but helpful.
[39:49] Jordan: For the long-tail test, what's the recommended load shape? We want sustained 200 qps with 5% spikes to 1k for 30s.
[39:58] Samir: We can model that. We'll also run staircase ramps and a randomized burst run.
[40:05] Tom: How do you capture cold starts for those spikes? We need to ensure cold v warm buckets are separated.
[40:11] Maya: The harness will label warmup windows; we'll exclude warmup when reporting steady state but include cold-start stats in a separate table.
[40:20] Priya: Any concerns with our post-filtering step (PII removal) adding variable latency?
[40:26] Samir: Post-filtering running in the adapter will add variance. Best to run a stripped-down version for perf tests, and a functional run for correctness. We'll keep both.
[40:36] (--- planning the actual handoff ---)
[50:05] Maya: Action checklist: we'll upload adapter template to the shared drive, Samir will upload the telemetry schema and ramp templates, Priya will produce two converted scripts, Tom will push traffic slice. We'll reconvene after scripts uploaded.
[50:19] Priya: One ask — can we redact session ids in logs before you ingest?
[50:24] Iris: Yes, we can accept redacted logs; if you want full logs we recommend a private tunnel.
[50:31] Jordan: Last Q: If streaming fails and fallback to chunked happens, how do you preserve ordering and session affinity?
[50:40] Samir: The adapter maintains session ids and sequence numbers; fallback is seamless from a session perspective if you choose the 'adhesive fallback' policy. We'll include that in the README.
[50:53] Maya: Great. Any blockers on timeline?
[50:56] Jordan: None now. We'll aim to have scripts by 11/18.
[51:02] Maya: Perfect. We'll send the deck and templates within 24 hours.
[51:06] (meeting close, quick recap)
[61:30] Maya: Recap: share adapter template, telemetry schema, ramp templates; customer to upload scripts and traffic slice; plan baseline week then streaming acceptance. Thanks all.
[61:45] Jordan: Thanks team.
[61:50] Priya: Thanks.

--- End transcript ---

document.content:
Fairband routing & key-mapping walkthrough - Sable Systems

Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes (recording stopped at 15:52)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Tom Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Sable Head of Platform), Jared Miles (SRE), Lena Ortiz (Security), Ben Hsu (Engineer)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
- Demo focused on routing: org vs project keys, fairband/burst lanes, sticky routing, and quota carve-outs.
- Customer constraints: multi-tenant marketplace with bursty traffic, strict audit logs, and residency controls.
- Action: pilot to validate latency and cost tradeoffs using two project keys and Dedicated burst lanes; share pricing and compliance docs.

Topics: routing policies, org/project keys, quotas, Dedicated vs Hosted, Optimize suggestions, security & compliance

[00:00] Maya: yeah good afternoon everyone thanks for joining, um I'm Maya with Redwood, I'll kick things off and Tom who's here is our SE so we'll do a quick walkthrough of how we recommend mapping org and project keys for multi-tenant workloads.
[00:12] Priya: hey Maya, thanks. We have about 45 minutes for the demo and then 10 for logistics? That's the plan.
[00:17] Maya: yep perfect. Quick intro round? Tom, you want to go?
[00:20] Tom: yeah hey folks Tom Alvarez, I'm the solutions engineer working on routing and performance at Redwood. I'll jump into the console demo and then run through a sample live config.
[00:29] Jared: Jared here, SRE, mostly concerned about tail-latency and how we handle spikes from our marketplace sellers.
[00:34] Lena: Lena from security team, quick flag we need SOC2 evidence, KMS integration details, and SSO/SAML flow.
[00:40] Ben: Ben, eng - focus is cost and how to shape traffic into predictable lanes.

[02:05] Tom: okay quick context: Sable is a multi-tenant marketplace, right? You said heavy bursts when product launches, and some tenants are very latency-sensitive.
[02:14] Priya: exactly. Some enterprise sellers have SLA requirements, others are fine with slightly higher cost to reduce latency. We want to avoid noisy neighbors blowing our monthly spend.
[02:26] Tom: perfect. So our pattern today is org-level key + per-project keys. We typically advise keeping an org-level master key for admin automations and then per-tenant or per-product project keys for traffic shaping. That lets you apply quotas and routing at different levels.
[02:45] Maya: I'll show a high-level diagram first - sorry screen share - pulling up the Console.

[03:05] [Tom screen share begins - Console visible]
[03:12] Tom: top left is the org overview. You can see active projects, aggregated token usage, and latency percentiles. On the right we have routing policies - these are where fairband and burst lanes live.
[03:25] Ben: is fairband like a token bucket?
[03:28] Tom: it's similar conceptually - we call it fairband because it slices capacity across tenants and then we allow controlled bursts using dedicated lanes. The implementation is leaky-bucket-ish with priority lanes for high SLA keys.
[03:40] Priya: how do we do sticky routing? We need the same tenant to always hit their pinned model variant during a rollout.
[03:47] Tom: good Q - we have sticky routing rules tied to project keys. You can pin model variants at project-key level and add sticky TTLs. So if you pin a canary for tenant A, all requests with that project key will hit the canary until TTL expires or you toggle.
[04:03] Maya: also worth calling out fallback policies - if a dedicated lane is saturated we can route down to a hosted compatible model or lower-cost quantized variant automatically.

[04:15] Jared: what's the observable impact? Will our p95 jump when fallback happens?
[04:20] Tom: depends on model variant and sequence length. We show per-route latencies in the Console, and our traces tag whether request used fallback. In practice we see small variance but one thing Optimize provides is recommendations - if a fallback is causing regressions, we suggest changing batch/quant profiles.

[05:05] [05:05 - 07:20 rapid config demo, timestamps every ~30s]
[05:05] Tom: creating a new routing policy: call it "marketplace-priority". Source is project key X, priority = 80, fairband slice = 15% of org baseline, burst lane = enabled with 500 TPS burst cap.
[05:25] Ben: wait 500 TPS per tenant? That's per project key right?
[05:30] Tom: correct, it's per project key. You can also set org-wide caps that gate total org usage.
[05:36] Priya: can we set different affordability tiers - like low-cost for analytics, high-priority for shopper-facing?
[05:43] Tom: yes, create multiple project keys and reuse a routing policy tag. Analytics keys can be mapped to a "bulk" routing lane with more aggressive batching and a quantized model.

[07:50] Maya: quick aside on billing: tokens are billed by model variant and token direction. In the Console you can view token breakdowns per project key to attribute cost. That helps avoid noisy neighbors.

[08:30] Lena: about audit logs - we need immutable logs that show key usage and routing decisions. Is that out-of-the-box?
[08:38] Tom: yes we emit per-request audit logs with routing metadata, model variant used, latency, and tenant key. Logs can be archived to customer S3/Vault or integrated with your SIEM. Note: retention is configurable.
[08:52] Lena: KMS? Our policy says keys must be in our HSM.
[08:56] Maya: we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for data at rest and can integrate with your provider for encryption of stored artifacts. For in-flight encryption we use TLS - standard.

[09:30] [09:30 - 16:10 - deeper routing examples & mis-transcriptions]
[09:30] Tom: demo: I'll attach a second project key for a large seller, call it "enterprise-ACME" - this key will have a pinned model variant (redwood-2b-quant) and a higher priority lane.
[09:44] Ben: typo - ACME is used as a placeholder but we can swap with "Northridge" later.
[09:48] Tom: sure. Then I'll configure a carve-out quota: monthly cap 50M tokens but with a soft reserve guaranteeing 10% of org capacity. That means even during a heavy month they keep a minimum share.
[10:05] Priya: what's the enforcement? soft reserve vs hard cap?
[10:09] Tom: soft reserve uses prioritization to favor that key during contention; hard cap rejects requests with 429. You can also set adaptive backoff to return a hint so clients can retry later.
[10:21] Jared: do you support multi-region routing? We have EU-only data residency for some tenants.
[10:26] Tom: yes, routing policies can be scoped by region. You can pin a project key to EU nodes only; we honor data residency and will avoid routing cross-region.
[10:34] Maya: note: Private deployments give you VPC/on-prem control if needed for regulatory constraints.

[11:10] Priya: can we do rate-limits per user inside a project key? We have thousands of sellers under a single project key and want per-seller caps.
[11:18] Tom: you can issue sub-keys or use metadata-based sharding. We also have namespace-level enforcement - you can include seller-id in the header and configure per-namespace quotas. Caveat: if you want strict per-seller enforcement at scale, it's often easier to mint per-seller project keys automatically.

[12:05] [12:05 - 18:20 - Optimize suggestions and cost controls]
[12:05] Tom: switching to Optimize view - here we surface recommended quantization, batch sizes, and cache policies by workload. For example, for short prompt patterns we recommend prefix KV caching which reduced token spend 18% in a similar workload.
[12:25] Ben: prefix cache meaning cached KV cache?
[12:28] Tom: yes, prefix/KV caching - sometimes transcribed as KV cash in old notes - it keeps earlier activations to avoid recomputing. For many chat-like patterns it helps a lot.
[12:36] Priya: do we have automated suggestions for batch vs latency tradeoffs?
[12:40] Tom: Optimize provides a slider and simulated cost/latency curves. We can generate a few candidate configs and you can test them in the pilot.

[13:30] Maya: quick pause - any compliance blockers?
[13:33] Lena: SAMEL - SAML integration for our SSO is critical, plus review of pen-test reports.
[13:40] Maya: we'll include SAML docs and SOC2/ISO pack in the follow-up.

[14:05] [14:05 - 22:00 - Pilot topology discussion]
[14:05] Tom: recommended pilot: two project keys representing two tenant profiles: 1) "latency-sensitive" pinned to Dedicated lane with reserved capacity and burst enabled; 2) "bulk-analytics" mapped to hosted lane with quantized model and high batching. Run 48 hours of production-like traffic (we can replay traces) to collect p50/p95/p99 and token unit spend.
[14:30] Priya: what about our current infra - we use K8s + Envoy in front, can we integrate easily?
[14:36] Tom: yes standard sidecar or Envoy route header injection works. We have SDKs and examples. For high-throughput you can use Redwood's batching proxy but Envoy header is common.

[15:12] Jared: for the pilot what metrics do you need from us?
[15:15] Tom: traffic traces (headers), expected seq length distribution, SLOs per tenant, and a representative token mix. We'll instrument latency histograms and token cost.

[16:00] [16:00 - 30:10 - Q&A, objections, and tradeoffs]
[16:00] Ben: I'm worried about cost spikes if a tenant goes viral. Do we have hard budget guardrails per-account?
[16:08] Tom: yes - hard caps at project or org level will reject beyond threshold. Plus you can set budget notifications and auto-fallback to lower-cost models when approaching spend ceilings.
[16:25] Priya: and if we use Dedicated, can we still have org-wide fairband?
[16:30] Maya: Dedicated provides reserved GPU pools but routing still happens in the control plane. You can carve out dedicated capacity for a set of project keys and let others use shared hosted nodes.

[17:05] Lena: one more: auditability of routing decisions. We need per-request proof for auditors.
[17:12] Tom: we can export signed routing events with trace IDs and include them in audit bundles. We support long-term S3 retention and can provide indexing to help compliance teams search.

[18:00] [18:00 - 36:40 - live JSON config & small demo glitch]
[18:00] Tom: I'll paste an example policy JSON - bear with me. (Tom copies/pastes, small lag)
[18:05] Tom: "policy": {"match": {"project_key": "enterprise-ACME"}, "route": {"lane": "dedicated-priority", "reserve_pct": 10, "burst_cap": 500}}
[18:20] Ben: weird, the Console shows an extra zero on the burst cap in our view, maybe a typo?
[18:24] Tom: ah yes that was me entering 5000 accidentally, fixing to 500. Sorry about that.
[18:30] Maya: good catch. Live demos are humble.

[19:10] [19:10 - 26:00 - pilot logistics and data residency details]
[19:10] Priya: for EU-only tenants we will need to pin keys to eu-west nodes. Cost likely different?
[19:18] Tom: yes regional cost differs by region and model variant; Console shows region breakdowns. We'll include region pricing in the follow-up sheet.

[20:05] Jared: how do you reconcile client-side retries when a request is 429 vs fallback? We don't want clients hammering.
[20:12] Tom: we return standard rate-limit headers and an optional retry-after; we also provide adaptive backoff suggestions via the SDK so clients implement exponential jitter correctly.

[21:30] [26:00 - 34:00 - security deep-dive by Lena]
[26:00] Lena: can you run through the SSO flow quickly? We need to see SAML assertions and how RBAC maps to project keys.
[26:08] Tom: yes, in Console you map groups to project-key roles. SAML assertions are parsed and we map group attributes to RBAC. We also support SCIM provisioning to auto-provision users.
[26:34] Lena: about logs - are they tamper-evident?
[26:38] Tom: we provide signed audit logs and can enable an append-only storage backend; customers can ship logs to their own bucket for additional guarantees.

[28:15] Maya: sounds like we're aligned on the pilot. Quick recap of recommended pilot config: two project keys, Dedicated lane for latency-sensitive tenant with pinned model + reserve; Hosted lane for bulk analytics with quantized model + aggressive batching; 48 hour replay, metrics: p50/p95/p99, token cost, fallback rate.

[29:00] Priya: that works. Any blockers from you, Lena?
[29:05] Lena: no blockers; need compliance pack and proof of KMS integration.

[29:20] Maya: we'll attach docs in the follow-up and include a sample policy JSON, pricing sheet, and pilot runbook.

[30:00] [30:00 - 38:00 - closing discussion and scheduling]
[30:00] Tom: plan for next week: I'll share pilot config and we can schedule the infra pairing.
[30:10] Priya: we have a window starting Feb 1 to run the pilot - engineering availability then.
[30:18] Maya: great, I'll schedule a kickoff.

[31:05] Ben: small nit - what about eviction policy for caches under memory pressure?
[31:12] Tom: we expose cache eviction stats and implement LRU by default; Optimize suggests cache sizes based on your traffic.

[32:20] Jared: will you include runbook steps for fallback analysis? We want to run an incident like scenario to see behavior.
[32:26] Tom: yep - included in the pilot runbook.

[33:00] [33:00 - 40:50 - pricing & contract wrinkles]
[33:00] Maya: quick pricing note - Hosted billed per token; Dedicated includes reserved capacity fee plus usage. For billing we can set org-level billing alerts.
[33:18] Priya: for Dedicated do we commit monthly or yearly? And what about burst units?
[33:25] Maya: Dedicated is monthly or annual commit; burst is metered and billed separately but can be capped. We'll provide exact numbers in the spreadsheet.

[34:50] Lena: legal will want to see the SLA and data processing addendum.
[34:54] Maya: yes we'll share SLA + DPA.

[35:30] [40:50 - 51:30 - final recap and explicit next steps]
[40:50] Maya: final recap: Pilot config, pricing sheet, compliance pack. Tom will run the pilot config and share benchmark plan. Priya to confirm start date. Lena to collect compliance questions.
[41:05] Priya: all good, we'll aim to finalize ASAP.
[41:10] Maya: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with notes and links.
[41:14] Jared: thanks.
[41:16] Ben: thank you.
[41:18] Lena: thanks.

Notes on transcription artifacts: occasional acronyms mis-heard (SAMEL for SAML), KV cache sometimes "KV cash", minor speaker overlap.

End of transcript.

KMS Rotation & Fallback Handoff - Postmortem Review

Quick postmortem of the Dec 29 KMS rotation-induced fallback where Verdant Labs experienced 30s spikes and partial decryption failures for private deployments. We reviewed root cause (staggered rotation + vault client TTL mismatch), agreed short-term mitigations (controlled rollback, increased circuit-breaker tolerance, audit log bundle), and mapped long-term hardening (HSM-backed rotation tests, canary rotations, improved observability). Explicit handoff of docs and runbooks to Verdant Ops and scheduling of a joint dry-run in staging.
Jordan to send KMS rotation runbook + rotated key audit export by 2026-01-06
Priya to schedule a 2hr dry-run session in Verdant staging w/ Marcus and Ravi by 2026-01-13
Verdant to provide a sanitized sample of failure traces and request IDs by 2026-01-07
Set up shared Slack channel for incident-playback: #rdw-verdant-ops (Jordan)
Jordan Hayes|Send KMS rotation runbook + audit export|2026-01-06
Priya Nair|Prepare dry-run checklist and test scripts for canary rotation|2026-01-12
Ben Chu|Share sanitized failure traces & request IDs|2026-01-07
Ravi Kapoor|Provision staging HSM test credentials (ephemeral)|2026-01-10
Marcus Lee|Coordinate observation run & post-run retro notes|2026-01-14
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-04
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46m
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Redwood CSM); Elena Morales (CISO, Verdant), Ben Chu (SRE), Ravi Kapoor (Platform Lead), Sana Iqbal (Ops)

-- Auto summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete) --
Verdant saw decryption/device failures during key rotation on Dec 29; fallback triggered to hosted key proxy which caused token latencies and partial errors. Discussed TTL mismatch between Vault client and rotate window, and a subsequent slow fallthrough to the Redwood fallback path.

[00:00] Jordan Hayes: hey everyone thanks for joining, we know folks are busy, we'll try to be tight. this is the postmortem + handoff on the kms rotation blip on december twenty ninth, is that right elena?
[00:08] Elena Morales: yes, thanks. we want the exact timeline, and, like, confirmation that the fallback won't leak any pii, and we need the audit evidence for compliance.
[00:18] Priya Nair: quick intro — priya, se on the infra team. i'll walk through observed traces and mitigation steps. Marcus is on for handoff notes.
[00:25] Ben Chu: real quick, we had a cascade — some requests saw 20 to 40 second tails, a subset failed crypto ops, and then clients retried, which amplified load.
[00:34] Ravi Kapoor: and to be clear, this was on our private deployment in eu-west-1 with customer-managed vault, right? not hosted?
[00:40] Jordan Hayes: correct, private deployment with Verdant-managed vault + our new fallback proxy. the fallback took longer than expected because of a TTL mismatch.

[00:55] Priya Nair: slide note, i'm paraphrasing logs — at 02:17 UTC the rotation job started, vault rotated keys but the vault-client had a 5m TTL and didnt refresh until 04:17 UTC, so the client attempted to use the old key for a period. some decrypt calls failed and triggered our fallback which tried to re-encrypt to proxy. that proxy endpoint had a brief capacity spike, leading to tokenization latencies.
[01:23] Elena Morales: so the mismatch was our TTL config plus rotation window — we didn't realize the client won't auto refresh mid-rotation?
[01:30] Priya Nair: yeah, it's a subtle interaction. the rotate job rotates and rotates metadata, but the client only checks at TTL expiry. Vault has multiple modes, and i think the client lib we shipped was using aggressive caching.
[01:43] Ben Chu: and for the record, some of the error messages in the logs were ambiguous — the stack said "decrypt failed" but it wasn't obvious it was key mismatch vs corrupted blob.

[02:01] Jordan Hayes: there's also an operational step: our fallback path re-encrypts with a hosted key which has different tokenization semantics. we should confirm no pii was exposed and that all writes were logged.
[02:12] Elena Morales: that's critical — SOC2 auditors will ask. we need a signed bundle of rotated keys audit and a list of request IDs that hit fallback.

[02:25] Priya Nair: actionably, we recommend: 1) short-term: revert the rotation for the smaller set while we patch the client TTL behavior, 2) widen CB (circuit-breaker) thresholds for the proxy, 3) export audit logs — which jordan will send, and 4) schedule a canary/dry-run in staging with HSM emulation.

[02:45] Ravi Kapoor: our question — why did the fallback hit the hosted proxy rather than a local cached key? we expected local in-memory cache to handle it.
[02:52] Priya Nair: the in-memory KV cache had evicted entries because of GC pressure — we saw memory churn around the same time due to another job. eviction+TTL mismatch equals no valid key locally.
[03:05] Sana Iqbal: uhh, can we confirm the eviction was due to our JVM flags? we bumped heap and saw spikes.
[03:12] Ben Chu: yeah, we changed -XX:MaxMetaspace and there was a permgen like effect, but the traces point to an OOM-ish GC pause.

[03:30] Jordan Hayes: ok realistic plan: immediate rollback of rotation for impacted keyset (we did this manually in the incident), but next steps are to instrument a canary rotation that uses a staged refresh step so clients refresh pre-rotation. that's priya's checklist.
[03:50] Priya Nair: i'll add automated client refresh in the client lib and publish a patch; we'll also provide a compat shim with toggles for rotation-window.
[04:02] Elena Morales: timeline expectation — auditors want documentation by next week. we need proof that the rollback didn't lose anything and the fallback didn't exfiltrate data.
[04:12] Marcus Lee: i'll assemble a compliance packet: signed audit export + list of fallback request ids + a short explainer. i'll hand it off to elena after jordan sends the raw exports.

[04:30] Ben Chu: and on capacity — the proxy had limited burst, which we should have foreseen. can we limit client retries to avoid thundering herd to the proxy?
[04:40] Priya Nair: yes, add jittered exponential backoff and a retry cap. also adaptive throttling on the proxy to shed non-critical traffic during rotations.

[05:01] Ravi Kapoor: longer term, we want HSM-backed rotations in staging, and to test rotation under load with the same heap settings as prod. can Redwood help provision ephemeral HSMs?
[05:10] Jordan Hayes: we can emulate HSM or do partner HSM in our dedicated infra. we'll propose both: emulation for quick tests, partner HSM for cert-level testing.

[05:25] Elena Morales: also, can you confirm RBAC for the fallback proxy logs? auditors will check who accessed keys.
[05:33] Priya Nair: yes, proxy logs contain actor identity (service principal). we'll include access control export and correlation ids.

[06:00] [interrupt] Sana Iqbal: quick nit — the client library name in logs was "redwood-priv" but in code it's redwood-private? little mismatch in naming in our internal docs so grep missed some traces.
[06:12] Priya Nair: ugh, sorry about that. that's on us — i'll normalize names in the runbook.

[06:28] Jordan Hayes: ok let's roleplay the postmortem timeline for the auditors — who did what and when. ben, can you recap?
[06:33] Ben Chu: at 02:17 rotate job starts, by 02:22 ~0.4% decrypts failing, 02:25 proxy accepts reroutes and starts spiking, 02:27 retries escalate load, by 02:40 ops notices elevated 5xxs, 02:50 rollback initiated and by 03:05 most traffic returned to normal. full recovery ~03:15.
[07:00] Elena Morales: that matches our internal timeline. we want the signed bundles and the runbook updates, and a plan for the canary.

[07:20] Jordan Hayes: agreed. next steps recap: jordan sends audit export + raw traces; priya publishes client lib patch and dry-run checklist; priya & rj (ravi) schedule the dry-run; marcus prepares compliance packet.

[07:43] Priya Nair: minor tech detail — we'll add a short-circuit in the client so if key-refresh fails it won't immediately go to proxy but will return a soft-failure that the caller can surface to the user gracefully. reduces proxy load.
[08:00] Ravi Kapoor: sounds good. one ask: can we have the dry-run simulate GC churn? we want to validate that eviction path is exercised.
[08:10] Priya Nair: yes we'll provide a stress script to create ephemeral GC pressure and observe behavior.

[08:24] Jordan Hayes: timeline for dry-run: target week of Jan 11-15. priya to pick exact date and share invite.
[08:32] Elena Morales: and auditors — we need the evidence by Jan 13 ideally.

[08:40] Ben Chu: i also want retros on instrumentation — add a specific metric for client key age and a histogram for time-since-last-refresh. that would've flagged this earlier.
[08:51] Priya Nair: noted, will add metrics and an alert threshold.

[09:05] [15 minute mark jump — summary handoff section]
[15:00] Marcus Lee: compliance packet items listed — signed key rotation audit (csv + GPG hash), fallback request id list, summary timeline, and mitigation plan. i'll assemble and run through internal QA before handing to elena.
[15:15] Elena Morales: thanks. on the packet, we might redact some PII before sending externally. we'll coordinate with Marcus.

[20:30] Jordan Hayes: bring up runbook handoff doc: https://redwood.example.com/docs/kms-rotation-runbook (note: link auto-captured, may require org access).
[20:40] Sana Iqbal: okay quick question — is the patch backward compatible with older client versions? we still have a small fleet on 1.2.
[20:47] Priya Nair: we'll publish the patch as opt-in toggle; full auto roll requires 1.3+. for older clients we'll ship a shim and a remediation guide.

[22:10] Ben Chu: any competitor notes — we looked at BigCompute's proxy approach but they require their hosted key, so not acceptable for us. good to know alternatives exist.

[23:05] Jordan Hayes: packaging notes: i'll send the raw exports to Marcus via the secure transfer and Marcus will produce the compliance bundle.

[24:00] [wrap-up]
[24:05] Jordan Hayes: final recap: immediate items sent by jan 6; dry-run scheduled by jan 13; patch in staging by jan 12; compliance bundle by jan 8. owners on action items in the chat follow.
[24:20] Elena Morales: thanks everyone, appreciate the clarity. this was helpful.
[24:30] Jordan Hayes: thanks all. we'll follow up with calendar invites and attachments.

-- End transcript --

Week 4 - Throughput & Latency Pivot with Polaris HealthSpan

Weekly POC sync to review week 4 benchmark results vs customer's incumbent provider, triage regressions at p95, discuss batching/kv caching and cost tradeoffs, agree next steps for 24h synthetic and security docs.
Throughput delta vs baseline
p95 / p50 latency tuning
Batching strategies and KV caching
Quantization impact and quality checks
Security readiness for private deployment
Alex Morgan: Share updated 24h synthetic test plan + traffic script (due: 2026-01-18)
Priya Shah: Run focused p95 profiling with KV caching off/on and share trace snippets (due: 2026-01-16)
Laura Chen: Provide sample request distribution and token histogram for production traffic (due: 2026-01-17)
Nadia Ortiz: Send list of compliance docs required for evaluation (due: 2026-01-20)
Redwood to run 24h synthetic load against Dedicated pool with customer's token distribution
Customer to provide long tail request logs and confirm success criteria for p95 <= 300ms
Schedule on-prem readiness workshop if 24h test meets throughput targets
AE to send updated pricing matrix including reserved capacity delta
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-01-14 14:30 PST
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan, Priya Shah, Tomás Rivera (Redwood) — Samir Patel, Laura Chen, Marcus Reed, Nadia Ortiz (Polaris)

Summary (auto): quick recap of last week, focus this week on p95 regressions and throughput peak behavior, a couple of anomalies in the evening run.

[00:00] Alex Morgan: alright everyone, thanks for joining, we got about 50 minutes today so we'll go through the week 4 numbers, dig into p95 anomalies and then triage a couple of tuning knobs.
[00:18] Samir Patel: yep thanks Alex, Laura and I will jump in — Marcus is on for infra stuff. we ran the smoke this morning too.
[00:27] Priya Shah: quick note, I'll share the dashboard link in the chat after the call — includes p50/p95 and per-shard throughput.
[00:35] Marcus Reed: perfect, we compared Redwood to our incumbent — um, the baseline provider had p95 ~410-450ms on our test, we saw Redwood at 220-260ms in the daytime but spiked to ~520ms overnight on one run.
[00:50] Tomás Rivera: okay that's helpful. do you remember whether the overnight run used the same batching profile? sometimes nightly retrains or log drains create skew.
[00:58] Marcus Reed: should have been same script but there was a higher fraction of long context requests. i.e., token distribution tail heavier.
[01:06] Alex Morgan: that aligns — our profiler flagged a KV cache miss storm during that window, KV 'cash' in the trace, so you likely saw more cold starts on the KV layer.
[01:15] Laura Chen: KV cash — yeah i saw some weird entry in the trace. is that the key value cache? could be miss rates.
[01:21] Priya Shah: yes it's KV cache — occasionally the client routing created micro-shards that lose local cache affinity, leads to more model cold steps and higher p95. we can simulate that easily.
[01:34] Samir Patel: baseline provider says their p95 is steady because they pin instances; cost is higher. we need to show both latency and cost delta at production traffic.
[01:44] Alex Morgan: totally — we put together a cost/perf slide that compares raw $/1M tokens, plus the reserved capacity monthly delta. Redwood's profile there was about 28% lower unit cost in our synthetic vs incumbent for similar QoS.
[01:57] Marcus Reed: can you remind us of the exact numbers? we need line items for infra team.
[02:03] Tomás Rivera: sure — rough numbers from the test: baseline provider 1M token cost $1,420; Redwood hosted path showed $1,020; dedicated reserved profile with autoscale came to about $1,150 once amortized. these are synthetic numbers and vary by batch size.
[02:18] Laura Chen: so dedicated still cheaper than baseline but a little higher than pure hosted, ok.
[02:24] Priya Shah: and throughput — on our peak 2h window Redwood sustained ~210 req/s with median tokens ~180, baseline was ~120 req/s under same hardware allocation. that gave Redwood higher overall throughput because of better batching + kernel selection for the model variant you picked.
[02:40] Samir Patel: that's promising. main worry is the p95 spike overnight. what are the hypotheses?
[02:46] Alex Morgan: one — KV cache misses due to shard affinity; two — larger context lengths hitting an unfavorable execution path causing extra kernel swaps; three — background maintenance tasks on your side (log ingestion) spiking I/O.
[02:58] Laura Chen: we did a large export at 01:12 UTC on that day — could have affected network I/O.
[03:03] Priya Shah: ok let's try to isolate. our plan: toggle KV caching off/on for a controlled run, run one with smaller max batch size to reduce latency tail, and run a run with pinned model variant (no fallback).
[03:15] Marcus Reed: what do you mean by pinned model variant?
[03:18] Tomás Rivera: we have lightweight fallback rules — sometimes if the preferred quantized variant is busy we fallback to a FP16 variant — that can change latency characteristics. pinning forces one path so we can measure.
[03:27] Samir Patel: got it. how much overhead to run those tests?
[03:30] Alex Morgan: low — we can spin controlled synthetic tests from our side using your token histogram; won't affect production. we'll need Laura's histogram.
[03:36] Laura Chen: i'll export and share it by EOD.
[03:39] Priya Shah: great. also one more note — we saw some tokenization differences between your preprocessing and ours; occasionally it increases effective token count by ~5-7% for clinical notes. that amplifies the p95.
[03:50] Nadia Ortiz: on the security front, we had a question about key management — if we go private, will KMS/HSM integration be supported?
[03:57] Tomás Rivera: yes we support KMS integrations and can run with customer-managed keys in the private plane. there was a small typo in the doc previously where we called it 'private plane' instead of 'private plane' — apologies, doc generation glitch. (laughs)
[04:12] Nadia Ortiz: ha, ok, just verifying that audit logs are going to the customer's SIEM and that retention options exist.
[04:18] Alex Morgan: yes audit logs + S3 export to your account is supported, and we can increase retention as part of the enterprise package. we'll attach the compliance matrix after this call.
[04:26] Samir Patel: great. i also want to drill into the p95 numbers you reported — what's the distribution? are we seeing a bi-modal tail?
[04:33] Priya Shah: looks like bi-modal-ish — a main cluster around 180-240ms and a smaller cluster 400-600ms. after we turn on KV caching simulation the smaller cluster shrinks.
[04:43] Marcus Reed: can you explain the caching impact briefly for the engineering team?
[04:47] Priya Shah: sure — continuous batching + KV caching stores prefix key-value states and avoids recomputation for repeated prefixes; if affinity is lost then you have to re-warm the cache which costs tokens and time, so p95 increases.
[04:59] Laura Chen: would a single-shard routing guarantee help?
[05:02] Alex Morgan: yes, pinned routing or setting affinity TTLs longer helps but increases memory footprint; it's a tradeoff. if you pin too long, you might not utilize GPU capacity well.
[05:11] Samir Patel: so what's the recommended starting config to hit p95 <= 300ms while keeping cost reasonable?
[05:16] Tomás Rivera: start with KV caching enabled, aff TTL at 10 minutes, batch max 16, prefer quantized variant with conservative fallback disabled for the test window. if p95 still >300ms, reduce batch max to 8 or increase affinity TTL.
[05:29] Marcus Reed: and what about quantization quality? we have clinical notes and can't afford hallucinations.
[05:34] Priya Shah: we used Q4_0 for the test and ran a quick eval on your 500-example prompt set — perplexity delta was small and we saw no hallucination uptick in sampled outputs. we'll share the eval artifacts.
[05:45] Laura Chen: please do share. those evals are critical for our clinical compliance team.
[05:50] Alex Morgan: action item — we'll push the eval summary and source prompts to the secure share.
[05:55] Samir Patel: excellent. another datapoint — cost sensitivity: if we go dedicated, network egress and reserved commit numbers will change our TCO. can you model a 6-month commit vs on-demand?
[06:06] Tomás Rivera: yes, we'll provide a 6- and 12-month commit model and include autoscale burst costs. that will be in the pricing sheet Alex will share.
[06:15] Marcus Reed: in terms of next steps for this week — what are the concrete runs we expect?
[06:19] Alex Morgan: Redwood runs: 1) 2 controlled runs with KV cache off/on, 2) pinned variant run, 3) reduced batch size run, all for 2 hours each and then a 24h synthetic with your token histogram. we'll start those Friday night PST to capture the overnight pattern.
[06:34] Laura Chen: Friday night works for us. we'll block a window and provide logs if anything spikes.
[06:38] Nadia Ortiz: for compliance, please include the network diagram for private deployments — we need to assess the traffic flows.
[06:43] Alex Morgan: noted, will attach network diagram and compliance matrix.
[06:47] Priya Shah: quick callout — we saw one rare error 'model mutex timeout' during the spike — logs included. we suspect lock contention when many long contexts force KV re-warms concurrently.
[06:57] Marcus Reed: okay, we can correlate with our job runs at that time.
[07:00] Samir Patel: anything else on benchmarks?
[07:02] Tomás Rivera: one more thing — we noticed the baseline provider used a slightly older CUDA stack that had a slower attention kernel on long contexts; small kernel changes drove a 10-15% difference in tail latency. our runtime picks best kernel based on sequence distribution which helps on those long tails.
[07:17] Laura Chen: interesting — might explain some of the observed differences.
[07:21] Alex Morgan: wrapping up — repeat next steps: Laura send token histogram and logs; Redwood runs the isolated experiments and the 24h synthetic; security docs and pricing to go out. we'll meet next Tuesday to review 24h results.
[07:36] Samir Patel: thanks team, appreciate the quick triage.
[07:39] Alex Morgan: thanks, we'll follow up with artifacts.

End of transcript.
