Lucida - Routes Visibility & Cost Playground Walkthrough

Redwood AE/SE walked Lucida through Console route-level visibility, usage analytics, and per-route cost breakdown. Discussed pilot with dedicated pool, required telemetry shape, SOC2/audit artifacts, and FinOps mapping. Customer interested in per-route SLOs, real-time cost alerts, and Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization. Agreed to run 2-week pilot benchmark; next meeting to align infra and pricing.
1) Intro & goals (Lucida pain: opaque route costs)
2) Console tour: per-route dashboards, usage heatmaps, attribution by tag
3) Cost breakdown: per-token, per-route, burst vs reserved usage
4) Optimize: batching suggestions, quantization profiles, cache hints
5) Pilot design and telemetry requirements
6) Security/compliance (SOC2, KMS, VPC)
7) Next steps and action items
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll keep this tight, want to show the route visibility and cost playground.
[00:22] Sofia Ramos: Thanks Maya. Quick context, we have about three routes in prod, but costs are spiking and it's hard to map to features.
[00:35] Ethan Cole: Yeah, that's very common. We'll go through the console and then talk pilot. Please interrupt if you want to see a specific metric.
[01:10] Derrick Huang: Quick q, are we mostly looking at hosted or considering dedicated right away? We're leaning dedicated because of data residency but open to hybrid.
[01:28] Maya Patel: Good call out. We'll show both flows — hosted for quick get-up, dedicated for predictability.
[01:55] Priya Menon: From FinOps side: we need per-route chargeback by team and ability to set alert thresholds when run-rate exceeds forecast.
[02:12] Ethan Cole: Absolutely. In the console you can tag routes, map to cost centers, and set per-route budgets — we'll demo that.
[02:40] [screen share begins] Ethan Cole: Alright this is the Routes page, top-left shows active routes, latency p50/p95, token consumption and estimated cost. The heatmap shows hour-by-hour token burn.
[03:05] Maya Patel: Note the top ribbon is configurable for burst vs reserved. Lucida, because you have spiky inference from the mobile app, the ribbon helps separate baseline reserved capacity from burst.
[03:33] Sofia Ramos: Does that map back to model variants? We have a quantized variant for some routes.
[03:44] Ethan Cole: Yes, variant-level breakdowns appear under the route detail. We also show fallback counts when a heavy model is not available and a smaller variant served.
[04:12] Derrick Huang: The transcript sometimes says K-V cash for KV cache, lol.
[04:20] Maya Patel: (laughs) yeah, fireflies does that. Back to the demo — clicking into a route.
[04:45] Ethan Cole: Here you can filter by tag, environment, and time-range. On the right we show cost attribution: raw token cost, infra overhead, and optimization savings.
[05:10] Priya Menon: How do you calculate infra overhead? Do you include GPU amortization?
[05:21] Ethan Cole: Good question. For Dedicated we include reserved capacity amortized across the committed window. For hosted it's the per-token bill plus a small platform fee. We show both line items.
[05:52] Maya Patel: We also surface suggested levers — e.g., enable L2 KV caching for this route, reduce max tokens for a specific model, or use auto-quantization.
[06:20] Sofia Ramos: Can Optimize recommend quantization levels safely? We have concerns about quality drop.
[06:33] Ethan Cole: Optimize recommends profiles tied to evals — you can run a quick eval set and see BLEU/ROUGE-like deltas. It's conservative by default.
[07:00] Derrick Huang: If we do a pilot, can we replay historical traffic? We want realistic perf numbers.
[07:12] Maya Patel: Yes, you can upload a traffic CSV or we can set up a shadow run. For the pilot we recommend a 2-week shadow with sampled production traffic.
[07:36] Priya Menon: About billing — can the console breakdown match our internal chargeback, i.e., cost center and project tag?
[07:48] Ethan Cole: Yup, tags map to cost centers. You can export daily granularity CSV for your billing system.
[08:10] [timestamp jump — demo deeper] Ethan Cole: Now in the cost insights tab, we surface per-route cost per 1k tokens, and compare model variants. You can see cost delta if we switch to a quantized variant or if we batch.
[08:44] Sofia Ramos: Show me an example where batching reduced cost but kept latency under 200ms.
[08:53] Ethan Cole: Sure — here's a route that was 120 rps, we configured dynamic batching with max latency 150ms and saw 28% token cost reduction while p95 stayed ~170ms.
[09:20] Derrick Huang: Are the batching knobs automatic or manual? We have concerns about tail latency.
[09:31] Maya Patel: There's an auto mode that learns traffic shapes and a manual mode for explicit SLOs. For production-critical routes many customers run manual with canary.
[10:00] Priya Menon: Security: we need to know about KMS, audit logs, and VPC peering.
[10:09] Maya Patel: For Private/Dedicated we support customer-managed KMS and we ship audit logs to your SIEM. VPC peering and private link are supported; we'll share the architecture diagram.
[10:35] Sofia Ramos: Any SOC2/ISO docs we can hand to our security team?
[10:41] Maya Patel: Yes — we'll send SOC2 summary and the control mapping. Action: I'll attach those docs.
[11:05] Ethan Cole: Back on console — the route timeline shows anomalies. We can create composite alerts: e.g., cost spike AND p95 > 500ms.
[11:25] Derrick Huang: Can alerts trigger auto-fallback to cheaper models?
[11:31] Ethan Cole: Yes, routing policies support automatic fallback to a variant or to a cheaper region. You can set priority and graceful degradation rules.
[12:00] [interaction — customer asks about a real metric] Sofia Ramos: Show the telemet— the telemetry fields you need.
[12:08] Ethan Cole: Basic shape: timestamp, route id, model id, tokens in/out, latency, request id, user id (hashed), and optional tags. We'll provide a schema.
[12:32] Priya Menon: Can we keep PII out? We require token redaction.
[12:38] Maya Patel: Absolutely — PII should be hashed before sending; the console ingests only hashed ids and aggregate counts.
[13:05] Derrick Huang: For the pilot, what's the expected infra delta? If we use dedicated pool, how many GPUs for our traffic?
[13:18] Ethan Cole: We'll need the traffic CSV; we'll do a capacity plan. For a rough estimate, the pilot uses a small dedicated pool with burst enabled — we size after an initial replay.
[13:45] Maya Patel: I'll coordinate sizing with you, Derrick — action item for Ethan to draft runbook.
[14:10] [15 min mark — Q&A continues] Sofia Ramos: What's the visibility into model-level KV cache hits?
[14:22] Ethan Cole: We show cache hit rate per route and per model; plus estimated token savings from caching.
[14:50] Priya Menon: Is Optimize able to recommend cache TTLs?
[14:56] Ethan Cole: Yes, based on request distribution. Recommend conservative TTLs to avoid staleness.
[15:30] [mid-call interruption — brief noise] 
[16:00] Derrick Huang: Sorry, connection glitch. Back.
[16:25] Ethan Cole: No problem. I'm pulling up the billing export example.
[16:42] Ethan Cole: Export shows columns: date, route, model, token_count, token_cost_usd, infra_overhead_usd, optimization_savings_usd, cost_center_tag. You can ingest into your FinOps system.
[17:05] Priya Menon: Nice. We need daily granularity and rolling 30-day window.
[17:12] Maya Patel: Export supports daily, hourly, and 5-minute windows depending on retention.
[17:40] Sofia Ramos: How long does detailed telemetry persist?
[17:45] Ethan Cole: By default hosted retains detailed logs 30 days; longer retention is an add-on. For Dedicated/Private you can set retention or ship to S3.
[18:10] Derrick Huang: On SLO enforcement, can Redwood do automatic throttling?
[18:18] Ethan Cole: Yes, rate limiters at route-level and client token-level, and we can integrate with your API gateway for backpressure.
[18:50] Maya Patel: Let's talk pilot scope: 2 weeks of shadow traffic plus daily cost reporting and a baseline eval.
[19:05] Sofia Ramos: Sounds reasonable. If the pilot shows >20% cost savings with acceptable quality, we'll move to a dedicated commit.
[19:18] Priya Menon: Who signs off on the pricing? It's FinOps + procurement.
[19:26] Maya Patel: We'll send a pilot quote and the renewal path.
[19:45] [walking through an example anomaly] Ethan Cole: Here's an instance where a route suddenly started using a larger variant due to missing prefix caching — the console shows cache miss rate increased and cost spiked. The fix was to enable prefix cache and reduce max context size.
[20:12] Derrick Huang: That example mirrors a bug we saw — good to know there's automated detection.
[20:40] Sofia Ramos: UX question: can product managers see these dashboards without seeing raw request ids?
[20:47] Maya Patel: Yes, RBAC allows role-scoped views; you can hide identifiers from PMs.
[21:10] Priya Menon: About SLA and uptime, do you provide SLOs for latency?
[21:18] Ethan Cole: For Dedicated we offer latency SLOs at the route level in the contract; hosted SLAs are at service availability.
[21:40] Sofia Ramos: What about multi-region? We need EU+US.
[21:48] Maya Patel: Supported — routing policies can keep EU data in EU region; private deployments can be region-isolated.
[22:10] Derrick Huang: Any gotchas for VPC peering? We run a strict firewall.
[22:18] Ethan Cole: We'll share a network checklist — ports, CIDRs, peering config. For on-prem there are additional steps.
[22:50] [demo wrap-up] Maya Patel: Quick recap — console has per-route cost attribution, Optimize recommends batching/quantization, routing policies allow fallbacks, and pilot plan is 2-week shadow with daily reports.
[23:20] Sofia Ramos: Looks good. Can you also include a runbook for rollback if quality regresses?
[23:28] Ethan Cole: We'll include rollback playbooks and canary steps in the runbook.
[23:50] Priya Menon: Please include example cost model showing projected savings vs commit levels.
[23:58] Maya Patel: We'll attach an example savings sheet.
[24:20] Derrick Huang: One more technical — how do you measure model quality during quantization tests?
[24:29] Ethan Cole: We run eval sets you provide and compute metrics (task specific). We show delta and flag samples where outputs diverge.
[25:05] [longer demo segment — console interactivity] Ethan Cole: Now switching to Alerts & Playbooks. You can create a playbook that on cost spike runs a limited rollback to cheaper variant and notifies slack.
[25:40] Sofia Ramos: Great — Slack integration is needed.
[25:46] Maya Patel: We support webhook, Slack, PagerDuty.
[26:10] Derrick Huang: How long to spin up a dedicated pool if we decide to commit?
[26:18] Ethan Cole: Depends on capacity — typically 48–72 hours for small pools if GPUs available; bigger commits take longer.
[26:45] Priya Menon: For pricing, do you offer month-to-month reserved or only annual?
[26:52] Maya Patel: We have monthly reserved and annual with discounts. Pilot is month-to-month.
[27:20] Sofia Ramos: Let's record the final acceptance criteria: 1) cost savings >=20% vs current baseline OR cost flat + improved latency, 2) no quality regression over eval set, 3) FinOps billing export maps to cost centers.
[27:42] Maya Patel: Noted. We'll include that in the pilot plan.
[28:10] [customer asks about data residency again] Sofia Ramos: Confirm that EU traffic never leaves region for EU routes.
[28:18] Ethan Cole: Yes, region routing policy can pin traffic and for Private you can keep control plane in-region.
[28:50] Derrick Huang: Any limitations on model types? We use some LoRA adapters on top of base models.
[28:58] Ethan Cole: We support LoRA and adapters; runtime shows adapter-level stats but will need model onboarding for custom kernels.
[29:30] Priya Menon: Is there an integration to our cost allocation system (Cloud FinOps tool)?
[29:36] Maya Patel: We provide CSVs and S3 exports; if needed we can wire a custom connector.
[30:05] [second half — pilot logistics] Maya Patel: Proposed timeline: kickoff next week, telemetry ingest day 1, shadow replay days 2-14, daily check-ins M/W/F, final review day 15.
[30:30] Sofia Ramos: That cadence works. We'll loop procurement/infosec after we see SOC2 docs.
[30:50] Derrick Huang: Do you have an estimated cost for the pilot?
[30:54] Maya Patel: We'll send a pilot quote — small infra fee plus usage; typically low cost to evaluate.
[31:10] Ethan Cole: I'll prepare the runbook and benchmark scripts.
[31:28] [questions about historical anomalies] Sofia Ramos: Does the console surface root-cause suggestions?
[31:35] Ethan Cole: It provides heuristics — increased cache miss, model fallback, or bad prompt expansions. It's guidance, not automatic remediation unless you want playbooks to run.
[32:00] Priya Menon: For billing transparency, can we see per-route hourly costs with tags flattened?
[32:08] Ethan Cole: Yes, hourly with tags and you can create aggregated views.
[32:30] Derrick Huang: Are there quotas for API? We might hit rate limits during replay.
[32:38] Maya Patel: For pilot we can lift limits; production has default quotas but can be tuned.
[33:05] [final wrap] Maya Patel: Ok final recap and I'll share SOC2, arch diagram, pilot quote, and runbook. We'll schedule follow-up Dec 1 for infra alignment.
[33:26] Sofia Ramos: Thanks, this was useful.
[33:33] Derrick Huang: Appreciate it.
[33:36] Priya Menon: Thanks all.
[33:40] Maya Patel: Thanks — we'll follow up with docs and next steps.
[33:50] [call ends — notes: meeting length truncated in export, actual 58 min; longer Q&A continued off-record]
[58:00]

document.content:
Hightower - transit architecture & private endpoint discovery

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-20
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Maya (Redwood SE), Jordan (Hightower SRE), Priya (Head of Cloud), Diego (SecOps), Emily (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough): Hightower is evaluating private/VPC deployment. Primary constraints: regulatory data residency, strict egress controls, transit-gateway topology, and limited peering ranges. Discussed private endpoints, VPC peering vs TGW, NAT/egress, route tables, KMS integration and SOC2 docs. Next steps: Redwood to share terraform examples and security pack; customer to share network diagrams and CIDRs.

00:00 Alex Rivera: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick intro — i'm alex, AE on the infra team at Redwood. today our goal is to understand how you'd like to run inference — private deployment in your VPC, looks like — and any network constraints.
00:22 Jordan Lee: hi, jordan here. yeah we're looking at private first. need to keep inference traffic inside our AWS footprint, "no public egress for payloads", and most compute should be in us-east-1 with DR in eu-west-1.
00:35 Priya Kapoor: and we have a transit-gateway based architecture, we've got three core accounts: prod, infra, and peering. so peering to an external provider needs to play nice with transit gw route tables.
00:50 Samir Patel: awesome, thanks. quick clarifying q — when you say "no public egress for payloads", do you mean both model input and logs, or logs can go to a logging endpoint we control?
01:03 Diego Morales: logs can go to our splunk forwarder inside the VPC, but payloads must never leave the org. encryption-at-rest and KMS integration also must be in place.
01:15 Maya Chen: good to know. for Redwood Private we can run a customer-managed control plane + private data plane or an on-prem bundle; most customers use our VPC endpoint model where we put an ENI/service endpoint in the customer's VPC and traffic never traverses the public internet.
01:35 Alex Rivera: a couple of network patterns we see: direct VPC peering, Transit Gateway attachments, or PrivateLink style endpoints. each has tradeoffs around route management, cross-account permissions, and bandwidth.
01:50 Jordan Lee: biggest operational ask: we need automatic failover to eu-west-1 for regional outage and predictable latency SLAs. also we have strict egress inspection — everything leaving an account must pass through NGFWs.
02:05 Samir Patel: gotcha. transit-gateway fits that with centralized inspection. we have customers who attach our infra as an additional TGW attachment in the same account or via a cross-account attachment; however you will need to add route propagation to the correct route tables.
02:20 Emily Zhang: question about private endpoints — is that AWS PrivateLink or an ENI we host inside our account?
02:30 Maya Chen: it's effectively a managed PrivateLink/ENI pattern. we can publish a service endpoint into your VPC and you call that endpoint using private IPs. for some deployments we also support cross-account TGW attachments where our compute lives in a dedicated account under your org.
02:48 Priya Kapoor: cross-account TGW sounds promising but our security team is picky about which accounts can assume roles. what's the auth flow?
02:56 Samir Patel: we generally use a short-lived cert-based or STS-assume-role mechanism depending on the pattern. for PrivateLink it's TLS mutual auth and certs if needed; for cross-account TGW we do a least-privilege IAM role with explicit trust. we'll share templates.
03:12 Diego Morales: any constraints on port ranges? we can't open 0-65535 broadly.
03:18 Maya Chen: standard: control plane uses 443 and some healthcheck ports, data plane is HTTPS to the endpoint — we can allowlist source IPs or use SGs to restrict. heavy throughput uses high-concurrency TCP, but it's still tunneled over HTTPS typically.
03:35 Jordan Lee: curious about NAT and egress for updates — if we host the model pieces in a Redwood-managed subnet attached to our TGW, will model fetches at boot contact public endpoints? we need to control that.
03:48 Alex Rivera: we can bake images in an air-gapped fashion or provide an update proxy that lives in your account. we also support bringing-your-own-images and supply signed model artifacts.
04:02 Priya Kapoor: good. compliance checklist — SOC2, encryption, audit logs. can you confirm audit logs are available and we can push them to our KMS and centralized logging?
04:14 Samir Patel: yes — audit logs (control plane and runtime) can be forwarded to your S3/CloudWatch/Splunk with KMS encryption using your CMK. we also retain audit trails in our control plane but can disable storage if you want everything in your account.
04:28 Emily Zhang: any region constraints? we prefer primary in us-east-1 for latency, with read/replicas in us-west-2 and eu-west-1 for DR. are all those regions supported for dedicated pools?
04:42 Maya Chen: us-east-1 and us-west-2 are standard, eu-west-1 is supported but with some instance-type limitations historically; we'll check current GPU availability. if you need deterministic hardware we can do a dedicated pool reservation.
05:00 Jordan Lee: and how does split-write / stateful KV cache behave across regions? we need low-latency KV local to the model serving region.
05:09 Samir Patel: KV cache is per-instance; cross-region synchronous replication is not recommended due to latency. typical pattern: keep state local to each region and use async replication for metrics/aggregates.
05:20 Diego Morales: that may impact our template for session-state. ok.
05:28 Alex Rivera: want to zone in on routing: if you're using TGW, we recommend creating explicit route table entries for the Redwood attachment and disabling broad 0.0.0.0/0 propagation for that attachment. also we provide a small set of IP ranges to allow in NGFWs.
05:45 Jordan Lee: can you supply those ranges? we have automated NGFW rule changes that need CIDRs.
05:52 Samir Patel: yes we'll generate the minimal CIDR list; in PrivateLink mode you don't need wide-range CIDRs, it's just the ENI in your subnet.
06:05 Priya Kapoor: what's the latency profile? if the model is in us-east-1 and our app is in the same region, we need 50ms p95 or better for single-turn calls — is that realistic?
06:20 Maya Chen: depends on model size and batch settings. for smaller 7-13B family models we often hit <30ms p95 on single-token generation when using a colocated dedicated pool with KV cache warm. larger models push that higher. we'll include sample SLOs.
06:38 Emily Zhang: what about streaming? we need partial responses as they generate for user UX.
06:45 Samir Patel: streaming over the private endpoint is supported — it's chunked HTTP/2. you just need to permit long-lived TCP in the SGs.
06:55 Jordan Lee: security: KMS integration detail — can Redwood encrypt with our CMKs? we don't want keys in your account.
07:05 Maya Chen: yes, we support customer-managed KMS keys; our control plane can encrypt request payload metadata but the customer CMK remains in your account and we only receive ciphertext. we'll send a whitepaper on the KMS flow.
07:19 Diego Morales: and SSO? we want RBAC via SAML.
07:23 Alex Rivera: Redwood supports SSO via SAML/OIDC and SCIM provisioning for user sync. admin roles, reader roles, and API key scoping are supported.
07:34 Priya Kapoor: explain rollback/fallback: if us-east has an outage, do you automatically route to eu-west? what about data residency — we can't have PII cross region unless masked.
07:45 Samir Patel: automatic geo-failover is policy-driven. default is no cross-region failover for in-flight PII; you can set policies to failover only for stateless requests or for non-PII traffic. many customers use a canary plus manual DR runbook.
08:02 Emily Zhang: ok can we talk about pricing form-factor? dedicated capacity vs private hosted?
08:10 Alex Rivera: yes — dedicated is reserved GPUs inside Redwood-managed pools for a customer (predictable throughput, enterprise SLAs). private-hosted (VPC endpoints) is a hybrid where compute can still be in our accounts but the network path is private. fully private on-prem lets you manage everything but has a higher onboarding cost.
08:28 Jordan Lee: licensing nuance: does Dedicated allow us to control model updates? we want to vet each model version before roll to prod.
08:36 Maya Chen: yes, you can pin model versions and control rollouts; we support canary rollouts and A/B testing. we also allow a manual model approval process in the private control plane.
08:50 Diego Morales: any egress metering? we need to bill back to teams.
08:55 Samir Patel: yes token-level metering and per-route cost breakdowns show up in the console and can be pushed to your billing export.
09:05 Emily Zhang: technical deep-dive possibility: we might want a follow-up with your infra SEs to run a short benchmark against a 13B model and our sample prompts.
09:14 Alex Rivera: absolutely — standard POC includes latency/cost benchmarks. we'll need a small corpus and some representative traffic patterns.
09:20 Jordan Lee: network nit: for TGW attachment we have strict route table segregation per account; will add route propagation require manual approval?
09:29 Samir Patel: depends on your policy. we can provide CloudFormation/Terraform that explicitly creates the attachment and route maps so you can review in PR flow.
09:38 Priya Kapoor: one potential blocker is VPC CIDR overlap — we use 10.0.0.0/8 ranges broadly. do you support NAT'd or translated IPs so we don't have to readdress?
09:50 Maya Chen: with PrivateLink we sit inside your subnet so no overlap. with TGW attachments you need unique prefixes — some customers NAT inside their transit VPC. we can document approaches.
10:03 Diego Morales: what about TLS termination? do we terminate at the ENI or keep end-to-end TLS?
10:10 Samir Patel: we support end-to-end TLS. if you want us to terminate, that's opt-in. for mutual TLS with client certs we can also do periodic rotation using your CA.
10:20 Emily Zhang: curious about observability — can we get token-level traces and request/response latency per route?
10:27 Alex Rivera: yes, console exposes per-route model latency, token counts, and sampling of outputs. for sensitive data you can disable content sampling and only send metadata.
10:40 Jordan Lee: integration question: we use Hashicorp Vault for secrets and an internal KMS proxy. can Redwood call our proxy to unwrap model keys or do you expect KMS in AWS?
10:52 Maya Chen: we can integrate with Vault via a signed attestation flow; typically customers either give us a CMK or we use an in-account proxy to perform unwraps. will need engineering touch.
11:05 Priya Kapoor: time for a quick recap and next steps?
11:10 Alex Rivera: yes — recap: 1) Hightower needs private/VPC deployment with no public payload egress, TGW-friendly design, strict NGFW allowlist, and KMS/SSO integration. 2) Redwood to share architecture doc, terraform templates, CIDR list, SOC2 + KMS whitepaper, and cost/latency spreadsheet. 3) Customer to share TGW diagram, CIDRs, and a small prompt corpus for bench. 4) follow-up POC week of 2026-03-30.
11:42 Priya Kapoor: sounds right. Diego, Jordan — anything to add?
11:47 Diego Morales: just verify the NGFW changes won't require us to change peering with internal partners. we'll surface that.
11:52 Jordan Lee: i'll pull route tables and send them to alex.
11:55 Alex Rivera: perfect. i'll also include a short runbook for TGW attachment and recommended route table entries.
12:03 Emily Zhang: one last quick thing — competitor evaluation: our procurement is also talking to Anthropic and OpenAI enterprise on private options; curious how you differ on operational tooling.
12:14 Samir Patel: two quick diffs: one, our runtime picks kernels and batching heuristics tuned for steady-state production workloads which tends to reduce cost/latency in long-running deployments; two, we provide model lifecycle + rollout automation and token-level cost breakdowns baked into the console.
12:34 Alex Rivera: ok we'll get the artifacts over today/tomorrow and coordinate on dates for the POC. thanks everyone.
12:45 Priya Kapoor: thank you all.
12:47 Meeting end.

Notes about transcription: occasional speaker labels were generic; some technical terms transcribed as 'K-V cash' or 'transit gateway' spelled inconsistently. External doc references: "Redwood private endpoint architecture" (link to be shared), "SOC2 + KMS whitepaper" (link to be shared), benchmark spreadsheet (link to be shared).

document.content:
Pilot sync: bench summary vs incumbent - Suncrest Health

Weekly pilot sync where Redwood presented lab benchmarks vs Suncrest's incumbent provider. Redwood shows materially lower median latency and higher sustained throughput in our config; discussed root causes of p95 spikes and KV cache warmup. Agreed next steps: share raw logs, provision VPC replay env, schedule deep dive on cache behavior and routing fallbacks.
Benchmarks: p50/p95 latency and sustained throughput
KV cache warmup and prefix caching
Routing & fallback behavior vs cost/latency tradeoffs
Security: data-in-flight, SOC2 mention and VPC peering
Next steps: logs, VPC test, deep-dive scheduling
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-20
Time: 15:00 UTC (42 min)
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Olivia (Suncrest CTO), Ethan (Lead ML Eng), Priya (Infra), Samir (PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): Redwood performance numbers looked better overall; some spikes at p95 from routing retries and cold KV cache. Action items recorded.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll kick off in a sec, and then diego will walk through the bench results from the lab runs this week.
[00:20] Olivia Park: yep thanks, good to see you - we've got the team here. quick ask, can you include the raw request traces, not just the summarized sheets?
[00:28] Maya Chen: absolutely, we'll include raw logs and token-level breakdowns. diego?
[00:33] Diego Ramirez: great, thanks. ok slide-free for speed: baseline here is Suncrest's current provider - meant to mirror their production params: 8k token sequence sampling, batch sizes ~16, 4 concurrent workers. Redwood run was our optimized config: quantized fp16, continuous batching with 64ms max wait, prefix KV caching enabled.
[01:05] Ethan Cole: couple quick clarifications - the incumbent runs used their managed endpoint with auto-scaling; did you emulate identical concurrency rhythm?
[01:15] Diego Ramirez: we replayed traces from Suncrest's logs with the same arrival pattern; there will always be small diffs but we used your production trace for 48h.
[01:25] Samir Patel: ok that helps. numbers?
[01:28] Diego Ramirez: p50 latency: Redwood 58ms vs incumbent 130ms. p95: Redwood 260ms vs incumbent 420ms. Sustained throughput (steady-state RPS): Redwood 420 req/s vs incumbent 190 req/s when holding at your target 200ms SLA.
[01:52] Priya Nair: those p50 numbers look great but p95 still feels high, what's causing the tail?
[02:00] Diego Ramirez: good call, two main contributors: first, cache warmup for long prefix-heavy prompts — when the KV cache is cold the first few tokens cost more. second, routing retries during short transient GPU saturations: our fallback rule spun up a compatible but lower-capacity model which increases latency for those requests until the pool stabilizes.
[02:27] Olivia Park: is that the automatic fallback you mentioned earlier? will that impact correctness or model outputs?
[02:34] Diego Ramirez: functionally outputs are from the same model family we configured for the fallback variant; we prioritize semantic parity but slight deltas are possible — we surface those in the quality monitor.
[02:48] Ethan Cole: do you have token-level cost numbers? that's something procurement will ask: tokens per second and cost delta vs incumbent.
[02:58] Maya Chen: yes we'll put a cost sheet next to the benchmark sheet. high level: because Redwood reduced avg latency and improved batching, the unit compute per request dropped ~28% in lab; that translates to about 22% lower per-unit cost in our estimates for this workload.
[03:20] Samir Patel: solid. how confident are you these lab numbers map to our on-prem replay? Priya?
[03:28] Priya Nair: we'll run the replay once VPC peering is up; our concern is network egress and any cross-region variability. we need to validate latency tail with our exact network path.
[03:40] Diego Ramirez: makes sense — we asked for VPC peering so we can run an end-to-end replay and capture identical network hops. that will resolve most of the discrepancy.
[03:50] Olivia Park: show us the timeline for follow-ups.
[03:53] Maya Chen: next steps captured: we'll share raw logs 48 hours, diego exports p50/p95 token breakdown, priya will open peering ticket.
[04:01] Ethan Cole: about the p95 spikes — can you annotate whether those correlate with model compaction/quantization changes? we saw in one run a 10% extra latency after switching quant profile.
[04:12] Diego Ramirez: good memory — we ran two quantization profiles: q4_0 and q8_0 as an experiment. the q8_0 path had slightly higher memory but was more stable under batching; the p95 spike correlated with q4_0 when we hit fragmentation in the allocator. we can pin to q8_0 for your pilot if you prefer stability.
[04:41] Priya Nair: would pinning to q8_0 meaningfully increase cost?
[04:45] Maya Chen: marginally — maybe 4-6% higher unit cost but lowers the tail and reduces retries which can offset the delta.
[04:55] Samir Patel: tradeoffs sound acceptable. can you walk us through the routing fallback logic?
[05:00] Diego Ramirez: sure — policy summary: we route by latency SLO primarily; when GPU pool reaches a soft-threshold we route new requests to a cheaper lower-latency-optimized variant or to an adjacent region with slightly higher egress. we also have automatic retry with jitter. in your pilot runs, the soft-threshold was triggered briefly at 2:10am in the replay window leading to ~120 requests routed to fallback for ~90 seconds. those requests had p95 ~620ms.
[05:28] Olivia Park: interesting. could that explain some of our user-reported blips?
[05:31] Ethan Cole: yeah we saw error reports around the same time in our logs but thought it was a client issue.
[05:36] Diego Ramirez: likely correlated. we'll annotate the raw logs with routing decision ids so you can see which requests hit fallback.
[05:43] Maya Chen: quick security check — Priya any blockers on the private pilot bucket or SOC2 artefacts we sent last week?
[05:50] Priya Nair: SOC2 docs look fine, just need confirmation on data-in-flight encryption policy with your peering. also need a short-term retention policy for logs (we prefer 90 days).
[06:02] Maya Chen: we support TLS in-flight and we can configure retention; we'll propose 90 days for the pilot.
[06:07] Olivia Park: perfect. another question: concurrency tuning — you mentioned continuous batching; will that add jitter to p50?
[06:15] Diego Ramirez: continuous batching introduces small added micro-wait to coalesce tokens, but with your arrival pattern we saw p50 improved because more effective batching happened; p95 is more influenced by cache warmup and routing; overall net improvement.
[06:30] Ethan Cole: do you have a suggested route for making p95 tighter? like pre-warming the KV cache or increasing minimal pool size?
[06:37] Diego Ramirez: yes: 1) proactive prefix caching for known templates, 2) slightly higher minimum reserved seats during peak windows, 3) pin to q8_0 to avoid allocator fragmentation. We can do a controlled run for each change and measure incremental benefit.
[06:54] Samir Patel: sounds like an experiment matrix. can Diego draft that?
[06:58] Diego Ramirez: will do — I'll include metrics to capture per-experiment.
[07:02] Olivia Park: any anomalies in the logs besides the routing events?
[07:06] Diego Ramirez: there were a handful of long tail events tied to a noisy neighbor on the shared test pool; we've isolated those in lab but in dedicated or your private pilot it won't occur.
[07:18] Priya Nair: that noisy neighbor concers me — what guarantees do we get with dedicated?
[07:22] Maya Chen: dedicated capacity gives you isolated GPU pools with guaranteed min throughput and SLA-backed latency targets; for pilots we can request a small dedicated slice so you can validate without full commit.
[07:35] Ethan Cole: procurement will want to see SLA language — can you put a draft into the sales folder?
[07:39] Maya Chen: yes I'll drop a draft SLA and also the dedicated offer in the deck.
[07:43] Olivia Park: one last technical curiosity — how do you handle KV eviction during long sessions?

[07:58] Ethan Cole: nice. will that be easy to integrate into our orchestrator?
[08:02] Diego Ramirez: yes we provide a simple REST endpoint and SDK hooks.
[08:06] Samir Patel: ok let's open the floor for any final clarifying questions.
[08:10] Olivia Park: can you confirm the raw RPS numbers again and where you measured them?
[08:14] Diego Ramirez: sure: Redwood sustained 420 req/s steady-state in our lab with <200ms median token step; incumbent plateaued at ~190 req/s before latency climbed above 250ms. numbers measured at the proxy ingress point in the replay harness.
[08:33] Priya Nair: that replay harness — will you share the harness config so we can run locally?
[08:38] Diego Ramirez: yes config and container image will be in the shared sheet.
[08:42] Ethan Cole: about cost delta again — 22% lower per-unit is compelling, can you show sensitivity if we pin q8_0?
[08:49] Maya Chen: yes we'll include cost sensitivity rows for q4_0 vs q8_0 and reserved vs burst billing.

[09:16] Olivia Park: any risk of data residency issues for our EU tenant? we have users in EU; will the replay hit EU endpoints?
[09:22] Maya Chen: in the pilot we were running in us-east but we can repeat in eu-west region and we support region pinning; if you'd like we can run a small set of replay tests in both.

[09:47] Maya Chen: ok final recap: Redwood shares raw logs & benchmark sheet by 10/22, Diego shares experiment matrix by 10/22, Priya opens VPC peering ticket 10/21, schedule cache deep dive week of 10/26. Any objections?

document.content:
ForgeWell LLM fit & hosting paths discovery

Intro call to scope model selection for customer-facing claims assistant. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private, context length needs (8k vs 32k), multilingual support, and tool-calling for policy lookups. Agreed to run a short Dedicated pilot and exchange benchmark materials.
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-08-14
Start: 15:30 UTC
Dur: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya R. (Redwood AE), Jamal N. (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Priya Menon (ForgeWell Head of AI), Ethan Cole (Platform), Liam O'Connor (Security), Sara Lim (Product)
Links shared: Redwood pilot deck (link), security pack (link), shared bench spreadsheet placeholder: /redwood/pilots/forgewell/benchmarks.xlsx

Auto-generated summary: short: ForgeWell building consumer claims assistant, needs long-context retrieval for multi-doc claims, multilingual support for EN/ES/FR/ZH, strong security/SSO and data residency asks.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, um I'm Maya from Redwood, i'll hand off to Jamal to do a quick tech run and then we'll talk hosting options and next steps
[00:12] Jamal: hey, thanks Maya. hi Priya, Ethan, Liam, Sara. quick check, is this still mostly about the claims assistant and live customer chat + backend policy lookup?
[00:20] Priya Menon: yep that's right. we have existing rules engine but want an LLM layer for summarization and auto-fill suggestions, and also retrieval across multiple policy docs, pdfs, attachments
[00:33] Ethan: and we need it to work across english and spanish first, french later, and maybe simplified chinese for a pilot region
[00:40] Jamal: great. couple of quick qualifiers: latency SLO you expect? per-query tokens? and any constraints on hosting — are you open to Redwood Hosted or do you require private VPC/on-prem?
[00:52] Priya Menon: latency ideally sub-600ms for the user-facing generation. for batch async tasks it's fine to be slower. on hosting — our security team prefers Dedicated or Private; we can do Dedicated reserved capacity if that's enough for isolation, otherwise Private VPC for on-prem sensitive data.
[01:10] Liam: (security) we need SOC2, SSO via SAML, audit logs for prompt history, and support for customer-managed KMS/HSM for keys. also data residency: EU for EU customers
[01:25] Maya: yep we support all of that, we have SOC2, SAML/SSO, RBAC and KMS integrations. for Private you'd get a managed control plane and customer-managed networking. we'll share the security pack after this call.
[01:40] Sara: question on context lengths — some claims involve dozens of attachments, pdfs, and long transcripts. what's realistic? 8k enough? 32k? more?
[01:52] Jamal: depends on approach. for retrieval+KV cache you'd usually keep the prompt window to 8k for cost/latency, and rely on tool-calling/retrieval to bring in the right snippet. we also support 32k models if you want fewer trips to retrieval but cost/latency goes up. for some open models we can do 32k context with quantized variants and get decent perf.
[02:15] Priya Menon: are you recommending hosted vs dedicated for that use case?
[02:20] Jamal: if you want predictable throughput and data isolation without managing infra, Dedicated reserved pools are a good middle ground. Hosted is fastest to start but shared. Private is for strict regulatory/air-gapped setups. many customers do a Dedicated pilot to validate latency/cost then move to Private if they need tighter network controls.
[02:36] Ethan: ok that matches our initial thinking. next, model selection — we want open models to reduce vendor lock and cost. are there specific open models you'd recommend for cross-lingual summarization and tool-calling?
[02:48] Jamal: yes. Quick callouts: Llama-family (Llama-2 variants) for strong base, Mistral picks up on many benchmarks, some newer 8/16/70B open models vary. for multilingual, some families handle spanish/french well, others less so — we'd test on your prompts. also function/tool-calling support differs; Redwood has structured tool-calling and streaming support across our runtime but model compatibility depends on function-tokenization semantics.
[03:18] Priya Menon: we care about hallucination suppression when pulling policy clauses and exactness for citations. how do you measure that?
[03:25] Jamal: we run evals tied to prompt sets — exact-match recall for citations, and we can run reranking + grounding via retrievers to reduce hallucinations. Redwood Optimize can recommend quant profiles and reranking thresholds. we'll demo that in the pilot.
[03:40] [00:04:00] Speaker 3: (mumble) um when you say retriever, are you talking about vector store?
[03:50] Jamal: yes, vector store + hybrid retrieval, and prefix KV cache so repeated prompts are faster. for attachments we typically chunk and embed then store in a vector DB.
[04:05] Maya: i want to call out costs — for 32k context models per-token costs are notably higher; part of the pilot is to show cost/bene tradeoffs. we'll include token-level cost breakdowns by route in the bench sheet.
[04:20] Ethan: also curious about throughput — we expect bursts during claims spikes; autoscaling?
[04:26] Jamal: Dedicated has configurable autoscaling and burst capacity policies; Private can autoscale but depends on infra you provide. fallback policies are available to route to a cheaper model if capacity constrained.
[04:40] Priya Menon: any constraints on tool-calling? we have internal APIs for policy lookup, payments, and a signature microservice. we want the model to call the right API and only surface sanitized outputs to users.
[04:53] Jamal: Redwood supports structured tool-calling and can enforce output schemas and sanitization rules; you can configure per-route policies. we also support function-like calls where the model emits JSON and Redwood validates it. there are a few caveats with some open models around tokenization of function markers which we note in the bench doc.
[05:12] Liam: on encryption, will logs contain prompts? we need redact for PII.
[05:18] Maya: you can configure prompt logging policies. for Private we can disable storage or store only hashed values; for Dedicated we offer retention controls and redaction pipelines. KMS integration for keys as requested.
[05:31] [00:10:00] Jamal: quick live example — we ran a small test on 8k context Llama-2-70b quantized and on a 32k Mistral variant. results: 8k Llama with retriever + rerank hit our latency target ~450ms median in Dedicated pool, 32k Mistral gave fewer retrieval hops but median latency was ~780ms and cost ~2.4x. caveat: Mistral 32k had better multilingual quality on Spanish prompts we checked but we need your prompt set to be sure.
[06:05] Priya Menon: that's helpful. can you put those numbers in the sheet?
[06:09] Jamal: yes, we'll populate as part of the benchmark doc.
[06:12] Sara Lim: about the pilot duration and ops — what do you recommend? 2 weeks? 30 days?
[06:18] Maya: most customers do a 2-week Dedicated pilot: we provision a small reserved pool, run your prompt set plus synthetic traffic, do a security review, and then iterate. if you need more time for regulatory signoff, we can extend.
[06:31] Ethan: fine. what infra access do you need from our side for Dedicated?
[06:36] Jamal: for Dedicated we need network peering or VPN, SSO metadata, and an initial data sample for evals; for Private we'd ask for an infra contact to install the package (if on-prem). we'll share an infra checklist.
[06:50] [00:20:00] Priya Menon: question on governance — version pinning and rollbacks? we want to avoid model regressions in prod.
[06:58] Jamal: Redwood Console supports version pinning, canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automatic fallback to previous variants if the new model underperforms per your eval suite. we also emit tracing for token-level cost broken down by route.
[07:15] Liam: and compliance: can we get audit logs for every prompt+response, and admin role separation?
[07:22] Maya: yes audit logs are available; RBAC with admin/engineer roles is standard. we'll include sample logs in the security pack.
[07:33] Sara Lim: a little concern — some vendors force you into API-first flows that are hard to migrate from. how portable is Redwood if we ever want to self-host?
[07:43] Jamal: portability is a goal — models and configs are abstracted; you can move from Hosted to Dedicated to Private with the same API and routing policies. model artifacts for Private are deployed under your control.
[07:56] Priya Menon: okay next — evaluation metrics: beyond latency and cost, we want hallucination rate, citation exactness, and multilingual BLEU-style metrics. can you measure those?
[08:08] Jamal: yes - we can run those evals; Redwood Optimize has hooks to run your tests and raise regression alerts on predetermined thresholds.
[08:18] [00:30:00] Maya: quick recap and notes on deliverables — we'll send the benchmark template, populate initial example numbers for 8k vs 32k on two model families, share security pack, and propose a 2-week Dedicated pilot for week of 8/21.
[08:34] Priya Menon: on the pilot — assuming acceptable security review and SLA, what ramp looks like after pilot?
[08:40] Maya: usually teams either expand Dedicated reserved capacity or go Private if they need extra network control. we can propose a tiered reserved commit to manage cost commitments.
[08:50] Ethan: another specific — multilingual: do you recommend separate multilingual models or single large multilingual model?
[08:56] Jamal: tradeoffs: single large multilingual models simplify pipeline but may be heavier and more expensive; language-specific models can be cheaper and faster but add routing complexity. for initial pilot we often test 1 multilingual and 1 language-specialized path.
[09:14] Sara Lim: ok let's talk about timeline — security signoff usually two weeks with our legal and security teams; procurement another month.
[09:23] Maya: understood — we'll align kickoff to your internal approvals and try to accelerate the security review with pre-filled docs.
[09:30] [00:40:00] Jamal: small tech caveat — some open models have spotty function-call semantics which can cause the model to format calls slightly differently; for critical tool-calling we recommend we either wrap the model responses with a lightweight validation layer or use a model variant that we've validated. we'll document exact model compatibility in the bench sheet.
[09:52] Priya Menon: any rough cost ballpark for Dedicated for a small reserved pool for 2 weeks?
[09:58] Maya: we'll provide a conservative estimate in the bench doc; initial ballpark is $Xk/month equivalent for the short pool — we'll convert to per-token + reserved cost in the spreadsheet.
[10:08] Liam: last question — data residency: EU-only for EU customers. can Redwood route requests so EU data never leaves region?
[10:13] Jamal: yes — smart routing by policy can keep requests in-region and fallback to same-region replicas. Private deployments can be fully localized.
[10:22] Maya: ok i'll summarize the immediate next steps in an email and attach the bench sheet and security pack.
[10:29] Priya Menon: thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[10:32] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with materials and proposed pilot dates.

End transcript.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker mislabels and minor garbled words (typical of call transcripts).

Developer Accelerator: SDK auth pairing lab

AE + SE walked through Redwood SDKs (Python + TypeScript) auth patterns and sandbox environment. Covered env var vs secret manager, Console sandbox for keys, basic optimize suggestions (batching, cache), and next steps to share sample repo + SOC2/KMS docs. Customer raised data residency and on-prem questions; SE suggested dedicated/private deployment options and offered spike for latency benchmarks.
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-04
Time: 15:00 PDT (48m)
Location: Zoom
Recorded: Yes
Attendees: Avery Park (Redwood AE), Tomás Rivera (Redwood SE), Sofia Lind (Fjord) , Marcus Dahl (Fjord), Priya Kapoor (Fjord)

Auto-generated topics: SDK quickstart, auth, console, optimize suggestions, dedicated vs hosted

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Avery: All right folks uh thanks for joining, really appreciate it. Quick intro — I'm Avery, AE on the account, and Tomás is our solutions engineer who will run the pairing lab. Sofia, Marcus, Priya, thanks for making time.
[00:12] Sofia: Thanks, excited. Quick note — we're trying to get a minimal integration running by end of next week.
[00:18] Tomás: Perfect, we'll focus on the Python + TypeScript examples, auth patterns, and then show the Console sandbox so you can generate ephemeral keys.
[00:28] Priya: Can you clarify ephemeral keys? We want to avoid leaking prod keys in CI.
[00:34] Tomás: Yep totally. There's two recommended flows: store long-lived secrets in your vault/KMS and mint short lived tokens for CI or front-end. We'll demo both.
[00:42] Marcus: And from security side, we need audit logs and KMS integration — SOC2 is a requirement.
[00:49] Avery: We'll attach the SOC2 + KMS integration docs after the call. I'll note that.
[00:53] Tomás: Ok starting the walkthrough — first step is environment variables for local dev. In Python: pip install redwood-sdk, then set export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk_live_XXX (demo only). In TS: npm i @redwood-inference/sdk and set process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY in the .env file.
[01:12] Sofia: Wait, small thing — your SDK package name is sometimes recorded as "redwood-infer" in older docs, we saw that. Which is correct?
[01:20] Tomás: Right now it's @redwood-inference/sdk for TS and redwood_sdk for Python — sorry docs overlap, we'll send the canonical package names in the repo.
[01:29] Tomás: Demo: quick Python snippet —
[01:32] Tomás: "from redwood_sdk import Client
client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
res = client.generate('Write a summary of my meeting')"
[01:45] Sofia: Looks straightforward. How do we do key rotation?
[01:48] Tomás: Console supports key rotation and per-key scopes. You can create a sandbox key scoped to embeddings-only for tests. We'll show that in the Console.
[01:56] Avery: Pulling up the Console now, excuse the slight lag.
[02:05] Tomás: On the Console dashboard — top-right you can create keys, set description, set expiration. The UI also exposes activity logs, which is handy for audit trails. Note: sometimes in transcription it's called "red-wood console" or "red wood" which is the same.
[02:28] Marcus: Are audit logs retained for 90 days by default? We need 365.
[02:33] Tomás: Hosted defaults are 90 days; for enterprise we can extend retention under the Dedicated/Private contracts. We'll call that out in the follow-up.
[02:40] Priya: For our CI, we use HashiCorp Vault — what's recommended?
[02:45] Tomás: Best practice is vault -> short lived credential minting. Either store Redwood long-lived key in Vault and use Vault to inject ephemeral creds into CI, or use an internal service to mint tokens via the Redwood session API if you want more rotation. We'll include example Vault policies in the repo.
[03:05] Sofia: Can you show the TypeScript sample?
[03:08] Tomás: Sure. sample.ts: "import { RedwoodClient } from '@redwood-inference/sdk'
const c = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })
await c.chat.create({ messages: [...] })". Real code lives in the sample repo link we'll share.
[03:26] Sofia: Nice. Any common gotchas?
[03:29] Tomás: A few: token not exported in sub-shells, Windows env differences, and build pipelines that strip env vars. Also watch for rate limits on sandbox keys if many parallel devs spin up.
[03:44] Avery: Switching to Optimize — this is our cost/perf toolkit. For a dev flow, Optimize suggests batching and prefix caching to reduce token costs while keeping p99 low.
[03:55] Marcus: We have a high throughput 1k rps workload in testing; would batching hurt latency for us?
[04:02] Tomás: It's workload-dependent. For many short requests, intelligent small batching helps throughput and unit cost. For latency-critical user-facing requests, you can disable batching on that route and enable for async workers. Optimize can propose per-route configs based on observed token lengths.
[04:20] Sofia: You mentioned quantization — will that impact model output quality?
[04:24] Tomás: Quantization profiles trade a small drop in quality for significant cost savings. Optimize provides model+quantize suggestions and evaluation harnesses so you can run regression tests against your prompt set. We'll include an eval harness example.
[04:39] Priya: For private deployment, do we need to change SDK endpoints?
[04:42] Tomás: Yes, for Private you'll point the SDK to your control plane endpoint (e.g., https://control.fjord.redwood.local) and supply certs or mTLS depending on setup. It's one config flag in the client.
[04:55] Marcus: We're interested in a canary rollout and A/B testing. Does the SDK handle routing?
[05:00] Tomás: Routing is mostly handled by server-side policies and model tags. Your SDK calls the same API, the control plane will route to variants according to rollout rules.
[05:10] Sofia: Let's try a live quickstart — can you walk us through creating a sandbox key step-by-step?
[05:15] Tomás: Yep. Console -> Developer -> API Keys -> Create Key -> name: fjord-dev-sandbox -> scope: chat, embeddings -> expire in 7 days. Copy the key.
[05:28] Priya: (typing) Trying to paste — getting a 403 when testing locally.
[05:32] Tomás: Hmm 403 on the test? Can I see the request?
[05:36] Priya: It's a curl: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_xyz" -d '{"prompt":"hi"}'
[05:44] Tomás: Two things: use the region endpoint we provisioned for you (us-west-2.sandbox.redwood.ai) and ensure the key has chat scope. Also JSON body needs content-type header. Example: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_xyz" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"input":"hello"}' https://us-west-2.sandbox.redwood.ai/v1/chat/generate
[06:05] Marcus: Ah that was the region mismatch. Good catch.
[06:08] Sofia: Any limitations in the sandbox compared to hosted prod?
[06:11] Tomás: Sandboxes are rate limited and may not have Dedicated performance characteristics. They are for dev/test. If you need throughput tests, we can provision a short-lived Dedicated pool for benchmarking.
[06:25] Avery: We'll record the ask: provisional Dedicated benchmark for 1k rps. Tomás will draft plan.
[06:31] Tomás: Moving to CI example — show GitHub Actions snippet where the key is pulled from Vault. (Tomás pastes a snippet).
[06:40] Sofia: Our infra team prefers short-lived JWTs rather than long-lived keys. Can Redwood accept OIDC tokens?
[06:45] Tomás: Yes, we support OIDC for private deployments and a token exchange mechanism for hosted as well — details differ by deployment mode. We'll include OIDC notes in the repo.
[06:58] Priya: On RBAC — can we restrict inside our org per-team keys?
[07:02] Tomás: Yes, Console supports per-key scopes and you can create service accounts with limited permissions. Dedicated also supports role sync from your IdP via SCIM.
[07:15] Sofia: Let's talk observability — what telemetry do we get by default?
[07:18] Tomás: By default you get per-request latency, token usage, model used, and errors. You can send traces to your own tracing backend via our tracing hooks. We also have cost breakdowns by token, per-route.
[07:34] Marcus: Do logs include prompt content? We need to avoid storing PII in logs.
[07:38] Tomás: Good point. Red-wood Console supports masking and configurable retention; customers can opt out of storing prompt text or route logs. For Private, you control everything.
[07:50] Avery: Ok I'm going to switch to the sample repo now — creating a branch 'fjord-quickstart'. You should receive invite.
[07:58] Priya: Received. Trying to run the Python quickstart...
[08:02] Priya: "ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'redwood_sdk'"
[08:06] Tomás: That indicates pip install didn't run in the venv. Did you run python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate? On Windows use venv\scripts\activate.
[08:18] Priya: Ah missed activate. Running now... ok working.
[08:25] Sofia: We saw a note about model pinning — can we pin to a specific model version for production?
[08:30] Tomás: Yes, you can pin model versions in your route config or via the SDK by supplying model: 'redwood-llama-v1@2025-05-01' so rollouts are deterministic. Optimize can recommend model variants.
[08:45] Marcus: For evaluation, will you run a regression test against our prompt set? We want to ensure quality doesn't regress with quantization changes.
[08:51] Tomás: Absolutely — we'll include an eval harness and walk through how to add your prompt set. Optimize can raise alerts if quality drops beyond thresholds.
[09:05] Priya: Can you talk about network egress — we have strict egress rules in prod.
[09:09] Tomás: For Private deployments you can run everything in your VPC or on-prem with no public egress. For Hosted we have regional controls and dedicated peering options. We'll include network diagrams in the follow-up docs.
[09:24] Sofia: A quick question about billing — how do sandbox usage charges appear in the Console?
[09:29] Avery: Sandboxes are typically free within a limit; beyond that they roll into dev credits or appear on the usage dashboard with a tag. Full billing shows per-token breakdown. We'll send pricing notes.
[09:40] Tomás: Now quick demo of Optimize UI — shows per-route suggestions, recommended batch sizes, and a simulated cost delta if you flip on prefix caching. (Tomás narrates).
[09:54] Marcus: For our transcripts feature, we have long context windows — 20k tokens — how does that affect KV cache?
[09:59] Tomás: Long contexts increase KV cache pressure; our runtime supports efficient KV eviction and prefix caching. For very long docs we recommend chunking and embedding-based retrieval. Optimize can recommend chunk sizes.
[10:15] Sofia: Let's do a quick smoke test end-to-end. Priya will trigger the TS client to call chat.generate and we'll watch logs.
[10:20] Priya: Running... getting 429 now.
[10:23] Tomás: 429 indicates rate limit — sandbox keys have low qps. For dev teams, either stagger requests or we'll provision a higher-limit sandbox.
[10:33] Priya: Understood. We'll add rate-limiting middleware in front of our dev harness.
[10:38] Avery: Quick compliance note — Marcus, you'll want the SOC2 and KMS docs; I'll attach them. Also we have a compliance whitepaper on private deployments.
[10:48] Marcus: Great. Also can you confirm encryption-at-rest and in-flight?
[10:51] Tomás: Data is encrypted in transit (TLS) and at rest. For hosted we manage keys but can integrate with your KMS for Dedicated/Private.
[11:03] Sofia: Any gotchas with npm workspaces? We use monorepo with Yarn.
[11:07] Tomás: Monorepos are fine; be mindful of pathing for env var injection during build and ensure you don't check keys into lockfiles. We'll include CI snippets for Yarn workspaces.
[11:18] Priya: For the benchmark plan, what metrics should we capture?
[11:21] Tomás: p50/p95/p99 latency, token throughput, error rate, cost per 1k tokens, and variance under load. We'll propose a test harness and synthetic workload generator.
[11:36] Avery: Recap: we'll send repo, SOC2/KMS docs, and Tomás will propose a benchmark plan. Marcus to share residency requirements. Next call we'll deep-dive private deployment if they want to proceed.
[11:50] Sofia: Sounds good. One last small ask — can you add a note about truncated prompts in the SDK logs? We sometimes see subtle truncation when content-type mismatches happen.
[11:58] Tomás: Yep we'll add a troubleshooting section for truncation, content-type, and common 4xx/5xx patterns.
[12:06] Priya: Thank you all, really helpful pairing.
[12:09] Avery: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up by EOD with links.
[12:12] (call ends)

--- End of transcript ---

References mentioned:
- sandbox console link: https://console.redwood.ai/sandbox/fjord (invite-only)
- sample repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/fjord-quickstart (will share invite)
- SOC2 + KMS notes: link to internal doc (shared post-call)
- Benchmark plan template: will be attached

Notes about transcript quality: medium — a few mis-heard package names and "red wood" tokens were present; speaker labels may be approximate in 2 places.

Avery Park: Share minimal mono-repo with Python + TS quickstarts and README by 2025-06-06
Tomás Rivera: Draft proposed benchmark plan for 99th p99 latency + throughput check for on-prem by 2025-06-10
Marcus Dahl: Provide data residency requirements doc and current cloud regions list by 2025-06-08
Send sandbox keys and sample repo link
Schedule 60m technical deep-dive for private deployment scoping (Tomás + Marcus + infra team)

Kestrel Health — Console Debug Playbook Intro (traces, request logs, fallbacks)

AE/SE intro followed by a console-oriented debug playbook demo. Focus on tracing, request logs, error analysis, KV cache fallbacks, and audit/security controls. Customer crowded with SRE and privacy questions; ask for sample traffic and KMS details. Agreed next steps: security pack, benchmark run, sandbox tenant.
Console trace capture and playback
Request logs and structured search
Error analysis and root cause triage
KV cache / prefix cache observations and 'fallback' behavior
Private deployment constraints (VPC/KMS)
Benchmarking and test harness setup
[00:00] Lydia (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Lydia from Redwood inference. quick roll call?
[00:08] Priya (Kestrel): hi this is Priya, engineering manager on inference infra, hey.
[00:11] Ethan (Kestrel SRE): Ethan here, SRE, will be running the benchmarks.
[00:14] Samantha (Kestrel Privacy): Samantha, privacy and data residency.
[00:17] Marcus (Redwood SE): Marcus, i'm the systems engineer, i'll walk through the console and debug flows.
[00:27] Lydia: agenda quick — show our console tracing + request logs, go through common failure modes and the playbook, talk about dedicated vs hosted fallbacks, and Q&A.
[00:35] Priya: sounds good, the two things for us are: one, low 99th latency spikes and two, audit logs for PHI.
[00:42] Marcus: noted. i'll surface the trace-first workflow — capture a slow request, replay it in the console, and inspect token-level latency and kernel attribution.
[00:52] Marcus: opening the console, um, we have the request inspector — you'll see a timeline bar, each segment maps to token generation, KV cash — sorry, KV cache — hits get highlighted. sometimes the transcriber swaps that word, but in the UI it's KV cache.
[01:10] Ethan: can you show a realistic example, like a multi-turn chat where latency jumps at turn 3?
[01:15] Marcus: sure — loading an actual sample trace from our demo tenant. here's the trace id — note this is synthetic but uses patterns similar to production.
[01:27] Marcus: see at 00:01:20 we have a spike, token generation time doubled. opening the request log panel shows a partial OOM fallback on the quantized kernel, fallback to fp16, which increased latency.
[01:40] Priya: when fallback to fp16 happens, is there a visibility for which kernel was chosen?
[01:44] Marcus: yes. the console annotates kernel selections; we also expose kernel hints in the raw request log, so you can filter by kernel name. sometimes kernel names are vendor specific — e.g. cuShmmv or something — we try to normalize.
[01:58] Samantha: for audit — are request logs redacted automatically? PHI concern.
[02:03] Lydia: good question. by default we mask tokens marked as sensitive in the prompt via our redaction rules, but we can integrate with customer-side redaction and provide redact-at-source guidance. also we have retention settings per route.
[02:18] Samantha: do you produce an audit trail that shows who accessed a specific trace?
[02:21] Marcus: yes, the trace metadata includes actor id from SSO, IP range, and an immutable audit log entry — that's accessible in the ops panel.
[02:33] Marcus: switching to request search — you can query by model, route, status code, latency > threshold, or custom tags. here's a saved query we use for 95p latency regressions.
[02:45] Priya: what's the time granularity? can we do sub-second histograms?
[02:49] Marcus: we store per-token timestamps, so you get high resolution. histograms are approximate but accurate for triage.
[02:56] Ethan: how does sampling work? we have very high qps and don't want to log everything.
[03:01] Marcus: there are adaptive samplers — deterministic sampling for error traces plus probabilistic session sampling. you can also set dynamic rules: e.g., sample all traces above N ms or when fallback occurred.
[03:15] Priya: show the error analysis playbook, like how you'd triage a 500 that only happens for certain contexts.
[03:20] Marcus: yeah — step 1: find failing requests via query; step 2: group by model+route+quantization profile; step 3: examine kernel and memory metrics; step 4: attempt playback with same inputs in the sandbox.
[03:33] Marcus: i'll demonstrate grouping; here we have a cluster of failures that all share the same prefix token length and the same custom embedding middleware. that hints at an input pattern.
[03:47] Lydia: i'd also call out our automatic regression alerts — if a saved eval set changes quality or latency, we create a linked incident and populate the playbook with suggested remediation.
[03:59] Priya: that eval set — can we upload our own prompts for regression checks?
[04:03] Marcus: absolutely, customers can attach prompt suites and expected outputs, and the console will run periodic evals and send alerts on drift.
[04:13] Ethan: about KV cache — we've noticed some cache-eviction patterns that cause cold starts for multi-turn sessions. any tooling to see prefix cache hit rates?
[04:24] Marcus: yes, in the request inspector you'll see prefix hit % and a timeline of KV hits. also the Optimize tab suggests idle TTLs and batch sizes to improve hit rate.
[04:36] Priya: you mentioned fallbacks earlier — can you explain the fallback hierarchy?
[04:40] Marcus: fallback chain is: primary kernel -> quantized alternative -> lower-memory model variant -> remote fallback (hosted) -> queue/429 depending on policy. in Dedicated setups you can pin rollouts to avoid remote fallbacks.
[04:55] Samantha: remote fallback concerns me for PHI — if remote fallback routes to hosted, is data sent off-prem?
[05:01] Lydia: by default, in Private deployments we disable remote fallback. we can also enforce strict routing policies and log any attempted fallback attempts as security events.
[05:12] Priya: good. show us a case where a route hit a fallback due to sudden load.
[05:17] Marcus: pulling a recent incident — you can see initial requests processed on-device, then at spike we hit memory pressure and the orchestrator routed new requests to a fallback model variant in a different region. the console marks that and shows the routing decision tree.
[05:32] Marcus: here's the trace overlayed with the autoscaler events — note the timestamp where a new pod came up and latency dropped back down.
[05:41] Ethan: is that autoscaler event correlated with capacity commits? we need to know billing impact of sudden scale-up.
[05:47] Lydia: yes, we surface cost delta per rollout in the console and you can set budget caps to avoid runaway spend.
[05:55] Priya: okay. show the replay feature — play a failing request in sandbox.
[06:00] Marcus: hitting replay now. the replay uses the exact tokenized input and forces the same kernel and config; you can toggle quantization on/off to see impact.
[06:12] Marcus: play back shows the same 2.4s token spike when quantized kernel is used, but when we force the fp16 kernel the median is higher but stable — helps narrow cause.
[06:27] Priya: do you capture GPU metrics like SM utilization and memory alloc?
[06:31] Marcus: yes, GPU telemetry is attached to traces for Dedicated or if the host exposes metrics in Hosted. SM utilization, tensor core activity, and memory headroom are all available.
[06:43] Samantha: is that telemetry retained with the trace or obfuscated to avoid PHI leakage?
[06:49] Marcus: metrics are numeric and not PHI; trace input is subject to redaction. we can also provide a policy to never store raw inputs in hosted mode.
[06:59] Ethan: for our POC we'll likely run a Dedicated pilot. what's the onboarding time for a sandbox with i-3 or A100 equivalents?
[07:08] Lydia: typical onboarding for Dedicated sandbox is 3–5 business days for reserved lanes; for quick proofs we can spin a hosted trial in hours.
[07:18] Priya: we need to decide by end of month. cost/latency tradeoff will drive it.
[07:24] Marcus: i'd recommend starting with hosted to run the first workload, capture traces, then move to Dedicated if we see predictable throughput needs.
[07:33] Marcus: next, overlaying the request log you can expand the raw headers — most people forget the client-side retry headers and we often see thundering retry storms. here's a real example where 3xx retries caused burst.
[07:47] Ethan: nice, that would explain the transient 503s we saw.
[07:50] Priya: security question — how is SSO mapped? we need per-route RBAC.
[07:55] Marcus: we support SAML/SSO with SCIM provisioning and per-route RBAC. audit logs map user IDs to actions.
[08:04] Samantha: can we configure redaction rules per route? some routes touch PHI, others don't.
[08:09] Lydia: yes, route-level retention and redaction policies. we can also export anonymized traces for external debug.
[08:18] Marcus: showing the timeline again — here's a compressed view and a raw view. raw view shows each token latency, kernel call, and the exact memory allocation when the token executed.
[08:33] Priya: what about long-running sessions? do you show end-to-end session time?
[08:37] Marcus: session aggregator groups related requests by session id or cookie; you can see cumulative token count and total time.
[08:45] Ethan: we'd like to capture cold-cache vs warm-cache behavior in charts.
[08:49] Marcus: Optimize tab surfaces cold-start heatmaps; we can export CSVs for your plotting.
[08:57] Priya: do you offer synthetic load drivers for benchmark fidelity?
[09:01] Marcus: yep — we provide a test harness that can replay traffic at scale with adjustable timing to mimic your real qps and prefix lengths.
[09:10] Marcus: moving to the incident playbook portion: once you identify a root cause, the console can create an incident, assign owners, and attach the failing traces + remediation checklist.
[09:22] Lydia: the checklist can be customized per customer — e.g., run KV cache TTL bump, increase worker pool, change batch size.
[09:30] Priya: can that be integrated with our PagerDuty?
[09:33] Marcus: yes, alerts and incidents push to PD, Slack, or email.
[09:38] Ethan: for the benchmark run, i assume we'll want to stress the quantized path since that's our expected production config.
[09:44] Marcus: we'll set the harness to prefer quantized kernels and also force fallback scenarios to measure tail latency.
[09:52] Samantha: please include a privacy-preserving mode for the harness so we can scrub inputs.
[09:57] Marcus: we can run harness with token-length preservation but replace semantic content with synthetic tokens.
[10:05] Lydia: quick aside, competitor question — you asked about OtherAI. we have a few customers that compared and picked Redwood for better traceability and fallback controls.
[10:15] Priya: do you support on-prem air-gapped installs?
[10:18] Marcus: yes, Private offers air-gapped install with a customer-controlled control plane; in that mode remote fallback is disabled by default and there's no outbound traffic.
[10:29] Priya: can you show the audit export? we need to hand that to compliance occasionally.
[10:33] Marcus: exporting now — it's a gzipped CSV with trace id, user id, event, timestamp. secure download link is time-limited.
[10:42] Ethan: one more operational question — how are rolling updates handled for model variants without causing cache churn?
[10:48] Marcus: rollouts are canaryed by routing percentage and we keep KV cache compatibility modes; we recommend warming caches by replaying a representative prefix set before migrating traffic.
[10:59] Priya: show how the console surfaces a canary failure and auto-roll back.
[11:03] Marcus: here's a sample where the canary showed regression on our evals; the console automatically marked the deployment unhealthy and routed 100% back to previous variant. rollback event logs are available.
[11:17] Lydia: that automation avoids manual firefights during deploys.
[11:22] Priya: everything looks promising. can we go deeper on the test harness and what we need to provide?
[11:27] Marcus: ideal: 24h sample traffic, SLO targets for p50/p95/p99, and a representative prompt set. we'll handle tokenization and match your production batch sizes.
[11:36] Ethan: sending that by monday.
[11:38] Samantha: on the doc side, please include language for our privacy team on data handling.
[11:42] Lydia: i'll include a short appendix with redaction and retention controls.
[11:48] Marcus: quick demo of a deep error trace — note sometimes the transcription will confuse acronyms like KV cash or KMS, but the console shows the exact field.
[12:00] Marcus: here's a trace where a model variant returned malformed structured output; we can rerun the request in a validation mode that checks schema and flags regression.
[12:13] Priya: can the console auto-roll back on schema violations?
[12:17] Marcus: yes, you can configure automatic block rules on certain failure types.
[12:22] Lydia: ok let's surface the practical next steps: we'll send security docs, set up a sandbox, and schedule the benchmark.
[12:29] Priya: agreed. any blockers on your side?
[12:32] Lydia: none, just need the sample traffic and KMS requirements.
[12:36] Ethan: we'll pull a 24-hour window and the SLO doc.
[12:39] Samantha: and we'll review the redaction appendix when you send it.
[12:43] Marcus: last thing — sharing a small ops playbook link in chat: https://redwood.ai/ops-playbooks/console-debug-playbook (this is a demo link).
[12:55] Lydia: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[12:59] Priya: thanks, helpful demo.
[13:02] Ethan: thanks all.
[13:04] Samantha: bye.
