POC Weekly: Access Validation, Credential Handover & SLO Adjust

Header:
Date: 2027-10-13
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~43 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee, Priya Menon (Redwood) / Daniel Ruiz, Mei Chen, Samantha Ortiz, Arjun Patel (CoveHealth)

Summary:
Quick weekly POC sync focused on access handover, a failing canary from last night, and an SLO adjustment proposal. We validated credential flows, identified a network egress rule blocking traceroute in one AZ, and agreed on a short microbench for latency numbers. Security had a few KMS/SOC2 follow-ups but no blocker yet.

Topics:
- Access & credential handover status
- Canary failure root-cause (investigation and temporary mitigation)
- SLO target tuning for 95th/99th percentiles given production-like traffic
- KMS integration timeline and audit log retention
- Next step microbench plan and data handoff

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll try to keep this tight — three main things: access, canary, and SLOs. Priya's gonna walk through the bench plan first, then we'll triage the canary.
[00:18] Priya Menon: hi all, yeah, quick agenda. microbench that we mentioned last week, it's a small script that fires 2,000 short generation requests across three sequence lengths. we instrument token breakdown and end-to-end latency. i'll share the script in the drive after the call.
[00:35] Daniel Ruiz: cool. before we dive, quick note, last night's canary threw 503s in one AZ, we rotated keys and it came back but we saw increased tail latency.
[00:48] Mei Chen: yeah i pulled the gateway logs, looks like an outbound rule from the staging-subnet to our egress proxy was blocked; traceroute died at hop 4. i've put the raw logs in the network folder.
[01:02] Samantha Ortiz: from a security perspective we want to confirm that the keys used are service-accounts backed by our KMS, not long-lived tokens. also need clarity on audit log retention for the private deployment.
[01:18] Jordan Lee: great, that's helpful. Priya, the microbench — what does it record exactly?
[01:25] Priya Menon: tokenized counts, runtime pre/post KV cache, and the model variant id. we tag requests with an id so you can correlate traces in your sidecar. note: the bench uses continuous batching emulation which might slightly underreport single-request p95 — that's expected.
[01:44] Arjun Patel: when you say KV cache, is that the K-V cash? sorry, how is that persisted?
[01:50] Priya Menon: (laughs) K V cache, yes. it's in-memory per serving shard with optional warmup from S3 for cold starts; for Dedicated we can persist snapshots to the PVC but for hosted it's ephemeral and warmed from prior traffic.
[02:09] Daniel Ruiz: okay, so snapshotting isn't enabled for our pilot currently. that explains some cold-start spikes.
[02:15] Jordan Lee: right, snapshotting is an opt-in config. we can enable periodic warm snapshots but that increases storage ops slightly — small cost tradeoff.
[02:29] Mei Chen: can you outline the immediate root cause for the canary 503s? i saw timeouts to the model node pool.
[02:36] Priya Menon: from our side the initial signal was connection resets when the autoscaler spun up new replicas; the gateway retried and hit a throttling limit in the load balancer. the network egress block in one AZ amplified it because it prevented fallback routing.
[02:52] Jordan Lee: so two factors: autoscaler warmup + AZ-level egress rule. mitigation — temporary lower concurrency on the canary and enable cross-AZ fallback.
[03:02] Daniel Ruiz: agreed, we can open that egress rule but need to whitelist the Redwood subnet only. Mei, do we have that open?
[03:07] Mei Chen: i can open a targeted rule to the IP ranges you sent last week, but please resend; i think the list has one obsolete CIDR.
[03:15] Jordan Lee: will resend updated CIDR list after the call.
[03:19] Samantha Ortiz: regarding KMS — we want to ensure Redwood's key-signing process integrates with our HSM-backed KMS. is there a recommended flow?
[03:28] Priya Menon: yes, we support external KMS via customer-managed keys (CMK). recommended is to provision an encryption key and add Redwood's service principal with encrypt/decrypt rights; for signing you can use an asymmetric key and we validate using public key material. we'll share our integration doc.
[03:45] Samantha Ortiz: also SOC2 question: are audit logs stored for 90 days by default for the private control plane?
[03:52] Jordan Lee: default retention in hosted is 30 days; for Private we can configure retention as part of the deployment; 90 days is supported but may require the audit add-on — i'll include pricing notes in the doc.
[04:06] Mei Chen: noted. for the microbench, can we get the exact launch config? like concurrency, inter-arrival times?
[04:12] Priya Menon: yep — we'll run 2k requests: 70% short (64 tokens), 20% medium (256 tokens), 10% long (1k tokens). concurrency ramp: start at 5 qps, ramp to 50 qps across 2 minutes, hold for 4 minutes, cool down 1 minute. script will output csv + latency percentiles.
[04:37] Arjun Patel: will you include server-side traces? we want to stitch with our APM.
[04:41] Priya Menon: yes request IDs map to opentelemetry trace ids we emit; put your APM agent id in the header and we correlate. there may be some minor misalignment if clocks are off.
[04:55] Daniel Ruiz: about the SLOs — our PM asked for 95th < 250ms and 99th < 750ms. is that realistic for your hosted config?
[05:05] Jordan Lee: depends on model and quantization. for a 7B model on standard quant we commonly see p95 around 180-260ms with continuous batching tuned; p99 can spike, especially under cold-start. Priya, do you want to add color?
[05:20] Priya Menon: p95 180-260ms is plausible if you use warmed replicas and a small KV cache hit rate. p99 is sensitive to queueing and autoscaler. that's why we suggested canary-based SLOs: start with 95th at 300ms and 99th at 900ms for pilot, then tighten after two weeks of microbenching.
[05:40] Mei Chen: can we set the SLO for canary only, not for production?
[05:44] Jordan Lee: yes, pilot SLOs can be looser. proposal: canary SLOs 95/99 = 300/900ms, production target later 250/750ms. we'll document rollback thresholds.
[05:57] Samantha Ortiz: one more on compliance: we need a data flow diagram that shows where tokens, embeddings, and KV cache snapshots live.
[06:05] Jordan Lee: we'll attach a high-level data flow diagram to the security doc.
[06:09] Daniel Ruiz: back to the canary: do you recommend disabling autoscale for the canary?
[06:15] Priya Menon: don't fully disable, but set a slower scale-up policy and a max replica count lower than prod; that prevents sudden churn and keeps latency stable.
[06:25] Arjun Patel: Arjun here — quick infra question: do you need IAM roles from our side to pull warm snapshots?
[06:31] Priya Menon: yes we need a read-only role for the S3 bucket + a service account mapping; for Private, we use the same pattern with your object store.
[06:40] Mei Chen: i'll prep the role and service account today and share the ARN.
[06:44] Jordan Lee: perfect. action item: Mei to share traceroutes + role ARN.
[06:49] Daniel Ruiz: about the microbench results, how will you present the data?
[06:53] Priya Menon: CSV and a small dashboard. we'll annotate p95/p99 and KV-hit ratios; also provide a per-route cost estimate using our cost model.
[07:02] Samantha Ortiz: what's in that cost model? does it account for snapshot storage ops?
[07:07] Priya Menon: yes snapshot storage and egress cost when warming from S3 are included; we give a per-1M token estimate so you can see cost tradeoffs.
[07:15] Jordan Lee: competitive note: some customers have looked at Anthropic for lower-latency short-turnaround tasks but we found their throughput profile trades differently; just flagging since procurement asked.
[07:27] Daniel Ruiz: okay, interesting. thanks.
[07:30] Jordan Lee: any blockers on the credentialing/handover to finish the week?
[07:34] Mei Chen: not blockers — just waiting on the CIDR list and we'll open the egress rule. also i need the exact service principal for KMS permissions.
[07:43] Jordan Lee: i'll send both items after this call.
[07:46] Priya Menon: i'll kick off the microbench tonight against staging and post results by Sunday. note: there may be some noisy samples during snapshot warmups.
[07:55] Arjun Patel: i'll verify our APM trace config and ingest the opentelemetry headers.
[08:00] Samantha Ortiz: can we get the security doc by Monday? we want to present to legal on Tuesday.
[08:05] Jordan Lee: yes, we'll prioritize security doc and include the data flow diagram + KMS steps; target Monday EOD.
[08:13] Daniel Ruiz: cool. last thing — can we add a short postmortem template for the canary incident?
[08:17] Priya Menon: absolutely, we'll add a one-pager with timeline, root cause, mitigation, and follow-ups.
[08:23] Jordan Lee: sounds good. recap: Redwood sends CIDR list, SLO playbook, security doc, and microbench artifacts. CoveHealth shares traceroutes, role ARN, and validates logs. next sync same time next week unless security needs earlier.
[08:38] Daniel Ruiz: thanks everyone. meeting adjourned.

Shared artifacts mentioned:
- Drive: /shared/poc/microbench (Priya will upload script and csv)
- Network logs: /shared/poc/network-logs/traceroute-2027-10-13.log (Mei)
- Security doc: https://drive.company/covehealth/redwood-security-draft (to be uploaded)
- Canary dashboard link: https://dash.covehealth.internal/canary/2027-10-13 (internal)

Questions (explicitly asked):
- Samantha: Are audit logs retained for 90 days by default for Private? (answered: configurable, may need add-on)
- Mei: Exact concurrency and ramp settings for microbench? (answered and put in action)
- Daniel: Are the proposed SLOs achievable? (answered with conservative pilot numbers)

End of transcript.

Prefix stability, tokenization impacts, and cache metrics review - Verdant Innovations

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-06
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Jenna Kim (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Redwood), Alan Park (CTO, Verdant), Sara Cho (ML Lead), Daniel Ortega (Infra), Maya Li (Product)

Summary:
Quick technical deep-dive focused on prefix/prompt caching strategy, how tokenization choices affect KV cache hit rates, eviction policies for multi-tenant safety, and tradeoffs with quantized models and batching under a VPC/private deployment. Action items and pilot next steps agreed.

Topics (auto):
- Tokenization boundary sensitivity and prefix stability
- Cache key design (normalized prompts, metadata tags)
- Hotset vs hotcache eviction simulations
- Quantization and KV size tradeoffs
- Batching and latency SLOs in private runtime

[00:00] Jenna: hey everyone thanks for joining. can we do quick intros?
[00:05] Alan: yeah alan here, CTO at Verdant. we run a customer-facing assistant, highly prefix-sensitive prompts, lots of identical opening system messages.
[00:12] Sara: sara, ml lead, i'm focused on quality — especially when responses vary by tokenization.
[00:17] Daniel: daniel infra, responsible for private cloud and VPC peering.
[00:21] Jenna: great. marco on the call?
[00:24] Marco: yep marco ruiz, se — i'll lead the technical bits on kv, batching and kernel/quant notes.
[00:29] Maya: maya, product — will be shepherding success criteria.

[00:45] Marco: ok quick agenda: first we examine tokenization and how small changes in the prefix --- like a trailing space or punctuation --- can break cache hits; then key normalization, deduping, tenant tags; eviction policies for shared cache; and finally how quantization increases kv size and affects throughput, and recommendations for the private pilot.

[01:12] Alan: our main worry is correctness — if a cached continuation is wrong for one tenant or prompt variant, that's a showstopper. cost and latency matter but safety first.

[02:05] Marco: totally, so two prongs: 1) improve hit-rate without loosening semantic correctness, and 2) isolate tenants and provide safe fallback.

[03:00] Sara: quick note: our prompts often include user metadata embedded in the system prompt, like "User: <firstName>" which changes every request. so naive full-prompt keys are useless.

[03:17] Marco: yep that's classic. we recommend building a normalized key blueprint: strip or hash ephemeral user fields, canonicalize whitespace, run deterministic tokenization, and optionally include a small sketch of the last N tokens (e.g., 32-token signature) rather than the full prompt. that keeps keys compact and improves hit rates.

[04:02] Daniel: does Redwood provide tokenizer determinism across hosted/dedicated/private? we cannot have different tokenizers in prod vs pilot.

[04:12] Priya: good question — runtime includes a reproducible tokenizer binary; we ship the same tokenizer artifacts to private. but note, quantized kernels may alter subword segmentation slightly if model variant differs. we recommend pinning model versions and tokenizer hash.

[04:40] Sara: wait slight differences in segmentation? i thought tokenizers are deterministic.

[04:47] Marco: generally deterministic, but when you use different model checkpoints (even quantized variants) the vocabulary or merge rules sometimes change in edge cases. and some tooling pipelines re-normalize punctuation differently. best practice: pin both model hash and tokenizer hash in the key.

[05:10] Alan: ok that adds operational overhead but seems necessary. what about using token-level prefixes (kv cache keyed directly by token ids) vs string keys?

[05:23] Marco: token-id keys are more stable across whitespace but can be large; we usually hash the token id sequence to a fixed-length signature. collision risk is low with 128-bit hash but you still need to tag by tenant and model-variant to avoid cross-tenant leakage.

[06:00] Maya: can you give expected hit-rate uplifts with normalization? we ran a simple analysis and saw ~3-4x difference depending on user field variance.

[06:15] Marco: sure, in our internal datasets normalizing ephemeral fields and canonicalizing formatting bumped hit-rates from ~6% to ~28% on chat-ish workloads where system prompts are stable. with token-signature strategies we saw up to ~45% for very templated prefixes. your mileage will vary.

[07:00] Sara: that's promising. are there tradeoffs with freshness? if we normalize too much we might accidentally serve stale context when the ephemeral user variable actually meaningfully changes the expected continuation.

[07:14] Marco: yep that's why we suggest multi-tier keys: a strict key (exact prompt hashed) for conservative correctness; a relaxed key (normalized sketch) that is only used when a confidence filter passes — e.g., semantic similarity score between the new prompt and the cached prompt above a threshold. When in doubt, fall back to live generation.

[08:10] Alan: how do you compute that semantic similarity cheaply? can't run an embed per request.

[08:18] Marco: two techniques: 1) use cheap fingerprinting Hj/MinHash on normalized tokens for a quick similarity estimate, or 2) precompute embeddings for canonical prompt families and tag keys with family ids. embeddings add cost but are amortizable for stable families.

[09:05] Daniel: on eviction policies for a shared KV store: we will be multi-tenant and resource constrained in initial pilot. how do you avoid one tenant's hotset overrunning others?

[09:20] Marco: use tenant-aware quotas and weighted LRU. i.e., maintain per-tenant token budget and global budget. when global pressure increases, evict from tenants over their pro-rata share first. also keep a cold-reserve for spikes to ensure tail latency.

[10:10] Priya: we also recommend time-decayed hotness metric: hits decay over time so short-lived spikes don't permanently dominate the cache.

[11:00] Sara: ok about safety — what if a relaxed-key hit leaks user-specific instructions?

[11:08] Marco: that's the big one. never apply relaxed-key hits to prompts that contain PII or user-specific instructions (e.g., "do not share" or legal texts). Use prompt classifiers (fast regex or small model) to tag prompts as sensitive; sensitive prompts go through strict-key path only.

[11:45] Alan: can we tag tenant and content-sensitivity flags in our app before calling Redwood? we'd prefer app-level hints.

[11:53] Jenna: absolutely — API supports hints like x-prefix-safety: sensitive|non-sensitive and tenant_id. those are used in key generation.

[12:20] Maya: walk us through a concrete example: user asks the assistant which plan to pick, the system prompt contains product mappings. how does the cache key look?

[12:35] Marco: simplified: key = hash(model_hash + tokenizer_hash + tenant_id + family_id + sketch32 + sensitivity_flag). where sketch32 is hashed last-32 tokens signature. If the incoming prompt differs only in user name, sketch matches and we may hit the relaxed key; if the user instruction changes, sketch diverges and only strict-key path applies.

[13:40] Sara: what about tokenization edge cases, like emoji, zero-width joiners? we saw mismatched token boundaries causing cache misses.

[14:00] Marco: those are common. recommended: normalize unicode (NFKC), replace or canonicalize emoji sequences to stable placeholders before tokenization, and log mismatches in an observability pipeline so we can iteratively expand normalization rules.

[14:50] Alan: can the Redwood runtime apply those normalizations server-side? we'd rather not change client code for a pilot.

[15:00] Priya: yes, we can offer optional server-side normalization layers but we flag changes in a compatibility report. for strict compliance you should test locally because normalization can slightly alter semantics.

[16:30] Daniel: moving to quantization: what are the practical kv-size differences when serving 8-bit vs 4-bit quantized variants?

[16:42] Marco: KV cache is mostly floating-point key/value pairs for attention caches. quantized models often reduce KV memory footprint — 8-bit can cut memory by ~2x vs fp16, 4-bit more but at cost of compute overhead to dequantize. However, quantization can change tokenization consistency if the model variant differs, so pin model hash.

[17:30] Sara: note: our primary production is sensitive to subtle generation differences — are quality regressions from 4-bit an issue?

[17:45] Marco: many teams see minor quality delta for completion tasks but it's model-dependent. recommended approach: run a side-by-side A/B run with your canonical prompts. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles per workload; for prefix-heavy workloads you might keep fp16 for critical families and use quantized for lower-priority routes.

[18:40] Maya: how does caching interact with quantization in terms of performance?

[18:50] Marco: caching reduces kernel calls; if your KV is warm, quantization overhead matters less because you skip full forward compute. but when cache misses spike, quantized backends may have higher latency due to dequantize steps — depends on kernel implementation and hardware. we include kernel-level benchmarks in the pilot.

[19:40] Alan: we run on-prem racks with A100-ish hardware. will Redwood's private runtime run optimized kernels or will we need to compile?

[19:50] Priya: private runtime ships with precompiled kernels for popular hardware (A100, H100 families). if you're on slightly older GPUs we may need a quick compile step; we give CI scripts to prebuild.

[20:25] Daniel: firewall/peering question: for private control plane + local runtime how do we handle KV metrics and audit logs — do logs leave our VPC?

[20:35] Jenna: logs are configurable: you can keep audit logs entirely on your side in Private mode, or ship summaries to Redwood for support. we also support local KMS and HSM integration.

[21:10] Sara: about batching: we have a mixture of interactive and batch flows. what batching strategies preserve our 200ms p95 interactive SLO while reducing cost for background tasks?

[21:22] Marco: continuous batching with latency targets is the sweet spot: maintain a small warm pool for interactive (no batching or micro-batches) and a separate pooled path for batch requests with higher latency allowance. Redwood runtime supports per-route batching policies and burst lanes for interactive traffic.

[22:05] Maya: any recommended numbers for micro-batching thresholds?

[22:12] Marco: for 200ms p95 interactive you want micro-batch windows ~1-3ms with prefetched KV; for background flows you can batch up to 16-32 tokens per request and window 10-50ms depending on traffic. these are workload-specific so we'll run tuning in the pilot.

[23:00] Alan: can we throttle specific tenants if they produce noisy huge prefixes?

[23:08] Marco: yes that's part of tenant-aware QoS: rate limits, token budgets, and dynamic throttles. we can apply soft-limits first and escalate to hard-limits if abuse observed.

[23:40] Sara: observability — we need to see per-key hit rate distributions and failure modes. what instrumentation does Redwood provide?

[23:48] Marco: per-tenant and per-route metrics: key-hit-rate, average prefix-length, eviction-rate, tail latency, model-variant diffs. we can stream metrics to your Prometheus, and there's also a console view with timelines. we also provide sampled transcripts and a mismatch detector for normalization failures.

[24:30] Maya: do you keep actual prompt text in logs? privacy is a no-go for us.

[24:37] Jenna: logs can be tokenized-only or hashed-only. we support PII redaction and local-only logging. all options documented in our security pack.

[25:00] Alan: what's the plan for the pilot and what success metrics should we set?

[25:10] Marco: pilot plan suggestion: 1) run 48-hour synthetic hotset run with your canonical prompts to exercise cache hit behavior; 2) run a shadow production replay for 1 week; 3) A/B a quantized variant on a subset of low-risk routes. Success metrics: p95 latency <=200ms for interactive, hit-rate uplift >=20% for targeted families, no cross-tenant leakage (0 incidents), and cost-per-1000 tokens reduced by >=15% on pilot routes.

[26:05] Daniel: can you provide the synthetic harness?

[26:10] Jenna: yes will share harness link and a docker image.

[27:00] Sara: another concern: collision risk with hashed signatures — is 128-bit enough?

[27:08] Marco: 128-bit collision is astronomically unlikely for your volumes, but we also keep a per-entry nonce and tenant tag so collisions can't cross-tenant. collisions are also logged to the mismatch detector.

[27:45] Alan: curious about fallback policies — if a relaxed-key match occurs but downstream safety checks fail, do you have an automatic regeneration path?

[27:52] Marco: yes, the runtime will re-run generation on mismatch or safety fail and also optionally trigger a negative cache entry for that sketch to reduce subsequent wrong relax-hits for a small TTL.

[28:30] Maya: show of hands — any blockers on security side to run the pilot?

[28:36] Daniel: need SSO and SOC2 docs, plus proof-of-concept for KMS integration.

[28:42] Jenna: we'll attach the security pack and KMS integration guide in the follow-up.

[29:10] Sara: i want to dig into the data we saw earlier: an internal run showed certain prompt families with 60% miss despite being templated; we suspect unicode and punctuation variance. can you run an analysis?

[29:22] Marco: yes we'll run tokenization diff on your sample. please share a dump of ~5k prompt headers.

[30:05] Alan: cost modeling — how should we think about dedicated vs shared private deployment for this workload?

[30:17] Marco: depends on concurrency and tail-latency needs. dedicated reserved capacity gives predictable throughput and lower unit cost at high scale. private with shared pools + strong caching may be cost effective early on because caching reduces consumed GPU cycles, but dedicated is more predictable for high-traffic tenants. we'll provide a cost model spreadsheet that lets you plug in expected hit rates and concurrency.

[31:10] Priya: also include the impact of prefix cache hit-rate on token throughput: each hit saves a variable number of token decodes — we'll help estimate median saved tokens per family.

[32:05] Sara: curious about one more edge case: if a cached continuation was generated under an older instruction set (different system prompt) and now the system prompt changed, how do you prevent stale responses?

[32:20] Marco: include a system_prompt_hash in the key and an optional TTL per key that invalidates on prompt schema changes. plus we support a 'prompt versioning' header so app can indicate major changes.

[33:05] Alan: great. what's the expected turnaround for initial benchmark results?

[33:12] Jenna: we'll share the benchmark skeleton within 48 hours and run first synthetic results within a week.

[34:00] Maya: any other Redwood notes about multi-tenant safety?

[34:06] Marco: two-layer defense: engineering controls (tenant tags, quotas, per-tenant eviction) and runtime checks (sensitivity classifier, strict vs relaxed key paths). also maintain audit trails for any relaxed-key hits used to seed responses.

[35:00] Sara: one tangential question: do you recommend storing prefix sketches in a separate high-availability KV (in-memory) or co-located on disk-backed store?

[35:12] Marco: hot KV should be in-memory (RAM/NVMe-backed with persistence off) for latency. we also persist checkpointed cold snapshots to disk for warm-starts. persistent cold store reduces warmup time after restarts.

[36:00] Daniel: what are operational costs for keeping a larger in-memory KV? we have limited RAM budget on-prem.

[36:08] Marco: that's where eviction policies and hotset sizing matter. you can configure a hot-reserve per tenant and cap global memory. plus Redwood Optimize can recommend sketch size and TTLs to stay within given RAM budgets.

[37:10] Alan: do you have example TTLs you recommend?

[37:17] Marco: for highly templated families, TTLs of hours are fine; for conversational ephemeral data, minutes. hybrid approach: hotset with short TTL and a warm backup with longer TTL.

[38:00] Priya: quick comment on observability: we'll provide dashboards with per-key sample traces so you can replay the request that created cached entry. those traces are scrubbed unless you opt-in to store plaintext.

[39:00] Sara: ok i'm convinced. let's talk about the actual pilot steps and who's responsible.

[39:10] Jenna: pilot scope: 48h synthetic run + 1 week shadow replay + quantized A/B on 10% traffic for non-sensitive routes. deliverables: harness, cost model, kernels for your infra, and security docs.

[39:40] Daniel: we'll provision a staging VPC and run the peering; tentative window 2026-05-18 to 2026-05-25.

[40:05] Marco: we'll need a short access window for metrics export — can be read-only.

[40:20] Alan: how will we validate zero leakage? do you run a negative test?

[40:28] Marco: yes we can run cross-tenant synthetic tests designed to detect leakage and verify tenancy isolation.

[41:00] Maya: any legal considerations for logs?

[41:06] Jenna: we'll include the legal/process docs in the follow-up; but main point: you can opt to keep PII redaction and audit logs on-prem.

[41:40] Sara: earlier you mentioned sketch sizes. what's the sensible sketch-length for us?

[41:48] Marco: start with 32-token sketch and measure. for long system prompts maybe 64. smaller sketches reduce KV size but may lower hit fidelity.

[42:30] Alan: what about cache key entropy and partitioning? we want to avoid hot partitions on certain cache shards.

[42:39] Marco: consistent hashing with tenant-aware sharding. also use salted hashes per time-window to spread writes if you see a single tenant hotspot. avoid sequential key patterns.

[43:10] Daniel: deep ops question: what's the eviction coordination mechanism across a multi-node cluster?

[43:17] Marco: we use a distributed lease protocol to coordinate evictions and to avoid thundering herds. evictions are lazy and often executed by local nodes first; global rebalancing runs asynchronously.

[44:05] Sara: any recommended instrumentation to detect repeated misses for the same family?

[44:12] Marco: yes an alert for family-miss-rate > threshold and repeated normalization mismatches. we can attach auto-tickets to your issue tracker if you want.

[45:00] Maya: quick question about compiled kernels: how long is typical compile time for custom hardware?

[45:06] Marco: usually minutes for common GPU types; rare architectures can take a few hours. we provide parallel compile infra.

[45:45] Alan: ok let's reiterate next steps so we have clear assignees.

[45:52] Jenna: recap: Jenna to share harness, cost model, security docs; Marco to run tokenization diffs and synthetic prefix warm/cold runs; Sara to provide prompt families; Daniel to provision staging VPC and share access window; all to reconvene after synthetic results.

[46:20] Sara: question — can the pilot include a short on-device test for offline inference? we have an edge node team.

[46:30] Marco: edge inference often needs smaller quantized models; caching strategies differ. we can scope that as a follow-up if you want.

[47:10] Alan: any gotchas you want to call out?

[47:16] Marco: main gotchas: 1) tokenization drift across environments, 2) relaxed-key safety false positives if sensitivity detection is off, 3) underestimated warm-up time after restarts if you don't persist warm snapshots.

[48:00] Priya: also note observability sampling rate — sample too little and you won't see rare mis-hits; sample too much and you leak privacy. configure carefully.

[48:45] Daniel: we'll review the security pack this week.

[49:05] Jenna: i'll send a follow-up with all links; also included is a short checklist for VPC peering and firewall ports.

[50:00] Marco: i'll kick off tokenization diffs once we get the prompt dump. expect initial notes in 3 business days.

[50:20] Maya: any final questions?

[50:25] Alan: none from me. thanks, very useful.

[50:30] Sara: thanks all.

[50:35] Jenna: thanks folks — we'll send notes and schedule the pilot kickoff.

Closing notes:
- Links to be shared: benchmark harness (docker + scripts), cost model spreadsheet, security pack, tokenizer diff tool, synthetic harness results template.
- Risk: normalization changes can affect semantics — recommended local verification.

Action items reiterated: see action_items field above.

End of transcript.

MosaicPath Console: route inspector & cost breakdown demo

Intro demo of Redwood Console route inspector, per-route telemetry and cost attribution. Customer focused on mapping traffic to billing and identifying high-cost routes. Discussed hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs, SSO/KMS requirements, and pilot next steps.
Meeting header: 2026-04-21 16:00 PT; duration ~42m; attendees: Daniela Park (Redwood AE), Marco Reyes (Redwood SE), Aisha Kumar (Redwood Solutions), Leah Chen (MosaicPath), Omar Diaz (MosaicPath), Priya Nair (MosaicPath), Samir Patel (MosaicPath Finance)

Summary (auto): quickconsole walkthrough, focus on per-route cost attribution and route inspector; collection of sample traffic; agreement to run pilot and share security artifacts.

[00:00] Daniela Park: hey everybody, thanks for joining. can you all hear me okay?
[00:05] Leah Chen: yes, can hear you. thanks da- uh Daniela.
[00:12] Marco Reyes: hi team, marco here, i'll be showing the route inspector and cost breakdown pieces. a couple of folks from infra on your end?
[00:20] Omar Diaz: yep that is me, omar, s-r-e. priya's on too.
[00:25] Priya Nair: yep, hi all. quick context, we're running a bunch of inference routes in-house today and billing is a black box across teams, our finance partner samir wanted to join to ask about chargeback.
[00:36] Samir Patel: thanks, yeah, want to see how costs map to teams, curious about per-route attributions and smoothing anomalies.

[01:02] Marco Reyes: great, quick agenda: 1) high level console view, 2) route inspector per-route telemetry and token-level cost where possible, 3) compare hosted vs dedicated economics, 4) questions and next steps.

[02:15] Marco Reyes: opening the console... this is the usage overview dashboard, shows total tokens, latencies, and cost estimate. notice the left nav under 'Routes' — when you click a route you get a breakdown of request volumes by model, avg latency, p95, and then cost split.
[02:40] Priya Nair: is that using our billing export mapping or is it an estimated cost model?
[02:48] Marco Reyes: good question. for hosted customers we use Redwood's internal unit pricing to estimate per-route costs. if you supply your reserved rates or committed pricing for dedicated, we overlay that so the numbers match your invoicing. occasionally the transcription may say 'we used committed rates' but it's an overlay, not a rewrite of your invoices.

[04:03] Marco Reyes: zooming into a route here — route inspector shows a time series of requests per minute, a token distribution histogram, and cost per 1k tokens. we also surface 'hot' request patterns that spike KV cash — I mean KV cache churn — apologies.
[04:20] Omar Diaz: KV cash, ha. yes cache churn has bitten us before. can you filter by model variant and sequence length?
[04:28] Marco Reyes: yes, you can facet by model variant, sequence length buckets, and by metadata tags like service, org, and customer id. the console supports custom route tags so you can map requests back to product teams.

[06:04] Leah Chen: how do you handle routing policies — if we have a canary or overflow to cheaper model during burst do we still get accurate cost attribution?
[06:12] Marco Reyes: we attach route context + fallback info. the cost attribution is tagged per actual execution: so if the request fell back to a quantized variant, the cost recorded is the variant's execution cost. smoothing across fallbacks is optional but we can show both 'logical route' and 'execution trace' views.

[07:30] Priya Nair: we're particularly worried about tokenization differences across open models — will the token counts be normalized?
[07:38] Marco Reyes: tokens are counted at the runtime tokenization step we run; there can be small variances between tokenizers, we surface 'model tokenizer' used in the trace. we also provide a conversion table for common models (gpt-style vs llama-style) in the mapping doc.

[09:05] Marco Reyes: switching to the cost drilldown: per-route breakdown has three panes — volume, tokens, and estimated $ cost. you can expand the cost pane to see unit cost contributors: kernel selection, batching efficiency, and sustained instance surcharge for dedicated pools.
[09:26] Samir Patel: sustained instance surcharge? can you unpack that?
[09:30] Marco Reyes: sure — for dedicated capacity there's a baseline reserved cost which we amortize across tokens; on top of that we show runtime-specific variable cost (e.g., increased kernel use for long sequences). the surcharge term is our label for the proportion of fixed reserved cost allocated to a route when utilization is low.

[11:10] Leah Chen: curious about how much of the cost savings come from caching vs batching. our traffic is very bursty.
[11:18] Marco Reyes: for bursty traffic, prefix/KV caching can save a lot if you have repeated prompts; batching helps for steady streams. our Optimize recommendations will suggest batching windows and quantization for routes with high p50 token lengths. we can run sample simulations if you share traffic traces.

[12:55] Omar Diaz: security — we need SOC2 docs, SSO via SAML, and KMS integration for keys. any gotchas for on-prem vs VPC?
[13:03] Daniela Park: yes, we have standard SOC2 and ISO artifacts; SSO/SAML is supported and RBAC maps to your IdP groups. for private deployments we support customer-managed KMS/HSM and detailed audit logs — you'll get audit events per request including route id and execution variant. we'll share the security pack after the call.

[14:45] Priya Nair: does audit logging include full prompt text or is that redactable?
[14:52] Aisha Kumar: logs are configurable — you can choose to redact prompt content, or store only digests/hashes for QA. retention policies are configurable per environment.

[16:20] Marco Reyes: demoing the instrumentation flow now: you can add route tags via header or SDK parameter, or set at the tenant-level in the API. we also ingest platform labels from telemetry systems like prometheus or Datadog if you forward them.

[17:55] Leah Chen: will we have to change our clients a lot to send these tags?
[18:01] Marco Reyes: minimal; if you already set a header for team or service we can read it. otherwise a small SDK patch to attach route metadata on request will do. we include migration snippets in our runbook.

[19:40] Marco Reyes: showing anomaly detection — console flags cost anomalies by z-score and by manual thresholds. you can set alerts to slack/email and create a ticket template that pre-populates with route traces and example requests.
[20:10] Omar Diaz: nice. can we backfill cost attribution for historical data?
[20:16] Marco Reyes: yes, if you provide request logs with timestamps and model/execution variant we can retroactively compute per-route costs for the last N months — there's a small processing fee for large backfills.

[22:03] Priya Nair: on accuracy, if we pin a route to a quantized variant for cost reasons, how do we manage quality regressions?
[22:12] Marco Reyes: great question — Redwood Optimize ties quality monitoring to prompt sets. you can define golden prompts and we run evals comparing outputs across variants. if regression exceeds threshold, we alert and can auto-fallback to a higher-quality variant.

[24:00] Samir Patel: what does the pilot look like? we want to start small with a few routes and get a chargeback-ready report for finance.
[24:08] Daniela Park: typical pilot is 2–4 weeks: we instrument 3–5 routes, import a week's of traffic, enable the route inspector and cost attribution, and deliver a chargeback-ready CSV plus a live dashboard for stakeholders. we'll also run a small benchmark to validate unit costs.

[25:12] Leah Chen: timeline wise we have a quarterly review on 05/18, it'd be great to have initial pilot numbers before that.
[25:20] Daniela Park: understood — we can aim to deliver pilot results week of 05/11 if we get traffic samples and finalize pilot scope this week.

[26:45] Marco Reyes: returning to the console, here's an example of route-level tags enabling team-level chargebacks: you can pivot by tag and create allocation rules to split shared infrastructure across teams by percent-of-requests or token-weighted allocation.
[27:05] Samir Patel: token-weighted allocation seems fairer for us given long-form generation in one of our products. can the console export a per-team monthly cost breakdown CSV?
[27:12] Marco Reyes: yes, exportable, and you can schedule recurring exports for finance. we also have a reporting API if you want programmatic ingestion into your billing system.

[29:02] Priya Nair: curious about dedicated pools — if we reserve gpus for high-throughput routes how does autoscaling and burst to hosted work?
[29:10] Marco Reyes: Redwood Dedicated supports configurable autoscale and burst policies; you can specify a fallback tier where overflow requests route to hosted cheaper instances or a smaller quantized model. the console will show both tiers and attribute cost to the actual execution.

[31:00] Omar Diaz: any readiness checklist for VPC/private deployments?
[31:06] Aisha Kumar: short checklist: network peering/vpn, routing rules, KMS access, NFS or object store for artifacts, and reserved capacity sizing. we'll send a detailed onboarding doc and a template security questionnaire.

[33:12] Leah Chen: do you support encryption-at-rest with customer keys?
[33:18] Daniela Park: yes, both at-rest and in-transit; customer-managed keys are supported in private deployments. for hosted we can also integrate with major cloud KMS providers.

[34:45] Marco Reyes: quick note on instrumentation: we recommend tagging early in the request lifecycle to capture full context including user id, product feature, and customer tier. small differences in tag placement can cause big mismatches in attribution.

[36:20] Priya Nair: one more thing — how do we handle ephemeral sessions where token reuse is high? does attribution credit repeated prefixes correctly?
[36:28] Marco Reyes: the KV cache and prefix caching logic are exposed in the trace; we show cache hits and attribute marginal token costs for each request. repeated prefixes will show lower marginal cost per request in the inspector.

[38:10] Samir Patel: pricing — will you send a pricing sheet that separates reserved capacity vs token-unit pricing for hosted?
[38:18] Daniela Park: yes, we'll send a tailored pricing sheet with sample math for your traffic patterns, plus the pilot pricing.

[39:25] Leah Chen: ok, quick recap?
[39:30] Daniela Park: recap — goals: instrument 3–5 routes, provide 1 week of anonymized traffic, run a 2-week pilot to produce a chargeback-ready report and dashboard. deliverables: pilot proposal/pricing, security pack (SOC2 + KMS docs), sample dashboard JSON, and scheduling pilot kick-off. owners: Daniela (pilot proposal & pricing), Marco (runbook + dashboard JSON), Priya (traffic samples), Aisha (security pack share).

[40:12] Priya Nair: sounds good. I'll sync with Samir and get the traffic files.
[40:18] Samir Patel: thanks — we'll try to get budget approved quickly.

[41:00] Daniela Park: great, i'll send notes and next steps after the call. thanks everyone.
[41:10] Marco Reyes: thanks, bye.
[41:20] Omar Diaz: thanks all, bye.

End of transcript.

Verdant Harbor - control scout: SSO/KMS/RBAC audit

Initial security/governance discovery with Verdant Harbor. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment tradeoffs, SOC2/ISO evidence requests, SSO/SAML and SCIM provisioning, RBAC mapping, audit log retention/granularity, and encryption/KMS options including BYOK and HSM. Agreed to share SOC2 report, KMS whitepaper, and draft RBAC mapping template. Next step: run a short bench & connectivity test; SE to propose sample RBAC model and SAML config checklist.
SE to send RBAC mapping template and SAML checklist by 2026-08-10
Redwood to share SOC2 type II report and encryption/KMS whitepaper
Schedule 30m connectivity/latency test for dedicated pool (w/ sample prompt) week of 2026-08-17
Customer to provide list of PII data flows and desired retention windows
Marco Ruiz: prepare RBAC role-to-permission mapping template (due 2026-08-10)
Jasmine Patel: attach SOC2 report and KMS whitepaper to CRM deal VH-2026-081 (due 2026-08-09)
Avery Cole: share high-level data flow diagram and retention matrix (due 2026-08-14)
Li Chen: spin up a short dedicated infra test and invite Verdant Harbor for connectivity check (target week 2026-08-17)
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-08-07 09:00 PT / 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jasmine (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Li (Redwood SE), Avery (Verdant Harbor Head of Platform), Samir (Security Architect), Rita (Compliance), Devin (DevOps)

[00:00] Jasmine: Hey everyone cc: thank you for joining, really appreciate you carving out time. Well do a quick intros then jump into security controls and your hosting preferences.
[00:18] Avery: Thanks, Jasmine. Short background — Verdant Harbor runs B2B SaaS for maritime logistics, lots of customer PII and regulatory needs in EU and US, so security and data residency are big.
[00:30] Samir: Right, were evaluating whether Redwood hosted will meet our compliance or if we need dedicated or private. Main gates are SOC2 evidence, SSO integration (SAML), RBAC, detailed audit logs, and KMS/BYOK.
[00:44] Marco: Great, thats exactly the checklist others have used. Quick outline from our side — Hosted (fastest), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools w/ tenant isolation), Private (VPC/on-prem for strict residency). There are tradeoffs around latency, cost, and control over keys.
[01:05] Rita: On SOC2, we need Type II plus the last six months of controls; also ISO27001 is in our roadmap — do you have either?
[01:14] Jasmine: We do SOC2 Type II and current ISO attestation is in process. Ill attach the SOC2 report after the call. Note: some vendor names in the report might be redacted.
[01:23] Samir: Fine, but well need the control mapping — mapping of Redwood controls to our control framework.
[01:30] Jasmine: Yes, we can provide a controls matrix.
[01:33] Devin: Quick Q on SSO — we use SAML 2.0 with Okta and SCIM for provisioning. How mature is your SAML/SCIM support?
[01:42] Li: We support SAML 2.0 SSO and SCIM for provisioning. Theres a standard SAML metadata exchange, and SCIM v2 for provisioning groups/users. There are a couple of known quirks with some IdPs where nameID formats cause mismatches, but we have a checklist.
[01:58] Samir: Do you support enforced MFA at IdP, session timeouts, and session re-authn for admin operations?
[02:07] Marco: We delegate auth to your IdP for SSO sessions. Admin ops in Console are RBAC-protected; we surface session creation timestamps and session termination APIs. We support SAML attributes for group membership to map roles.
[02:22] Rita: For RBAC, we need role separation: platform-admin, infra-ops, compliance-viewer (read-only logs), and app-service accounts. Can your teams map fine-grain permissions to these roles?
[02:34] Li: Yes — our RBAC model supports resource-level permissions (model endpoints, deployments, audit logs) and we can add custom roles. Marco: Weve seen customers define about 8-12 roles to stay manageable.
[02:47] Samir: How about service accounts and key management? We want keys to be customer-managed (BYOK) with automatic rotation every 90 days and HSM-backed storage (FIPS 140-2).
[03:00] Marco: Dedicated and Private support BYOK. Hosted supports an envelope encryption pattern where your KMS (KMS in your cloud) can be used to wrap keys in some plans. For HSM/FIPS, dedicated/private can integrate with HSM-backed KMS or on-prem HSM appliances.
[03:18] Avery: So with hosted wed lose BYOK? Thats the tradeoff?
[03:21] Jasmine: Hosted has options — we have a hosted tier that allows customer-managed keys (theres some integration work), but the highest control (full HSM in customer's VPC) is only with Private.
[03:33] Devin: What about at-rest encryption for model artifacts and cache? And transit? Do you have TLS everywhere?
[03:38] Li: All traffic in transit is TLS 1.2+; at-rest encryption is AES-256. Model artifacts and KV cache are encrypted by default. If you opt for BYOK, keys are wrapped by your KMS.
[03:51] Rita: Audit logs — granularity and retention. We need immutable logs for admin auth changes, model deployments, inference requests for audit sampling. Retention policy target is 18 months for logs and 7 years for certain audit artifacts. Is that feasible?
[04:08] Marco: We can export audit logs to your storage (S3/GCS/Azure Blob) with a configurable retention. Our default retention in hosted is 90 days; dedicated can be extended, and private gives you full control. For 7-year archival, customers use exported buckets with lifecycle policies.
[04:24] Samir: How real-time is the log export? We need near real-time for alerting.
[04:29] Li: We push logs to a streaming endpoint — typical delivery within seconds to minutes. For near real-time alerting youd forward into your SIEM (Splunk/Datadog).
[04:38] Avery: Any information on tokenization and PII redaction before logs? Wed prefer PII not appear in logs.
[04:46] Marco: We redact certain prompt fields by default in hosting — but prompt-level auditing can be configured. If you need to avoid storing raw prompts, we can use prefix/KV caching strategies that avoid logging content, or redact at ingestion. We should map exactly which fields you consider PII.
[04:59] Samir: Data residency — some EU customers require EU-only processing. Can Redwood guarantee region pinning for hosted requests?
[05:07] Jasmine: Yes, region routing policies are supported. Hosted can pin to EU regions; Dedicated can be placed in specific regions; Private obviously runs in your VPC. We do cross-region fallbacks only if allowed by policy.
[05:21] Rita: Regarding SOC2 evidence — we will need to get the SOC2 report and also evidence of encryption controls, key rotation schedules, and incident response playbooks.
[05:32] Jasmine: We'll provide the SOC2 Type II and an overview of key management controls and playbooks. Some of the deeper artifacts require an NDA but we can share redacted extracts.
[05:42] Devin: Latency/tradeoffs — if we go dedicated to meet residency/BYOK and fine-grain logging, what's overrun on cost and latency compared to hosted?
[05:52] Marco: Dedicated is higher fixed cost but gives predictable throughput and locality. Latency is comparable to hosted in the same region; the biggest delta is cost model — dedicated has committed units. We can run a quick bench with your sample requests to show per-token latency and throughput.
[06:06] Avery: On the RBAC side, does Redwood support SCIM group sync so we can manage access via Okta groups?
[06:12] Li: Yes, SCIM group sync is supported. You can map SCIM groups to Redwood roles. Well share the SCIM schema and a short checklist for Okta.
[06:21] Samir: One subtlety — we want an immutable audit trail for any admin changes, with who changed what and before/after values for role grants. Does your audit do diffs?
[06:31] Marco: We record admin actions with metadata and old/new values for config-like changes. For some actions we include diffs; for others we include snapshots. We also persist the actors identity (SAML subject) when available.
[06:44] Rita: For compliance, we also need a record of subprocessor locations and a data processing addendum.
[06:50] Jasmine: We'll provide a subprocessor list and DPA template.
[06:54] Devin: Any known issues integrating with our custom key rotation policy? We do forced 90-day rotations and emergency key revocation.
[07:02] Marco: Emergency key revocation is supported on Dedicated/Private. Hosted supports revocation in our wrapped-key model but there are steps to rewrap and re-encrypt artifacts which wed coordinate with your team.
[07:14] Samir: For performance-sensitive endpoints well probably want dedicated pools; can we do a hybrid where critical workloads use Dedicated and lower-sensitivity use Hosted?
[07:23] Li: Absolutely — smart routing can route by policy (latency, cost, or sensitivity). You can set rules to send certain traffic to dedicated pools and fall back to hosted variants if capacity is low.
[07:35] Avery: Great. Quick question on data deletion: if a customer asks for data to be deleted, how quickly can you remove cached keys or prompt history?
[07:44] Marco: We support deletion APIs; cached KV/prefix caches can be purged. Retention windows apply to exported logs. For hosted, depending on SLA, deletion may take up to X hours to propagate; for Private you control retention fully. Well provide exact SLAs in the follow-up.
[08:00] Rita: Well need to validate the deletion flows as part of our PIA.
[08:05] Jasmine: Noted. Well include a deletion flow doc in the follow-up pack.
[08:12] Li: One operational note — when you bring BYOK, you own key rotation and Redwood needs a rewrap window to re-encrypt stored artifacts. We have a standard rewrap handshake to avoid downtime.
[08:26] Samir: Sounds good. Anything else on your side we should know?
[08:30] Jasmine: Two quick asks — 1) can you send a short list of the controls youre most concerned about (we heard RBAC, KMS, audit logs, SSO), and 2) confirm stakeholders for next call (security, platform, devops).
[08:42] Avery: I will send a two-page control priority doc. Also will invite our infra lead to the bench test.
[08:49] Jasmine: Great. To close, well circulate SOC2, KMS whitepaper, RBAC template, SAML/SCIM checklist, and draft connectivity tests.
[08:58] Rita: Thanks.
[09:00] Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: auto-generated with some misheard items (e.g., "wrap" sometimes transcribed as "rap", IdP spelled as IP). There was brief crosstalk at 03:00-03:20.

Inference wellness and budget standup - Alpenglow Diagnostics QBR

Quarterly health check focused on usage patterns, unexpected cost uptick in June, latency outliers on patient triage flow, and roadmap alignment for private deployment proof-of-concept.
June cost spike analysis
Triage endpoint latency and p95 targets
Dedicated vs hosted for PHI/hipaa workloads
Pilot runway and next quarter roadmap
Meeting header
Date: 2026-07-08 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jamie (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Priya (Head of ML - Alpenglow), Carlos (Eng Mgr - Alpenglow), Emma (Security Lead)

[00:00] Jamie: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we've got about 50 minutes, wanted to run the quarterly health standup. quick round of intros?
[00:12] Priya: hi i'm priya, we run the inference models for patient triage, thanks for having us.
[00:18] Carlos: carlos here, i own the infra side and the rollout schedule.
[00:22] Emma: emma from security - i'll be focused on compliance and data flow.
[00:26] Jamie: perfect, and im jamie from redwood, and marcus our solutions eng will cover the deeper perf bits. marcus do you want to intro?
[00:34] Marcus: yeah hi everyone, i look after latency tuning and pilot ops, happy to dig in on the p95s and batching.
[00:42] Jamie: ok jump into the headline — priya you had flagged a cost spike in june, can you summarize?
[00:50] Priya: yeah so overall tokens are up ~28% in june because triage throughput doubled during the clinic trial, but the cost increase was larger than expected. some of that is long context conversations where we hit higher seq len, and i think we also had some routes fall back to hosted larger models when the dedicated pool was saturated. so cost per request went up.
[01:15] Carlos: to add, we saw a lot of small bursts at 2am UTC that look like retries from our batcher. not sure if that's our client side or a connectivity flake to the region. those retries multiplied.
[01:28] Marcus: okay a couple of things — retries can blow up cost quickly because prefix caching / K V cache doesn't help an entirely new request, and if a route falls back to the Redwood dedicatE pool it could pick a higher-capacity model variant. we saw that in the telemetry.
[01:43] Jamie: (laughs) yes, the fallback logic sometimes picks a compatible variant with larger embedding dims which increases token work.
[01:50] Priya: is that something we can pin? we want predictable unit cost during trials.
[01:55] Marcus: totally — you can pin model versions per route, and we can set a stricter routing policy so it doesn't fallback to higher-cost variants. i'll add a proposed policy in the pilot diagram.
[02:05] Emma: quick question on data residency: for the pilot we'll be processing PHI, we need private VPC or on-prem. do you have an updated compliance packet?
[02:15] Jamie: yes we have a private deployment option — Redwood Private — though i might say the export says 'Redwood private control plane' sometimes transcribed as 'redwood private plane' in docs — but yes, private with K-M-S integration and audit logs. we'll share the SOC2 + HIPAA notes.
[02:30] Emma: ok please add specifics about key rotation and HSM options.
[02:33] Jamie: noted.
[02:36] [03:00] Marcus: on the latency side, you mentioned p95 spikes on the triage endpoint last week. i pulled the traces: most p95 spikes correlate to long sequence lengths and cold KV cache after restarts. additionally some traffic hit a region fallback which added ~90ms. or, ah, 90ms per call isn't that big but when you have tight 300ms SLO it matters.
[03:21] Carlos: our target is p95 <= 300ms end-to-end from request arrival to response. some of the spikes were 450-600ms.
[03:29] Marcus: we can address that three ways — smaller model variants for short-turn prompts, smarter batching thresholds, and persistent KV cache warming during deployments. also we recommend burst capacity in the dedicated pool to avoid region fallbacks.
[03:42] Priya: curious about quantization. you mentioned earlier that benchmark said our model could be q4_0 without quality degradation?
[03:49] Marcus: yes for the patient triage model q4_0 looked acceptable on the eval set, but we should run an A/B with your golden prompt set — that will give us signal on accuracy vs token-efficiency.
[03:59] Priya: ok let's do that as part of the pilot.
[04:02] [05:10] Jamie: switching to costs again — jamie: we will send the line-item cost export that breaks down by model, route, and time bucket. for june we'll highlight the fallback incidents and the retry storms.
[05:22] Carlos: that helps — also can you show how batching parameters map to cost? our dev noticed we were using a very small max_batch_size that kept requests single-shot.
[05:31] Marcus: yes small batch sizes mean less GPU efficiency. we saw many single tokens which is expensive; we can suggest dynamic batching with latency SLO awareness — Redwood Optimize recommendations will propose specific numbers. sometimes the doc refers to 'Redwood opti-mize' in notes.
[05:48] Priya: can the optimize recommendations be simulated against our logs so we can estimate savings before changing prod?
[05:54] Marcus: absolutely — we can run a cost-savings sim offline against a one-week sample and share a projection.
[06:00] Emma: regarding security, can we get an NDA or data processing agreement for pilot? we need that before any PHI touches your hosted infra.
[06:08] Jamie: yes we'll attach the DPA and the pilot addendum; for private/on-prem the DPA extends — we'll include HSM/KMS options.
[06:14] [09:00] Carlos: timeline — we are aiming to start the pilot in early august; the main blocker is security signoff and confirming infra sizing.
[09:10] Jamie: for sizing marcus will propose the dedicated capacity commit and a burst plan; we typically do a 4-week pilot with capacity left-shifted.
[09:20] Marcus: i'll include a recommended pool (2xA10s equivalent) and autoscale config that keeps tail latency in check.
[09:27] Priya: on models — we'll need version pinning for the pilot and the ability to rollback quickly if quality regresses after quantization. how does rollback work?
[09:36] Marcus: rollouts are canary-based with automated fallback. you can pin the serve config to an exact model digest and we keep previous model artifacts for fast rollback. there might be a small cache-warm penalty but it's quick.
[09:48] Emma: audit logs — do you provide token-level tracing and exportable logs for SOC2 evidence?
[09:53] Jamie: yes we provide per-request tracing, route level latency and cost, and an exportable audit log for admin actions. we'll share a sample export.
[10:02] [12:00] Priya: real quick — we sometimes use an internal self-host for low-sensitivity inference, any lock-in concerns if we use both Redwood hosted and our self-host?
[12:10] Marcus: the api surface is consistent — if you maintain model artifacts you can move between modes. the main difference is the runtime optimizations and the kv-cache semantics which are runtime-specific — but we provide a migration guide.
[12:25] Carlos: ok good.
[12:28] [15:00] Jamie: let's recap and call out immediate items: we'll send the june cost export, marcus will prepare pilot architecture and recommended pool and batching config, emma will send the compliance checklist, and carlos will confirm workloads. schedule the pilot kickoff week of 7/20.
[15:20] Priya: thanks, that timeline works for us.
[15:24] Emma: can you also include the HSM key rotation frequency in the packet?
[15:27] Jamie: yep — we'll include rotation policies and KMS/HSM options.
[15:30] Marcus: one more thing — to validate q4_0 quality we propose a 1-week A/B with 10% traffic on the pilot env then measure precision/recall on golden prompts.
[15:42] Priya: agreed.
[15:45] [20:00] Carlos: minor note — our infra team wants a runbook for failure modes (region outage, ded pool saturate). can you provide a sample runbook?
[20:08] Marcus: yes i'll attach a runbook with fallbacks and recommended circuit breakers and retry policies.
[20:15] Jamie: ok great. any other questions?
[20:18] Priya: none from me.
[20:20] Emma: no.
[20:22] Jamie: cool we'll follow up with the artifacts, thanks everyone.

Meeting end

Call ended with agreement to start pilot planning; immediate emphasis on cost breakdown and security packet. There was moderate transcription noise around product names (Redwood Private vs redwood private plane) and technical jargon (KV cache transcribed as K V cash).
Redwood to share line-item cost breakdown for June (by route/model) by 2026-07-10
Customer to confirm compliance questions list for Private deployment (Emma) by 2026-07-12
Schedule 2-hour on-prem pilot planning workshop (Marcus + Carlos) week of 2026-07-20
Jamie: send June token/time cost export + short explainer (due 2026-07-10)
Marcus: prepare pilot architecture diagram and ops checklist for private deploy (due 2026-07-17)
Emma: collate PHI dataflow questions and SOC2/HIPAA checklist items (due 2026-07-12)
Carlos: confirm list of test workloads and SLA thresholds for pilot (due 2026-07-15)

Peninsula Health Console Telemetry Sherpa Walkthrough

Intro + console walkthrough focused on per-route usage, billing breakdown and telemetry. Customer has hybrid architecture, strong compliance needs (data residency, KMS), worried about latency spikes during patient-facing flows. Agreed to trial Dedicated pool and run bench to validate latency vs cost tradeoffs.
Meeting header: 2028-06-07 15:00 UTC | Duration 52 min | Attendees listed above

[00:00] Jamie: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Jamie Ortega from Redwood, with Priya and Marco from our eng team. How's everybody?
[00:08] Mark: Morning — Mark here, CTO at Peninsula. Sorry for the background noise, we had a pager.
[00:12] Aisha: Aisha, hi. We're mostly here to see the console telemetry and how we can map route costs back to product teams.
[00:18] Jamie: Great, that's exactly what Priya will walk through — per-route dashboards, chargeback, and how optimize suggestions drive down token cost.
[00:27] Priya: Quick agenda: show the usage lens, per-route cost breakdown, demo chargeback export, then a short section on Dedicated and private options — and security. We'll leave 10 mins for Q&A.
[00:38] Liam: One ask up front — any demo data can you make sure it masks PHI, we can't upload patient info.
[00:43] Marco: Absolutely, we'll use synthetic traces. Note about transcription: sorry if some names get munged.

[02:10] Priya: (screen share) Starting at the Usage Overview — token volumes over time, top 10 routes. You can see we automatically attribute tokens by route id, user-id hashing optional. For Peninsula, the interesting bit is the two patient-facing routes show high latency variance.
[02:28] Mark: Can you slice by api-key / team tag? We tag requests at our gateway.
[02:33] Priya: Yes, we map headers (x-team, x-route) — the console shows hierarchy: tenant -> route -> model variant. Exports are CSV or parquet.
[03:05] (crosstalk)

[05:15] Priya: Now per-route dashboard: call volumes, p50/p95 latency, token mix (prompt vs completion), and cost per route. Cost is a raw compute + model premium estimate — we include batching and cache savings as separate columns.
[05:32] Aisha: How are you calculating the cache savings? Our app has lots of repeated prompts for EHR lookups.
[05:38] Priya: We estimate prefix-KV cache hit rates from the request fingerprints and your configured cache policy. You can toggle assumed cache hit rate to simulate savings. It's an estimate, we also provide sample playback for validation.

[07:02] Jamie: Quick qualification — what's your current model hosting? On-prem for PHI or cloud?
[07:09] Mark: Hybrid. Most dev traffic in cloud, but anything with identifiable patient data lives in our private VPC on-prem.
[07:17] Jamie: Good to know — we can support Private deployment with customer-managed KMS.

[08:40] Marco: Demo: chargeback export — you can map cost slices to GL codes or service owners. We support per-route tagging and a rules engine for automatic allocation.
[08:57] Liam: Do tags survive cross-region routing if you fallback? We route to standby region sometimes.
[09:03] Priya: Tags are preserved; fallback routes are annotated with the original route id. Fallbacks show up as separate color in the route timeline.

[11:30] Aisha: Security — SOC2? We need audit logs and proof of data segregation for our compliance team.
[11:38] Jamie: Redwood is SOC2 Type II; we also provide detailed audit trails per-request (who requested, route id, model version) and can integrate with your SIEM over S3 or syslog. I'll send SOC2 docs.
[11:50] Sofia: For KMS, can you use our HSM? We require customer-managed keys for encryption at rest.
[11:56] Marco: Yes, Private deployment integrates with customer KMS/HSM. For Hosted we use BYOK for stored artifacts and can provide key-rotation schedules.

[13:20] Priya: Back to cost — here's the per-token breakdown: model compute, GPU time, and orchestration overhead. The optimize tab suggests quantized variants or batching config changes that estimatedly reduce per-token cost by up to 35% for some routes.
[13:45] Mark: That 35% — is that from quantization alone or batching? We can't degrade quality on patient summaries.
[13:55] Priya: It's a mix. You can pin quality thresholds — e.g., allow int8 for non-diagnostic summarization routes, keep fp16 for critical flows. Console shows expected quality delta and sample diffs.

[16:00] Liam: Latency concerns: patient triage route must be <= 120ms p95. How do we guarantee?
[16:07] Marco: For SLOs like that, we recommend Dedicated pools pinned to the model variant with reserved slots and local KV cache. Also, we can set routing policies to prefer low-latency region and automatic fallback to a lighter model only if latency would be violated.
[16:25] Aisha: What's the real-world p95 with dedicated vs hosted? Any benchmarks?
[16:30] Priya: Typical p95 on Dedicated with optimized kernels and 1s sequence length can be sub-100ms for small instructed models. We'll run a bench with your payloads — that's part of next steps.

[18:10] Mark: How much operational burden to run Private? Our infra team already has a few infra projects.
[18:18] Marco: Private has a control plane option where Redwood manages orchestration but the inference plane is in your VPC. We provide playbooks and an ops runbook; initial onboarding is heavier but day-to-day is light.

[20:05] Priya: Walkthrough of the alerting: thresholds on p95, error-rate per route, token surge alerts. Alerts can create JIRA tickets automatically or hit PagerDuty.
[20:20] Liam: Can we set a budget cap per route? We want auto-protect so experimental routes don't blow the budget.
[20:25] Priya: Yes — you can set hard caps or soft caps with throttling or automatic fallbacks to cheaper model variants.

[23:00] (demo continues with sample export)

[27:10] Priya: Now the telemetry detail: sample payload playback allows you to replay a request against different model variants to see diff in tokens and output. Useful for quality gating before rollouts.
[27:30] Aisha: If we replay patient data, again must be masked — is masking built-in?
[27:36] Marco: We provide a redaction helper for playback. It removes names and identifiers and supports custom regex rules.

[29:50] Mark: Pricing questions — if we go Dedicated with reserved capacity, what's the commit vs burst model?
[29:58] Jamie: Dedicated is a monthly commitment for reserved slots; we support burst capacity at a premium. Pricing sheet I'll attach, but rough rule: reserved capacity gets discount and predictable unit economics.

[32:12] Aisha: Competitors: we've looked at Bedrock + Anthropic for some use cases. What differentiates Redwood here?
[32:20] Jamie: We emphasize consistent serving primitives across hosted/dedicated/private, observable per-route economics, and traction on high-throughput production use cases. Also better tooling for prefix/KV cache and automatic batching suggestions.

[34:45] Liam: On telemetry retention — what retention windows? We need 2 years for audits but don't want to pay cloud egress costs.
[34:52] Marco: Retention is configurable per-tenant and per-data-class. We can keep high-fidelity request traces for 90 days and aggregated metrics for multi-year, and exports for long-term retention into your S3.

[38:00] Priya: Demo close: show how to create a rollout with canary traffic split and automatic rollback if quality drops. The console links to your evals and prompt sets.
[38:20] Sofia: Who signs the DPA? We need a DPA and assurance that data doesn't leave EU for certain flows.
[38:28] Jamie: We have EU-region private deployments and DPA templates. I'll attach legal contacts.

[41:15] Mark: Ok, let's make this actionable — we'll start with a pilot on two routes: patient-triage and medication-check. We'll expect the trial Dedicated pool to be provisioned for 2 weeks.
[41:28] Jamie: Great. Priya, can you confirm sandbox plan?
[41:32] Priya: Yes — we'll provision a dedicated sandbox cluster with synthetic data and invite Liam + Aisha. Expect invite by 2028-06-12.

[44:10] (Q&A: small bits about model version pinning, canary size 5-10%)

[48:05] Liam: One last ask: can you provide a sample route-level cost forecast based on our current monthly tokens? We'll share the sheet.
[48:12] Jamie: Yes, send the CSV and we'll return a modeled forecast with recommendations.

[50:00] Jamie: Recap — Redwood to share SOC2 + DPA, provision telemetry sandbox, provision Dedicated trial, Peninsula to share route CSV, schedule bench for latency/cost.
[50:20] Mark: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[50:25] Aisha: Thanks.
[50:30] (call ends)

Halcyon Labs - capacity top-up & EU on‑prem pilot discussion

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-04
Start: 09:30 PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Olivia (Redwood CSM), Liam (CTO Halcyon), Priya (Head Infra), Daniel (Procurement)
---
Summary:
Quick renewal + expansion checkin. Customer wants a modest capacity top‑up for Q1 traffic spike, plus an EU on‑prem pilot to satisfy data residency and KMS requirements. Discussed pricing model for top‑up, timeline for a 6‑week pilot, SOC2/audit deliverables, and initial perf benchmarks. Action items and follow ups agreed.
Topics:
- Current usage and projected Q1 ramp
- Dedicated vs hosted top‑up economics
- EU on‑prem pilot scope (network, kms, audit)
- Contract amendment and pilot success metrics
---
Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, um quick agenda, chances are we start with current usage and then get into the pilot, sound good?
[00:07] Liam: yeah that works, we've got about 18 minutes for slides but mostly just want to confirm numbers and next steps, sorry typos in calendar, pulled up the dashboard now
[00:15] Priya: hi all, quick context, halcyon is launching two new products in Q1 so we expect a 25‑35% bump in requests, plus EU regulatory push, which is why we want the on‑prem pilot scoped.
[00:30] Maya: ok great, can you remind us current committed capacity and latency SLAs you see?
[00:38] Liam: current committed is two dedicated GPU pools, avg latency around 180ms p95 for gen traffic, cost is creeping up because of lots of short‑lived prompts, so we're trying to smooth it with batching suggestions
[00:51] Samir: thanks, sounds inline. for the top‑up we're recommending a 30% reserved bump for Q1 with burstable credit; that keeps price predictability and avoids per‑token surprises.
[01:05] Priya: can you send the pricing table that compares reserved vs on‑demand for the bump? I want the per‑hour and per‑token numbers side‑by‑side.
[01:12] Samir: yes we'll send a detailed matrix. also wanted to check interest in a shorter pilot of Redwood Private in EU — you mentioned KMS and local audit needs?
[01:22] Priya: correct. our compliance team requires customer‑managed keys (HSM/KMS) and audit logs retained on premise for 90 days. in our ideal world the control plane stays in our VPC.
[01:34] Maya: we can support a Private deployment package — note some bits of the control plane remain in the Redwood service for orchestration, but the data plane can be in your VPC and we support KMIP/HSM integrations.
[01:47] Liam: ok that's promising, can you outline the network topology required? specifically, do we need to open a bunch of CIDRs outbound?
[01:54] Maya: we'll share a minimal egress list, typically a few management endpoints and NTP, and then the internal model nodes talk over private peering, we'll capture that in the onboarding doc.
[02:06] Daniel: procurement question — how does billing look for a pilot vs production reserved capacity? is the pilot refundable?
[02:12] Samir: pilot is typically a time‑boxed contract with a pro‑rated fee; if you convert to reserved capacity within 30 days we'll apply a credit from the pilot spend.
[02:23] Daniel: ok that's reasonable, we'll need that in writing for our legal team.
[02:29] Priya: on the perf side, we want to run your kernels against our real prompts. is there a checklist we should follow to make benchmarks reproducible?
[02:37] Maya: absolutely — we'll send a benchmark checklist: prompt set formatting, sequence length distribution, target tokenization, and a recommended runbook for KV cache warmup. also, note we have quantization variants that change latency/cost tradeoffs.
[02:50] Liam: you said quantization variants — will that affect output quality? our product is fairly sensitive to hallucination on long form answers.
[02:58] Maya: there's typically a small delta; we can run a quality regression with your golden prompts during the pilot. if we see delta above your threshold we can dial quantization back or use a higher precision model variant.
[03:12] Samir: curious — any other vendors you are evaluating?
[03:15] Priya: we're talking to BigCloudAI for a managed endpoint and VendorX for a self‑managed runtime, mostly to compare costs and control model weights.
[03:24] Samir: good to know — we'll include a cost comparison for the same workload in the quote.
[03:29] Olivia: just to flag, our deployment playbooks include SOC2 artefacts and audit logs export; we can attach those to the pilot SOW.
[03:39] Liam: good, for timelines we need pilot completed by mid‑January to feed product release; can you make a 6‑week window work starting early December?
[03:47] Maya: yeah 6 weeks is doable if we get network access and a golden prompt set in week one. rollouts: week1 onboarding, week2 perf runs, weeks3‑4 tuning, week5‑6 validation/hand‑off.
[04:02] Daniel: put me on the contract thread, we'll need a purchase order for the pilot and a list of what triggers conversion to reserved contract.
[04:10] Samir: we'll include conversion language and a conversion credit in the SOW.
[04:15] Priya: regarding KMS, we have an HSM partner and will need an integration contact. who owns that on Redwood?
[04:22] Maya: I'll be primary, and our infra security lead, Aaron Cole, will help with the KMS/HSM specs — I'll include his contact.
[04:31] Liam: any redlines we should expect in the amendment? support levels, uptime SLA, and data residency statements are our main ones.
[04:39] Samir: yes SLA language and support response tiers will be included. for data residency we'll state the data plane will be hosted in your EU VPC for pilot, logs can be exported to your SIEM.
[04:50] Priya: on logging, retention policy needs to be configurable up to 12 months, is that possible?
[04:56] Maya: out of the box we do 90 days, but we can extend retention with an optional archiving module to your S3/GCS in EU — that will be in the ops addendum.
[05:08] Liam: ok sounds good. any blockers to starting the pilot from Redwood side?
[05:13] Samir: main dependency is an NDA + signed SOW for the pilot and a network window for onboarding. we'll draft both.
[05:20] Daniel: procurement will need estimated invoice schedule, deliverables, and contact for invoicing.
[05:25] Olivia: noted, Samir will add billing cadence.
[05:30] Liam: just to surface one worry — we've had poor experiences with noisy bursts causing latency spikes. how does Redwood handle graceful degradation?
[05:39] Maya: we have automatic fallbacks — routing to compatible model variants and throttling policies. for dedicated pools we can set burst caps and queueing policies to preserve p95 targets.
[05:50] Priya: okay and for monitoring, can we get token‑level cost breakdowns and per‑route dashboards?
[05:56] Maya: yep console gives per‑route token and latency breakdowns, and we can provision a shared dashboard for your SREs.
[06:04] Samir: recap — we'll send: updated capacity quote with reserved top‑up pricing, pilot SOW and timeline, benchmark checklist, and SOC2/audit artifacts.
[06:14] Liam: perfect. let's aim for Samir's timeline. thanks everyone.
[06:18] [crosstalk] Priya: thanks both, we'll start internal approvals this week.
[06:23] Olivia: I'll follow up with a calendar invite for kickoff as soon as SOW is signed.
[06:28] Samir: great — end of call.
---
End summary / recorded notes:
Call felt productive; clear runway to pilot in Dec if SOW signed. Key asks: pricing matrix, benchmark checklist, KMS contact, and contract amendment with conversion credit.
