IDP provisioning & privilege boundaries kickoff with Solstice Bio

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (AE), Priya Desai (SE), Liam O'Connor (CSM) — Solstice: Maya Lin (CTO), Andre Gomez (Dir Infra), Sofia Chen (Security), Rajat (DevOps), Elena (Legal)

Summary:
Redwood-led security kickoff to align on SAML/IdP integration, SCIM provisioning, RBAC role slices and least-privilege model, audit log retention and routing, and customer-managed key (CMK) options for encryption at rest. Customer priorities: EU data residency, SOC 2 evidence, minimal blast radius for service accounts, and cert rotation policies.

Topics: IdP metadata, SAML assertions & attributes, SCIM groups & mapping, RBAC role templates, audit log streaming to Splunk, KMS/CMK integration, data residency & Private deployment options, SOC2/ISO artifacts.

[00:00] Jordan Park: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call please.
[00:06] Maya Lin: Hi, Maya here, CTO at Solstice.
[00:09] Andre Gomez: Andre, infra.
[00:11] Sofia Chen: Sofia, security.
[00:12] Rajat Patel: Rajat, DevOps.
[00:14] Elena Ruiz: Elena, legal.
[00:16] Jordan Park: Great. I'll hand off to Priya to run through the technical flow and then we can dive into SCIM and RBAC.
[00:22] Priya Desai: Hi all. High level — we want to confirm three things: how you want to connect your IdP to Redwood, how users/groups map into Redwood roles, and how you want logs and keys handled. I'm going to sketch an example SAML flow then SCIM mapping. Please stop me if anything sounds off.
[00:38] Priya Desai: For SAML, we support IdP-initiated and SP-initiated. Assertion needs to include NameID (email) and we like to receive an attribute for role or groups, e.g., groups claim with full DN or a simple group array. Some IdPs send group IDs, some send names — either works but we need mapping.
[00:55] Andre Gomez: Quick question — we use Azure AD but have a proxy in front that rewrites some claims. Will that break anything?
[01:02] Priya Desai: It can. If claims are rewritten you'll need to either change the rewrite rules to keep the group attribute intact or provide us a mapping table. For example if group claim is "grp_names" vs "groups" we'll map accordingly. We can accept multiple attribute names.
[01:18] Sofia Chen: On encryption — we require customer-managed keys for any workspace that touches PHI. Do you support CMK with rotation and KMS integration?
[01:26] Priya Desai: Yes, we support CMK for Dedicated and Private deployments. For Hosted API we offer envelope encryption with Redwood-managed keys or optional Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) in supported regions; rotation is supported with a staged rewrap process. Note: the Private deployment path gives you full control over keys via your KMS/HSM.
[01:44] Maya Lin: If we go hosted with BYOK, can we ensure the keys never leave EU?
[01:50] Priya Desai: We can pin key material to regional KMS endpoints — if you require EU residency we recommend Private or Dedicated in EU region. Hosted BYOK is possible in EU, but we need contractual language for residency guarantees.
[02:04] Elena Ruiz: We'll need that in the contract; also want SOC 2 evidence before any pilot.
[02:09] Jordan Park: Understood. We'll send SOC 2 bundle and ISO references after this call.
[02:14] Priya Desai: Switching to SCIM — we support group sync for automatic provisioning and deprovisioning. SCIM can be configured to sync group membership to Redwood roles. Typical pattern: SCIM group = RBAC role, with admin groups mapped to higher-perm roles.
[02:31] Rajat Patel: Our concern is blast radius. We have some CI service accounts that should not be admins. How do you carve those out?
[02:37] Priya Desai: Two approaches: 1) Use a dedicated service account OU in IdP that maps to a tightly scoped role in Redwood; 2) Use attribute-based mapping — e.g., an attribute 'serviceAccount=true' that SCIM sends so those accounts get a sandbox role. We can also exclude certain users from SCIM by filter.
[02:56] Andre Gomez: Filtering sounds ideal. Is filtering evaluated server-side or by our IdP?
[02:59] Priya Desai: Filters are on Redwood side during provisioning — we evaluate SCIM list endpoints or incoming patch operations and apply filters you provide. We log all provisioning events.
[03:10] Sofia Chen: About auditing — we need immutable logs for SSO events and admin actions, and ability to forward to Splunk. Retention 7 years for some artifacts. Is that supported?
[03:20] Priya Desai: We forward syslogs/events via secure streaming. Default retention in hosted is 90 days, but for Dedicated/Private you can configure retention and export to your SIEM. 7-year retention typically requires you to archive externally — we can stream to an S3 bucket in your account or to your Splunk HTTP collector.
[03:37] Sofia Chen: Ok we'll probably archive to our S3 with lifecycle rules.
[03:40] Jordan Park: Note — we'll include an example Splunk HEC config and sample event schema in follow-up.
[03:47] Priya Desai: On RBAC design, we recommend role slices: Admin, Power-User (can run infer jobs), Viewer (read-only), Service (CI/service accounts). Keep number of roles small to reduce complexity.
[03:58] Andre Gomez: Can roles be scoped per team or per project?
[04:01] Priya Desai: Yes, we support role scoping at workspace and route level. For example "DataScience:Power" vs "Infra:Admin". We also support least-privilege via policy templates that restrict API surfaces.
[04:13] Maya Lin: About policy templates — can we define a custom policy that prevents model deletion and restricts model rollout? We want to limit that to ops only.
[04:20] Priya Desai: Absolutely. We have policy primitives for model:create, model:delete, rollout:execute. You can combine them into templates and bind to groups.
[04:28] Rajat Patel: How do you handle SAML certificate rotation — if our IdP rotates certs every 30 days how smooth is the handoff?
[04:35] Priya Desai: We support metadata URL ingestion and offline metadata upload. For aggressive rotation, we advise setting up both old/new certs in metadata (IdP supports key rollover) or use metadata URL so we pick up changes. If you rotate daily, we can accept an automated push; otherwise manual update via Console/API.
[04:53] Elena Ruiz: Legal question — what data do you store in logs? Do we get PII?
[04:58] Liam O'Connor: We typically log identifiers (user id, email) for auditability but can mask or hash on request. We don't store raw PII in trace logs; sensitive payloads are redacted. We can provide a log schema doc.
[05:10] Sofia Chen: Will those logs include request payloads or model outputs?
[05:14] Priya Desai: By default we log metadata about the request (timestamps, user, route, model id, token count). Model outputs are not logged unless you enable debug/eval mode. For compliance, many customers disable output logging and only retain usage metrics.
[05:30] Jordan Park: Customer question — if we need SOC 2 scoping for Redwood's hosted offering, are there shared responsibilities?
[05:36] Priya Desai: Yes; Redwood's SOC 2 covers our controls for the service but you remain responsible for access management and secure usage in your account. We'll send a shared-responsibility matrix.
[05:46] Andre Gomez: We want to do a POC that demonstrates: SAML SSO, SCIM sync, RBAC least-privilege, and logging to our Splunk collector. How long to spin up a Dedicated sandbox in EU?
[05:56] Priya Desai: Typical start is 5–7 business days for dedicated sandbox in EU, assuming networking and infra approvals. Private on-prem is longer. We can do hosted test with EU region quicker if you accept Redwood-managed infra.
[06:10] Maya Lin: We need proof that keys are never exported for BYOK — what's the guarantee?
[06:14] Priya Desai: For BYOK we use envelope encryption; the KMS never sends key material to Redwood. Redwood only receives wrapped keys. In Dedicated/Private, keys can be in your KMS in your account so we never touch raw key material. We'll attach a technical note.
[06:28] Sofia Chen: On SCIM schema — can you accept custom attributes we use, like employeeType and orgSlice?
[06:34] Priya Desai: Yes, we map custom attributes. We suggest canonical names during mapping to avoid drift. We'll share a mapping template.
[06:40] Jordan Park: Quick aside — any competitors you considered?
[06:42] Maya Lin: We've looked at AuthFlow and CloudAIEndpoints; main gap was model-specific RBAC and audit granularity.
[06:49] Priya Desai: Noted. We'll highlight our per-route traceability in follow-up.
[06:54] Rajat Patel: How do we isolate internal staging workloads from prod? Do we need separate workspaces?
[06:59] Priya Desai: Best practice is separate workspaces with distinct VPC/subnets and KMS keys. That gives you strong separation for billing, logs, and keys.
[07:10] Andre Gomez: Is there automation for provisioning new project workspaces via API?
[07:13] Priya Desai: Yes, you can create workspaces via API and programmatically bind groups/roles via SCIM or the Redwood management API.
[07:18] Sofia Chen: For long-term audit retention, is streaming to our S3 enough for compliance?
[07:22] Priya Desai: Yes, streaming to your S3 with lifecycle set to keep objects is common. We provide event formatting docs so you can parse.
[07:29] Elena Ruiz: Who signs the Data Processing Addendum (DPA)?
[07:32] Jordan Park: Our legal team will sign the DPA. We'll attach a copy in the follow-up.
[07:36] Maya Lin: On the SCIM side, if we deprovision a user, how quickly does that revoke tokens and sessions?
[07:42] Priya Desai: Token revocation is near-real-time for interactive sessions; for long-running inference jobs we provide revoke hooks and job-level ACL checks. We invalidate session cookies and issue a revoke to active tokens. There can be short windows (seconds) but it's immediate in practice.
[07:58] Rajat Patel: Any limitations on number of SCIM groups? We have thousands and want to avoid hitting quotas.
[08:03] Priya Desai: We support large group counts; for scale we recommend delta sync (patch operations) instead of full list on every run. We'll share best practices doc.
[08:12] Sofia Chen: For role separation, can we require MFA for role elevation to admin?
[08:16] Priya Desai: Yes, we support admin elevation workflows that require step-up auth — integration with your IdP's MFA is supported.
[08:24] Jordan Park: Ok time check — we've got about 30 minutes left, any high-risk items we should surface now?
[08:31] Sofia Chen: Data residency and long-term logs are high risk, plus legal needs on DPA and contract language for residency. Also key handling if we go hosted.
[08:41] Priya Desai: Action-wise: we'll share SOC2 bundle, SCIM mapping template, Splunk HEC example, and a proposed pilot timeline for Dedicated EU sandbox. We'll also include a short KB on key rotation.
[08:53] Andre Gomez: For pilot, can we test a CMK rewrap cycle to see performance impact?
[08:59] Priya Desai: Yes, we can instrument a rewrap test in the sandbox. We expect small latency impact per rewrap but it's manageable. We'll include tokenized metrics from prior tests.
[09:10] Maya Lin: On rollback/fallback — if Dedicated capacity is unavailable during a canary, do you fallback to hosted model? We want deterministic routing.
[09:18] Priya Desai: We have routing policies: you can prefer Dedicated and fail closed or prefer Dedicated with fallback to hosted. For strict isolation you can set fail closed. We'll document tradeoffs.
[09:29] Jordan Park: Let's capture next steps and owners.
[09:32] Priya Desai: Action items recap — (1) Priya: SCIM mapping + sample CSV, (2) Jordan: SOC 2 + ISO links, (3) Redwood: Splunk HEC example and event schema, (4) Solstice: IdP metadata and cert cadence, (5) Solstice: list of admin/service accounts.
[09:50] Elena Ruiz: We'll also need standard contract language for EU residency and BYOK assurances. Add that to the list.
[09:58] Jordan Park: Will do. Any final questions?
[10:02] Sofia Chen: One last: can you produce a short runbook for emergency key rotation or key compromise?
[10:07] Priya Desai: Yes, we'll share a runbook with steps for rotation, revoke, and rewrap.
[10:12] Jordan Park: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts within 48 hours.
[10:16] Maya Lin: Thanks, appreciate it.
[10:18] Meeting end."
Priya Desai: Share SCIM attribute mapping doc and sample CSV (due 2026-08-10)
Jordan Park: Provide SOC 2 artifact link & ISO cert location (due 2026-08-06)
Rajat Patel: Send current IdP metadata and cert rotation cadence (due 2026-08-09)
Sofia Chen: Provide desired audit retention window and SIEM endpoint (due 2026-08-12)
Redwood to share SOC 2 Type II evidence bundle link
Priya to send SCIM attribute mapping template and example CSV
Schedule technical pilot for dedicated VPC + CMK test (target week of 2026-08-17)
Customer to confirm list of admin service accounts for RBAC carve-out

Procurement & Legal: Pilot terms, technical acceptance, MSA/DPA prioritization

Redwood AE + SE ran procurement and legal intake with Atlas Retail Labs to prioritize MSA/DPA redlines, confirm SLA/acceptance criteria for a two-week pilot and surface security docs (SOC2/KMS/SSO). Main disagreements were on egress charges and encryption key ownership. Agreement to run a 2-week technical pilot on Dedicated capacity with isolated VPC peering, legal to review proposed DPA redline by 2027-07-20.
Lena Park - Send pilot commercial term sheet and pricing deck (due 2027-07-15)
Ravi Menon - Share benchmark plan and test harness repo + sample prompt set (due 2027-07-16)
Maya Ortiz - Provide onboarding runbook and support contacts for pilot (due 2027-07-18)
Sofia Lin - Return DPA redline notes (due 2027-07-20)
Priya Nair - Share Atlas minimal compliance matrix and any required attestations (due 2027-07-19)
Redwood to provision Dedicated pilot environment (isolated VPC) and share access details
Atlas legal to circulate DPA redlines to Redwood (deadline 2027-07-20)
Schedule technical onboarding session and latency benchmark run (target 2027-07-17)
Redwood to send SOC2 type II report and network diagrams
Set up SSO/SAML test account and KMS key exchange plan
[00:00] Lena: Okay hi everyone, thanks for joining — we can get started. I'm Lena from Redwood, AE. We've got Ravi on the line for technical, Maya for onboarding.
[00:17] James: Hey Lena, quick context — procurement lane. We need to lock pilot terms and make sure legal has the DPA route.
[00:32] Sofia: Hi all. We'll be focused on the DPA redlines, specifically data residency, subprocessors and key management.
[00:45] Ravi: Quick note, for the pilot we usually offer either hosted or dedicated; given Atlas's constraints it sounds like Dedicated + VPC peering is preferred, yes?
[00:58] Markus: Yeah, Platform team prefers Dedicated. We need isolated KV cash (sic) and no cross-tenant caching, and we want option to bring our own KMS if possible.
[01:12] Lena: Absolutely — we can do customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integration, and we will note that in the DPA appendix. There is an operational note though: BYOK adds a small egress key-exchange step.
[01:27] Tom: Egress fees — that's the other issue. Procurement is worried about open-ended egress charges if usage spikes.
[01:34] Lena: Understood. For the pilot we can cap egress at a pre-agreed threshold and then propose per-GB rates beyond that. We'll put that in the pilot term sheet.
[01:46] Priya: Security question — do you have SOC2 type II? Also ISO? We need evidence of controls, and audit logs retained at token- or request-level for 90 days.
[01:58] Maya: We have SOC2 and can share the report; audit logs are configurable per-customer and retention can be extended via the Console.
[02:10] Sofia: When you say "logs configurable" can we get a signed commitment in the DPA for retention?
[02:16] Lena: We'll propose language in the DPA appendix committing to retention for the pilot window; long term we can discuss retention SLAs.
[02:26] James: What about SLA? We need a 99.9-ish availability SLO for production but for pilot we can be more flexible — what's Redwood's typical latency SLO?
[02:38] Ravi: For hosted we aim for p50 in 100-200ms depending on prompt length, p95 varies; on Dedicated with GPUs we can target 95th < 500ms for our small- to mid-size models. We can run a latency benchmark during the pilot to show numbers.
[02:52] Markus: Important that 95th is stable across bursts. Also, KV cache warming and continuous batching might change numbers.
[03:03] Ravi: Right — our runtime does per-request batching, KV cache and prefix caching. Quick note: the transcript may say "KV cash" above — that's the speech engine.
[03:12] Sofia: On the DPA, subprocessors list — we need names and regions for any cloud infra vendors used. Can you provide a list?
[03:20] Diego: Yes we can share subprocessors and regions; for Dedicated we typically use managed infra providers in the same cloud region as the customer, and we can provide contractual commitments for regions used.
[03:31] Tom: Pricing — two main asks from FinOps: 1) a predictable committed rate for the pilot or a reservation discount, 2) clarity on token pricing and how embeddings are billed.
[03:42] Lena: For the pilot we'll propose a short-term reserved capacity rate — not full year commit but a two-week reserved block so you get predictable cost for benchmarking. Embeddings billed per-embedding-unit, we'll put sample costings in the deck.
[03:55] James: Can you include a sample benchmark sheet with expected token volumes? Procurement needs that to compare against internal P&L.
[04:01] Maya: We'll attach a simple benchmark template and sample cost projection.
[04:10] Sofia: On keying — Atlas wants BYOK with customer-controlled keys; are you able to do HSM attestations and a key-rotation cadence?
[04:20] Ravi: Yes BYOK with HSM is supported in Dedicated path; rotation cadence can be set and we will send the HSM attestation doc. There's an operational integration step to establish a key-access policy.
[04:33] Priya: Also we need to confirm that redact or delete commands can be actioned on demand for pilot data — is that immediate?
[04:42] Diego: We support data deletion and have an expunge workflow; we'll outline SLO for deletion in the DPA appendix. For pilot we'll commit to 48hr removal of cached artifacts.
[04:53] James: Timing — procurement goals are to make a go/no-go decision by end of next week — can legal and Redwood exchange redlines quickly?
[05:02] Lena: Yes the plan: Redwood sends pilot term sheet & pricing today/tonight; Atlas legal returns DPA redlines by 2027-07-20. Pilot provisioning and a technical onboarding session we'll aim for 2027-07-17.
[05:18] Sofia: We'll read redlines but any MSA changes we'll try to limit to DPA appendix and operational exhibits.
[05:24] Tom: One more on egress: if you host models in EU and we have EU customers then residency is fine; but if we push production traffic to US, how is data-in-transit handled?
[05:35] Ravi: Data in transit is TLS 1.2+/mTLS where required. For cross-region we can set routing policies to keep inference in the EU region; if not possible then we can include data transfer assurances in the DPA.
[05:49] Markus: For the benchmark, we want 3 prompt templates: agent assist, search re-rank, and checkout chat. We'll run against a 10k prompt sample.
[05:59] Ravi: Great — I'll post the test harness repo and example prompt sets — sample load harness is JMeter-based and an adapter for the Redwood SDK.
[06:10] Lena: On the commercial side — pilot period pricing, reserved block for 2 weeks, plus agreed egress cap. We'll also offer a follow-on discount if you convert to 12-month reserved Dedicated.
[06:22] Tom: That helps procurement. Also checkpoint — what about backups and snapshot exports? We need to know retention for model artifacts we upload.
[06:31] Diego: Snapshots are customer-owned and can be exported; retention policy is configurable. We'll include that in the runbook.
[06:40] Sofia: A legal detail — employee access logs and subprocessor transfer notifications. Can Redwood notify us 30 days in advance of subprocessor changes?
[06:50] Maya: Standard is notification window, we can propose 30-day notice in the DPA.
[07:00] James: Are there any legal hold or eDiscovery features if we needed them in future?
[07:06] Diego: We have an enterprise add-on for eDiscovery and extended retention — not in pilot by default but available.
[07:15] Priya: Security posture — can you provide the pen test report and the SOC2?
[07:20] Lena: We'll share SOC2 Type II and a sanitized pen test summary — full report under NDA if needed.
[07:29] Sofia: NDA will be signed; we'll coordinate.
[07:34] Tom: One more finance flow — invoicing cadence and tax treatment. Do you invoice monthly or can you do upfront for the pilot?
[07:43] Lena: We can invoice upfront for the pilot reserved block or net-30 after pilot depending on procurement preference. We'll put both options in the term sheet.
[07:53] Markus: On the routing side, if we want automatic fallback to a lower-cost variant during capacity pressure — is that supported? We don't want to lose availability.
[08:03] Ravi: Yes smart routing exists — fallback to compatible model variants, with configurable quality thresholds. We'll document expected quality delta in the pilot notes.
[08:15] James: Okay this is helpful. Let's recap next steps.
[08:20] Lena: Recap: Redwood sends pilot term sheet & pricing by end of day; Ravi shares benchmark harness and prompt set by Friday (2027-07-16); Atlas legal to return DPA redlines by 2027-07-20; schedule technical onboarding on 2027-07-17; Redwood to provision Dedicated pilot env and share credentials.
[08:40] Sofia: Confirmed, we'll review redlines and flag any hard stops.
[08:45] Maya: I'll be your onboarding POC, reach me for test accounts.
[08:50] James: Thanks all, we'll reconvene after redlines.
[08:54] Lena: Thanks team. We'll follow up in writing with links to SOC2, runbook, pricing deck and the benchmark template.
[09:01] (end recording)

MeridianWorks — Console: inference economics & route playbook

AE + SE walked MeridianWorks through Redwood Console's per-route usage and cost telemetry, demonstrated Optimize suggestions for batching and quantization, and scoped a short pilot to validate inference economics against MeridianWorks' LLM workloads. Security and routing policies were discussed; action items include sharing pricing, security pack, and a benchmark run with their prompt set.
Alex Chen: Share tailored pricing sheet and route-playbook deck by 2026-06-09
Priya Nair: Schedule pilot benchmark session and request sample prompt set (due 2026-06-10)
Aisha Khan: Provide current traffic distribution CSV and examples of 3 high-traffic routes by 2026-06-08
Liam O'Neill: Confirm procurement timeline and budget window (answers in email)
Daniel Park: Share short list of privacy/regulatory requirements for pilot (by 2026-06-11)
Send pricing + security packet
Set up pilot with dedicated two-week benchmark
Run 48-hour traffic replay against Redwood Hosted and Dedicated variants
Follow-up call to review benchmark results (tentative 2026-06-18)
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-05 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen, Priya Nair (Redwood) — Daniel Park, Aisha Khan, Liam O'Neill (MeridianWorks)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect): Redwood console walkthrough focusing on per-route cost and a playbook for reducing token spend. Showed Optimize suggestions such as batching and quantization profiles; discussed pilot and security controls.

[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, I think we should give like a quick agenda — we'll do a 5‑10 minute context q, run through the console per‑route dashboards and then Priya will demo the optimize suggestions and the bench plan, and then q and as and next steps. Sound good?
[00:15] Daniel Park: yeah works for me. quick background — we're building an assistant and some summarization pipelines, traffic's pretty spiky, we care about latency under 300ms for search re-rank routes but other routes can be batchy.
[00:28] Aisha Khan: and security is a hard requirement, we need SSO, audit logs and KMS for keys, also we have an internal requirement for data residency in eu-west for some workloads.
[00:45] Alex Chen: totally, we'll call out those controls. quick q — are you currently hosting models yourself or using a vendor?
[00:52] Daniel Park: hybrid — some internal endpoints for proprietary models, and we use ProviderX for high‑throughput generation right now. We're exploring dedicated capacity for predictable latency.
[01:08] Priya Nair: cool, that hybrid pattern aligns with a lot of customers. so when we show the console you'll see you can route per‑route by policy — region, latency target, or cost — and also pin a model version for rollouts.
[01:24] Liam O'Neill: say more about the cost telemetry, we need to attribute to product teams and routes for internal chargeback.
[01:33] Alex Chen: yeah that's the core of today's walkthrough. jumping in — this is the Console home, token spend overview at the top, quick filter by time range and routes. notice the 'route map' — it's a mapping from API key / route name to cost and p95 latency.
[01:55] [screen share noise]
[02:10] Alex Chen: okay, clicking into the 'summarization' route — you can see requests per minute, model variance, and a cost per 1k tokens breakdown. the console estimates per‑token unit costs by model and hardware profile.
[02:28] Daniel Park: hmm the per‑token cost for the 8k context variant looks lower than our current billing from ProviderX, are those estimates or actual bill numbers?
[02:38] Priya Nair: good q — for Hosted those are actual billed units. for Dedicated we estimate based on reserved capacity and observed throughput; for Private on‑prem it's based on your reported capacity config. sometimes transcription shows 'de‑dedicated' but I meant Dedicated, sorry.
[02:58] Aisha Khan: there's a chart labeled 'KV cash hits' — is that the KV cache metric?
[03:06] Priya Nain: (laughs) yes KV cache hits — sometimes the transcript turns into cash — it's the same KV cache and prefix caching that reduces re‑compute in multi‑turn apps.
[03:20] [04:00] Alex Chen: next, we have 'per‑route breakdown' which is what most finance teams love — total spend, tokens, average input length, output length, and a normalized 'cost per success' if you attach a success metric. you can slice by tag or team.
[04:22] Liam O'Neill: can we export route assignments to our billing system? we use an internal billing engine.
[04:29] Alex Chen: yes CSV or direct S3 export. you can also map routes to chargeback owners and auto‑populated labels via the API.
[04:40] [05:00] Priya Nair: now i'm jumping to Optimize tab — this is where we run static analysis and live profiling to suggest batching, cache TTLs, and quantization levels. it surfaces expected savings with an estimated quality delta.
[05:20] Daniel Park: how do you estimate quality delta? that's a key point for us.
[05:27] Priya Nair: we run a small eval on your provided prompt set — we compare logits and output similarity on a holdout. it's not perfect but it gives a directional metric, plus we pin the model to a canary and do A/B so you can measure production quality.
[05:44] Aisha Khan: curious about quantization — will that be automatic? we worry about hallucinations.
[05:51] Priya Nair: quantization profiles are recommended per‑model and per‑workload; we recommend starting with int8 for non‑critical routes and run the eval. we also provide fallback policies to send requests to the full‑precision variant on anomalies.
[06:10] [06:30] Alex Chen: ok demo time — Priya will show a real example. Priya?
[06:35] Priya Nair: sure, I'll replay a recorded trace from a 48‑hour window. here's the 'search‑rank' route — you can see spikes around 11am UTC; we overlay latency and cost. you can also run a 'what‑if' — tweak batching to 8 and the console shows estimated latency change and cost reduction.
[07:02] [07:30] Priya Nair: note the 'batching heatmap' — it suggests routes that are safe to batch without violating SLOs; the color coding is based on p95 latency and sensitivity.
[07:45] Daniel Park: interesting — for search‑rank we need strict SLOs. the suggested batching would add like 30ms which might be ok, but we need to test.
[07:55] Priya Nair: exactly, that's what the pilot is for. the console also has a simulated replay mode where we run your traffic and show a tokenized diff and cost estimate across variants.
[08:15] Liam O'Neill: replay — does that use our keys or is it synthetic?
[08:21] Alex Chen: you provide an anonymized traffic dump; we replay it in a sandbox within Redwood and we never persist PII — that's covered in the security packet we'll send.
[08:33] [09:00] Aisha Khan: on security, we need SSO (SAML), audit logs, and KMS integration. can we have HSM support?
[09:09] Priya Nair: yes SAML SSO is standard, audit logs stream to your SIEM, and we integrate with customer KMS; HSM options are available for Private customers. Redwood is SOC 2 Type II — we'll attach the report.
[09:26] Daniel Park: what about data residency — can we pin some routes to eu‑west and others to us‑east?
[09:34] Alex Chen: yes routing policies allow region pinning. you can also have mixed deployments — Private for regulated routes and Hosted for others.
[09:43] [10:00] Priya Nair: back to costs — here's a 'cost waterfall' view: model compute, token usage, and misc infra overhead. you can drill into per‑route percent variance month over month.
[10:18] Daniel Park: our biggest spend is prompt engineering — we have long contexts for summarization. can Redwood help optimize prompts?
[10:28] Priya Nair: yes we surface prompt length contributions by route and give suggestions: prefix caching, truncation heuristics, and rewriter templates to reduce input tokens for common forms.
[10:41] [11:00] Alex Chen: another feature is 'route fallbacks' — if a dedicated pool is saturated, we can fall back to a cheaper hosted variant with rate limiting. that keeps things online.
[11:15] Liam O'Neill: do we get alerts if observed cost deviates from predicted by more than X%?
[11:21] Priya Nair: yes configurable alerts; you can tie them to a cost budget for a route and trigger webhooks to Slack or PagerDuty.
[11:33] [12:00] Daniel Park: practical q — what's the timeline for a pilot and what resources are needed from our side?
[12:08] Alex Chen: typical pilot is two weeks: we ask for sample prompt set, anonymized traffic dump, and a point of contact for infra. Redwood provides a sandbox account, config the routes, and run the replay and live canary.
[12:24] Aisha Khan: we can carve out 8 hours of infra time to provision the traffic dump.
[12:30] Priya Nair: great. i'll note we need three sample routes: summarization (high tokens), search‑rank (low latency), and chat assist (multi‑turn).
[12:45] [13:00] Alex Chen: quick note on pricing — hosted is usage priced, Dedicated is reserved capacity commit, Private is license plus infra. we can send line items in the pricing deck.
[13:15] Liam O'Neill: can you include modeling for blended costs if we run hybrid? i.e., some percent on Dedicated and the rest on Hosted?
[13:23] Alex Chen: yes we'll include blended scenarios in the sheet.
[13:30] [14:00] Priya Nair: switching to failure modes — if a quantized variant returns lower quality we have automated rollback; the runtime supports automatic fallback to a full‑precision host based on similarity thresholds.
[14:20] Daniel Park: curious about infrastructure logs — can we get token‑level traces for compliance?
[14:28] Priya Nair: we provide request headers and token counts; we don't log raw PII payloads unless you opt in for debug and sign an NDA for that limited window.
[14:44] [15:00] Alex Chen: ok let's sketch the proposed pilot timeline — week 1: onboarding and traffic export, week 2: replay and small live canary, week 3: results and tuning.
[15:15] Daniel Park: that aligns with our internal window. procurement wants a budget decision by 2026‑06‑22.
[15:24] Liam O'Neill: yes and we need to check legal for data residency constraints before production.
[15:30] Aisha Khan: we will share the CSV and sample prompts by Monday.
[15:36] Priya Nair: great, i'll send calendar invites for the pilot kickoff once we have the artifacts.
[15:45] [16:00] Alex Chen: any competitors or other vendors you're evaluating?
[16:05] Daniel Park: we have POCs with Anthropic and in parallel some infra vendors, but Redwood's per‑route billing is compelling.
[16:13] Alex Chen: good to know. we'll include comparison notes in the follow up.
[16:20] [17:00] Closing recap: Alex Chen: recap — we'll send pricing + security pack, Priya will coordinate pilot and request artifacts, MeridianWorks provides traffic dump and prompts. follow up meeting to review results around 2026‑06‑18.
[17:22] Daniel Park: thanks all — appreciate the detail.
[17:30] Alex Chen: thanks everyone talk soon.

Notes and links mentioned: "route playbook deck (shared link)"; "security packet (SOC2, SAML, KMS guide)"; "benchmark sheet (CSV template)".

Transcript end.

document.content:
Emberfin security review — audit logs, approvals, change control (Hosted canary rollouts)

Emberfin (regulated fintech) reviewed Redwood’s audit logging and governance model for Hosted canary rollouts (percentage traffic splitting). Customer asked for concrete evidence of: (1) what audit events are emitted for rollout create/start/step-change/pause/approve/rollback, (2) how approvals and RBAC are enforced (including separation of duties), (3) retention and export to their SIEM, and (4) how emergency rollback is handled and logged. Redwood Security (Marcus/Kevin) described audit event fields (actor identity, tenant, route, before/after config, timestamps), retention expectations, and options for export/integration; Dylan covered control-plane enforcement and approval gates. Action items captured for Redwood to send the audit events spec, sample redacted audit log payloads, RBAC role/permission matrix (including rollout-approver role), and SOC 2 / security package links. Emberfin will confirm internal retention requirements and preferred export format and schedule a follow-up focused on SIEM ingestion + a short tabletop scenario for change-control evidence.
Customer asked: Are rollout approvals required or optional per-tenant? Can we enforce separation of duties (requester != approver)? What events are logged for auto-stop / auto-rollback? Do audit logs include diff of traffic percentage changes and model version IDs? What is default retention and can it be extended? Can audit logs be exported to Splunk/QRadar (or via webhook/S3)? How do you log break-glass actions during an incident? Do you support SAML/SSO and SCIM today? How do you prevent noisy audit events during step progression? Can we scope who can view rollout metrics vs who can execute rollout actions?
Redwood (Kevin Osei) - Send audit event schema doc + examples for rollout actions (create/start/pause/approve/step-change/rollback/auto-stop) with redacted sample payloads - Due 2025-03-07
Redwood (Marcus Lin) - Share security package: SOC 2 report, encryption/KMS overview, and audit log retention statement - Due 2025-03-07
Redwood (Dylan Brooks) - Provide RBAC matrix for rollout permissions (create/start/approve/rollback) and notes on separation-of-duties capabilities/roadmap - Due 2025-03-10
Emberfin (Markus Feld) - Confirm internal requirements for audit log retention (months/years) and preferred SIEM ingestion path (Splunk HEC vs S3 polling vs webhook) - Due 2025-03-10
Redwood (Simran Kaur) - Schedule 30-min follow-up: SIEM export + change-control evidence walkthrough (tabletop scenario) - Due 2025-03-11
Redwood to email audit logging spec + sample events and RBAC permission mapping.
Emberfin to validate retention/export requirements and identify which teams need access (SecOps vs Platform).
Follow-up call to cover SIEM export options and run through an example: request rollout -> approval -> canary step -> auto-stop -> rollback with all evidence artifacts.
Meeting header
Date: 2025-03-05
Time: 9:00 AM Pacific
Duration: 58 min
Title: Emberfin security review — audit logs, approvals, change control (Hosted canary rollouts)
Attendees (Redwood): Simran Kaur, Marcus Lin, Kevin Osei, Dylan Brooks
Attendees (Emberfin): Priya Shah (CISO), Markus Feld (GRC), Elena Ruiz (Platform Eng), Tariq Hassan (Procurement)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Reviewed audit logging and governance features related to Hosted canary rollouts.
- Discussed approval gates, RBAC roles, and change history.
- Covered retention and export/integration patterns for audit logs.
- Captured evidence/documentation requests and follow-up steps.

Transcript
[00:00] Simran Kaur: Alright, cool. Um, thanks everybody for the time. This is the security review follow-up on the safe rollouts / canary rollout workflow in Hosted. Goal today is mostly audit logs, approvals, and change control. Marcus and Kevin are here from security. Dylan from Console and the control plane side.

[00:20] Priya Shah: Great. Thanks, Simran. We have Markus from GRC, Elena from platform, Tariq from procurement. We’re basically validating governance before we let any teams touch production model changes.

[00:33] Marcus Lin: Makes sense. Happy to go deep. We’ll keep it concrete.

[00:39] Simran Kaur: Quick agenda: (1) what actions exist in the rollout workflow, (2) what audit events we emit, (3) RBAC and approvals, (4) retention/export. Then next steps.

[00:52] Elena Ruiz: Yep, and I’ll probably ask about separation of duties and how you handle emergency rollback.

[01:00] Dylan Brooks: Cool, that’s right in scope.

[01:05] Simran Kaur: Priya, anything to add?

[01:08] Priya Shah: Just that we need evidence. Like, “show me example audit event payloads,” not just “we have audit logs.”

[01:16] Kevin Osei: Totally fair.

[01:19] Simran Kaur: Alright. Dylan, can you give a 60-second overview of the workflow as it exists in Hosted?

[01:26] Dylan Brooks: Sure. So, Hosted routes can have a rollout object attached. You pick a baseline model version/config, you pick a canary model version/config, then define traffic steps like 1%, 5, 25, 50, 100. Each step has a minimum soak time. The console and backend orchestration progress steps; smart routing enforces deterministic traffic split.

[01:53] Dylan Brooks: Actions are: create rollout draft, validate, start, progress to next step, pause, resume, rollback to baseline, and complete. There’s also “approve” if the tenant policy requires approvals for certain actions.

[02:10] Markus Feld: When you say “tenant policy,” is that like a config we set, or Redwood set?

[02:15] Dylan Brooks: It’s configurable per tenant, with defaults. In enterprise plans we can set required approvals, max step size, min soak. Some of it is guardrails we enforce globally too.

[02:27] Priya Shah: So approvals are optional? We need them mandatory.

[02:31] Marcus Lin: We support mandatory approvals per tenant and per action category. For example: start rollout requires approval, or step above X percent requires approval.

[02:43] Elena Ruiz: And can you enforce that the approver is different from the requester? That’s a core SoD control for us.

[02:50] Dylan Brooks: Today, we can enforce approver role vs executor role via RBAC. The strict “must be different human” check—there’s partial support; we can do “two-person rule” for certain operations in our policy engine, but I want to be careful: it depends on identity context we get from SSO and whether the action is API vs Console.

[03:14] Marcus Lin: Let’s break that down. Our audit events always record an actor identity: user ID, email if present, auth method (SSO vs API key), and the role/permission that authorized it. For SoD, we can either enforce by roles (requester doesn’t have approve permission) or by a rule “approver != initiator.” That latter one is in our roadmap for GA rollouts; I don’t want to overpromise if you need it day one.

[03:43] Priya Shah: We likely need it day one for production changes. At least for the percent increases beyond, say, 5%.

[03:50] Kevin Osei: Understood. We can also support an operational workaround: require “rollout-approver” permission be held by a different group. So functionally separation of duties. We’ll document that.

[04:03] Tariq Hassan: Just to clarify, is this something that comes with the platform, or an add-on?

[04:08] Simran Kaur: Audit logging and RBAC are included in enterprise plans; specific governance policies may map to the plan. We can follow up with packaging, but today we’ll focus on whether controls exist.

[04:22] Markus Feld: Okay. Let’s talk audit logs. What events do you emit, exactly? And are they immutable?

[04:28] Kevin Osei: For rollout actions we emit audit events for: RolloutCreated, RolloutStarted, RolloutStepChanged (includes percent change), RolloutPaused, RolloutResumed, RolloutApprovalRequested, RolloutApproved or ApprovalDenied, RolloutRollbackInitiated, RolloutRollbackCompleted, RolloutAutoStopped, and RolloutAutoRollbacked—sorry the name might be slightly different, but we log the automated control-plane action too.

[05:02] Kevin Osei: Each event includes: timestamp, tenant/org ID, project/workspace ID (if applicable), route identifier, rollout ID, baseline model version ID, canary model version ID, region scope, action type, actor (user/service), source (Console/UI vs API), request ID / trace ID, and a before/after diff of the config object.

[05:25] Elena Ruiz: When you say diff, is it literally a JSON diff? Or just “changed fields list”?

[05:31] Kevin Osei: It’s a structured “before” and “after” snapshot of the relevant fields. For high-volume configs we don’t dump everything, but for rollout it’s manageable. We can provide examples.

[05:44] Priya Shah: We need actor and device context. Like IP address, user agent.

[05:50] Marcus Lin: We capture request metadata, yes: IP, user agent for Console sessions, and for API it’s the client ID / key ID and source IP. If SSO is used, we store the SSO subject ID and email.

[06:08] Markus Feld: Is the audit log tamper-proof? Like, can a Redwood admin modify it?

[06:13] Marcus Lin: Internally, we treat audit logs as append-only. Customers do not have write access. Redwood staff access is restricted and logged. The store is write-once semantics at the application layer; we can also provide controls around retention and export so you can maintain your own copy.

[06:33] Priya Shah: Okay. How long do you retain?

[06:36] Kevin Osei: Standard retention for audit events is 90 days in-product. Enterprise can extend. For regulated customers we often do 365 days or more, and/or recommend SIEM export for long-term retention.

[06:52] Markus Feld: We need 7 years for certain change records.

[06:56] Simran Kaur: Seven years typically implies SIEM or your own archive. We can talk about export patterns.

[07:03] Elena Ruiz: Export is key. Can we stream audit events to Splunk?

[07:09] Kevin Osei: We have a couple options: (1) periodic export to object storage (like S3) in JSONL format, (2) webhook delivery to your collector endpoint, or (3) we integrate through common pipelines—some customers use Splunk HEC, some use QRadar via a relay. We’ll confirm what’s available in your region.

[07:32] Priya Shah: You said “region.” We’re US-only for now.

[07:36] Kevin Osei: That simplifies.

[07:39] Markus Feld: Also, what about audit logs for auto-rollback? We need evidence of the system making the decision.

[07:45] Dylan Brooks: Yeah, for auto-stop/rollback, the orchestrator will emit an event with the stop condition and metric that tripped. For example “p95 latency regression above threshold for N minutes” or “5xx error rate above X%.” It includes the threshold values and the evaluation window.

[08:08] Elena Ruiz: Are those thresholds configurable per rollout?

[08:12] Dylan Brooks: Default thresholds exist, and you can override within guardrails. So you can’t set it to “never stop.” But you can tune sensitivity.

[08:23] Priya Shah: I’m going to ask the annoying question: where do those metrics come from and can they be spoofed?

[08:30] Marcus Lin: Not annoying. Metrics are generated in the data plane and aggregated centrally. The decision engine uses our telemetry pipeline. Customers cannot write into that pipeline. There are integrity checks, and we log the decision and the source metric IDs. We can provide a description of the chain of custody.

[08:52] Speaker 1 (Markus Feld): So the audit event would show the metric? Like the actual number?

[08:56] Dylan Brooks: It will show the observed value and threshold at the time of the decision, yes. Not like a whole timeseries.

[09:05] Elena Ruiz: And can we see the same in the UI?

[09:08] Dylan Brooks: Yes, the rollout timeline in Console shows “Auto-paused due to latency breach,” and there’s a link to the comparison charts baseline vs canary.

[09:19] Priya Shah: Okay, approvals. Walk me through “approval required.” Is that a button? Is it an email? How is it enforced?

[09:27] Dylan Brooks: In Console, when a user with create permission submits a step change that requires approval, the system creates an approval request. That request is pending until someone with “approve rollout changes” permission approves. If you attempt to bypass via API, policy engine denies and returns a message.

[09:49] Marcus Lin: Enforcement is in the control plane policy engine. The data plane just enforces the current active split config; it won’t accept an unapproved config because it’s never published.

[10:05] Markus Feld: Can an approver approve via API? We like everything via code.

[10:10] Dylan Brooks: Yes, approvals can be via API. Same audit events apply.

[10:17] Elena Ruiz: SSO—do you support SAML? And SCIM provisioning?

[10:22] Marcus Lin: SAML SSO is supported. SCIM is supported for enterprise tenants for provisioning and deprovisioning users and groups.

[10:32] Priya Shah: And MFA? We require MFA.

[10:35] Marcus Lin: If you use SSO, MFA is enforced at your IdP. For local auth, we support TOTP but we strongly recommend SSO.

[10:46] Tariq Hassan: Sorry, can I ask: does “rollout approver” map to a named role we can reference in contract language?

[10:53] Kevin Osei: Yes, there is a “rollout-approver” role in the RBAC bundle. It’s basically permission to approve and also to rollback if allowed. We’ll send the mapping.

[11:08] Markus Feld: I need to see the permission set. Like, can approver also start? That would violate SoD.

[11:14] Marcus Lin: Permissions are granular. You can separate “start rollout” from “approve step change.” We’ll provide the matrix. Also, even if one person holds both permissions, you can administratively separate by assigning to different groups.

[11:33] Priya Shah: We prefer technical enforcement. But okay, matrix first.

[11:38] Simran Kaur: We’ll capture as an action item.

[11:41] Elena Ruiz: Another question: audit logs for read access. If someone views the rollout or downloads data, is that logged?

[11:49] Kevin Osei: We generally log administrative and configuration changes. Read events for dashboards are not always logged due to volume. For sensitive objects, we can enable “read audit” but it’s not default. For rollouts specifically, we log change actions as the primary compliance control.

[12:12] Priya Shah: For us, view access to audit logs themselves should be logged.

[12:17] Marcus Lin: That’s a reasonable ask. Let’s see if we can enable that. We’ll check current capabilities and follow up.

[12:26] Markus Feld: Also, can you show how the system proves “what was running” at a given time? Like model version in production.

[12:34] Dylan Brooks: For Hosted, the route config includes the model version and the rollout state. Every config publish is versioned and you can query history. Rollout timeline plus the audit trail gives a time-based view. Additionally, request logs/metrics are tagged by cohort (baseline/canary) during a rollout.

[12:57] Elena Ruiz: Tagged at request time? With rollout ID?

[13:00] Dylan Brooks: Exactly. We tag requests with rollout_id and cohort. That powers baseline vs canary comparison charts.

[13:09] Priya Shah: Is that tag included in our logs? Like can we correlate individual requests?

[13:13] Dylan Brooks: In aggregate metrics yes; request-level logs depend on what you have enabled. For privacy we don’t dump prompt content; but we can include rollout ID in request metadata returned and in traces.

[13:27] Markus Feld: Prompt content aside, we need to show auditors that change X happened, approved by Y, then traffic increased from 5 to 25 percent at time Z.

[13:37] Kevin Osei: That’s exactly what the audit events cover: a step-change event with before/after percent and the approver event referencing the approval request.

[13:49] Priya Shah: Are those events correlated? Like shared IDs?

[13:52] Kevin Osei: Yes, approval_request_id and rollout_id. And request_id for the API call.

[14:00] Elena Ruiz: How about emergency rollback. If we hit an incident at 2 AM, can on-call rollback without approval?

[14:08] Marcus Lin: You can define a policy that allows rollback without approval, but that’s your choice. Many customers allow “break-glass” rollback to protect availability, and require an audit event and post-incident review.

[14:24] Dylan Brooks: And rollback is a first-class action. It switches routing back to baseline immediately. We also support auto-rollback if SLO thresholds are breached.

[14:34] Priya Shah: “Break-glass” has to be logged and ideally notifies security.

[14:39] Kevin Osei: Correct. Rollback event includes actor, reason if provided, and we can trigger notifications to your configured channel (email/webhook). We’ll outline options.

[14:55] Markus Feld: Do you support JIT access? Like time-bound elevated role.

[15:00] Marcus Lin: Not natively in-product as “JIT.” But many customers do that at the IdP level with group membership timeouts. Our RBAC uses group claims from SSO.

[15:13] Elena Ruiz: Understood.

[15:15] Simran Kaur: I’m going to pause and check: are we hitting the main concerns? Audit event coverage, approval enforcement, export/retention.

[15:23] Priya Shah: Mostly. I want to understand your “change control story” for SOC 2 / ISO. Like do you have an internal SDLC and do those controls extend to customer config changes.

[15:34] Marcus Lin: Internally we have SOC 2 Type II and standard change management. For customer-initiated changes, our controls are: RBAC, approvals, audit logs, and immutable history. We can share our SOC report and a short statement describing how customer configuration changes are recorded.

[15:56] Priya Shah: Good. Also: do you have a public doc about audit event fields?

[16:02] Kevin Osei: We have a spec doc. It’s not fully public yet but we can share under NDA / in the security package.

[16:10] Tariq Hassan: That’s fine.

[16:12] Elena Ruiz: Can we go through an example payload? Even redacted.

[16:16] Kevin Osei: I can describe one now and send examples after. Example: event_type=RolloutStepChanged. It includes route_id “support-agent-prod”, rollout_id “rlt_…”, from_percent=5, to_percent=25, baseline_model_version “mvl_123”, canary “mvl_456”, actor “priya@emberfin.com” (or user id), auth “saml”, ip “x.x.x.x”, decision “allowed”, policy “max_step=25, min_soak=30m satisfied.”

[16:50] Markus Feld: It includes policy evaluation results?

[16:53] Kevin Osei: It includes which policy gate was evaluated and whether it passed. We avoid dumping entire policy objects in every event.

[17:03] Priya Shah: That’s good. We’ve had vendors where they log “changed config” but not why it was allowed.

[17:10] Marcus Lin: Yeah, we include the authorization context.

[17:16] Elena Ruiz: Deterministic cohorting—does that matter for audit?

[17:20] Dylan Brooks: It matters for correctness, less for audit. But if you ask “why did user X see canary output,” deterministic hashing is the reason. Also for retries / streaming, we keep stickiness so a request doesn’t flip cohorts mid-stream.

[17:38] Elena Ruiz: Okay.

[17:40] Markus Feld: What about multiple regions? If the rollout is global, is it 25% in each region or 25% overall?

[17:48] Dylan Brooks: It’s applied per region consistently, with the same config, but enforcement is region-aware. Metrics are broken out by region too. We can send the ADR but that may be too deep for this call.

[18:03] Priya Shah: Just tell me: can I prove to an auditor which regions were affected.

[18:07] Kevin Osei: Yes, region scope is included in the rollout config and audit events.

[18:13] Priya Shah: Great.

[18:16] Simran Kaur: Switching to retention/export. Kevin, can you talk about how customers typically integrate with Datadog/Splunk.

[18:24] Kevin Osei: Sure. For audit logs, common patterns: (a) export job writes JSON lines to an S3 bucket in your account, then you ingest to Splunk/Datadog. (b) webhook push to your endpoint which forwards to SIEM. For metrics, separate story: we have dashboards in Console and can export metrics via APIs.

[18:49] Elena Ruiz: Do you support “near real-time” export? Like under 5 minutes.

[18:54] Kevin Osei: Webhook is near real-time. Batch export is typically hourly, configurable.

[19:02] Markus Feld: If you push to us, how do you handle retries? We don’t want dropped events.

[19:07] Kevin Osei: We have delivery retries with backoff; and for webhook we can provide a replay window. Also we keep the events in our store so you can backfill.

[19:18] Priya Shah: And if your service is down, does that block model traffic? I don’t want audit logging to become an availability dependency.

[19:27] Dylan Brooks: The data plane doesn’t depend on audit logging. For control-plane actions, if audit pipeline is degraded, we can still accept changes but we’ll flag it. For strict customers, we can also configure “fail closed” for approvals. We need to decide what’s safer for you.

[19:49] Priya Shah: Default should be fail closed for governance actions, not for serving.

[19:54] Marcus Lin: Agree.

[19:56] Elena Ruiz: Another thing: do you have change tickets? Like integration with Jira? We require change request ID.

[20:03] Dylan Brooks: Not integrated as a first-class workflow yet. We do have a “reason” field you can enter. Some customers put their change ticket ID there. That gets logged in audit events.

[20:20] Markus Feld: That’s acceptable. As long as it’s enforced required.

[20:25] Dylan Brooks: We can make it required by policy for your tenant, yes.

[20:31] Priya Shah: Great. What about model config changes outside rollouts? Like just switching a route.

[20:38] Kevin Osei: Those are also audit logged. Route config changes are a broader category of events.

[20:45] Elena Ruiz: And are there API endpoints to query audit events?

[20:49] Kevin Osei: Yes, there’s an audit log API: filter by time range, route, actor, event type. Again, we’ll provide docs.

[21:03] Priya Shah: Okay. I’m going to ask about “who inside Redwood can see our audit logs.”

[21:10] Marcus Lin: By default, Redwood staff do not access customer audit logs. Access is restricted to a small set of on-call/security personnel for support cases, and any access is itself logged and reviewed. We can provide our internal access control statement.

[21:31] Priya Shah: And data residency, but we can do that offline.

[21:35] Simran Kaur: Yep.

[21:37] Speaker 2 (Tariq Hassan): I have a procurement-ish question: do you have a standard DPA that covers this logging/export?

[21:44] Simran Kaur: Yes, we do. We’ll include with the security package.

[21:50] Elena Ruiz: Back to approvals: is approval synchronous? Like you click approve and it immediately progresses the step.

[21:57] Dylan Brooks: Approval unlocks the action. The requester then can click “Apply step” or we can optionally auto-apply once approved. For governance, many customers prefer explicit apply.

[22:12] Markus Feld: Audit log should include both approval and apply.

[22:15] Kevin Osei: It does.

[22:18] Priya Shah: What about paused rollouts. If auto-paused, who can resume?

[22:22] Dylan Brooks: Resuming is an action governed by policy and RBAC. Usually it requires the same or higher permissions than step change.

[22:33] Priya Shah: Okay.

[22:35] Elena Ruiz: Can the system automatically roll back to baseline or does it just pause.

[22:40] Dylan Brooks: Both are supported: auto-stop (pause) or auto-rollback. Which one is configured depends on the stop condition policy.

[22:52] Markus Feld: Again, log everything.

[22:55] Kevin Osei: Yes.

[22:57] Priya Shah: Let’s talk about “evidence.” What can you send that would satisfy an auditor.

[23:03] Marcus Lin: We can send: (1) SOC 2 Type II report under NDA, (2) audit event schema for rollout actions, (3) sample redacted audit events, (4) RBAC permission matrix including rollout-approver, (5) a short write-up about retention/export.

[23:23] Priya Shah: Good. Also maybe a screenshot of the UI timeline.

[23:27] Dylan Brooks: We can do that too.

[23:30] Elena Ruiz: And a tabletop “here’s an incident and rollback happened.”

[23:34] Simran Kaur: We can schedule that as a follow-up.

[23:38] Markus Feld: Can you also answer: are audit events delivered exactly-once.

[23:43] Kevin Osei: For webhook, it’s at-least-once delivery, which is typical. Events have stable IDs so you can dedupe.

[23:52] Markus Feld: Okay.

[23:54] Priya Shah: Another question: do you log changes to the policies themselves? Like max step size and soak time.

[24:01] Kevin Osei: Yes, policy config changes are audit logged too, including who changed them and before/after.

[24:10] Priya Shah: That’s important.

[24:12] Elena Ruiz: If a user tries to do an action they’re not allowed, do you log that attempt.

[24:18] Marcus Lin: We log authorization failures at the security event level. Not all are in customer audit logs by default, but we can make sure you have visibility for governance-related denies. We’ll clarify.

[24:34] Priya Shah: Please do. Attempted changes are important.

[24:39] Dylan Brooks: In Console, the user sees an error message that includes which guardrail blocked it. That’s from the policy engine.

[24:47] Elena Ruiz: Good UX.

[24:49] Simran Kaur: We’re about halfway. Any other key requirements we haven’t hit.

[24:54] Priya Shah: One more: are audit logs searchable by “route name” and “model version.”

[25:00] Kevin Osei: Yes. Filter by route_id and model_version_id.

[25:06] Markus Feld: And can we pull in bulk via API.

[25:09] Kevin Osei: Yes, with pagination.

[25:12] Tariq Hassan: Do you charge for audit log retention.

[25:15] Simran Kaur: Longer retention is typically an add-on. Export is the recommended long-term approach.

[25:22] Priya Shah: Okay. Elena, anything else.

[25:26] Elena Ruiz: I want to confirm: You said SAML and SCIM are supported. Do you support group claims mapping to roles.

[25:33] Marcus Lin: Yes, group-to-role mapping. You can map IdP groups to Redwood roles.

[25:39] Elena Ruiz: Great.

[25:41] Markus Feld: For SoD, we’ll likely create two groups: rollout-operators and rollout-approvers.

[25:48] Dylan Brooks: Exactly.

[25:50] Priya Shah: But again, we might require “different individual.”

[25:54] Marcus Lin: Understood. We’ll take that back as a requirement. For the immediate phase, role separation covers most auditors.

[26:05] Priya Shah: Depends on auditor.

[26:07] Simran Kaur: Yep.

[26:09] Dylan Brooks: Another control: approval can be required only when increasing traffic past a threshold. For example 1% and 5% can be self-serve, but 25% requires approval.

[26:23] Priya Shah: That’s helpful.

[26:25] Elena Ruiz: And max step size guardrail prevents jumping 5 to 100.

[26:28] Dylan Brooks: Exactly.

[26:31] Priya Shah: Okay, let’s shift to “audit log format.” Are you using a standard like CloudEvents.

[26:38] Kevin Osei: It’s JSON, similar to CloudEvents but not exactly. Includes event_id, event_type, occurred_at, actor, resource, metadata.

[26:50] Markus Feld: Fine. Send schema.

[26:54] Simran Kaur: We will.

[26:56] (crosstalk)

[27:00] Priya Shah: Sorry, one thing: do you log the actual prompt or output.

[27:05] Marcus Lin: No, not in audit logs. Audit logs are about administrative actions. Prompts/outputs are not stored by default; there are separate logging features with customer control.

[27:18] Priya Shah: Good.

[27:20] Elena Ruiz: What about “reason” field. Is it free-text.

[27:24] Dylan Brooks: Yes. We recommend including change ticket ID and summary.

[27:31] Markus Feld: Okay.

[27:33] Simran Kaur: Let’s capture action items now so we don’t miss them. Kevin will send audit event schema and examples. Marcus will send SOC report and security package. Dylan will send RBAC matrix and comment on SoD enforcement. Markus, you’ll confirm retention and SIEM ingestion preferences.

[27:55] Markus Feld: Yes.

[27:57] Priya Shah: We also want a follow-up to walk through a scenario.

[28:02] Simran Kaur: I’ll schedule.

[28:05] Elena Ruiz: Can we include your on-call / runbook for “rollout stuck” or “bad split.” That’s relevant to operational governance.

[28:13] Dylan Brooks: We have internal runbooks. We can share a customer-facing troubleshooting guide. For deep runbooks, we can share excerpts.

[28:24] Priya Shah: That would help.

[28:27] Marcus Lin: We can include a short runbook excerpt with steps and escalation paths.

[28:34] Tariq Hassan: That’s great.

[28:36] Simran Kaur: Alright. Any other competitor comparisons needed? I know you asked about Bedrock earlier.

[28:43] Priya Shah: No, not today.

[28:46] Elena Ruiz: We do want to understand if you integrate with AWS audit trails.

[28:51] Kevin Osei: If you deploy in your VPC, we can integrate more directly. For Hosted, we provide our own audit logs and export. We can align with your cloud logging pipeline via export.

[29:06] Elena Ruiz: Okay.

[29:08] Markus Feld: One more: do you have an SLA around audit log availability.

[29:13] Marcus Lin: We have platform SLAs; audit log UI/API has a target availability. For compliance, we recommend export so you have your own copy. We can share numbers.

[29:27] Priya Shah: Please send.

[29:30] Simran Kaur: Will do.

[29:33] Dylan Brooks: Maybe worth noting: the rollout timeline view in Console is derived from the same event stream, so customers get a human-readable history.

[29:43] Priya Shah: That’s nice, but again we need raw events for auditors.

[29:47] Kevin Osei: Understood.

[29:49] (brief pause)

[29:51] Simran Kaur: We have about 25 minutes left. Priya, do you want to go deeper on any specific control.

[29:57] Priya Shah: Yes. Access controls. Can we restrict who can view audit logs vs who can execute rollouts.

[30:05] Marcus Lin: Yes. Separate permissions: view_audit_logs and manage_rollouts, for example. You can also scope access by project/workspace in some setups.

[30:18] Elena Ruiz: And does that apply to API keys too? Like service accounts.

[30:22] Marcus Lin: Yes, API keys are bound to a principal with permissions. We recommend separate service accounts for CI/CD vs human admins.

[30:35] Markus Feld: Do you have service account audit identity in logs.

[30:39] Kevin Osei: Yes, it will show as “svc_…” principal with key ID.

[30:45] Priya Shah: Great.

[30:47] Elena Ruiz: Another nuance: if a rollout step is scheduled (like automatic progression), who is the actor.

[30:55] Dylan Brooks: If it’s auto-progression, actor is a system service principal. The event will show “system/orchestrator” plus the original rollout owner in the metadata.

[31:09] Markus Feld: That’s acceptable.

[31:11] Priya Shah: As long as the approval step is still human.

[31:15] Dylan Brooks: Exactly.

[31:18] Elena Ruiz: Let’s talk about “approval notifications.” Do you integrate with Slack/Email.

[31:23] Dylan Brooks: We have email notifications and webhook notifications; Slack via webhook.

[31:30] Priya Shah: Okay.

[31:32] Markus Feld: Data classification: are audit logs considered customer data. How are they encrypted.

[31:38] Marcus Lin: Yes, they’re treated as customer metadata. Encrypted at rest and in transit. For some plans we support customer-managed keys (KMS) for certain data stores; we’ll confirm if audit logs are included in CMK scope.

[31:57] Priya Shah: That’s important. Put it in the follow-up.

[32:01] Kevin Osei: Will do.

[32:03] Simran Kaur: I’ll note: CMK coverage question for audit logs.

[32:08] Elena Ruiz: Also, is there rate limiting on audit log API.

[32:12] Kevin Osei: Yes, but high enough for typical use; export is better for bulk.

[32:18] Markus Feld: Okay.

[32:20] Priya Shah: So, what’s the status of this feature? Beta or GA.

[32:25] Simran Kaur: Hosted canary rollout workflow is targeting GA. Some customers are in beta. Governance features like audit events and RBAC are part of the GA bar.

[32:38] Priya Shah: We don’t want to be beta for security.

[32:41] Simran Kaur: Understood. We’ll align on timelines and can gate enablement.

[32:48] Dylan Brooks: For what it’s worth, audit event coverage is already implemented for the rollout actions. We’re finishing some polish on exports and policy edge cases.

[33:01] Priya Shah: Okay.

[33:03] Markus Feld: Can you also provide a list of event types. Sometimes we need that for Splunk parsing.

[33:09] Kevin Osei: Yes, we’ll provide the enumeration.

[33:12] Elena Ruiz: A small concern: cardinality. If you include rollout_id and route_id in metrics, does that blow up.

[33:19] Dylan Brooks: For metrics, we limit tags and aggregate by cohort. There are guardrails to prevent unlimited series. Audit logs are not metrics; they can be high volume but are manageable because rollout actions are low frequency.

[33:35] Elena Ruiz: Okay.

[33:37] Priya Shah: What about “rollback completed” event. How do you know it completed.

[33:42] Dylan Brooks: Orchestrator updates state after config is published and confirmed by the routing layer. If there’s a failure, it emits a failure event and leaves rollout in a safe paused state.

[33:57] Markus Feld: Failure states must be logged too.

[34:00] Kevin Osei: Yes, errors are captured with error_code and message.

[34:04] Priya Shah: Great.

[34:06] Simran Kaur: We can do a mini tabletop now if helpful. Like: user creates rollout, gets approval, step increases, latency spikes, auto-pauses, rollback. Would that help.

[34:17] Priya Shah: Maybe in the follow-up. Today I want docs.

[34:21] Simran Kaur: Okay.

[34:23] Tariq Hassan: For procurement: we’ll need the SOC report and DPA anyway.

[34:28] Marcus Lin: We’ll send in the security package.

[34:31] Markus Feld: Also, what about audit log deletion. Can a customer delete their audit logs.

[34:37] Kevin Osei: In-product, you can’t selectively delete audit events. You can manage retention windows, but not delete individual events. For privacy requests, we can handle per policy, but audit logs are generally retained as compliance records.

[34:55] Priya Shah: That’s good.

[34:57] Elena Ruiz: Do you support “legal hold.”

[35:00] Kevin Osei: Not as a product toggle today; export to your SIEM is the path. We can also support retention extensions contractually.

[35:11] Priya Shah: Okay.

[35:13] Simran Kaur: Anything else on export format or delivery.

[35:18] Markus Feld: Include timestamps in UTC, ISO 8601.

[35:22] Kevin Osei: Yes.

[35:24] Markus Feld: And include stable event IDs.

[35:27] Kevin Osei: Yes.

[35:29] Elena Ruiz: Does the audit log include the model name and version, or just an internal ID.

[35:35] Kevin Osei: Both. Internal IDs and a display name, if available.

[35:41] Priya Shah: Great.

[35:43] Simran Kaur: We’re good. I’ll do recap and confirm owners.

[35:48] Simran Kaur: Redwood: Kevin sends audit schema + sample payloads by Friday. Marcus sends SOC report and security package by Friday. Dylan sends RBAC matrix and notes on separation of duties and required “reason” field policy by Monday. Emberfin: Markus confirms retention requirements and preferred SIEM path by Monday. Simran schedules follow-up by next Tuesday.

[36:14] Priya Shah: That works.

[36:16] Markus Feld: Yes.

[36:18] Elena Ruiz: Yes.

[36:20] Tariq Hassan: Fine.

[36:22] Simran Kaur: Any final questions.

[36:25] Priya Shah: Just one: we’d like to see a written statement that any Redwood internal access to customer audit logs is logged and reviewed.

[36:34] Marcus Lin: We can provide that as part of the security package and point to SOC control descriptions.

[36:40] Priya Shah: Great.

[36:42] Simran Kaur: Alright, thanks everyone. We’ll follow up via email.

[36:47] (Call continues with light scheduling chatter)

[37:05] Simran Kaur: Elena, what days are best for the SIEM follow-up.

[37:08] Elena Ruiz: Tuesday afternoon or Thursday morning.

[37:12] Simran Kaur: Cool, I’ll propose times.

[37:15] Priya Shah: Thanks.

[37:17] (end)
